en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Sagāthāvagga of the Saṃyuttanikāya.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Work 1.
At the commencement of the commentary, the homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of making known the origin, the support, and the purity of the Dhamma that is to be commented upon.

Furthermore, this is for the purpose of generating great respect among the wise toward the commentaries on the Dhamma, so that they may properly achieve the qualities of learning, memorization, and so forth regarding it.
It is for the purpose of accomplishing all benefit and happiness through right practice.

Alternatively, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem in this commentary is performed because it is auspicious, because it constitutes a preliminary duty in all undertakings, because it has been practiced by the wise, and because others in the future might follow one’s example upon seeing it.
Alternatively, the making of homage to the Triple Gem is for the sake of generating a specific merit consisting in the worship of those worthy of worship.
This alone is the purpose intended by the Master here: namely, to provide reinforcement for the power of that karma which has its sign in the success he himself has attained;
to prevent any contraction of it in the interim; and to bring both of these to completion without obstacle through the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
For he will say: "Thus, with a mind full of confidence... [and so forth]."
"By its power. For the worship of the Triple Gem is an unsurpassed field of merit;

it possesses immeasurable majesty as an excellence of merit that is capable of destroying all defilements that act as obstacles within the worldly existence—even amidst manifold hindrances—and it wards off calamities such as fear.
As it is said: "For one who worships those worthy of worship," and likewise: "Those who..."
“Monks, those who have faith in the Buddha have faith in the foremost; for those who have faith in the foremost, the result is foremost,” and so forth.
“The rapture that arises in the body of one who praises the Buddha— That rapture alone is indeed superior to the entire Jambudīpa.”
“Dhamma,” and so forth; “Sangha,” and so forth; and “Jambudīpa.
Likewise: “Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion,” and so on.
“In the forest or at the foot of a tree... there will be no fear, nor trepidation, nor horripilation.

Regarding this, he spoke the three verses beginning with “whose heart is cooled by compassion” in order to demonstrate the possession of preeminent qualities in the Triple Gem which one wishes to worship.
For it is through the possession of such preeminent qualities that they become worthy of veneration.

And the homage rendered to one worthy of homage accomplishes the intended purpose. In this regard, the teaching for which he intends to provide a commentary is neither primarily characterized by compassion like the teaching on the Vinaya, nor is it primarily characterized by wisdom like the teaching on the Abhidhamma;
rather, it is primarily characterized by both compassion and wisdom. First, concerning that very [teaching] which is the primary basis of the Perfectly Enlightened One’s...
Because it is the root of all other jewels, it is said: “A heart cooled by compassion,” and so forth. In this context, *kirati* means compassion (*karuṇā*);
the meaning is that it scatters away or removes the suffering of others. Alternatively, *kiṇāti* means compassion;
the meaning is that when there is suffering in others, it afflicts or troubles the compassionate one. It is the trembling of the virtuous when there is suffering in others.
Alternatively, it is *karuṇā* because it causes distress (*kheda*) to the heart. Or else, *ka* means happiness (*sukha*); it is *karuṇā* because it obstructs that [happiness].

For its characteristic is the desire to remove the suffering of others; thus the meaning is that, due to the lack of regard for one's own happiness, it obstructs—that is, hinders—the happiness of those who are compassionate.
"Cool with compassion" (*karuṇāsītala*) means cool by means of compassion; he whose heart possesses this coolness of compassion is [so described].

One whose heart is cooled by compassion, that is, one whose heart is cooled by compassion. In this regard, although loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) also function in a manner that severs the burning within the mental continuum of beings—

due to their inherent nature of not desiring the removal of others' welfare, happiness, and so forth, and due to their being the direct opposites of ill-will (*byāpāda*) and aversion (*arati*)— [compassion is distinguished here].
Although the cause for the state of mental coolness is found [in all three], nevertheless, it is specifically compassion (*karuṇā*)— which, by its activity of removing the suffering of others,
has the essence of not enduring the affliction of others and is of the nature of non-harming— that is said to be the sign of the coolness of the Blessed One’s mind,

like mental tranquility (*cittapassaddhi*). Or rather, it should be understood that through the medium of compassion, loving-kindness (*mettā*) and gladness (*muditā*) are also stated to be causes for the state of coolness in the heart.
Alternatively, it is said that "the heart cooled by compassion" refers to the Great Compassion itself— which, being the basis for the distinction of the sixfold uncommon knowledge and which,

like the knowledge of omniscience, has attained the state of Great Compassion by pervading its entire range of objects— acting as the cause for the Blessed One’s heart to become cool through its intensity.

Alternatively, although loving-kindness (*mettā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) are also causes for the cooling of the heart due to their preeminence, compassion (*karuṇā*) alone is said to be "the cause of the state of coolness in the Blessed One's heart" because it is the cause of all the specific qualities of a Buddha.
Indeed, all the qualities of a Buddha have compassion as their source; for the Blessed One’s heat of suffering in *saṃsāra* was extinguished by the power of compassion.
Out of a desire to remove the suffering of others, even throughout many incalculable eons, his state remained as if untiring;
he was destined for the complete accumulation of the qualities that constitute a Buddha and had attained mastery over the Dhamma.

Thus, even when the causes for the tormenting of his heart—such as being placed upon a stack of seven layers of iron—were present, there was not even the slightest change in the coolness of his mind. And in this interpretation of the meaning, in all three stages...
It should be understood that the Blessed One’s compassion is inclusive.
"Pajānāti" (he understands) means wisdom (*paññā*); the meaning is that he penetrates [things] through various modes according to their true nature.

Wisdom itself is the "light of wisdom" (*paññāpajjoto*) in the sense of illuminating the true nature of phenomena through various modes by way of abandoning the veil of the knowable. It is especially so because it abandons even the latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).
"Destroyed" means eradicated, demolished. "Demolished by the lamp of wisdom" means destroyed by the lamp of wisdom (*paññāpajjota*).
It is called "delusion" (*moha*) because one is deluded by it, or it itself is deluded, or because its very nature is merely to cause delusion; it is ignorance (*avijjā*).

That same [ignorance] is called "darkness" (*tama*) because, like darkness, it acts to conceal the true nature of objects. One for whom the darkness of delusion has been demolished by the lamp of wisdom is "one for whom the darkness of delusion has been demolished by the lamp of wisdom."

To him, whose darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom— for although the darkness of ignorance has indeed been dispelled by the lamp of wisdom for all those whose taints are exhausted,
there exists a distinction in the abandonment of defilements by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones compared to the disciples who have attained vision and the Paccekabuddhas,
just as there is for those resolved through faith; this is because [the Buddhas] possess a preeminent quality due to the total eradication of even the latent tendencies (*savāsanā*).
Praising the Blessed One by way of his abandonment of ignorance, he said: "By the lamp of wisdom, the darkness of delusion is destroyed.

Alternatively, because he has produced within his own continuum the total disappearance of the darkness of ignorance without depending on the instruction of others, and likewise because he has attained mastery over omniscience and the [ten] powers, and because of the power of his excellence in teaching the Dhamma to the mental continua of others—
Because it was he alone who brought that [wisdom] forth correctly, the Blessed One alone is especially to be praised for the disappearance of the darkness of delusion;

thus he said, "The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom. And in this interpretation of the meaning, it should be understood that by the phrase "the lamp of wisdom," both the Blessed One’s wisdom of penetration (*paṭivedha-paññā*) and his wisdom of teaching (*desanā-paññā*) are included through a general designation, or by the method of mentioning one of two similar things (*ekasesanaya*).
Alternatively, because the Blessed One’s knowledge has as its limit all that is knowable, and because the darkness of delusion—
which obscures the true nature of all knowable phenomena— has been dispelled by the lamp of wisdom known as unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*),

which is capable of awakening to the true nature of every knowable phenomenon, it is said, "the darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," considering that the destruction of the darkness of delusion is unique to the Blessed One.

And here, because it has been attained in the destruction of the darkness of delusion, the "unobstructed knowledge" (anāvaraṇañāṇa) should be understood as the "destruction of the darkness of delusion" within one's own continuum by way of a metaphorical designation for its cause.

For the abandonment of the obscurations to the knowable (ñeyyāvaraṇa), which consists in the abandonment of the defilements along with their latent tendencies through the perfection of the resolution (abhinīhāra), is indeed the destruction of the darkness of delusion;
however, in the case of another's continuum, it is [called so] by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit, because it serves as the cause for the destruction of the darkness of delusion.
Unobstructed knowledge is called "the dispelling of the darkness of delusion.

But what is the reason that, among the various forms of excellence in abandonment, only the eradication of ignorance is taken as the basis for praising the Blessed One, and not the abandonment of all defilements without exception, which is even more preeminent?
It is because by the very mention of its abandonment, the abandonment of those [other defilements] associated with it is also implied.
Because it possesses the nature of illuminating the total eradication of the entire mass of defilements;
for there is no such defilement that is not abandoned through the abandonment of ignorance without remainder.
Alternatively, like true knowledge (*vidyā*), it is the cause for the arising of all wholesome states and the non-arising of all unwholesome states without remainder.
Since ignorance is the primary cause for the occurrence of saṃsāra, by the statement regarding its destruction, the eradication of the entire mass of defilements is already expressed;
thus it is said: "The darkness of delusion destroyed by the lamp of wisdom.
Humans and gods are *narāmarā*; together with humans and gods is *sanarāmara*; and that world is *sanarāmaro loko*.
"Sanarāmaraloka-garu" means one who is honored by the world of humans and gods; thus, "sanarāmaralokagaruṃ" refers to him who is honored by the world of humans and gods.
By this, he shows the Blessed One’s quality of being a benefactor even to the remaining beings—just as he is to gods and humans—by bringing about specific virtues appropriate to each.
Nor should one raise the objection regarding a distinction between primary and secondary importance here; for the order of words is one thing, while the order of meaning is another. In such cases...
For in compound words, even that which is primary is designated as if it were secondary, as in the expression "the assembly together with the king.

Although, in this context, the world is threefold by way of the world of beings (*satta-loka*), the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*), and the world of space (*okāsa-loka*), the meaning should nevertheless be understood according to the world of beings alone, since it is the world of beings that is capable of being treated with respect, and it is that which is intended here as the object of veneration. For it is there that beings are "worlded" (*lokiyanti*).

Merit and demerit, along with their respective results, are called "the world" (*loka*). Furthermore, by the inclusion of the term "immortals" (*amara*), the gods of rebirth (*upapatti-devā*) are intended here.

Alternatively, the word *loka* has the sense of a collection; it is so called because it is "perceived" (*lokīyati*) or "designated" (*paññāpīyati*) as a whole. Together with humans (*nara*) they are "with humans" (*sanarā*);

those who are both "with humans" and "immortals" (*amara*) are "humans and immortals" (*sanarāmara*); the world of these is the "world of humans and immortals" (*sanarāmaraloka*), according to the same method as before.
It should be joined [to the following]. And here, by the word *amara* (immortal), the purified deities (*visuddhideva*) are also included.

For they are, in the ultimate sense, immortal due to the absence of death; yet the mention of "humans and immortals" (*naramarānam*) alone is by way of a pre-eminent designation (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*), just as in the expression "the Teacher of gods and humans.
Thus, [this teaching] is unsurpassed, being preceded by the avoidance of all that is harmful and intent upon the provision of welfare and happiness without exception.

Because of his perfect application of means, his being of ultimate benefit to the world including its devas and humans, and his possession of immeasurable, incomparable, and distinguished qualities of power, the Blessed One—the supreme among all beings—is the highest object of veneration for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems.
Therefore it is said: "Venerated by the world of men and gods."

He is the "Sugata" because his going (*gata*)—his movement—is beautiful (*sobhana*). For the Blessed One’s approaching of those people who are to be converted is beautiful, since it results exclusively in their welfare and happiness.

Likewise, due to his physical body being adorned with the primary marks and secondary characteristics, his gait is free from defects such as haste, slowness, stumbling, dragging, pressing down, crouching, crookedness, or confusion; it surpasses the movements of royal swans, bulls, elephants, and lions.

The movement of the body and the movement of knowledge—accompanied by the specific qualities of vast, stainless compassion, mindfulness, energy, and so forth—are indeed beautiful in their faultlessness from the initial aspiration until the attainment of Great Enlightenment.

Alternatively, through self-arisen knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), one thoroughly understands the entire world by way of the realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*). Through that knowledge...

He is the Sugata because he has gone rightly and understood; likewise, having abandoned the origin of the world by means of the clear realization of abandonment, he has rightly gone beyond it by bringing about its state of non-arising—thus he is the Sugata.
Having rightly gone to and attained the cessation of the world, which is Nibbāna, by means of the clear realization of actualization—he is the Sugata.
[And] by means of the clear realization of development, [he has rightly gone] the path leading to the cessation of the world...

He is the Sugata because he has gone rightly and practiced rightly. This meaning should be clarified by such methods as: "He is the Sugata because he does not go back to, does not return to, and does not re-enter those defilements which were abandoned by the path of stream-entry," and so forth.
Alternatively, he is the Sugata because he has gone to, or attained, a beautiful state—namely, perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) or Nibbāna itself. Because...
Or, he speaks the Dhamma that is real, true, beneficial, and appropriate for those to be trained, at the right time;
therefore, because he speaks rightly and well, he is called *Sugata*—the letter *da* being changed to *ta*. Thus, he is the *Sugata* because of his beautiful gait and other such qualities;
[one approaches] that *Sugata*.
They are called *gatis* (destinies) because they are to be gone to by way of rebirth through merit and demerit;
they are specific types of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*). These, moreover, are fivefold, consisting of the hells and so forth.

Since even all karma leading to existence has been turned back by the attainment of the Noble Path through making it incapable of ripening, the Blessed One is well-liberated and dissociated from all five destinies; thus he said, "liberated from the destinies" (*gativimutta*).
By this, he shows that the Blessed One is not included within any [of these realms], which is why the Blessed One is called “the god beyond gods. Therefore he said:
“By what one might be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba, or as a bird;
by what one might go to the state of a yakkha, or attain the human state—”
“Those taints of mine are exhausted, shattered, and rendered baseless.

For because the kamma and defilements that lead to various states of existence were completely abandoned by the Supreme Path right at the foot of the Bodhi tree, there is no inclusion of the Blessed One within any state of rebirth;
thus, the Blessed One is absolutely beyond all realms of existence, wombs, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings.
"Suparimutto" (well-liberated). "Gativimuttaṃ" means that which is liberated from the [five] destinies. The meaning is: "I pay homage to it," "I bow down to it," or "I praise it.
Alternatively, by saying "liberated from the destinies," he praises the Blessed One for the attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
For here, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two aspects: from the perspective of his own welfare accomplished and from the perspective of his practice for the welfare of others.

Among these, the accomplishment of one’s own welfare is to be understood as resulting from the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, the absolute abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies, and the reaching of *nibbāna* without residue.
The practice for the welfare of others is to be understood as resulting from the teaching of the Dhamma that leads out of all suffering by one whose mind is indifferent to gain,
honor, and the like, and from the arrival of the time for the maturation of knowledge through a constant inclination toward the welfare of others, even toward those who are hostile.

Furthermore, herein, the practice for the benefit of others is shown to be twofold—by way of disposition (*āsaya*) and by way of application (*payoga*)—and the accomplishment of one’s own welfare is shown to be threefold. How so?

By the phrase “whose heart is cooled by compassion,” the practice for the benefit of others is shown by way of disposition; by the word *Sugata* in the sense of “one who has gone rightly,” the practice for the benefit of others is shown by way of application;
and by the phrase “whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom, and who is liberated from rebirth,” [the accomplishment of one’s own welfare is shown].

By these [qualities]—namely, the meaning of the penetration of the Four Truths expressed by the word "Sugata," and the remaining meaning expressed by the phrase "whose darkness of delusion has been destroyed by the lamp of wisdom"—all forms of the attainment of one's own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others are revealed.
Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood through three aspects: from the perspective of cause, fruit, and benefit. Therein:
The cause is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which is shown by the first word. The fruit is fourfold:

perfection of knowledge (*ñāṇasampadā*), perfection of abandonment (*pahānasampadā*), perfection of power (*ānubhāvasampadā*), and perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāyasampadā*). Among these, the perfection of knowledge and the perfection of abandonment are manifested by the second word through the sense of the penetration of the truths, and by the term "Sugata" (*sugata*);
furthermore, the perfection of power is [manifested] by the third word, while the perfection of the form-body...
It should be understood that by the term *sugata* in the sense of the beauty of the body and gait as previously described—
since that [beauty] is absent without the perfection of the primary and secondary marks— the teaching of the Dhamma of liberation through the three vehicles is an immediate benefit,
not an external one; this is what is revealed by the term *sugata* in the sense of "one who has spoken rightly" (*sammāgadanattha*).
In this context, by the phrase "whose heart is cooled by compassion," he shows the root of perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
For it was because his mind was impelled by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that the Blessed One made the formal resolve to lift sentient beings out from the mire of *saṃsāra*;
having fulfilled the perfections (*pāramīs*) in due order, he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Thus, compassion is the root of perfect enlightenment.
The Root: By the phrase "He whose darkness of delusion is destroyed by the lamp of wisdom," he demonstrates Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).

For path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*) has unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*) as its proximate cause, and unobstructed knowledge has path-knowledge as its proximate cause; this is what is called Perfect Enlightenment.

By the term *Sugata* in the sense of "one who has gone rightly," he demonstrates the practice leading to Perfect Enlightenment—a practice free from the two extremes, such as the adherence to lethargy or agitation, the accumulation [of karma], devotion to the pleasure of sensual indulgence or to self-mortification, and the dogmatic insistence on eternalism or nihilism.
The word *Sugata* is used because he has proclaimed the Middle Way, which is embraced by compassion and wisdom.

By means of the other [epithets], he shows the purpose [of his teaching] as being distinguished by what is primary and what is secondary regarding Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). Herein, the primary purpose is the crossing over of sentient beings from the great flood of saṃsāra;
anything other than that is secondary. Among these, by means of the primary [purpose], he shows the practice for the benefit of others.

By the former [phrase], he shows the Blessed One’s attainment of his own welfare; by both together, he shows that among the four types of persons—those practicing for their own welfare and so forth—the Blessed One is the fourth type of person.

And thereby, he shows his state as the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*dakṣiṇeyya*), his state as the supreme object of veneration, and his own status as having become a field (*khetta*) for the act of paying homage.

And here, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), the Blessed One’s perfection of all mundane qualities is shown, because it illustrates his uncommon qualities that have attained the state of loftiness among mundane things;

by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), his perfection of all supramundane qualities is shown, because it illustrates the knowledge of the path which has the knowledge of omniscience as its proximate cause.
For the meaning established by the mention of both is expressed by the words “the teacher of the world of men and gods,” and so forth.

"It is manifested" (*vipañcīyati*). By the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows that his approach is free from defilement; by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), he shows his departure [from the world].
Likewise, by the mention of compassion, he shows the Blessed One’s activity in accordance with worldly convention, since compassion is within the domain of worldly discourse;
by the mention of wisdom, he shows his non-transgression of that convention. For it is through the failure to realize the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena that...

By transcending conventional designations (*samañña*), there occurs the grasping of a "being" and so forth. Likewise, by the mention of compassion (*karuṇā*), he shows the dwelling in the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*);

by the mention of wisdom (*paññā*), [he shows] unimpeded knowledge regarding the three times, the knowledge of the Four Truths, the knowledge of the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), and the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*).
Since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is already included by the mention of compassion, the remaining unique knowledges are [implied].

He demonstrates the range of his knowledge by way of many such classifications of wisdom (paññā), including the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā), the unshakable knowledges regarding the eight assemblies, the ten powers (dasabala), the fourteen Buddha-knowledges,
the sixteen modes of conduct of knowledge (ñāṇacariyā), the eighteen qualities of a Buddha (buddhadhamma), the forty-four bases of knowledge (ñāṇavatthu),
and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion (karuṇā)...

By the inclusion of wisdom (*paññā*), there is the perfection of true knowledge (*vijjā*). By the inclusion of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is self-mastery; by the inclusion of wisdom, mastery of the Dhamma.

By the inclusion of compassion, there is the state of being a protector of the world; by the inclusion of wisdom, the state of being one's own protector. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, there is the quality of being a pioneer;
by the inclusion of wisdom, there is gratitude. By the inclusion of compassion, there is the absence of self-torment.

By the inclusion of wisdom (paññā), there is the state of not being tormented by oneself. Alternatively, by the inclusion of compassion (karuṇā), the qualities that constitute a Buddha are established;

by the inclusion of wisdom, the state of Buddhahood itself is established. Likewise, by the inclusion of compassion, the rescuing of others is shown; by the inclusion of wisdom, one’s own rescue is shown.
Similarly, by the inclusion of compassion, a mind of assistance toward all beings is indicated; by the inclusion of wisdom, a mind of detachment from all phenomena is indicated.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the beginning of all the qualities of a Buddha because it is their causal source; wisdom (*paññā*) is the end, because there is nothing further to be done beyond it.
Thus, by showing the beginning and the end, all the qualities of a Buddha are shown.

Likewise, by the mention of compassion, the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), preceded by the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), is shown; for compassion is the source of that [virtue].
Virtue (*sīla*) arises from the practice of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, and that [virtue] is associated with the three jhānas.

By the term "wisdom" (*paññā*), the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) is indicated. Furthermore, since virtue is the beginning of all the Buddha-qualities, concentration is the middle, and wisdom is the end, all the Buddha-qualities are shown by way of this method through the demonstration of what is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
Because it has been shown. For this alone is the means for seeing the qualities of the Buddha without remainder, namely, the grasping of the method;
otherwise, who indeed would be capable of showing the qualities of the Blessed One in their entirety, word by word? Therefore he said:
"Even a Buddha, were he to speak the praise of a Buddha..."
“Even if one were to speak of another for an eon,
and that eon were to be exhausted after a very long interval,
the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”

And for that very reason, even the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, while intent on discerning the qualities of the Buddha, having rejected [the idea of such discernment] by saying, “Certainly not, Bhante,” stated: “But, Bhante, the sequence of the Dhamma (dhammanvaya) is known to me.
Having thus praised the Blessed One in brief through all his qualities of omniscience, he now spoke the verse beginning with “The Buddha too... in order to extol the True Dhamma (saddhamma).
In that context, “Buddha” is a designation of the agent (kattuniddesa); “the state of being a Buddha” (buddhabhāva) is a designation of the object (kammaniddesa).
"Bhāvetvā" (having developed) and "sacchikatvā" (having realized) are designations for actions occurring at a prior time. "Yaṃ" (which) is an indefinite designation for the object.
"Upagato" (approached) is a designation for an action occurring at a subsequent time. "Vande" (I revere) is a designation for the action itself. "Taṃ" (that) is a restrictive designation.
"Dhammaṃ" (the Dhamma) is the designation for the object of the action of revering. "Gatamalaṃ" (free from stain) and "anuttaraṃ" (unsurpassed) are its qualifiers.

In this regard, first, the meaning of the word *buddha* should be understood according to the method of explanation [found in the Niddesa]: “He is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is a Buddha because he awakens the generation,” and so forth.

Alternatively, he is called a Buddha because he has woken up (*buddhavā*) due to the absolute departure of the sleep of ignorance along with its latent tendencies, or due to the blossoming of his awakening (*buddhi*), by way of the meanings of waking and blossoming. Or else:

Since there is no knowable object (*ñeyyadhamma*) that has not been understood by him, and because there is no specific knowable object that can be grasped as an object of action (*kamma*), there is no desire for a verbal expression of an object;
thus, the designation of the agent (*kattuniddesa*) is obtained solely in the sense of "having understood" (*avagamatthavasena*).

Therefore, he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened (*buddhavā*), just as one says, "The initiated one does not give. In terms of its meaning (*atthato*), however, [he is so called] because of his self-arisen knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) which is fully matured by the perfections (*pāramitā*).

The Buddha is the continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) which, together with its latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), has destroyed and eradicated all defilements without remainder, and which is the locus of an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

As it is said: "Buddha means that Blessed One who is self-become (*sayambhū*) and teacherless (*anācariyaka*), who by himself awakened to the truths regarding phenomena unheard before; and therein he attained omniscience in the [ten] powers."
"And mastery. The word *api* (also/even) is used in the sense of esteem (*sambhāvana*).

By it, he demonstrates esteem for the qualities of the Dhamma that are about to be mentioned, implying: "The Blessed One is indeed endowed with such distinguished qualities. "Buddhahood" means perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). "Having developed" means having produced and increased.
"Having realized" means having made manifest through direct experience (*paccakkha*). "Attained" means reached; "achieved" means arrived at.
The meaning [of *attha*] is this: it connects with the phrase "the state of a Buddha" (*buddhabhāva*). "Gata-mala" means free from stain; the sense is that it is faultless.
"Vanda" means I bow down to, or I praise. "Anuttara" means devoid of anything superior; the sense is that it is supramundane (*lokuttara*). "Dhamma":
it is called *dhamma* because it supports (*dhāreti*) those who practice according to its instructions, preventing them from falling into the states of misery or into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

This is the summary of the meaning here: Thus, even the Blessed Buddha, endowed with such a multitude of diverse qualities, having developed the Dhamma known as the Noble Path and realized the Dhamma known as the fruit and Nibbāna, attained unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment;
and that very state, which is the cause of the Buddhahood of all Buddhas, is free from all stains of defilement by virtue of its being superior to anything else.

"I pay homage to the supreme True Dhamma of penetration. Here, the inclusion of the True Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-saddhamma*) should also be understood, because it too elucidates that [Dhamma].
Alternatively, since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "He reached the ocean of the Abhidhamma method;
he comprehended the three Piṭakas," the mode of realization and comprehension (*sacchikiriyā-sammasana-pariyāya*) applies to the Dhamma of the scriptures as well.
It should be understood that this too is stated here.

Likewise, because it is said, "having developed and realized which Dhamma," it should be known that here, by the word *dhamma*, the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and the rest during the preliminary stage are included along with the perfections (*pāramitā*), which constitute the qualities that make one a Buddha.
For these [perfections] are indeed "stainless" because they are the opposite of defilement, and "unsurpassed" because they are not shared by others.

Thus, for the sake of all beings' escape from the entire suffering of saṃsāra, he made a great resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) and possessed a noble disposition characterized by the dwelling of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
He fulfilled more than a hundred thousand [aeons] of supreme qualities—such as giving, self-control, restraint, and so forth—which were purified and stainless by the excellence of wisdom (*paññā*).

For four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*), through diligent, uninterrupted, and exhaustive practice of meditation and direct realization regarding karma and other phenomena, the Blessed One attained mastery;
possessing marvelous, inconceivable, and great power, he reached the supreme pinnacle of perfection in higher virtue (*adhisīla*) and higher mind (*adhicitta*).
Then, by directing the Great Vajra-Knowledge through twenty-four million four hundred thousand gateways concerning the modes of conditions (*paccayākāra*), he [attained] the unsurpassed...
“Fully awakened to perfect enlightenment.

Herein, by the word “having developed,” he praises the Dhamma through the perfection of true knowledge (*vijjā*); by the word “having realized,” he praises it through the perfection of liberation (*vimutti*).
Likewise, by the first [phrase] he praises it through the perfection of jhāna, and by the second, through the perfection of deliverance (*vimokkha*). By the first...
Or, by the first [factor] there is perfection of concentration, and by the second, perfection of attainment.
Alternatively, by the first there is the state of the knowledge of destruction (*khayeñāṇa*), and by the second, the state of the knowledge of non-arising (*anuppādeñāṇa*).

Or, by the former there is likeness to lightning, and by the latter, likeness to a thunderbolt. Or, by the former there is the attainment of dispassion (*virāga*), and by the latter, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*). Likewise, by the first there is the state of deliverance (*niyyāna*).
He praises the Dhamma by means of its second quality of deliverance. Or, he praises it by means of its first quality as a cause, and its second quality as the unconditioned.
Or, he praises it by means of its first quality as vision, and its second quality as seclusion.

Or, he praises the Dhamma by means of its first quality as sovereignty, and its second quality as the deathless. Alternatively, [he praises it] thinking: "Having developed this Dhamma, the Buddha attained the state of Buddhahood."
By this [phrase], he praises the Dhamma for its being well-expounded; by "having realized it," he praises it for its being directly visible.
Likewise, by the former [phrase] he praises it for its being timeless, and by the latter for its being inviting one to come and see.

Or alternatively, by the former he praises the Dhamma for its leading onward, and by the latter for its being personally verifiable. By the phrase "with stains gone," through the illumination of the absence of defilement—
It shows the complete purity of the Dhamma. By the term "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), it demonstrates its vastness and perfection through the indication that there is nothing else superior to it.
Alternatively, by the first [term], it shows the Dhamma’s excellence in abandonment; by the second, its excellence in intrinsic nature.

Or else, the state of being free from stain (*gata-mala-bhāva*) should be applied to the Dhamma because it is to be developed (*bhāvetabba*); for by the power of development, it [removes] the defilements.
“He is one who eradicates”: the state of being unsurpassed should be understood here in the sense of that which is to be realized.
For it is called "unsurpassed" because, once its realization has been produced, there remains nothing further to be done and because it is not shared by others.

Likewise, by the term “having developed,” the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom belonging to those in training (sekha) are shown together with the preliminary virtues and so forth. By the term “having realized,”...
By this, the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom belonging to those beyond training (asekkha) in relation to the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) have been shown.
3. Having thus praised the True Dhamma in brief by means of all its qualities, he now spoke the words beginning with "of the Sugata" in order to extol the Noble Saṅgha.
Therein, "of the Sugata" is a statement of relationship. To that [is added] "of his sons."
By this, the connection [is established]. "Oraṃsānaṃ" (of the legitimate sons) is a qualification of the sons.

"Mārasenamathanānaṃ" (of those who crush Māra’s army) is a statement of the reason for their status as legitimate sons. By this, he shows that the very abandonment of the defilements is the reason for the Blessed One’s status as having them as his legitimate sons.
"Aṭṭhannaṃ" (of eight) is a statement defining the number. And by that, even though they possess the nature of being distinguished beings, [the number is specified].
This shows that even when their number reaches many thousands, they do not exceed this numerical limit, because they do not transcend the state of being established in the paths and fruits.
"Assembly" (*samūha*) is a designation for a collection. "Noble Saṅgha" (*ariyasaṅgha*) is a designation for the state of being a group distinguished by its virtues.

By this, he shows that even though there may be no physical unity among the noble persons, they possess the nature of a "Noble Saṅgha" because they are united through the commonality of view and virtue.

In this context, those who exist in the breast, are born from it, and are connected to it are called *orasā*. Just as the legitimate sons (*orasaputta*) of beings, by virtue of being born from their own [parents],

are especially entitled to the inheritance belonging to their father, so too these noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), by virtue of being born through the noble birth at the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma from the Perfectly Enlightened One,
[are entitled] to the bliss of liberation and the jewel of the noble Dhamma belonging to the Blessed One.

And "exclusive sharers" means they are like those born from the breast (*orasā*). Alternatively, by the very power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, noble disciples—both those entering and those who have entered the plane of the Noble Ones—are, in the primary sense, to be called the Blessed One’s "breast-born sons" (*orasā puttā*), because they are born of the effort generated by his breast.
For even when the teaching of the Dhamma is being carried out by the disciples, it is [still] "the Blessed One’s..."
This is called "the teaching of the Dhamma" because it is rooted in that [Dhamma] and because it lacks specific characteristics such as those [of the other three paths].

Even though, at the time of the noble disciples' attainment of the Noble Path, neither a son of the gods (devaputta-māra) nor the host of Māra necessarily attempts to obstruct them— as they did for the Blessed One— nevertheless, regarding the reasons why they ought to be dissuaded by them...
Since they too are indeed crushed when [he] is crushed, he says, "of those who crush Māra’s army.

However, in this context, although one should say "of those who crush Māra and Māra’s army," it should be understood that the term "mārasenamathanānaṃ" is formed by the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpeka-sesa* (retaining only one member of a similar group).
Alternatively, just as with the *khandha-māra*, the *abhisaṅkhāra-māra*, and the *guṇa-māra*, the same applies to the crushing of the *devaputta-māra*.
The body of the power of the defilements is called "an army" because it approaches as an ally. As it is said: "Sensual desires are your first army," and so forth.

And that river of defilements—divided into one thousand five hundred types, or indeed infinite types—is specifically crushed, shattered, and scattered by those noble disciples using the weapons of the qualities such as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and serenity;
thus they are "crushers of Māra’s army. By this, their...
This shows that the Blessed One has a son who is born after him.

They are called "noble ones" (*ariya*) according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), because they are far removed from defilements, because they do not proceed in what is not the right way, and because they proceed in the right way.

Alternatively, they are so called because they are to be approached (*araṇīya*) and resorted to by the world including the devas as a refuge, and because for those who have approached them, their purpose is accomplished.
The noble ones (*ariya*). The community of the noble ones is the "Noble Saṅgha" (*ariyasaṅgha*). Alternatively, it is the "Noble Saṅgha" because it is both noble and a community.

It should be understood that the words "I revere with my head" are spoken right here in this context to demonstrate the great benefit of this Noble Saṅgha, showing that after the Blessed One’s passing, even the attainment of the jewels of the Buddha and the Dhamma depends upon the jewel of the Saṅgha.
And here, by the phrase "the legitimate sons of the Sugata," he shows the excellence of the Noble Saṅgha’s origin;
by "the destroyers of Māra’s army," he shows the excellence of its abandonment, because it demonstrates the abandonment of all defilements;

and by "the assembly of the eight," he shows the excellence of its knowledge, because it demonstrates the state of those established on the paths and those established in the fruits. By the term "Noble Saṅgha,"...
It demonstrates the perfection of power by showing the pre-eminent status of all the Saṅghas.

Alternatively, the phrase "the legitimate sons of the Sugata" demonstrates that the Noble Saṅgha possesses a pure basis. "Crushers of Māra’s army" demonstrates that they have entered upon the practice of right, straight, and proper conduct.
"The assembly of the eight" demonstrates their state as those worthy of offerings and so forth. "The Noble Saṅgha" demonstrates its status as the unsurpassed field of merit.
Likewise, by the phrase "the heart-born sons of the Sugata," he illuminates the nature of the Noble Saṅgha’s supramundane going for refuge;
for it is through that supramundane going for refuge that they became the Blessed One’s heart-born sons.
By the phrase "the destroyers of Māra’s army," he shows their prior right practice accomplished through the perfection of their initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*). Those who have made such a resolve...

For those who have practiced rightly indeed conquer Māra and his retinue. By the phrase "the assembly of eight," he shows the states of the trainees (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha) which have penetrated their respective opposites;
this is because the states of the path and fruit are explained by way of reference to the individuals (puggalādhiṭṭhānena).
By the term "the Noble Saṅgha," he shows its status as the most worthy of offerings. And the going for refuge [is the duty] of the disciples.
The beginning consists of all virtues; the middle consists of the aggregates of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth belonging to those in training (sekkha), together with their preliminary practice;

and the end consists of the aggregates of virtue and so forth belonging to those beyond training (asekkha). Thus, in brief, all the virtues of the Noble Saṅgha are shown to be excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
4. In this way, by means of these three verses, through the concise recitation of all virtues, homage is paid to the Triple Gem.
Having thus performed that act of homage, he now spoke the words beginning with “Thus to me,” dedicating it toward his intended purpose.
In this context, they are called *ratana* (jewels) in the sense of generating delight; these are the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.

For when one adverts to their qualities as they truly are—beginning with “Such indeed is the Blessed One”—an abundant joy and gladness arise, which serve as the cause for attaining the Deathless. As it has been said:
“Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
on that occasion his mind is directed straight, having the Tathāgata as its object. With a mind directed straight...”
"Furthermore, Mahānāma, the noble disciple gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma;
in one who is joyful, rapture arises," and so forth.
Or, the sense of "jewel" is the state of being honored and so on. For this has been said:
“Because it is esteemed, of great value, incomparable, difficult to behold,
and enjoyed by beings who are not ordinary, it is therefore called a ‘jewel’ (ratana). Furthermore,
qualities such as being esteemed and so forth are found only in the Buddhas and others, and are not shared with anyone else.
“Consisting of homage” (*vandanāmaya*) means consisting of the act of homage (*vandanā*), just as one speaks of what “consists of giving” (*dānamaya*) or “consists of virtue” (*sīlamaya*).

Here, homage is the state of being inclined toward the qualities of the Three Jewels through body, speech, and mind, or it is their praise. It is called “merit” (*puñña*) because it produces the fruit of becoming worthy of honor, or because it purifies (*punāti*) one’s own continuum.
“With obstacles well-destroyed” (*suvihatantarāyo*): this means with obstacles thoroughly destroyed. By this, [the author indicates] his own possession of serene confidence (*pasāda*).
It shows that, by virtue of the excellence of the Triple Gem as a field of merit, that merit is capable of destroying obstacles and calamities that hinder the exposition of the meaning.
*Hutvā* (having been) is a word expressing a prior action; its connection is with the phrase "I shall expound the meaning.
*Tassa* (of that) refers to that merit consisting of the homage to the Triple Gem. *Ānubhāvena* means by the power.

5. Having thus shown the purpose for making obeisance to the Triple Gem, he now states "adorned with the Saṃyutta-vagga" and so forth, in order to introduce by way of praising the qualities that specific teaching of the Dhamma whose meaning he intends to comment upon;
the meaning is: "adorned with the Saṃyuttas such as the Devatā-saṃyutta, and with Vaggas such as the Naḷa-vagga."
In this context, "Saṃyutta" and "Saṃyoga" are identical in meaning. Of what is it the connection? It is the connection of the *suttas* and the *vaggas*.

For just as a collection of phonemes is a word (*pada*), so too a collection of words with a delimited sense is a sentence (*vākya*), a collection of sentences is a *sutta*, and a collection of *suttas* is conventionally termed a *vagga*; likewise, a collection of *suttas* and *vaggas* is conventionally termed a *Saṃyutta*.
"Those which are joined together" (*saṃyujjanti*)—here, because they are joined by groups of suttas, it is called *Saṃyutta*.

Although, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), there is no such thing as a "whole" (*samudāya*) apart from its constituent parts (*avayava*), nevertheless, just as the conventional designations (*samaññā*) such as "word" (*pada*) and so forth are applied based on the parts themselves when distinguished by their respective arrangements, so too are the conventional designations "Sutta-group," "Saṃyutta," and "Āgama" applied. Even though [the whole] does not exist ultimately, [it is still designated].

A collection, when apprehended as if it existed by way of a form imagined by the intellect, is conventionally designated as the locus for its constituent parts, just as one says, "the branch is on the tree. Therefore, it is said: "of that which is adorned by the Saṃyutta-vagga.
One might object: "Is not the Saṃyutta-vagga itself the Āgama? By what, then, is it adorned? This objection should not be raised. For it is so.

For even when the substance (*vatthu*) is not different, there is a "distinguishing manifestation" (*bhedaka-samudācāra*) because it makes known the specific quality intended, such as in the expression "the body of a stone statue.
*Āgama* means that one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth, come (*āgamissanti*) to this, by this, or from this.

It is *vara* (excellent) in the sense of being supreme due to the perfection of qualities such as being "good in the beginning," and because it is to be chosen (*varitabba*) by the wise as the cause for the success of whatever they aspire to. Thus, it is *āgama*.

And that which is excellent (*vara*) is the "excellent scripture" (*āgamavara*). Or, it is called "excellent" because it is esteemed as scripture; thus, being both "connected" (*saṃyutta*) and "excellent scripture," it is the "Connected Excellent Scripture" (*Saṃyuttāgamavara*), [a commentary] on that.

Those who have awakened after the Buddhas are the "Buddhas-awakened-after-Buddhas" (*buddhānubuddhā*); these are the noble ones, such as the Chief Disciples, who have penetrated the Truths by following the Buddhas' penetration of the Truths.
By them, through the qualities of their expositions of the meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇanā*) and expositions of the virtues (*guṇasaṃvaṇṇanā*)...
...by way of what has been thus described.
Alternatively, it should be construed as "the Buddhas and those who have awakened after the Buddha" (*buddhānubuddhā*).

For indeed, that very meaning which was first analyzed by the Fully Enlightened One himself—by way of various incidental teachings and so forth regarding the Vinaya, Suttas, and Abhidhamma—is precisely [that which is intended here].
Subsequently, they were compiled by the reciters (*saṅgītikāra*) according to their thematic exposition (*atthavaṇṇanā*).

In this context, "Saṃyutta-vaggas" refers to groups or collections of *saṃyuttas*, such as the Sagāthāvagga and so forth. Alternatively, because they are included within the *saṃyuttas*, the "vaggas" are the "Saṃyutta-vaggas," such as the Naḷavagga and so forth.
Or, the *saṃyuttas* themselves are the "vaggas," thus "Saṃyutta-vaggas. All three [interpretations] are valid according to the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*).
Having taken this up, it is said: "Adorned with the Saṃyutta Vaggas.
In that regard, in the Sagāthāvagga there are eleven Saṃyuttas and thirty-eight Vaggas. In the Nidānavagga there are nine Saṃyuttas and thirty-nine Vaggas.
In the Khandhavagga there are eleven Saṃyuttas and fifty-nine Vaggas. In the Saḷāyatanavagga...
There are nine Saṃyuttas and thirty-eight Vaggas. In the Mahāvagga, there are twelve Saṃyuttas and forty-eight Vaggas. This is the measure of the Saṃyutta sub-divisions and Vaggas herein.
Regarding the phrase "for the generation of the differentiation of knowledge":
it is because of the abundance of discourses on dependent origination, the aggregates, the sense bases, and so forth, which elucidate the profound course of wisdom.
“Of him who produces the analysis of wisdom. Here, however, this tradition is praised as “the generator of the various modes of wisdom”;

and it is the custom of this Master in his commentaries (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) to offer such praise at the beginning of each commentary by extolling the specific qualities of the particular Dhamma to be commented upon. For instance, this is seen in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the *Papañcasūdanī*, the *Manorathapūraṇī*, the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, and others.

And praise was offered for it in due order, beginning with: "Of the Abhidhamma which brings forth faith, which crushes the arguments of opponents, which generates diverse eloquence in the preeminent preachers of the Dhamma, which has been fathomed by profound knowledges, and which is constantly varied by manifold methods. 6.

It is called *aṭṭhakathā* because the meaning (*attha*) is explained (*kathīyati*) by means of it; thus, it is simply a commentary (*atthakathā*), with the substitution of the letter *ṭṭha* for the letter *ttha*.
Having established it as, for example, "the meaning of oppression is suffering. "From the beginning" means at the start, in the first council (*saṅgīti*).

Because they were endowed with the supreme mastery over the mind through the possession of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and because the fivefold mastery over the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth was possible, the elders such as Mahākassapa and others were "mastery-possessors" (*vasī*).
By their five hundred [disciples]. "Yā" refers to that commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Recited" (*saṅgītā*)...
In the places where it was appropriate to explain the meaning, [the commentary] was spoken by summarizing it as "this is the meaning of this, this is the meaning of that.
It was also recited subsequently by the Elder Yasa and others during the second and third councils. By this, he demonstrates the purity of the lineage of his own sub-commentary.

7. Because he was taken from and born of a lion (Sīha), he is a Sihaḷa; because they were born of his lineage, the khattiyas in the island of Tambapaṇṇi are [called] Sihaḷas, and it should be understood that the island of Tambapaṇṇi itself acquired the status of being "Sihaḷa" due to their residence there.

"Brought" means brought from Jambudīpa. "Then" means afterwards. For at a later time, in order to prevent confusion with the tenets of other schools (nikāyantara), [the text was rendered] in the Sihaḷa language.
“[The commentary] was composed. By this, he shows that because the original commentary (*mūlaṭṭhakathā*) is not common to all, this exposition of the meaning must be performed exclusively [by him].
For this very reason, he says, “for the sake of those dwelling on the island (*dīpavāsīnamatthāya*).
Here, the construction is: “for the sake of those dwelling on the island”—meaning either those dwelling on Jambudīpa or those dwelling on the island of Sīhaḷa—it was composed in the Sīhaḷa language.
8. "Having removed" means having removed the Sinhalese language, which is like a bodice. "From that" means from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). "I" refers to himself.
"The delightful language" refers to the Māgadhī language; for it, being the natural mode of expression, delights the minds of the wise.
For this very reason he says, "conforming to the method of the Thread" (*tantinayānucchavika*), meaning it is in accordance with the course of the Pāḷi and follows the shadow of the Pāḷi.
The meaning is as follows: "Free from fault" (*vigatadosa*) means devoid of unrefined expressions, verbal obscurities, and foreign words.
"Not transgressing the occasion" (*samayam avilomento*) means not contradicting the established doctrine (*siddhanta*). By this, he states the absence of defects in the meaning.

For it is precisely because they are non-contradictory that even the doctrines of the Elders (*theravāda*) will be elucidated here. "Of those who illuminate the lineage of the Elders" (*theravaṃsadīpānaṃ*): by means of the stable aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth.

Because they were endowed with these qualities, [they were called] the Elders (thera), such as Mahākassapa and others. The lineage of the Elders (theravaṃsa) is the succession of teachers derived from them.

Being included within that [lineage], because they are perfected in both scripture and realization, they cause it to blaze forth by means of the lamp of wisdom; thus, they are the "Lamps of the Elder Lineage" (theravaṃsadīpa), namely the inhabitants of the Mahāvihāra.
That which is determined in various ways is a "determination" (vinicchaya), [referring to] the knotty points.

A discourse that cuts through doubt proceeds in the manner of crushing all remaining obstructions (*khila*). "Those for whom there is a very skillful and subtle discernment" means those who possess such discernment.
Alternatively, "discernment" (*vinicchaya*) refers to the knowledge that investigates the aforementioned objects;

thus it should be construed as "those for whom there is a very skillful, clever, and discerning investigation. By this [phrase], [the lineage] descending from the Elder Mahākassapa and the other Elders is indicated.
And for that very reason, he demonstrates that the judgment of those dwelling in the Great Monastery (Mahāvihāra) is unerring, gentle, and subtle, and serves as its authoritative standard.
Regarding the phrase "and for the sake of good people" (*sujanassa ca*), the word *ca* has the sense of inclusion.

By this, he shows: "It is not only for the sake of those dwelling in Jambudīpa, but also for the sake of pleasing virtuous persons. And by that, [he indicates] even for those dwelling on the island of Tambapaṇṇi...

The meaning "for the benefit" is established because it is easy for them to grasp and so forth, and because it is of great assistance to them. "For the sake of long endurance" means for the purpose of long-lasting persistence;

that is to say, for its continued existence over a long period of time. For this exposition of the meaning (atthappakāsana) functions for the long endurance of the True Dhamma, as it serves as the means for the correct application of words and phrasing without error and for the proper method of interpreting the meaning. Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the true Dhamma.
Which two? Well-settled phrasing and syllables, and well-expounded meaning.
11–12. Desiring to provide a commentary on this meaning, [the author] says “Sāvatthī and so forth” in order to avoid the charge of excessive prolixity.
It has been said. For that very reason he said: “I shall not provide further detailed exposition here; I shall not investigate that here.
Regarding the phrase “of the two compilations,” this refers to the Dīgha Nikāya and the Majjhima Nikāya.
To show the basis for the general statement “I shall not provide further detailed exposition here,” the passage beginning with “But as for the suttas” was spoken.
14. Desiring to compose this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the author provides instruction to his listeners, stating that the *Visuddhimagga* should be taken as representing a portion of its contents.
He thus presents the doctrines discussed therein by way of enumeration, beginning with the words "Discourse on Virtue" (*sīlakathā*) and so forth.

Therein, "Discourse on Virtue" refers to an extensive explanation of virtue (*sīla*) by way of what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided. "Ascetic Practices" (*dhutadhammā*) refers to the factors such as the practice of eating only almsfood (*piṇḍapātikaṅga*) and the rest.

The thirteen factors for shaking off the defilements (*kilesadhunanakadhammā*). "All meditation subjects" (*kammaṭṭhānāni*) refers to the thirty-eight mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the two mentioned in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*);

these are, without exception, the bases for the practice of the development of yoga. "Accompanied by the method of temperament" means accompanied by the classification of temperaments such as those dominated by lust (*rāgacarita*), and so forth.
The "jhanas" are the four fine-material-sphere jhanas (*rūpāvacarajjhāna*), and the attainments (*samāpattiyo*).

The four formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*); or alternatively, the eight meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) that have been merely acquired, which are called "attainments" because one has attained mastery over entering them;

or alternatively, "meditative absorptions" refers to the fine-material and immaterial-sphere absorptions, while "attainments" refers to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The six superknowledges (*abhiññā*), distinguished as mundane and supramundane, constitute all superknowledges. The "determination through the calculation of wisdom" (*paññāsaṅkalananicchaya*) is the conclusion reached by categorizing and synthesizing wisdom according to the methods taught in such texts as the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga*, beginning with the singlefold classification and so forth.
16. The "mode of conditionality" (*paccayākāra*) is the state of being a root-condition and so forth for the conditioned phenomena that arise from roots and so forth;

the "teaching on the mode of conditionality" is the instruction on that. The meaning is: the discourse on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). Furthermore, it is perfectly pure because it is free from the confusion of the tenets of other schools;

it is subtle and refined because the analytical resolution of the compact mass [of phenomena] is extremely difficult to achieve; and it is accompanied by the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*) and the rest.

And because it has been investigated there, he says, "by means of perfectly pure and subtle methods. Because it was investigated without setting aside the methods as they appear in the *Paṭisambhidā* and other texts, it is "a path whose finality is not yet released" (*avimuttantimaggā*).

Regarding the phrase "Thus, all this": the word *iti* indicates completion; the word *pana* is an ornament of speech. The meaning is, "all this [which has been stated]. "Here" refers to this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). The intention is: "I shall not investigate that here, for fear of redundancy."
18. Now, determining the sole cause for that very lack of deliberation, he says: "The Path of Purification stands in the middle," and so forth.

Therein, by the phrase "standing in the middle"—which illustrates its state of being central—it is shown that the *Visuddhimagga* is specifically the common commentary (*sādhāraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) for the four Āgamas, and not, like the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and others, an uncommon commentary (*asādhāraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).

[The author] shows this. Furthermore, the phrase "specifically" (*visesato*) is stated with the understanding that the *Visuddhimagga* likewise serves as a commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma as appropriate.
(19) "Thus indeed" (*icceva*) means "just thus. "That too" (*tampi*) refers to the *Visuddhimagga*. "By this" (*etāya*) refers to the *Sāratthappakāsinī*.
And here, by the words “brought from the Island of Siṃhala,” etc., he shows the cause for composing the commentary;
by the words “for the benefit of the inhabitants of the island and for the satisfaction and long endurance of the Dhamma of the virtuous,” he shows the purpose;
by the words “I shall explain the meaning of the excellent Saṃyutta Āgama,” he shows the summarized meaning; and by the words “having set aside the Sinhalese language from that point on,” etc.
By the phrases beginning with “Sāvatthipabhūtīnaṃ” and “Sīlakathā,” etc., the manner of composition is indicated.
For even the non-discussion here of matters already examined in the lower Nikāyas and in the *Visuddhimagga* constitutes a mode of composition in this work.
The commentary on the introduction to the treatise is concluded.
1. Devatāsaṃyutta 1.
Naḷavagga 1. Commentary on the Oghataraṇa Sutta (The Discourse on Crossing the Flood)

Since the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of things that possess distinctions occurs precisely through the demonstration of those distinctions, [the author] first stated, "In this regard, what is called the Saṃyutta-Āgama," and so forth, in order to show the divisions of the Saṃyutta-Āgama by way of its Suttas in the Saṃyutta-vagga and other sections.
Therein, "therein" (tattha) refers to that statement which was said: "I shall explain the meaning of the excellent Saṃyutta-Āgama. "Therein" (tattha) [refers to]...
Or, regarding the phrase "Understand the meaning based on the *Saṃyutta* through this commentary," as for the mention of the *Saṃyutta* made therein:
that which has five sections is "the Five-Sectioned" (*Pañcavagga*). The analysis (*viggaha*) is by way of its parts; the collective whole is the meaning of the compound.
Now, desiring to comment upon it from the beginning, [the author] first relates how it was included in the First Great Council (*paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*) by means of his own commentary.
In order to show that it proceeds according to the very sequence in which they were laid down, it was said: "Among its sections, the Sagāthavagga is first," and so forth.

Therein, *saṅgīti* means the chanting or reciting together of the Dhamma and Vinaya that had become scattered—because they were taught and established in various places according to specific requirements—by collecting them together;
and because of its vast scope and its venerable nature, [it is called the Great Recital].
A great recitation is a *mahāsaṅgīti*. The first great recitation is the *paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti*;
the time when that took place is the *paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāla*, and it is at that time of the first great recitation.

It is called a *nidāna* because it lays down (*nidadāti*) the teaching—making known what was previously unknown—by way of the teacher, the time, and so forth; thus it is a "source" (*nidāna*). As for that which...

In the world, it is called "the extraction of a knot"; here, this "knot" should be understood as the text beginning with "Thus have I heard," and not, as in passages such as "Bhikkhus, I teach the Dhamma with its source," as the cause for the arising of a teaching based on one's own inclination or other such factors.
For this very reason, he said: "The passage beginning 'Thus have I heard' was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council."
"The introduction is first. Here, although one who wishes to provide a commentary following the sequence established during the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti) ought to state it in detail,

[the author] says "But that [introduction]" and so forth, avoiding the excessive bulk of this commentary by noting that since it has already been explained in detail in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, it should be taken from there.

1. Having thus extended the instruction regarding what is to be said concerning the external nidāna, the passage beginning with "But as for this" (*yaṃ panetaṃ*) was spoken in order to comment upon the internal nidāna starting from the very beginning.

In that context, since one who provides a commentary must first show the word-analysis (*padavibhāga*) and the meaning of the words (*padattha*) for the phenomena to be commented upon, and only thereafter provide the commentary by way of showing the summarized meaning (*piṇḍattha*) and so forth—
[These things] must be done; therefore, showing the words first, he said: "‘Evam’ is a particle-word," and so forth.

In this context, *padavibhāga* means the distinction (*visesa*) between words, not the grammatical analysis (*viggha*) of words. Alternatively, *padavibhāga* refers to both the words (*padāni*) and the distinction between words (*padavibhāgo*).
Or, by means of the *ekasesa* (single-remainder) rule, the words and the word-analysis are both included under the term *padavibhāga*.
It should be understood as "spoken. In that regard, the grammatical analysis (*padaviggaha*) is to be seen in compound terms such as "the grove of Jeta is Jetavana," and so forth.
"From the meaning" means from the meaning of the words. Showing that word-meaning first, according to the sequence for extracting the meaning, he says "first of all, the word *evaṃ*...
and so on. Regarding the phrase "limitation and so forth," here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes meanings such as "this," "purpose," "question," "measure," and others.

The inclusion [of the term *evaṃ*] should be understood. For instance, in such expressions as “various crafts and occupations have come to be thus (*evaṃgatāni*), of such a kind (*evaṃvidho*), of such a form (*evamākāro*)” and so forth, the word *evaṃ* has the same meaning as the word *idaṃ*. Indeed, the word *gata* is a synonym for *pakāra* (manner/type), as are the words *vidha* and *ākāra*.
For common people use the words *gata*, *vidha*, and *ākāra* in the sense of *pakāra*. “Thus indeed you were well-bathed and well-anointed...”
In such passages as, "With hair and beard trimmed, wearing garlands and ornaments, dressed in white garments, endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, they sport about,
just as you do now along with your teachers," it refers to a question.
In such passages as, "Thus swift is its revolution, thus is its limit of life," it refers to a measure.

But is it not the case that in the passage, “Thus indeed you are well-bathed, well-anointed, thus indeed is the limit of your life,” the word *evaṃ* (thus) expresses both the manner of questioning and the measure [of the life-span], and therefore the word *evaṃ* has the sense of a mode (*ākāra*)?

No, because there is a distinction. For the word *evaṃ* denotes a mere mode and is intended to have the sense of a mode—as in “thus explained” and so forth—but it does not denote a specific mode. And thus...
Having done so, the examples in the similes, such as “Thus by a mortal who has been born,” become appropriate.

For instance, in the passage beginning “Just as... much,” here the heap of flowers stands for the collection of causes for merit—such as rebirth as a human, reliance upon a true person, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and the attainment of wealth through acts like giving—which possess qualities such as beauty and fragrance.

Since abundant meritorious deeds, which resemble garlands and flower-clusters, ought to be performed by a mortal being because of the inherent nature of death, these are like heaps of flowers and garlands;

thus, as the manner of comparison is stated non-specifically by the word "thus" (yathā), it is appropriate to state that "the word 'evam' has the sense of concluding the manner of comparison. However, when that manner of comparison is specified...
"In meaning it is simply a simile," he said, "it has come down as a simile.

Likewise, regarding the perfection of deportment appropriate for a recluse, which is being pointed out by such phrases as "one should advance in this manner" and so forth—the manner of pointing that out is, in meaning, simply an instruction;
thus it was said: "In this way for you... [etc. ...in the instructions. Likewise: "It is so, Blessed One; it is so..."

And here, in the phrase “Sugatas,” *sampahaṃsana* refers to the gladdening and uplifting by various means of the qualities existing therein, performed by those who understand the aforementioned meaning without error.
It should be construed as: "whatever manner of gladdening exists therein. Likewise, in this context, it should be construed as:
"the manner of censuring," which is indicated by the presence of disparaging terms such as "outcaste" (*vasalī*) and so forth.

It is understood that [the meaning] is made manifest here by the word *evaṃ*. And just as it is here, so too should it be seen that the forms of similes (*upamākāra*) and so forth are used by way of similes and the like, due to the proximity of words such as "heap of flowers" which have been spoken [in that manner].

However, the phrase "Yes, venerable sir" (*evaṃ, bhante*) is used by the monks—who have been directed toward the careful hearing and attention of the Dhamma—as a way of acknowledging their own state of being established therein.
Because it has been stated here, the word *evaṃ* is said to have the sense of "accepting what is spoken.
By that [word], "Evaṃ, bhante" means "Well said, bhante; very well, bhante.
And regarding the phrase "Speak thus," the manner of speaking which is now to be described—namely, "Speak to the ascetic Ānanda exactly as I say"—is indicated by the word *evaṃ*.
It is said that "the sense of illustration" is expressed here. Regarding the phrase "it is so for us":

even here, in order to produce a firm conviction regarding the fact that those aforementioned phenomena bring about harm and suffering, a question is posed by way of seeking consent—"Do they lead [to such results] or not?
What is your view on this?"—and because the reply given is "It is so for us," the word "evam" (thus) expresses the firm conviction of that specific mode.
"Vibhāvita" is understood as "discerned. However, since that mode of these phenomena—which leads to harm and suffering—is being delimited, it serves the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*);
thus he said: "In 'thus it is for us here,' etc., [the term refers to] restriction.

"Skilled in various methods" refers to those consisting of unity, diversity, non-activity, and the nature of things (*evaṃdhammatā*), and those consisting of the "Joyous Turn" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*), the "Fertile" (*tipukkhalā*), the "Lion’s Play" (*sīhavikkīḷita*), and the "Goading Hook" (*aṅkusasamālocana*).

Or, "various methods" (*nānānayā*) refers to various methods according to the distinctions of the basis (*ādhāra*) and so forth. Alternatively, "methods" (*nayā*) refers to the ways of the texts (*pāḷigatiyo*);

and these [ways] exist by way of basic rules (*paññatti*) and supplementary rules (*anupaññatti*), by way of categories such as pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth, mundane (*lokiya*) and so forth, mixed with both (*tadubhayavomissaka*) and so forth, wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, compendiums (*saṅgaha*) and so forth, liberation from time (*samayavimutta*) and so forth, setting aside (*ṭhapanā*) and so forth, roots of the wholesome (*kusalamūla*) and so forth, and by way of the triads and dyads (*tikappaṭṭhāna*) and so forth.
"And of various kinds" means of various methods; "skillful in those various methods" means subtle, delicate, and refined by means of them.

"Inclination" (*āsaya*) is the same as "disposition" (*ajjhāsaya*); these are manifold through their divisions such as eternalism and so forth, and through their divisions therein such as having little defilement and so forth.
Alternatively, it is that which has its origin and cause of arising in self-disposition and the like; thus, it is "originated from manifold dispositions. "Endowed with meaning and phrasing" means...
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as follows: it is "complete in both meaning and phrasing" because there is nothing further to be added;

and it is endowed with six factors of meaning—namely, revealing, manifesting, explaining, analyzing, making plain, and prescribing—and with six factors of phrasing—namely, letters, words, phrases, modes, etymological definitions, and explanations.

Regarding the phrase "various miracles" (*vividhapāṭihāriya*), they explain the meaning of the word *pāṭihāriya* here as follows: "It is called a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*) because it removes opposing factors, that is, because it eliminates the defilements such as lust.

However, since the Blessed One possesses no opposing factors such as lust that need to be removed—just as the supernormal power (*iddhividha*) exists even in ordinary persons whose minds are free from corruption and endowed with the eight qualities, having destroyed their opposing factors—[the term is used here in a different sense].
Because it occurs [only] there, it cannot be called a "miracle" (pāṭihāriya) here by way of the conventional usage current in that context.
However, if the defilements residing in those to be trained are the adversaries of the Blessed One, the Great Compassionate One, and because he removes them, it is called a "miracle";
in that case, this is appropriate. Alternatively, [it refers to] those who are adversaries of both the Blessed One and his Teaching.
Regarding the *titthiyas*, it is a "manifestation" (*pāṭihāriya*) because of its taking away (*harana*).
For they are taken away and removed by means of supernormal power, mind-reading, and instruction, through the removal of their views and because of their incapacity to manifest those views.
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "after," as in such examples as: "When he had entered [the city], another brahmin arrived."
Therefore, "display" (*paṭihāriya*) refers to that which is to be brought forth and put into operation after the mind has been concentrated, freed from defilements, and has accomplished its task;
or alternatively, it is the subsequent bringing forth (*pacchā-haraṇa*) once one’s own defilements have been removed by the paths of the fourth jhāna.

Furthermore, the supernormal powers (*iddhi*), the direct teachings (*ādesanā*), and the instructions (*anusāsani*) are [performed] for the benefit of beings by one who is free from defilements and has accomplished his task.
Furthermore, they are to be performed again; and because they remove the defilements of other beings from one’s own fields of green grass, they are called *paṭihāriya*.

Indeed, that which is a *paṭihāriya* is a *pāṭihāriya*. Alternatively, each individual member within the collection consisting of psychic power (*iddhi*), manifestation (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsanī*) is called a *pāṭihāriya*.
Or else, the fourth jhāna and the Path are called *paṭihāriya* because they remove opposing factors.
*Pāṭihāriya* means that which is born therein, or that which has that as its sign, or that which has come from that.
