Since it is found in the teaching of the Blessed One in many ways—through the classification of psychic powers (*iddhi*) and so forth, and through the classification of its objects—he says "various wonders" (*vividhapāṭihāriya*).
"Not otherwise" means not otherwise than the manner in which it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One; but it does not mean [not otherwise] from the Blessed One...
From the perspective of the manner of teaching. For the Blessed One’s teaching possesses an inconceivable power.
And by taking it thus, the statement, "Who is capable of understanding it in every aspect? is justified;

furthermore, this does not contradict the demonstration of the power of retention, because what is intended is that there is no contradiction with the manner in which it was heard. For here, there is no need for an avoidance of a difference in meaning between the two.
This is because they have the same object. Otherwise, it would follow that the Elder was both capable and incapable of receiving the Blessed One’s teaching in its entirety.

This is because [the term "self"] is applied to one's own continuity, which is designated as "internal" (ajjhatta) in the sense of being "one's own" (niyaka), as stated in the passage: "That which is not another is self."
Although the word *me* appears in only one sense, he says,
"The word *me* is seen in three senses," with reference to the existing distinction based on its designation as the instrumental,

the dative, and the genitive. Although a prefix qualifies the action, nevertheless, because it is merely indicative, even when that [prefix] is present, it is the verbal root (*suta*) itself [that conveys the meaning].

Showing that there is no contradiction in including the term with a prefix (*saupasagga*) when explaining the meaning of the word *suta* without a prefix (*anupasagga*)—namely, that it means "he speaks of this or that self"—the author says:
"Both with and without a prefix. "Of it" refers to the word *suta*.

Since both the objective (*kamma*) and the abstract (*bhāva*) modes of derivation are possible here for the word *suta*, he states: "Or, 'having been considered' (*upadhārita*) or 'consideration' (*upadhāraṇa*)."
"Or else, the meaning is 'may'. When there is the sense of "may," it means when the word *me* functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of the agent;
that is the meaning. When there is the sense of "mine," it means when it functions as a possessor (*sāmin*) by way of a relationship.
It is stated that, in the proximity of the word *suta*, the word *evaṃ* employed [there] must be one that illuminates the act of hearing.
"‘Thus’ is a demonstration of the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness and so forth.

By the word “and so forth” (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of the five-door consciousnesses beginning with receiving (sampaṭicchana), as well as the mind-door consciousnesses brought forward by those [preceding moments].

Since all sentences possess the sense of the particle *eva* (only/just), the meaning “heard only” is obtained for the word “heard” (suta); thus he said, “by way of negating the state of not having heard.”

By this restriction, he shows its freedom from attachment. And just as "what is heard is indeed heard" must be delimited, he says, "the demonstration of grasping that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor erroneous," because it is properly heard.

Alternatively, since a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words, the meaning of "heard" is that it is not unheard; thus it is said, "by the negation of the state of being unheard."
By this, he effects a turning away from [the claim that it was] seen and so forth.
This is what is meant: "This was not seen by me, nor realized through self-become knowledge;
rather, it was heard, and that too correctly. For this very reason, he says: "It is an indication of a grasp that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor perverted."
Alternatively, when the word *evaṃ* (thus) is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇatthe*), this application of meaning is made;

thus, the meaning of the word *suta* (heard), which depends on that [restriction], is stated as "by way of negating the state of not hearing. For this very reason, he said: "It is an indication of grasping [the teaching] without deficiency, without excess, and without error.
And here, the word *savana* (hearing) should be understood as having the sense of the object (*kamm-attha*), as in "it is heard" (*suyyati*).

Having thus shown the application of the meaning of the three terms in one way by means of the hearing-cause and the distinction of hearing, he now says “In the same way,” etc., in order to show it by other ways.

Therein, “of that” (*tassā*) refers to that cognitive process of mind-door consciousness which occurred in the manner of hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One; for that [process] is of various kinds.
[They] are capable of occurring with respect to an object. And thus it has been said: "by way of the ear-door.
"In various ways" means in the manner of the manifold apprehensions of the phrasing and meaning that are about to be explained.

By this, he indicates that in this construction, the word *evaṃ* (thus) is taken in the sense of "manner" (*ākāra*). "The manifestation of the state of occurrence" is the making manifest of the existence of occurrence.

“Sutaṃ” means “an exposition of phenomena” (dhammappakāsana). It is stated as such because the object upon which the aforementioned course of consciousness (viññāṇavīthi) proceeds in its various modes is itself a phenomenon (dhamma), not because the word *suta* has the meaning of "phenomenon" (dhamma).
The clarification of that very same meaning is given by the passage beginning with “This is below,” and so forth.

In that context, the term “course of consciousness” (*viññāṇavīthiyā*) is used in the sense of an instrument (the ablative case), while “by me” (*mayā*) is used in the sense of an agent (the instrumental case).
Thus, the word "evam" (thus) is employed for the purpose of indication (*nidassana*) alone, as it serves to reveal the manner in which something is to be demonstrated;

this is because there is no distinction between the act of indicating and that which is to be indicated. By means of that word "evam," he shows that the entire sutta is referred back [to what precedes].
Since the word "suta" (heard) is a verb (*kiriyāsadda*), and because the act of hearing is connected to a common continuum of consciousness (*viññāṇappabandha*).
And therein it is said, "the designation of a person (puggalavohāra)," because it is stated: "‘Suta’ is the manifestation of a person’s function.
For the act of hearing is not possible in a continuum of phenomena (dhammappabandha) devoid of the designation of a person.
Regarding the phrase "of whichever mental continuum," etc., one may take the word *evaṃ* in the sense of manner (*ākāra*) and provide an alternative construction to the previous one.

This was stated in order to demonstrate the eightfold application (*atthayojana*). In that context, "designation by way of mode" (*ākārapaññatti*) is precisely "designation by way of dependence" (*upādāpaññatti*), so called because it takes as its basis the modes of occurrence of phenomena.

"The heard" (*suta*) is a designation for the object; it is stated thus because the phenomenon that constitutes the object of hearing is the locus of occurrence for the person who is the agent of the act of hearing, by way of that act of hearing.
[As for] "that which is distinct from the continuum of consciousness" (*cittasantānavinimutta*)...

Although in the ultimate sense there is no agent whatsoever, according to conventional linguistic usage, and with the desire for a term that expresses a distinction imagined by the intellect, it is said—
treating the possessor [of the mental continuum] as if it were distinct from the mental continuum itself— that "the possessor [is known] by means of the mental continuum.
Furthermore, the dhamma that is the object of the act of hearing is, in this context, the mental continuum occurring by way of the act of hearing.

In the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), because of the state of being an agent, or because the activity of hearing exists only as the occurrence of consciousness by way of listening, it becomes the object of the agent of that activity; thus it is said: "the object of the agent belonging to that [state].
And because the Elder, who possesses the mode of hearing, has correctly determined [the matter], he says: "the conclusion of grasping. By this, or for the sake of emphasis—
It should be understood that by taking the word *evaṃ* (thus), this application of meaning (*atthayojanā*) has been made.

The word *evaṃ* has the nature of manifesting the determination, the indication, or the ascertainment of the form of the meanings and phonemes—designated as "suttas"—which were previously heard in their various arrangements;
it is the very means for the determination of such forms and so forth.

Because the designation of a person (*puggalapaññatti*) consists in the functioning of a continuity of phenomena (*dhamma*) that serve as its basis, it is said: “‘Thus’ is a description of the function of a person.
However, since even for a proponent of a person (*puggalavādin*), the act of hearing does not exist independently of consciousness, it is specifically the function of consciousness;
thus he says: “‘Heard’ is a description of the function of consciousness. Because the occurrence of the word ‘I’ has exclusively a sentient being (*satta*) as its object...
And because the function of consciousness must be integrated right there [in that person], it is said: "‘Me’ is a designation for a person endowed with both functions.

Since the meanings of the words *evaṃ* and *suta* respectively consist in the nature of non-existent designation (*avijjamāna-paññatti*) and existent designation (*vijjamāna-paññatti*), he shows them as being the activity of the continuum of phenomena (*dhamma-pabandha*) which serves as the basis for such designations.
He said: “‘Thus’ is a designation for the function of the person (*puggala*); ‘heard’ is a designation for the function of consciousness (*viññāṇa*).

And here it should be understood that the four applications of meaning, beginning with the accusative case, are shown by way of illustrating the specific distinctions of instrument, action, agent, and object; by way of demonstrating the activity of the person as the domain of the person's operation;
by way of designating the specific distinctions of the mode of grasping, the grasper, and the object of grasping; and by way of designating the agent and the operation of the instrument.
Since one must proceed by way of the designation (*paññatti*) alone for every meaning that is to be understood through words,
and since all designations are included within the sixfold classification of designations— beginning with "existent" (*vijjamāna*)— he states,

"‘Thus’ (*eva*) and ‘mine’ (*me’)," etc., while determining the specific nature of those designations such as "thus" and so forth. Therein, regarding that which is called "thus" (*eva*) and "mine" (*me*):
Because phenomena such as the aspects of the truths lack their own specific characteristics (asallakkhaṇa), they are non-existent designations; thus it was said:

"Non-existent designation in terms of the true and ultimate sense" (*saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena*). In this context, "in terms of the true and ultimate sense" means in terms of the actual reality and the supreme reality.
This is what is meant: that which is unreal, like a magical illusion or a mirage, and which is to be grasped through hearsay and the like—

And that which is not the unsurpassed goal—that nature of visible forms, sounds, and so forth, or the nature of being subject to change, experiencing, and so forth—is called the "truely real" (saccikaṭṭha) and the "ultimate" (paramattha) meaning;
it is not, however, the meaning of the words "thus" (evaṃ) and "this is mine" (meti).

To make this very point more evident, the passage beginning with "What is the reason for this? was stated. As for the word "heard" (suta), he says it with reference to the sense-base of sound (saddāyatana).
“Designation of what exists” (*vijjamānapaññatti*). For this very reason it is said: “Whatever there is here that has been apprehended by the ear.
However, when it is stated that [something] is “apprehended by way of the ear-door,” everything including both the meaning (*attha*) and the phrasing (*byañjana*) is thereby included.

“Because it can be spoken of in dependence on this or that” means that in dependence on those phenomena that have come within the range of the ear, one refers to them by way of their determined aspects and so forth, saying “thus.”
The meaning is that it is to be called "mine" by depending upon the aggregates included within one's own continuity (*sasantatipariyāpanna*).

Although the conventional usage of "heard" (*suta*) occurs with respect to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*), which is devoid of the intrinsic nature of being seen and so forth—just as the expressions "second" or "third" occur—it nevertheless proceeds by depending on the first [seen] and so forth;
thus he said, "because it is to be expressed in relation to what is seen and so forth. For [it is said]: "that which was not heard does not exist..."
"‘Sutta’ means this matter has been made manifest.
The Elder replied, "It is thus," referring to the specific modes of the Sutta as they have been personally realized by himself; therefore, he said, "it illuminates non-delusion.
By the phrase "one becomes capable of various modes of penetration," he indicates the manifold nature of the Sutta that is about to be explained.
And it shows that which is difficult to penetrate. "It illustrates the non-confusion of what has been heard" is said because the mode of what was heard is being shown according to its true nature.
"By means of non-delusion" means by the absence of delusion; or rather, it refers to the establishment of wisdom at a later time through the very wisdom that arose at the time of hearing.
The same should be said regarding the phrase "by means of non-confusion. The mode to be penetrated in the case of the phonemes is not excessively deep.
In this context, since "the retention of what has been heard exactly as it was" is what must be done, the function of mindfulness (*sati*) is predominant, while wisdom (*paññā*) is subordinate;
thus it is said, "preceded by wisdom," and so forth, taking wisdom as the precursor. Here, being a "precursor" means being primary, as in such expressions as "mind is the precursor.
Alternatively, by way of being a precursor, [wisdom acts] like the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) in relation to eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*) and the rest.
The meaning "wisdom precedes this [speech] because it is its primary factor" is also appropriate;
this being so, the meaning of the term *pubbaṅgamāya* (preceding) should also be understood according to the context, by way of the reverse of what was stated above.
Regarding the phrase *atthabyañjanasampannassa*: it means "endowed with both meaning and phrasing," by way of announcing, elucidating, explaining, analyzing, clarifying, and describing.

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as: "endowed with six bases of meaning" (atthapada) and "endowed with six bases of phrasing" (byañjanapada), namely by way of letters, phrases, syllables, grammatical forms, etymological definitions, and explanations.

By means of the word "thus" (evaṃ), he illustrates appropriate attention (yoniso manasikāra), which serves the purposes of indicating a mode, pointing out, and determining those things being spoken of.
The intention is that its object is the true Dhamma free from perversion.

It "illuminates non-distraction" because it is said that the hearing of the Sutta—which is about to be explained and whose occurrence in this treatise is prompted by questions such as "Where was the *Oghataraṇa-sutta* spoken?"—is not possible without concentration (*samādhi*).
The passage beginning with "of one whose mind is distracted" serves to corroborate that very point.
It has been said: "By all perfections" means by the perfection of meaning, phrasing, teaching, purpose, and so forth.

Just as right attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) [is established] by the aspects, indications, and determinations that have the true Dhamma (*saddhamma*) as their unerring object, and just as non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is [established] by the hearing of the true Dhamma, so too, by means of right attention—which is the fruit—[one understands] the state of having rightly directed oneself and the state of having performed merit in the past.

Success (*siddhi*) is stated because it is inseparable from that; thus, by means of non-distraction itself as the fruit, the success of the causes—the hearing of the true Dhamma and reliance upon a good person—should be demonstrated, since these do not exist for one who has not heard [the Dhamma] and lacks reliance upon a good person.
Furthermore, by the statement "For one whose mind is distracted," etc., which expresses capability, non-distraction as the cause is shown through reliance upon a good person.
And the accomplishment of hearing the true Dhamma, which is the fruit, has been shown. However, this following interpretation would be more appropriate here:
the support of hearing the true Dhamma and relying upon a person of integrity are not exclusively causes for non-distraction, because they are external factors.
Non-distraction, on the other hand, like reliance upon a person of integrity, is an exclusive cause for hearing the true Dhamma; thus it is also [the case].
The demonstration that the accomplishment of relying upon a true person (*sappurisūpanissaya*) is not possible without non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is not incorrect;

it is not the case that it is impossible, because for those with distracted minds, the goal is not accomplished due to the absence of attending upon a true person. Herein, the first is a demonstration of the establishment of the cause by means of the fruit, like the presence of rain upstream inferred from the swelling of a river.
The second is a demonstration of the establishment of the fruit by means of the cause.
It is to be seen as the occurrence of rain following the emergence of a cloud that rains unceasingly.

It is said, "Such is the auspicious manner," because it is the cause for fulfilling the welfare of others without remainder—the mode of plunging into the excellence of the entire Dispensation by way of the distinctions and divisions of the meaning and phrasing of the Blessed One’s word. For it does not exist [otherwise].

The connection [is as follows]: "The attainment of the final two wheels" refers to the pair of qualities known as right aspiration for oneself (*attasammāpaṇidhi*) and merit performed in the past (*pubbekatapuññatā*).
Furthermore, they are called "wheels" (*cakkāni*) because they function in succession, or because by means of them sentient beings move through fortunate existences (*sampattibhava*).
It is with reference to these that it was said: "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels; endowed with which, gods and humans..."
“The four wheels turn,” and so forth. Here, the distinction between “prior” and “subsequent” should be understood according to the sequence of the teaching.
“By means of the accomplishment of the latter two wheels” means by way of the existence of the latter two wheels.
One whose self is rightly directed has previously performed merit and possesses a pure intention, because the defilements that are the causes of its impurity have been distanced; thus he said.
“Purity of disposition becomes accomplished. For it has been said: “A mind rightly directed makes one better than before,” and “You have done merit, Ānanda;
apply yourself to striving, and soon you will be free from the taints. Therefore he said:

“Through purity of disposition, there is the accomplishment of proficiency in attainment. Regarding “purity of application”: [it refers to] that which is preceded by wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
This is due to the clarity of the application of listening to the Dhamma. Thus it is said: "The accomplishment of proficiency in the scriptures.

Alternatively, it is because of the faultless nature of all bodily and verbal application. For one whose bodily and verbal application is completely pure becomes undistracted in mind—due to the absence of remorse—and thus gains confidence in the scriptures.
By the passage beginning with "indicating various modes of penetration," etc., he demonstrates the application of the meaning by way of the four analytical knowledges (*catu-paṭisambhidā*),

because it illustrates the Elder’s lack of confusion and non-forgetfulness regarding both the meaning and the phrasing through the words *evaṃ* and *suta*. Therein, by the phrase "indicating the penetration of the distinctions of what is to be heard," it is shown that this word *suta*—
due to its proximity to the word *evaṃ*, or by virtue of its reference to what is yet to be spoken— is, in a general sense, [the means of indicating] the specific qualities of the Dhamma to be heard.

He illuminates [the meaning of] "touching. Since the thorough investigation and deep penetration of the teachings (pariyatti-dhamma) through mental views are specifically dependent upon attention (*manasikāra*), these should be connected with the word "thus" as explained by the method already stated which illustrates wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
Furthermore, since the hearing, retention, and verbal mastery of the teachings are specifically dependent upon the application of the ear (*sotāvadhāna*), these...

By connecting this with the word "heard" (*suta*), which indicates non-distraction according to the method already stated, he demonstrates how one generates enthusiasm for hearing the Dhamma as a perfection of the Dispensation.
In that context, "Dhammas" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti*). "Examined with the mind" means examining it with the mind according to such methods as:
"Herein virtue is taught, here concentration, here wisdom; herein there are so many connections," and so forth.

“Not disregarded”: well-penetrated by means of a view that has become one of reflective acceptance (*nijjhānakkhanti*), or by means of a view consisting of full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*);

that is, having properly defined the various material and immaterial phenomena mentioned here and there as “this is form, such is the extent of form,” and so forth, they have been thoroughly penetrated.
"By the entire statement" is said because it was previously joined separately with each of the three phrases.

"Not attributing to himself" means not establishing [the thought] "this is mine" within himself; here, this genitive case is used in the sense of a locative. "The plane of the bad person" refers to ingratitude.
As it is said: "In this case, a certain evil bhikkhu, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, attributes it to himself."
Thus has been stated the stage of ignoble speech; that very stage of ignoble speech is the non-Dhamma (*asaddhamma*).

But is it not the case that the statement regarding the transcendence of the plane of the unworthy and so forth is purposeless, given that the Elder Ānanda lacked the overweening pride of thinking, "This is my word," and the Elders Mahākassapa and others likewise lacked any suspicion thereof? This is not so. "Thus have I heard... [and so on].
This meaning is also clarified by the statement, "It was heard," which shows that it was seen [by the Buddha].
However, some say: "Such an objection—that those words were spoken with regard to the reflections of the deities—is out of place.
For at that moment, a reflection arose in the minds of certain deities: "The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, and this Venerable One is skilled in teaching."
"He is now teaching the Dhamma; he is one born of the Sakyan clan, the Tathāgata’s brother, the son of his paternal uncle.

Does he teach the Dhamma that he has realized for himself, or is it merely the word of the Blessed One as he has heard it?"—thus, by way of such doubts and the like, and by way of the entry into the plane of a person of no integrity and so forth, the "transcending" and other factors are explained. He enters.
It shows. It is a "guide" (netti) because it leads beings, as appropriate, toward the goals pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal;
thus, the Dhamma itself is the guide, a "guide to the Dhamma" (dhammanetti).
Doubt (vicikicchā) is a state firmly rooted as uncertainty; while perplexity (vimati) is a mere division of thought that does not extend very far. Lack of faith (assaddhiya) is...
It is "destroyed" because it was spoken by the Blessed One, because it was received directly from him, and because there is no fault of grasping at slips of the tongue or harsh speech.
Herein, the first three applications of meaning are shown by taking the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "manner" (*ākāra*) and so forth, without grasping any specific distinction;
the four following [applications] are elucidated by taking the word *evaṃ* specifically in the sense of "manner. The final one...

However, it should be understood that the three [instances] have employed the word *evaṃ* respectively for the purpose of indicating a mode, for the purpose of illustration, and for the purpose of restriction.
The word *eka* is seen in the senses of "other," "best," "without companion," and "number," and so forth; for instance, in the passage: "The self and the world are eternal..."
In such passages as, "And some assert: 'This alone is the truth, all else is vain,'" the word *eka* is seen in the sense of "other.
In "one-pointedness of mind" (*cetaso ekodibhāva*), it means "excellent. In "alone, withdrawn," it means "without companion.
In "Bhikkhus, there is indeed one moment and one occasion for living the holy life," it refers to "number. Here too, he shows that it refers to number.
He said: "The term 'one' is a designation for the delimitation by counting. "Time" (*kāla*) and "occasion" (*samaya*) refer to the appropriate time and the completeness of conditions.
"Moment" (*khaṇa*) means opportunity. For the appearance of a Tathāgata and so forth is the opportunity for the holy life of the path, because it is the cause for obtaining its requisite conditions.
Furthermore, the moment itself is the occasion; the sense is that what is called a "moment" and what is called an "occasion" are one and the same. Thus, "the great occasion" (*mahāsamaya*).
“Mahāsamūho” means a great assembly. “Samayopi kho” means even the cause for fulfilling the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). “Samayappavādake” means those who proclaim their own doctrines (*diṭṭhi*);
for it is there that the non-Buddhist teachers (*titthiya*), sitting together, proclaim their respective doctrines.

“Atthābhisamaya” means the attainment of benefit. “Abhisamayo” is that which is to be fully realized; thus, “abhisamayattho” means the purpose of full realization, because [the truths] such as oppression (*pīḷana*) and so forth are to be fully realized.

They are spoken of by bringing them into a state of unity. Alternatively, the meaning that constitutes the object of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) or penetration (*paṭivedha*) is the "meaning of clear realization" (*abhisamayattha*);
thus, those very [terms] are spoken of as such through their oneness. In this context, "affliction" (*pīḷana*) is the harming of one who possesses the truth of suffering, making him non-expansive;
"torment" (*santāpa*) is the burning and scorching by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and so forth.
In this context, *samaya* means a collection (*samavāya*), because the auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*) meet (*sameti*) and come together (*samaveti*).
It is a *samaya*—meaning a moment (*khaṇa*)—because the holy life of the path (*maggabrahmacariya*) meets and comes together with the persons who are its support.

It is a *samaya*—meaning time (*kāla*)—because a being (*satto*), a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), or [the factors of] arising and so forth, meet (*sameti*) in it, or come together (*saṃgacchati*) by means of it, such as through co-nascent factors (*sahajātādi*) or through arising and so forth.

For although time does not exist as a substantial entity (*attha*), it is nevertheless spoken of by way of a mere conceptual construct—as a locus or an instrument for the occurrence of phenomena—by means of a form established through mere imagination. "Samaya" means the simultaneous or equal movement, proceeding, or persistence of parts;
it is a collection, just as in the term "samudāya. For it is precisely the simultaneous persistence of parts that constitutes a "samaya."
It is called *samaya*. It is a *samaya* because, through the coming together (*samāgama*) of the remaining conditions, the fruit comes (*eti*) from it, arises, and proceeds;

thus it is a cause (*hetu*), as in the term "origination" (*samudaya*). Or, it is a *samaya* because beings come (*eti*) into connection (*sameti*) with their own objects due to the state of being fettered (*saṃyojana*), or because they proceed (*ayanti*) in accordance with their adherence (*abhinivesa*) through this firm grasping (*daḷhaggahaṇa*); thus it is a *samaya*.
*Diṭṭhi*. For by means of the fetter of views (*diṭṭhisaṃyojana*), beings are bound exceedingly tight. *Samaya* means meeting, gathering, or coming together; it is acquisition.
It is the vehicle (*yāna*) to cessation (*sama*), or the correct (*sammā*) vehicle, departure, and non-occurrence;
it is abandonment. *Abhisamaya* means that which is to be approached correctly and attained face-to-face through knowledge; it is the non-perverted [realization] of phenomena.

It is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). It is called *abhisamaya* because one approaches, proceeds toward, and awakens to by way of being face-to-face; it is the unerring realization of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
In this manner, the application of the term *samaya* should be understood with respect to each respective meaning.

In the enumeration of the meanings of the word *samaya*, the example of the word *abhisamaya* should be understood according to the method already stated. *Assa* means "of the word *samaya*. *Kālo* (time).
Because meanings such as "conjunction" (samavāya) and so forth are impossible here, and because time must be referred to as the introduction (nidāna) of the discourse—
just as the place, the teacher, and the assembly are—
why then is time indicated here in an unrestricted manner rather than being restricted by way of seasons, years, and so forth?

He said, “In that regard, although... and so forth. Showing that this merit is also obtained when the word *samaya* is used without restricting it to specific times such as the seasons or the year, he said, “Or these which...,” and so forth. For a general designation settles upon a particular instance.

In that context, the occasion for dwelling in happiness in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra-samaya*) consists of the daily attainments of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) and the fruits of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*).

The period of passing away consists specifically of seven weeks. "Well-manifested" means they are made evident through such things as the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system and the appearance of radiance.
To show that even within the aforementioned classifications of time, certain portions can be subsumed under other categories, he says, "And that which...
and so forth. For thus, the occasion for the function of knowledge and the occasion for practicing for one's own welfare are both included within the occasion of full enlightenment.

The occasion for noble silence, the occasion for dwelling in happiness in this very life, the occasions for the practice of benefiting others through compassionate duty and for discourses on the Dhamma—these alone are the occasions for teaching.

The connection is that the description is made by means of the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*). "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the Abhidhamma, the Suttas other than those [mentioned], the phrases, and the Vinaya.

"In such a way" (*tathā*) refers to the locative and instrumental cases. The sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the sense of support (*ādhāra*). "State" (*bhāva*) is indeed action (*kiriyā*); it is the characterization of another action by means of that [action].
The characteristic of a state by means of a state. In this regard, just as time— though itself non-existent in the ultimate sense—

is known as a support delimited by states possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma), because of the absence [of those states] prior to and subsequent to that moment when they arise at a particular instant—
as in such expressions as "born in the forenoon" or "going in the afternoon"— and just as a collection, though non-existent separately apart from its constituent parts, [is likewise known].

It is designated as the locus of its parts by way of mere conceptual construction (*kappanāmatta*), just as in such cases as "the branch on the tree" or "produced in a heap of grain," and so too here; showing this, he said: "For the locus... of phenomena.
At whatever time, or within whatever heap of phenomena, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, at that very time, within that same heap of phenomena—
And the meaning there is that contact and so forth also exist. Just as in the expression, "He went while the cows were being milked;

he returned when they had been milked," the act of going is indicated by the act of milking, so too here, when it is said, "at whatever time" (*yasmiṃ samaye*), the sense of "being present" (*sati*) is understood simply because the referent of the word lacks an absence of existence.
At the moment [of consciousness], the activity of arising of the mind and the activity of the manifestation of contact and so forth are characterized within the activity of the sevenfold process.

"At whatever moment" means at whatever ninth moment, or when whatever cause such as appropriate attention exists, or when there is a concurrence of conditions, a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen; it is at that very moment, in that cause, or in that concurrence of conditions.

Since contact and the other [factors] are also present, he says, “...is characterized (lakkhīyati),” showing that in both instances the locative case is used for the word *samaya* because it is connected with the state of being a characteristic (*lakkhaṇabhūtabhāva*).
Both the sense of cause (*hetu*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) are possible, as in: “he dwells by means of food,” “he dwells by means of knowledge,” or “he cuts with an axe.”
As in the passages beginning with "he digs with a spade," the Blessed One— having heard of a transgression, having convened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
having questioned the individual involved in the matter, and having censured him— proclaims the training rules at the very time the respective matter occurred,
without letting that time pass, while taking into account the cause for the proclamation of those training rules.
As in the case of the third *pārājika* offense and others.
From the very beginning of the undertaking until the conclusion of the teaching. By means of the dwelling in compassion, which is designated as the practice for the benefit of others.
"For the purpose of indicating that meaning" means for the purpose of indicating the sense of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*). This is a designation of the accusative case.
It is formed just as in the expression “he recites for a month. “The ancients” refers to the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathās.

“A distinction consisting merely of verbal expression” means a difference by way of mere wording; by this, he shows that the analysis of case-endings (*vibhatti*) and gender (*liṅga*) has been made in the Suttas and the Vinaya.
“Best” (*seṭṭha*): the word expressing “best” is called “best” because it is associated with the quality of being best; likewise...

“Also here [in the word] ‘supreme’ (uttama). “Worthy of reverence” (gāravayutta) means connected with a state of respect due to being endowed with weighty qualities, or connected with reverence because it is worthy of being held in high esteem.
The meaning is that this has already been stated, and need not be repeated here, because this commentary is but a portion of the *Visuddhimagga*.

Another method: He is the Blessed One (bhagavā) because he possesses fortune (bhāga); he is the Blessed One because he has nourished (bhatava); he is the Blessed One because he desires fortune (bhāge vani); he is the Blessed One because he desires excellence (bhage vani); he is the Blessed One because he has overcome (bhattava); he is the Blessed One because he vomits out excellence (bhage vamī); he is the Blessed One because he vomits out fortune (bhāge vamī).
“Possessor of fortune, nourisher, desirer of fortune, And desirer of excellence, possessor of what is overcome;
Vomiter of excellence as well as fortune— Thus the Victor is called the Blessed One.”

In this context, how is he "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One)? Those aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue and so forth, which are portions of qualities and divisions of qualities, exist and are found in the Tathāgata, being unique and unsurpassed.
For his virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation, moral shame, moral dread, faith, energy, mindfulness, and clear comprehension [are all thus].
Purification of virtue, purification of view, serenity, insight, the three roots of the wholesome, the three types of good conduct, the three right thoughts,
the three blameless perceptions, the three elements, the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the four noble paths, the four noble fruits, the four [foundations of mindfulness]...
the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*); the knowledges that delimit the four modes of birth; the four noble lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*); the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*);
the five factors of striving (*padhāniyaṅga*); right concentration with five factors; right concentration with five knowledges;

the five faculties (*indriya*); the five powers (*bala*); the five elements leading to escape (*nissāraṇīyā dhātu*); the five knowledges of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*); and the five factors that ripen liberation.
Perception; the six bases for recollection; the six respects; the six elements leading to emancipation;
the six constant abidings; the six unsurpassed states; the six perceptions conducive to penetration; the six direct knowledges; the six unique knowledges; the seven qualities that prevent decline;
the seven noble qualities; the seven noble treasures; the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven...

The qualities of true persons; the seven bases for the wearing away [of defilements]; the seven perceptions; the teaching on the seven types of persons worthy of offerings; the teaching on the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed;
the teaching on the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom; the eight forms of rightness; the transcendence of the eight worldly conditions;
the eight bases for exertion; the teaching on the eight inopportune moments; the eight thoughts of a great person; and the teaching on the eight bases of mastery.
The eight liberations; the nine states rooted in wise attention; the nine factors of exertion for purification;

the teaching on the nine abodes of beings; the nine ways of removing resentment; the nine perceptions; the ninefold diversities; the nine successive dwellings; the ten qualities that make one a protector;
the ten kasiṇa bases; the ten courses of wholesome action; and the ten rightnesses.
The ten abodes of the noble ones, the ten qualities of one beyond training, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the eleven benefits of loving-kindness,
the twelve modes of the Wheel of Dhamma, the thirteen ascetic qualities, the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha,
the fifteen qualities that ripen liberation, the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing, the sixteen things that burn away the future, and the eighteen qualities of a Buddha.
There are nineteen knowledges of review, forty-four bases of knowledge, fifty knowledges of arising and passing away,
more than fifty wholesome states, seventy-seven bases of knowledge, the Great Vajira-knowledge that traverses meditative attainments numbering twenty-four trillion,
the infinite modes of knowledge for the analytical investigation and review of the *Paṭṭhāna*, and likewise throughout infinite world-systems.

Furthermore, there exist and are found infinite and immeasurable varieties of such qualities—unique, unsurpassed portions and categories of virtue—as the knowledge that discerns the inclinations and so forth of infinite beings.
Therefore, because he possesses these aforementioned portions of virtue, he should be called "Bhāgavā"; however, by shortening the vowel *ā* to *a*, he is called "Bhagavā."
Thus, first of all, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he possesses fortune (*bhāga*). As it is said:
"Because all the portions of qualities (*guṇa-bhāgā*), beginning with virtue (*sīla*), exist without exception in the Sugata, therefore he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*)."
"How does one become a bhante? the Blessed One asked.

"It is by fulfilling the ten perfections—generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—which must be brought to completion by Great Beings (mahābodhisatta) who have made the great aspiration for perfect enlightenment after having combined the eight qualities beginning with human birth, and who have exerted themselves for the welfare of the entire world."
The thirtyfold perfections (*pāramī*)—consisting of the ten perfections, the ten secondary perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*);
the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*) beginning with giving; the four foundations (*adhiṭṭhāna*) beginning with truth;

the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*)—namely, the renunciation of limbs, life, kingdom, sons, and wife; the prior application (*pubbayoga*), the prior conduct (*pubbacariyā*), and the proclamation of the Dhamma.
The practice for the benefit of relatives, the practice for the benefit of the world, the practice of wisdom, and so forth— in brief,
all the accumulations of merit and knowledge that constitute the qualities making one a Buddha— from the time of the Great Resolve onwards, for four incalculable eons plus a hundred thousand aeons,
these [qualities] do not become conducive to decline, conducive to defilement, or conducive to stagnation; rather, they...

They become progressively more distinguished; thus, because he has "honored" (*bhata*)—meaning he has fully and continuously honored them without exception—one should say "one who has honored" (*bhata-vā*).
However, by way of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), the letter *ta* is changed to *ga*, and thus he is called "Bhagavā.
Alternatively, "bhata-vā" means that those very qualities which constitute the factors of Buddhahood, as previously described, have been "carried" (*bhari*) in the manner already stated.
The meaning is: "you have accumulated" (*sambhari*), "you have fulfilled" (*paripūresi*). Thus, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he has "honored" (*bhatavā*).
"The Protector has honored all the requisites for perfect enlightenment, beginning with the perfection of giving; therefore, too, he is considered the Blessed One."

How is it that the Blessed One is called "Bhāge vanī" (the one who has chosen his portion)? Those portions of meditative attainments which are utilized daily, numbering twenty-four hundred thousand million, he chose, cultivated, frequented, and practiced extensively for all time—without exception—for the sake of the welfare of the world and for the sake of his own dwelling in happiness in this very life;
thus, because he chose his portion, the Blessed One is called "Bhāge vanī. Alternatively, among the things to be directly known, such as the wholesome states and so forth...
And among the aggregates and so forth, there are those fourfold portions of clear realization categorized briefly as "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) and so on;
but in detail, there are numerous portions to be fully understood, such as: "The eye is to be fully understood, the ear... [and so on]... aging-and-death is to be fully understood";
and [numerous portions] to be abandoned, such as: "The origin of the eye is to be abandoned... [and so on]... the origin of aging-and-death is to be abandoned."

The categories of phenomena to be abandoned (*pahātabba-bhāga*); the categories to be realized (*sacchikātabba-bhāga*), such as "the cessation of the eye... [and so on]... the cessation of aging-and-death is to be realized";

and the various types of categories to be developed (*bhāvetabba-bhāga*), such as "the path leading to the cessation of the eye" and "the four foundations of mindfulness"—he frequented (*vane*), that is, he cultivated, all of these according to their respective spheres of activity and modes of cultivation.
He practiced by means of these. Thus, he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because he has sought (*vanī*) these portions. Alternatively, with great compassion he sought (*vani*) and aspired:

"How might I establish these aggregates of Dhamma—these portions and segments of qualities such as virtue and the rest, which are shared with disciples—within the mental continuums of those to be trained?
And that aspiration of his brought about the fruit exactly as intended.
"Thus he has partaken of the portion," said the Blessed One.
"Because the Tathāgata partook of and aspired for the portion of the qualities of the attainments regarding what is to be known,
for the welfare of beings, he is therefore called 'Bhagavā'."

In what sense is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) "one who possesses fortune" (*bhage vanī*)? Briefly stated, those things which are shared out according to one's resources by those who have performed merit and are endowed with skillful means are called "fortunes" (*bhagā*);

these are mundane and supramundane attainments. Regarding those, first, in the mundane sphere, while the Tathāgata was still a bodhisatta prior to his full enlightenment, he "possessed" (*vani*), "shared," and "cultivated" (*sevi*) those [attainments] that had reached the highest excellence, and established himself therein without remainder.

While possessing the qualities that produce a Buddha, he brought the Buddha-qualities to full maturity; and having become a Buddha, he acquired, cultivated, practiced, and frequented those blameless, unsurpassed,

and extraordinary supramundane states— both in terms of worldly sovereignty, such as regional kingship, universal monarchship, and the attainment of divine royalty, and in terms of superhuman states, such as the meditations (*jhāna*),

liberations (*vimokkha*), concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*), the development of the path (*magga-bhāvanā*), and the realization of the fruits (*phala-sacchikiriyā*).

And [the word *bhaga*] has many meanings not shared by others: fortune (*bhaga*), acquisition (*vani*), sharing (*bhaji*), and service (*sevi*). Thus, because he acquired fortune, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*).
“Whatever prosperities there are in the world, and those that transcend the world in their variety— The Fully Awakened One acquired them all;
therefore, too, he is considered the Blessed One.”
"How is it that the Blessed One is 'possessed of devotion' (*bhattavā*)? [It is because] he has many devotees who are firm in their devotion; thus he is "possessed of devotion.

For the Tathāgata is the supreme among all beings by virtue of his possession of immeasurable and incomparable excellences of power and qualities, such as great compassion and omniscience; and he is devoted to the accomplishment of the welfare and happiness of others without exception, preceded by the removal of all that is harmful.
By virtue of his unsurpassed perfection of practice, his state of being of ultimate benefit to the world including its devas and humans,
and his physical body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor characteristics, the fathom-wide radiance, and other unique qualities not shared by others;

and by means of the vast and utterly pure [glory] consisting of the epithets such as "Thus indeed is the Blessed One," which proceed according to the actual qualities he has attained and pervade the three worlds.
Because he is endowed with the sound of "thuti" (praise), because he is well-established in such qualities as fewness of wishes and contentment which have reached the highest perfection,

and because he possesses extraordinary and distinguished qualities such as the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence, he is one who has measure in form and confidence in form, who has measure in voice and confidence in voice,
who has measure in austerity and confidence in austerity, and who has measure in the Dhamma and confidence in the Dhamma.
Thus, because it is beautiful on all sides by virtue of its quality of inspiring confidence within this world-system consisting of four continents,
it is the supreme object of love and devotion for immeasurable beings, including gods and humans, as it serves as a locus for their respect, esteem, and reverence.
Those who are established in his instruction and endowed with verified confidence (aveccappasāda) become unshakable by anyone.
This serene confidence and devotion cannot be overcome by a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, or Brahmā.
For even when they must sacrifice their own lives, they do not abandon that confidence therein, owing to the firmness of their devotion to his command.
Therefore it was said:
“He who is grateful and mindful of what has been done, wise, a good friend, and firm in devotion.
“Just as, monks, the great ocean is stable in nature and does not overstep its shore, even so, monks,”
“Whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, that my disciples do not transgress even for the sake of their lives.
Thus, [the Blessed One] is called *bhattavā* (one who possesses devotion) according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), having elided one *ta*-sound and changed the other to a *ga*-sound.
“For he who is endowed with preeminent virtues, seeking the welfare of the world...”
“Because many have partaken [of his teaching], the Blessed One is therefore called ‘Bhagavā’.

How does he vomit forth fortune (*bhaga*)? Because even while he was a Bodhisatta, throughout immeasurable births, while fulfilling the perfections (*pāramī*), the Tathāgata vomited forth—that is, he ejected—fortune, sovereignty, and glory, which are designated as *bhaga*, just as one ejects a lump of spittle.
Just as he had previously cast them aside without regard, even in his final existence, he disregarded as if they were mere blades of grass the sovereignty over the four continents—
which was like the lordship of the deva-world, accompanied by the glory of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), supported by the excellence of a universal monarch,
radiant with the seven treasures, and endowed with fame— and having renounced it without longing, he went forth and attained supreme perfect enlightenment; therefore...

He vomited up these fortunes, beginning with beauty, thus he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*). Alternatively, "fortunes" (*bhagā*) refers to the constellations; they proceed and move together with them, hence they are called fortunes.
Furthermore, the splendors that depend upon the specific features of the receptacle world—such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and the Himavat mountains—possess a state that endures for an eon;
these too the Blessed One vomited up by transcending the abodes of beings dwelling therein, through the abandonment of desire and lust attached to them.
"He has abandoned" (*pajahī*). Thus, because he vomited out the "fortunes" (*bhaga*), he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*).
"Because the Sugata, the Blessed One, abandoned the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, fame, sovereignty, happiness, and the mind of the world, for that reason he is the Blessed One."
In what sense does the Blessed One vomit out the portions? "Portions" refers to the constituent parts of phenomena that possess such portions;
these are manifold, categorized by way of aggregates, bases, and elements, and within those, further by way of form and feeling, earth and so forth, and the past and so forth.
And the Blessed One, having utterly severed all conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), all fetters (*yoga*), all ties (*gantha*), and all bonds (*saṃyojana*), [vomits them out].
Attaining the deathless element, he vomited it up; being without regard, he discarded it and did not vomit it back again.
For thus he [discarded] the earth, water, fire, and air everywhere; the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; eye-consciousness... pe... mind-consciousness.
Eye-contact... [and so on] ...mind-contact; feeling born of eye-contact...
[and so on] ...feeling born of mind-contact; perception born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...perception born of mind-contact;
volition born of eye-contact... [and so on] ...volition born of mind-contact; craving for forms... [and so on] ...craving for mental phenomena; thought concerning forms... [and so on].

By means of the classification of phenomena according to their sequence—starting with "thought of mental objects" (*dhammavitakka*), "sustained thought on forms" (*rūpavicāra*), and so forth, up to "sustained thought on mental objects" (*dhammavicāra*)—he vomited up and disgorged all categories of phenomena without exception, casting them away through a relinquishment free from attachment. For it has been said:
"That which, Ānanda, was abandoned, vomited up, released, relinquished, and cast off—that the Tathāgata [does not regard again]..."
"He will turn back"—this possibility does not exist. Thus, he vomits out [the world] in its parts; therefore he is the Blessed One (*bhagavā*).

Alternatively, "he vomits out in its parts" means that through the gateway of noble path-knowledge, he vomited out, ejected, renounced without regard for, and abandoned all phenomena—both wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, dark and bright—which are in mutual opposition. And he [established others] in suchness.
He taught the Dhamma. And this has been said: "Bhikkhus, even states that are Dhamma must be abandoned, how much more so those that are not Dhamma.
Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping," and so forth.
Thus, too, he vomited out (vamati) the parts [of defilements], and so he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā).
“Since the Great Seer has vomited out the dark and bright portions of phenomena— such as the aggregates, bases,
and elements— for that reason too he is considered the Blessed One.
Thus it was said.
“He has enjoyed his portion, he has enjoyed his fortune, he has conquered in battle;
he vomits forth his fortune as well as his portion—thus the Conqueror, the Blessed One.
He makes the body of the Dhamma manifest: “Ānanda, that Dhamma and Vinaya which have been taught by me to you...”
It is stated thus because there exists a figurative designation of the Dhamma as the Teacher, based on the words: “That which has been laid down by me is your teacher after my passing away.
His body is like a diamond-mass (*vajirasaṅghāta*) because his physical frame is indivisible by others; for no one is able to cause an obstacle to the Blessed One’s material body (*rūpakāya*).
He demonstrates the excellence of his teaching (*desanāsampatti*) for the entirety of what is about to be explained...
It indicates the excellence of the discourse through the demonstrative particle "thus" (evaṃ).

It demonstrates the excellence of the disciple by showing that what was heard was heard by me, a great disciple established by the Blessed One as foremost in five respects because of my attainment of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā);
and furthermore, it was heard by me personally, not heard secondhand, nor brought down through tradition—this is how it illuminates this meaning. It demonstrates the excellence of the time.
Because the word *samaya* (time), when used in conjunction with the word *bhagavā* (the Blessed One), illuminates the fact that [this time] is adorned by the arising of a Buddha.
For the excellence of time has the arising of a Buddha as its supreme limit. Therefore, it is said:
"In this Kali age, the dregs of an eon, the arising of a Buddha—oh, what a great marvel!"
"A lotus arisen in the midst of a fire, with its nectar fully gathered.

By "the Blessed One," he indicates the excellence of the teacher, because it reveals his state as the supreme being distinguished by special qualities and because it is a designation used out of profound reverence.
"Without distinction" means not by way of a specific distinction, but by way of the commonality of the state of abiding (*vihāra*). "In postures... [etc. ...in dwellings" (*vihāresu*).

Regarding the four dwellings—the dwelling in the postures (*iriyāpathavihāra*), the divine dwelling (*dibbavihāra*), the sublime dwelling (*brahmavihāra*), and the noble dwelling (*ariyavihāra*)—the term "manifestation of possession" (*samaṅgīparidīpana*) means the manifestation of the state of being possessed. "This" refers to the word "dwells" (*viharati*). For it is used in such passages as:
"Here, a certain person dwells in association with householders, sharing their joys and sorrows," and so forth, in reference to the dwelling in the postures.

It has arrived. Regarding the passage: “Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... attains and dwells in the first jhāna,” this refers here to the divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*).
Regarding passages such as: “He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,” this refers to the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
“Aggivessana, at the conclusion of that very discourse, right there... [the text continues].
In such passages as, “Upon that same former sign of concentration, I settle the mind within myself, I compose it, I unify it, I concentrate it;
by means of which I indeed dwell throughout the entire life-span,” this refers to the noble abidings (*ariyavihāra*).

Therein, *iriyā* means moving about or proceeding, which is bodily exertion. Because standing and so forth are the means for the occurrence of that [exertion], they are called “postures” (*iriyāpatha*).
For one who possesses a posture (*ṭhānasamaṅgī*) might perform some action with the body, such as walking and so forth;
or it is that by which the personal existence (*attabhāva*) moves or proceeds, thus it is "posturing" (*iriyā*), which is bodily activity.

Because it is the means for the occurrence of that [activity], it is both "posturing" and a "path" (*patho*); hence, "posture" (*iriyāpatho*), namely standing and so forth. And that, in its actual sense, occurs in the manner of ceasing motion and so on.
It is simply the continuity of the fourfold stream of existence. "Abiding" (*vihāra*) means either the act of abiding, or that by which one abides;
thus, it is the postures themselves that constitute "abiding," hence "posture-abiding" (*iriyāpathavihāra*). That which exists in the celestial realm (*divi*) is "celestial" (*dibba*);

the meaning is that it exists in the divine worlds such as those of the *Brahmapārisajja* gods due to frequent occurrence there. Alternatively, it is "celestial" because it conduces to that celestial power, by way of the exertion for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Or, because it leads to a great destination, it is divine (*dibba*); and since it is both divine and an abiding (*vihāra*), it is a "divine abiding" (*dibbavihāra*):

the four meditative attainments of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). The immaterial-sphere attainments (*āruppasamāpatti*) are also included herein. The abidings of the Brahmas, or the abidings that are Brahmas, are the "divine abidings" (*brahmavihāra*): the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*).
The abidings of the Noble Ones, or the abidings that are Noble Ones, are the "Noble abidings" (*ariyavihāra*): the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
For it was said, "Indeed, [the body] obstructs one posture," and so forth;

even though the Blessed One is able to maintain his physical existence for a very long time by means of even a single posture, this was nevertheless stated to show that such is the inherent nature of a body sustained by clinging (*upādinnaka*).
Or rather, because the Blessed One, wherever he dwelt, taught the Dhamma to those to be trained (*vineyya*), [he spoke thus].

Because he dwells passing his time through various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he "brings" (*harati*)—that is, conveys, leads toward, and produces—the manifold welfare and happiness of beings and of himself;
therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "he brings manifold [benefit].
He "conquers" (*jināti*) his adversaries, thus he is *Jeta*. For the word *jeta*, like the word *sota* (ear), exists as a term denoting the agent (*kattusādhana*).
He is called Jeta because he was born at a time when the king had conquered his enemies;

for the prince was called Jeta because the king attributed his own victory to him, saying, "He has conquered," thus he is Jeta. Alternatively, the name Jeta was given to him out of a desire for auspiciousness;
therefore, it should be understood that the word "Jeta" is used in the sense of "one who is to be conquered" (jeyya). Of that Prince Jeta—at the forest, etc. from the beginning.
In order to show that from the very beginning it was his property, the words "That indeed" (*taṃ hi*) and so forth were spoken.
Because he possessed all desirable things, because he was free from the stain of stinginess, and because he was endowed with qualities such as compassion, he always provided alms for the destitute;
thus, he is Anāthapiṇḍika—one who has alms for the destitute—and [the text refers to] him, Anāthapiṇḍika. If it is Jetavana, how...
Regarding the phrase "Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery," he said "by Anāthapiṇḍika" and so forth.
It is called an *ārāma* because those who have gone forth find delight (*āramanti*) therein due to its perfection in the five factors of a lodging; it is in that monastery.
Even though that plot of land was purchased by the Great Merchant with a layer of crores, the trees were not sold by Jetā; therefore, it is to be designated as "Jetavana."
They say he "obtained" it. Or rather, both terms are used there for the purpose of praising the excellence of the relinquishment by both parties;
for even the wealth obtained by Jeta through the sale of the ground was applied there toward the construction of the gatehouse.
Because the grounds of Sāvatthī and Jetavana were distinct, it is said: "Indeed, it is not possible [to build] in both places with one..."
"To dwell in harmony.
"Unfamiliar" means not well-known by such names as Sakka or Suyāma.

Although the word *aññatara* (one or another) is seen even among those who are well-known, it is stated, "We recognize him," and so forth, to show that it refers to anyone belonging to that same class. *Ahuṇā* means "just now. This is a term used in a general sense.

Having included the divine state within [the category of "deity"]. A deity itself is a "devatā," because it can be applied even to a male. For this very reason, he said, "But in this sense," and so forth.
Now, is it not the case that beings of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) lack the male faculty (purisindriya), by virtue of which they might be called "men"?
Even though the male faculty is absent, they are nonetheless designated as "male persons" (purisapuggala) on account of their male physical form and male appearance.
They are so called because of their nature as the types of men.
*Abhikkanta* means "transcended" (*atikkanta*), which has the sense of "gone beyond"; thus he said, "it is seen in the sense of destruction.

For it is for this very reason that it is stated later: "The first watch has passed away" (*nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo*). *Abhikkantatara* means "exceedingly more desirable" (*ativiya kantataro*). And such [a state] is beautiful.
"He is called Bhaddaka" means "he is seen as beautiful. "Ko? means among the gods, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so forth, who is which?
"Me" means mine. "Pādāni" means the feet. "Iddhiyā" means by means of such supernatural power (*iddhi*) as this.
"Yasasā" means by means of such a retinue and following. "Jalanti" means shining brightly. "Abhikkantena" means exceedingly.
"With lovely, desirable, and beautiful appearance" means with the color of the skin, the radiance of the body's complexion.
"Illuminating all directions" means shining upon all quarters, making them a single mass of light and a single expanse of brightness, like the moon and like the sun;
such is the meaning of the verse. "Beautiful" means of sublime form, of perfected form.
The phrase "of skin" (*chaviya*) is stated with the intention that the "skin resembling gold" (*kañcanasannibhattaca*) is already included by the mention of "golden-colored" (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇa*).
However, others hold that it is the color-element (*vaṇṇadhātu*) residing within the skin itself that is included here by the mention of "color" (*vaṇṇa*) in the expression "golden-colored.

"Color" (*vaṇṇa*) means praise, proclamation, or eulogy; it is so called because it is praised. Alternatively, it is so called because it is "colored" (*vaṇṇīyati*), meaning it is defined as distinct from other things.
The section on color (*vaṇṇa*) and the section on lineage (*kula*). It is called "color" (*vaṇṇa*) because by means of it the fruit is described—that is, manifested according to its true nature;

thus, it is a cause. It is called "color" because it is the description—the configuration—by way of being long, short, and so forth; thus, it is shape. It is called "color" because it is described—that is, measured—by way of smallness, greatness, and so forth;
thus, it is dimension. It is called "color" because, when undergoing transformation, it manifests the state that has entered the heart.

"Color" (*vaṇṇa*) refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). In this way, one should understand the application of the word "color" to various meanings according to their respective causes for its occurrence.
"Having manifested psychic power" means having fashioned divine psychic potency by emitting radiance from one's clothes, ornaments, body, and so forth.
Beings belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) are able to come even without [such] deliberate preparation because of the grossness of their physical form.
For they subsist on physical nutriment (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra). Those belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) are unable [to do so] because their form is subtler than that.
Therefore he said, "Of them," and so forth. Therein, "extremely subtle" refers to the primary rebirth-linking form (mūla-paṭisandhi-rūpa).
By this it is meant that there is no performance of postures (iriyāpatha-kappana); thus, even in the Brahma-world, the Brahmas mostly exist by means of created form (nimmita-rūpa) alone.
This shows that they "occur. For the other [type of] matter is exceedingly subtle; it exists merely as the support and basis for the arising of consciousness, remaining possessed of shape.
"Entirety" means completeness. "Abundance" means being in great measure. "Unmixedness" means the absence of confusion with what is of a different nature.
For what is intended there is non-intermixture with pleasure. Non-excess, being beyond that, is the absence of distinction.
"Entirely" (*kevalakappaṃ*) means having made it entirely firm. "For the sake of schism in the Saṅgha" means for the sake of dispute in the Saṅgha, for the production of contention.
"Entire" (*kevalaṃ*) refers to Nibbāna because of its seclusion from all conditioned things; one who possesses that is a "possessor of the entire" (*kevalī*), one who has realized cessation.
One whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). Therefore he said: "The meaning is dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
Now, this word *kappa*, whether with a prefix or without a prefix, is intended to show the mere word *kappa* as it occurs in the compound *okappaniya*;
otherwise, the word *kappa* would be entirely unindicated. [The phrase] "by means of the ascetic-standards" (*samaṇakappehi*)...
By means of the conventional designations established by the Vinaya for recluses. "Always" (*niccakappa*) means at all times. "Designation" (*paññatti*) is a name.
For that venerable one, this is indeed the name, namely, "Kappa. "One whose hair and beard are trimmed" (*kappita-kesa-massu*) means one whose hair and beard have been cut with a razor.
"The two-finger-breadth allowance" (*dvaṅgula-kappa*) refers to the permitted extent of two finger-breadths once the time of midday has passed. "Pretext" (*lesa*) means a reason or ground.
Even for a radiance capable of pervading without remainder, there might be a partial pervasion due to some cause;
however, in order to show that this [radiance] pervades entirely, the word *kappa* is taken in the sense of "all around" (*samanta*), thus he said: "without remainder, all around.
*Kevalakappaṃ* means slightly incomplete, or simply "entirely. Nothing at all remained unpervaded by the Blessed One’s radiance.
For the deities illuminate that place with their own radiance. Indeed, the radiance of the Blessed One is not overcome by the radiance of anything else;
rather, it remains surpassing even the radiance of the sun and other luminaries.
Or, as for the phrase "by which reason," this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). For the cause of an action is indeed the purpose of the cause; it is not...

The meaning of "action" (*kiriyattha*) is like that of an instrument (*karaṇa*); therefore, since the action of approaching here is for the purpose of attaining various specific qualities, that instrumental expression is properly used in the sense of a cause (*hetuattha*), as in the cases of "he dwells by means of food" or "he dwells by means of knowledge," rather than in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇattha*), because [the latter] would be inappropriate.

Thus it was said: "or by which reason," and so forth. This is because the Blessed One possesses the fruit of the True Dhamma, which is ever-present, unsurpassed, sweet, vast, and most excellent in flavor.
The Blessed One is compared to a great tree that constantly bears sweet fruit.

For by the very act of taking [the fruit] with the intention of enjoying its sweet fruit, the state of having sweet fruit is attributed to the Greatly Compassionate One. "He approached" (*upasaṅkami*) means he had approached (*upasaṅkantā*).
For one who goes to some place out of a desire to reach it approaches by passing over various points; thus, he is to be called "one who has approached."
He obtains it. Therefore he said, "It is stated as 'gone' (gata)," meaning "approached" (upagata).

He said, "The illumination of the conclusion of the act of approaching," because "having approached" (upasaṅkamitvā) is a designation for the prior action. "From there" means from that place which was reached when it was said, "he approached."
Because sitting is, in the sense of turning back from walking, common to standing, it is said:
"Standing to one side by virtue of skill in sitting. For even those who are seated are indeed said to have turned back from walking, since they must stand before sitting;
thus, the aforementioned positions and so forth are also included within "sitting. By way of rejecting what is too far or too near, [one stands] neither too far nor too near.
The name has been mentioned. That, however, should be understood—at the very least—as the touching together of the outstretched hands of both.
"Having extended the neck" means having extended it by way of turning the neck.
Granted, "how" (*kathaṃ*) is a question regarding manner; here, the manner of crossing over is what is asked. And that manner of crossing over, in terms of its meaning, is as follows:

He said, "It is indeed the cause," [asking], "In what way? This is a question regarding the cause. He is manifest through the appearance of many wonders at the time of his full enlightenment, such as the great earthquake and so forth.
He is *mārisa* in the sense of being worthy of respect (*marisana*), and in the sense of overcoming (*abhibhavana*) evils and misfortunes such as disease;
thus he is free from suffering. Therefore it is said, "He is without suffering. Furthermore, this is a figurative expression used as a term of endearment even when addressing one on the side of hell.
As in the expression “beloved of the gods. For this very reason, he said, “If it were so,” and so forth.

Suppose a stake, having been driven in from the top down to the region of the heart, were to pierce through; and another stake, having been driven in from the sole of the foot up to the heart, were to pierce through and meet the first stake at the region of the heart—at that very moment when those two stakes meet.
You should understand this as being like the time when a word has transcended its original restricted application.

When a word that originally functioned with reference to a specific cause is applied to something that lacks that cause, it is called *ruḷhī* (conventional usage). This is like the word "cow" (*go*) when applied to a ball of rice that possesses the characteristics of being a gift and so forth, even though it lacks the act of walking.

Regarding the phrase "crossing the floods" (*oghātaraṇa*): in order to show, both by way of enumeration and by their specific nature, those floods whose crossing was asked about, the words beginning with "four" were spoken.
Why, however, are only four floods mentioned here, and why are they specifically the flood of sensual desire (*kāma*) and so forth?
This is not to be questioned, because the Blessed One—who knows the specific characteristics of the intrinsic nature and function of all phenomena—has [disclosed] the entirety of the knowable.
Having fully awakened to things as they truly are, [he realized]: "Only this many floods have been taught, and these very ones have been taught.

They are called *oghā* (floods) because they flood and cause one to sink in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). They flood by striking [beings] from below and driving them along; thus, they are said to drive beings downward.
This meaning will be explained later in the Commentary itself with the words, "And all this," etc. In the sense of being desired...
“Kāma” means sensual pleasure; and because it is a flood (ogha) in the sense already stated, it is called the “flood of sensual pleasures” (kāmogha).

To show that the “flood of existence” (bhavogha) is craving for existence (bhavarāga), it is said: “It is desire and lust for the realms of form and formlessness, and attachment to meditative absorption (jhāna-nikanti).
However, in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī* and other works, it is stated: “And it is lust accompanied by the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi). Of these, the first...

Attachment to rebirth-existences (*upapattibhava*) is the first; the second is attachment to kamma-existence (*kammabhava*), because there is no view-approach (*diṭṭhigata*) that is not already included within the sixty-two views.

Since it has been stated that "the sixty-two views constitute the flood of views," and since all that is to be known is subsumed within the Four Noble Truths, he said that "ignorance regarding the Four Truths constitutes the flood of ignorance."
Now, in order to show the source of origin for those evil states termed "floods" (ogha), the passage beginning with “therein” (tattha) was spoken;

as for their sphere of occurrence, the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa) and so forth have already been shown. Regarding the statement, “Lust and desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure is the flood of sensuality” (kāmogha), it would be logical that, setting aside the flood of existence (bhavogha), all greed constitutes the flood of sensuality.
[This applies to] that which is accompanied by the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi).

In the Commentaries, lust is called the "flood of existence" (*bhava-ogha*) because it is associated with the view of existence; however, in the Canon, it is stated that the flood of existence arises only in those states dissociated from views.
For this very reason, it is said: "The flood of existence arises in the four types of consciousness-moments accompanied by greed and dissociated from views.

Therefore, it would be logical for greed accompanied by views to also be included in the "flood of sense-desire" (*kāma-ogha*), for [it is a cause] of the sufferings pertaining both to the present life and to future lives.
The taints (āsava) such as sensual desire, which function as causes, are also stated to be twofold; likewise, the floods (ogha) are simply the taints themselves.

In the exposition of the sensual-taint, the phrase "in sensual pleasures" (kāmesu) means "in the objective sensual pleasures belonging to the three planes, which serve as the objects (ārammaṇa) for sensual lust, lust for views, and so forth"—this meaning is possible.
For not all craving (taṇhā) arising therein receives the name "sensual desire" (kāmacchanda) and the rest.

If, however, it is argued that because lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is called the "flood of sensuality" (kāmogha), the status of being the flood of sensuality must be denied to the lust for the celestial palaces of the Brahmās and so forth,
as well as to the lust for views (diṭṭhirāga)— then, in that case, there would have to exist a greed that is distinct from both the flood of sensuality and the flood of existence (bhavogha).
When such [greed] arises in relation to states dissociated from the sphere of views, then [the mind] is associated with it.

Regarding the statement "the flood of ignorance is dissociated from the floods," one might argue that for this [ignorance] as well—just as in the case of [states] associated with displeasure, doubt, or restlessness—it should be said that it is dissociated from the floods.

For it could be said: "In the four types of consciousness-arising accompanied by greed and dissociated from the [wrong] views, the delusion that has arisen may be associated with the floods, or it may be dissociated from the floods. [The answer is: "In the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed, the flood of sense-desire..."

Because of the statements, "It arises among the arising of states of consciousness," and "Dependent on the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha) are the flood of views (diṭṭhogha) and the flood of ignorance (avijjogha)," it cannot be said that the flood of sensual desire is not accompanied by views.
