Likewise, in this context, it is merely stated that "the flood of existence (bhavogha) consists of desire and lust for the fine-material and immaterial realms, as well as attachment to meditative absorption (jhānanikanti)"; it is not stated that "lust accompanied by the eternalist view."
"In the sense of going downwards" means in the sense of proceeding toward the lower realms.

Here, it is stated "and the higher existence," etc., to show that downward proceeding is not only by way of leading to the states of loss (*apāya*), but also by way of being obstructed from crossing over the ocean of *saṃsāra*.

Granted, Nibbāna is locationless because it is formless (*arūpin*), yet its inclusion as "higher" is not by way of a physical place, but because it has escaped from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*).
However, because it deserves to be called "above all existence" (*sabbassapi bhavassa upari*), it is stated: "Nibbāna is the higher existence" (*uparibhavaṃ nibbānaṃ*).
In such passages as "the great flood of water" (*mahāudakogho*), the word *ogha* has the sense of a "heap" (*rāsa*); thus it is said: "This is a great heap of defilements.
This applies to the others as well—that is, to the flood of existence (*bhavogha*) and so forth.
"Not standing" (*appatiṭṭhahanto*) means not remaining due to the influence of defilements and so forth; the meaning is "not sinking.

"Not exerting" (*anāyūhanto*) means not exerting oneself through the influence of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) and so on, but rather being swept away by over-exerting oneself and thus transgressing the Middle Way. Therefore he said, "not striving" (*avāyamanto*);
the intention is that one does not strive by way of wrong effort (*micchāvāyāma*). "Hidden" (*gūḷha*) means restrained (*saṃvuta*). "Concealed" (*paṭicchanna*)...

This is a synonym for that very [term]. It is "concealed" (*saṃvutta*) in the sense of meaning, and "hidden" (*paṭicchanna*) in the sense of sound, being unmanifest in places such as an inner island where one must remain. "Exerting themselves" means striving with their hands and feet.
This is the group of meanings, or this is the answer.
Now, in order to show the underlying intention with which the Blessed One posed the question by making it thus obscure, he said, "But what [is the meaning]? and so forth.
"By way of censure" means by way of censure as a means for disciplining those who are to be trained. Therefore he said, "Those who imagine themselves to be wise," and so forth.
"Having sifted again and again" means having winnowed repeatedly.
That son of the gods was one whose pride had been humbled, for he did not understand the meaning of what had been stated.

The word *yathā* (as) is an indefinite term that is specified by a restrictive definition; and since it is connected with the interrogative phrase *kathaṃ* (how), he spoke thus—“Tell me as I understand it”—in order to show the meaning of both.
*Yadāssu ahaṃ*: here *assu* is the particle *asu*, which is merely an indeclinable (*nipātamatta*), as in expressions such as *yadidaṃ kathaṃ sū*.
*Sabbapadesu*: in all three phrases, namely in *tadāssu saṃsīdāmī* and so forth. *Ataranto*: not making an effort to cross for the purpose of surmounting the floods (*oghā*).
*Tattheva*: right there, within those very floods that cause one to sink. *Osīdāmī*: I am sinking; I am being submerged by the floods.
"I am overwhelmed" means I am submerged by the floods. "I am being swept away" means I am carried off by the floods. "Unable to stand, sinking down" means I am unable to remain steady;
"I am drifting away" means I pass beyond what is useful, that is, I fail in right practice through lack of aspiration—this is the meaning.
"In steadiness and effort" means seeing the fault in both steadying oneself and in the exertion, according to the analysis to be explained later.
Having seen the danger in establishing and accumulating—which consists of sinking and pushing up, and acts as an obstruction to crossing over.
This was spoken by the Blessed One with reference to the preliminary attention he himself had previously practiced at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
"Neither standing nor striving" means not sinking, by way of avoiding the defilements and other factors that cause establishing and accumulating.

"Not having attained final liberation. Even by that deity, that matter was penetrated because she possessed the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) and because the qualities conducive to the maturation of liberation had reached full development.
However, it was not manifest to those who understand through elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*) and the like;

rather, it was as manifest to her as it was to those who understand through brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññū*). The seven pairs, whose nature will now be described, are shown in the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*).
"By way of defilements, he stands still" means that, being overwhelmed by greed and the other defilements, he remains established in *saṃsāra*;
through his failure to practice rightly, he is said to "sink right there.

"By way of volitional formations" means that, intending there with the volition of volitional formation, he is said to "be carried away" by passing over the opportune moment suitable for right practice. In this same manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining pairs as well.

And here, "defilements rooted in the round" refers to the persistence in saṃsāra by means of those defilements, which brings about rebirth in various states of existence through respective kamma; the defilements, however, are merely the condition for that.
The first dyad is stated by way of showing this meaning: that one is "carried along in saṃsāra," repeatedly taking birth in various states of existence.
These beings wandering in *saṃsāra* are of two types: those of craving-temperament (*taṇhā-carita*) and those of view-temperament (*diṭṭhi-carita*).

The second dyad is stated by way of showing this meaning: that for those factors which have become the leaders in *saṃsāra*, there is a "stabilizing" (*saṇṭhiti*) by way of their own nature, and for others, there is an "accumulating" (*āyūhana*) by way of the conditions for their occurrence.
[This refers to] the nature of seeing gratification in things that are subject to fetters (*saṃyojaniya-dhamma*).

The third dyad is stated to show that, specifically by way of craving, there is a firm establishment [in existence], and likewise, by way of views, there is an exertion due to the misapprehension of a path to liberation where there is no path to liberation. As for the intention of the fourth dyad, it has been elucidated in the commentary itself.
For one who adheres to the view "the self is eternal" clings to immaterial lust (*arūparāga*) or to the non-liberation of the non-percipient realm (*asaññūpaga*).
Having grasped [the notion] "liberation," one clings to saṃsāra itself. Therefore it was said: "For the adherence of clinging is the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*).

Furthermore, because one who adheres to the idea that the self is annihilated and destroyed upon reaching any state of existence whatsoever—such as the realm of sense-desire (*kāma-bhava*)—and that it does not exist after death, fails to practice the right path that brings about liberation from existence.
It overreaches that. Therefore it is said: "The views of non-existence [arise] from overleaping and dogmatic adherence.
"Remaining stuck through sluggishness" means not practicing rightly due to falling into contraction by way of indolence and so forth.
"Exerting oneself through restlessness" refers to the fifth dyad, spoken of in terms of distraction due to the absence of right concentration.
Just as there is no concentration for one who has entered into sensual pleasure because the mind is defiled, so too there is none for one devoted to self-mortification because the body is defiled.

Thus, these two extremes, which cause defilement of the mind and the body respectively, are stated in the sixth dyad as the causes of sinking and being swept away due to their reliance on craving and views.
Previously, the phenomena subject to defilement were mentioned only in a limited sense.

The phrase "the sign of sinking" was shown [previously]; now, by way of showing it without exception, and because previously the conditioned phenomena (*abhisaṅkhāradhammā*) were shown in a general sense as "the sign of burning," the seventh dyad is stated here by way of showing specifically the meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations (*puññāneñjābhisaṅkhāre*) as "the sign of accumulating.
For in this way, by way of rebirth in the miserable destinies and the happy destinies...
The states of sinking and struggling have been shown by way of analysis. For this very reason, he said, "And it has also been stated," and so forth.
They lead to the lower region, that is, to an unhappy destination (*duggati*), hence they are called *adhobhāgaṅgamanīyā*, with the nasal vowel not being elided.
Likewise, they lead to the upper region, hence they are called *uparibhāgaṅgamanīyā*.
And here, when asked about crossing the flood, the Blessed One showed only the factor for its abandonment—namely, "without a foothold, without exertion"—and not the factor for its association.

This should not be viewed in that way; rather, it is a demonstration of the states opposed to it by means of the negation of both that which constitutes a foothold and that which constitutes exertion. For this is not...
The syllable *a-* is used solely in the sense of negation; however, it can also signify the opposite, as in such expressions as “unwholesome states,” “harmful,” or “non-Dhamma.

Therefore, the meaning here is: “not finding a footing and not exerting effort,” occurring by way of being the opposite of finding a footing and exerting effort, and thus acting as the cause for such an occurrence.
The particle *kho* is a fixed expression (*nipāta*) used in the sense of emphasis, as in “he indeed heard” (*assosi kho*).

...as it were. By this, he shows the categorical certainty (*ekaṃsika*) regarding the absence of a foundation. This word *kho* should also be brought over and applied to the phrase "without exertion" (*anāyūha*).
For even non-exertion is indeed categorical; its opposite is the Noble Path together with insight (*vipassanā*).
By that alone does the crossing of the flood (*oghataraṇa*) occur, and not otherwise. Thus has this teaching been presented according to the logical connection (*anusandhi*).
The deity, having penetrated the path together with insight (vipassanā), was established in the first fruit [of stream-entry]. Therefore it was said:
"This answer to the question," and so forth.

Regarding the word "after a long time" (*cirassā*), he stated "after a long period of time" (*cirassa kālassa*) to show that this is another term of identical meaning, just as in the case of "my... (*mamaṃ*).
Or, monks: here, the word *mamam* has the same meaning as the other term *mamā*.

"One who has not seen before" means one who has not seen [the Buddha]. And this state of not having seen should be understood as the failure to accomplish the duty that ought to be performed after seeing.
Otherwise, what kind of deity could there be that had not seen the Blessed One? Therefore he said, "But what of her," and so forth. Seeing...

It is appropriate to say this "on account of" (*upādāya*); that is to say, whenever one sees someone who is dear, on account of that sight, it is fitting to say—whether referring to someone never seen before or one previously seen—"Ah, we have not seen the Venerable One for a long time!
This shows that such is the conventional usage established in the world. Or, the Noble Path is called "Brahma"; of that...
He is a brahmin because of his non-speaking, his knowing, and his penetrating. "By the extinction of defilements" means:
by means of *nibbāna*, which is defined as the absolute eradication of defilements, he is extinguished—meaning that all the distress and fever of the defilements have been perfectly stilled.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "clinging, entanglement, etc.," it includes such modes as being ensnared and so forth. For this has been said:
“*Visatā* means *visattikā*; it is *visattikā* because it has spread out (*visaṭā*); it is *visattikā* because it is extensive (*visālā*); it is *visattikā* because it cleaves (*visakkati*);

it is *visattikā* because it is deceptive (*visaṃvādikā*); it is *visattikā* because it carries off poison (*visaṃ harati*); it is *visattikā* because its root is poison (*visamūlā*); it is *visattikā* because its fruit is poison (*visaphalā*);
it is *visattikā* because its enjoyment is poison (*visaparibhoga*). Or rather, that craving is *visālā* with respect to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.”
“‘Attachment’ (visattikā) means it is spread out (visatā) and extended (vitthata) among tactile objects, phenomena, clans, and groups.

In this context, “spread out” (visatā) means extended; it is said that [the craving] is “spread” (visaṭā) by way of pervading the phenomena of the three planes, such as form and so forth—this is simply the previous word with the letter *ta* changed to *ṭa*.
“Vistāra” means extensive. “Visakkati” means it moves about (parisakkati); it endures (*sahati*).
Or: for one who is lustful, even when struck with a foot by the object of that lust, endures it.
They also say that "visakkana" means shrinking back or struggling. It is "deceptive" because it grasps the impermanent and so forth as permanent and so forth.
It "carries away" (visaṃ harati) because, by seeing the advantages in sensual pleasures in various ways, it functions in diverse modes directed away from renunciation.
It withdraws and contracts the mind; "poison" (*visa*) means it carries away or bears the burden of suffering (*dukkha*).
It is "rooted in poison" (*visamūlā*) because it is the cause for kamma that produces suffering. Alternatively, it is "rooted in poison" because feeling overwhelmed by suffering is its root.

It is "fructifying as poison" (*visaphalā*) because suffering, such as form and so forth, is its fruit due to the origination of suffering. Through craving, there is only the enjoyment of suffering, such as form and the rest.
"Not from what is not nectar" refers to the consumption of poison; in all cases, the formation of the word should be understood according to its etymological derivation (*nirukti*).
However, in order to show the primary meaning here, it is stated again: "Or rather, 'wide-spread' (*visālā*)," and so forth.
In this way, the meaning of the term *visattikā* should be understood. [The phrase] "by three" means by the first and second paths. "Having crossed over" means by the third path.
"Crossed over" means by means of the fourth path.
"Gave his approval" means he gave his consent properly. Therefore it is said: "He was of one intention.
"Vanished" means he went out of sight. To show how he vanished, it is said: "The body, which was conditioned," and so forth. "With garlands" means...
It is stated with a change of gender; some read "mālāhi," which is an expression made by omitting the letter *y* that should have been "malyehi.
This, first of all, is the commentary on the hidden meaning according to the Aṭṭhakathā. Now follows the commentary on the method of the *Netti*.
Now, we shall provide a commentary on the meaning of the text according to the method of the treatise (*pakaraṇa-naya*).

Since that commentary is easy to compose and easy to understand once the origin, purpose, and the recipients of the teaching, as well as its summarized meaning, have been determined, we shall first determine the origin and other factors of this sutta’s delivery.
Among these, first, the origin: [The remainder of the text follows.]
The source of the teaching (*desanānidāna*) is twofold: common and uncommon. Therein, the common is also twofold, distinguished as internal and external.
Among these, the common internal origin is the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Lord of the World.
For it was by being impelled by that [Compassion] that the Blessed One’s mind arose for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those to be trained; with reference to which [it is said]:
It is said: “Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye,” and so forth.

Herein, it should be understood that great compassion (mahākaruṇā) is included even in its causal state, because it arises solely for the purpose of ferrying beings across the great flood of saṃsāra by means of the gift of the hand of the True Dharma’s teaching.
And just as with great compassion, so too with omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), the ten powers of knowledge (dasabalañāṇa), and the rest.
And these [factors] should be described as having their origin within the teaching itself.

For the Blessed One, knowing all knowable phenomena in their true nature—the modes in which they should be taught and the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings—set forth his diverse methods of teaching in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained, through his skill regarding what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna*) and so forth.
As for the external, common origin, it was the Great Brahmā Sahampati, accompanied by a retinue of ten thousand great Brahmās.

The Exhortation. For after that exhortation, the Master of the Dhamma, having allayed the indolence born of reflecting upon the profundity of the Dhamma, became intent upon teaching the Dhamma. Furthermore, [that profundity] is twofold, distinguished as internal and external.
Therein, the internal is that great compassion and that knowledge of teaching by which this Sutta [was taught].
Both of these should be understood as external; for this sutta was introduced by that deity’s question, since the delivery of a sutta depends upon a question.
This is indeed already contained in the Pāḷi.
Furthermore, the purpose (payojana) is twofold: common and uncommon. Among these, the common [purpose] extends in sequence up to final Nibbāna through non-clinging.
This is because the Blessed One’s teaching is characterized by liberation. For this very reason, he said: “For this purpose is discourse, for this purpose is counsel,” and so forth.
However, the vision of that deity and the attainment of the Path are not shared [with others]; both of these are merely external.
But if the purpose—consisting of the accomplishment of the power of the teaching—resides within the mental continuum of those to be trained, it is due to the fulfillment of the intended aim.
One might consider that even for the Blessed One, the Greatly Compassionate One, this [teaching] is indeed a purpose for the sake of accomplishing his intended goal;
by this method, it may also be regarded as being internal to him.
Furthermore, the failure of that deity to understand, as it truly is, the manner of crossing over the flood is the origin of this teaching.

The purpose is the understanding of that [teaching]. For it is this [understanding] that prompts the Blessed One to deliver this teaching, considering the teaching to be directed toward its accomplishment.
Indeed, whatever fruit is to be achieved through a teaching is called the "purpose" because it prompts the teacher to engage in the teaching, since that fruit is what is desired.
Likewise, there is here the posing and answering of questions for the sake of establishing deities and other disciples.
The purpose is as follows: the turning back of the wheel of saṃsāra, the setting in motion of the wheel of the True Dhamma, the refutation of eternalism and other forms of wrong conduct,

placing right speech foremost, the uprooting of the roots of unwholesomeness, the planting of the roots of wholesomeness, the closing of the doors to the states of misery, the opening of the doors to heaven and liberation,
the pacification of the outbursts of defilements, the eradication of the underlying tendencies, and the thought, "Being liberated myself, I shall liberate others."

The purposes to be understood here include: not deceiving one’s previous promise, not deceiving the aspirations of those who hold opposing views, crushing the doctrines of the heretics, and establishing the Buddha’s Dhamma;
just as the deities were leaping with doubt regarding the crossing of the flood, so too were others who had investigated the Dhamma [doubtful] toward the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Furthermore, those who do not know the practice, whose intellects are perverted by hearing, retaining, and habituating themselves to what is not the true Dhamma (asaddhamma),

and who are averse to hearing, retaining, and habituating themselves to the true Dhamma (saddhamma)— yet who seek liberation from existence— are the disciples suitable as vessels for this teaching. As for the summarized meaning (*piṇḍattha*), however,

regarding the two phrases "without a foundation" (*appatiṭṭha*) and "without exertion" (*anāyūha*), it is by way of application to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths (*catusaccakammaṭṭhāna*).
Frequent application of wise attention, conjunction with the roots of the wholesome, freedom from sinking and over-exertion, non-abandonment [of the task], dispelling of obstacles to skillful means,

distancing oneself from false attachments, purification of craving and ignorance, the means for severing the three rounds of existence, dissociation from the taints, floods, bonds, destinations, the arising of craving, and clinging,
the removal of mental rigidity, the warding off of delight, transcending social entanglements, the relinquishing of the root of dispute, and the destruction of the paths of unwholesome action.

It is the transcending of wrongness, the cutting off of the root of underlying tendencies, the subsiding of all defilements, distresses, fevers, and aggressions; it is the teaching of seeing and hearing,
the designation of the Dhamma as being like lightning and a thunderbolt, the manifestation of the Dhamma that leads to dismantling, the illumination of the three abandonments,
the application to the three trainings, the undertaking of serenity and insight, the accomplishment of development and realization, and the purification of the aggregate of virtue and the rest.
These and others are to be understood in this way.
Therein, that by virtue of which defilements and so forth one becomes established or sinks, and that by virtue of which volitional formations and so forth one is carried along or swept away—
both of these constitute the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*), as they are produced from it and dependent upon both of them.

The aggregates are the truth of suffering; both of these constitute the meaning. The teaching—which conceals the intended meaning of "without foundation and without grasping"—is the means, because by way of subduing pride, it serves as the cause for that deity’s realization of the truths.
Through the instruction on the negation of foundation and grasping, [the path] is free from the two extremes for those seeking to cross over the four floods.
“The middle way of practice is to be undertaken”—this is the Blessed One’s injunction here; this is the "mode of teaching" (desanāhāra).

It is stated by way of a question—"How indeed?"—due to the desire to know and because of the inclination to resolve the doubts of others. It is stated as "you" because of being face-to-face and because of being a single individual.
[It refers to] the state of being worthy of nothing other than the weightiness of one who has reached the ultimate excellence.
It is called "Sādhū" because it illuminates the burden of the True Dhamma; it is called "Mārisa" because of its possession of qualities such as the virtue of being dear;
it is called "Ogha" because of its dragging down and its state of being a mass;

and it is called "iti" because the meaning intended to be known has been accomplished and brought to completion, since the establishment characterized by sinking has not been made and is entirely unmade.
“It is ‘without foundation’ (appatiṭṭha),” it is said. This non-doing is stated with the emphasis of a categorical certainty (*ekamsika*).
And because that lack of foundation pertains to one’s own continuum (*sasantatigata*), and because he was asked, “Are you [the one]? (*tvaṃ*), it is stated, “I am” (*ahaṃ*).
Because of addressing the deity and as a term of endearment, “Friend” (*āvuso*) is said. [This refers to] accumulation (*āyūhana*), which has the characteristic of being cast out (*nibbuyhana*).
It is said that they are "without exertion" (*anāyūha*) because they are entirely unconditioned and have not been produced.

Because the three modes [of craving] are not desired as floods (*ogha*), doubt regarding them has not yet departed; and since there is no distinction in the crossing over of the floods, it was asked: "In what way, then?
Likewise, because there is no difference in meaning between the characteristic of sinking, the state of being established, and the settling within *saṃsāra*.

It is simultaneous. Likewise, because there is no difference in meaning between "the characteristic of burning away" (nibbuyhanalakkhaṇa) and "exertion" (āyūhana), and because it is the transcending of right practice, it is said to be simultaneous: "When I... [etc. ...then indeed I burn away.
Because it is the opposite of both of those and because it wards them off, it is said: "Thus indeed I... [etc. ...I have crossed the flood."
It is said "after a long time" because of the vast interval of time, being separated by the appearance of a single Buddha.

It is said "indeed" (*vata*) because of the state of having never been seen before and because of its wonder-inspiring nature. It is said "I see" because of its being presently perceived and because it is directly witnessed by oneself.
It is called "Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇa*) because of the expulsion of evil and because of the attainment and penetration of the Noble Path, which is itself Brahman.
It is so called because it has completely extinguished the burning of the defilements and the burning of suffering;

thus it is said to be "fully extinguished" (*parinibbuta*). It is so called to be "crossed over" (*tiṇṇa*) because the application for crossing has been accomplished and there is nothing further to be crossed.
It is so called as "the world" (*loka*) because it is to be beheld with the eye of knowledge, and because it disintegrates and falls apart.

It is called "clinging" (*visattikā*) because it arises and becomes attached to sense objects. It is called "this" (*idaṃ*) because it is directly perceived by knowledge and because it is the conclusion.
It is called "I have spoken" (*avocaṃ*) because it has been uttered and completed.
It is called "that deity" (*sā devatā*) because she was first mentioned and is being referred back to. Because there is no negation and because the meaning is to be rejoiced in—
“He was pleased” is what was said. He is called the “Teacher” because he trained [disciples] and because of his attainment of the ultimate goal.
He is called “disappeared” because he went out of sight by passing beyond the range of vision. This is the Mode of Conveying Investigation by Investigation of the Successive Order.
Crossing the flood is appropriate through non-establishment and non-exertion, because of the relinquishing of defilements and volitional formations and the successful attainment of the further shore.
It is logical that there is sinking into *saṃsāra* for one who stands still through all defilements—

by way of craving, views, the bases of craving, eternalism, and so forth— because the cause is well-established. When the mental formation of defilements exists in the function of volitional formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*),
for one who exerts effort by way of adherence to all views, over-reaching adherence, and so on, [there is immersion] by the great flood of *saṃsāra*.

"It is fitting that there is 'emerging' because of the transcendence of right practice. It is fitting that there is the state of a *brāhmaṇa* because of the debtlessness toward, and the penetration of, the Noble Path which is the Brahmā;
for one has banished evil (*bāhitapāpa*). It is fitting that there is the state of being 'fully extinguished' (*parinibbuta*) because of the attainment of the truly peaceful Dhamma;
for all defilements, along with their latent tendencies, have been abandoned. And likewise, it is fitting that there is the state of having 'crossed over' the attachment."
It is fitting that not even a trace [of it] is seen, because it has been eradicated by the supreme path; this is the Mode of Conveying the Logical Reason (*yuttihāra*).
Establishment by way of the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) is specifically the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the cycle of kamma.

Accumulation by way of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) is the proximate cause for the cycle of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*). Non-establishment and non-accumulation are the proximate causes for crossing the flood (*oghataraṇa*).
It is the crossing over of the flood, leading to nibbāna without residue. The basis for its establishment is the contemplation of gratification with respect to craving.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, for one who contemplates gratification in things that fetter, craving increases.
Ignorance regarding the aggregates, contact, perception, and thought, as well as improper attention and evil friends, are [the conditions] by way of views through the influence of another's voice.
It is the proximate cause for establishing. As it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "The aggregates are a basis for views;
ignorance is also a basis for views," and so forth. It is the proximate cause for accumulation by way of the craving, views, delighting, and the remaining defilements and volitional formations.
In this manner, according to what is appropriate, [it is the proximate cause] for establishing and accumulation by way of craving, views, and so on.
The state of being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) must be stated. The rest here is to be clearly determined from the text itself.

This is the Mode of Conveying the Proximate Cause (*padaṭṭhāna-hāra*). By answering with the negation of "standing" and "exertion" in the phrase "without standing, without exertion," right practice—which brings about deliverance—is grasped, because it is exclusively the means for crossing over the flood.
And by grasping that [right practice], all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) are likewise included.
They are grasped as having a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of leading out (*niyyāna-lakkhaṇa*);

this is the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*). This very meaning has already been stated: that there was a lack of understanding, as it truly is, of the manner in which this deity crossed the flood.
Furthermore, others who, by relying on this teaching, penetrate the means for crossing the flood—they too are the "source" (*nidāna*) of this teaching.

They are to be seen. Herein, the Blessed One’s intention is this: "How might those who, by means of this teaching, penetrate it correctly and cross over the fourfold flood, thereby transcend the entire great flood of saṃsāra, and establish others therein as well?
Etymology (*nirutta*) is the analysis of words; it refers here to the introductory phrases beginning with "Thus" (*evaṃ*).

Regarding the Pāli words beginning with "katham," we have not elaborated upon them here for fear of excessive prolixity, as they are easily understood by following the method set forth in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and its sub-commentary (*līnatthavaṇṇanā*).
There are five kinds of connection (*sandhi*): by way of word (*pada*), meaning (*attha*), teaching (*desanā*), arrangement (*nikkhepa*), and sutta. Among these, regarding the word...

The connection between one word and another word is *padasaṇdhi*. Likewise, the connection between the meaning of one word and the meaning of another word is *padattha-saṇdhi*, which is called the "connection between action and its factors" (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*).
For a discourse with multiple transitions, the connection is the respective transition from one point to another;

however, for a discourse with a single transition, the connection between what precedes and what follows is *desanā-saṇdhi*, which is described in the Commentary as "the transition following a question" (*pucchānusandhi*).
The connection of underlying intention (*ajjhāsayānusandhi*) is analyzed in three ways as "according to the sequence" (*yathānusandhi*).

Here, underlying intention should be understood as twofold: one's own intention (*attajjhāsaya*) and the intention of others (*parajjhāsaya*). The connection of presentation (*nikkhepasandhi*) is to be understood by way of the four modes of presenting a discourse (*suttanikkhepa*).
Whatever else needs to be said here should be taken according to the method explained in the *Papañcasūdanī-ṭīkā*.
The connection between the suttas here should be understood by way of the first placement [of the *oghatarana-sutta*].
Now, why does the inquiry—"But why was the *oghatarana-sutta* placed first here?"—not arise anywhere?

Furthermore, it is because [the sutta] functions by way of the negation of both a foothold (*patiṭṭhāna*) and an exertion (*āyūhana*), as in: "He crossed the flood without a foothold and without exertion."

This sutta has been placed here first of all because it elucidates the Middle Way by way of avoiding the two extremes; for the teaching of the Buddhas consists primarily in making known the Middle Way practice without falling into either extreme.
Furthermore, as for the correlation of one teaching with another teaching:
This is also a connection in the teaching (*desanā-sandhi*). It should be understood here as follows:
the teaching beginning with “Without a foothold... [passage] ...he crossed the flood without exertion” is this teaching:
“At all times endowed with virtue, wise, and well-concentrated;”
Ardent in energy and resolute, he crosses the flood that is so difficult to cross.
Free from the perception of sensual pleasure, having transcended the fetter of form,
and with delight and lust utterly destroyed, he does not sink in the deep.
By faith one crosses the flood, by diligence the ocean.
One should cut off five, abandon five, and master five further;
the bhikkhu who has overcome the five attachments is said to have crossed the flood.
“Therefore, a person who is always mindful should avoid sensual pleasures;
having abandoned them, he crosses the flood, like one who has boarded a boat and reached the further shore.
The one who sees the end of birth and its origin understands the solitary path with compassion for the welfare of others.”
"By this path they crossed over in the past, they will cross over, and those who are crossing over the flood.
It is through such teachings that [the text] is brought into harmony; thus, this is the Fourfold Array (catubyūha) method.
Regarding "without a foothold, without exertion," here "foothold" and "exertion" refer to the defilements (saṃkilesa). By means of that, there is improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra).
It is illuminated by way of the pacification of the defilements through non-accumulation, which is wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
In this regard, for one who attends unwisely, craving and ignorance increase. Among these, by the mention of craving, those phenomena rooted in craving are included;
by the mention of ignorance, the entire wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) rooted in ignorance is included. And by the mention of wise attention, those things rooted in wise attention [are included].
The phenomena revolve around the fourfold wheel of success. Furthermore, right practice is illustrated by way of its foundation, accumulation, and negation;
and that, in brief, is comprised of virtue and the rest. Therein, by the mention of virtue, the eleven benefits of virtue revolve;
by the mention of concentration, the five-factored right concentration and the five-knowledge right concentration [revolve].

The requisites for concentration also recur. By the inclusion of "wisdom," wisdom and right view—meaning that all factors of the Noble Path are included within the manifestation of right view—this is the Mode of Convergence (*āvatta-hāra*).
The foundation is sevenfold by way of the defilements and so forth. The exertion is sevenfold by way of volitional formations and so forth.
Likewise, by way of their opposites, there is non-establishment and non-accumulation. This is the analysis of the states (*dhamma-vibhatti*) herein.
The analyses of the proximate causes and the planes, however, should be understood according to the method explained below. This is the Mode of Analysis (the Mode of Analysis of the States).
Having properly accomplished the preliminary practice and having coupled serenity and insight, [one should perform] meditation...
By striving, one crosses the flood that is without support and without effort, because of distancing oneself from defilements and the like, and because of not sinking or being swept away by them.

However, by sinking and being swept away through the power of defilements and the like, one does not cross the flood, because of finding a footing in saṃsāra and because of the exertion toward the production of renewed existence in the future. This is the method of the "turning-back" (parivatta-hāra).
"Not finding a footing, not standing, not sinking, not emerging, and not emerging again" is a synonymous expression;
"not striving, not struggling, not thinking, and not fashioning" is a synonymous expression; "the flood, the ocean of defilements" is a synonymous expression;
"crossed over, transcended, and gone beyond" is a synonymous expression. By this method, [the same applies] to the remaining phrases as well.
"It should be understood as a term of method" refers to the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacana-hāra).

Regarding the phrase "without a footing, without exertion": here, "footing" is a designation for the performance of the functions of the defilements; it is a designation for the manifestation of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna);
it is a designation for the growth of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra); it is a designation for the gratification of craving (taṇhā); [and] of views (diṭṭhi).

It is a description of the accomplishment of what has been fully realized. It is a description of the adherence to existence through the view of existence. It is a description of perversion through the view of non-existence.
It is a description of the craving for sensual pleasures through the pursuit of sensual pleasure. It is a description of self-mortification through the pursuit of self-torment.

Furthermore, "unsupported and without exertion" is a description of the direct knowledge of those phenomena that are to be directly known. [It is a description] of those phenomena that are to be fully understood...

The designation of full understanding (*pariññā-paññatti*). The designation of the abandoning of states to be abandoned for one crossing over the flood (*ogha-matarin*) is the designation of the path as cultivation (*bhāvanā-paññatti*).
The designation of the realization of cessation (*nirodha*) is the designation of its verification (*sacchikiriyā-paññatti*).

This is the method of designation (*paññatti-hāra*). In the phrase "without a foothold and without exertion" (*appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhaṃ*), by the mention of "foothold" (*patiṭṭhāna*) and "exertion" (*āyūhana*), and by the mention of the "flood" (*ogha*), the truth of the origin (*samudaya-sacca*) is indicated.
"Grasped" is included. By the three terms "unsupported," "unaccumulated," and "crossed over," however, the truth of the path is grasped;
and since the inclusion of that which possesses a cause is established by the inclusion of the cause itself, the truths of suffering and its cessation are indeed grasped by implication.
This is the entry by way of the truths. In this context, there are the five mundane aggregates, by means of which the establishment and accumulation [of suffering] are accomplished. Those...
The four supramundane aggregates (*khandhā*), by means of which the success of crossing the flood is achieved—this is the entry by way of the aggregates (*khandhamukhena*).

Those same five aggregates, twelve bases (*āyatanāni*), and eighteen elements (*dhātuyo*), [when reduced] to those four aggregates, two bases, and two elements—this is the entry by way of the bases and the elements (*āyatanamukhena* and *dhātumukhena*). Likewise, one enters "without a foothold" and "without exertion."
Here, by the inclusion of "establishment" (*patiṭṭhāna*) and "accumulation" (*āyūhana*), the defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and so forth, are included.

The defilements, volitional formations, and the rest, as well as the floods (*ogha*), the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*), and the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*),—together with the mention of "non-establishment" and "non-accumulation," and the expression "crossing the floods"—the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*) is thereby described. And thus, the aggregate of mental formations is the base of mental phenomena.
And since the dharma-element is included, there is likewise entry by way of the aggregates, by way of the bases, and by way of the elements.
If insight is the contemplation of impermanence, it is the door to liberation by way of the signless;

if it is the contemplation of suffering, it is the door to liberation by way of the desireless; if it is the contemplation of non-self, it is the door to liberation by way of the empty. Thus, [there is entry] by way of the doors to liberation.

The entry: the factors such as the aggregate of virtue belonging to those in training on the path, as well as the base of mental objects and the element of mental objects that are untainted—this is indeed the entry by way of the aggregates and so forth;
this is the Mode of Conveying Entry (*otaraṇa-hāra*). "Without a foundation" is the commencement (*ārambha*).

"Without exertion" is the purification of the word, not the purification of the commencement; likewise for "flood. But in "they have crossed," there is both the purification of the word and the purification of the commencement; this is the Mode of Conveying Purification (*sodhana-hāra*).
"Without a foothold, without exertion"—this is a resolution by way of the state of being a recluse (*sāmañña*).

It is a specific statement made after having formulated it as "crossing the flood," considering it to be a negation of both footing and exertion in their commonality through craving, views, and so forth.
For the crossing of the flood consists of the four noble paths. Among these, the first and second paths are, without distinction, the crossing of the flood of views.
The third path is the crossing of the flood of sensuality, and the highest path is the crossing of the remaining floods—this is the Mode of Conveying a Foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*).
Unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) is the cause for establishment by way of defilements (*kilesa*). Defilements are the causes for the accumulation of formative forces (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
However, wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) and abandonment (*pahāna*) are, respectively, the causes for non-establishment and non-accumulation.
The contemplation of gratification in things that fetter is, according to the case, the cause for craving by way of craving. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Bhikkhus, for one who contemplates gratification in things that fetter, craving increases.
The aggregates, ignorance, contact, perception, applied thought, improper attention, evil friends, and the voice of another are the bases for the establishment [of views] by way of views.
These are the causes. Therefore it was said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "The aggregates are a basis for views; ignorance too is a basis for views," and so forth.
Craving and delighting are the causes for the accumulation [of kamma] by way of the remaining defilements and volitional formations.
Following this method, the analysis of the causes for establishment and accumulation should be determined according to the appropriate application of craving and views, and by way of their opposites.
"Of non-establishment and non-accumulation. For, seeing the danger in the arising of defilements is the cause for non-establishment;
seeing the danger in volitional formations is the cause for non-accumulation; and exerting oneself in insight is the cause for crossing the flood.
This is the "Requisite Mode of Conveying."
Through the absence of a footing and the absence of exertion—by means of the aforementioned divisions—there is the complete purification of all four floods (*ogha*).

Furthermore, through the absence of a footing and the absence of exertion, there is the restraint and the total closing off of the streams; thus, the specific closing off and the bringing about of non-occurrence of all four floods occurs.
For, by means of the cultivation of the Noble Path, there is no footing by way of defilements (*kilesa*) and no [volitional] formation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) by way of [karmic] formations.

The accumulation (*āyūhana*) has been severed; for him, all floods (*ogha*) have been crossed, have been fully crossed over, and have been abandoned—this is the "Method of Coordination" (*samāropana-hāra*).

In the phrase "without a foothold and without accumulation," by the mention of the "foothold" (*patiṭṭhā*), craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*) are included, for it is through their influence that a being establishes itself in this or that state of existence.
By the mention of "accumulation," the conditioned phenomena (*abhisaṅkhāra-dhamma*) that arise with those as their conditions are included.
[They] are grasped. Therein, specifically, material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) are the basis for craving (*taṇhā*), and immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) are the basis for ignorance (*avijjā*).
Their respective antidotes are serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*); these are expressed by the phrases "without a foothold" and "without exertion," [crossing] the flood.
Among them, the fruit of serenity is liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*), and that of insight is liberation by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*).

For it is described as being distinguished by the terms "fading away from lust" and "fading away from ignorance. In this context, craving, ignorance, and volitional formations constitute the truth of the origin;
the material and immaterial phenomena that serve as the basis for these constitute the truth of suffering; their non-occurrence constitutes the truth of cessation;
and the practice that leads to the realization of cessation—the way of crossing over the flood—is stated here as the truth of the path. By the inclusion of craving...

And here, the unwholesome side should be understood by way of deceit, fraud, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, evil desire, association with evil friends, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, and so forth. By the inclusion of ignorance (*avijjā*), the unwholesome side should be understood by way of distorted attention, anger, enmity, denigration, spite, envy, avarice, aggression, stubbornness, the view of existence, and so forth.
By the opposite of what has been stated, [the wholesome side] should be understood by way of non-deceit, non-fraud, and so forth, as well as non-distorted attention and so forth.

Likewise, the side of purification should be understood by way of the faculty of faith and other factors belonging to serenity (samatha), as well as the perception of impermanence and other factors belonging to insight (vipassanā).
This is the ground for the method of the Conversion of Delight (nandiyāvatta-naya).

Furthermore, among the phenomena belonging to the categories of craving, ignorance, and their concomitants, which have been grasped according to the aforementioned method, craving is greed (lobha) and ignorance is delusion (moha).
When ignorance is associated with greed, it is like pus when blood is present; likewise, when craving is present, resentment arises as hatred.

Thus, when the three unwholesome roots are grasped, by their very opposition and through such expressions as "without a foothold," the three unwholesome roots and the three wholesome roots are established.
Here too, greed includes all wholesome roots that are subject to the taints (*sāsava*).

The application of the Truths (*saccayojanā*) should be applied as follows: the nature of accumulating (*āyūhanadhamma*) is the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*), while the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandhā*) produced by that [origination], which serve as their basis and objective field, are the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), and so forth.
Furthermore, the fruit (*phala*) here should be determined by way of the three liberations (*vimokkha*);

[the cause] is by way of the three unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*), the threefold misconduct (*duccarita*), the stains of defilement (*saṃkilesamala*), and unwholesome perceptions, thoughts (*vitakka*), and so on.

The unwholesome side is to be led forth; likewise, the purification side is to be led forth by means of the three wholesome roots, the threefold good conduct, right wholesome perception, thought, concentration, the doors of liberation, and so on—this is the ground of the Tipukkhalo method.
Likewise, among the phenomena belonging to the side of craving and ignorance taken up according to the stated method, specifically regarding craving and views:
By way of [ignorance], the perversions of perceiving the foul as "beautiful" and the suffering as "pleasurable" arise;
by way of ignorance and views, the perversions of perceiving the impermanent as "permanent" and the non-self as "self" are to be understood.

As their antidotes, through the words beginning with "without a foothold," and by means of the faculties of mindfulness, energy, concentration, and wisdom thus obtained, the four foundations of mindfulness are indeed established.
In this regard, four types of persons are to be demonstrated by means of four faculties. How so? For those of craving-temperament (taṇhācarita) are of two kinds:
those with dull faculties and those with sharp faculties; likewise for those of view-temperament (diṭṭhicarita).

Among them, the first type—grasping at the perverted notion of "beauty" in what is ugly—by the power of mindfulness observes the true nature of the body as it really is, and through the power of meditation eradicates that perversion.

He enters the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*). The second person, who grasps what is not happiness as "happiness" through a perversion of perception, dispels the opposing factor by means of the power of energy—which consists of the restraint of energy—as described in the passage beginning with "he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire.
Having destroyed that perversion through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*), he enters the certainty of rightness. The third person, regarding what is impermanent...
One who grasps [the notion] "permanent" incorrectly, having concentrated the mind through the power of serenity (samatha) and perceiving the momentary nature of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra),
eradicates that perversion through the power of cultivation (bhāvanā) and enters the certainty of rightness (sammattaniyāma).

Fourthly, because of the deception caused by the density [of appearance] regarding continuity, collection, function, and object, one [perceives] as self what is merely a heap of phenomena such as contact (phassa), which is actually non-self.

One who holds the wrong adherence that "this is self" destroys that wrong adherence by means of mental attention to the emptiness of the fourfold alternative (catukoṭika-suññatā), and thus realizes the fruit of recluseship.
The application of the truths should be understood as follows: the truth of the origin consists of the four perversions, such as the perception of beauty and the perception of pleasure;
and the five aggregates of clinging, which serve as their basis and object, constitute the truth of suffering, and so forth.
As for the fruit here, it consists of the four fruits of asceticism (*sāmaññaphala*).

Here, the unwholesome side is to be understood by way of the four perversions (*vipallāsa*), the four taints (*āsava*), floods (*ogha*), yokes (*yoga*), bodily ties (*kāyagantha*), wrong courses (*agati*), the arising of craving (*taṇhuppāda*), the seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and non-penetration (*apariññā*) and so forth; likewise, the side of purification is to be understood by way of the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), the fourfold abiding in jhāna, the factors conducive to happiness, the immeasurables (*appamaññā*), the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), and so forth.
This is the ground of the "Lion’s Play" method (*sīhavikkīḷita-naya*).
Furthermore, with the establishment of these three methods of meaning (*atthanaya*), the two methods of expression (*vohāranaya*) are necessarily established as well.

For indeed, the observation of phenomena that serve as the directions for the methods of meaning is "observation of the directions" (*disālocana*), and the bringing together of those [phenomena] is the "hook" (*aṅkusa*);

thus, it should be understood that all five methods are applied here. And this discourse belongs to the section on penetration and the part pertaining to training within the sixteenfold *Suttantapaṭṭhāna*.
It should be understood that by way of negation (*byatirekamukhena*), establishment (*paṭṭhāna*) and accumulation (*āyūhana*) are included;
thus, it should be seen as pertaining to the defilements (*saṃkilesa*), penetration (*nibbedha*), and the stage of training (*sekkhabhāgiya*).

Furthermore, in the twenty-eightfold *Suttanta-paṭṭhāna*, it should be known as mundane and supramundane, based on sentient beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*), consisting of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and the knowable (*ñeyya*), vision (*dassana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), our own doctrine (*sakavacana*), that which is to be answered (*vissajjanīya*), wholesome (*kusala*), and permitted (*anuññāta*).
The commentary on the Oghataraṇa Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Nimokkha Sutta:
"First arrived" means the words that have appeared first in the first sutta and so forth by way of the sequence of commentaries. "Of clear meaning" means...
For the sake of clarity. Indeed, only a word whose meaning is not previously known and whose meaning is difficult to understand should be commented upon.

Regarding the phrase "jānāsi no," he says "jānāsi no" means "do you know? because the particle *no* has the same meaning as the interrogative particle *nu*. It is called *nimokkha* (liberation) because beings are liberated from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) by means of it;
that is, the Path (*magga*). And because they are released by means of it, it is called *pamokkha* (release); however, regarding the state of being released...
The fruit that is to be realized is called "liberation" (*pamokkho*), just as Arahantship is called "the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion.
"Those" refers to sentient beings. "Is secluded" (*viviccati*) means it becomes separate and unmixed;

the meaning is that it departs. It is "seclusion" (*viveko*) because suffering is secluded from it. In the second interpretation, however, [it is secluded] from the entire suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
“Beings are released (*nimuccanti*), liberated (*pamuccanti*), and secluded (*viviccanti*) therein”; thus *nimokkho*, *pamokkho*, and *viveko* should be understood to mean Nibbāna.
Furthermore, the locative case in *ettha* should be seen as expressing the sense of a cause or basis (*nimitta*).
The particle *kho* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), as in expressions such as *assosi kho*.

Existence rooted in delight (*nandīmūlaka-bhava*) is "existence as delight" (*nandībhava*); this is by eliding the latter member of the compound, just as "one who eats vegetables and lives on vegetables" is called "vegetable-liver" (*sākabhakkho paṭṭhavo sākapaṭṭhavo*).

Having first stated the meaning where the round of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*) is predominant, he now speaks the words beginning with "And through delight" (*nandiyā ca*) while stating the meaning where both [defilements and kamma] are predominant.
"In the former manner" means that existence as kamma rooted in delight is "existence as delight."
In this context. By the term "craving for existence" (*nandībhava*).

"By way of the threefold formative activity of karma" means by way of the three types of formative activity of karma—namely, meritorious formative activity and so forth—and by way of the three types of bodily formative activity and so forth.

The aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is included because volition (*cetanā*) is predominant within the aggregate of formations. [The phrase] "by perception and consciousness" (*saññāviññāṇehi*).

“By the terms ‘perception’ and ‘consciousness’ as stated in the phrase *saññāviññāṇasaṅkhayā*. And “associated with that” means precisely those associated with the aforementioned aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
“Two aggregates” refers to the aggregates of perception and consciousness. [Objection:
Is it not the case that the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) is not included here? [Response: It is not that it is not included; showing this, he says “But by those...,” and so forth.
"By three aggregates" means by the aggregates of perception, formations, and consciousness. They are included because they are inseparable [from feeling];
for there is no arising of consciousness that is devoid of feeling. "Of those not acquired through clinging" refers to the wholesome and unwholesome [states].

What is intended here is not the non-occurrence of functional (kiriyā) aggregates. "By way of non-occurrence" means by way of having reached the state of being subject to non-arising. By way of non-generation.

That which is grasped by means of kamma and defilements is *upādi*; this refers to the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*). What remains for one who possesses such grasping (*upādino*) is the "residue of clinging" (*upādisesa*);
together with that residue of clinging is "with-residue" (*saupādisesa*). Nibbāna is described here because it illuminates the state of the complete subsiding of all kamma and defilements.

Since the two preceding terms included the aggregates not yet grasped (*anupādiṇṇaka*), the term "of feelings" (*vedanānam*) here specifically refers to those aggregates that have been grasped (*upādiṇṇaka*).
It is appropriate [to say], "of the appropriated feelings. By "cessation" (nirodhena) is meant their ceasing by way of the cessation of the desire and lust connected to them.
By "pacification" (upasamena) is meant their absolute pacification through non-occurrence. And by doing so, the inclusion of the word "and" (ca) is justified.
"Of those" (tesaṃ) refers to that feeling and the three aggregates associated with it. "By way of basis and object" (vatthārammaṇavasena).
This is by way of all material phenomena that are appropriated (*upādiṇṇaka*), whether they serve as the basis (*vatthu*) or as the object (*ārammaṇa*).
But why were only the four immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) mentioned above, while the material aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*) was not included?

Because of its distinct nature. For in the attainment of Nibbāna with residue remaining (*saupādisesa-nibbānappatti*), just as there are appropriated material phenomena, there are also non-appropriated material phenomena.
There is simply no occurrence [of them]. "In the second method" refers to this position: "of both delight and existence.

By the mention of "delight," the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) is included because it accompanies it. By the phrase "the aggregate of form consisting of rebirth-existence," he speaks specifically of appropriated material phenomena.

By the inclusion of that [aggregate], those [phenomena] produced by temperature and nutriment which have it as their cause are included; and by the mention of "consciousness," those produced by mind are included.
In this context, it should be understood that the form belonging to the four continuities is included.

By "perception and so forth," the three aggregates—perception, consciousness, and feeling—are included; however, this is done without making a distinction between what is clung-to (*upādiṇṇa*) and what is not clung-to (*anupādiṇṇa*), but rather without qualification.
For Nibbāna is the non-occurrence of the five aggregates without qualification. Therefore he said: "Thus... Nibbāna is spoken of."
For here, by the term "Nirvana," the great Nirvana of the Deathless (amata-mahānibbāna) is intended. And they lead to this very one; this refers specifically to the second method mentioned above.
One who upholds the four Nikāyas is a *catunikāyika*. The Elder named Bhaṇḍika is the Elder Bhaṇḍika.
The word "iti" is a reference to the manner already stated. "By way of Nirvana alone" refers to the Nirvana with residue (*saupādisesa-nibbāna*) in the first method.
And regarding the Nibbāna without residue, in the second [verse], however,
the Blessed One concluded and finalized the teaching entirely by means of Nibbāna itself, described as the "great Nibbāna of the Deathless.
The commentary on the *Nimokkha Sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Upanīya Sutta:
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, it is said that "it is brought near (*upanīyati*)," meaning "it is exhausted" or "it ceases.
The sense is "it perishes. Alternatively, "it is brought near" refers to the very nature of life.
He said, "The approaching of death has been stated," explaining: "Or it approaches; the meaning is that one gradually attains death.

Here, although the word "is led" (*upanīyati*) refers to a specific type of kamma that is not explicitly manifest—just as it is said, "All health ends in illness, all youth ends in old age, and all life ends in death"—it is used in this context.
Because it was said, "Life is being led away," it was stated that "one approaches death. This was stated by way of the agent (*karmakartṛ*).
Now, in order to show the meaning by way of the object (*karmasādhana*), the passage beginning with "Or, as... was stated. A herd of cows is led by a cowherd to whatever place he desires.
Beings live by means of it, or co-arisen phenomena live [by means of it], thus it is "life" (*jīvita*); that very thing—
Because it possesses sovereignty in their preservation, it is called a "faculty" (*indriya*); thus he says, "life is the life-faculty.
"Limited" (*paritta*) means short-lived; therefore he says, "brief. Here, the function of life is intended as the condition for the non-interruption of the continuity [of the aggregates];
thus he says, "and because of its limited nature by its own essence," and so forth. Furthermore, "lifespan" (*āyu*) here refers to the maximum lifespan, and that—
This should be understood according to the present time.
For in this current arising of a Buddha, this discourse is intended to illustrate the extreme brevity of life;

thus, in order to define the exhaustion of life by way of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), he said, "it lasts for only the duration of a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittappavattimatto*)," referring to a single...
The meaning is: "It lasts for only the moment of the arising of the consciousness. Now, in order to clarify that point by means of a simile, the passage beginning with "Just as if" was stated.
Therein, "while it is revolving" means that the wheel-rim of a chariot revolves; the intention is that it revolves by means of only one portion of the rim in a single moment.
The same method applies here to the phrase "it stands by means of only one [rim]. "Lasting for a single moment of consciousness" (ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ).

[It exists] for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇa*). "In that consciousness" means in whichever single consciousness it may be. "Merely having ceased" means as soon as the state of cessation has been reached.
"Is called 'ceased'" means that, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), the being endowed with that [consciousness] is called "dead.
However, those who do not discern the distinction observe the "cessation" (*nirodha*) of the continuity of what is not being cognized by the immediately following [moment].
In order to clarify the aforementioned point by means of a sutta, the passage beginning with “As it has been said” was stated.
By this, he shows that for sentient beings in all three periods of time, life and death in the ultimate sense occur solely by way of mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).
“Life” (*jīvita*) refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). “Personal existence” (*attabhāva*) refers to the remaining phenomena, excluding life, feeling, and consciousness.
These are intended [here]. "Pleasure and pain" refers to pleasant and painful feelings;
here, equanimity is also included within pleasure and pain because it possesses the nature of being either desirable or undesirable. "Exclusively" means unmixed with itself or with permanence.

"Associated with a single consciousness" means conjoined with a single consciousness. It is "light" because, according to the method already stated, it lasts for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇika*).
The moment of life and so forth passes exceedingly swiftly.

"Those that have ceased for one who is dying" refers to those aggregates which, for a being passing away—that is, for a being undergoing death—should be said to have ceased subsequent to the act of falling away (*cuti*).
Or, "for one who is staying here" refers to those [aggregates] which, for one staying—that is, for one persisting—here in the course of existence (*pavatti*).

The aggregates that have ceased through the occurrence of dissolution—all of them alike, all of them having gone to the same state, having set, having passed away without re-linking—have departed because of the absence of a new rebirth-linking upon returning again. For just as the aggregates at the moment of death do not arise [again], so too were the aggregates prior to that.
Therefore, the intention is that the life of sentient beings lasts for only a single moment of consciousness.
"One born with the unarisen has not been born" means that one is not born with a mind that has not yet arisen, because it can be said:
"In a future moment of consciousness, he has not lived, does not live, and will not live. One lives by means of the present, functioning mind;

such a person is called "living," for he neither has lived nor will live [once that moment passes]. "The world is dead through the dissolution of the mind" refers to everything just as it does to the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).
With the dissolution of each respective state of consciousness, this world is said to have "passed away" in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), because it can be said:
"In the past moment of consciousness, he lived; he does not live now; he will not live [in the future]," since that which has ceased is without reconnection (*appaṭisandhika*).
Even so, there is a conventional designation (*paññatti*) based on the ultimate reality, by means of which, depending upon each respective occurring consciousness, one speaks of "three..."

The conceptual designation of a continuity (*santānapaññatti*)—which is the objective domain for the occurrence of such statements as "Phussa lives" or "Phussa is living"—is here ultimate (*paramatthiyā*) and constitutes an ultimate reality (*paramatthabhūtā*).
For it has been said: "Name and clan do not decay.
There are no refuges for one who has reached old age; nor, because of that [old age], is there any [refuge] for an evildoer from his evil kamma.
For those who perform meritorious deeds by way of providing service, there is mental suffering due to separation from loved ones;

for both types of people, there is no small amount of physical suffering arising from the cutting of bonds and so forth, as well as the onset of delusion. Therefore, there are none who can protect them.
Thus he said: "There are none at all capable of being a refuge, a shelter, or a resort. That from which one fears is...
Because fear and the cause of fear are [both] included, he said "bases of fear" (*bhayavatthu*). By that inclusion, fear—characterized by mental terror—is indeed already grasped;
for when there is a cause, the effect must necessarily exist.

"Prior volition" refers to the volition of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) occurring in either a single-advertence cognitive process (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*) or a multiple-advertence cognitive process (*nānāvajjana-vīthi*). "Subsequent volition" refers to [the volition occurring] by way of attaining mastery.

The volition of attainment (*samāpatti-cetanā*) is that which occurs by way of entering [the attainment] from another state. The volition of relinquishing (*muñca-cetanā*) is the volition of the first absorption (*appanā*) occurring by way of suppression.

Meditative pleasure (*jhāna-sukha*) is the pleasure found in the fruition-absorptions (*vipāka-jhāna*) of a wholesome absorption. Here, the word "pleasure" (*sukha*) is used as a synonym for "desirable.
Attachment to absorption (*jhāna-nikanti*) is the longing for absorption. By way of the gratification of absorption...
The craving that has arisen is the relish for jhāna. It is because of this that those various Brahmās, having emerged from jhāna, utter the words, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!

Just as the gods who abound in happiness—those possessing triple-root rebirth—are capable of attaining jhāna when they proceed [to meditate], but others are not, it is said, "among the sense-sphere gods. And these include both the sense-sphere gods and the higher gods.
And the term "devas of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacaradeva*) should be understood as a *sarūpaka-ekasesa* (a collective compound based on partial similarity).

By this, the inclusion of both certain humans and all humans is established, because they constitute the object of aspiration and imagination. Therefore he said: "O, may these... [and so forth] ...remain.
A place where there are large, spreading drops is called *thullaphusitaka*; it refers to a dark region.
Or: in that context of heavy raindrops.
Because it was said, "One should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness," it is stated that "he speaks a discourse on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) which does not lead to liberation.

In the sense of breaking down and falling apart, it is the world (loka); and because it is to be grasped by defilements, it is also "worldly bait" (lokāmisa). This is the non-figurative (nippariyāya) sense of "bait."

Furthermore, that which is called "worldly bait" (*āmisam*) in the world is "worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*). It is called a "synonym" (*pariyāya*) because it makes something known by way of a transformation of its essential nature;
thus, it means a hint or a reason. Therefore, he said, "the four conditions are [taught] in their non-synonymous sense" (*nippariyāyena*);

for since the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is exclusively to be grasped by the foolish worldlings, it is described as having the nature of "synonymous bait. Here, however, the intended meaning is the opposite of the round of existence.
Because it is desired. For abandonment depends upon the four requisites.

Since for some there is even a condition for the abandonment that depends upon the entire round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he says "it is indeed permissible" with apprehension. He says "designated as Nibbāna" because it is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) where all the suffering of the entire round is stilled; thus it is "peace" (*santi*).
The commentary on the Upanīyasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Accantasutta: 4.
They pass away, they spend [time], thus they are "kālā" (times). For times such as "before the meal" and so forth are, in the ultimate sense, merely the occurrence of mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
Although non-existent, they are established merely by worldly convention;

because that very process of phenomena never turns back once it has proceeded, they seem to exhaust and destroy each respective manifestation of phenomena, as if they themselves were passing away along with them.
Therefore he said: "Time devours all beings, including oneself. And: "The nights carry one away."

The meaning here should also be understood according to the method already stated. Since it is said, "Perceiving this danger in death," the meaning expressed is that [the stages] carry the person across toward the arrival at death.
Regarding the phrase "stages of life" (*vayoguṇā*), here "stages" (*guṇā*) refers to divisions.

For the followers of other sects apply the designation "age" (*vaya*) to the entire collection of consciousness by means of the final moment of consciousness; thus he says: "of the first, middle, and last stages of life."

The meaning of *guṇa* is "qualities" (*rāsa*). The meaning of *guṇa* as "benefit" (*ānisansa*) is seen in such passages as: "I wore a garment of bark, having attained twelve qualities. However, in such passages as:
"I shall make it threefold (*tandiguṇa*), it would increase twofold, twofold," the meaning of *guṇa* is "the occurrence of that state" (*tabbhāvavutti*). [As it is said:
"The names of the Great Seer are incalculable, along with his qualities (*saguṇena*)."

In such passages as, “The name should be engraved with a quality, even if it be worth a thousand,” the sense of *guṇa* (quality) should be understood as the sense of praise (*pasaṃsa*). In the phrase, “The qualities of age are gradually abandoned,” the meaning is the same method as that stated for the expression “time passes.
Here, the inclusion of the word “first” in the compound *paṭhamamajjhima-vaya* (the first and middle ages) [is intended to include all stages].
This was stated to show that for one who has reached old age, there is no returning again. For this very reason, it was said: "At the moment of death, however, all three stages of life are abandoned.
Here, in the text, the passing away of time is shown in general by the phrase "the times pass away";

then, in order to show that same process specifically, the other two [stages] were mentioned. In the commentary, however, with reference to one of dull faculties, the qualities of the stages of life...
It is said, “they abandon them gradually,” and with reference to one of medium faculties, it is said, “the nights pass away.

With this intention, it is stated that “times” refers to times such as before the meal and so forth. Therefore, it should be understood that in that context, by the word “etcetera” (ādi), the divisions of time consisting of the subdivisions of time—such as after the meal, the first watch of the night, and the muhutta—are included. “The rest” refers here to the latter half of the two verses.
For this [term] is referred to here because its meaning has already been understood and because it was stated in the immediately preceding sutta.
The commentary on the Accent-sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Katichinda-sutta.
5. "Chindanto" means cutting off completely. "Kati chindeyyā" means how many evil states (pāpadhamma) would he cut off, and bring them to the state of non-arising?

"In the remaining phrases as well" means in the other two phrases as well. By the phrase "this same method applies," he extends [the principle] to this meaning: "Abandoning, how many would he abandon?
Developing, how many would he further develop? This refers to the fourth phrase.
But the meaning has been shown by its very nature. "One in meaning" means one in terms of the sense (bhāva). If this is so, for what purpose was another synonym taken? To this he says:
"But [for the sake] of the composition of the verse," and so forth. Since there is indeed repetition in meaning here, he says: "avoiding repetition of words.
"He transcends attachment" means he is "one who has gone beyond attachment" (saṅgātiga); thus he says: "this is precisely that meaning."

"Below" (*oraṃ*) refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*); they are called "lower-fettering" (*orambhāgiya*) because they partake of that [realm] by way of being conditions for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Furthermore, in this context, they are "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) because they yoke beings to suffering—namely, through karma to its result, and through the result to suffering—and specifically:
personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), and aversion (*paṭigha*). Above...
The four formless elements (arūpadhātu) are so called; because they partake of those [elements] in the manner already described, they are the "higher fetters" (uddhambhāgiyāni), namely:
attachment to the fine-material and immaterial realms, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

He spoke thus—"One should cut off five, abandon five"—in accordance with the very words employed [by the deity], for the sake of making it easy for that deity to grasp. It was not merely in accordance with the words spoken by that deity...
Thus, in order to show that these fetters can also be described from another perspective, the passage beginning with "Or alternatively" was stated.
By this it is meant that the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) are heavy and difficult to sever because they constitute a firm bondage;
therefore, with reference to them, it is said, "one should cut the five."

The higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), however, are light and easy to sever because they are to be abandoned through the method of development (*bhāvanā*) following the sequence of practice that has already occurred below;
therefore, with reference to them, it is said, "one should abandon the five. Thus he said: "Like a bird bound by a snare on its feet," and so forth.
"Distinction" means the distinction of the developments—that is, developing, arising, and causing to increase the development of insight (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*).
And increasing [them]. In the sense of binding one to the mire of saṃsāra, lust itself is the "fetter of lust" (*rāgasaṅga*). This same method applies to the others as well.

Since, in this context, lust, delusion, views, the view of self-existence associated with those [views], adherence to rules and observances, sensual lust, and ignorance are in substance the very floods (*ogha*), while the others are merely their concomitants, therefore the Blessed One, by means of the abandoning of the fetters and the surmounting of the bonds...

He spoke on the crossing of the flood (*oghataraṇa*). Both mundane and supramundane [teachings] were spoken because the phrase "one should cultivate" (*bhāvaye*) was intended for the development of the path in its prior stage (*pubbabhāga*).
The commentary on the *Katichinda-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Jāgara-sutta*.
6. *Jāgaratan* is a term of address used out of disregard. Therefore he said, "while the faculties are watchful.
Regarding the phrase "but in the verse of response," the connection is with the words "this meaning is to be understood.
