The intention is that the meaning of the verse of the question is likewise to be understood by this same method. In the expression "five sleepers who are watchful," the word "sleepers" (*suttā*)—

In relation to the word *pañca*, the nominative plural form is to be transformed according to the principle of concord with the word *jāgarata* (be awake), thus becoming "be awake for the five" (*pañcannaṃ jāgarata*).
Therefore he said: "while the five faculties are awake.

The meaning is that they are awake by virtue of being unbound [to defilements], being capable of their own functions through not being dormant in their respective duties. Just like one who is asleep...

They are "asleep" because of the presence of the sleep of negligence (*pamāda-niddā*). To demonstrate that very state of being asleep by means of a discourse focused on the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna-kathā*), it was said, beginning with "Why?
and so forth. One who is negligent, or one in whom negligence exists, is called *pamāda*; the state of that is *pamādatā*.
By that—meaning, by way of the state of being negligent—is the sense.
Having thus explained the meaning of the first quarter-verse, the words "evam suttesu" and so forth were spoken in order to explain the second.

Its meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. Because, by way of the activity of non-abandoned sleep, in a person possessed of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), unarisen dust of passion and the like arise, and arisen [dust] increases; therefore it was said: "By the hindrances alone..."

"It takes up the king of defilements. For this very reason, he said "the former," and so forth. Here, "taking up" (ādiyana) refers to the state of being a condition for the successive arising of the preceding and succeeding [moments].

"It is purified by the five faculties" means that it is purified from all defilement by means of the five faculties beginning with faith, which are included within the Path. For the faculty of wisdom itself consists of the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty and the others.
And the others are the "conformable" (anvaya) suttas.
The commentary on the Jāgara-sutta is finished.
7. The commentary on the Appaṭividdha-sutta.
7. Since the Dhamma that distinguishes between the occurrence [of saṃsāra], the cessation [of saṃsāra], and the causes of both is also included within the Four Noble Truths, it is said:
“Dhammas means the Dhammas of the Four Noble Truths. For all four Noble Truths are indeed included within the Four Noble Truths.

“Unpenetrated” means not yet realized by way of the full understanding through clear comprehension (*pariññā-abhisamaya*) and so forth. “In the doctrines of speculative views” means in those doctrines designated as “speculative views” (*diṭṭhigata*).
“They are set in motion by views on speculative positions. Regarding the phrase “others than these,” this means others besides those belonging to this dispensation (sāsana).

“By their very nature” means by their inherent character; the sense is that they proceed of their own accord. “They go” means they continue to exist, persisting while having adopted a doctrine of views.
“By another” means by one who holds a speculative position. “They are led” means they are incited toward embracing a doctrine of views. Therefore he said, “Therein,” and so forth.

"To awaken" means to awaken from the sleep of negligence. It is "auspicious" because it proceeds with wise attention (*yoniso*) due to the teaching of the Dhamma as it was declared, and because of its awakening. "By way of cause" means by way of the method (*ñāya*).
"By way of reason" means by way of the application that brings about the full realization of the Four Noble Truths. [It is clear] like an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of one's hand.

One who knows all that is knowable (*ñeyya*) is "all-knowing" (*sabbaññū*); by virtue of that very awakening to omniscience (*sabbaññutā-abhisambodha*), he is a "Buddha," thus an "All-Knowing Buddha" (*sabbaññu-buddha*).
One who has awakened to the Truths (*sacca*) through individual, independent self-knowledge (*sayambhu-ñāṇa*)—that is, knowledge not shared with others—is a "Private Buddha" (*paccekabuddha*).

One who awakens to the Four Truths through the instruction of another is a "Buddha of the Four Truths" (*catusacca-buddha*). For it is thus that, due to the absence of self-dependent realization, [he is so designated].

He is called solely the "Buddha of the Four Truths. One who has awakened to the objects of knowledge (*ñeyya*)—the classification of the aggregates and so forth—by means of learning (*suta*), that is, by knowledge consisting of what has been heard, is a "Buddha by learning" (*sutabuddha*).

Excluding the Omniscient Buddha and the Paccekabuddhas, the remaining ones—the Chief Disciples, the Great Disciples, the ordinary disciples, those free from passion, and all others whose taints are destroyed—are included.
This is because of such statements as, "The three former ones are Fully Enlightened Ones," and so forth. He dwells together.

By this [phrase], "abiding" and "conduct" are indicated. "Abiding in the world" (*lokasannivāsa*) means the world's abiding; in that [abiding]. In the unevenness consisting of bodily misconduct and so forth.
Or, in the unevenness of the classes of beings due to the loss of mindfulness. For that [abiding] is uneven because of its association with unevenness.

Or, in the unevenness of the arisen defilements such as the unevenness of lust. Having abandoned that unevenness, having looked upon that unevenness with equanimity, [one dwells] evenly and similarly.
It is fitting; or rather, they conduct themselves and act in a manner equal and identical to the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
The commentary on the *Appaṭividita-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Susammuṭṭha-sutta*.
8. *Susammuṭṭhā* means "completely and exceedingly confused. For the seven trainees (*sekkhā*) have become utterly bewildered and ruined.

But how is it that they are said to have "lost" what they had not yet attained? To this he says, "Just as... and so forth. The connection is: "of one who has attained" (*adhigatassa*), meaning "one for whom there has been attainment. "He speaks" (*so vadan*)—this is the syntactical link. "The rest" refers to the passage beginning with "the phenomena" (*dhammā*). It is exactly like the previous [case].
It is exactly as stated in the immediately preceding verse.
The commentary on the Susammuṭṭha Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Mānakāma Sutta.
9. One who wanders about having failed to abandon pride regarding distinctions such as one’s bed and so forth, and having instead embraced it, is said to be "one who desires pride.

Thus it is said: "of one desiring, that is, longing for, pride. It is called *dama* (taming) because by means of it the mind is tamed; thus *dama* refers to the factors conducive to concentration (*samādhipakkhika*), such as the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*) and others.

It is called *dama* because it tames the six sense faculties with the mind as the sixth; thus it is the restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*). It is called *dama* because it tames—that is, abandons—the defilements (*kilesa*).
*Taming* (*dama*) and *wisdom* (*paññā*). It is called *taming* because it tames bodily action and so forth by means of fasting; thus, it refers to the Uposatha observance.

It is called *taming* because it tames and disciplines anger, malice, intolerance, pride, and the like; thus, it refers to patient endurance (*adhivāsanakhanti*). "By that very [term]" means that because only those factors belonging to the side of concentration (*samādhi*) are intended by the word "taming.
Furthermore, the reading is "there is no silence" (*na monaṃ atthi*), where "of one who is unconcentrated" (*asamāhitassa*) indicates the negation of concentration.
Because it is spoken of as the crossing to the further shore of the realm of death (*maccudheyya*), it is said that "silence" (*mauna*) is the knowledge of the four paths;
for that cannot be achieved by anything other than that. "He knows" means he penetrates by way of penetration through non-delusion.

It is called the "realm of death" (*maccudheyya*) because death dwells therein; it refers to the five aggregates because they are subject to death. "Of that very same" means of the realm of death itself.

The "far shore" (*pāra*) is Nibbāna, which has become the further bank. Regarding the word "should cross over" (*tareyya*), he says that "crossing over" here refers to the activity of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), thus stating:
"one should penetrate it" (*paṭivijjheyya*) and "one should reach it" (*pāpuṇeyya*). For he will likewise say later: "What is called 'penetration-crossing' has been stated.
Therefore, the reading "one would not cross over, one would not penetrate, or one would not reach" is appropriate here. Otherwise, [the following] "this... [would be inconsistent].
Otherwise, statements such as "it has been said" would be contradicted. "Dwelling alone in the forest" means dwelling in the forest having become solitary.
Granted that the abandonment of certain types of conceit can be obtained even through the lower paths;

however, because its abandonment is complete only by the supreme path (agga-magga), it is said: "having abandoned the ninefold conceit by means of the path of Arahatship. This is preceded by access concentration (upacāra-samādhi).

Regarding the statement "by access and absorption concentration" (*upacārappanāsamādhīhi*), this is said because it would be inappropriate to conclude each sentence by referring merely to "concentration" alone, [namely] "access concentration" (*upacārasamādhi*).
For there is no supramundane jhāna that has not reached absorption (*appanā*).

As for the term "of one with a bright mind" (*sucetaso*), it is a description of the characteristic of the mind being accompanied by knowledge; thus he says, "by way of association with knowledge," and so forth.
For it will be said: “In the phrase ‘one of pure mind,’ wisdom is indicated by the term ‘mind.

Regarding the phrase “completely liberated in every respect,” this means that one whose mind is dissociated from all states of existence (bhava) and the like is entirely detached from the aggregates (khandha) and so forth;

thus it is said, “having become completely liberated from all aggregates, bases (āyatana), and so on. Thorough penetration through full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha) cannot exist without penetration through realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha).
He said, "There is not," [concluding] with "stated... of the three planes.
Because one engages in misconduct based on conceit (*māna*), this conceit is called a destroyer of virtue (*sīla*). Therefore, because conceit is the opposite of virtue;
by this description of the abandonment of its opposite, the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*) is stated in its own essential form—this is the intended meaning.
And here, by the word *suci* (pure), the mind (*citta*) is qualified as a "well-purified mind. The phrase "therefore" (*tasmā*) is used because it has been shown by means of wisdom (*paññā*).

By this term, namely "of pure mind" (*sucetaso*), the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*), the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-sikkhā*), and the training in higher wisdom (*adhipaññā-sikkhā*) are stated, having thus qualified virtue and the other factors.
Showing that there can be both co-occurrence and deviation [between a quality and its possessor] when one speaks of a qualifier and the qualified, he says: "The higher virtue... and so forth.
Having stated, "When virtue exists, [concentration] arises," and so forth, the passage beginning with "Therefore" was spoken in order to show both of these through their respective divisions.
Since the first method proceeds by way of confusion, the second method is stated with "Furthermore," etc., in order to show them without confusion.
In the phrase "having attained," the connection is also made by supplying the words "by one aspiring for Nibbāna. Regarding insight (vipassanā):

The distinction from the previous method lies in this meaning: although it has not yet attained the status of being a foundation (pādaka), it has nonetheless entered into that state by way of its arising and so forth for that purpose.
However, as there is no distinction from the previous method regarding higher wisdom (adhipaññā) here, it was not mentioned.

"Having combined" means having gathered them together both by way of their synonyms and their essential natures. "The entire Dispensation" refers to that which comprises the three trainings, precisely because the three [trainings] have been explained.
Thus the entire teaching has been explained.
The commentary on the *Mānakāma-sutta* is finished.
10. The commentary on the *Arañña-sutta*.

10. "Of those whose defilements are stilled" (*santakilesānaṃ*) means of those for whom the fever of the defilements has been calmed. Because they possess qualities such as virtue and because they have attained the stilling of fear, the wise are called "the peaceful ones" (*santo*);
therefore it is said, "or of the wise. By this he says, "Truly, the peaceful ones," and so forth.
"Of those who practice the best conduct" (*seṭṭhacārīnaṃ*) means of those who walk in the highest conduct. Because [they are superior] to the virtuous worldlings (*puthujjanakalyāṇa*),...
From that point on, a bhikkhu is said to dwell in the holy life of the path; therefore, it says, "dwelling in the holy life of the path.
However, there is no need to speak of the clarity of the complexion of the Noble Ones.
"The basic meditation subject" refers to the meditation subject for practical application. "Dissimilar continuity" refers to the mental continuity proceeding toward various objects. That...
For, due to the agitation of distraction, the continuity of the concentrated mind is a dissimilar continuity (*visabhāga-santati*).
"It enters" means that the continuity of consciousness, which is similar to concentration (*samādhi-sabhāgā*), enters the path of serenity (*samatha-vīthi*).

"The mind becomes serene" is said with reference to the developing mind (*bhāvanā-citta*) that delights in the meditation subject (*kammatthāna*); having become serene, it proceeds. "The blood becomes serene" is because of the absence of mental turbidity.
It becomes red and unclouded. They are pure because of the purity of their cause.
The phrase "the color of the face of a palmyra fruit" (*tālaphalamukhassa*) should be connected with the word "face" (*mukha*) at the beginning [of the compound].

For in this way, the inclusion of the word "omitted" (*pamutta*) is justified, owing to its similarity to the excellence of the color of the face of a palmyra fruit. *Tebhūmaka* is simply *tibhūmaka*.
“They do not grieve for the past”: having made the acquisition of conditions in the past their characteristic mark, they do not grieve nor do they lament.
They do not construct [expectations] by way of craving for wishing; thus he said, “they do not long for. “By whatever means” means by this or that other way.
“By what is obtained at that very moment” expresses the absence of enjoyment through hoarding. “By the threefold cause” means in a threefold manner.

“By cause” means the sign of contentment with the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*). “Destruction” means the cause of destruction. They are called “destruction” because things are destroyed by them; these are greed, hatred, and the evil states associated with them.
Since it is the cause of the body’s specific state of dryness, just as it is for the formless body (*arūpakāya*), he said, “by these two causes. “Lutō” means cut down (*lūno*).
The commentary on the Arañña Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Naḷavagga is finished.
2. The Nandanavagga.
1. Commentary on the Nandana Sutta 11.
Regarding the statement "Therein the Blessed One," it is not as smooth in its phrasing (*byañjana*) as when it is stated "Therein, indeed, the Blessed One";
thus he says, "by way of the smoothness of the phrasing. "The elders of the assembly" means those who are the seniors in the assembly.
They were especially fit vessels for that teaching. "The monks who are the leaders of the assemblies" means the monks who are the foremost among the four assemblies;
for the assembly of monks is the eldest of the four assemblies because it arose first.
"Addressed" means he called out to them; and since calling out is making known, he said "he made them know. "Venerable sir" (*bhadante*) is a term expressing reverence, respect, and deference.
As for the meaning: "May it be auspicious for you, Venerable Sir" (*bhadante*)—it is auspicious because of its own conclusion and completion, and because it brings about the welfare of others.
Regarding the phrase "they replied to the Blessed One" (*bhagavato paccassosuṃ*): here, the genitive case *bhagavato* is used as a form of address;
the intention is that it depends upon the word expressing the related sense [of the verb], thus he says, "they listened back to the word of the Blessed One."
The term "Bhagavatā" here is a dative case used in connection with the act of assenting, as in the expression, "he assents to Devadatta.
Whatever else needs to be said on this point will be addressed in the commentary on the first sutta of the Nidāna-vagga.
"Tāvatiṃsakāya" refers to the class of deities known as the Tāvatiṃsas. "The second heavenly world" refers to the second among the six worlds of sense-desire.
The world of the gods (*devaloka*). Thirty-three persons, together with the one who performed the meritorious deed, were reborn there;

the place associated with them is called *Tāvatiṃsa*. Those who dwell there are also named *Tāvatiṃsa* according to the principle of association. Therefore, he said, "By the young man Magha," and so forth.
However, since this particular doctrine had fallen into disrepute, he used the word "they say" (*vadanti*) when announcing it. Demonstrating its state of being discredited:
He said, “But because...,” and so forth. For he will say later: “For in this way the term becomes faultless.
“A mere designation by name” means that it is simply a conventional expression established independently of the actual referent.
They call it a *vana*; thus it is an *upavana* (grove). Even when one has entered it again and again and fallen into suffering, it gladdens [the person] with its own excellence.
In order to show that they do not even reach a state of suffering, the passage beginning with “in the five [aggregates]” was stated.
“Of those who have entered” means even those who have entered by way of being enclosed within the womb.

It is said, “they melt like a lump of snow,” referring to those who pass away while only slight changes are visible at the very moment of death. However, as for those who disappear suddenly without visible changes, [the following applies]:
With reference to them, they say it was stated that [the flame] "goes out like a lamp-flame. It gladdens both those who are by nature joyful and those who are dejected.
In the park named *Nandana* after this very meaning; the word "surrounded" is expressed in the feminine gender based on the term "deities," for he is actually a son of the gods (*devaputta*).

Because they exist in the heavens (*divi*), he said "dibba" (divine), meaning "be reborn in the world of the gods. Because they are desirable, they are [referred to] by the term *kāmabandhana* (bonds of sensual desire);

likewise, because their individual natures are not intermingled with one another, they are [referred to] by the term *kāmakoṭṭhāsa* (spheres of sensual desire). *Upetā* means arrived at, endowed with.

*Paricārayamānā* means enjoying themselves. Indeed, having regard for this word, the expression *kāmaguṇehi* (by the strands of sensual pleasure) is an instrumental case used in the sense of the agent.
In the sense of being conjoined with [the previous], it is said "delighting" (*ramamānā*) because they were moving while delighting, having regard for what preceded.
Alternatively, "sporting" (*paricārayamānā*) means causing to move about completely or on all sides; thus he says, "moving their faculties about.
For in the first method, the word *paricaraṇa* has the sense of experiencing, whereas in the second method, it has the sense of turning around. And as for that phrase, "at that time":

The time has been stated. *Adhunā* means "now. "He wandered about" (*so vicarī*)—this is the connection. "By means of the strands of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇehi*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of a cause.
"Enveloped" (*ovuto*) means having a mind thus obscured that its true nature is not known; "shrouded" (*nivuto*) and "enveloped" (*pariyonaddho*) are synonyms for that same state.
Therefore he said, "the conqueror of the world" (*lokābhibhūto*). "Pre-eminent" (*āsabhim*) means excellent, as when one speaks like the Bodhisatta: "I am the foremost in the world," and so forth.
To the question, "What is the purpose of mere seeing? he says: "by way of... pe ...vasena. The meaning is: by way of experiencing the portions of sensual pleasure established in that Nandana Grove.
"Naradevānaṃ" means of those deities who are male; hence he says "devapurisānaṃ" (of divine males).
It is said that "three times ten" because a number that is slightly more or less than what is required for calculation does not count. "Tettiṃsānaṃ" (of the thirty-three).

This is indeed a conventional usage (*ruḷhī*) that must be stated. The intended meaning is [that they are endowed with fame] by way of what is called a retinue (*parivāra*), not by way of what is called reputation (*kitti*).

For reputation has as its cause qualities such as virtuous conduct (*sīla-ācāra*) and so forth. When glory (*yasa*) is intended—as in the statement, "The Tāvatiṃsa gods are long-lived, beautiful, and abound in happiness"—it is possible to say "endowed with glory" without making any distinction at all.
“Noble female disciple” means a stream-enterer; some say it refers to a once-returner.
“Having turned back her intention” means having reversed the intention of that deity by showing that the true nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva) is not as you, O foolish one, imagine it to be.
Nibbāna alone is what is called absolute happiness. For sense pleasures are suffering and subject to change—this is the intended meaning.
Having rejected her intention: although formations belonging even to the fourth plane are indeed impermanent, they do not come within the range of comprehension (*sammasana*);

therefore, the inclusion of the three planes is made by way of comprehension. "Having been" means having come into being and arisen through the convergence of conditions where they previously did not exist;
by this, their aspect of existence is shown. "In the sense of non-existence" means...
By the state of destruction, which consists in the cessation of continuity.

They are impermanent (anicca) and unstable; for that very reason, they are impermanent because one does not desire them, thinking, "These pleasures are mine. Their intrinsic nature is arising and passing away;
that is, their nature is to arise and cease moment by moment. Therefore he said: "[The synonyms] beginning with 'arising... [are] a synonym for the former.
Or, it is said that "yasmā vā" (or because) and so forth is a synonym for the final cause. "Tadanantara" means in between those two, arising and passing away.

"Vemajjhaṭṭhāna" (the middle position) refers to the moment of stability (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*). As for those who say, "There is no stability of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārānaṃ ṭhiti*)," their view is incorrect.
For just as the state of destruction (*bhaṅgāvatthā*) of that very same phenomenon is distinct from its state of arising (*uppādāvatthā*), [so too is the state of stability].
One falls into the position that what is desired arises as one thing and ceases as another;

thus, the state of that which has arisen when it is facing dissolution must be accepted, and that very state is the moment of duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*). For it is not possible to understand that "that which is arising is simultaneously perishing.
"Designated as tranquility" means that Nibbāna alone, designated as ultimate tranquility, is happiness, and not the sensual pleasures intended by you—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the *Nandanasutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Nandati-sutta*:
Regarding the word "rejoices" (*nandati*), he says "is satisfied" (*tussati*) because here rejoicing is the function of sensual craving accompanied by rapture; therefore—
The meaning is that he is joyful and delighted by the satisfaction of his desires. "Puttimā" means "one who has sons.
Since the word *mā* can also signify abundance, he says "bahuputto" (one with many sons). Showing the purpose for including the state of having many sons, he says "tassa hi," and so forth.
"Of grain" (*dhaññassa*) is a genitive case used in relation to the word "filling" (*pūrenti*). He said this; that is, he spoke with reference to this meaning.
The meaning is: "having such an intention. *Gosāmiko* means "one who possesses cows" (*gomā*). Here too, the word *mā* signifies abundance.
*Gorasasampattiṃ* means "the excellence resulting from cow-products. *Upadhī* is the plural form of the personal pronoun. *Hi* is a particle used in the sense of a reason.
They are called *nandanā* because they cause delight, that is, they generate joy and gladness. Granted that [they are so called] because they serve as the basis for suffering...
In the absolute sense (*nippariyāyato*), sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) deserve to be called "substrata" (*upadhī*); however, with reference to that deity's intention, it was said:

"because they are the basis for pleasure. Since the other two terms have as their cause the ground for the defilements (*kilesavatthu*), although all suffering in *saṃsāra* has the defilements as its cause, it is especially the evil states (*pāpadhammā*) that produce rebirth in the woeful states (*apāyūpapatti*).
He said: "The defilements (kilesa) also [are so called] because they serve as the basis for the suffering of the states of misery. "Bringing near" means leading toward or producing.
One who is of human birth but, due to the scarcity of food and clothing, is full of suffering like a hungry ghost (peta), is thus a "human-ghost" (manussapeta).
One who is of human birth but, being of the aforementioned nature, is struck by misfortune and harmed by others as if he were one in hell, is thus a "human-hell-being" (manussanerayika).
It is like one who causes a fruit to fall from a tree by [shaking] it.

"In the same way, in nine ways" means that just as one who has children grieves for the sake of his children due to the destruction of those children across the three periods of time, so too does one who has cattle grieve for the sake of his cattle in nine modes.

The construction is: "The five bases of sensual pleasure also cause a person to grieve. "Of him" refers to one who further craves after them. "Of the one desiring" refers to one in whom sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) has arisen.
"Jantu" means a living being (*satta*). "If they decline and if they perish": "like one pierced by an arrow" means like one who has been struck by a shaft;
"is afflicted" (*ruppati*) means it undergoes transformation, which is to say, it grieves. For a person, grieving is the condition for the onset of sorrow.

"There are no acquisitions" (*upadhayo natthi*): Granted, the acquisitions consisting of defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), and the physical substrate (*upadhi*) are indeed non-existent for one whose taints are exhausted, due to the attainment of the Path.

Since the elements have been ceased, how then can there be the acquisitions of the aggregates? Even at the time when he still possesses a residue of clinging (*saupādisesa*), those [acquisitions] do not exist as causes for the arising of further existence;
this, moreover, is the case at the time when there is no residue of clinging (*anupādisesa*). Therefore it is said: "He is without acquisitions, one whose great taints are destroyed.
The commentary on the *Nandatisutta* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the *Natthiputtasamasutta* 13.

Because "affection for a son" (*puttapema*) is included by the mention of "son" (*putta*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound, he says "equal to affection for a son" (*puttapemasama*).
"Equal to cows" (*gosama*) means made equal by cows. Therefore, he says "equal to cows. "Equal to the sun" (*sūriyasama*) means equal to the sun.

And this possessive suffix [in *sūriyābhāya*] refers to a part [of the whole]. Here, it is understood that "light" (*ābhā*) is a part, because it is spoken of as being "immediately following" [the sun];
thus he says, "equal to the light of the sun," and so forth. They are called *sarā* (lakes) because they are remembered (*saranti*) for their state of great floods;
they are vast reservoirs of water. All of them have the ocean as their limit (*samuddaparamā*), because its further shore is unseen by those on this side.
The meaning of this verse should be understood according to the method explained in the first verse of the *Natthi attasamaṃ pemaṃ* (There is no love equal to self-love) collection:

namely, that there is no love equal to love for oneself. This is illustrated by the story of the woman who, unable to endure the heat of the summer in a waterless wilderness, laid her crying infant on the ground in her lap and stood over him until she died.
It should be illustrated. Therefore he said: “For even having abandoned mother, father, and so forth, [one abandons] sons, daughters, and so forth. And likewise he said:
“Having searched all directions with the mind, one finds nothing anywhere dearer than oneself.”
"Thus, the self is dear to others as well;
therefore, one who desires their own welfare should not harm another.
There is no wealth equal to grain, for it is upon that [grain] that the livelihood of beings who subsist on food depends.

"At such a time" means at a time of famine. "Shining only in one part" is said because even the sun is incapable of pervading the four great continents with its radiance at a single moment, let alone others;

however, through the power of the Bodhisatta’s knowledge of arising and passing away, the entire field of his birth became a single expanse of light—thus it is said, "Wisdom... is able. Darkness... [is dispelled].
It is called "dispelling" because it proceeds all at once, pervading without exception that state wherein wisdom—such as the knowledge of past lives and so forth—occurs.
However, the statement "as far as the Ābhassara realm when rain falls" is said according to common usage.
The commentary on the Naṭṭhaputtasama Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Khattiya Sutta* 14.
One is called a *khattiya* because he protects beings from disputes concerning territory (*khettato*). The deity speaks according to his own inclination.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "bipeds, etc.," quadrupeds, wives, and children are included. By the word "etcetera" in "the Buddhas, etc.,"... [the rest of the passage continues].
The noble thoroughbred, the good horse, and the son of a good wife. Regarding the phrase "the best of bipeds," it is not intended here as a restrictive rule that he is the best *only* among bipeds;

rather, it is intended that he is simply the best. Therefore, the meaning here is this: the Fully Awakened One is indeed the best among bipeds and others because he has arisen therein, since there is no one superior to him among all beings.
Therefore he said, “But when this [mind] is arising,” and so forth. One who understands what is the cause and what is not the cause is called *ājānīya*.
“Have it seized,” meaning: have the wild beast seized in such a way that it does not get wet with water. Some read “*asussūsā*”;
*āsuṇamāna* means one who, being respectful, accepts what is said.
The commentary on the *Khattiya-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Saṇamāna-sutta*. 15.
"When midday has stood": this refers to when midday has stood, having passed the first half [of the day] but not yet reached the second half.
"Sannisinnesu" means when they have completely sat down for the purpose of dispelling fatigue. The designation is made by changing the letter *da* to *va*.
Therefore he said: "in those who are sitting down, resting. "Of all beings" refers to all beings who subsist on nutriment;
it is the time when their bodies are heated by the heat of summer and the postures (iriyāpatha) are weakened—referring to the postures such as standing and so forth.
The time when [the forest] was not yet capable [of producing sound]. "It seems to hum" means it makes a sound, just as another great forest would according to the method to be described.
Therefore he said: "This is like that," referring to the joints of a hollow bamboo—meaning the joints of a large bamboo that has split and become hollow.
Not finding a second companion, she spoke thus out of agitation due to dissatisfaction. "Not small happiness" means abundant.
"Exalted is the bliss of seclusion.
This refers to one who has entered an empty dwelling for the sake of living alone; by this, he shows physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).

"Of one whose mind is tranquil through the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth by means of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth"—by this, he shows mental seclusion (*cittaviveka*). [This is said] because of seeing the danger in *saṃsāra*.

For a bhikkhu who has attained both kinds of seclusion and has thus gained a delight that transcends human states—a delight that is superhuman—this refers to the delight of meditative development (*bhāvanārati*).
"In front" means in the preceding part; "behind" means in the subsequent part.
"Another" means someone else. Alternatively, "in front" means in the future, with reference to the future; "behind" means in the past, with reference to the past.
Because it does not obstruct practice. "Another" (*para*) refers to anger (*kodha*), due to its nature of defiling the mind. "Not another" (*apara*) refers to greed (*lobha*);
if that does not exist, by this he shows the absence of both longing for the future and grieving for the past.
"It becomes exceedingly comfortable" means that with the disappearance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), which is the foremost of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the hindrances are suppressed.
By means of *jhāna*, there is an exceedingly comfortable dwelling. "Living alone" refers to one who dwells in seclusion in the forest with craving as his only companion.
"The rest is just like that": whatever else needs to be said here is exactly the same as what was stated in the first verse.
The commentary on the Saṇamāna Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Niddātandi Sutta: 16.
In the last month [of the rains], having returned from his almsround after the meal, he spread out his outer robe folded fourfold.
Having abbreviated the text to simply "mindful and clearly comprehending on the right side," it is stated that "he has fallen asleep.
The stream of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-sota*) unmixed with functional consciousnesses is neutral sleep. For that is capable of arising even in those whose taints are destroyed;
however, what is intended here is the sloth and torpor that arises in the periods preceding and following that [neutral sleep].
Sleep (*niddā*) generally occurs at indefinite times for those whose taints (*āsava*) have not been destroyed. To show that its opposite exists at definite times, he said:
"Excessive eating... [etc. ...the idleness of a newcomer. Idleness (*tandī*) refers to the four unwholesome aggregates that are the opposites of energy (*vīriya*) and are caused by physical sloth.
*Tandī* is a designation of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). *Tandiyanā* is a designation of its mode of manifestation (*ākāra*).
*Tandīmanatā* is the state of the mind having become languid. *Ālasya* is the taking up of a state of laziness. *Ālasyāyitattaṃ* is the arrival at a state of laziness.
*Kāyavijambhanā* is the stretching out of the body. *Ukkaṇṭhitatā* belonging to the unwholesome side is dissatisfaction associated with the unwholesome side.
*Bhattakilamatha* is the exhaustion arising in the body due to the food, which has the meal as its basis, as previously described.
"Defiled" means one whose mind is defiled by the weakening of wisdom. Because the mind is not concentrated, its manifestation is obstructed.
Since the "illumination of the Noble Path" is simply its arising, he said: "The meaning is that it does not shine, it does not become manifest.
For the Noble Path does not proceed under the name of "non-light" (ajoti).
"By energy co-nascent with the path" means by energy co-nascent with both mundane and supramundane paths; for here, the "mixed path" is intended.

"Having brought forth" (*nīharitvā*) means "for the sake of bringing forth. This word *tvā* has the sense of a causal suffix, as in such expressions as "and having seen with wisdom" (*paññāya cassa disvā*).
By this, the statement "the path is purified" is justified. Some read it as "the noble path is purified" (*ariyamaggaṃ visujjhati*).
The commentary on the Niddātandī Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Dukkarasutta: 17.
"They endure what is hard to endure" means they endure suffering that is difficult to bear; and because it is difficult to undertake, that suffering is hard to endure.

“Difficult to endure” means by way of its constant application. “By one who is unskilled” means by one who is not proficient due to the absence of that wisdom termed *veyyattiya* (dexterity), which is capable of discerning those factors that are conducive or non-conducive to the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*). Therefore he said, “by a fool.
He said, “the duty of a recluse” (*samaṇadhamma*), meaning that state in the presence of which one is called a recluse. By this [he refers to the verse]: “Difficult to do and difficult to endure...”
By this half-verse, "and by the asceticism of one who is incompetent," he shows this; that is, he shows the following matter now being stated.
"Abhidanta" means a tooth that overcomes; the meaning is "the upper tooth.
For it functions by specifically overcoming the other [lower tooth], which is like a mortar [overcoming] a pestle, especially at the time of chewing something. "Ādhāya" means by way of pressing down.
"Setting aside. "Striking against the palate" means as if striking the region of the palate. "With the mind" means with a wholesome state of consciousness (*kusala-citta*).
"The mind" refers to an unwholesome state of consciousness (*akusala-citta*). "Having restrained" means having suppressed it by way of affliction so that there is no excessive manifestation.
"To the end of life" (*āpāṇakoṭika*) means having the limit of the end of life; the meaning is "living until the very end. "It constricts" means it is a constriction (*sambādha*).
"Obstructive": by way of unwise thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, there are many perils (*parissaya*).
"Foot" (*pada*) means that the mind goes (*pajjati*) therein; it refers to the object (*ārammaṇa*). A "foot" that is itself a posture is a "posture-foot" (*iriyāpathapada*).
"Neck and four feet" means those five, with the neck as the fifth. Or, they are "conjoined" (*samodahanti*) or have the cause for being conjoined (*samodhāna*); this is the meaning here.
He said: “‘Having joined together’ means having properly placed [the mind] inside, having caused it to enter within.
He speaks of the internal sphere of the range of activity (*gocarajjhatta*) within one’s own objective sphere (*ārammaṇakapāla*). “Joining together” means while joining together.

“Independent” means not dependent upon any phenomenon belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) by way of craving, views, or dogmatic adherence. “Non-injurious” means through the abandoning of the signs of injury.
“Established in the nature of rescuing” means established in the form of lifting one out from the ruin of virtue;
the meaning is that it is endowed with compassion. Therefore he said, “depending on compassion.
The commentary to the *Dukkarasutta* is concluded.
8. Commentary on the *Hirīsutta* 18.
“He restrains” means he prevents [the speech] and does not allow it to proceed. “The deity asks.
“He removes” means he takes away; the meaning is that he guards [the speech] so that there is no basis for abuse whatsoever. “He awakens” is a term for a charioteer.
A noble steed does not strike at its own body, for it understands what is appropriate.
There is no one truly free from false and groundless abuse among foolish people, because of their constant engagement in slandering others. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“They blame the one who sits in silence; they blame the one who speaks much.”
“They blame even one who speaks moderately; there is no one in the world who is not blamed.

Or, *tanuyā* means “a few. Therefore he said, “few” (*appakā*). “Always mindful” (*sadā satā*) is a statement of the reason for the state of being restrained by moral shame (*hirī*). “Having reached” (*pappuyya*) means having attained or arrived at. It is called *nibbāna* because it has emerged from craving (*vāna*);
it is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). The commentary on the *Hirīsutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the Kuṭikāsutta 19.

"Inside" (anto) means within the belly. "In the sense of a dwelling place" (vasanaṭṭhānaṭṭhena) means by way of being a residence. "Family lineage" (kulapaveṇi) means family custom or family tradition.
"In the sense of continuity" (santānakaṭṭhena) means by way of being the bond for the continuity of the family. Thus, [the meaning] of the question asked by all the terms—
It is stated that "the particle [is used] in the sense of granting permission" (*anujānanavasena*) with the words "one-shoulder-speech" (*ekamsavacane*).

Having established that Mahāpajāpatī was her maternal aunt, her foster-mother, and her mother, it is stated without distinction as "because she went forth after abandoning [the world]. The connection is made by supplying the word "there is none" (*natthi*) following "because she went forth after abandoning.
Furthermore, by the very statement of the absence of dwelling in a mother’s womb and so forth, [the absence of] bondage within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is shown.

It was not grasped because its non-existence had been demonstrated. It is said that this deity did not understand [the Buddhas' qualities] in the same way that ordinary worldlings do not know the qualities of the Buddhas;
therefore, she said, "Having bound on my armor," and so forth.
The commentary on the Kuṭikāsutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta. 20.
Because it causes burning through its scorching nature, it is called *tapodā* (a "scorching stream"). This is the name of that lake. Thus he said, "of the lake of hot water.
From there—from the water-lake in the abode of the Nāgas—a river named *tapodā* flows forth. For that is the river.
"It ascends to the surface of the earth. The phrase "born such as this" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

They say that by "the world of the departed" (petaloka), the hells such as the Iron Cauldron (lohakumbhi) are intended here. However, many departed beings dwell within the forests at the foot of the mountains starting from the edge of the lake;
this matter should be illustrated by the *Petavatthu-pāḷi* and the *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta*. "From where it flows" means from which lake this [water] comes. "Sweet water" (sātodaka).
“Sweet-watered” (*madhurodaka*): “Setodaka” means water that is completely pure, that is, untroubled water. “From there” (*tato*) means from the Tapodā and other such sources.
“Prosperous” (*samiddha*) means well-succeeded through the perfection of its constituent parts; hence he said, “handsome,” and so forth.

“Devoted to striving” (*padhānika*) means one who is intent upon the dhamma of contemplation (*sammasana*), or one for whom that [striving] exists here. A “lodging” (*senāsana*) is one where the doors and windows are well-secured.
Having caused them to take up the temperature by covering [the water] with them.
"Going while making it public" means going while entering a state free of water, as if before the time of bathing.

In order to reject what is improper (*avatta*) and to demonstrate what is proper (*vatta*), it was stated first: "In that regard... one must not descend," and so forth. [This concludes] the surveying of all directions.
Just as [trees] are established near water for the purpose of making known to people that the bathing place is secluded;

the purpose of establishing stumps and so forth is for the purpose of placing robes and other items. The purpose of clearing away [obstructions] is for the purpose of removing non-human beings (*amanussa*).
The purpose of the inverted position is to prevent the upper body from being straightened or uncovered even at that moment. It should be placed right on top of the robe.
"Having set it aside here or there. "Near water" means in the vicinity of water. "The place where it has been soaked" refers to the spot that has become damp with perspiration.
"It should be spread out" for the purpose of drying it. "Storing it away" is for the purpose of easily taking it up again and wearing it.
"Descending to the measure of the navel" is because at that point it attains the characteristic of being concealed from the water. "Without causing waves," and so forth.

This is a demonstration of acting with restraint. "Having wrapped around the lower garment" means having thrown on and fastened the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) so that it completely encircles the region of the waist.
The intention is that even his physical appearance became serene for one who truly experiences the recollection of meditation (*bhāvanānussati*). A recluse (*samaṇa*).

"To restrain" means to restrain one's own mind that has fallen under the sway of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Led by sensual desire" (*kāmūpanītā*) means having a mind that has approached sensual pleasure;
or alternatively, having a mind led toward the Elder by the defilement of sensual desire.
"Without enjoying" means without experiencing. Since [the object] is already implied by the sense [of the context], he says "the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇe*).
“Bhikkhasī” means you beg. And that is by way of the practice of begging for alms; thus he says, “you wander for alms.
The time for the heavy indulgence in sensual pleasures is specifically the stage of early youth; thus he says, “the time of tender youth. “Obhaggena” means with a body bent in the middle.
For at the time of old age, the body of beings becomes bent at the waist.
*Voti* is a mere particle, as in such phrases as *ye hi vo ariyā*. *Sattānaṃ* is a general term, not referring exclusively to human beings.
*Dehanikkhepanaṃ* means the place where the physical body is laid down. *Animittā* means those for whom no sign exists;
the meaning is that they are devoid of signs by which one might recognize them, such as [the thought], "This one lives for so long," and so forth. *Na nāyare* means they are not known.
"From this point on" (*ito paraṃ*) means "at another time" (*paraṃ*) in this context. By this, inclusion even for a short period of time is established.

Furthermore, "onward" (*paraṃ*) is intended here as the period from the maximum lifespan down to the minimum, because beyond that there is no life for sentient beings. "Due to the absence of delimitation" (*vavatthānābhāvato*) means due to the absence of delimitation by way of time.
And in this context, "delimitation" (*vavatthānaṃ*) should be understood as a boundary (*paricchedo*), not as non-confusion (*asaṅkaro*).

*Vavatthānaṃ* means determination or certainty. In the phrases "the stage of the *abbuda*" and so forth, the word *kāla* (time) should be applied individually to each, as in "the time of the *abbuda*" and "the time of the *pesī*.
Here, *kāla* refers to the specific periods such as morning (*pubbaṇha*) and so on. Therefore he said, "even in the morning," and so forth. The connection here is:
"one must fall [from existence] with this very body. "In many ways" means: for those born in a city, [to a village], and for those born in a village...
"Those born in a city [return] to a city; those born in a forest [return] to a forest; those born in a countryside [return] to a countryside," and so forth in many such ways.
"By one who has passed away from here" means by one who has passed away from this destination. "Here" means in this destination.

"Like an ox yoked to a machine" means that just as an ox yoked to a machine does not overstep the machine, even so time [does not overstep] the five destinations (*gati*); thus should the application of the simile be understood.
“This is the time” means this is the time of death. “In the final period” means in the latter stage of life. “The three boundaries of age”:

by one who has transgressed the three boundaries of age beginning with the first. For having completely transgressed the boundaries of the first two stages of life and having transgressed the initial boundary of the final stage, he is described in that way.
[As it is said: “For this duty of the recluse... it is not possible to perform.”
Having stated that matter, the words beginning with "Then indeed" were spoken in order to demonstrate it in detail.

"To grasp" means to grasp by way of fixing [the teaching] in the heart, both according to the text and its meaning. "To enjoy" means to experience the happiness of maintaining the Dhamma as it has been taught.
From the speaking of one person, he first recites a verse or a sutta; when that is finished, the other Dhamma-preacher...
Expanding upon that very [teaching], he delivers a discourse on the Dhamma; this is a *sarabhañña* (recitation) discourse on the Dhamma.
Following the sequence of the suttas and verses until the conclusion, the chanting is a *sarabhañña* discourse on the Dhamma. Saying, "May time not pass me by," he speaks thus:
"This is my time for performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*). Beyond that, [he says] "the final stage... another..."
He says, "It is time. By saying, "I shall eat at the right time... [etc. ...therefore I go for alms without eating," he explains his own practice together with its cause and its benefit.
This is said with reference to that reason for his reverence: "Then that deity, having established herself upon the earth..."
This has been said. He spoke the words beginning with "But as a youth," because [the state] was attained through being overcome by greed.
"Endowed with all success" means endowed with all forms of success, namely, success in wealth and success in retinue. "Adornment and avoidance" refers to the act of adorning oneself.
"One who has not played" means one who has never played before. And here, "playing" refers to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; thus he says, "one who has not eaten."
"Play with unfulfilled desires" means the application of experiencing desires that have not yet been fulfilled. "Visible" (*sandiṭṭha*) means they are seen by oneself;

being visible, they are "visible-in-this-life" (*sandiṭṭhika*), meaning visible through one's own direct personal experience. "Temporal" (*kālika*) means those for whom a specific time has arrived; they are the temporal ones.
"Immediately after thought" means immediately after the thought that was desired; the meaning is: in whatever mode of object one has desired. For this very reason, he said:
“Immediately after the mind, the experience of whatever object one desires does not occur,” and so forth.
“Because it is to be obtained immediately after the mind” means because the fruit is to be obtained immediately after the concentration-mind that has no interval.

“Even among those who have gathered” means even among those who have assembled. “One whose desire is fulfilled” means one whose desire has been realized. “Picture-makers by the acquisition of forms, book-makers...”
Image-makers are those who fashion forms from ivory, wood, metal, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), actors and others who assume various forms and disguises are included.
Regarding the phrase "at the other doors," those such as perfumers, florists, and cooks should be mentioned here.

"He" refers to the Elder Samiddhi. "By means of the attainment of his desired [objects]" means by means of the attainment of his retinue, enjoyments, and requisites. "Of the suffering that is to be reached..."
Of bodily and mental suffering that is to be obtained by way of encountering and guarding against sensual pleasures (*kāma*).
Of despair (*upāyāsa*): of intense distress that has arisen. Some read "of one who is dissatisfied" (*vissātassa*). Some read "by means of reviewing-knowledge" (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇena*).
"Time" (*kāla*) refers to that which is to be awaited thus: "At such-and-such a time the fruit occurs"; that which is not such is "non-time" (*akāla*). "In this" (*ettha*): in these [cases].
Regarding the nine supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*). "The method of 'Come and See'" (*ehipassavidhi*) refers to the verbal expression of the method occurring as "Come and see.
Alternatively, *upaneyya* means that which is to be led; that itself is *opanayyika*. "By the wise" (*viññūhi*) means by those who have penetrated the truths.

Since these are exclusively those such as the *ugghaṭitaññū* (those who understand through a condensed statement) and so forth, he says "by the *ugghaṭitaññū* and others. Regarding the term "individually" (*paccattaṃ*):
The meaning should be understood according to the locative case as "in oneself," hence he said, "in oneself, in oneself" (*attani attanī*).
"Connected with all the phrases" means that it should be understood as being connected individually with each [phrase], such as: "How is the danger here greater? How is it timeless?
"New" means young, not having been ordained for long. Referring to those who have reached the characteristics required to be instructors of bhikkhunīs, [he says] "from twenty years..."
It is said, "starting from the Elder. Here, by "the Dispensation" (sāsana), he means the Three Pitakas which comprise the Three Trainings; thus he says, "by the Dhamma," and so forth.
In that context, "Dhamma-vinaya" means the Discipline (vinaya) herein [is established] by means of the Dhamma, without the use of force or weapons.
Or, "Dhamma-vinaya" means the Discipline herein is for the sake of the Dhamma, not for the sake of material gain. Or, it is discipline according to the Dhamma, not according to what is non-Dhamma.
The Dhamma-Vinaya. Or, the Blessed One is the Dhamma, the Lord of the Dhamma, because he has the Dhamma as his body;

it is the Vinaya of that Teacher who is designated as "Dhamma," and not [the Vinaya] of those who rely on mere reasoning—thus it is the Dhamma-Vinaya. It is discipline within the Dhamma, not discipline outside the Dhamma.

And it is called "Dhamma" because it sustains (dhāreti) beings who practice according to the instructions, preventing them from falling into the states of misery, [protecting them] from all defilements.
It is called *vinaya* because it disciplines (*vineti*); thus, it is the *dhammavinaya*. Therefore, he said: "Both of these are names for the Teaching (*sāsana*) itself.
*Dhammavinaya* means discipline that is joined with the Dhamma; it is like a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses.

Alternatively, *dhammavinaya* means both the Dhamma and the Vinaya; [the compound refers to] that *dhammavinaya*. For the perfection of the state of being *dhammavinaya* is established through the statement that the Teacher is the very embodiment of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
Because the Dhamma and the Vinaya distinguish one another. In the Abhidhamma as well, there is the term "Vinaya," thus establishing the pair of Dhamma and Vinaya;

and because they are spoken of as the taught and the formulated, the Dhamma and Vinaya are established. The Dhamma is taught in four ways: by way of demonstration (*sandassana*), instigation (*samādāpana*), incitement (*samuttejana*), and encouragement (*sampahaṃsana*);

the Vinaya is formulated in four ways: by way of virtue (*sīla*), conduct (*ācāra*), and defeat (*parājita*). The practice of the Dhamma is one's own domain, while the formulation of the Vinaya is the domain of others.
The domain of the Buddha. The Dhamma is taught by way of a method (pariyāya), while the Vinaya is established by way of the non-method (nippariyāya).

The teaching of the Dhamma has the intended meaning as its primary focus; the establishment of the Vinaya has the literal meaning of the words as its primary focus. The Dhamma has ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca) as its primary focus; the Vinaya has conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) as its primary focus. The Dhamma has purity of disposition (āsaya) as its primary focus; the Vinaya has purity of practice (payoga) as its primary focus.

Through the accomplishment of the two types of action, there is the accomplishment of the Dhamma and the Vinaya. For by means of the Dhamma, the accomplishment of instruction is achieved; by means of the Vinaya, the accomplishment of exhortation is achieved.

By means of the Dhamma, the accomplishment of discourse on the Dhamma is achieved; by means of the Vinaya, the accomplishment of noble silence is achieved. Through the avoidance of the two kinds of blameworthy conduct, there is the accomplishment of the Dhamma and the Vinaya.

For by means of the Dhamma, the accomplishment of the relinquishment of natural (pakati) blameworthiness is specifically achieved; by means of the Vinaya, the accomplishment of the relinquishment of conventional (paññatti) blameworthiness is achieved.
The accomplishment of the two qualities—both common and uncommon—to householders and those who have gone forth.

From the pair of being "much-heard" (*bahussuta*) and "inspired by what is heard" (*sutasaddha*), there arises the accomplishment of the Dharma and the Vinaya through the distinction between mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*), their thorough study (*pariyāpuṇana*), and dwelling in the Dharma (*dhammavihāra*);

and from the distinction between the upholders of the Dharma (*dhammadhara*) and the upholders of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*). Through the accomplishment of the two refuges, there arises the accomplishment of the Dharma and the Vinaya. Herein, for sentient beings...
The refuge is twofold: the Dhamma and the self. Therein, the Dhamma well-practiced is a refuge, for it is said: "The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by the Dhamma.
A well-tamed self is also a refuge, according to the statement: "The self is indeed its own lord. Therefore it was said:
"By the establishment of the two refuges, there is the establishment of the Dhamma and the Vinaya. Therein, as for its establishment of the Dhamma:

And since the accomplishment of the Vinaya depends on both of these, he said, showing both: “For herein, the two Piṭakas are spoken of by means of the Dhamma, and the Vinaya Piṭaka by means of the Vinaya.
“Having arrived recently” means having approached just now, not long ago.
“Having placed him in a great place” means in a place of great importance, for the purpose of demonstrating his high status, together with his own retinue.
Having announced that she had been set aside. "By the great assembly" means by the customary practice of approaching, paying homage, and engaging in conversation.
It is said that all those sitting down sit while leaving that spot vacant. "By way of making firm" means by way of strengthening.
It is said that this deity was endowed with wisdom and of a proud nature; therefore, she would not listen to my teaching without first abandoning her pride.

Thinking that it might be possible to penetrate [the truth], the Blessed One, speaking at the outset in a way difficult to understand for the purpose of subduing pride, spoke two stanzas beginning with "those who perceive what is expressible" (*akkheyyasaññino*), thereby distinguishing for those desiring to know the temporal nature of that [Dhamma] and the directly visible nature of the Dhamma itself.
It is called "what is expressible" (*akkheyya*) because it can be expressed in various ways by means of such things as the marks of a householder, designations, and specific names. Thus he said:
"Because they are the basis for the discourses. "Of these" means of beings (*sattānaṃ*). "Established" means set forth or occurring; that is, they are attached (*āsatta*).

Let them be attached by way of the five attachments such as sensual desire (*kāmasaṅga*); but how is it with the others? For even one who has gone toward what is undesirable, when doubting in the manner of "Is this so?
and so forth, is indeed said to be "attached" to that object because he does not abandon it; likewise, one who has fallen into distraction is attached to the object of distraction.
As for the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), there is simply nothing more to be said regarding their state of attachment.

"The yoke of Death" means the bond of Death; the meaning is the nature of being subject to death. Because those who have not fully understood the basis [of existence] have not transcended death, they are to be employed by Death according to its will;
and because they remain within the very range of the successive commands hurled here and there, therefore—

It is said: “They come with their application... [and so on]...”. Since the phenomena of the three planes are called *kāma* in the sense of being desirable, and because they are to be obtained at a particular time, their temporality (*kālikatā*) is proclaimed here by the word "to be told" (*akkheyya*). Therefore he said:
“Thus, by this verse, the temporal *kāmas* are spoken of. For all phenomena of the three planes are desirable, and because they are temporal, [they are included].
The true nature of sensual pleasures has been thus described. This verse also illuminates that very same meaning; therefore, these [verses] have been spoken by you for that purpose alone.

Furthermore, those beings who are established in the five aggregates through views, craving, and so forth, and who, clinging to them as "woman," "man," "I," or "mine," enjoy sensual pleasures—they do not transcend death. Thus it is here.
It is said that "the meaning of 'timeliness' regarding sensual pleasures has been explained" by stating, "sensual pleasures have been declared to be timely.

This is "full understanding through knowledge" (ñātapariññā), which is the wisdom that delimits phenomena—both material and immaterial—after having understood them according to their characteristics and so forth. Therefore, he says, "having thus made them known," and so on.
Furthermore, by the very mention of their "proximate cause" (padaṭṭhāna) here, the conditions for those material and immaterial phenomena are also implied.
"Grasped" (*gahita*) should be understood as including the discernment of conditions (*paccaya-pariggaha*). "He traverses" (*tīreti*), "he weighs" (*tuleti*), "he investigates" (*vīmaṃsati*).

By the phrase "by forty-two aspects," he shows the great insight (*mahā-vipassanā*) that has reached its culmination. Those aspects, however, are to be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*.
[This is shown] by such passages as, "By the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), one abandons the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*)," and so forth, even at the moment of insight.
Abandonment can indeed be attained by way of partial relinquishment; however, demonstrating full understanding through abandonment (*pahānapariññā*) by way of complete relinquishment, he said:
"By the supreme path... this is full understanding through abandonment. And likewise he said: "Thus, by means of the three kinds of full understanding," and so forth.

"The declarer" (*akkhātāraṃ*) means that which is to be declared, not that which is to be spoken of (*akkheyyaka*). Therefore he said: "The agent by way of action," and so forth. "The agent" (*kārakaṃ*).
And he states the proof: "He does not conceive" means he does not set in motion conceiving; "the declarer" refers to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

Alternatively, "for that [cause] does not exist for him" means that cause does not exist or is not found in that one whose taints are destroyed—namely, that cause consisting of views, craving, and so forth, by which the five aggregates, the objects of declaration, might be called "Tissa," or "Phussa," or "woman."
Or, one might speak while adhering to the notion that it is a "man"—thus the meaning here should be understood.
Because they are worthy of worship by humans, nāgas, and others, the term "yakkha" is a common designation for all deities; thus, even a daughter of the gods is called a "yakkhī.
"The ineffable" (akkheyya) refers to the path of abandonment through the full understanding of abandonment, and Nibbāna, which is its object, is also included.
"He does not conceive" means that for one whose taints are destroyed, there is the attainment of the fruit; thus it is said, "the ninefold supramundane dhamma has been explained.
"Superior" means better by way of superior birth and so forth.

When those are taken, that is, when those three types of conceit—conceit of superiority, etc.—are taken, the three conceits of superiority, the three conceits of equality, and the three conceits of inferiority are indeed included. He...
"Person" (puggala) refers to that person who has not abandoned conceit. "By that very conceit," meaning by that which serves as the cause.
Regarding the phrase "by the first half-verse," he says, "the sensual pleasures of the present life were spoken of," because the objects of desire (vatthukāmā) were mentioned in the first portion.
"Mode" (vidhā) means that which is established or placed in a distinct manner; it is a division. "Of what mode? means how it is established.

The meaning is: "In what manner does it proceed? It is *vidhā* because it burns in various ways (*vividhena ākārena*) according to its inferior and other qualities, and because it sustains (*upadhāraṇa*).
Regarding the word *mānesu*, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause; thus, the meaning is "on account of conceit" (*mānahetu*).
"It does not waver" means it does not tremble, because it does not abandon its own perfectly pure nature.

Wisdom (*paññā*) is described as "reckoning" (*saṅkhā*). Wisdom is the thorough reflection (*yoniso paṭisaṅkhāna*). A "reckoner" (*saṅkhāyaka*) is an accountant by way of counting, summing up, and so forth.
"Conceptual proliferation-reckoning" (*papañca-saṅkhā*) refers to the portions of proliferation such as conceit and the like.

That by which those various phenomena are correctly reckoned—that is, established according to their true nature—is "reckoning," namely wisdom. It is the calculation, the delimitation, by means of "one, two," and so forth.
*Saṅkhā* means calculation (*gaṇanā*). It is called *saṅkhā* because it is reckoned (*saṅkhāyati*), that is, analyzed into parts; thus it is a portion (*koṭṭhāsa*).

It is called *saṅkhā* because it causes one to perceive [something] as "a being," "a person," and so forth; thus it is a designation (*paṇṇatti*) such as "day" and so on. The one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) has abandoned them—meaning he has thoroughly relinquished them—because of the complete abandonment of lust and the other defilements.
The meaning is: "ninefold" in its detailed classification, and "threefold" in brief. "Ninefold" means...
Alternatively, in the reading *navabhedattā*, the meaning is that there are nine kinds by way of internal subdivisions.

A *vimāna* is so called because the womb (*gabbha*) is measured (*mānīyati*) specifically by means of particular conditions, such as the specific state of being female; thus, it is the abode of the womb. "He did not approach" (*na upagacchi*) means he will not approach.
Therefore he said: "The past tense is used for the future sense. For "he did not attain" (*nājjhagā*) is the past tense for "he will not go."
"Atthe" means: "He cut [the bonds] with the sword of the Noble Path. "Looking upon rebirths in the dwellings of beings" means:
in the places where beings are reborn. He spoke only of supramundane dhamma because it was taught for the sake of Arahatship.
The word *attha* should be brought forward and explained as "it is fitting to explain the meaning (*attha*) of the verse. It may also be understood by way of the Eightfold Path.
The same method applies here as well. Mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*) are called the cause for the pursuit of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*);

thus it is said, "the cause for the ten courses of wholesome action. Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the verse by way of the Eightfold Path, this is the detailed method now being stated.
"In that place" refers to the occasion of answering the question asked by the deity. [This was done] to bring about the ripening of the deity's knowledge.
Having observed him, there was a great Dhamma teaching consisting of a progressive discourse together with a penetrating instruction.

"Having directed his knowledge" means having fixed the knowledge of meditation (*bhāvanāñāṇa*) that proceeds through the successive stages of purification attained by recollecting the Teacher’s teaching.
"Established in the fruit of stream-entry" means because of the excellence of the Teacher’s teaching and because his own knowledge had reached maturity.
Having attained the first fruit, he spoke thus; that is, he uttered the verse beginning with "One should not do evil" in such a manner.
It is not a factor [of the path] because, just as livelihood becomes defiled by way of vocal and bodily action, so too does it become defiled when these succeed.
Therefore, it belongs to the side of vocal and bodily action, and is thus already included by the mention of those two. Effort, mindfulness, and concentration are included.
By way of inclusion in the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*). Right view and right intention are included by way of inclusion in the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*).
The avoidance of the two extremes is included in its own essential form; this is the intended meaning. "Thus," etc., is the conclusion.
The commentary on the *Samiddhi-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Nandanavagga is finished.
3. The Sattivagga: 1.
Commentary on the Satti Sutta.

21. "The summary of the teaching" (*desanāsīsanti*) means a statement characterized by the terms of the teaching; this is the intended meaning. "Struck down" (*omaṭṭho*) refers to a blow delivered with the face turned downward.
In this very context, the passage beginning with "There are four" is stated in order to show the classification of blows.
"Standing above" means standing above elephants and so forth. "A blow delivered with the face turned downward" refers to [striking with] swords, daggers, and the like.
Having turned it face down, the blow has been struck away. "Ummaṭṭha" (rubbed) should be understood as the opposite of what was said [before].
"Vimaṭṭha" (scraped) means various blows. Having stated, "Omaṭṭha means seized," the passage beginning with "So hi" (For he...

was spoken to show the reason for that very seizing. Internal corruption refers to foul-smelling worms and so forth. "Having bound him together with the bed" refers to the merchant person on whichever bed...
Having laid him down there, having secured him well, while those making the foot-end upward must make the head-end downward.

Therefore he said, "He should be made to lie with his head downward. "Paribbaje" means he would move about. Since that movement is associated with the dwelling in meditation (*bhāvanāvihāra*), he said, "he should dwell."

“Extraction of the dart” (*sallassa ubbahanaṃ*) means the extraction of the dart. This is because the intended meaning of the simile is the abandonment through suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), which is established by taking a limited sense.
Therefore he said, “Again and again,” and so forth. It continues as a consequence because it is shown that the abandonment of sensual lust for deities is liable to arise when conditions are present.
[Objection: Should not the teaching have been concluded by the Blessed One with the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmimagga*)?

No, because the teaching must be delivered in accordance with the power of the other’s knowledge; for the Master of Dhamma teaches the Dhamma in a manner that accords with the inclinations of those to be trained.
The commentary on the Satti Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Phusatisutta 22.
"Kamma does not touch" means it does not touch the contact of kamma; the meaning is that it does not perform kamma.
"Resultant [contact] does not touch" means the contact of resultant does not touch; resultant simply does not arise due to the absence of its cause. Thus...

Having explained the meaning by establishing a connection between the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result (vipākavaṭṭa) through the method of negation (vyatireka), he now speaks the passage beginning with "Kamma alone... while explaining the meaning solely by way of the cycle of kamma.

In that context, "it is not done by one who does not do" means that kamma is not performed by one who does not act; the sense is that there is no such thing as kamma performed without intention. Now, regarding that same point...

The passage beginning with “And touching” was stated in order to show [the relationship] by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Therein, “therefore” means because of touching. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
To show that same meaning clearly by way of a surrounding context and together with its cause, the passage beginning with “Therefore, while touching” was stated.
“Natural law” (*dhammatā*) means that the consequence of the ripening of karma follows only the agent, not the non-agent; this is the inherent nature (*sabhāva*) of the ripening of karmic results.
"Returns" means it approaches and follows along. "Evil" refers to unwholesome karma and its fruit.
This meaning should be illustrated by the story of a monk who, out of fear while being pursued by hounds sent by a hunter in the forest, climbed a tree;
meanwhile, the hunter’s robe fell upon him, and he was devoured and killed by those very dogs.
The commentary on the Phusati-sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Jaṭā-sutta: 23.
To show the specific sense in which craving is called a "tangle" (jaṭā), it is stated as "of the net-like" (jāliniyā).

For she is called "the ensnarer" (*jālinī*) because she possesses snares (*jālā*) that are her own constituent parts, distinguished by the hundred and eight modes of craving’s movement (*taṇhā-vicari-ta*).
Now, in order to show her mode of occurrence as a tangle (*jaṭā*), the passage beginning with "She indeed" (*sā hi*) was stated.

Therein, the phrase "in objects such as form" (*rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu*) indicates the sphere of her activity; for there is no objective domain of craving apart from the sixfold objects consisting of form and the rest.

"By way of non-existence. "In the order of low to high" means by way of their occurrence from below to above: sometimes on a visible-form object and sometimes on objects up to mental-phenomena; and sometimes on a mental-phenomena object and sometimes on objects down to visible form.

Here, the sequence from low to high should be understood according to the order of the teaching, and this meaning should also be understood by way of sensual lust and so forth regarding formations (*saṅkhārānaṃ*).
Because there is a continuous binding together here through the arising of one state after another in a momentary succession, it is said: "in the sense of binding together by way of repeated arising.
This demonstrates the relationship by which *jaṭā* (tangle) is used as a simile for craving (*taṇhā*), showing how the simile and the thing compared correspond.
The meaning here is this: just as the net-like branches of a bamboo thicket and their clusters, etc., [entwine] by means of their own parts...
“Tangles” (*jaṭā*) are so called because they are woven together and interlaced; craving (*taṇhā*) is likewise so called because its intrinsic nature is that of weaving together.
These beings, conceiving of what is grasped as “this is mine” to be non-different from themselves, make it internal.
Since the word “internal” (*anto*) signifies the state of being inside, craving—which arises even toward one’s own belongings—is called the “inner tangle” (*antojaṭā*).
[These things] have been mentioned. For one who has gone forth, the bowl and so forth; for a householder, the elephant and so forth—these are one's own requisites (*sakaparikkhāra*).
"Self" (*atta*) means that which is the object of conceit (*abhimāna*); thus it is "selfhood" (*attabhāva*), namely the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha-pañcaka*).
Some say it is the body. Through craving (*taṇhā*) for one's own selfhood and so forth, such as: "My selfhood is beautiful," or "May my selfhood be like that of so-and-so," and so on.
The mode of arising should be understood as follows: one’s own internal bases such as the eye, and one’s own and others’ external bases such as visible forms, or all [bases] belonging to others;
or alternatively, the internal bases such as the eye included within one’s own and others’ continuums, and likewise the external bases such as visible forms included therein.
This applies even to their occurrence within limited (paritta) and sublime (mahaggata) states of existence.

The state of craving as an internal tangle and an external tangle is to be understood. For the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), because no defilement has been suppressed and it is not liberated from anything, serves as a specific condition for internal grasping; thus it is called "internal" and "inside.
By contrast, fine-material and immaterial existence (*rūpabhava* and *arūpabhava*) are called "external" and "outside. Therefore the Blessed One said: "One who is fettered internally..."
“...the person, the person with external fetters.

Although craving is divided into many types according to the distinction of its objects and the distinction in the manner of its occurrence, it is taken as a single unity by virtue of the commonality of its state as a tangle (*jaṭā*);
thus it is said: “by that very tangle arising in this way. Furthermore, that [craving] is included within the continuum of beings (*sattasantāna*) mentioned by the term *pajā*.
Having thus become entangled again and again, it proceeds by being matted and bound; therefore he said, "The world is matted by a tangle.
For although, in the ultimate sense, there is no whole distinct from its parts, yet a single part is not called a "whole";
thus, distinguishing the whole from its parts, he shows the simile and the subject of the simile: "Just as..."
"Entangled by reeds, matted hair, and so forth... [he said]. The connection is with the word "this tangle" (*imaṃ jaṭaṃ*).

By entangling it through a weaving that leaves not even a single one of the three elements (*dhātu*) remaining, it stands as a tangle of the three elements (*tedhātukaṃ jaṭetvā*). By this, he expresses its vast scope and the extreme difficulty of disentangling it.
