With the words "Who is able to disentangle it? (*vijaṭetuṃ ko samattho*), he shows that the term "disentangle" (*vijaṭaye*) has the sense of capability (*satti*), not the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*).
Thus, when asked with the words “The inner tangle,” and so forth, the Blessed One, answering that matter for him, spoke the passage beginning with “Having established oneself in virtue.

Here, “virtue” (sīla) refers to wholesome virtue. Since that must be sought as something entirely pure among its divisions such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha, he said, “in the fourfold purity of virtue” (catupārisuddhisīle).
One who says "I am not," "I do not go," is a *nara*, a person (*purisa*). Granted, even a woman is capable of disentangling the tangle of craving;
however, he said "a man" (*naro*) to indicate the being who is preeminent [in this task], just as one says "the Teacher of gods and men.

In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated "a man means a being" (*satto*) in order to show that this is a general term for a person without distinction. Of that which has become fruition...

"One who possesses wisdom" (*sapañño*) means one who exists together with wisdom (*paññā*). For it is by virtue of that wisdom—which, from the very beginning, proceeds extensively as a continuous stream—that this being deserves to be specifically called "one possessed of wisdom.
Indeed, even resultant wisdom (*vipākapaññā*), through its specific continuity, serves as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for the arising of developmental wisdom (*bhāvanāpaññā*);
this is because such a condition is absent in those [beings] born without roots (*ahetuka*) or with two roots (*duhetuka*). Regarding "the wisdom of the kamma-born, rootless rebirth-linking":

“Wisdom is known in the three-rooted rebirth-linking born of kamma”—thus, the term *tihetuka* (three-rooted) should be connected with the word *paṭisandhi* (rebirth-linking), not with the word *paññā* (wisdom).

For wisdom itself is not three-rooted. Wisdom that proceeds from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards is called “wisdom in rebirth-linking” because it is rooted in that [rebirth-linking], and not because it occurs only at the very moment of rebirth-linking.

It is called *citta* because it thinks (*cinteti*) and closely contemplates (*upanijjhāyati*) an object; thus, it is concentration (*samādhi*). For that [concentration] has the function of close contemplation to an exceptional degree.
Indeed, initial application (*vitakka*) and the other factors do not accomplish that purpose without concentration, whereas concentration accomplishes it even without them.

Furthermore, it is called *citta* because, by bringing about a state of proficiency and strength through its conditions, it accumulates (*cinoti*) the mind—that is, one's own mental continuum. Thus, it is concentration.

Because of the variety of consciousness through the first jhāna and so forth, and because of the production of consciousness for the various modes of psychic power (iddhividha) and so on, the designation "consciousness" (citta) can indeed be applied to concentration even without instruction from another.

However, in the Commentary, it is stated—taking the word *citta* to be conventionally established in the sense of "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*)—"Here, the eight attainments are spoken of under the heading of 'consciousness'. This is according to its true nature.

It is called *paññā* (wisdom) because it knows by way of various modes. Although that wisdom is manifold—being divided into categories such as the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth—it is intended here as that which is to be developed (*bhāvetabba*), based on the statement "develop it. Showing this, he says: "Insight (*vipassanā*) is spoken of under the name of wisdom.
Although the abandoning of defilements is indeed an exertion (*ātāpana*) common to right view and the other factors as well, the word *ātappa* (ardor/exertion), however—
The word *ātāpa* is established specifically in the sense of energy; thus he says, “*Ātāpī* means one possessed of energy.

Just as the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is carried out and maintained by that wisdom, so too does that [wisdom] serve that purpose for the practitioner; thus he calls it “wisdom for carrying out” (*pārihāriyapaññā*).
It leads all tasks, such as advancing and so forth, by delimiting them through such factors as clear comprehension of what is beneficial; thus it is the “guide of all tasks” (*sabbakiccapariṇāyikā*).
Since the verse was spoken with reference to a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), he spoke the passage beginning with "Just as a man" in order to show a simile likewise with reference to a person.
In that context, *sunisitaṃ* means well-sharpened; the meaning is "extremely keen.
The sharpening of the sword to its keenest state occurs on the whetstone, and its being raised by the strength of the arm is [the next step].
Having established both of these as the subject of the comparison, the simile was spoken; thus, showing both of them as the objects of comparison, he said:
“Well-sharpened on the whetstone of concentration... lifted up by the hand of wisdom. For it is through the quality of concentration that wisdom becomes sharp, as it is said:
“One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are. And energy is its support, because it provides the exertion.
“Vijaṭeyya” means he would be able to disentangle. For when insight leading to emergence is present, the practitioner of yoga is indeed capable of disentangling the tangle of craving.
And here, “disentangling” refers to abandonment by way of complete cutting off; thus he said, “he would cut it off and crush it.”
At the moment of the path, however, this is called "unraveling," and at the moment of the supreme fruit, it is called "having unraveled all the tangles. Therefore he said, "Now," and so forth.
Since the unraveling of the tangle occurs by means of the Noble Path, and that indeed comes about by resorting to Nibbāna, he said with reference to that:
"the place for the unraveling of the tangle. In order to show where that [tangle] is unraveled, he says:

“Wherein name and... and so forth is stated. In the phrase “Resistance and perception of form,” the nasalization (*sānunāsika*) is used for the sake of metrical ease in the verse; thus, it means “perception of resistance and form.
By way of the perception of resistance, the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) is included, because it is comprised within that [perception].
Perception of forms such as the earth-kasina is “perception of form. In both cases, it is designated by way of the term “perception” (*saññā*).
Only the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) is grasped. By "the compression of existence" (bhavasaṅkhepa) is meant the state of being compressible by way of the nature of existence;

the meaning is that they share a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of existence. Or, because they can be described as dispassion toward form, they are here called "perception of form";
in this way, it should be understood that the immaterial existence (arūpabhava) is also included here. "Name and form" (nāmañca rūpañca) refers to them without remainder.
Others maintain that since "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is included here, the inclusion of the formless existence (arūpabhava) and the non-percipient existence (asaññabhava) is thereby established.
"In the place of exhaustion" means in Nibbāna, which is the cause of exhaustion and the sign of total depletion. Therefore he said: "Nibbāna... is thus shown.
The commentary on the *Jaṭāsutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Manonivāraṇasutta* 24.

"Those who hold such a view" means those whose perspective is as follows: "The arising of consciousness is in every way accompanied by suffering; a state of being entirely without consciousness is better;
therefore, the mind should be restrained from whatever [object] it may turn toward. "He" refers to the sentient being. [This is] a discourse that does not lead to liberation.

She speaks thus, saying that it prevents the mind from being unwise. "Having attained a state of restraint" means having properly entered into a state of restraint by refraining from indulging in passion and so forth.
For when the mind proceeds by way of the practice of the Dhamma, there is not even the slightest indulgence in passion or the like;
neither in the present nor in the future will there be any harm for such a person. Therefore, that mind [is restrained] from everything.
Because it is blameless in its conduct, it should not be restrained. Therefore he said, “I shall give a gift,” and so forth.
“From whatever” means from whatever instance of blameworthy conduct or from improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*). “That” refers to the mind, which must be restrained because it brings about harm.
The commentary on the *Manonivāraṇa Sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Arahantasutta 25.
*Katāvī*: one who has done what was to be done; the meaning is that he stands having performed and brought to completion the tasks such as full understanding (*pariññā*).
Therefore it is said: "one who has accomplished his task by means of the four paths. This meaning is understood from the proximity of words such as *arahant*. Thus, "I..."
He asks in such a manner as "I speak," and so forth.

"Skilled in the aggregates and so on" means one who is proficient in the aggregates, bases, and so forth, as well as in their specific characteristics and so on, both in terms of their collective nature and their individual occurrence, and who knows them as they truly are.
"Discourse based on the acquisition of a self" means having abandoned discourse based on the acquisition of a self (*attūpaladdhi*). "Distinction in conventional expression" (*vohārabheda*)...
"Not doing so" means that one might say "I," "mine," relying merely on worldly convention (*lokasamaññā*) without violating or destroying worldly usage by saying, "I know the ultimate truth.
By such statements as "the aggregates eat," he demonstrates the violation of conventional usage and the danger therein.
Pride (*māna*) is indeed the equal partner of views. For thus, in the second path and so forth, it is through right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) that there is the realization of abandonment.
The accomplishment of practice occurs when one is opposed to what is contrary [to it]. Therefore he said:
"Having thought, 'If he does not speak by way of views, does he perhaps speak by way of conceit? "Vidhūpita" means scorched, burnt by the fire of knowledge.

And since those [defilements] are then called "destroyed," he said "vidhamitā" (dispelled). The notions of "mine" and so forth proceed as long as there exists the continuity of a being (*sattasantāna*).
By this [term] "delusion" (māya), it means conceiving (maññanā). Because delusion itself is "the state of being deluded" (mayatā), he said: "The state of being deluded is conceiving.
The commentary on the *Arahantasutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Pajjotasutta*.
26. "By day and by night" means not only by day like the sun, nor only by night like the moon, but rather both by day and by night.
"In this or that place" means in whichever specific location it is blazing;
it does not illuminate the entire great quarters and the intermediate spaces of the directions like the sun or the moon. It is light produced through the power of knowledge.

They call it the light of knowledge (*ñāṇāloka*). However, from the statement: "Bhikkhus, regarding these things unheard of by me before, the eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, and light arose: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering’"—the path is the light of knowledge.
Or, from the statement: "Darkness was dispelled; light has arisen," it is the light of the threefold true insight (*vijjā*).

The light of knowledge (*ñāṇāloka*). It is the expansion of joy that arises just as at the first full enlightenment; or, specifically, it is the bodily radiance produced by the joy arising from the investigation of the *Samantapāsādikā* (the Great Commentary) in the Jewel House.
The light of confidence (*pasādāloka*) is the very light produced by the confidence that arose on that same occasion.
It is the light of confidence that arose [when he said] during the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma: "O Koṇḍañña, you have indeed understood!"
And they say: "In every respect, the Teacher’s Dhamma-teaching is the light of the Dhamma-discourse that dispels the darkness in the hearts of beings.
By the phrase "all the light arisen from the manifestation of the Buddhas," he shows that even the light of the Dhamma produced in disciples through the teaching is the power of the Buddha.
The commentary on the *Pajjota-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Sara-sutta*. 27.
Because they proceed by way of continuity without interruption, the succession of the aggregates and so forth is called a "series" (*sara*). Therefore he said: "These..."
“From the ocean of saṃsāra. From what? By what cause, or in what respect? Therefore he asks, “Having come from what?

It does not find a footing because of the absence of conditions. By the passage beginning with “water,” etc., the non-existence of the sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) and the fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*) is shown through the designation of the non-footing of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
By showing the non-existence of both of those, the immaterial existence (*arūpa-bhava*) is also [shown to be absent] according to the method explained below.
Non-existence is indeed shown; or rather, the meaning here should be understood according to the literal expression.
For since the first two have been taken up, and the subsequent meaning proceeds only after having grasped the meaning already taken up.
The commentary on the Sara Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Mahaddhanasutta 28.

It is called a *nidhāna* because it is stored (*nidhīyati*). The meaning is that which has become something to be stored, or that which is already stored (*nihita*). "Pearls, gems, and so forth" refers to pearls, jewels, beryl, coral, silver, gold, and the like.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "gold, silver, vessels, and so forth," one includes coins, storehouses of grain, merchandise, and other such items. That too...
For it is called "wealth" (*bhoga*) because it is enjoyed by way of providing constant maintenance.
"They covet one another" means they covet what belongs to each other. Therefore he said, "they long for. "Unadorned" means not sufficient or adequate;
thus their minds are made such, being overcome by lack of contentment and great greed. Therefore he said, "unsatisfied and having become inadequate."
"Ussukkajātesu" means those who have developed zeal for their respective duties. "Nānākiccajātesu" means in various kinds of duties, or among those in whom various duties have arisen.
"Vaṭṭagāmikapasutena" means among those following the stream of the round of existence.
Because it is a dwelling place for craving, it is called both "geha" (home) and "agāra" (house); thus he said, "the home together with women. "Virājiyā" indicates the sense of a cause.
The commentator says, "having made them shine," for this particle *tvā* also has the sense of a causal reason (*hetu*).
The commentary on the Mahaddhanasutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Catucakkasutta.
29. *Iriyā* is said to be the activity to be performed by means of the body; because it is the locus for the occurrence of that activity, it is called a *iriyāpatha*, such as walking and so forth.
Because it proceeds from one to another, it is a "wheel. Therefore, he said: "The four wheels" means the four postures (*iriyāpatha*). "Nine doors" refers to the body born of karma (*karajakāya*).
And since that [body] is filled with impurities such as hair and so forth, he said: "Full" means full of impurities. Of craving...

"Accompanied" (*saṃyutta*) means accompanied by craving (*taṇhā*). By this, it shows that it is not only impure in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), but also in terms of the phenomena dependent upon it.

It is "born in mud" (*paṅkajāta*) because it is born in the mire of impurity known as the mother's womb, and it is also "born in mud" because it is born from the mire of impurities such as hair and so forth.
"Departure" (*yātrā*) means removal. By this, [it is shown] to be impure both in its intrinsic nature and in the phenomena dependent upon it.
He asks: "How might there be a departure from the body? Therefore he says, "Of this," and so forth.

In the sense of binding and fettering, *naddhi* here is intended as *upanāha* (enmity); thus he says, "*Naddhi* means *upanāha*. Furthermore, that [enmity] was previously called anger (*kodha*) at an earlier time;
thus he says, "at an earlier time," and so forth. [This refers to] what is indicated in the text by the term *upanāha*, etc.

In this text, with the exception of the defilements already specified, the remaining seven defilements—view, doubt, and so forth—should be understood as "thongs" (*varattā*) because they are difficult to release.
Although this single phenomenon is one and the same in its essential nature of grasping an object, it is nevertheless differentiated according to its modes of manifestation:
in the sense of wishing, in the sense of aspiring, it is "desire" (*icchā*); and in the sense of being greedy...
Greed is so called in the sense of devouring (*gijjhana*). "Arising for the first time" means having arisen for the first time with respect to a single object or on a particular occasion.
"Arising repeatedly" means that which arises again and again. Greed is attachment (*āsatti*) toward an object not yet obtained, characterized by a longing for what has not been attained.
"Having torn out" means having extracted it from one's own continuum (*sasantāna*).
The commentary on the Catucakkasutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Eṇijaṅghasutta:
"Like the legs of an eṇi deer" means like the legs of an eṇi deer. This genitive case is used here to express a relationship of part to whole.
Because the flesh of his calves is even all around, he has well-rounded shanks. "Lean" (*kisa*) indicates the negation of stoutness, not the manifestation of an excessively emaciated state;
thus it says, "not stout, with a symmetrical body. "Withered by the sun" means having a body withered by asceticism due to the state of scorching the sense-faculties.
For this very reason it says, "withered by heat," and so forth; likewise, it is said in the Pāḷi:
“‘Little food, not greedy’—just as ‘the state of a hero is heroism’ (vīriya) characterizes heroism by way of the hero’s state, so too the state of a hero arises from heroism;

thus it is said: ‘A hero is one who possesses heroism. ‘Having eaten four or five morsels, one should drink water’—according to this rule stated by the General of the Dhamma, moderation in eating constitutes being one of little food.”

“Knowing the proper measure. Having said “moderate food,” he further spoke of “limited eating at the proper time” and “meager food” in order to show that there is moderation even in eating at restricted times.
[He says this] because of being free from greed regarding the four requisites, since greed has been entirely abandoned right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Indeed, by the phrase “regarding the four requisites,” the departure from greed is shown in all respects.
"Or it is illuminated": this is a rejection of craving for flavors, because after saying "one who eats little," it is stated "one who is not greedy.

Regarding the phrase "or like a lion," he says, "like a solitary lion, like a solitary elephant," bringing over the word *iva* (like) from the context of "solitary" (*ekacara*) here as well, since it must be connected there too. They are solitary and heedful through their being alone.

Form (*rūpa*) is included by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), because they have the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of form. Name (*nāma*) is included by way of the mind (*manas*), because the mind has the intrinsic nature of name.

By the term "inseparable phenomena" (*avinibhuttadhamma*), phenomena that are not found apart from one another are understood. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth are included.
Here, by the mention of the "strands of sensual pleasure," the five physical bases (*vatthu*) are indeed included through their commonality as being of the nature of form.
By the inclusion of "mind," the base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) is included; thus, the twelve bases are grasped.

In this same manner, the inclusion of the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth should also be applied accordingly. Therefore he said: "In this context, the locative case should also be applied by way of the five aggregates and so on.
"In this context" means in the Pāli text. "Kāmavatthu" is the locative case.
The commentary on the Eṇijaṅgha Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Satti Vagga is finished.
4. The Satullapakāyika Vagga.
1. Commentary on the Sabbhisutta: 31.

Because they proclaim (*ullapanti*) the Dhamma—consisting of the going for refuge, virtue, and so forth—of the virtuous ones (*sataṃ*), or because they proclaim and speak of that Dhamma through their own recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati*), they are called "those who proclaim what is true" (*satullapā*).
They are the deities; their body is the assembly, therein...
They are called *satullapakāyikā*. Therefore he said, “the Dhamma of the good,” and so forth.
Having spoken by way of undertaking [the precepts], and not merely by way of giving a descriptive account—“therein” means in that state of being *satullapakāyikā* for those deities.
“This is the basis” means this is the reason. “Sea-traders” means merchants (*saṃyattika*). “With the speed of a discharged arrow” means with a speed like that of an arrow released from a bowstring.
The meaning is "by a swift current. It rises up, thus it is a "risal" (uppatati); misfortune occurring in a risal is "risal-born" (uppātika).
A foundation for welfare is a "foundation of benefit" (hitapaṭṭhā). It brings about welfare and happiness in the next world and is a cause for fearlessness.
"A hundred legs" means a hundred men; for he speaks of men by the term "legs," because of their state of being companions. He undertook the five precepts. Among those near and far...

Because it ripens first for one who is near [to death], it is said: "relying on virtue undertaken at the time of death. "By way of a multitude" means by way of a collection. "By the good" (sabbhī) means by the virtuous;
for they are called "peaceful" (santa) because they are praiseworthy due to their accomplishment of the welfare of themselves and others, and because they possess the quality of peace.
Since they, moreover, are endowed with the characteristics of the wise, he says: "by the wise" (paṇḍitehi).
"Should associate" means "should dwell together"; this is the intended meaning here, as he says: "In all modes of conduct," and so forth.

"Friendship" (mittasanthava) means the binding together of loving-kindness (mettī). For loving-kindness is characterized by the desire for the welfare of beings, and since that [welfare-desire] is accompanied by knowledge and preceded by knowledge, friendship is undefiled;
the other [type of association] is defiled. Therefore, he said: "It should not be formed with anyone."
“Saddhamma” means the beautiful Dhamma that brings benefit in this very life and so forth. “Seyyo” (better) refers to the state of increasing welfare and so on; thus he says “growth.
“Of the good ones” (sataṃ) means of the virtuous, of the wise—this is the meaning here.

Because the word “other” (añña-) has as its scope the opposite of that, he says “from another, from the blind fool. By the elision of the final member of the compound, the word “soka” (sorrow) here signifies the cause of sorrow, the reason for grief.
He said, "Seized," and so forth, beginning with "grounds for sorrow. The "grounds for sorrow" are thieves and the like, because they cause sorrow to others by means of plundering and so on.
"Followed by sorrow" means having reached sorrow.
"Of the Elder" refers to the Elder Saṅkicca. Because she was his own elder sister, he addressed her as "you. This [is] "here..."
Thinking, "The thieves have set out; he does not even consider us as much as a blade of grass," some said, "Let us kill him.
Out of compassion, others said, "Let us release him. *Mantetvā* means having spoken.
*Ahu* means *ahosi*, which signifies that it happened in the past. *Araññasmiṃ brahāvane* means in such a vast forest, in a great wilderness.
The meaning of "resident" is "a hunter. "Traps" refers to snares and the like. "Having set" means having prepared them.
"The hare" refers to the animal; "alarmed" means terrified with fear. "In a single night" means in just one night.
"Loss of wealth" refers to the loss of the property that travelers receive as provisions, [thinking]: "He even kills a recluse; why should he feel shame toward us?"
The intention is that because the travelers will not return, they will not receive even the provisions for a single day.
"Relatives" refers to kinsmen such as mother, father, brothers, sisters, and so forth.
It is said that while those traveling toward Adhimutta’s sister approached her, they encountered him on the way; Adhimutta, guarding his word of truth, [faced] the danger of robbers...

He did not inform them. Therefore it was said, "of them too," and so forth. Because he had gone forth in dependence upon him, it is said, "in the presence of the novice Adhimutta," and not as his preceptor for full ordination.
Hence he said, "having made them his own pupils.
Through the preservation of truth and the attainment of unsurpassed qualities, he shines in the midst of his kinsmen.
*Sātataṃ* means "constant" (*satataṃ*). For here, the substitution of *sā-* for *sa-* occurs, as in the case of words such as *sārāgo*.
Alternatively, *sātatabhāvo* means "the state of being constant"; thus he says, "or happiness. "By that cause or another" means by this or that specific reason.
The speech of all those [others] is well-spoken, but the speech of the Blessed One is pre-eminently well-spoken. And this meaning is established by the very words of the respective verses.
To extract and demonstrate what is implied by the phrase "it is understood," the passage beginning with "not only" was stated. By this,

it is shown that just as associating with noble persons and devotion to the true Dhamma are the certain causes for the growth of beings and the acquisition of wisdom, so too— when the conditions for sorrow exist—

are they the causes for the state of being free from sorrow, for splendor in the midst of kinsmen, for going to a happy destination, for long-lasting happiness, and even for liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra.
It should be understood that it has already been stated [in the previous section] that this is not shared with others.
The commentary on the Sabbhi-sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Macchari-sutta.
32. Non-apprehension occurring in the manner of negligence is *pamāda* (heedlessness). Because of this, they are entirely devoid of mindfulness;
thus it is said, "by way of the characteristic of the absence of mindfulness. Furthermore, wrong view, doubt, and so forth are included here precisely within heedlessness.
Now, in order to show how giving is not bestowed because of the cause of stinginess and the cause of heedlessness, [the text says]: "A certain person..."
"‘Hī’ and so forth was said. ‘Will go to complete exhaustion’ means it will undergo the loss of wealth. ‘Play and so forth’:
by the word ‘and so forth,’ one includes adornment, decoration, festivals, lunar observances, calamities, and the like. ‘Bestower of fame’ means a giver of renown, glory, and the fame of retinue.
‘Bestower of splendor’ means a giver of good fortune. ‘Bestower of success’ [means] through success in lineage, wealth, beauty, and enjoyments."
"Bestowing success. Or, "merit" (*puñña*) here should be understood as the fruit of merit, as in such passages as "thus this merit increases," and so forth.

"There is a fruit of giving": herein, [the text points out] the instability of the object to be given, its being common to many, its having to be relinquished, the faultiness of the joy directed toward it, and the fact that the practice of giving is not shared by others.

It should be said that [the donor] knows the following: its capacity for accompaniment, the blamelessness of the joy pertaining to its object, the dispelling of evil states such as greed, and its status as a decisive support (upanissaya) for other merits.

"That very fool" refers to one who is miserly; fools are those whose nature is not to give. Some do not even enjoy wealth themselves out of fear of its depletion through use, like the merchant Atilobha; therefore, it is said: "in this world and the next."
Because a certain person who is by nature ungenerous, even when seeing travelers, does not truly see them;

even when hearing their talk, he does not truly hear it; he himself says nothing at all; and he remains bound by the pillar of the desire not to give—therefore, the signs of death are indeed found in that state.
Thus it was said: "By death through the lack of a generous nature, they have died. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, having taken up only the act of giving, the phrase beginning with “Just as... was spoken in order to show its similarity to death.
But the characteristics of the nectar of generosity and virtue should be understood by reversing what has been stated. The singular number is used for the plural;
therefore, he said “going together” because it was spoken with a change in grammatical number. The qualities such as generosity and virtue are ancient, not merely of today.
That which is eternal (*sanantana*) exists among these [wise ones], thus they are the "eternal ones" (*sanantanā*), meaning the wise (*paṇḍita*).
It is said that "this Dhamma belongs to them," and thus the Dhamma is eternal; hence it is stated: "This is the Dhamma of the eternal, wise ones.
Even when there is but a small amount of property to be given, some give a gift while others do not, due to their state of stinginess. A single offering is like a thousandfold gift.
Because of the loftiness of the volition of relinquishment, it is like the giving of a thousand.

"Difficult to follow" means it is hard for one who does not possess [the requisite qualities] to follow. And because the non-following of this Dhamma is itself the failure to fulfill it, he said "difficult to fill.
"One should practice the Dhamma"—this practice of the Dhamma is undertaken with reference to the householder.
He said: "He practices the dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action. Therefore he said: "And he supports his wife.
"Samuñjaka" means the gathering of grain discarded on the threshing floor by means of a broom or similar tool, after the farmers have finished their own work and the harvest has been spread out.
Therefore he said: "Even he who... practices *samuñjaka*. By this [phrase], the offering of a hundred thousand times a hundred thousand is included.
Alms-food was presented for ten crores of monks. By supplying the word "given" (*dinno*), the construction is completed.
Or, "alms-food for ten crores of kahāpaṇas" means alms-food prepared by means of the expenditure of ten crores of kahāpaṇas.
This is considered to be an offering equivalent to the gift given by those who perform a thousand sacrifices a hundred times over.
It has been said. "Even while gathering *samuñjaka* grass" means even after having gathered *samuñjaka* grass; the sense is "for the purpose of gathering *samuñjaka*.

The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. The construction is: "Even while supporting a wife, one practices the Dhamma; even by giving away only a small amount, one practices the Dhamma.
"Of such a person" refers to the practice of Dhamma belonging to one who is of that kind, who thus practices the Dhamma.
These givers of a thousand-fold sacrifice do not equal even a fraction of that [merit] by virtue of their own giving of a thousand-fold sacrifice. The passage beginning with "By that poor man...
is an exposition of that very same meaning. "Of all those" refers to all those mentioned as "the givers of a thousand-fold sacrifice to hundreds of thousands.
"The others" refers to persons other than the one previously mentioned as "of such a kind. "The gift of ten thousand koṭis" means...
The "thousandfold gift" (sahassadāna) is so called because it consists of many thousands of items, numbering ten million.
Regarding the phrase "it does not equal even a fraction," this was said because this particular gift is more exalted, more abundant, and yields more abundant fruit than those other gifts;
thus he says, "How indeed is this to be understood as having greater fruit?"
It has reached greatness by way of its specific conditions, thus it is "magnificent" (*mahaggata*); the meaning is "exalted. Therefore he said: "This is a synonym for 'vast' (*vipula*).
"By the even" means by the right method; the meaning is "by the Dhamma. "Uneven" means not even, having attained the characteristic of stinginess.
"Having cut" means having crushed. Showing that crushing to be a striking, he said "having struck. "Tear-faced" means mixed with tears flowing from the face.
"Having caused others to weep. "Great giving" (*mahādāna*) refers to a great gift by virtue of relinquishing the many objects of charity as previously described.
"Due to impurity in its origin" means because of the defilement of the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) and the search for the object of charity.
"The other" is the gift produced through righteous conduct (*dhammacariyā*). "Limited giving" (*parittadāna*) is so called by way of the limited nature of the object of charity.
A small gift. Regarding "through the purity of his own arising" and "through the purity of his intention and the search for the object to be given":
he spoke thus, saying, "Thus [he was] the giver of thousands upon thousands. In that context, "thousands" means hundreds of thousands;
the mention of "hundreds" was not made for the sake of the ease of the verse composition. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the Maccharisutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Sādhusutta: 33.
"He uttered an udāna"—he uttered it because it was to be vomited forth by the force of joy; he expressed it as an outpouring. And this [udāna] is so called because...
The speech was produced by rapture; therefore it is said, "he uttered an utterance" (*udāhāraṃ udāharī*).
To show how that speech is called an "inspired utterance" (*udāna*), the passage beginning with "for just as... was stated.

In the phrase "by means of faith" (*saddhāya*), the letter *ya* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). For faith is the specific condition for the volition of relinquishment, since such volition is absent in one who lacks faith. The particle *pi*...
This is the purpose of summarizing the meaning of what was stated. The word *sāhu* should be understood as having the same meaning as the word *sādhu*.
How so? The intention is that giving and battle have opposite natures. "Both these" refers to this pair: giving and battle.
"One who fears for his life" means one who fears the destruction of life. "One who fears loss" means one who fears the loss of wealth. "Speaking" means...
This proclaims their attachment to life and, for that very reason, their inability to fight. "Cutting" (*chejja*) means the severing of hands, feet, and so forth.

"Exerting" (*ussahanto*) means applying effort. "Thinking, 'I will thus protect my wealth,' or 'I will thus ensure my wealth is not exhausted'"—this proclaims greed for wealth in this world, and for that very reason, their inability to give. "Thus" (*evaṃ*) means in this way.

Because of his lack of regard for life and wealth, giving and fighting are equal for him. "Endowed with faith and so forth" means being possessed of such qualities as faith, virtue, livelihood, wisdom, and morality.

For even when giving only a small amount due to the meagerness of the object to be given, he increases his own abundant and sublime merit through the excellence of his mind and the excellence of the field;
[he thus abandons] the manifold types of greed, hatred, envy, stinginess, wrong view, doubt, and so on.
It overcomes its opposite, and for that very reason it becomes of great fruit and great benefit.
In the commentary, however, it is stated simply as "it crushes stinginess," because that [generosity] is its direct antithesis.

"For the sake of others" means in the next world. The story of the one-clothed brahmin should be cited by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and the story of the sprout by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

One who has obtained the Dhamma by this means is called "one who has acquired the Dhamma" (*dhammaladdha*); the grammatical formation of this term should be understood as being like that of the word *aggi-āhita*.
They say: "Exertion (*uṭṭhāna*) is bodily energy, while energy (*vīriya*) is mental. Exertion is the state of being engaged and intent upon the production of wealth;
energy is the corresponding effort. That which is the locus for the operation of his commands—even the Vetaraṇī River [cannot stop him]—the others [likewise cannot].

"And having transcended the Niraya [hell]. They, however, say there are thirty-one hells by dividing Avīci tenfold according to the Abbuda and other hells, and by dividing each of the remaining great hells into three according to the distinctions in the lifespan.
The threefold nature of that lifespan should be understood through the sharp, middling, and mild degrees of the karma that leads to the Sañjīva and other hells. Others...
However, they say: "There are eight great hells (mahāniraya), sixteen supplementary hells (ussadaniraya), and the first four cold hells counted as one, making seven cold hells;
thus, there are thirty-one great hells. By including the term "great hell," the first four cold hells are treated as a single hell.

"Of these" refers to the conditions that have been selected after investigation. The ninety-five types of sectarian divisions are to be understood according to the method explained in the *Papañcasūdanī* commentary.

"Therein" means in those two kinds of investigation. He spoke of the investigation of the recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇā*), for similes indeed exist solely for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the thing to be illustrated.
By this, the investigation of those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*) should also be understood as being included within the selection of a good field.
By the phrase "restraint regarding living beings" (*pāṇesu saṃyamo*), he shows the tenfold nature of the wholesome path of action (*kusalakammapatha*).
For just as "restraint regarding living beings" is said to be restraint from depriving sentient beings of life, so too is it restraint from seizing their property,
from violating another's wife, from deceiving, from causing mutual dissension, from striking with harsh speech, and from idle chatter.
Restraint arises from not coveting what belongs to others, from not thinking of their destruction, and from not holding wrong views. Therefore it was said:
"She began to describe the benefits of virtue. Here, however, restraint from harsh speech is stated explicitly by its own name.
"Through fear of being censured by others" means through the fear of being spoken ill of by others on account of one's own evil deeds. Regarding "fear of censure":
"Due to the fear of being censured": wishing, "How indeed might others not censure us?", they do not commit evil.
"The state of the Dhamma alone" means that the portion of the unconditioned Dhamma (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*) alone is better and superior.

Since all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*) are impermanent, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation, therefore, for the sake of attaining that [unconditioned state]...
It shows that effort must be made. Since the word *pubba* (formerly) refers to a specific time, he says: "And formerly, even at the time of Kassapa Buddha and others," and so forth.
Furthermore, since it does not refer to a specific time but rather to a general location (the sense of the locative case), he says: "Or all [of them]," and so forth.
In that context, "all of them" means that these Lokanāthas, beginning with Kassapa Buddha, being such [beings], have indeed calmed the burning heat of all defilements (*kilesa*).
Because of possessing all truly existing virtues.
The commentary on the *Sādhu-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Na santi-sutta*.

34. "Kamanīyāni" means "desirable. For that very reason, these desirable objects, pleasant objects, such as forms and so forth, are either *vatthukāmā* (sensual pleasures as bases) or *kilesakāmā* (sensual pleasures as defilements) which take those as their object. The statement, "There are no sensual pleasures among humans," is merely a heading for the teaching;
in reality, sensual pleasures are indeed impermanent. "Maccudheyya" means that wherein death dwells. One does not return [to it] again.
"Herein, that is non-returning. This is because one does not go back to what is termed "nibbāna without remainder" (apuna-āgamana). The passage beginning with "Nibbāna, indeed...
is an exposition of the very meaning already stated. "Bound" means having a mind attached. "Negligent" means having fallen into the negligence of indolence (*vossagga-pamāda*).
[Suffering] is born from craving and desire because they are its specific conditions. It destroys what is desired, thus it is *agha*, which is suffering (*dukkha*). Here...
However, by way of exhaustive inclusion, it is said that "the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.

Because the removal of craving is the removal of misfortune (*aghavinaya*), there is the cessation of the fruit through the cessation of the cause; thus, having spoken of *nibbāna* with residue remaining (*saupādisesa*), he speaks of *nibbāna* without residue remaining (*anupādisesa*) as "the removal of misfortune is the removal of suffering" (*aghavinayā dukkhavinayā*).

The term *citrāni* (various) refers to the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*) as well, which exist through the distinctions of association with feeling, views, and so forth, and through differences in their modes of manifestation, such as being accompanied by distress or free from distress;
therefore, in order to distinguish them [from those], it is said "objects of consciousness" (*ārammaṇacittāni*).

"Lust for what is intended" (*saṅkappitarāga*) is lust for an object intended by way of [perceiving it as] beautiful and so forth. Defilement-sensual-desire (*kilesakāma*) is called simply "sensual-desire" (*kāma*), because its status as sensual-desire is established here specifically by way of that [intentional object].

It is to be clarified by the *Pasūra-sutta* through the passage beginning with “These are not sensual pleasures,” because that [explanation] occurs in the context of that subject. Now, explaining that same matter in brief, he says: “The wanderer Pasūra...

“Those which are variegated in the world are not sensual pleasures”: if those variegated objects in the world, such as forms and so forth, are not sensual pleasures; “you have known them” means only...
If you say, having made desire [consisting of] the passion of intention (*saṅkapparāga*), "He will come," the meaning is "he will be.
"While hearing delightful sounds, the Teacher too will become an enjoyer of sensual pleasures"—this is a separate verse, but here it is shown in an abbreviated form.
As for "the wise" (*dhīrā*), he says "the learned" (*paṇḍitā*) because they are endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*).
"Of him": of one who has abandoned anger and conceit, who has completely transcended the fetters, who does not cling to name-and-form, and who is free from the burdens of passion and the like.
The Elder named Mogharāja was one of the sixteen attendants of the Brahmin Bāvari.
The intention is that the meaning is not yet fully concluded according to the sequence of the discourse; there is something further to be said. Completely...
Because of his liberation, gods and humans pay homage to him who practices accordingly. What happens to them? Is it that nothing at all occurs? Is this the specific point here?
He spoke thus with reference to the One of Ten Powers (*dasabala*) by way of the highest description (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*).
"By practicing in accordance" means by following after the practice and engaging in it. "They pay homage" means they revere him.
"Having known the Dhamma of the Four Truths" means having penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Truths realized by him.
And thus, because of the Buddha’s perfect awakening, they become free from doubt; hence it is said, "having abandoned doubt.

Thereafter, however, through the gradual attainment of the supreme path, they also transcend all attachments. They are to be praised for the fulfillment of the qualities of one beyond training (*asekkha*).
"There is also praise from the wise.
The commentary on the *Nasanti-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Ujjhānasaññi-sutta*.
35. They possess perception that proceeds by way of disparagement; or, they perceive by way of disparagement, thus they are "those who perceive with disparagement" (*ujjhānasaññī*).

"Let him cause [it] to be made" means let him cause a limit to be set for those things already made. "Causing it to be made with a limit" means causing it to be made with a boundary; the meaning is that it is a limited statement.
By way of being the opposite of rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) and so forth, silk (*pattuṇṇa*), fine cloth (*dukūla*), and so on are mentioned. This is the name.
By the word *gahita* (taken), it is shown that in the phrase *ujjhānasaññikā*, the particle *ka* signifies "perception" (*saññā*).
"Existent in another mode" means the self (*attā*) existing or being found in an impure mode other than the mode by which one perceives oneself.
"Having deceived" means having misled. Of that deceiver. That [refers to] the four requisites.
"Enjoying. "Comprehending" means they know by delimiting his practice. "The doer" (kāraka) means the agent of right practice; the sense is "one who practices rightly.
"This" (idaṃ) is stated with a change of gender; the sense is "this one" (ayaṃ). "Practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (dhammānudhammapaṭipadā) refers to the Dhamma of Nibbāna...
The practice is appropriate and conforms to the Dhamma. It is firm because it does not slacken in the destruction of opposing factors.
Regarding the phrase "by mere speaking and by mere hearing," the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of excluding a qualification;
thus, it excludes the distinction of right practice from what is merely spoken or merely heard. "The worldly convention" (*lokapariyāya*) means the thorough investigation of the world.
The transformation of formations by way of their arising and ceasing. Therefore he said, "the rising and falling of the world of formations.
This meaning occurs only through the penetration of the Truths; thus he said, "and having understood the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
"They do not act thus" means that while not revealing the qualities existing within themselves, they say, "They do not act in the way you describe."
The meaning is that he declares its non-existence.

"Only one who has not committed [the offense]" means one who has not committed the fault. "Acceptance of the transgression" means forbearance; thus, when it is confessed by the teacher, it is said to have been removed from him. Therefore he said: "May he accept it" means "may he forgive it.

"By way of its own nature" means according to its true nature (*sabhāvato*). "Identical with one" means even though one knows the mental conduct of others, one is together with those who do not know it.

"Acting in a manner identical to one [who has committed an offense]. "From another" means subsequently. "When a discussion has arisen" refers to when a discussion such as "In whom do transgressions not exist?
is underway; having then illuminated the power and majesty of the Buddha by saying, "Of the Tathāgata, the Buddha," and so forth.
"I shall forgive" means I shall accept the confession of the transgression. For here, it is the acceptance of that [confession] which is intended by the term "forgiveness."
The Teacher, however, is always forgiving.
One who has anger within his mind is called *kopantara*. One for whom hatred (*dosa*) is heavy—that is, to be held in high regard—is called *dosagaru*.
Alternatively, the reading is *paṭimuccati*, which has the same meaning. *Accāyika-kamma* is an action performed impulsively, without prior reflection. *No cidha*: not at all.
“If not here. *Idha* is a mere particle. *Apagataṃ* means removed or taken away. “If there were no fault,” by that way of speaking, it means if there were no such thing as an offense.
“They would not settle” means they would not be pacified. “Virtuous” (*kusalo*) means blameless.

By the two words “wise” (*dhīro*) and “mindful” (*sato*), he speaks of one who has cut the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭachinda*). The meaning of “Who indeed is always wise? is [to be understood] from the verse beginning with “Whose transgressions... and so forth.

This is the meaning of the question verse. Since the word *tathāgata* has been explained in detail in the commentaries on the *Dīgha Nikāya* and *Majjhima Nikāya*, he says, "for such reasons as these, [the title] of the Tathāgata.
By the phrase "by his Buddhahood and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the reasons set forth in the *Niddesa*, beginning with "the awakener of the world.
Liberation (*vimokkha*) refers to the Noble Path; its "end" (*anto*) is the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*).
In this context, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to a designation (*paññatti*); it is by means of that [designation] that he illuminates the power of a Buddha.
Now, he shows that what was scattered is being gathered together in brief.
The commentary on the *Ujjhānasaññīsutta* is finished.
6. Saddhāsuttavaṇṇanā 36. Regarding the phrase *tatvassā*:

it is said that this is a grammatical description (*niddesa*) formed by substituting the letter *va* for the vowel *o* and eliding the letter *a*, thus resulting in "from that, [there is] confidence" (*tato assā*).
Alternatively, the reading is *tatassā*; and the meaning of "from that" (*tato*) is "because of confidence" (*saddhāhetu*). "Do not follow" (*nānupatanti*) means they do not occur.
“They become negligent” means they are heedless; the meaning is that they practice wrongly. “Characteristics” refers to the characteristics of impermanence and so forth.

“He contemplates closely” means he looks upon [them] by approaching with the eye of knowledge; the meaning is that he observes them. “The duty of what has come” means the duty of what has been brought;

this is the reading, or alternatively, *āhata-kiccaṃ*. “He accomplishes” means he brings to completion by way of penetration through non-delusion; [this refers to] the truth of cessation, which possesses such characteristics.
The meaning of "he contemplates" (*upanijjhāyati*) should also be stated in the context of the Path, because without it, penetration through non-delusion is impossible.
"Having the kasiṇa as its object" (*kasiṇārammaṇassa*) is a statement of its characteristic; for there are indeed attainments that have objects other than the kasiṇas.
And just as those with the kasiṇa as their object [serve] for the eight attainments and for the remaining states that take them as objects by way of reviewing...
Because those objects were grasped by the mind in such a manner, it is said, "of the kasiṇa-object.
Arahantship is called "supreme happiness" because it is to be described as the highest and most excellent happiness.
The commentary on the *Saddhā-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Samaya-sutta* 37.

"In dependence upon an exclamation" (*udānaṃ paṭicca*) means: in dependence upon an utterance of joy spoken by the Kukkura-sons (*ukkākaraññā*) for the purpose of avoiding confusion regarding their birth, based on the purity of their own lineage. [It refers to those] who, by way of clan (*gotta*), received the name "Sakka. If even one...
Regarding the country (*janapada*), as to why it is plural, he says: "By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhīsaddena*).

For those who contemplate syllables (*akkharacintika*) desire gender and number as if they were appropriate in such instances; this is the conventional usage here, as in the case of "Avantī" and "Kurū.
However, when the word *janapada* is used as a qualifier for those [countries], it is singular because it is a class-term (*jātisadda*). "Aropima" means not planted by anyone.
"By a barrier" means by a dam. "Having had it bound" means having had the embankment made firm with yellow leaves, stones, clods of earth, and so forth.

"They cultivate crops" means that, it is said, because of the intensity of the heat in the month of Jeṭṭha, the snow in the Himavat melts and flows down, eventually entering the Rohiṇī River; having bound [the river] there, they cultivate their crops.
To make clearer the meaning stated briefly as "Having struck at their birth, they increased the quarrel," he said, "The Koliyan laborers spoke.
"Niyutta-amaccānan" means of those high ministers appointed to that work of guarding the crops.

38. "That park was known as Saṅkha"—this is the connection. Those who seize with a bow and arrow, strike, and afflict are called *dhanuggahā* (archers).

Because he is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), and because he has thoroughly understood the danger and the escape regarding the entire collection of bases for the origin of the sustenance by which all beings subsist—let alone [the danger and escape regarding the specific objects]—his mind is not overwhelmed by whatever arises. Thus, it is said:

"Having become one who endures feelings...," because he has correctly established mindfulness and clear comprehension. "Not being oppressed" means not being afflicted. Granted, [this applies] to what is undesirable...

There is no such thing as being touched by feeling and not being oppressed by it; however, because its basis has been fully understood (*pariññāta*), one who does not fall under its power is called "unafflicted.

They are unable to lie down because of the arising of suffering. "This lion’s posture" refers to this aforementioned lion’s posture.

41. "Head" (*sīsa*) is a term for the teaching; it refers to designating something as the head among other things that ought to be stated in the teaching.
Therefore, he said, "By lust and so forth," and so on. "By giving" (*dānena*) means by relinquishing to others what belongs to oneself.

“Without having eaten two or three meals” means without having eaten food for two or three times.

The status of being a vehicle is also stated for things such as umbrellas. Therefore, it is said: “It is a giver of vehicles; it is a giver of happiness.
A lamp is called a “giver of eyes” because it acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārīkāraṇa*) for the function that must be performed by the eye.
To show in detail the meaning that was stated in brief as “it is a giver of all [faculties] such as strength,” [the text continues]:
“Two or three [houses] in a village,” and so forth, was said. A *paṭissaya* is a dwelling because it is to be resorted to by means of sitting and other such postures.
It is as if placed [there], because fatigue is dispelled. “For one wandering outside” means for one who, not having obtained a *paṭissaya*, wanders in the open space outside.
“He is scorched” (*jhāyati*) means he is being scorched; the meaning is that he is exhausted. This occurs due to opposing conditions such as cold, heat, and so forth.

Dissimilar continuity (*visabhāga-santati*) should be understood as occurring within one’s own continuum; conversely, similar continuity (*sabhāga-santati*) is to be understood from the opposite perspective.
"Pleasure" (*sukha*) arises both from the avoidance of conditions for suffering and from the occurrence of conditions for pleasure;

showing that one obtains both of these by way of reliance, he said, "As he was walking abroad on his feet," and so forth. "The bliss of the joy of the Dhamma" (*dhammapītisukha*) [refers to] through the reviewing of the Dhamma.
“Arisen joy and bliss” means the bliss that occurs through the subsiding of the defilements.
It is said, “It is as if one has descended into a well,” referring to how darkness falls for one who has entered a shelter with closed windows and, having shut the door, stands therein.
Therefore it is said, “The bed, chair, and so forth are not discerned. This is due to the fault of fatigue from having exerted oneself outside while in meditative absorption.
Nor is it through the fault of ingratitude. Therefore he said, “for a moment,” and so forth.
That by which one does not die is *amaraṇa* (the state of non-death), such as the attainment of Nibbāna and the like. The giving of that is the teaching of the Dhamma; he gives that.
Therefore he said, “he who instructs in the Dhamma. As to how this instruction in the Dhamma occurs, he said, “the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*),” and so forth.

“He expounds the commentary” means he provides an exposition of the meaning of the text whose wording has not yet been opened up; furthermore, he causes those who have not yet studied it to recite the text.
In various places, he answers the questions asked; this, first of all, is the duty regarding the scriptures (*ganthadhura*).
As for the duty regarding practice (*paṭipattivāsadhura*), he explains the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*); for both of these, there is the hearing of the Dhamma.

He performs [these]. "All giving" refers to the aforementioned giving of material goods (*āmisa-dāna*) and the giving of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*). "The gift of the Dhamma" refers to the teaching of the Dhamma.
"Delight in the Dhamma" is the delight in the Dhamma of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). "The flavor of the Dhamma" is the joy and gladness based upon the true Dhamma.
The commentary on the *Kiṃdada-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Anna-sutta* 43.

"They long for" means they desire. To show by way of examples those places where his approach became more widely known in the world, he said, "as in the case of the householder Citta, Sīvali Thera, and others. "Food" refers to the fourfold food known as *anna*.
...the condition. Having taken all the donors together as one, it is stated in a general sense as a single unit:
"only the donor. And as it is said: "Who indeed is that *yakkha* who does not delight in food? In that context, "*yakkha*" means a being (*satta*).
Furthermore, because a general designation refers to a manifold range of objects, [it continues]: "those who give it with faith, with a serene mind..."
"With the mind, he partakes of that very food"—thus it is said. Herein, the letter *ma* is used for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*); the meaning is "those very [qualities].
He follows after the donor's non-renunciation just as a wheel follows the hub.
The commentary on the Discourse on Food is finished.
4. Commentary on the Ekamūla Sutta 44.
It has a single root (ekamūlā) in the sense of being established; that is, it has one root known as ignorance (avijjā). That is the "single-rooted" [suffering].

Just as craving arises through the contemplation of gratification (*assādānupassanā*) regarding things conducive to fettering (*saṃyojanīya*), so too does non-comprehension arise through the domination of craving.
Ignorance is the root of craving, and craving is the root of ignorance. This principle is stated by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*);
however, this mutual state of being roots by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) is indeed evident.
But here, in this verse, that which is intended as the "single root" is craving. Therein, the craving for existence turns toward the view of eternalism.
It turns back by way of the craving for non-existence (*vibhava-taṇhā*) through the view of annihilationism; thus there is a double turning.

"By way of the point of co-nascence" means even by way of the point of co-nascence, let alone for one who has fallen into confusion, there may be defilement due to the powerful state of the craving that is currently occurring.
"By way of the point of decisive support" means precisely by way of the point of decisive support, because [craving] cannot exist at the point of co-nascence.
“Places of spreading” (*pattharaṇaṭṭhāna*) means the ground where [the craving] proceeds after having become extensive. Therefore he said: “In those [three], it spreads.
It is called the ocean in the sense of being a sea (*samudda*). Because it is sufficient (*alaṃ*) and capable for the purpose of crossing over due to its unfordability, it is a “pit” (*pātāla*);
furthermore, it is a “pit” because it is like a pit. Therefore he said: “in the sense of being without a foothold. The meaning is: by way of its unfathomable depth.
The commentary on the Ekamūla Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Anoma Sutta: 45.
"Anomanāma" means having a name that is not deficient. For the Blessed One’s names are based solely upon his qualities; and of those qualities...
He said, "Because it is complete, it is called 'of no deficient name,'" adding, "because it is endowed with all virtues," and so forth.

Furthermore, names such as "one possessing the three knowledges" (*tevijja*) or "one possessing the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñña*) are not "names of no deficiency" because their scope is limited;

however, the Blessed One’s names such as "Teacher," "Omniscient One," and "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*Sammāsambuddha*) are indeed "names of no deficiency" because their scope is vast and they possess no deficiency.
Therefore he said, "It is called 'independence' (avekalla). "The aggregates and so forth" refers to the specific distinctions among the aggregates and the like.

"Meanings" (atthe) refers to those things that are to be known as they truly are by means of knowledge. "For the attainment of subsequent wisdom" means for the acquisition of supramundane wisdom (lokuttara-paññā).

"The way" (paṭipadaṃ) refers to the way of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). By virtue of the defilements and sensual desires, because they are to be clung to, sensual desires themselves are the "attachment" (ālaya).
It is said “moving with pleasure” (*kamamāna*) because it attained a state of pleasantness precisely in the past; it is not so now, as that [state] is absent. Therefore he said:
“But this was said with reference to the past. It refers to those who are great by virtue of their great majesty and other qualities.
The commentary on the *Anoma-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Accharā-sutta* 46.

Regarding the verse beginning with “Resounding with the clapping of hands,” since the intention with which the son of the gods sang it cannot be understood without a gradual narrative (*anupubbikathā*), the author speaks starting from its origin, saying: “It is said that this son of the gods... and so forth.
In this context, "in the Dispensation" means in the Dispensation of this very Teacher. "Action and non-action" refers to the determination of what constitutes action.

Because he prioritizes the welfare of others and possesses few personal concerns, he lives a simple life. "The portion for lying down" is the part of the day permitted for resorting to a bed for the purpose of resting the body when it is fatigued from devotion to meditation during the daytime and the first watch of the night.
"Internally" means within the belly; because the food is scanty, there are winds that cut like knives due to their sharpness—winds that are like knives.
"Precisely in the battle" means in the very struggle against the Māra of the defilements, or while standing at the head of the sphere of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*) teaching the Dhamma.
Due to the dullness of the necessary conditions and the immaturity of his knowledge, he did not reach the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*) before his time.
"Having done so" is the construction. "Standing above" means standing above the celestial cloth by way of being an accessory (parikkhāra).
"He remained exactly thus" means that even though they spoke to him in that manner, he remained exactly as he had been before.
"The golden plate" refers to the golden plate to be obtained after winning at dice. Because he had committed no transgression, his virtue was entirely unbroken. Since, in that regard...
When they were coming into the presence of the Teacher, they also came along with him; therefore it is said, "surrounded by a host of nymphs" (*accharāsaṅghaparivuta*).
"Resounding" (*saṅghosita*) means resounded together; it was resounded here and there by way of the sound of the nymphs' singing.

He speaks of them as a "host of *pisācas* (ogres)" because of their lack of desire and passion. "Because of a mind fixed on certainty" (*niyāmacittatāya*) means because of a mind inclined toward the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*).
“By way of veneration” means by way of occupying a position of respect, because one does not act under their control. “Sustenance” (yātrā) refers to sustenance directed toward Nibbāna.
Since that, however, is the departure from the round of existence (vaṭṭa), he asked, “How will there be a departure?

“One who is exceedingly austere” (atisallekhata) means one whose mode of life is such as to scrub away the defilements (kilesa) to an extreme degree. “One who has not formed a resolve” means one who is not devoted to the cultivation of meditation (bhāvanā).

"For one who has not yet initiated insight" means for one who has not yet begun the practice of insight. "Of the practitioner" means of one who practices rightly by following the instructions of the Sugata. "Insight into emptiness" means insight that illuminates emptiness through dwelling alone by distancing oneself from misconduct and craving.
"He shall have a single path" means that for him there shall be only the supramundane path in the future; however, the preliminary path is already well-practiced—this is the meaning.
"Of bodily crookedness and so forth" means because of the non-existence of bodily misconduct and the like, due to their having been completely severed and being no longer found.
"Fearless" (abhaya) means that there is no fear here, or that for the person who has attained this, there is no fear.

It is so called because, in proceeding across the wilderness of saṃsāra to the secure, deathless state known as Nibbāna, it serves as a well-prepared vehicle provided by the Charioteer of the Sugatas.

The "chariot" refers specifically to the Noble Eightfold Path. They are called "wheels of the Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) because they do not deviate from the Dhamma and because they arise one after another.

"Fear of wrongdoing" (*ottappa*) is also included by virtue of its inseparable connection [with moral shame]. "Support" (*apālamba*) means a refuge. "Retinue" (*parivāra*) means equipment, due to its being prepared.
In the sense of making the path, the Dhamma is right view as it is comprised within that [path]. "By way of impermanence, etc. means by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth.
"When the [defilements] have been purified and are being abandoned": "the cycle obtained by the plane" (*bhūmiladdhavaṭṭa*) refers to the cycle known as the "plane-obtained.
In this context, the five aggregates are called the "plane" because they are the locus for the occurrence of insight;

the mass of defilements that is liable to arise therein due to the nature of the karma of the cycle is the "cycle obtained by the plane. "Thoroughly understanding" means by way of delimitation and by way of transcendence.

Understanding and penetrating [the truth], why did the deva-son establish himself in the fruit of stream-entry alone, given that this teaching was delivered by the Blessed One with the four paths as its primary focus? To answer this, he said, "For just as... and so forth.
The commentary on the *Accharā-sutta* is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Tree-Planting (Vanaropasutta) 47.

Regarding the word *ke*: the term *ke*, which is expressed according to its own grammatical base (*sāmiva*), should be transformed here into the nominative plural (*paccattabahuvacanavasena*), as in the phrase "those established in the Dhamma, endowed with virtue" (*dhammaṭṭhā sīlasampannā*).
For the transformation of case endings occurs according to the sense. Or, in the phrase "Who are the people? (*ke janā*), the term *kesa* is used.

Having brought [the subject] forward by way of the lion’s gaze, one should apply it; thus he says: "Who are those established in the Dhamma? Who are those perfected in virtue? By the word "asks," he states the reason for that.
A *ārāma* is so called because beings delight (*ramanti*) therein due to the excellence of its fruits and other qualities.

Those who plant and establish such groves are *ārāmaropā*. That which is frequented (*vanīyati*) and resorted to because of the excellence of its shade is a *vana*. Regarding that, the characteristic of a small grove (*upavana*) is as follows:

The forest is included by the mention of the monastery grounds (*ārāma*) itself; thus, he speaks of the characteristics of a penance grove (*tapovana*) with the words, "having enclosed the boundary," and so forth.
"Uneven" refers to a place that is rough due to water and mud. A *papā* is so called because they drink drinking water (*pānīya*) there;
or, it is a *papā* because water is drunk (*pīyati*) there. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "tanks and so forth," he includes irrigation channels (*mātikā*).
"Referring to the meaning of this" means that by this [phrase], he rejects [the idea that merit] has reached the level of a path of action (*kammappatha*).
For when one recollects the merit performed by oneself, much merit is generated on account of that [act]; however, the merit as it was performed does not increase of its own accord.
"Because of being established in that Dhamma" means because of being firmly established in that Dhamma, such as the planting of groves and so forth. By that too...

"Endowed with virtue" means that, having stood upon the virtue practiced in accordance with the aforementioned qualities, one is possessed of other virtues as well, characterized by restraint of body and speech.
The ten wholesome states are fulfilled because of the avoidance of misconduct. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the *Vanaropa-sutta* is concluded.
8. Commentary on the *Jetavana Sutta* 48.

They are called *isī* (sages) because they have sought after [virtuous] qualities and because their qualities are sought after; this refers to those beyond training (*asekha*), those in training (*sekha*), and noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*). The assembly of sages is the "Sangha of sages" (*isisaṅgha*). That which is frequented by the Sangha of sages is [described as] "frequented by the community of monks" (*bhikkhusaṅghanisevita*).

For one who causes that [monastery] to be built, there is [merit] by way of the perfumed chamber (*gandhakuṭi*), the palace (*pāsāda*), the gabled hall (*kūṭāgāra*), and so forth, as well as by way of trees and creepers with glossy, dense shade.
Furthermore, that Jeta’s Grove delights the mind because of its excellence of location, which is uniquely and exceedingly beautiful, as well as because it is a dwelling place for the Noble Ones;
thus he said, “Having thus described the praise of Jeta’s Grove with the first verse.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Wherever Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful. [This refers to] volition leading to diminution.
It brings about the purification of beings by leading to the destruction of karma; thus it is said, "Karma is the volition of the Path.
It is *vijjā* (clear vision) in the sense of making known the Four Noble Truths and in the sense of piercing the defilements;
thus it is said, "*Vijjā* is the wisdom of the Path," meaning right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*). The factors belonging to the side of concentration are right effort, mindfulness, and concentration.
Just as true knowledge (*vijjā*) belongs to the side of true knowledge, so too concentration (*samādhi*) belongs to the side of concentration.
Because he possesses virtue (*sīla*), it is called "virtue"; thus it is said: "The life of one established in virtue is supreme.

"Views and intentions" refers to right view and right intention. In that context, the state of being "true knowledge" is predicated of right intention by virtue of its being an aid to right view. For it is thus: [he]...

It is said to be "included within the aggregate of wisdom. And just as right intention and the others are included within the aggregate of wisdom, so too are effort and mindfulness included within the aggregate of concentration; thus he says, "effort, mindfulness, and concentration.
For here, by "dhamma," concentration is intended, as in such passages as, "Those Blessed Ones were of such a nature (evaṃdhammā). [The remaining factors are] speech, action, and livelihood.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these are included as being comprised within the path itself. Therefore he said, "by this eightfold path.
The noble path is to be developed by means of the method or procedure. Therefore he said, "the states conducive to concentration.
This refers both to the states of insight conducive to right concentration and to the states of the path. "Monks, I shall teach you the noble right concentration..."
For according to the statement, "together with its proximate cause and its requisites," the path factors beginning with right view have right concentration as their requisite.
"One should investigate" means one should examine; the meaning is that one should develop. "Therein" is a locative expression used for the sake of indicating the cause.
For the purification of beings has the Noble Path as its cause. Therefore he said, "one is purified therein by means of the Noble Path. [This refers to] the phenomena of the five aggregates.
"Vicineyya" means one should clearly see the five aggregates in the present.
When these are being clearly seen and insight has reached its peak, at that very moment the truth of suffering is penetrated through the penetration of full understanding;
at that same moment the truth of the origin is penetrated through the penetration of abandonment; and the truth of cessation is penetrated through the penetration of realization.
"The truth of the path is penetrated by means of penetration through cultivation"—thus, in these four truths, one is purified.
In this context, the locative case is used in the sense of the "sign" (nimitta); the meaning is: "while those truths are being penetrated.
The term *avadhāraṇavacana* is a word of definition; the meaning is "determination" (*avadhāraṇa*). And [the phrase] "Sāriputto vā" (or Sāriputta).
The definitive statement, "Among disciples, Sāriputta alone is the best," illustrates this meaning because of his preeminent status.
By the phrase "through the pacification of defilements," it shows that the Great Elder possessed such a tranquility of defilements.
He attained perfection in wisdom within the domain of his disciples. If this is so, then regarding the verse: "Even a bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore would be at most only this much."
This should be understood as stated specifically by way of those Buddhas who have reached the perfection of wisdom within the domain of knowledge.
Furthermore, the restriction [implied] regarding liberation is stated with reference to those who have gone beyond by means of the three liberations. Therefore he said:
“Gone beyond means gone to Nibbāna,” and so forth. There is no one found superior to the Elder; indeed, such a one is found.
The intention is that it might be obtained in exactly this way.
The commentary on the *Jetavana Sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Macchari Sutta*.
49. "Maccharino" means those who possess stinginess (*macchera*), those who are endowed with stinginess; thus he says, "endowed with stinginess. *Macchera* and *macchariya* are one in meaning.
"He does not pay homage" means he does not perform even the mere act of salutation, much less giving;
this is the intended sense. "To do service" is to be construed as "he performs a sweet welcome. This...
"Even so, he does not show his own self as one who is soft toward stinginess, considering it to be 'stinginess' itself.
"Do your feet ache? Surely it is your own feet that ache from coming and going; what do these people cut?"—this is the intended meaning.
"He does not even perform proper etiquette, so how could there be giving?"—this is the intended meaning. They go to their respective destinations according to their karma.
The noble ones (*ariya*) are so called because they approach (*upagacchanti*). However, those who are base (*kucchita*) noble ones are "miserly" (*kadariya*), meaning they are stubbornly stingy.

Indeed, there is nothing more base than stinginess, for it is the most inferior of all things; this is because it obstructs generosity—the root of all success, such as the attainment of wealth—since it overcomes all virtues.
This is expressed by such statements as "one's own destroyer. [One becomes so] through the pursuit of stinginess.
It is the destroyer of the attainment of a fortunate rebirth for wholesome states.
*Samparāya* refers to the world beyond (*paraloka*), so called because one must pass away from or approach it according to one’s merit or demerit.
*Kāmaguṇarati* is the gratification based upon the strands of sensual pleasure. *Khiḍḍā* refers to physical play, verbal play, and mental play.
Thus it is threefold. "This is the result" means that the difficult acquisition of robes and so forth is such a kind of result (*vipāka*).

"The world of Yama" refers to the other world. Regarding the word *upapajjare*, the particle *iti* here has the sense of "manner"; by this, it includes what is stated in the Canon as "hell and the animal realm.
"They beg" refers to the noble begging (*ariya-yācanā*). For it is said: "The Noble Ones stand with reference [to others]; this is the begging of the Noble Ones."
Those who share [their wealth] are called "generous" because they act upon what they know ought to be done.

"By the radiance of the celestial mansions (*vimāna*)" is merely an illustration; for the radiance of the pleasure groves, the wish-fulfilling trees, and even the radiance of the deities' garments, ornaments, and bodies likewise illuminate the heavenly realm.
Alternatively, "they shine" means they are manifest, not unmanifest as in the world of the miserable states (*apāya*). "In those things produced by others" means...
Without having acquired them oneself, [one enjoys] the articles of comfort provided by others. Therefore, it is said in the Pāḷi:

"They rejoice like those who wield power" (*vasavattīva modare*); the meaning is that they rejoice through the possession of happiness, just like the sons of the gods who wield power over the enjoyments created by others (*paranimmitabhogesu vasavattī devaputtā*).
