"The future life spoken of thus" means these are the heavenly realms (*saggā*); this refers to the future life described above. "Of both" means...

Of these two aforementioned types—those who perform evil deeds and those who perform good deeds—after passing away from there, that is, after passing away from hell or the heavenly realms and so forth, they are reborn among human beings.
Among them, he who was miserly and is reborn among humans becomes poor;
yet, due to the influence of his previous conduct, remaining miserly, he kills fish, turtles, and other creatures for the sake of supporting his wife and children.

Furthermore, he is reborn in hell. The other, possessing a pure intention, having become prosperous and having performed further meritorious deeds by virtue of his past conduct, would be reborn in heaven. Therefore it was said: "In the future life as well, there is only an unhappy destination or a happy destination.
The commentary on the *Maccharisutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta 50.
Regarding the phrase “*upapannāse*,” this is an expression formed by the addition of the letter *se*; its meaning is simply “reborn,” as he explains by saying “approached by way of rebirth.
Because they do not fall away from their own excellence, they are called the *Aviha* (the Unfallen); the Brahma-world of those [beings] is the *Avihā-brahmaloka*.
"In that" means at the very moment of rebirth, that is, in the first stage itself. "By the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship" means by the liberation of one beyond training (*asekkha-vimutti*).
However, they were already liberated by the liberation of one in training (*sekha-vimutti*) even before being reborn in the Aviha heaven;

thus, it is said: "They transcend the human body by way of abandoning mental defilements"—this is a demonstration of the cause by means of the fruit. Therefore he says: "The human body here... and so forth.
“...are said. That which exists in the divine realm (*divi*) is *dibba*; it refers to the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) designated as the state of a Brahmā.

Regarding that, the term “fettering bond” (*saṃyojanakoti*) is used, as it is said: “The divine bond (*dibbaṃ yogaṃ*) consists of the five higher fetters (*pañca uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni*). “Of this one” refers to the son of the gods (*devaputta*).
“Having abandoned the human body, he has reached the divine bond”—this refers to their welfare through the abandonment of all transgressions.

“He speaks what is blameless” means that you say he is one who is skillful (*kusala*). By applying a metaphorical identity between the meaning and the word, it is said that his speech is profound; thus he says, “profound in meaning,” because of the profundity of the meaning itself, not of the word.

Because of the complete eradication of sensual lust and the total abandonment of the objects of sense-desire, the non-returner (*anāgāmī*) is called a “brahmin practitioner of the spiritual life free from the fleshly. This is the place where he dwells.
"One who has the same village as this" means "a resident of the same village.
The commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Ādittavagga is finished.
6. The Chapter on Aging (Jarāvagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Aging (Jarāsuttavaṇṇanā) 51.
It is "good" (sādhu) because it accomplishes what is beneficial; for whatever kind of benefit there may be, that is to be obtained by one who desires welfare.
Because it is obtained through service, it is called "auspicious" (*bhaddaka*) in the sense of being excellent; thus he said, "What is obtained as 'well done' (*sādhu*) is auspicious.
To clarify from the opposite perspective the meaning already stated—that "virtue is well done until old age"—it was said, "By this, he shows this.
"This" refers to this group of meanings.

“Established” means having gained a footing within the continuum of consciousness, such that it cannot be led away by anything. Therefore he said, “arrived by way of the path. “By way of being honored, etc.
refers to its state of being worthy of worship and so forth. For this has been stated in the Porāṇa-ṭīkā: “It is ‘honored’ because it is a treasure;
for in the world, this which is called a treasure is honored by virtue of its worth being a thousand pieces of gold and so forth. And those who...
In the world, those such as the Kṣatriya scholars, the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, and Mahābrahmā are held in high esteem;
he is esteemed by them because they must go to him for refuge and so forth. "Bringing joy" means bringing the bliss of rapture (*pīti*).

"By the bliss of the delight of jhāna" refers to both kinds of the bliss of the delight of jhāna. "To weigh" means to delimit. "The supreme limit of qualities" means the pinnacle of excellence regarding qualities.
“Hard to find” (*dullabho*) means that it is impossible to obtain even after passing through many incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*). “Matchless” (*anomo*) means not deficient, but complete.
In this regard, because he is especially enjoyed by matchless beings, he is to be recollected as “the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One”;
thus [the author] says, “The Blessed One is matchless in virtue,” and so forth.
"Only the wisdom of the Noble Path (ariyamagga-paññā) is intended here," thus he said: "But here, wisdom is called a 'jewel' in the sense that its manifestation is difficult to obtain.
Because it produces meritorious fruit and because it purifies one's own continuum, volitional merit (puññacetanā) is called "merit" (puñña).
However, because it belongs exclusively to the one in whom it has arisen and is not shared with others, it is "not brought by anyone," as stated in the Commentary.
However, it is stated that [it is] "due to its formlessness.
The commentary on the *Jarāsutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Ajarāsutta*.

52. "By non-decaying" means by not arriving at a state of being worn out. This is a term for a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) used in the sense of reaching non-destruction. Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'by way of non-failure'. "Should be expelled" means it should be removed.
The commentary on the *Ajarasā-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Mitta-sutta*.

53. It is called a *sattha* because it moves together with goods (*attha*); it is a group of people who travel to foreign lands and such places for the purpose of trade, taking merchandise and capital.
Therefore he said, "one who travels together" (*sahacaro*), meaning one who goes along with [them]. A "friend" (*mitta*) is one endowed with the duty of a friend through the application of affection.
To show the specific type intended here, he said, "when illness has arisen," and so forth. "Of such a kind" (*tathārūpe*)...

[It refers to one who is] loathsome or difficult to treat. Just as a man who has gone abroad is a source of dependence for those left behind when his wealth is lost, so too a mother is a source of dependence for her son within the household due to her affection for him; thus it is said:
"A mother is a friend in one's own home. Regarding the phrase "of one whose purpose has arisen," he says "of one whose duty has appeared" to mean that a specific objective has been established.
"Beneficial for the future life" means bringing about welfare in the life to come.
The commentary on the *Mittasutta* is concluded.
4. Commentary on the *Vatthusutta*.
54. *Paṭiṭṭhāti* means "stands as a support. *Guyhassa* means "of that which is to be hidden, of a secret. He is called the "supreme friend" because he occupies a position of extreme affection.
The commentary on the *Vatthusutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Paṭhamajanasutta*.
55. *Vidhāvatīti* means it runs toward various forms; the meaning is that it proceeds according to its desire.
The commentary on the First Janasutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Second Janasutta.

56. "From the suffering of the round" means from the suffering of *saṃsāra*. For *saṃsāra* revolves because of the successive arising of defilements (*kilesa*), karma, and their results (*vipāka*). And that suffering is [called] "suffering" because it is merely suffering, being a mass of various kinds of suffering.
The commentary on the *Dutiyajanasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Tatiyajanasutta*

57. *Nipphatti* (accomplishment) means accomplishment because of the bringing forth (*nipphajjana*) of desirable and undesirable results (*vipāka*). For that very reason, it is a support (*avassaya*); the meaning is that it is the basis, the foundation, and the cause for the result that has been accomplished.
The commentary on the Third Janasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Uppathasutta.
58. "Not the path" means it is not the path; it is not the means. "The wasting away of night and day" is said because the moment of its passing away is manifest there.
For even the moment already spoken of passes away of its own accord. The "remaining external impurity" consists of such things as clothing and the body.
For it is said: "It can be cleansed by washing with ashes, lye, and so forth. "Corrupted" means the continuum of beings (sattasantāna) has been defiled.
It is not possible to make one pure by inducing a state of internal impurity. "A woman" refers to one who creates an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"Offspring" refers to the group of seven; one becomes attached—that is, forms an attachment—to them when failing to see their danger as it truly is.
Asceticism (*tapas*) is so called because it scorches the defilements (*kilesa*); thus he said, "all of them," and so forth.
The commentary on the Uppatha Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Second Sutta: 59.
Regarding the phrase "In what" (*kissa*), he said "in what is he delighted? because it is a genitive case used in the sense of a locative. Faith (*saddhā*) has the nature of being blameless.
Therefore, because it brings about mundane and supramundane welfare and happiness, he said: "She is the companion for one going to a happy destination and to Nibbāna.
She instructs by virtue of being a guide in the practice of what is beneficial.
The commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Kavi Sutta: 60.

Regarding "gāyattī and so forth": among the twenty-six meters, the meter beginning with *gāyattī* and ending with *ukkatikā* is the source and origin of verses (*gāthā*), in the sense that "by means of this they arise. However, by those [other meters], there is the *anuṭṭhubhā* and so forth.

It is said: "Zeal is the source of verses. Verses that establish what has gone before are those verses uttered for the purpose of generating mindfulness—like an initial announcement—at the beginning of a Dhamma discourse.

For it is said that "a syllable generates a word"; since a collection of syllables is a word (*pada*), and a collection of words is a verse (*gāthā*), and a collection is manifested by its constituent parts because they bring about its occurrence, therefore...
A syllable (*akkhara*) is that which stands as a phoneme; a collection of those is a word (*pada*).
Since a word is like one who manifests or generates [meaning], it is said that "the syllable generates the word.

For although a syllable, once uttered, perishes and exists for only a single moment, it is grasped as a word when it is brought together as a whole through the process of synthesis by the mental consciousness-stream (*manoviññāṇa-vīthi*) as it proceeds subsequently.
It manifests the meaning according to convention. The same principle applies here as well in the statement, "a word generates a verse. A verse (*gāthā*) reveals the meaning;

that is to say, a collection of words designated as a "verse," being connected through the relations of action and its factors (*kāraka*), clarifies the intended meaning in accordance with the speaker's intention—meaning that which is reflected upon, repeatedly observed, and coherently joined.
It is based on designations such as "ocean" and so forth, precisely by way of reliance upon conventional usage (*vohāra*).
Having established that [the word] means "it proceeds," he said, "beginning the verses," and so forth. He said "refuge" (ālaya) meaning "support" (avassaya), and "basis" (patiṭṭhā).
"Poet" (kavi) refers to one who speaks with variety and so on.
The commentary on the *Kavisutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Old Age is finished.
7. The Chapter on the Swift (Addhavagga). 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Names (Nāmasutta).

61. "Names" refers to names divided into categories such as common names (*sāmañña-nāma*) and so forth. "All" means the entire range of designations (*paññatti-patha*) and the entire range of the occurrence of the knowable (*ñeyya-pavatti-patha*).
Regarding the phrase "it has overcome": although the past tense is used in the text, that is merely for the sake of the grammatical characteristic (*lakkhaṇa-matta*).

By the words "it overcomes" and "it follows after," it shows that "overcoming" (*abhibhava*) is "following after" (*anupatana*), which is to say, its occurrence (*pavatti*). Furthermore, this overcoming of it—
Without referring to those of limited scope, he speaks the words beginning with "or by means of spontaneous birth" (*opapātika*) in order to show [beings] according to their vast scope.
"It has a name" means that for that tree, rock, and so forth, there is a designation (*samaññā*) such as "nameless"; the sense is that people perceive it in that way.
The commentary on the Sutta on Names is finished.
2. Commentary on the Citta Sutta (62).
"Those who fall under the power of the mind" refers specifically to those who have not fully understood the basis [of existence]. "Without remainder" means a complete inclusion;
for those who have fully understood the aggregates and have abandoned the defilements do not fall under the power of the mind.
They bring that [mind] under their own control.
The commentary on the *Citta-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Taṇhā-sutta*.

63. In the third [verse], the phrase “all have come under its sway” refers to the complete and exhaustive inclusion of those who fall under the sway of craving (*taṇhā*). This meaning is indicated by the expression “the same method applies.
The commentary on the *Taṇhāsutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Saṃyojanasutta*.

64. Regarding the phrase "What is its fetter? (*kiṃ-su-saṃyojano*), he says it is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*). Thus he asks, "Of what fetter is it? (*kiṃ-saṃyojano*). They wander by means of these; thus they are "wanderings" (*vicāraṇā*), meaning feet. Although the plural should have been used, the singular has been employed.
"Of that" refers to the world. The commentary on the *Saṃyojana-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Bandhana-sutta*.
65. In the fourth [sutta], the meaning is exactly as stated in the preceding one; since only the phrasing differs, he says, "The same method applies to the fifth as well.
The commentary on the *Bandhana-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Attahata-sutta*.
66. With the intention that the reading is “kenassubbhāhato,” he said, “the syllable *su* is merely a particle.
However, in the reading “kenassabbhāhato,” there is a euphonic conjunction (*padasaṃdhi*) through the elision of the vowel *u*.
“Scorched by the smoke of desire” means tormented and burnt by craving, which is characterized by longing for objects not yet attained. Therefore, he said, “blazing with desire.”
The commentary on the Attahata Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Uḍḍita Sutta: 67.

"Ullaṅghita" means having leaped up after having hanged oneself. "In the elephant-stalls for sounds, etc. means that the ears and other [senses] were suspended in the elephant-stalls for sounds and so forth.
Because one is bound by the strong fetter of the rope of craving (*taṇhārajjuna*) and does not transcend it. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the world of the sense bases (*āyatana*).

Since the application of meaning has been made in this way, the application should also be made by way of the world of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth. It is not distant because it is the immediately succeeding existence (*anantarabhava*).

Since there is an interval of the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), there is no awakening to the karma of that single mind-moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); such being the case, why [is it not distant]?
He said, "Because beings do not awaken," and so forth, beginning with "by the powerful one.
The commentary on the Uḍḍita Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Pihita Sutta.
68. *Pañho* means the matter desired to be known. Regarding *pucchito* (asked):
because the first half-verse of the seventh sutta was made the second half and the second half was made the first by the deity in the eighth sutta, it is said, "asked in reverse order.
That "the answer is in accordance with the question" is established even without being stated; therefore, it was not mentioned [here].
The commentary on the Pihita-sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Icchā-sutta. 69.
Regarding the ninth [verse], "vinayāya" means "by means of discipline" (*vinayena*). This dative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. "Kissassu" means "of what? (*kissa*).
The syllable *su-* is merely a particle. "It cuts all bonds" means it completely severs all ten kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
For there is no bond of defilement whatsoever that remains unsevered once craving has been severed.
Since this meaning is easy to understand, he said, "All is quite clear."
The commentary on the *Icchāsutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Lokasutta*. 70.
Regarding the phrase "When what?"—in what being present? Since its state of existence occurs precisely through the mode of arising, he said: "When what has arisen?"
"The world has arisen" is said because of the conventional designation (*lokasamaññā*) for that which is without grasping (*anupādāna*).

"In the six"—here too the same method applies—[refers to] "they become intimate," meaning they produce excessive affection (*adhikasineha*), because the internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*) serve as the objects for such excessive affection.

"Depending upon" (*upādāya*) is taken as a verb (*kiriyāpada*) by way of ellipsis (*vacanasesa*), since an action at a prior time depends upon an action at a subsequent time; thus, [the full sense is] "it proceeds" (*pavattati*).
What, then, proceeds? The world, meaning the conventional designation "world. The word "in six" (*chasu*) is used in the locative case in the sense of a cause;
for all suffering has the sixfold base (*chaḷāyatana*) as its cause. "This" refers to the world of sentient beings. It is said to be "arisen" because the sixfold base is the root of all sufferings.
One forms an intimacy with the external bases, especially with visible forms and so forth.
Because they have craving as their basis. Since, by way of satisfying the eye and so forth, one grasps at forms and so on, this leads to being pursued by the world;
therefore it is said: "The six... [is oppressed].
The commentary on the *Loka-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Addhavagga is finished.
8. The Chapter on Cutting (Chetvāvagga). 1. Commentary on the Sutta on Cutting (Chetvāsutta).
71. "Having struck" (*vadhitvā*) means having killed or destroyed. "Because of not being scorched" (*aparidayhamānattā*) means because of not being oppressed.

Because grief and lamentation have perished, one does not grieve, due to the absence of the suffering of mental pain. "Poison" (*visa*) is so called because it is undesirable; its root cause is anger, as it results in what is undesirable. Therefore, he said:
"Of the poison-rooted" (*visamūlassa*) means "of that which has the ripening of suffering. "Of one who is reviled" (*akkhuṭṭhassa*) means of one who has committed the offense of verbal abuse.
For, in connection with the sense of "striking with abuse," the term *kuddhassa* is used in the dative case (*sampadāna*) in the sense of the accusative.
Happiness arises and anger perishes. With reference to the arising of happiness, this anger is called "sweet at the end" (*madhuragga*), meaning it has a happy conclusion.
The commentary on the verse beginning with "having cut" is finished.
2. Commentary on the Rathasutta 72.

"Paññāṇa" (knowledge) is the characteristic and the means of discerning it. "Disvā" (having seen) means by reason of seeing. Just as "the kingdom of King Coḷa" is known as "the Coḷa kingdom," so too is the kingdom made known by the king.
The commentary on the Rathasutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Vittasutta 73.
“By means of faith” (*saddhāya*) means for the sake of faith as a cause. “Perfection of family” (*kulasampadā*) refers to excellence such as being born into a *khattiya* lineage and so forth.

Because it is the cause for obtaining all mundane and supramundane wealth, it is specifically called the “wealth of faith. Regarding all blameless qualities that have arisen by way of the three doors mentioned below—
Because it encompasses [all wholesome states], it is said: "Dhamma is the ten courses of wholesome action. It is undefiled happiness; it is non-material (nirāmisa) happiness.
Comparing that very [happiness] with material (sāmisa) happiness, he says "undefiled" because it is being held in high esteem.

Furthermore, because it generates delight through its quality of being unsatiating, because it is difficult to find dear, and because it brings about freedom from hatred even in one who indulges in it for a long time and to a great extent—
Truth alone is sweeter. For truth does not deserve to be called "flavor" (*rasa*) merely because it is to be drunk, tasted, or experienced.
Now, in order to show its great worthiness even by way of its fulfillment of function and its benefits, the passage beginning with "In truth indeed...
was stated. Therein, the turning back of the river is to be illustrated by the story of Mahākappina and others; the remaining [points]...
These matters are to be illustrated by the Kaṇhadīpāyana-jātaka, the Sutasoma-jātaka, and the Maccha-jātaka.
"They crush" means they overcome. "Sweeter" means more beautiful; the sense is "among the best. "One who lives by wisdom" (paññājīvī) means one whose mode of living is by means of wisdom;
the sense is "one whose conduct is preceded by wisdom. Furthermore, "one who lives by wisdom" means that his life proceeds and functions by way of wisdom.
Showing that the meaning is "he causes to proceed," he said, "He who lives by wisdom," and so forth. Some read "jīvatan" (living), the meaning of which is:
"Of those living, they say the one who lives by wisdom is the best.
The commentary on the Vittasutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Vuṭṭhisutta* 74.
"Of those springing up" means of those rising up by splitting the earth. It is called "sevenfold" because it is referred to as "the best," or because the others conform to that.
It is "secure" (*khema*) due to the absence of famine and calamities. Therefore he said, "well-supplied with food" (*subhikkha*).
“Falling” means moving with their faces downward. “Wandering” means having the habit of wandering;
since they are called "mobile" (jaṅgama) and are not stationary like trees and so forth, he says “of the mobile.
“Cows” means milch-cows; by this term, the inclusion of buffaloes and others should also be understood. “Speaking” means speaking about a matter that has arisen.
"By her own patience" means by her own inclination or preference for what has been accepted. The other deity, not being satisfied with her answer, said:
"As far as 'one who destroys' (*padhaṃsī*)"—meaning one who destroys virtues, because she causes the loss of the qualities obtainable through the teaching of the Teacher.
"Shameless" (*pagabbā*) means endowed with impudence; just as she was harsh through verbal impudence, so too must she be in speech.
*Mukharāti* means *mukhakharā* (one with a harsh mouth). Desiring to hear the meaning connected to the Three Jewels—which is gentle and subtle—she questioned the One of Ten Powers (*dasabala*).
In responding to that deity, [the Buddha] spoke in accordance with her disposition (*ajjhāsaya*). *Uppatamānā* means rising up;

he eradicates it specifically. *Vaṭṭamūlakamahāavijjā* (the great ignorance rooted in the cycle of existence) is a specific description of reality (*bhūtakathana*) for the purpose of showing its disadvantage (*ādīnava*).
“Of those sinking” (*osīdantānaṃ*) means of those sinking downward by way of their opposites; the sense is “of those uplifting.
“Become a field of merit” (*puññakkhettabhūto*) is a qualifying statement regarding what has occurred, explained as the meaning of the phrase “for those walking on foot.
“Whatever kind of son he may be” is said because the deity previously used the term “son” in the preceding phrase.
The commentary on the Vuṭṭhisutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Bhītāsutta:
Regarding the phrase "Kiṃ sūdha bhītā," he says that *su* and *idha* are merely indeclinable particles, thus [the meaning is] "Kiṃ bhītā" (What are you afraid of?). And the path...
“Expounded in many bases” means it was expounded—that is, taught—by providing numerous reasons and various types of grounds for realization.
Therefore he said, “By way of thirty-eight objects,” and so forth. “While this is so” means:
since you have thus proclaimed the path leading to Nibbāna through many bases common to all, why is this people, though a secure path is available, afraid and has gone astray due to perverted views?
"Does it mean 'he took'? Thus the deity, by means of the first half-verse, made known to the Teacher the matter she had thought of according to her own desire;
by the second half-verse, she asks about her own doubt. "Of great wisdom" means of broad wisdom. "Of abundant wisdom" means of superior wisdom.
"Having set aside" means having restrained. "One who shares" means one whose nature is to distribute food properly during its consumption.
Therefore he said, “With a snap of the fingers,” and so forth; the meaning has already been explained above. “By mind” means by the apprehension of the mind.
“A factor of prior purification” means a factor that constitutes prior purity. “In the four” means included within the aforementioned factors.
“Requisites for sacrifice” means the instruments of giving. “In these qualities” refers to these very ones.

Regarding the qualities such as faith: just as one who possesses faith, having established the requisite conditions, becomes a specific condition for the relinquishing of material things because they have direct conviction in the fruits of karma and the next world, so too is one with a tender heart.
For it is one with a tender heart who, having attained compassion (*anudaya*), gives whatever belongs to himself to others. And he who is of a nature to share—
Even with only a small amount belonging to himself, he shares his enjoyments with others.

Being generous, he fulfills the desires of those in need at the proper time, knowing that it is appropriate for one who is disposed to give; thus it is said: "Thus... [as before] ...he spoke regarding the four.
The three factors beginning with speech illustrate the perfection of the threefold virtue (*sīla*). For one whose virtue is perfected does not [fear] the next world...

He would speak. Faith is one factor because it illuminates purity of application and intention. For one whose intention is pure and who stands in right application, how could there be fear of the next world?
The method of pairs (*dukanaya*) is the application of four factors by way of the [two] pairs.
"Established in these four qualities" means established in these four virtues comprised within the aforementioned pairs.
The commentary on the *Bhītāsutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Najīrati-sutta*. 76.
"Name and clan" (*nāmagotta*) refers to such things as the name and clan of Tissa Kassapa Gotama. This is merely an illustration.
Therefore, it should be understood that this is a statement of the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) for all designations (paññatti).

"It does not decay" means that because it is a dharma lacking intrinsic nature (asabhāva-dhamma) and is devoid of arising and passing away, it does not reach aging. Thus he said: "It does not have the nature of decaying.
Because it is designated by that same conventional term even at a later time due to the persistence of the designation, he said: "Because of past Buddhas... it is called 'it does not decay.'"
*Ālasya* means the state of being lazy, a stubborn indolence. Therefore he said, “by which,” and so forth. *Ṭhiti* means activity.
Negligence due to sleep is the non-performance of what ought to be done. Negligence due to defilements (*kilesa*) is also the performance of what ought not to be done.
*Kammasamaye* means at the time appropriate for performing an action. *Kammakaraṇavīriyābhāvo* means the absence of that energy which gives rise to the execution of that action.
However, in terms of its actual meaning, it is an unwholesome state of mind that is the opposite of energy (*vīriya*), not merely the absence of energy.
Lack of restraint in virtue is immorality (*dussīlya*). Immoral conduct is called "lax behavior. Excessive sleepiness is "drowsiness.
For even a man with strong hands is overcome by sleep; therefore he said, "By that," and so forth. Regarding "excessive hunger" and so on, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes...
It includes “overcoming” and so forth. The laziness of one who is a visitor is not an inherent state like the laziness previously mentioned.
Regarding the phrase “those six holes,” he says “those six holes” because it is stated in the text with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
They are called “holes” because there is no opportunity for the arising of wholesome consciousness. Therefore the Blessed One said: “Where wealth does not stay. In every respect...
The intention is "without leaving even a remnant.
The commentary on the *Najīrati-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Issariya-sutta*.
77. "The rust of the blade" (*satthamala*) means the rust of the sword; by which the sword becomes tarnished.
Here, by the mention of the "rust of the blade," it is the tarnished sword itself that is intended; thus he says, "a sword seized by rust.
"The exercise of command" (*āṇāpavattana*) refers to their desire for sovereignty, which consists in dwelling according to their own will over whatever is small or great.
Even a jewel, because it belongs to the category of things to be given away, is not called the "supreme commodity";
however, a woman is indeed the supreme commodity because she cannot be relinquished even by a woman who has abandoned the conduct of her family. Therefore he said:

"A woman is the best of commodities. Indeed, because she is the source of birth for various noble men and is a mine for the supreme jewels, a woman is the best of commodities. She is like a sword coated with rust.
Because it obstructs the function of awakening. Like rust on a blade, it is "rust on the sword of wisdom" (*paññāsatthamala*) because it causes the absence of qualities in the sword of wisdom.
"Abbu" refers to misfortune; that which gives this is "abbuda," meaning a cause of destruction.

[Objection: Is it not improper for a renunciant to take [what is not given]? [Response: It is proper. Demonstrating its propriety through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [the author says]:
He said, “‘Salākabhatta and so forth,’ etc.
The commentary on the *Issariya-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Kāma-sutta*.
78. Because it is stated in the Pāḷi as “one who desires his own welfare,” he says, “excluding all Bodhisattvas.
For they, being entirely engaged in the welfare of others, are great compassionate ones who desire the welfare of others; thus, they do not have what is called a “desire for their own welfare.
And even that practice of theirs which brings about their own welfare is undertaken solely for the sake of the welfare of others. This is stated in the Porāṇa-Ṭīkā.

Because Bodhisattvas, while fulfilling the perfections through their practice for the benefit of others, surrender themselves to others when encountering such circumstances due to the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī), it is therefore said here: "excepting all Bodhisattvas.
"Kalyāṇa" means auspicious. Because it refers to speech, he says: "gentle and soft."
"Evil" means base and inferior. Furthermore, he shows that very thing by its specific form as "harsh speech.
The commentary on the *Kāmasutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Pātheyyasutta*.

79. "Faith binds the provisions for the journey": faith indeed binds the pack of provisions and prepares the travel rations for a being who, by way of death, is traveling along the great road, entering upon the great wilderness, and plunging into the great abyss.
How so? It says: "Having generated faith," and so forth. This is what was stated: "Faith binds the provisions for the journey."
This verse-line was spoken by the Blessed One. *Sirī* (glory): it is attended to by those who have performed merit; it is acquired by them, thus it is *sirī*.
*Issariyaṃ* (sovereignty) means power. *Āsayo* (abode): because it is to be dwelt in, it is an abode; the meaning is a dwelling place (*niketa*). *Parikaḍḍhati* (drags along):
it drags the person, who is subject to desire, here and there.
The commentary on the *Pātheyya-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Pajjota-sutta*: 80.
That which illuminates various even and uneven places is called "light" (*pajjota*). A lamp, having dispelled darkness, [makes things] directly evident.

It shows what belongs to the category of form (*rūpagata*); likewise, the lamp of wisdom, having dispelled the darkness of ignorance, shows the form that constitutes the ultimate reality (*paramattha*) of phenomena.
"Like a wakeful brahmin" means like a brahmin whose taints are destroyed and who is awake;
for he is always awake due to the full development of mindfulness and wisdom. "Cattle" refers to those of the bovine species; this is a general inclusion of both cows and oxen.
“Kamme” is the locative case used in the sense of the instrument. “Jīva” means life; “sajīvino” means those together with life.

Therefore he said, “of those living together with their work,” which means those living by performing such work as farming, trading, and so forth. “Together with herds of cattle” means together with a group of cows.
Without them, farming and other such works do not arise, nor can there be the production of dairy products or the accomplishment of plowing and carrying loads.
Furthermore, certain agricultural works, some commercial activities, and so forth, succeed. Regarding "of the body of beings":

although those who subsist on food maintain their livelihood otherwise, agriculture is the primary cause for the mode of life based on farming, because it is the instrumental cause for the production of fruit.
And "posture" (iriyāpatha) is the means for the occurrence of the acts of moving about. They say that "cold" refers to the cold work of the plow.
The commentary on the *Pajjota-sutta* is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Araṇa-sutta* 81.
They are called *raṇā* because beings cry out (*raṇanti*) due to them; they are lust and the other defilements. For it is through being overcome by them that sentient beings [suffer] in various ways.
They weep and lament; yet, because they are entirely without conflict (*raṇa*), they are "without conflict" (*araṇā*). They are free from defilements and have exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsavā*).

"One who has lived the life" (*vusitavāso*) means one who has completed the dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacariyavāsa*). "Freedom" (*bhojisiya*) means the state of being independent (*bhujissabhāva*); thus he said, "the state of no longer being a slave.

"Ascetics" (*samaṇā*) refers to those who have stilled evil; thus he said, "ascetics whose taints are exhausted. At the time when they are virtuous worldlings (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), by means of mundane full understanding (*pariññā*),...

In the prior stage, those in training (sekkhā) fully understand and delimit the five aggregates of the three planes—which are to be fully understood—by means of mundane full comprehension; at the time of reviewing, they do so by means of both mundane and supramundane full comprehension. Those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), however, have already fully understood that which was to be fully understood.
For they enjoy [the fruit] as masters. It is said, "They honor him who is established," referring to the state of being worthy of honor.
And because of the perfection of virtue, he said: "Established means established in virtue. "In this world" means in this world.
Regarding the term "khattiya," he said "not only khattiyas," etc., to show that it is a general designation.
The commentary on the Araṇa Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on Cutting is finished.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Devatā Saṃyutta of the Sāratthappakāsinī,
the sub-commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya, is completed.
2. Devaputtasaṃyutta 1.
First Chapter 1.
Commentary on the First Kassapa Sutta
82. A son of a god is a *devaputta*. Since there is no relationship between gods as progenitor and the procreated, how can he be called a "son of a god"?
To this he says, "Of the gods," and so forth. The statement, "One who is not manifest is called 'a certain one' (*aññataro*)," is said by way of general rule;
for even one who is manifest is sometimes called "a certain one. In the *Devatāsaṃyutta* mentioned below, it says: "Those who are not manifest..."
Having said, "a certain deity," it is here stated as "the manifest devaputta. For thus his clan-name, Kassapa, was mentioned;
and that indeed was by way of a conventional designation established through a previous birth. *Anusāsanaṃ* means instruction; he who gives that instruction is *anusāsaṃ*.
*Bhikkhuniddese* means in the exposition of the word *bhikkhu*. *Bhikkhuovādaṃ* means [instruction] that brings about the state of being a bhikkhu.

[He spoke] the exhortation. But if he had not heard it, how did he speak this question? He spoke the question based on what he had heard from another, but not by virtue of having heard it directly from the Blessed One.
"Of those" refers to the three types of persons already mentioned. For, by the words "desiring to speak," and so forth, the fourth [type] is indicated here.

It has been extracted. Regarding that, the Blessed One does not make the question of the first three [questions] a burden because of the deficiency of one factor each and the deficiency of two factors respectively;
however, because the fourth possesses both factors in their entirety, he makes it a burden, thus he said, "But this," and so forth.
In the verse, the genitive case in "subhāsitassa" is used in the sense of the accusative; therefore, he said, "one should train in what is well-spoken."
"One who trains in the Buddha’s word, which is based on the Four Truths and so forth, is said to train in the fourfold verbal good conduct";
thus he says, "one should train... based on the Four Truths," and so on. By means of this restriction, he excludes its opposite.
"To be attended" means to be cultivated, developed, practiced repeatedly. "The meditation subject consisting of thirty-eight divisions."
This was said with the fact that this [first] term has insight as its proximate cause kept in mind. For it is said:
"By the second term, the training in higher wisdom is explained. However, for those who read: "By the second term, the training in higher consciousness;

by the calming of the mind, the training in higher wisdom," according to their reading, the meditation subject consisting of thirty-eight varieties would be [limited to] only the pure serenity meditation subject.
The term "grasping" (gahaṇa) is to be understood [in this sense]. If that is so, how is it that the phrase "by way of the eight attainments" is stated?
They say: "It is stated by way of those attainments which have insight as their foundation.
And by taking it thus, the statement "by the second term, the training in higher wisdom" is justified. Since "training" means "cultivation," he says: "the meaning is 'he should develop'."

“Upāsana” means attending upon (*payirupāsana*). And showing that this is by way of mastering what has not yet been heard, supporting the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and so forth, he said, “That too,” and so on.

The training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) has been explained by the method of taking the characteristic (*lakkhaṇahāra-naya*). For since verbal good conduct has the nature of virtue (*sīla*), by the mention of that [verbal conduct], bodily good conduct—which shares the same characteristic—and the other [mental good conduct] are also already included. And here, regarding the training in higher virtue...
Seclusion of mind is taught for the training in higher wisdom; seclusion from acquisitions is taught for the training in higher consciousness;
and seclusion of body is mentioned by its own specific form in the text. Thus, it should be understood that all three kinds of seclusion have been made manifest.
The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the First Kassapa Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Second Kassapa Sutta: 83.
"By means of two jhānas" refers to the two jhānas characterized by contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇa-ūpanijjhāna*). "Through liberation from the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna-vimuttiyā*)...

By means of the liberation obtained through devotion to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he speaks of the liberation by way of its factors (*tadaṅga-vimutti*) and the suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*).
Because it is the heart, the inner core, of the Teacher’s dispensation, it is the attainment of the non-occurrence [of defilements] by the mind;

and since that, in terms of its actual meaning, is none other than final knowledge (*aññā*), he says "Arahatta" (Arahantship). For one desiring to attain that, craving and views must be absolutely abandoned.

Because those [two] succeed when that [arahatta-phala] is present and fail when it is absent, to the same extent that they are dependent upon it by way of its production, this [arahatta-phala] is also said to be dependent upon them.
Thus he says, "independent," and so forth. Arahantship is called "the benefit" (ānisaṃsa) in the sense that it is to be benefited;
that which has this as its benefit is "the benefit of arahantship" (arahattānisaṃsa). For one desiring to attain arahantship, the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) must be sought.

And therein, the very first application to the subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna-attānuyoga*) is not included here; thus he said, "the preliminary stage of the Dhamma of the Thread" (*tantidhammo pubbabhāgo*).
In this context, "Dhamma of the Thread" (*tantidhammo*) means the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhammo*).
The commentary on the Second Kassapa Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Magha Sutta 84.
"Magha" is the name of Sakka, inherited from his previous birth. "He himself" means Sakka himself. "By conduct" means by the practice of dharma such as attending upon one's mother and father.
"Others" refers to having overcome evil states that ripen in future existence (*upadhivepakkapāpadhamme*). "The Asura" refers to the Asura who was the enemy of Indra.
The commentary on the Magha Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Māgadha Sutta: 85.

"The fourth sutta has the same meaning as already stated" means that its meaning has already been explained in the *Devatāsaṃyutta*; therefore, the intention is that no further explanation need be given here.
The commentary on the Māgadha Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Dāmali Sutta: 86.
“By that cause” means by that exertion acting as the cause; the meaning is: the motive for the performance of exertion.
Whatever existence there may be—whether small or great, inferior or superior. "Exertion over a long duration" means the undertaking of energy for a long time.
"The completion of what is to be done" means the final accomplishment of one's task. "Just as before" means just as it was prior to the arising of Arahantship;
even after that, one should likewise make firm the energy called "exertion of the intellect," so that it does not become like something subject to disturbance.
One speaks while conceiving [notions]. However, the exertion of energy for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) and so forth is indeed desirable.
They are "unmixed" (*asaṃkiṇṇa*), meaning they are not intermingled, because they have not been included elsewhere. Therefore he said, "By the Blessed One," and so on.
If that is so, why was this stated specifically here? To this he replied, "But here," and so on. A river is called such because its banks are unstable.
This is the place where one should be established.
The commentary on the Dāmalī Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Kāmada Sutta.
87. *Pubbayogāvacaro*: one who was a practitioner (*yogāvacara*) in the past, devoted to meditation in a previous existence.
It is said that this person, having gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa, practiced the duties of an ascetic for many thousands of years, yet did not produce any distinction.
To show this matter along with its cause, [the text] says: "Because of the abundance of defilements," and so forth.

It has been said. "Of one who is entirely pure" means: of one who is completely purified and entirely unstained, in such a way that it brings about further distinction. "Concentrated by virtue" means:

having properly established the mind and well-perfected the mind, in such a way that virtue brings about successive distinctions and pertains to penetration (*nibbedha*). Being thus, they are endowed with that.

He said "endowed" because they possess these qualities. "Firmly established in their own nature" means that, being trainees (sekha), they have a nature firmly fixed by the Dhamma as it has been attained, remaining unshakable.

The Blessed One said, "Contentment brings happiness," thinking, "If I were to accept contentment [as the answer], the son of the gods would say, 'Contentment is hard to find. Thus he said, "for the purpose of raising a further question."

One who has gone forth is called a forest-dweller, a dweller at the foot of a tree, or one who lives in the open air, having entered the homeless life; but as for one living in a monastery, he asks "how?
and thus says "in a seven-storied [palace]," and so forth. "Contentment with the four requisites" means contentment regarding the four requisites achieved through devotion to meditation.
By this, he shows that satisfaction is obtained through the calming of the mind. "Through the cultivation of the calming of the mind" means...

The construction is: "one whose mind delights in the cultivation that specifically pacifies the mind by means of the cultivation that pacifies the defilements of the mind, and by making the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth, free from their habitual range.

And herein, through the pacification of the faculties, the concentration of the mind becomes perfected; for it is through the cultivation of the faculties that the concentration of the mind is fulfilled.

Because it distances one from unwholesome actions. Through the concentration of higher mind (*adhicitta-samādhi*), contentment with the four requisites becomes especially pure and complete, owing to the nature of renunciation regarding both the gain and loss of those requisites.
Furthermore, for one who is content in the manner described, the virtue (*sīla*) undertaken according to his vow becomes purified and reaches fulfillment;
being thus established, he applies himself to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.

By the words beginning with "Those who, night and day," he shows this meaning: that one who is engaged in the sequence of the path, completely severing the defilements, becomes one who has seen Nibbāna.

Why would they not go? They certainly will go; however, he speaks with apprehension, intending to show the difficulty of right practice apart from the cultivation of the Noble Path. Therefore he said: "But this..."
“The Blessed One’s path is difficult to traverse, uneven.
Regarding this, some say: “But ‘this one’ refers to the deva-putta. For having heard the Blessed One’s words, ‘The Noble Ones are going,’ he spoke thus:
‘The Blessed One’s [path] is difficult to traverse,’ and so forth. That is not tenable, because [the Blessed One said], “This is true,” and so on.
This was shown by providing a synonym for that very [term];
therefore, while you said, "the path by which the Noble Ones go," the son of the gods said, "O Blessed One, this path is difficult to traverse and uneven.
Granted, the Noble Path is sometimes called an "extremely painful practice" (*atidukkhā paṭipadā*), but that is only with reference to the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*); however, this—
It is exceedingly easy to traverse because it avoids the difficult terrain of all defilements;

it is not uneven because it keeps far away from the unevenness of bodily misconduct and so forth, as well as the unevenness of passion and so forth. Therefore he said, "of the preliminary practice," and so on.
"Of this" refers to the Noble Path. For the Noble Path has many perils by way of its being something that must be fortified through the training in higher virtue and the rest.
"Thus it was said" means it was said that "it is difficult to traverse and uneven.

"Upside down" means having their heads turned downward because they do not stand up; for among the factors of wholesomeness (kusalaṅga), right view is the head because it is the most excellent, and the ignoble ones fall and do not stand up because of their wrong practice. Therefore he said, "with the head of knowledge," and so forth.

“The ignoble path” means the wrong path. Therefore he said, “on the uneven path. Because they follow that path, the ignoble ones—having failed to reach the path of the noble ones and having been abandoned by it—fall into the states of misery and into the entire suffering of saṃsāra.
“That very [path]” means this path which can never be traversed by the ignoble ones, but is entirely [accessible] to the noble ones, those beings who are purified.
He is equal through his attainment. Because they are possessed of bodily unevennesses and so forth, [others] are unequal within their own bodies;
but because those [defects] have been entirely abandoned by them, they are indeed equal in every respect.
The commentary on the Kāmadassu Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Pañcālacaṇḍa Sutta 88.
"In the extreme confinement" (*sambādhe*) means in that which is most congested due to the pressure of the defilements of craving and so forth.

For what is intended here is the confinement of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), which is like an exceedingly foul place of refuse; for that is difficult to handle, and in its absence, the confinement of the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) finds no opportunity.
It is just as it was for Mahākassapa and the others. "Opportunity" (*okāsa*) is a name for *jhāna* because of the absence of the confinement of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
For here, *jhāna* is called "opportunity" by virtue of its unconfined nature, and that is due to its being a state of absolute non-confinement and its serving as a basis for insight (*vipassanā*).
Thus, it is said in the Pāḷi: "He found" (*avindī*), and so forth. In that context, "he found" (*avindī*) means he attained (*vindi*).
He attained. "Bhūrimedhasa" means one of great wisdom; the sense is "possessed of wisdom. "Abujjhī" means he awakened, he penetrated.

"Paṭilīnaseṭṭha" means the best among those who have withdrawn, or the best of those who are withdrawn. One who has abandoned conceit is called "withdrawn" (paṭilīna) because of having withdrawn from the state of being puffed up by the influence of pride.
"Paṭilabhiṃsu" [means they attained] even amidst the confinement of the strands of sensual pleasure: "These strands of sensual pleasure [do not belong] to people like me..."

"What will they do? Having overcome [their doubts], they attained right mindfulness for the sake of reaching Nibbāna. Through the supramundane concentration associated with that [mindfulness], they were also well-composed.
It is said that this son of the gods, in a previous existence prior to this one, had been an attainer of the first jhāna; having passed away from there, [he was reborn here].
Having been reborn among the Brahmakāyika devas and there experienced the bliss of jhāna, he passed away from there and was now reborn in the realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava).

Therefore, reflecting upon that jhāna and praising the Blessed One for the quality of being "one who has attained such bliss of jhāna," he uttered the verse beginning with "In a crowded place indeed... Then the Blessed One [spoke to him].

Just as a mustard seed is nothing compared to Sineru, the king of mountains, which rises six million eight hundred thousand yojanas high, so too the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere is nothing compared to the infinite and immeasurable qualities of a Buddha.

Demonstrating this, he proclaimed the attainment of unsurpassed qualities with the words beginning, "Those who have mindfulness," and so forth. In that context, "mindfulness" refers to insight-mindfulness (*vipassanā-sati*).
Together with noble path-mindfulness. "Well-composed" means they are perfectly composed by both mundane and supramundane concentration.
For they are absolutely well-composed; it is not merely because they have attained the jhānas that they possess an unshakeable nature.
Some, reading the text as "well-composed in their work," explain the meaning as "composed in the Path."
The commentary on the Pañcālacaṇḍa Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Tāyana Sutta. 89.
Because he produced that view by his own personal effort in a previous birth, he was formerly a *titthakara* (founder of a sect). Therefore, he said:

"Having generated a view. Others say: "In the past he was a *titthakara* (founder of a sect) because he possessed a *titthakara*—that is, by way of grasping [him] as 'this is my teacher'; he was a follower of a *titthakara* in his former existence.
They explain: "'Having generated a view' means having taken up and grasped the view of that teacher. A "ford" (*tittha*) refers to the sixty-two views.
Because of the absence of false doctrine (micchāvāda) for one who has abandoned [wrong views]. "Those attached to a sect" means *titthikā*;
they are called *titthiyā* by changing the letter *ka* to *ya*. "Of that" refers to the aforementioned wholesome karma (*kalyāṇakamma*).
"By way of its outflow" means by way of its fruit (*phala*). "Connected with energy" means it is an illumination of energy; this is the sense.
*Aniyamitāṇatti* means an unrestricted injunction; it is a statement of a rule by way of non-restriction. *Taṇhāsotaṃ* means the stream of craving, the continuous flow of craving.
*Nīhara* means abandon with equanimity. *Ekattaṃ* means one-pointedness; therefore he said "jhāna.
*Upapajjati* means it does not arise or reach [the goal]; thus he said "he does not obtain. *Na osakkeyya* means he should not fall into contraction or retreat. From household life...
*Paribbaja* means wandering away from all sides; thus it is *paribbaja*.

Because of the lack of firmness in undertaking the vows of one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*), and because of performing those duties without diligence, there is a lax grasp. *Atireka* means more than even the previous time of going forth.
*Upari* means higher and higher. "It is better that the wrong-doing (*dukkata*) remains uncommitted" means that it is beneficial for misconduct to remain entirely unperformed in every respect.
"Whatever" means whatever kind of kamma. "Performed laxly" means performed and set in motion by way of lack of earnestness (*asakkaccakāritā*).
"Of just such a kind" means of a kind similar to that which is touched upon in common parlance, because it resembles subsequent remorse, conduct, and so forth.
"Defiled" means defiled by the corruption of craving (*taṇhā-saṃkilesa*). "Suspected and apprehended" means from the beginning and on all sides.
“Suspected by others. The beginning of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) is the “initial holy life” (*ādibrahmacariya*);

those engaged therein are “pertaining to the initial holy life” (*ādibrahmacariyikā*), meaning they are the preliminary practice for the holy life of the Path. Therefore he said, “become the beginning of the holy life of the Path.
“Becoming the primary exertion” means becoming the first undertaking.
The commentary on the Tāyana Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Canda Sutta: 90.
Since the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) is mentioned, its inhabitant is also included; thus it is said: “the son of the gods dwelling in the moon mansion.”

"Everywhere" (*sabbadhi*) means: "O Blessed One, you are completely liberated from every miserable state; therefore, please grant me liberation as well from this cramped place"—this is the intended meaning.
Thus he said: "Be my refuge. "Compassionate toward the world" (*lokānukampaka*) means:
because you have favor toward the entire world, [the same applies] to you and to this moon. "Just like such [beings]" (*tādisā eva*) means: being equal [to them].
"Thus. "You release" means you have released. Therefore he said: "A present tense verb used in the sense of the past.
The commentary on the *Candimasutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Sūriyasutta*.
91. Regarding "andhabhāvakaraṇe" (the maker of blindness), others say it means "the maker of darkness for the world. Therefore, he said "tamasī" (darkness). "Virocati" means it shines.
Granted that the first deity was mentioned by way of a son of the gods, yet because Rāhu’s activity occurs in his celestial mansion (vimāna), he said, "Maṇḍalī means having the shape of a circle.
He speaks [then] because he has seized [the moon] with his mouth. With his mouth...
In this context, "seizing" (*gahaṇa*) is intended in the sense of "swallowing" (*gilī*), and not merely "ingesting"; thus he says, "he speaks of swallowing.
Now, in order to show his capacity to seize with his mouth, the passage beginning with "For Rāhu... was stated. The phrase "He...
and so forth is the demonstration of the cause for his seizing of the moon and sun. "The deities residing therein" refers to the deities who serve as attendants to the moon and sun.
"Speeding with velocity": for he is exceedingly difficult to restrain when facing anyone, being established by the fixed law of karma.
"The crown of the head" refers to the upper part of the neck; some say it means the very top of the head. "He would emerge" because of the sharp, swift, and powerful nature of his speed.
"Having dragged him back" means having dragged him toward the direction of his own departure. "Him" refers to Rāhu. "Even though he wished to leap upward..."

He would have been unable to reach them. By these two phrases, he shows that although he possessed a massive body and great strength, the velocity of the movement of the moon and sun was entirely impossible for him to restrain.
"With his celestial vehicle" means with the moon’s vehicle during a lunar eclipse and with the sun’s vehicle during a solar eclipse—along with both vehicles simultaneously.
For on the new moon day, the two vehicles are separated by a distance of only one *yojana*.

Having sacrificed, they proceed together. If both sons of the gods had attained the fruit of stream-entry, then why was it said only in the *Sūriya-sutta* (The Discourse on the Sun), "My offspring," and not in the *Canda-sutta* (The Discourse on the Moon)?
It is said that he, having passed away from there before long, was reborn elsewhere, and another deity indeed resided there at the time when the Blessed One [spoke] regarding that lunar eclipse.
They say that the sun does not speak verses, but at a later time, Rāhu occasionally seizes it even there.
The commentary on the Sūriya-sutta is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Chapter on Anāthapiṇḍika 1.
Commentary on the Candasasa Sutta 92.
A place where a river flowing down from a mountain slope turns back is also called a *kaccha* because it is a narrow, confined spot.
Viyāti said: “One who dwells among mountain clefts. Because it rises as something unique by virtue of being remote from its opposites and by virtue of its excellence, it is called *ekodi*;

thus, it is one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*). Because they are joined to that, those with one-pointed minds are here called *ekodī*. They are called *nipakā* because they settle and purify themselves from their opposites;
they are the wise. Therefore he said: “Those with one-pointed minds,” and so forth. [The object] is the object distinguished by body and so on.
They are "mindful" (satā) because they remember with preeminent mindfulness; thus he said, "possessing mindfulness" (satimanto).

"They will go safely" means that just as wild animals in the aforementioned places will live safely, unharmed by calamities, so too those who have attained jhāna will live safely, unharmed by the defilements.
It is said that this son of the gods perceived the Brahma-world as Nibbāna, and therefore spoke thus. The Blessed One...
“This son of the gods, while not being one who goes to Nibbāna, perceives himself as going to Nibbāna; come now, I shall show him the way to Nibbāna,” he thought, and spoke the second verse.
Because it is the further shore of the four floods, or indeed of the great flood of saṃsāra, Nibbāna is called the “further shore.
A fish is “born in the water” (*ambujo*). Just as fish cut through a net of cords, so too [the wise] [cut through] the net of defilements.
"Having broken through, they will go forth.
The commentary on the Candimasasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Veṇḍusutta.
93. *Payirupāsiya* means "for the sake of attending upon. *Sikkhanti* means they train in the three trainings. *Siṭṭhipade*:

because it instructs regarding the defilements and because it provides protection from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), it is called "instruction" (*siṭṭhi*); it refers to the "words" (*pade*) because one must practice according to what has been instructed.
Thus, the meaning is "in the True Dhamma. Therefore he said, "in the words of instruction. In that context, "instruction" (*anusiṭṭhi*) is the True Dhamma.
"At the proper time" means at the appropriate and opportune moment. "Diligence" refers to the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
The commentary on the Veṇḍu Sutta is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Dīghalaṭṭhi Sutta.
94. "He appeared just so" means he appeared with a long staff; thus it became his conventional designation.
The commentary on the Dīghalaṭṭhi Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Nandana Sutta.
95. It is "unobstructed" (*anāvaṭa*) because there is no obstruction (*āvaṭa*) or covering for it.
There is no cognitive obstruction (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*) capable of overwhelming it, such as a tree or a mountain, which act as obstructions to the natural vision of sentient beings. "Of what kind?
means of what configuration, or of what nature. "Suffering" (*dukkha*) refers to the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
The commentary on the Nandana Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Candana Sutta: 96.
"Below" means in the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*). For one wandering there, a firm footing is generally difficult to find.
Beings are indeed submerged; therefore, saṃsāra has no foothold below. "Above" refers to the sublime realms (mahaggatabhava).
For one reborn there, it is difficult to find a support for ascending to Nibbāna;
because of their delight in jhāna, attachment to that very state becomes strong for them. Therefore, saṃsāra has no support above. "With mind directed" means toward Nibbāna.
"With mind sent forth toward the husband": there are three formative volitions (*kammābhisaṅkhāra*), namely the three volitions beginning with meritorious volition (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).
Therefore, having stated that "existence as kamma has delight as its precursor," it is said, "having generated delight.

By means of the heading "perception of sensual desire" (*kāmasaññā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is included; and by this, the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) headed by sensual desire are also included.

He said: "By the mention of 'perception of sensual desire' (kāmasaññā), the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) are included. "Form-existence" (rūpabhava) means form (rūpa); here, the word *bhava* is elided.

By the mention of "form-existence," the remaining existences are also included therein. By the mention of "fetters" (saṃyojana) for that, the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) are included.
"In the great flood" (mahoghe) means in the great flood of saṃsāra. "Of those" refers to sensual existence and the others.

By means of inclusion, because it possesses the same characteristic as the state of existence (*bhava*). The formless existence (*arūpabhava*) is included by way of the method of taking the characteristic. The remainder is easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Candana-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Vāsudatta-sutta*.
97. The sixth [sutta] has its meaning already explained in the commentary on the *Devatāsaṃyutta* below.
The commentary on the *Vāsudattasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Subrahmasutta*.
98. *Subrahmā* is the name of that son of the gods. To show the reason for his approaching the presence of the Teacher, [the author] said, "It is said that he...
and so forth. That very sorrow was the occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) for that son of the gods.
"Surrounded by a host of nymphs" means surrounded by a host of nymphs numbering about a thousand. "Sporting in the Nandana" means sporting in the Nandana Grove. "The hand..."
"It comes" means it becomes something that can be grasped by the hand. "They tie" means that here even the winding of a garland should be understood as occurring through a state of playfulness;
otherwise, it would simply mean that the flowers themselves, by various mental dispositions, come to the hand in the form of a garland.
"By way of interrupting karma" means that while there is still a remainder of life in that divine world, [it occurs] due to that which harms it.
“By the power of evil karma that has found its opportunity. “A stroke” (pahāra) refers to the third part of the day; therefore, “all at once” means at one and the same time.
“By grief rooted in the beloved” means by grief caused by the beloved as its object. “Being afflicted” means being oppressed. In the seventh [verse]...
"On the seventh day" means on the seventh day according to human reckoning.
"Right there" means that he was to be reborn in that very same hell because he had previously committed that evil deed together with them. "Distressed" means he fell into mental terror.
"To expel" means to drive out or remove. "Having gone into the presence of the Teacher" [means] together with those five hundred nymphs.
Having gone together into the presence of the Blessed One, he says "this" (*idaṃ*) to show his own mind, because it is immediate and directly perceived. He says "constant" (*niccaṃ*) meaning always.

Since this sense of "constancy" must be understood according to the underlying intention (*adhippāya*), he states "in the world of the gods" (*devaloke*) and so forth, showing therein what is to be abandoned and what is to be grasped.
It should not be taken [as occurring] prior to the occurrence of the cause, because that fear does not exist before then. "In those" refers to the sufferings;
for since they are to be produced by causes and conditions, they are called "in difficulties" (*kicchesu*) in the verse.

Alternatively, "in difficulties" means "on account of difficulty. For the meaning is: on account of those failures in application (*payoga-vipatti*) by which those sufferings might arise, it is "on account of that cause."
For those failures of application and failures of rebirth would have been eliminated by his approaching the presence of the Teacher.

"The sufferings seen by way of those reborn" means the sufferings seen through the lens of those who have been reborn; and "in those sufferings"—in every case, the locative case is used in the sense of a sign (*nimitta*).
"As if burning" refers to the burning of the continuum of consciousness.

"Bodhi" is that which awakens to and penetrates all four truths; it is the assemblage of states such as mindfulness and so forth. Therefore, they are "factors of awakening" (*bojjha*) because they arise from awakening (*bodhi*).

Furthermore, since that awakening occurs precisely through the mode of development (*bhāvanā*), and because the word "bojjha" is used in the ablative sense (*nissakkavacana*) in connection with the term "from" (*aññatra*), he shows this meaning by referring to the word "having released" (*muñcitvā*) and stating: "the development of the factors of awakening" (*bojjhaṅgabhāvanā*).
He said: "The 'quality of austerity' (tapoguṇa) refers to the ascetic practice (dhutadhamma). For it is called 'austerity' (tapa) because it scorches (tapana) one who is greedy with craving;

and it is called a 'quality' (guṇa) because its own nature is that of a quality and because it is dependent upon qualities. Therefore he said: 'the quality of austerity known as the ascetic practices' (dhutaṅga).

It is the 'renunciation of all' (sabbanissagga) because everything included within the realm of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra) is relinquished therein; thus he said: 'from the renunciation of all, that is, from Nibbāna.'"
The restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara) alone is to be understood first, because it is the very first stage in the sequence of practice.
To show that sequence of practice, he said, "In the restraint of the faculties," and so forth.

Since, in the ultimate sense, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are comprised only within the path, he said, "the factors of enlightenment together with insight. "Of him" means of that yogi who exists in such a state.
Because the Teacher spoke that verse to the deva-son and subsequently proclaimed the Truths, it is said:
"The Blessed One concluded his teaching by means of the Four Truths. The deva-son was established in the fruit of stream-entry;
while it is true that his own specific attainment arrived here, he was [established] in the fruit of stream-entry together with approximately five hundred nymphs.
"It should be understood that he was established [in the fruit]. Therefore, it is said in the commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta:

"At the conclusion of the teaching, having been established in the fruit of stream-entry together with five hundred nymphs, and having made that attainment stable, he went back to the world of the gods."
The commentary on the Subrahma Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Kakudha Sutta: 99.
When [the Buddha] said, "I rejoice," the son of a deity, wishing to urge that "delight" (*nandī*) is indeed a stain for one who has gone forth, asked, "Do you rejoice? (*nandasī*)?
He asked. Then the Blessed One, rejecting his position, said, "What joy have you found? By this he shows:
"For you, there is not even a condition for the 'joy' (nandi) intended by me here; how then could that joy exist? Therefore he says, "That which is called satisfaction," and so forth.
Then the deva-son, challenging him by saying that in the absence of joy there must be sorrow, and that sorrow is a stain for one who has gone forth—
He said, "In that case, ascetic, do you grieve? The Blessed One, rejecting that as well, said, "What has been lost?
and so forth. The meaning is: "What is it that defeats me? [The opponent thinks:
"If you have neither joy nor sorrow because of the absence of both the gain that is a cause for laughter and the loss [of what was dear], then for one who dwells alone..."
But [the Blessed One] said, "Should one not be free from discontent? thus: "I hope that while you sit alone, discontent does not overwhelm you.
When that too was rejected by the Blessed One, he then spoke the verse beginning with "How are you... asking for the reason why even those [pleasures, sorrows, and discontents] were absent.
Then the Blessed One, proclaiming that reason to him, spoke the verse beginning with "Of one born into misfortune..."
In that context, *aghajātassa* means "born into suffering. Therefore he said, "standing in the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkhe ṭhitassa*).
For one in whom craving has arisen—that is, one whose craving is not abandoned—the suffering of the round has indeed arrived because its cause has not been abandoned.
Demonstrating that very cause's non-abandonment, he said, "For it is said: 'The sufferer yearns for happiness. This refers to the occurrence of suffering.
That very process of craving has also been shown by him. By means of the words "Thus" (*iti*) and so forth, he demonstrates the aforementioned meaning as a conclusion.
The commentary on the Kakudha Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Uttara Sutta.
100. The *Uttara-sutta* of the *Navama-vagga* has its meaning already explained in the commentary on the *Devatā-saṃyutta* below.
The commentary on the *Uttara-sutta* is concluded.
10. The commentary on the *Anāthapiṇḍika-sutta*.
101. In the tenth [chapter], although it belongs to the *Devatā-saṃyutta*, these very same verses appear, beginning with “For this is that Jeta’s Grove.
Therein, the introductory setting (*nidāna*) “a certain deity” has been supplied. Because it follows the method already established below, it is not written in the manuscripts;
however, here in the *Devaputta-saṃyutta*, the setting in the village is stated as “Anāthapiṇḍika, the son of a deity.”
And as for his having arrived there, it was stated by the son of a god (*devaputta*) by way of proclaiming the qualities of the Teacher in the manner already described.
However, the Teacher, in making that matter known to the monks, said, "A certain son of a god.

In showing the reason for proclaiming it in that way, he said, "Of the Elder Ānanda," and so forth. "By means of inferential cognition" (*anumānabuddhiyā*) means by means of inferential knowledge (*anumāna-ñāṇa*). "For the purpose of manifesting his majesty" means for the purpose of illustrating his power.
The commentary on the Anāthapiṇḍika Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. The Chapter on Various Non-Buddhist Sectarians (Nānātitthiyavagga).
1. Commentary on the Siva Sutta. 102.
"The first of the third chapter" means it is the first sutta in the third chapter. Its meaning has already been explained above in the first sutta of the Satullapakāyika Chapter.
The commentary on the Siva Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Khemasutta 103.
*Paṭhamameva* means "even before," that is, prior to the actual occurrence of aging, death, and so forth. *Balavacintanaṃ cinteti* means he reflects with intense anxiety;
just as a cartwright, driving his cart along an uneven road without realizing it, becomes pained and dejected when the axle breaks and he is unable to repair it.
One who thinks powerful thoughts experiences great mental anguish; likewise, one who speaks contrary to the Dhamma, having fallen into the jaws of death, experiences powerful mental anguish.
Therefore, one should not be negligent in practicing the Dhamma.
The commentary on the Khemasutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Serīsutta 104.
“Whatever gift I give”: whatever object of giving I bestow upon another. “Being its master”:
being its overlord by thoroughly overcoming greed regarding that object, I give it because it cannot be dragged away by him. “Not a slave... [and so forth].

Having stated, "there is no companion," the passage beginning with "For he who... was spoken in order to demonstrate both of these through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya* and *vyatireka*).
He gives as a slave because he has entered into the state of servitude to craving (*taṇhā*). He gives as a friend because he does not relinquish his affection for him.
He gives as a master because, having liberated himself from the slavery of craving and having overcome it, he proceeds [to give] with mastery. It is similar to the enjoyment of a master.
"This [term] occurs because of this cause.
Alternatively, it shows that the person who is a giver by virtue of their generosity and moral conduct is of three types according to the distinction in their engagement with giving:
the slave of giving (*dānadāsa*), the companion of giving (*dānasahāya*), and the master of giving (*dānapati*). To demonstrate these three types in detail, he says: "He who..."
The passage beginning with “hī” has been stated. In the sense of being something to be given, it is “giving” (dāna), such as food, drink, and so forth.
In that regard, whatever one consumes for oneself, because one acts under its sway through being overwhelmed by craving, one becomes like a slave to it.
As for that which is given to others, this is said even there—by way of the commonality of food and drink—“having become a slave to the object of generosity (deyyadhamma) known as giving, he gives.”
He gives as an associate by establishing equality between what he himself should consume and what he must give to others.
He gives as a servant because, instead of remaining subject to the nature of the gift itself, he brings it under his own control.
According to another method: one who, having consumed something excellent for himself, gives something inferior to others, is called a "slave to giving."
Because of falling into a state inferior to that [object] on account of it.

He who gives to others exactly what he himself consumes is called a "companion in giving" (*dānasahāya*), because by relinquishing an object that is neither inferior nor superior to it, he attains a state of equality.
He who, having consumed something inferior himself, gives something excellent to others is called a "lord of giving" (*dānapati*), because through that act he attains a state of excellence.
For the result corresponds to the action; therefore, by saying “a lord of giving,” the son of the gods shows that “I was such a person.
To explain in detail the matter stated briefly in the text as “giving was given at the four gates,” the passage beginning with “It is said of him” is spoken.
“Giving” (dāna) means what has been sacrificed (yiṭṭha), and that indeed was performed for the common benefit of all.
He said, “The ascetics... [and] the beggars. Those who have gone forth into homelessness are those who have entered any kind of renunciant life.
He addresses those who merely claim the status of brahmins by the term *bhovādino*. Because the world was then empty of Buddhas, they did not obtain [anything].
"Wretched" means those who lead miserable lives, whose livelihoods are difficult; therefore he says, "poor people. They were unable to carry out livelihoods such as agriculture or trade.
Here, it is intended that “the wretched” refers to those such as the one-eyed or the club-footed; thus he says, “the one-eyed, the club-footed, and so forth. “Travelers” means wayfarers.
“Beggars” refers to those who solicit by praising the virtues of donors or the fruits of their actions, such as the naked ascetics (nirgranthas) and others.
