Therefore he says, “A desirable gift has been given,” and so on. “The measure of a handful” is stated with reference to grains of rice and the like. “The measure of a bowl” is stated with reference to rice gruel, cooked rice, and so forth.
Just as the acquisition of a village is income arising within a village, so too is the acquisition of a gate there; thus he said, "in that place where hundreds of thousands arise.
They gave a more extensive gift because their other wealth had been expended.
"With reference to that" means with reference to that more extensive gift which was performed. For the king’s gift there was greater than the gift of the women’s quarters.
He said "a turning back" because it turned back as if overcome. "Koci" is a nominative singular used in the sense of the locative.
Therefore he said "somewhere. Because he arose during a time when the lifespan was many thousands of years, that king gave gifts for eighty thousand years.
The commentary on the Serīsutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Ghaṭīkārasutta: 105.
The fourth [sutta] has its meaning already explained below in the commentary on the Devatāsaṃyutta.
The commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Jantu Sutta 106.
Those who are ignorant of the Vinaya are not skilled regarding those things that lead to defilement and those things that lead to purification; whatever [they may say]...
Those who act [wrongly] do not have much remorse. In them, unarisen restlessness arises, and arisen restlessness increases and reaches full development;
thus he said: “Because of the perception of what is improper as proper... they are of a restless nature. Because it is empty due to a lack of essence, it is like a reed (*naḷa*);
pride (*māna*) is called a "reed," thus he said: “*Unnaḷā* means those with upraised reeds. Therefore he said: “Those whose empty pride has arisen.”
For conceit (*māna*) is particularly empty when it occurs [thinking] of one who is superior, "He is superior," or of one who is equal, "He is equal.

By "fickleness" (*cāpalla*) is meant the state of being fickle; the meaning is "restless with craving. "Harsh-mouthed" (*mukhakharā*) means harsh by way of the mouth; the meaning is "speakers of harsh words. "Scattered-speech" (*vikiṇṇavācā*) means having diffuse speech;
due to idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*), their speech is without limit. Therefore he said, "unrestrained in speech," and so forth. In the "Fierce Current" (*caṇḍasota*).
"Like those in a shipwrecked boat": by this he shows their state of unstable activity.
Those beings who possess such a state are unable to stand or sit in one place, but wander here and there. "With unsteady minds" means having minds that do not remain fixed upon a single object.
"With unrestrained faculties" means having the eye and other sense-faculties that are not controlled.

When one who lacks virtue is spoken of alongside those with virtues, his lack of virtue becomes manifest, just as the defect of a glass gem is revealed when it is placed near a birth-gem (*jātimaṇi*).
"Those who live happily" means those established in happiness; that is, they lead their lives easily and without hardship, such that they are easy to support for their donors.
Therefore he said, "In the past, monks," and so forth.
One who leads the affairs of a village according to his own whim is a *gāmaṇi*; however, he speaks of them with contempt as "village-leaders" (*gāmaṇikā*).
"Having abandoned" means having abandoned through the loss of mindfulness; "by the intoxication of defilements" means by the intoxication of craving, which is characterized by great greed.
For it is with reference to the misconduct of those who are actually virtuous that the son of the gods speaks. [The phrase] "only those who are worthy of being spoken to" means...
They are indeed to be assisted by me with my exhortation. "Cast away" means abandoned by their teachers, preceptors, and others;

for that very reason, they are without a protector and without a support. "Ghosts" (petā) means those whose life has departed, the dead. Just as ghosts are, so too are they [the dead], because they are incapable of benefiting themselves and are objects of loathing for the wise.
The commentary on the Jantu Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta: 107.
"In one place" means in a single location designated as the boundary of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). "On earth" refers to "where."
This is a statement concerning the earth-plane; although it is spoken in a general sense, because of the statement "that is the end of the world," its scope is indeed specific.
Having said "he is neither born nor dies," why was it further stated that "he does not pass away nor reappear"?
To this he says: "This... is included as successive [rebirth]. "By going on foot" means by traveling by way of feet. Of the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka).
He speaks with reference to the end, desiring to reveal the truths that follow. For the end of the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) is Nibbāna.
One who possesses a bow that is firm and strong is a "strong-bowed one" (*daḷhadhanvā*). He is thus called "one of firm nature" (*daḷhadhamma*). Therefore he said, "the strong-bowed one.
"By the supreme measure" means by the measure of a thousandfold strength. He is an archer because of his training in the art of archery, not merely by being an archer.
He said: “A ‘bowman’ is a teacher of archery. Having said “bowman,” when it is further stated “trained,” it is understood that he is trained in the art of archery;
and since such training reaches its peak only after a long period for one who is capable, he said:
“Trained in the craft of archery for ten or twelve years. “Even the measure of a bull” means twenty *iṭṭhis* (spans) is a bull.
In that space the size of a bull. "A hair-tip" (*vālagga*) means the end of a hair. "One who has practiced his hand" (*katahattha*) means one whose hand is well-trained.

"One who has practiced his bow" (*katasarakkhepa*) means one who has become skilled in archery by way of demonstrating the range of the bow's reach; therefore he says, "one who has displayed his craft. Some say "one who has mastered his craft" (*katasippa*).
"A missile" (*asana*) is that by which one throws; it is an arrow. "Palm-shade" (*tālacchāyā*) means the shade of a palm tree; however, that [shade] is only a cubit (*ratana*) in extent.
Or four fingerbreadths wide.
"From the eastern ocean" refers to the eastern ocean within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). By the term "ocean," he means the rim of the eastern world-system.
The same principle applies here for the "western ocean. "Without conceptual proliferation" (*nippapañca*) means not being made dark by ignorance. "Attained" (*sampatta*)...
"Having arrived" refers to having arrived with such speed. Regarding the word "Anotatta," the term "having arrived" (*sampatte*) is to be supplied here to complete the connection;
likewise, it is to be supplied in the phrase "having chewed a tooth-stick of *nāgalatā*. "Then" (*tadā*) means when he was a seeker of the world's end.
"The time of long life" (*dīghāyukakālo*) refers to a period during which the lifespan is many thousands of years. "Of the world-system" (*cakkavāḷalokassa*) is used in its general sense.
The singular number [is used]; the meaning is "the world-system of a thousandfold universe" (*cakkavāḷaloka*). He was born in this very world-system through a craving established by former service.

By the phrase "in one possessing perception," he shows that it is not merely a matter of form-phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), but rather the aggregate of the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*). "One who has stilled evil" means one whose defiled states (*saṃkilesadhamma*) have been utterly eradicated.
The commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta and the Nandivisāla Sutta. 108–109.
The seventh and eighth suttas, the Nanda Sutta and the Visāla Sutta, have already been commented upon below; thus, their meaning is as previously stated.
The commentary on the Nanda Sutta and the Nandivisāla Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Susīma Sutta: 110.
"Is it even for you?"—the word *nu* is used here in the sense of an inquiry; therefore, he asks this because he wishes to speak of [your] qualities.
The intention [is as follows]. "It is not fitting" means it is not logical; "spoken" means having begun to speak. Therefore he said, "it does not reach the culmination.
To demonstrate that very failure to reach the culmination, the passage beginning with "for he... was stated.

Because of his lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension, he is "of ox-like character" (*gorūpasīlo*); he is deluded and of faltering wisdom. For one whose character is like that of an ox is called "of ox-like character. He is of a similar nature.

Because of the state of having a single form of mind. The "likeness among the Noble Ones" (ariyānaṃ sabhāgatā) is by way of their possessing virtues; thus he said, "having gained confidence in each other's virtues.

Regarding "sixteen-fold wisdom": this refers to sixteen kinds of wisdom, namely, the six beginning with great wisdom (mahāpaññā), the nine wisdoms of the successive meditative attainments (anupubbavihārasamāpatti), and the wisdom of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayapaññā). The sixty-three knowledges shared by disciples (sāvakasādhāraṇañāṇa) are also included right here.

They go to the gathering and the assembly. "Ānanda," he said to the Elder. "Conduct" (ācāra) refers to the virtue of behavior (cāritta-sīla). "Range" (gocara) refers to success in one's range of activity (gocara-sampatti). "Abiding" (vihāra) refers to the abiding in meditative attainment (samāpatti-vihāra).

By the words "advancing" and so forth, he refers to the abiding in the postures (iriyāpatha-vihāra). In the phrase "for you too" (tuyhampi), by the word "too" (pi), the Blessed One includes himself as the first.
Having done so, he spoke the words beginning with “It pleases me” in order to show that the elder’s own inclination was made clear to all other wise people.
In this context, although the Elder Ānanda is also included among the eighty great elders,
by saying “It pleases the eighty great elders” and then adding “It also pleases you,” [the author] indicates that it is the Dhamma-Senāpati who...
"It should be understood as [the desire] to have his complexion described.
"Between the garments" means between the lower robe he was wearing. "Having found an opportunity" means having gained the chance to take what was found between the garments while making a wager.
"I shall obtain" means "indeed, I shall obtain. "Becoming the banner of the island" means [becoming the banner] spread over one hundred yojanas.
It is the banner of Jambudīpa. "Carrying away persons who are like chaff" means carrying away those persons who, due to the absence of inner substance, are like chaff.

"By way of foolishness" means by way of the absence of preference, inclination, and so forth. "By way of wickedness" means by way of being difficult to deal with. "By delusion" means by way of great stupidity. Some, however, say:
"The fool, by way of foolishness—that is, by way of delusion and by virtue of his natural state as a fool—does not know. The deluded one, by way of delusion..."
They say: "Even though one is oneself not a fool, when one is overwhelmed by delusion (*moha*), then through that delusion one does not know;
this is the distinction between these two [terms]. "One whose mind is perverted" means one whose mind is distorted by possession by a spirit (*yakkha*) or by a derangement of bile (*pitta*).
To show the fourfold skillfulness (*kosalla*) mentioned in the phrase "in the four skills," he says: "For it is said... and so forth.

It has been stated. In that context, one who understands the eighteen elements as they truly are—in terms of their arising, their passing away, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them—is skilled in the elements (*dhātukusala*).
One who is skilled in the sense-bases (*āyatana*) according to the method already described is skilled in the sense-bases (*āyatanakusala*).
One who is skilled in the twelve factors of dependent origination, beginning with ignorance, is skilled in dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādakusala*). "This belongs to this... [and so forth].

"The place [of an effect] is its cause; this is not the place, not the cause"—one who understands such a "place" as a place and a "non-place" as a non-place according to reality is skilled in place and non-place (*ṭhānāṭṭhānakusala*).

Furthermore, one who has gone from here—that is, proceeded—by means of knowledge (wisdom) known by the name "the wise one" (*paṇḍita*), which moves with unattached course through the thorough comprehension and clear realization of these elements and so forth, is called "wise."
Because he grasps great matters, his wisdom is great; thus he is "one of great wisdom" (*mahāpañño*).
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well, which is why it is said: "The meaning is that he is endowed with great wisdom and so forth.
As for "diversity" (*nānatta*): this is the diversity of those qualities such as great wisdom, by being endowed with which the Elder is praised as "one of great wisdom" and so on.

This is the distinction. Since the "greatness" of any particular immaterial dhamma should be understood through the accomplishment of its function, he said, "He comprehends the great aggregate of virtue," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that accomplishment of its function.
In this context, [greatness] is by way of greatness of cause, greatness of condition, greatness of support, greatness of classification, and greatness of function.
The greatness of the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) should be understood by way of the greatness of its fruit and the greatness of its benefits.
In this context, the causes are non-greed and so forth. The conditions are moral shame (*hiri*), moral dread (*ottappa*), faith (*saddhā*), mindfulness (*sati*), energy (*viriya*), and so forth.

The supports are the fixedness toward the enlightenment of disciples, the enlightenment of paccekabuddhas, and perfect enlightenment, as well as the specific types of persons endowed with them. The classification is the division into conduct (*cāritta*) and so forth. Its function is the removal of the opposite by means of its factors and so forth.
The dispelling [of defilements]. The fruit is the attainment of heaven and the attainment of Nibbāna. The benefit consists of being dear and agreeable, and so forth. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*, the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*, and other such texts.

In this same manner, the greatness of the aggregate of concentration and the other aggregates should also be determined and understood as appropriate. Regarding the "proper and improper occasions" (*ṭhānāṭṭhāna*), etc.

Furthermore, its greatness should be understood through its vast scope. In this regard, the vast scope of the possible and the impossible is to be understood by the method set forth in such discourses as the *Bahudhātuka*;
that of the abidings and attainments, by the method determined in the *Samādhi-khandha*;
that of the Noble Truths, because they encompass the entire Teaching, by the method set forth in the *Saccavibhaṅga* and its commentaries; and that of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth—
According to the method presented in the *Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga* and its commentaries;
because the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) constitute the production of great benefit, great happiness, great welfare, and great security from bondage (*yogakkhema*);

and because of their state of being peaceful, sublime, subtle, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, and to be experienced by the wise; and because the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) possess a great accumulation of requisites, a great objective range, a great function, great power, and a great fruition.
And: its greatness should be understood from the accomplishment of the great purpose, beginning with the intoxication-subduing of Nibbāna.

"Grasps" (pariggaṇhāti) means it grasps by delimiting [the object] from its intrinsic nature and so forth; the meaning is that it knows and penetrates it. Furthermore, "that" refers to the state of great wisdom. Regarding "wide wisdom" (puthupaññā):
here, knowledge operates upon various aggregates, such as "this is called the aggregate of form" … pe … this is... [and so on].
"The aggregate of consciousness is called 'name'": thus knowledge proceeds based on the differentiation of the five aggregates.
Among them, the aggregate of form is of one kind; the aggregate of form is of eleven kinds; the aggregate of feeling is of one kind;
the aggregate of feeling is of many kinds; the aggregate of perception is of one kind; and the aggregates of mental formations and consciousness [are likewise distinguished].
Thus, knowledge proceeds by way of discerning the differentiation of each aggregate according to its singlefold nature and so forth, as well as according to its pastness and so forth.
Likewise, knowledge proceeds by way of discerning the differentiation of the sense bases (*āyatana*), such that: "This is called the eye-base... [and so on]... this is called the mental-object-base.
In that regard, ten sense bases belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while two belong to all four planes; thus knowledge proceeds by way of discerning the differentiation of the sense bases.
"In various elements" means: "This is called the eye-element... pe ...this is called the mind-consciousness-element.
Therein, sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), and two belong to the four planes [of existence]. Thus, knowledge proceeds by way of the differentiation of elements;
it should be understood that this is stated with reference to the clung-to (upādiṇṇa) elements, for [it applies] to the Paccekabuddhas and to the two Chief Disciples.
Knowledge proceeds only with respect to the distinctions among the appropriated elements (*upādiṇṇadhātu*), and even that only partially, not exhaustively;
furthermore, they do not know the distinctions among the non-appropriated elements (*anupādiṇṇakadhātu*) at all.
There is nothing at all to be said regarding the other disciples, for it is only because of the abundance of this particular element among the omniscient Buddhas that [this distinction exists].
The trunk of one tree is white, while this one is black; this one has smooth bark, this one has thick bark, and this one has thin bark;
the leaf of this one is of such-and-such a color, shape, and so forth;
the flower of this one is blue, yellow, red, or white, fragrant or foul-smelling; the fruit is small, large, long, round, or well-shaped.
Whether it be bitter, harsh, fragrant, sweet, pungent, sour, acrid, astringent;
whether a thorn be sharp or not sharp, straight or crooked, copper-colored, red, or white—knowledge proceeds in dependence upon the diversity of elements (*dhātu*).
"There are" refers to the objects of perception, such as visible forms and so forth. "In various dependent originations" refers to the distinction between internal and external.

And regarding the various classifications according to their structural distinctions among the factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*): for each individual factor, beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), is designated as "dependent origination.
Therefore, it is said in the *Saṅkhāra Piṭaka*: "There are twelve conditions; there are twelve dependent originations.

Regarding the phrase "in various voidnesses, in non-apprehensions": this refers to those things of various natures which, due to being devoid of permanence, essence, and so forth, are of a void nature; from that...

Thus, regarding those intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) that are not apprehended by way of being female, male, self, or belonging to a self; here, the syllable *ma-* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*padasaṃdhikara*).

"In various meanings" (*nānāatthesu*) means in various kinds of meanings within the domain of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), such as the distinctions between conditioned phenomena and so forth.

"In phenomena" (*dhammesu*) means in various phenomena such as conditions and so forth within the domain of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*). "In expressions" (*niruttīsu*) refers to those very same [meanings and phenomena]...
In the etymologies (*nirutti*) consisting of words that distinguish between meanings and phenomena. Regarding "in inspired insights" (*paṭibhānesu*):

this refers to the knowledges that have attained the name "inspired insights" because they manifest and establish themselves in various ways toward their objects—such as the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)—thinking, "These [words] illuminate this specific meaning.
Regarding "in the various individual aggregates of virtue" (*puthu nānāsīlakkhandhesu*) and so forth: this refers to the multiplicity and diversity of virtue.
This has already been stated. As for the others, they are clearly understood by following the method already explained.
However, since Nibbāna is actually one and undivided, its plurality must be understood here by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra); thus it is said:
“having transcended the states common to ordinary people. By this, its plurality is illustrated here through such expressions as “the crushing of intoxication” and so forth.
Having thus shown the greatness and diversity of wisdom by way of its objects, it is now said, "What is laughing wisdom (*hāsapaññā*)?

and so forth, in order to show its state of laughter by way of associated states, its state of impulsion by way of its mode of occurrence, and its state of sharpness and so forth by way of its function.
In that context, "abounding in laughter" means abounding in rapture (*pīti*). The remaining terms refer to that [wisdom].

Synonyms: "He fulfills virtue" means that, being joyful and exceedingly elated, he fulfills the other threefold virtue by means of wisdom accompanied by rapture (*pīti*), having set aside the Pātimokkha virtue because it has already been separately included under what is more specifically "laughter-inducing.
For wisdom accompanied by rapture and mental joy (*somanassa*) is, through its delight, fully blossomed and expanded toward its object.
It proceeds as if [associated with joy], not accompanied by equanimity. The same method applies to the aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), and so forth.
By the words "the Elder" and so on, he shows that the Elder’s wisdom was characterized by laughter due to the success of his aspiration.
Because it quickly and swiftly moves toward all form from the perspective of the characteristic of impermanence, it [knows] the aggregate of form as impermanent with great speed.

Because the prior kamma-formations have been rendered exceptionally powerful by the distancing of their opposites through the process of development, one penetrates the characteristic [of impermanence] without hesitation, like Indra’s hurled thunderbolt;
thus, one penetrates the characteristic of impermanence in the aggregate of form with speed.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is called "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Thus, by way of insight having the characteristics as its object...
Having shown swift wisdom (*javanapaññā*), the passage beginning with “form” (*rūpa*) was stated in order to show it by way of powerful insight (*balavavipassanā*).
Therein, “in the sense of destruction” (*khayaṭṭhena*) means because of its nature of destruction, since wherever it arises, it breaks up at that very moment.

“In the sense of terror” (*bhayaṭṭhena*) means because of its terrifying nature. “In the sense of being coreless” (*asārakaṭṭhena*) means because of its lack of a self-essence and its lack of a permanent essence, and so forth.
"Having weighed" means having weighed with insight (*vipassanā*) which has become a scale. "Having scrutinized" means having scrutinized with that very same [insight] which has become a scrutiny.
"Having discerned" means having revealed them as they truly are, having made the five aggregates discernible and manifest.
"In the cessation of form" means by way of being inclined, sloping, and leaning toward *nibbāna*, which is the cessation of the aggregate of form.
Now, in order to show impulsion-wisdom (*javanapaññā*) by way of insight that has reached its culmination (*sikhāppattavipassanā*), the passage beginning with “matter” (*rūpa*) is stated again.
Some say it is “by way of insight leading to emergence” (*vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā*).

The state of the sharpness of knowledge (*ñāṇatikkhabhāva*) should be understood specifically in terms of the thorough eradication of opposing factors; thus [it says] “swiftly the defilements... (*khippaṃ kilese*).
Having stated, "He is one of keen wisdom because he cuts [them off]," he spoke the passage beginning with "arisen sensual thought" in order to demonstrate those defilements by way of classification.

He said, "One of keen wisdom possesses swift direct knowledge and his practice does not waver," and so on, stating, "The four noble paths were attained in a single sitting," etc., in order to show the keen wisdom of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) through the words "And the Elder... and so forth.
This shows that [the insight] has reached its peak.

The penetration of the truths is accomplished through seeing things as they truly are: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, conditioned, dependently arisen, and subject to destruction, decay, fading away, and cessation."
The phrase "not otherwise" is stated by way of its cause in order to show penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhikapaññā*).

In this context, "abounding in urgency" means that, according to the method already described, one frequently experiences a sense of spiritual urgency regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).

"Abounding in trepidation" means that, through the power of knowledge-trepidation, one's mind is repeatedly terrified of all conditioned phenomena. By this, he refers to the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*).
By the phrase "full of weariness," he refers to the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*);

by "full of aversion" and so forth, he indicates its repeated arising. "Outward-facing" means having the face of knowledge directed toward *nibbāna*, which lies outside all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), or having the face of liberation directed in that same way.
"Nibbijjhana" means penetration; it possesses this quality, or it penetrates. Thus, it is called "penetrative."

Or, that very wisdom which is piercing is "penetrative wisdom" (*nibbedhikā paññā*). Furthermore, whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning is easily understood because it follows the method already explained below.

"One of few desires" means the concealment of one's own virtues; that is, the hiding of the qualities existing within oneself, such as erudition, the ascetic practices (*dhuta*), morality, and so forth.
The concealment of the quality of realization and moderation in receiving—by this alone, moderation in seeking and in enjoyment is also stated.
"By three kinds of contentment" means by three kinds of contentment for each of the four requisites; thus, there are twelve in total.
"By one who is secluded" refers to those whose bodies are withdrawn from society and who do not delight in company. "Delighting in renunciation" refers to...
To those who have entered the going-forth; whose minds are pure and free from mental defilements;
who have attained supreme serenity through the realization of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), having reached an exceedingly high degree of serenity and purity;

who are "without substrate" (*nirupadhi*) due to the absence of the substrate of defilements (*kilesa-upadhi*) and so forth; and who are "beyond formations" (*visaṅkhāra*) because they have emerged from all conditioned phenomena by means of the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*).
Nirvana. One who has attained these three kinds of seclusion is "secluded" because he is secluded in various ways.
*Saṃsagga* (association) is the arising of intimacy through frequent contact; association that arises by way of hearing is "hearing-association.
The same method applies to the others as well. *Samullapana* (conversation) is talking and chatting. Association by means of this object of association is "use-association."
Regarding the term *āraddhavīriyo* (“one who has aroused energy”): here, the arousal of energy (*vīriyārambho*) means the exertion and fulfillment of energy.
Showing that this, moreover, consists in the complete suppression of the defilements (*kilesā*), he said, “In that regard,” and so forth.
“A practitioner of the shaking-off” (*odhunanavatto*) means one who practices by way of shaking off any defilement whatsoever that is blameworthy. Therefore, he said, “Of the bhikkhus,” and so forth.
“Transgressed fault” (otiṇṇaṃ vajjaṃ) means a fault that has been committed and reported. “Not transgressed” (anotiṇṇaṃ) means not reported.

“By way of the thread” (tantivasena) means by way of the Dhamma of the Canon; the meaning is “by way of the word ‘yutta’. One who censures and feels disgust toward evil persons and evil qualities is a “censurer of evil” (pāpagarahī).
Therefore he said, “toward evil persons,” and so forth. “One who sees one thing” (ekadassī) means one who sees only a single existence, one who sees merely this world.
“Seeking only the happiness pertaining to this present life. “On all sides” (*samantā*) means from every direction;
the construction is: “May it not exist for me anywhere. “With sixteen phrases” means with sixteen sections. “Unshakable” (*akuppa*) means incapable of being shaken by anything.
This discourse on the virtues of the General of the Dhamma, following the words of the Teacher, pervaded ten thousand world-systems; to demonstrate this, [the text] says “Thus,” and so forth.
It has been said. There are four kinds of radiant color (vaṇṇanibhā) because it arises from sublime joy and gladness. It shines beautifully, thus it is "beautiful" (subho).
Because of its excellence in radiance, the gem is auspicious; therefore he says, "beautiful means handsome. It is of noble birth (jātimā) because it originates from a completely pure mine.
Even specific types of gems such as the *kuruvinda* type are rooted in the purity of their source; therefore he says, "endowed with noble birth" (*jātisampanno*).
"By means of preparatory work such as washing" refers to the preparatory work consisting of washing on four stones, removing impurities, heating, and smoothing.
Because the natural color is established by means of a red woolen cloth (*rattakambala*), the beryl gem shines exceedingly; thus he said, "placed upon a pale cloth" (*paṇḍukambale nikkhitto*).
"Placed" (*nikkhitto*) refers to the object (*bhaṇḍa*). And an object made of little gold does not shine.
Regarding the phrase "of vast splendor," it is said: "an ornament made of more than five measures of gold. "Gold" (suvaṇṇa) is a designation for five *dharaṇas*.
Therefore, what is intended here by the term "necklace" (*nikkha*) is a variegated ornament consisting of twenty-five measures of gold;
for that is vast, not meager. Regarding the phrase "in the river flowing beneath the great jambu branch," [it refers to] beneath the great jambu branch.
"Born in a river. That gem, it is said, was red. "Well-worked by a skilled [artisan]... pe ... well-beaten":
it has been thoroughly heated with a torch by a highly skilled goldsmith and properly beaten, having undergone well-prepared refinement through processes such as immersion.
"In the *Dhātuvibhaṅga*" refers to the *Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta*. "A finished article" means an object fashioned into the form of an ornament.
"Not too high, not too low" refers to the "morning sun. This means it possesses the color brought by the Teacher and has its qualities manifested.
"He does not rejoice even in death" means he does not rejoice even in his own death, because the falling away of oneself is blameworthy.
However, the Bodhisatta relinquishes his own personal existence for the sake of others out of compassion; thus...
Since relinquishing [the body] leads to the fulfillment of the ultimate perfections (paramattha-pāramī), disciples are unable to do so because of the training rules (sikkhāpada).
He does not long for life because his craving for life has been utterly severed. "A brief day" means a wage delimited by a portion of the day, such as:
"Today you must perform this work; this is your wage. For such is the hired laborer.

He looks only toward the end of the day, not toward the completion of his work. "Like a hired laborer seeking his wages" means he is like a man who, desiring his fee and hire, watches for the exhaustion of time.
The commentary on the Susīma Sutta is finished.

10. Commentary on the Discourse to the Disciples of Various Sectarians (Nānātitthiyasāvakasutta) 111. "Disciples of various sectarians" means disciples of many different non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthika*). "In cutting off" refers to acts of mutilation such as the amputation of hands and so forth.
"In killing" refers to the act of taking life. "He does not perceive any evil" means he does not see that there is any evil whatsoever [in these acts].
And he proclaims it thus to others. "Vissāsanti" means the state of being confident.
By saying, "There is no result even for those who have performed deeds," one generates confidence and a sense of security in those who have committed evil and those who have not performed merit.

"Tapojigucchāya" means by means of asceticism—such as nakedness and so forth—and by the loathing of evil, thinking, "I am purifying evil," through the undertaking of nakedness and other such practices.
The meaning is as follows: for one who stands firm in that undertaking and possesses a mind restrained by restraint, he is indeed called "guarded";
thus it is said, "well-restrained in self," and so forth. There are four watches (*yāma*) or parts; these four watches themselves are the *cātuyāma*.
Here, the word *yāma* has the sense of a "part," as in the expression "the first watch of the night. Furthermore, in this context, that part is characterized by restraint.

He said, "Well-restrained by the fourfold restraint. The meaning is: well-restrained by the restraint consisting of four parts. "One who has rejected all cold water" means one who has renounced the use of all cold water.
"Endowed with the warding off of evil in every way" means possessed of the warding off of evil characterized by every mode of restraint.
"One who has shaken off evil" means one who has shaken off evil even by the warding off of evil characterized by total wearing away (*nijjara*).

"Touching" means touched by the complete warding off of evil, which is characterized by the destruction of karma through the exhaustion of all eight types of karma and the attainment of non-distraction;
having touched that, he stands firm. "Not concealing" means speaking exactly as he has seen and heard, not for the sake of concealment.

"A supporter of various sectarians" means a supporter of all other teachers (tīrthikas), being full of faith toward them in a general sense. "Reached the pinnacle" means having reached the noble limit to be attained in the ascetic life (śramaṇadharma) through the attainment of liberation.
“Merely by associating” means merely by making a sound together with the lion’s roar. It is like a jackal merely making its own jackal-cry while a lion is roaring his lion-roar.
“A small kotthu” means a tiny jackal. “One whose conduct is suspected” means one whose conduct is suspected both by oneself and by others. “Of true persons” refers to the Buddhas and others.
"Of him" means of that son of the gods who was filled with speed. "He entered the body" means he entered as if having actually penetrated the body.
"He resolved" means he determined in such a way that the mind did not function according to what had been grasped [by others], but rather functioned under his own control.
"Engaged" means connected through seeing. "Seclusion" refers to [the seclusion of] hair-cutting, clothing, food, and lodgings.
The state of seclusion. Therefore he said, “They, it is said,” and so forth. “Attached to form” means firmly adhered to the phenomena of the eye and visible forms.
Therefore he said, “Established by craving and views. “Desiring the longing for the world of the gods” means desiring only the longing for the world of the gods.

“Of a mother” because of the nature of being subject to death. Therefore he said, “‘Of a mother’ means of mortals. “For the sake of the other world” means for the sake of the world’s attainment of higher excellence.

“Of similar color to radiance” (*pabhāsavaṇṇā*) means having a color equal to radiance. To the question “Whose radiance? he says, “of the moon’s radiance,” and so forth. The phrases “having a color like the radiance of saffron-red” and “having a color like the radiance of Indra’s bow” are to be applied respectively.
“Flesh” (*āmisa*) is that which has rawness (*āma*)—the stench of raw flesh—as its characteristic. “For slaughter” (*vadhāya*) means for the purpose of destroying.
“Forms” (*rūpa*) refers to material phenomena such as the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
“Of those belonging to Rājagaha” means those situated near Rājagaha. Regarding the word “white,” he says “white means Kelāsa” because the peak of Mount Kelāsa is intended.
“Agha” means that which cannot be struck by anything; thus he says “going to the agha” means “going to the sky.
“Udadhi” is that in which water is held; [thus] it is the great ocean. “Vipula” refers to Mount Vepulla. “Of the Himalayan mountains...”
Of the regions of the Himavat mountains. The Buddha is supreme through all his qualities, such as virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The commentary on the Suttas concerning various non-Buddhist teachers and disciples is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the *Devaputtasaṃyutta* of the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyuttanikāya*, is completed. 3.
*Kosalasaṃyutta*.
1. First Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the *Dahara-sutta*. 112.
"He exchanged greetings with the Blessed One": the King of Kosala, being unaware of the Blessed One's virtues, [acted] out of his own pride as a kshatriya.
He exchanged greetings only with the Blessed One. For when the Teacher first arrived, the words beginning with "just as" were spoken in order to show the manner of his greeting.

"Just as he asked about his well-being and so forth" means that the Blessed One’s initial exchange of greetings with the king was in the form of asking, "Is it bearable for you, Great King? Is it sustainable? and so on.
The construction is as follows: by means of the previous speech and by imitating that, the king also came to share the same joy as the Blessed One.
To illustrate that shared joy through a simile, it is said, "like cool water," and so forth.
In that context, *sammoditaṃ* means blended or unified; it refers to the equality and uniformity of the act of greeting.
"Is it endurable? means: "This body, consisting of four wheels and nine doors, is by its very nature difficult to endure due to the abundance of suffering;

can it possibly be endured? He asks this. "Is it sustainable? means: "Since its existence depends upon the [four] requisites, can it possibly be sustained for what is called a long-term maintenance? [He asks this] because of the absence of afflictions such as diseases of the head.
"Is there little affliction?"—this refers to the absence of a miserable livelihood. "Is there little illness?"—this refers to the ease of exertion in performing various duties.
"Is there lightness?"—this refers to the possession of strength corresponding to that [lightness]. "Is there well-being?"—this refers to the occurrence of a pleasant dwelling.
The meaning should be understood by applying the word *kacci* ("I hope") to each respective instance. [The phrase] *balavappattā* means having attained strength.
*Pīti* is simply rapture (*pīti*). *Pāmojja* is fresh rapture. It is called "conducive to amity" (*sammodanīya*) because it generates and produces gladness.
Furthermore, showing the meaning as "that which is to be greeted with amity," he said: "because it is appropriate for greeting.
"Because of the state of being remembered" means because of the state of being recollected. Although it should have been called "saraṇīya," it is stated as "sāraṇīya" by lengthening the vowel.
"By its sweetness when being tasted" refers to its initial sweetness; "by its sweetness when being recollected" refers to its delightful quality when being reflected upon.
"By the purity of the phrasing" refers to the eloquence of the speech in that discourse by virtue of its natural expression;
"by the purity of the meaning" refers to the absence of defilement in the meaning. "By numerous methods" means by numerous reasons.

"Because it has not been seen" means because it has not been seen by way of approaching [the Teacher]. "By way of qualities and non-qualities" means either its profound nature by way of qualities, or its superficial nature by way of non-qualities.
"Having made it the core of the palm of the hand" means having made it the substance to be grasped within the hollow of the palm.

"Questions on the departure from the world and the entry into existence" refers both to questions concerning the state of having emerged from the world and to questions concerning the initial ascent into existence.
For when asking about the Teacher’s state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One (sammāsambuddha), he asks: "Is Master Gotama escaped from the entire world, and is he the eldest among all beings?

Indeed, he asks this because, just as the Teacher's state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One is understood through his escape from the world, so too is it understood through his status as the eldest and most excellent among all beings. This meaning is established by such discourses as the *Aggapasāda Sutta*.
It is to be made manifest. But how is perfect Buddhahood (sambuddhatā) to be known? From his teaching of the Dhamma without error.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā* and other such works.
The king, not knowing the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma without error, for that very reason did not have faith in his Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).

Thinking, "If even those who are senior and have long been ordained cannot attain the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), how could it be attained by one who is the opposite of them?", he will say, "But what about Master Gotama? and so forth.
The King does not ask out of his own personal conviction, because they themselves had admitted in his presence that they were not Perfectly Enlightened Ones. Since they...
Because they falsely claimed through lying that their own attendants and others were "Buddhas," it is said:
"He asks by way of the claims accepted by the world. This matter will become clear later.

"The Buddha’s lion’s roar" refers to the lion’s roar unique to the Buddhas alone. Granted that omniscience has the knowledge of the path as its proximate cause, yet in the knowledge of full enlightenment—
However, when that [term] is taken, it is already understood by implication; thus it is said: "Right Self-awakening, which is designated as omniscient knowledge.
By the mere act of entering into any kind of renunciation (*pabbajjā*), one is a recluse (*samaṇa*), not because of having stilled evil deeds (*samitapāpa*).
By virtue of birth alone, one is a brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*), not because of having banished evil deeds (*bāhitapāpa*). The term *saṅgha* refers to the community (*samūha*) of those who have gone forth.

The intention is that the *saṅgha* [is so called] merely by virtue of being a collection of those who have gone forth (*pabbajita*), not because of its being a unified body through the commonality of liberating views, purity of virtue, and the ascetic life.
"It belongs to these" means it exists as an attendant to these who claim omniscience.

"That very same" refers precisely to what is designated as the collection of those who have gone forth. Some, however, [say]: "By way of the collection of those who have gone forth; [the term] *saṅghin* [is used] by way of the collection of householders."
When they say "of the group-leader" (gaṇin), that is merely their own opinion, because in the world the term *saṅgha* is conventionally established only for a community (*gaṇa*).

"By way of training in conduct" means by way of training in conduct such as the practice of the naked ascetic’s vow (*acelaka-vata*). "Manifest" means made known by virtue of being a member of a community (*saṅghī*) and so forth.
Having said "of few desires," in order to show the state of having few desires found therein, [he says] "by way of having few desires."

It is said, "They do not even wear a lower garment. For among those [heretics], the quality of fewness of desires—characterized by concealing one's existing virtues as is done by those within the Dispensation—is not found.
*Yasa* means fame or reputation. Because they are considered to be those by whom the flood of saṃsāra is crossed, it is called a *tittha*;
thus he says, "Titthakaras are makers of tenets (*laddhi*). *Sādhusammatā* means "considered 'good'."
“They are not esteemed by the virtuous,” he said, [explaining] “the noble ones... [down to] the worldling.
“The tumult of the aeon” (*kappakolāhala*) means the clamor arising from the aeon; it is the great sound proclaimed by the sons of the gods, crying out, “The emergence of the aeon will take place!
“These” refers to Pūraṇa and the others. “The tumult of a Buddha” (*buddhakolāhala*) is the proclamation of a Buddha’s appearance made by the deities. “Having waited upon” (*payirupāsitvā*)—
Having heard it through a succession of oral tradition from men. The "Cintāmaṇi-vidyā" is a science for knowing the minds of others.

It appears as "maṇikā" in the *Kevaṭṭa-sutta*; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes the *Gandhāri-sambhava-vidyā* and others. Therein, it demonstrates the miraculous transformations of Gandhārī.
"In one's own being" (*attabhāve*) means in the body. "The splendor of kings" (*rājusmā*) means royal majesty.
"Pure dhamma" means faultless dhamma, the state of being free from defilement.
"Having taken this up" means having taken up the words spoken by them in his absence—"We are Buddhas"—and then, in his presence, [hearing] "We are not Buddhas.
"He spoke thus" means he said: "Those who, Master Gotama... [as before] ...are new in their going-forth. "Having taken up his own admission" means: "No..."
Having taken the admission uttered by them before him, [the Buddha said], "We are Buddhas. In such a context, the word *kiṃ* functions as a term of negation;
thus it is said, "The word *kiṃ* is a word of rejection," meaning for what purpose would he claim this?
"They are not to be despised" means they are not to be censured, for this prefix *u-* has the sense of censure. Because of the addition of the word "young" (*daharo*),...
And because it will be explained later, it is said: "A khattiya is a prince. It is called an *uraga* because it moves by means of its breast (*urasā*);
while this refers to any snake in general, he says "a venomous serpent" (*āsīvisa*) here to show the specific one intended.

By saying "a bhikkhu," he indicates a virtuous renunciant in a general sense; however, here [the term is used] because of the Blessed One’s statement, beginning with "Bhava also [said], 'O Gotama... and so forth.
He initiated the discourse by way of a specific reference; therefore, the Blessed One made himself the internal subject.
Even if a particularity is already manifested by a general statement, the inclusion of the term "spoken" (vutta) excludes it from being merely an indicator of the arising of doubt.
Thus he said, "By skill in teaching," and so forth. Now, in order to demonstrate [the fault] through the application of contempt and disparagement:

The passage beginning with “And here” has been stated. In that context, the manifestation of contempt through the manner of not showing respect is intended as the state of being manifest through disparagement;
thus, contempt is shown by way of bodily application, while disparagement is shown by way of verbal application.
However, both are included in their specific varieties for both [contexts], since both contempt and disparagement occur in both places.

"Pariggaha" (comprehension). "All that" means all those things such as contempt and so forth. None of these should be practiced in any of the four cases, because they bring harm both in the present and in the future.

"Tadatthadīpanā" (the illumination of its meaning) is the elucidation of the meaning stated at the beginning. "Visesatthadīpanā" (the illumination of its specific meaning) is the elucidation of a meaning more distinguished than that.

“Lord of the fields (khetta), thus a khattiya”—this etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*) should be understood as the grammatical establishment of the term. The worldlings say: “He protects beings from disputes regarding the fields;
thus he is a khattiya. Among these [terms] that have come down in such passages as “Mahāsammata, the khattiya, the king,” this is the second.

*Akkhara* means conventional designation (*samaññā*). For it is called “syllable” (*akkhara*) because it never decays (*na kadāci kharati*) due to the absence of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya*).
Thus it was said. Therefore he said: "Name and clan do not decay. "One of noble birth" means one whose birth is accomplished, one of extremely pure birth.
"The three castes" refers to the Brahmin, Vessa, and Sudda castes. "Having surpassed" means having overcome them by means of one's own excellence of birth.
Since only a noun phrase was stated and it requires a verb phrase, he said: "Indeed, there exists a reason (thānaṃ hi) [for this]."
"With an uprooted staff" means with a staff—that is, a teaching—uprooted from all sides;
[it refers to] a powerful, forceful, and grave [offense], even against a king. "One should avoid that kshatriya" means one should avoid the kshatriya by not treating him with contempt or disdain.
Therefore he said, "one should not strike."
He explains the reason for perceiving the various colors of the serpent with the words beginning, "By whatever... *Bahubhakkaṃ* means one that eats much, a consumer of all things.
*Pāvakaṃ* (the purifier) is so called in the sense of cleansing, by burning even what is impure.
*So* refers to the path. *Kaṇhavattanī* means that which has a black course (*vattanī*). Having become a great mass of fire, it reaches as far as the Brahma-world.

To show that at the time of the end of the eon (*kappa*), when a forest is consumed by fire, it is only after some time that wood, grass, trees, and so forth arise again, he says "there they grow" (*jāyanti tattha pārohā*) in the text; demonstrating this, he says "therein" (*tatthā*) and so on.

[The fire] is unable to burn [them] because of the crying out for protection and other such acts. They perish because they have been destroyed by the spiritual power (*teja*) of the ascetics (*samaṇa*). "Not of that... (*na tassa*)... [and so on].
In this context, having brought forward the letter *na-* from the word "vindare" (they find), it should be connected [to the verb]; thus he says, "they do not find.
"Remaining as mere location" means that only their place remains for them, while they themselves perish entirely along with their wealth; such is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "one should act rightly," he shows by way of analysis how one should act rightly toward kings and others.
He said, “First, a khattiya,” and so forth; that is indeed easy to understand. “Three types of excellence of family” refers to the khattiya, brāhmaṇa, and gahapati mahāsāla families.
There are nine brahmā-worlds: five in the world of form-brahmās and four in the formless-brahmā worlds—this is by way of classifying them as *kammabhava* (existence as kamma);
the remaining enumerations are by way of classifying them as *upapattibhava* (existence as rebirth).
“*Abhikkantaṃ*” means exceedingly desirable. As for its desirability, it is due to its being exceedingly wished-for, heart-pleasing, and beautiful;
thus he said: “The meaning is ‘exceedingly wished-for,’ ‘exceedingly agreeable,’ and ‘exceedingly beautiful.
The neuter designation is used in reference to the word “*abhikkantaṃ*,” whereas the word itself refers to the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma; therefore, it was spoken in that way.
Or rather, this is merely for the sake of indicating the meaning; therefore, the change of gender and case-ending should be understood according to the sense.
The same method applies to the second phrase as well.
"Placed face downwards" means placed face downwards by someone. "Naturally facing downwards" means [facing downwards] by its very nature.

"Born. "He should uncover" means he should open it. "Taking by the hand": without saying "Go facing east or facing north," and so forth, but rather taking him by the hand and making him free from doubt, he should say, "This is the path," and then say, "Go.
"The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight" means the fourteenth day of the dark half of the month. "He should turn what was overturned upright" means...
One should turn upside up a vessel that is without a base for what is to be placed within it, by means of making it into a base for that [content].

Because ignorance faces [the truth], it has arisen with its face turned downward; thus, being averse to the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*), it falls into the non-True Dhamma (*asaddhamma*) precisely because of that downward-facing state.

In this way, these two phrases should be applied according to their respective meanings, not according to their numerical order. Granted, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the other [hindrances] are also [included].
While there are concealers [of faults], wrong view is especially a concealer; thus he said, "concealed by the thicket of wrong view.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I declare that wrong view is the supreme fault.

The "bad path" (kummagga) is the path leading to all states of misery, so called because it is a "contemptible path" (kucchito maggo). Wrong view and the others are the direct opposites of right view and the rest.

The eight states of wrongness constitute the wrong path. It is precisely with reference to their being the opposites of both [the right path and the right practice] that it is said: "by one revealing the path to heaven and liberation.
A lamp dependent on ghee and such is not as bright as one dependent on oil; hence the mention of an "oil-lamp.
"By these various modes" means by these types of similes to be illustrated, such as turning what is overturned upright, uncovering what is hidden, and so forth.
*Pasannākāraṃ*: the honor to be performed by those who have faith. *Saraṇaṃ*: a refuge, a resort, a final destination. *Ajjatā*:
here the word *tā* is merely an extension of the word *ajja*, just as in the term *devatā*. *Pāṇehi upetaṃ*: accompanied by life;
[it means] "may it hold me as one who has gone for refuge for as long as my life-breaths endure."
He declares his own going for refuge as lasting until the end of life. Therefore he said, "As long as I... and so forth.
Whatever is not explained here in terms of its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Dahara-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Purisa Sutta 113.

"In the previous sutta" means in the teaching of the previous sutta. For there, at the time of approaching [the Buddha], he did not know the Teacher’s qualities and merely engaged in polite greetings.
However, having heard the teaching and come to know the Teacher’s qualities, he went for refuge.
Here, in this assembly, he paid homage and saluted with the fivefold prostration. Regarding "internally" (*ajjhattam*):
having taken oneself as the basis, with reference to, and not abandoning oneself, those phenomena that occur directed toward oneself are "internal.

This is a nominative singular used in the sense of the locative, in the sense of grasping them collectively within. And although this word *ajjhatta* [is used] in the senses of internal object (*gocara-ajjhatta*), internal field (*visaya-ajjhatta*), and internal self (*atta-ajjhatta*).

[The defilements] proceed. However, since those [definitions] are not applicable here, it is said “internal in its own right” (*niyakajjhatta*); the meaning is “among internal phenomena known as ‘one’s own’.

Therefore, he says “in one’s own continuity. “Characterized by greed” means characterized by longing; the meaning is that its intrinsic nature is the firm grasping of an object. “Characterized by hatred” means characterized by anger;
the meaning is that its intrinsic nature is malevolence. “Characterized by delusion” means...

Its characteristic is ignorance; the meaning is that it is a state of delusion regarding the intrinsic nature of the object. "They afflict" means they oppress by destroying what is beneficial and producing what is harmful.
For that very reason, he said "they destroy and disperse," meaning they act so that [the path] is not seen on the paths to heaven as it would otherwise be.
"Arising within oneself" means produced within one's own continuum (saṃtāna).
The commentary on the Purisa Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Jarāmaraṇa Sutta: 114.
“Apart from aging-and-death” means without aging-and-death. Is there anyone who is born devoid of aging-and-death?
*Ko* means "who," [used here] to ask a question. In the canonical text (*pāḷi*), *jātassa* is the genitive case used in its own sense (*paccatte*).
By the form *mahāsālā*, it shows that the letter *ra* has been changed to *la*, as in the expression "the easterners" (*puratthiyā*) being called "pulatthiyā.
*Mahāsārappattā* means having attained great wealth and value. "A hundred million pieces of wealth"—this is the very reading [of the text]. "A *kumbha* is said to be ten..."
They say, "We shall provide [them] with vessels. "Masters" means masters by virtue of their wealth and power.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "gold, silver, vessels, etc.," one includes clothing, beds, dwellings, and so forth. Because exclusive wealth is already in the form of a hoard, it is said, "of that which has not been placed in a hoard.
"Of that which brings satisfaction" refers to the means of happiness such as palaces, litters, and the like.

"Far from defilements" (*ārakā kilesehi*): he states the etymological derivation according to the rules of grammar (*niruttinaya*). "Far" (*āraka*) means distant from them because they have been completely eradicated.

He is "Worthy One" (*arahant*) because of the destruction of lust and the other [defilements], because of the absence of shame (*raha*) in committing evil deeds, and by virtue of being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), and so forth.
Although this is an explanation based on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, he says that the method of the Abhidhamma alone is the non-figurative (*nippariyāya*) sense.

“Four taints”: the dwelling in the holy life (*brahmacariya-vāsa*) refers to the dwelling in the holy life of the Path (*magga-brahmacariya-vāsa*). “He emerges, having emerged”: [he emerges] by means of the four paths.

“To be done by the four paths” means that which is to be performed individually by each of the four paths—the clear comprehension (*pariññā*), abandoning (*pahāna*), realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and development (*bhāvanā*)—of the truths.
Thus, when combined, it becomes sixteenfold. They are called “burdens” (*bhāra*) because they are like burdens in the sense of causing one to sink down. Therefore he said: “Burdens indeed...”

"The five aggregates," and so forth. Because it is bound up with a self and does not abandon the self, and because it is taught as the ultimate reality (*paramattha*), the ultimate reality is arahantship.
Granted that this state—being comprised within a continuity of all success and being a faultless phenomenon—is possible due to its unshakable nature;
yet it is especially predominant in arahantship, which is the foremost among those states characterized by non-decline. It is not...
Regarding the phrase "in the others," it is stated: "designated as arahantship," and so forth.

The tenfold fetter (*saṃyojana*), divided into those pertaining to the lower and those pertaining to the higher, is called the "fetter of existence" (*bhavasaṃyojana*) because, by acting as the condition for the rounds of defilement (*kilesa*), karma, and result (*vipāka*), it binds one to existences by way of not permitting escape.
For even though there are other factors belonging to their class, they do not constitute fetters without these.

Their state of being conditions exists; the determination of existence (*bhavaniyāma*)—comprised of the lower and higher fetters—is also the determination of the karma that produces this or that specific existence.
Furthermore, since even karmas performed by one whose fetters are severed do not produce existence, the meaning of "fetters" should be understood as applying to those [fetters] alone.
"Having known correctly through reasons" means: according to the method (*ñāya*), he should know them as they are to be known regarding suffering and the rest.

Having understood thus, the following was stated beginning with "by means of path-wisdom" (*maggapaññā*) in order to show how the activity of a subsequent time occurs, being liberated from the activity of a prior time.
Its nature of breaking up is due to its dependence on the moment;
its nature of being laid down is due to its being subject to death. This body is [characterized by] the departure of heat, life-force, and consciousness.

Regarding the nature of things that are subject to being discarded: since that upon which something is established must be described as dissociated from the continuum of that thing, it is said, "For even for one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava), there exists that which is subject to non-decaying. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"In this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, I proclaim the world and the origin of the world."

"...and the cessation of the world," and so forth. Regarding this one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), setting aside that which is "not subject to decay" as previously stated, [the Buddha] spoke thus—"this body of his is subject to breaking up"—in order to show what is subject to decay.

For it is only when one has reached old age that there is the certainty of its breaking up and being cast aside; it is with reference to this meaning that the teaching of the Sutta proceeds. Of this meaning...
*Uppatti-aṭṭhuppatti*: that which has this as its origin is *aṭṭhuppattika*. The word *kira* signifies tradition;
by it, he indicates that this meaning is arrived at through oral tradition and is not found in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. Therefore, he says, "they say.
To show the reason (*hetu*) by which this meaning is *aṭṭhuppattika*, it is stated: "Having sat in the Sivika hall, it was spoken. "He dwells..."
It should be understood in such a way that it does not contradict the introductory statement, "In Jeta’s Grove.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the delivery of this sutta was prompted by a question? [Response: That is true; however, the statement regarding its origin (*aṭṭhuppatti*) refers specifically to a portion of the sutta.
Some, moreover, say: "The King had arrived having mounted a vehicle; [the sutta] was spoken after showing him the chariot upon which the King was to ride."
What need is there to say anything regarding a body that is like a lump of foam? They proclaim it "together with the good" (*sabbhi*);

for indeed, there is never anything to be done by the good together with the good. Therefore, because the defilements—which are by nature subject to sinking—have reached their dissolution, Nibbāna is called "the good" (*sabhi*). Regarding the first phrase: "The Dhamma of the good does not age..."

Showing the reason for the phrase "does not undergo aging" (*upeti*) by way of contrast (*byatireka*): The Dhamma of the noble ones (*sataṃ dhammo*), which is Nibbāna, does not possess the nature of sinking or decaying due to defilements;
therefore, having come to that, one does not undergo aging. Defilements, however, are the cause of that [decay].
Thus, for the reasons stated, one does not undergo aging. Therefore he said, "This," and so forth. Or alternatively, it is a synonym for "excellent" (*sundara*).
This word “sabbhi” (by the good) is used because it illustrates that which is not subject to falling away; the meaning is “that which has become the nature of all things.
Therefore he said: “Dispassion is declared the foremost among them; there is nothing equal to that state.
The commentary on the Jarāmaraṇa Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Piyasutta 115.
*Rahasi gatassa* means having departed from the crowd of people.

*Nilīnassa* means as if one who is secluded (*paṭisallīnassa*) by sitting to one side in solitude through that very separation from people; hence he says, "of one who has become alone" (*ekībhūtassa*). This was spoken by the Omniscient One.
Acting thus, he said, having accepted his words with the thought, "It is even so," and repeating those words accordingly.
Because he was seized by the Ender (Death), he was abandoning his human existence, including fields, lands, silver, gold, and so forth.
*Anugaṃ* means followed; the meaning is that it follows him alone. *Nicayaṃ* means that which has been accumulated through successive increases. *Samparāyikaṃ* means beneficial for the future life.
The commentary on the Piyasutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Attarakkhitasutta 116.
“Pīdahana” means restraint. “Of one who has not reached a breach of the courses of action” means that it occurs as a mere mental occurrence, like the time of a dream.
"Of one who has not entered into the specific path of action. "Of action" means of unwholesome action (*akusalakamma*). "Restraint" (*saṃvara*) indicates the state of being restrained;
however, the state of restraint for the other [type of action] has already been shown by the preceding three terms.

Shame (*ottappa*) is also indeed included, because it is inseparable from that [restraint]. For there is no loathing of evil devoid of fear of evil, nor is there fear of evil devoid of loathing of evil.
The commentary on the Attarakkhitasutta is finished. 6. Commentary on the Appakasutta 117.

Since the word *uḷāra* is seen to mean both "excellent" and "much," he said: "both excellent and much. "By means of pride and intoxication" (*mānamajjanena*) means by way of pride and the attainment of arrogance. They "transgress" the fault characterized by the overstepping of the proper bounds of good conduct. A "trap" (*kūṭa*) is a snare.
The commentary on the *Appakassutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Aḍḍakaraṇasutta*: 118.
Since a being speaks a deliberate lie for the sake of sensual desire, therefore sensual desires are its basis and condition.

He says "the cause" and so forth, beginning with "with sensual desire as the cause. The meaning is that he attends to Viṭaṭūbha by means of the auspicious face (Bhadramukha) through the practice of auspiciousness (*bhadropacāra*).
A "court of justice" (*aḍḍakaraṇa*) is so called because legal decisions (*vinicchaya*) are made therein; it is a place of adjudication. "Khippa" refers to a hook (*kūṭa*);
it is also acceptable to understand it as a fish-hook. "Set" (*oḍḍita*) means caused to fall [into the water] by way of being cast down.
The commentary on the Aḍḍakaraṇasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Mallikāsutta 119. [Question:
"Why does she ask? [Answer: Having raised the reason for the question, it is said: "This [is] to show [the answer] starting from the origin (samudaya)."

"Kira Mallikā," and so forth, was said. "Having gone to the flower garden" means having gone for the purpose of protecting his father’s flower garden and for the purpose of gathering the remaining flowers.

"In the village of Kāsi" means in a village of the kingdom of Kāsī. It is said that this village had been given by the Great King of Kosala for the sake of providing the root of flowers for his daughter when she went to her husband's home; it was for that reason. By his nephew...
By Ajātasattu. "His" refers to King Pasenadi. "She" refers to Mallikā.

"To turn back" means to turn back according to her nature, that is, to reject her words. Regarding "he did not obtain": since this is a past tense used in the sense of the present, he said, "he does not attain.
"A separate self" means the self of those beings.
The commentary on the Mallikāsutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Yaññasutta 120.
*Thūṇa* means a sacrificial pillar. *Upanītāni* means brought forward for the purpose of beginning the sacrifice. *Ettāvata* means "to this extent": "In this world... [and so forth].
[He spoke] with this much of the text: "Venerable sir... weeping, she performs the preliminary rites.
"Determination" means not finding or knowing the certainty as to whether "I shall obtain that woman or not.
"Like froth on the surface" means just as where something has boiled, froth rises up but does not settle, so [it was] many times.
Having raised up foam. "On that day" means on the day the king could not sleep and lay in pain.
"Looking toward the light" means looking toward the great light that had appeared at the rim of the opening of the iron cauldron.
[He spoke] his own words for the purpose of making the king understand the situation. A great cry arose: "The king [is performing] such a sacrifice!"
"...he causes [it] to be made. He intended to speak, but being unable to speak, he uttered "Sa" and sank into the iron cauldron.
"He intended to recite this verse"—this is the connection here. This same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
They caused the drum of the Dhamma to be beaten, saying, "Let no one kill any living being. That man, the husband of the woman, [attained] the fruit of stream-entry.
The Teacher established himself through the perfection of his own supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*), and the King through the perfection of the Teacher’s skill in teaching;
however, because the Great Bodhi tree is by nature subject to cessation, the King did not attain any particular distinction.
"Bases of conciliation" (*saṅgaha-vatthūni*) refers to the causes for winning over the world. From the nine portions of the harvested crop, [one portion goes] to the farmer...
Having granted the kings the taking of one share or the taking of a tenth share, the farmers, being joyful and satisfied, brought forth their crops;
thus it is said, "the meaning is 'one who is wise in bringing forth crops. It is said that thereafter, the taking of a sixth share arose.
"Sufficient for six months" means enough for each of six months. "He lays out" means he arranges it as if in a snare.
Through speech, one should perform the work of speech that is pleasing and brings pleasure to those who are dear. Because the kingdom is entirely prosperous and so forth, it is secure (*khema*).

It is free from the *abbuda* hell because there is an absence of thieves. Indeed, this kingdom is called "thiefless" (*acoriya*) and "boltless" (*niraggaḷa*) because its houses have doors that are never closed.
"Having uprooted" means having pulled out by the roots. "By two sacrifices" refers to the period preceding the Great Sacrifice (*mahāyañña*).
And with the two subsequent offerings of attendants that were to be performed. "Twenty-seven...

[etc. ... "It perishes" means: by the slaughter of six hundred and nine animals in total—comprising three hundred and twenty-seven domestic animals together with twenty-two horses and so forth, and two hundred and sixty wild forest animals—it was terrifying and brought fear to those who dread evil. For thus they say:
“Harnessed oxen are yoked; they slaughter cattle in the midst [of the sacrifice], even nine more than required for the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) ritual.
*Sammanti* means that which is to be inserted as a bolt into the hole of the yoke. *Pāsentī* means they throw or fasten. *Saṃhārimehi* means by means of carts.

“With sacrificial posts that ought to be carried. It is said that formerly a certain king, while performing the Sammāpāsa sacrifice on the bank of the Sarassatī River, sank away as soon as a fissure opened in the earth.
Following him blindly, ignorant brahmins—thinking, “This is the path by which he went to heaven”—established the Sammāpāsa sacrifice there.
Therefore it is said: “From the place where he sank, etc.”
A *yāga* with a goat (*ayūpa*) lasts for few days; a *satrayāga*, however, which includes a bull (*sayūpa*), can be accomplished over many days.

The term *vāja* refers to ghee and honey prepared according to the formulas of the mantras. It refers to a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of seventeen items, such as gold, bullion, cows, and buffaloes.
Because there is no bolt (*aggaḷa*) on the doors of the innermost storerooms and other such places, it is called *niraggaḷa*. In that sacrifice, it is said, [one gives] one's own...
The inheritance is surrendered without remainder and without concealment. "Great undertakings" (*mahārambha*) refers to those involving the killing of many animals.
However, since it will be stated in the commentary, "Wherein various [animals] are slain," the meaning "great tasks" (*mahākicca*) is given;

whereas here, because it is said, "Great undertakings means goats, sheep, and so forth, by way of elaboration," the meaning "those involving the killing of many animals" is given. "Without undertaking" (*nirārambha*)...
The meaning here should also be understood according to the method already stated. "Anukula" means "following the family"; the sense is that it is "conforming to the family.
Therefore he said: "That which is the regular meal, etc.… [the rest as above] … the meaning.
The commentary on the Yañña Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Bandhana Sutta 121.
"This" refers to the statement beginning with "Here, venerable sir. "Those bhikkhus reported" is the syntactical connection.
"Among them" means among those people who had been caused to be bound by the king. "They reported the performance of good deeds" means they reported the practice of virtuous actions, not merely—
[This refers to] the fact that those men were caused to be bound. Now, in order to show that matter in detail, the passage beginning with "It is said of the king" was spoken.
*Aṭṭhavaṅko* means having eight corners. *Antogharacārino* means those who dwell within the inner apartments.
*Ukkaṭṭhe* means in battle. *Mantīsū* means among those who keep counsel secret. *Akutūhalaṃ* means self-restraint. *Piyaṃ* means that which is to be loved.
"When sweet food and drink have been consumed": this refers to when they have been eaten. "When a matter has arisen" means when a duty or obligation has come about.
"Firmly" means they do not speak [of it as firm], because it can be removed by the mere strength of the body. "Deeply dyed, dyed" means being exceedingly dyed, thus "dyed.
"By its essential nature" means by way of its essence, through the perception of its essential nature. "Carrying downwards" means having the habit of carrying away what is below.
He said: "It is that which drags one into the four states of misery. "Loose" means having a loose appearance, but it is not actually loose.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Difficult to release.
The commentary on the *Bandhana-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Second Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Sutta of the Seven Hair-matted Ascetics.
122. "In what is called the Eastern Park" means that it is designated as the Eastern Park (Pubbārāma) because it was established in the eastern direction of the city of Sāvatthī.
"Therein" refers to the brief expression "in the palace of Migāra’s mother.
This "graduated discourse" (anupubbikathā) now being spoken is a sequential account starting from the beginning. She made a request to be the foremost attendant of that Blessed One.
Seeing a certain female lay disciple, she desired that position for her. "Of Meṇḍaka’s son" means of the son of the merchant Meṇḍaka.
She placed her in the position of a mother, having recognized her helpfulness and her sense of reverence.

"In the palace built by her" refers to the palace built by that great lay disciple on a plot of ground measuring one *karīsa* at a cost of nine crores, after she had commissioned the great *latāpasādhana*, and which was adorned with a thousand chambers.
"Parūḷhakacchāti" means having the hair of the armpits grown long. "Kamaṇḍalughaṭikādiṃ" refers to the requisites of one gone forth, such as a water-pot and a small jar.
"Naggabhogganissirikānan" means of those who are naked, of those who are humpbacked, and of those who are lacking in splendor. For they are indeed naked because they are without clothes;

they are humpbacked because their bodies are deformed by practices such as the vow of nudity; and they are lacking in splendor because they are devoid of beauty. Having concealed what he himself had seen and heard...
"It would not be right for them to speak"—this is not the reason, because they were spies employed by the king.
However, if this were done, they might think, "He knows that there are other renunciants as well," and thus he acted with a deceitful mind;
this can be understood. For, being dissatisfied with that point, he said, "Moreover," and so forth.
“Kāsikacandana” means brilliantly shining sandalwood. It is said that, by way of its color, it is intensely radiant and luminous;
for that very purpose, they make it smoother. Therefore he said: “‘Kāsikacandana’ means smooth sandalwood.

“For the sake of color and fragrance” means both for the sake of the beauty of the color and for the sake of the state of being sweetly fragrant. “For the sake of color and fragrance” also means for the sake of coloring the skin.
And for the sake of fragrance. By the words "by a householder" and so forth, he shows that the Arahants are difficult to understand by one who dwells thus in negligence.
Showing that "association" here means approaching at the proper time, he said "by one who approaches. Even by one unrestrained in body and speech, there may be the appearance of restraint;
even by one with unguarded faculties, there may be the appearance of guarded faculties. [Thinking: "I shall encompass them."
“I shall investigate whether it is pure or not. “By one who is wise” means by one possessing the wisdom that examines ethical conduct (*sīla*).
He is unable to know because he does not maintain the intrinsic nature of the existing ethical conduct.
“By speaking” means by speaking back and forth; for he will say later, “In the case of some,” and so forth. “Noble expression” (*ariyavohāra*)...
