“Designation by way of what is seen, etc. refers to the verbal usage expressed as “seen,” “not seen,” and so forth.
Taking the cause of that [usage] alone, he says, “In this case, it is volition. This same method applies to ignoble designations as well;

for in the ultimate sense, truthful speech and the like, as well as false speech and the like, have the characteristic of volition. “Designation by way of convention” is so called because things are designated in various ways accordingly.
Thus he said: "O Great King, purity is to be known through common practice.

"The domain of knowledge" (*ñāṇathāma*) means the power of the qualities of knowledge, by which one completes urgent duties and tasks through such things as spontaneous presence of mind (*ṭhānuppattika-paṭibhāna*).
"Through discussion" (*saṃkathāya*) means through right discourse proceeding by way of investigating the meaning. "He leaps up" (*uppilavati*).

Because of their lightness of being. "Spies below" means those who move about at a low level. Regarding those who, having entered [among others], act for the purpose of testing the secrets of others, the designation "spies" (*ocaraka*) is used;
thus it is said, "for they are spies," and so forth.
"By color or shape" means either by color, or by shape, or by the excellence of color, or by the perfection of shape.
Or: "He is well-born and amiable; he is to be trusted"—this is the construction. "With a light glance" means with a limited vision, like a flash of lightning.
"With an article of requisites" means with an article that serves as a requisite for one who has gone forth.
"A copper half-māsaka" means a half-guñja-weight coin made of copper.
The commentary on the *Sattajaṭilasutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Pañcarājasutta*. 123.

"Forms" (*rūpa*) refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) designated as form. Although these are divided into many varieties by way of blue and so forth, they are nonetheless the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Because they do not transcend the state of being cognizable by the eye, he said: "the objective field of visible form, distinguished as blue, yellow, and so forth.

Since the word *to* (in *tadā*) has the same temporal meaning as the word *dā* (in *yadā*), he said: "*yato* means *yadā*" (when). It is "agreeable" (*manāpa*) because it pleases or increases the mind;
it is "delightful" (*manorama*). "The production of what is agreeable" means that which is cherished by the mind of that person, by virtue of its excellence.
The meaning is that it proceeds having made the ultimate limit its boundary.

"Pleasant to the person" (puggalamanāpa) means that, without considering the intrinsic nature of the object, it is called "agreeable" (iṭṭha) because of its state of being agreeable by way of the person alone. "Conventional designation" (sammuti) means a common appellation.
He says this because one grasps even what is contrary [to reality] as "pleasant to the person" due to the perversion of perception, taking it to be of another nature.
“That which is desirable and pleasing to one person... and so forth. Now, demonstrating this by way of what is cognizable by the tongue, he says, “To those living on the borderlands,” and so on.

“This is agreeable to a particular person” means that, just like the aforementioned object cognizable by the tongue, any other similar object that is grasped as agreeable by this or that particular person is called “agreeable to a person.”
The intention is that there is nothing in the world that, even when analyzed by the world through the act of seeing, could be grasped as something sweet once it has been analyzed.
Therefore he said, "But it must be shown after being analyzed.

Even for a divine aeon (*dibbakappa*)—that is, even for something comparable to what is included within the heavenly worlds—it appears unpleasant due to the lack of familiarity with sublime and exquisite objects.
But for those of intermediate capacity... [and so on] ...it should be analyzed according to how the agreeable appears as agreeable and the disagreeable appears as disagreeable.
Even there, showing that the definition of the desirable and the undesirable is to be understood in the absolute sense (*nippariyāyato*), he says: "And furthermore, this...
and so forth. And furthermore, this object which consists of the desirable and the undesirable, in the impulsions (*javana*) of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*)...
Because it generally proceeds by way of the unwholesome, the occurrence of the unwholesome alone is shown there with the words "it lusts and it hates.
However, its occurrence by way of the remaining sense-sphere [consciousness] is certainly possible as well;
for it proceeds toward what is not repulsive by way of a repulsive aspect, and toward what is repulsive by way of a non-repulsive aspect. Resultant consciousness is both desirable and undesirable.
One discerns that it is not possible to deceive the result (vipāka). For wholesome kamma is exclusively desirable, and unwholesome kamma is exclusively undesirable;
therefore, the resultant consciousness arising therein proceeds according to its own intrinsic nature.
As for what is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*—namely, "there is nothing called 'undesirable' born of wholesome kamma"—that is said only in this limited sense.
That, however, should be regarded as a mere illustration. By that [example], it might be conceded that even unwholesome karma-born beauty is desirable for certain beings;
but they say that what is born of wholesome karma is desirable for all.
For instance, the human form is unpleasant to some animals, such that they flee upon merely seeing it. And humans [find] the form of deities [unpleasant].
Seeing it, they are afraid; yet even for them, the resultant consciousness arises as a wholesome result (kusalavipāka) directed toward that form.
However, it should be understood that because they lack such merit, they find no delight therein.
Just as there is an absence of undesirable things born of wholesome karma, so too there must be said to be an absence of beautiful, desirable things born of unwholesome karma.
For even elephants and such beings, when born from unwholesome karma, are objects for the unwholesome result of human beings;
however, that which is born from wholesome karma and arises during the course of existence is an object for the wholesome result.

Because it is mixed with desirable objects, one can say that the small portion born from unwholesome karma will not be the cause for the arising of a predominant unwholesome result. Now, regarding that very same [point]:
The phrase beginning with "Even though" was stated in order to clarify the distinction between desirable and undesirable objects by way of karmic result (*vipāka*).

That [distinction] was stated for the purpose of classifying what is agreeable according to conventional usage (*sammuti*); however, it is not analyzed in that way here, which is why he said, "But the Blessed One," and so forth.
That lay follower is known as "Candanaṅgalika" because he was born in the village of Candanaṅgala, and as "Candanavilāsa."
"Of some": the construction is "inspiration arose for that lay follower. "Those kings, seeing [them] with their luster destroyed and their beauty lost"—this is the connection.
"Sprinkled with water" means consecrated with water. "Like embers" means like a pit of glowing coals. "At an early hour" means even before dawn.
"Not devoid of fragrance" because it was blooming at that very moment. "Such a statement" refers to a statement of this kind, namely, "you have covered [it]."
The commentary on the Pañcarājasutta is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Doṇapākasutta: 124.
Regarding the phrase "doṇapākakura," it is stated as "doṇapākaṃ kuraṃ" because the case ending has been elided in the presentation.
"Of a *doṇa*" means of four *āḷhakas*; the meaning is "of sixteen *nāḷīs*. "Suitable for that" means corresponding to that;
the meaning is "appropriate for the measure stated for it. "Previously" means on days prior to that day. "Powerful" means great.
"The fever of hunger" means caused by the indigestion of food. On both sides of this king, palm-leaf fans were held.

They fan him with pairs of palm-leaf fans. "A comfortable dwelling" means the state of dwelling in happiness obtained through moderation in eating; for one who knows the proper measure in food dwells in comfort.
Therefore he said: "For one who is moderate, sensations become slight; he ages slowly, preserving his life. "For one who is moderate" means for that person who is moderate;
the meaning is that there are no discordant sensations arising from the condition of having eaten.
"Gradually" (*saṇikaṃ*) means slowly and gently; the meaning is that it is free from danger. "It decays" (*jīrati*) means that the food consumed undergoes digestion.
"Guarding the life-span" (*āyupālayaṃ*) means protecting the life-force (*jīvita*) which is cessation and devoid of sensation.

Alternatively, "it decays gradually" means that such a person who knows the proper measure in eating, by virtue of moderation in food, decays slowly—that is, it takes a long time for it to reach digestion—while guarding his life.
Regarding the phrase "having mastered": in order to show how he mastered everything and how he subsequently practiced it, the words "together with the king," and so forth, were spoken.
The connection is made by bringing in the phrase: "you might take that much rice and a corresponding amount of curry.
"This is a man's portion" means this is the portion to be eaten by a man of middle size, namely, the measure of a *nāḷika* of boiled rice.
"Having polished the body" means having applied effort so that all feverish distress is stilled, as if the body were being scraped smooth and has attained a state of broadness.
It was said that "virtue is for the sake of the future life," but from where does this virtue come? To answer this, he says "in food," and so forth.
"It becomes a factor of virtue" means it becomes one part, one portion, of the fourfold purification of virtue (*cātupārisuddhisīla*).
The commentary on the Doṇapāka Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the First Saṅgāma Sutta: 125.
One who acts and conducts herself by means of wisdom is called *Vedehī*; she was the sister of the King of Kosala and the mother of Ajātasattu. She...

It is said that they are by nature possessed of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). Therefore, it is called "a synonym for the wise. It is "fourfold" (*caturaṅginī*) because it possesses four factors.

"Between the two kingdoms" refers to the interval between the kingdom of Kāsī and the kingdom of Magadha; however, that village belonged to the kingdom of Kāsī. "Evil ones" (*pāpā*) means those of base and inferior conduct.
*Metti* is so called because one is affectionate (*mejjati*) and fond (*siniyhati*) [of them]; those in whom this exists are "friends" (*mittā*). Together with...

They go together and proceed together, thus they are "companions" (*sahāya*). "Well-bent" (*sampavaṅka*) means thoroughly inclined. Having seen a cause for victory, he spoke; for it was said by way of delimiting time:
"Today, during this night, he lies in suffering. "The destruction of enemies" refers to when there is a person who is an enemy;
thus he said, "he encounters a person who is an enemy."
The commentary on the First Saṅgāma Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Second Saṅgāma Sutta: 126.
Having said, "Listen," there is an ellipsis of the word "having spoken. "It serves" means it is possible; "it is capable" means it is able to be done.
It is possible. Regarding the phrase "and when others," he says "when others" because the word *ca* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*).

"They plunder" means they bring about destruction or seizure. "He is plundered" means that because one who has plundered another's property does not own it, he himself is plundered by another—just as if he were experiencing the karmic fruit in this very life—and suffers the loss of wealth.
He encounters [misfortune]. For he thinks, "This is the cause"; thus, he regards his own evil deed as a cause that brings him benefit.
A victorious person, thinking "I am winning this," also meets with defeat because of it. "One who strikes" refers to the ripening of evil karma.
"By the turning away of karma" means by the cessation of karma, having obtained an opportunity through the acquisition of conditions.
The meaning is: by means of karma that has been turned back and made to disappear.
The commentary on the Second Saṅgāma Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Mallikā Sutta.

127. "Ekacca" means the wise ones who possess discernment (*paññā*). "Seyya" means excellent. He says, "having parents as deities" (*sassudeva*), because for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukhatthaṃ*), the syllable *sa* of the word *sasura* has been elided.
Thus, it means "those who have their mother and father as deities. "The elders of the quarters" (*disājeṭṭhaka*):

he refers to the world by way of the "elders" in all four directions. "Of such a kind" (*tādisāya*) means by a conduct characterized by qualities such as intelligence (*medhāvitā*). "By a good wife" (*subhariyāya*).
The meaning is: "to a beautiful woman who has become like a fertile field.
The commentary on the Mallikā Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Appamāda Sutta.
128. *Samadhiggayha* means having grasped thoroughly and exceedingly, having grasped specifically by way of the proper method (*ñāya*).
*Kārāpaka-appamāda* is the diligence that sets the three bases of meritorious action into motion. *Samavadhāna* means inclusion within the interior.
*Upakkhepa* means the state of being thrown in, not remaining outside. Like the remaining groups of terms, the [remaining] phenomena are included because they possess specific locations.
They converge upon diligence because it is all-inclusive. Diligence is the foremost, the best, and the greatest among all other states.
"In the sense of being a means of acquisition" means by way of being the cause for attainment. "Even though it is mundane" means even though it belongs to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
For what is intended here is the diligence that occurs in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) leading to the sublime (*mahaggata*) and the unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
The construction is: "The wise praise [it]. Regarding the state of diligence being praiseworthy, he states the reason with the words "these," etc., because it must be practiced exclusively.
In this construction, the word "in meritorious deeds" is connected with the word "diligent. Since the wise praise diligence, and since one is diligent in meritorious deeds...
One attains both goals; therefore, one who aspires for long life and the rest must practice heedfulness alone.
According to the second interpretation, however, the wise praise heedfulness. Where? In the performance of meritorious deeds. Why?

Because of the passage beginning with "one who is heedful," etc. Thus he said: "Because... [is] the goal. The attainment of goals refers to the attainment of welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth.
The commentary on the *Appamāda-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Kalyāṇamitta-sutta*: 129.
One who possesses a friend that is "good" (*kalyāṇa*)—meaning a friend endowed with qualities such as virtue—is a "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*); this is the teaching concerning him.

It is called "well-expounded" specifically because of the good friend, since one accomplishes the duty that must be done after hearing it. Therefore he said, "it fulfills the purpose. "Of the other" means of the evil friend.
"By that" means by the fulfillment of the purpose. "This" refers to this statement: "And that indeed belongs to one with a good friend.
"The Dhamma of the teaching" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma); for that is to be obtained directly from a good friend.
Others, by means of that very support and through their own individual personal efforts, obtain a virtuous friend; such is the meaning to be understood.
For this teaching has come down according to the case of the *śrāvaka* and the *bodhisattva*. Indeed, for the other types of *bodhisattvas*, there is no need for instruction from another.
"Half of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) comes from a virtuous friend" means that for one leading the holy life, half of its merit is obtained from a virtuous friend.
"Half by one's own personal effort" means that for one who applies the other half of knowledge through one's own personal exertion (*purisakāra*).

This matter is well known in the world as well: "Half of the state of possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijjatā*) is to be obtained from the teacher, and half is to be obtained by one's own personal effort.
Therefore, the Elder thought in that way. "Without remainder" means completely. "From that" means from the good friend (*kalyāṇamitta*).
"It comes as a half" means that the quality of a half approaches one who is practicing. "By many men":

there is no separation or distinction because it is impossible to distinguish the meaning when it is gathered together. "This" refers to the meaning being established through the voice of another, the first person, and personal effort.
"So much" means such a portion. If it cannot be obtained, then why [is it said] "a half"?
He said, "By means of good friendship," and so forth. It is not possible to obtain [the factors] among right view and the rest.
Since they cannot be accomplished merely through the voice of another, the whole [set] is not possible;

however, it is stated as "the whole indeed" for the purpose of illustrating their status as primary causes. "The cause for obtaining the prior stage" means the reason to be obtained in the prior stage.

Because nothing further or more distinguished can be attained without the instruction of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*). "In the ultimate sense" (*atthato*) means from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramatthato*).

Having stated, "The spiritual friend... [etc. ...the four aggregates," the meaning is "having heard. Since those qualities, such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, are included within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), he says:
"They are indeed called the aggregate of mental formations as well."
*Māhevaṃ* is a compound (*mā aha evaṃ*); *aha* is a mere particle, and *mā* is a particle used for prohibition. Therefore he said, "Do not speak thus.
When the Blessed One said, "Do not speak thus, Ānanda," it was at this point that the Dhamma-keeper of the storehouse [thought]:
"For one such as you, Ānanda, who cultivates the qualities of a spiritual friend, it is not fitting to speak in such an untruthful manner."
Showing that the refutation is appropriate by way of praising his qualities as they truly are, he said, "One who is learned," and so forth.
The connection is: "The Blessed One spoke this [word]"; "this" refers to this statement. Here, the word *hi* has the sense of a reason;

by it, the cause for that refutation—namely, "lest [it be otherwise]"—is illuminated, though not stated in its own form. This is shown by the passage beginning with, "For one who has a virtuous friend," and so on.
But since that has been shown according to its specific form, he said: “Now... [etc.]... he states the beginning.
“To be expected” (pāṭikaṅkhitabba) means to be expected in the sense of being desired, not by way of a sign for expectation; thus he said: “The meaning is ‘inevitably occurring.
“Here” (idha) is a term containing an internal restriction; the meaning is “right here. For it is only in this very teaching (sāsana) that there is the cultivation of the Noble Path.
"Not elsewhere" means only in the initial terms; that is, only in the terms such as "right view" (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) and so forth, which are stated at the very beginning of each respective sentence.
"Characterized by right seeing" means having the essential nature of seeing correctly by way of the full understanding and clear realization of the four noble truths.
"Characterized by right placing" means [placing] the associated mental states upon the object known as Nibbāna.
Its intrinsic nature is that of right application. Regarding "having the characteristic of right embracing":
because false speech and so forth have the function of deceiving and the like, they are harsh and non-embracing; right speech, as their opposite, has an embracing nature.
It embraces associated states through its smoothness, and it embraces the person who hears the well-spoken words as a condition for right speech; thus, it has the characteristic of right embracing.

Just as a bodily action (kāyikakiriyā) gives rise to something that is to be done and itself constitutes an arising or an effort, so too the joy of abstinence (viratipīti) termed right action (sammākammanta) should be understood as having the characteristic of giving rise [to other states].
Alternatively, "giving rise" (samuṭṭhāpana) is the lifting up of associated mental factors, like the lifting of a burden by a bodily action. Of a living being...
It is the purity and cleansing of either the associated states, the maintenance of life, or the livelihood itself.

Right effort has the characteristic of right exertion, being the nature of uplifting the associated states so that, just as there is the increase of the attainment of the meaning of abandoning arisen faults through the Dhamma and the non-arising [of new ones], so too there is the increase of the attainment of the meaning of abandoning and non-arising through the Dhamma.
Furthermore, it is the grasping of the body, feelings, mind, and mental objects, and the abandoning of the graspings of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self.
Right mindfulness has the characteristic of being correctly established by way of dispelling [distractions].
Right concentration has the characteristic of correct concentrating, for its nature is the making of one-pointedness of the associated states.
There are three functions: with respect to opposing states, objective states, and associated states, [these functions] occur in one and the same moment.
These are the specific modes of activity occurring at that moment. Now, in order to show them according to their actual nature, the passage beginning with “namely” (*seyyathidaṃ*) was stated.
By the word “together” (*sahidha*), it is shown whether the defilements mentioned as “others” are identical in function (*ekaṭṭhā*) or not identical in function (*anekaṭṭhā*) with wrong view.

One abandons [them], and having abandoned them, one penetrates [the truth]. Regarding “cessation” (*nirodha*): one takes *nibbāna* as the object and penetrates it through the penetration of realization (*sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha*).
Showing that the path factors are not only to be understood in the manner already stated, but also by another method, he said, "Moreover," and so forth.
They are "of different moments" because they arise again and again; "of different objects" because they consist of the contemplation of impermanence and so on;
"of one moment" because they arise all at once; and "of one object" because their domain is Nibbāna. Thus they receive four names.

It receives three names by way of its occurrence through the full understanding of realization (*pariññābhisamaya*) and so forth. It receives these three names by way of its occurrence through the abandoning of sensual intention (*kāmasaṅkappa*) and the rest; for it acquires these three names precisely by way of the abandoning of their opposites. This same method applies to the others as well.

They are both abstinences (*virati*) and volitions (*cetanā*), because they occur by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) in the preliminary stage; however, at the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*), they are exclusively abstinences.
Because the function of the path is the eradication of opposites. For volition (cetanā) is not the intrinsic nature of the path.
By way of the four right efforts and the four foundations of mindfulness, it receives four names because of the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and the increase of wholesome states.
"In the prior stage as well as at the moment of the path" means that just as in the prior stage by way of the first jhāna and so forth...
It is manifold. The same applies at the moment of the path (magga).

For not even a single instance of path-concentration receives the names of first-jhāna concentration and so forth, because—unlike right view and the other factors—it lacks differentiation by way of function. Therefore he said: “At the moment of the path, it is simply right concentration.
The connection is: “having known, what is to be known. Growth means expansion, increase, and repeated arising.
He said: "It generates again and again. "Produces" (*abhinibbattetī*) means it produces while causing [the result] to increase. "Seclusion" (*vivittatā*) is the state of being secluded.

For that which is to be secluded is secluded from what is to be separated; and that which stands having been secluded—both of these are here called "seclusion" (*vivittatā*) by way of their commonality as a state of being secluded.
Among those two, the former is so called because it is being secluded from what is to be separated.
The collection of phenomena (dhammasamūha) that possesses the activity of seclusion is understood as "seclusion" by virtue of that very activity of seclusion;
the other [type of seclusion] is so called because its intrinsic nature is entirely secluded from that [defilement].

In this context, the mass of phenomena in which right view arises occurs only by depending on that which is designated as "seclusion," precisely because it is being secluded in the manner already described.
But the other [type] lacks that inclination toward and taking as an object; thus it is said, "dependent on seclusion" or "based on seclusion.
Or, just as jhāna that occurs by way of seclusion is called "born of seclusion," so too right view that occurs by way of seclusion should be understood as "dependent on seclusion.
And this dependence refers to the paths and fruits by way of insight and the path.
It should be understood that even though there is no temporal sequence of "before and after" among them, in the context of the term *paṭiccasamuppāda*,

there can exist a development based on a single undifferentiated dharma-substratum, just as there is the arising of conditions. Having stated its dependence on the seclusion of partial suppression (*tadaṅga-viveka*), eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*), and escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*),
its non-mention of dependence on the seclusion of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-viveka*) is because it is being spoken of in terms of the cultivation of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga-bhāvanā*).
For one who has developed the path, those states which are yet to be realized—namely, their function—is seclusion by way of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-viveka*).
By way of aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*) means: by way of the great aspiration, "I shall realize Nibbāna.

For even though at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*) the mind has conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as its object, once one has clearly seen the danger in conditioned phenomena, the mind inclines toward Nibbāna, which is their opposite; thus it is by way of aspiration.
It is dependent on seclusion as an escape, like a person overcome by heat whose mind inclines toward coolness.

Some, however, say: "Just as there is dependence on seclusion as an escape according to its intrinsic nature and according to one's inclination, so too there may be dependence on seclusion as subsiding.
For to the same extent that there is an inclination toward Nibbāna, there may also be an inclination toward the fruit.
“May I indeed attain and dwell in that base”—this is because of the cultivation of such an aspiration.
Since the cessation of lust is, in meaning, not distinct from the seclusion intended here, just as it is from the discipline of abandonment (*pahānavinaya*), it is therefore said:
“This same method applies to those based on dispassion (*virāga*) and so forth. Thus he says: “For dispassion and the rest have seclusion as their very meaning.”
The word *vossagga* has the sense of relinquishment and the sense of launching forth; thus, the twofold nature of relinquishment is stated.
For relinquishing (*vossajjana*) consists of both abandoning and proceeding without apprehension due to a state of letting go.

Therefore, at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), there is relinquishment through the factor of specific counteraction (*tadaṅga-vasena*), and at the moment of the Path (*magga*), there is relinquishment through total eradication (*samuccheda-vasena*) of the opposing side. Likewise, at the moment of insight...
Relinquishment (*vossagga*) should be understood as the state of having abandoned its own inherent nature by inclining toward that [object] and by taking it as an object at the moment of the Path.
For this very reason, it is said: "In this context, relinquishment is abandonment" and so forth. "This right view" refers to right view spoken of in a mixed sense.

"In the manner already described" means by way of abandoning through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*) and abandoning by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*), and by way of inclining toward that and taking it as an object.
Since the meaning of "resting" (*vossagga*) was already stated previously, he says, "by the entire phrase.
"Transforming" refers to the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), while "transformed" refers to the moment of the path (*magga*). Here, "transformation" means ripening;
thus he says, "ripening and fully ripened. And this ripening consists in the ability to abandon the defilements, which is obtained through the power gained by cultivation (*āsevana*).
The state of being sharp and pungent [refers to the mind] in order to leap into Nibbāna. Therefore he said, "This," and so forth.
"This method" means that this method which was stated regarding right view in the passage beginning with "dependent on seclusion" applies to the remaining factors as well, such as right intention;

the meaning is that it should be applied there in the same way. "Dependent upon" (paṭicca) means relying upon. "Having the nature of birth" (jātisabhāvā) means having the nature of arising. "Entire" (sakalo) means...
"Without remainder" means "all. No path whatsoever can exist as having a remainder;
for when the lower path has arisen, the higher one is indeed said to have arisen, because it arises immediately thereafter. "In the sense of relinquishment" means in the sense of utterance.
"They describe" means they expand upon [it] by way of describing its qualities.
The commentary on the *Kalyāṇamitta Sutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the First *Aputtaka Sutta*. 130.
The word *diva* is synonymous with *divasa* (day), just like the word *divā*; therefore, when the word *diva* is used as a qualifying attribute, it refers to the day.
He said, “During the day of the day,” and so forth, to illuminate a specific meaning. *Saṃ* means wealth;
its master is *sampati*, the owner of wealth. Because it brings about his welfare, it is called *sāpateyya*; thus he said, “*Sāpateyya* means wealth.
Because the goods made and unmade in his house were exceedingly numerous, the King, struck with amazement, said, “What more can be said?”
*Kāḷaloha* is the name for iron ore. They also set out gold and other materials in the forms of tortoises and so forth.
*Sakuṇḍakabhatta* is cooked rice mixed with either *sakuṇḍas* (small grains) or *sathusas* (thick gruel). *Bilaṅga* refers to grain-sour; it is also called *āranāla*.
That which has this as its second [ingredient] is called *bilaṅgadutiya*. For that is called *kañjika* because it is produced from sour gruel (*kañji*).
“Three-flap clothing” (*tipakkhavasana*) refers to a lower garment made from three pieces of cloth. Thus he said: “Three... [etc. ...lower garment.
An inferior person who is base is called a “worthless person” (*asappurisa*); thus he said: “a lowly man.

Because it is the point of entry through its being produced by karma, the fruit is called “foremost”; because its peak points upward due to having gone to a higher plane, it is “upward-pointing” (*uddhaggika*).
“Dakkhiṇā” means giving. “Sagga” refers to existence as rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (kāmabhava);
because it causes one to be born there, it is said to be “conducive to heaven” (saggassa hitā). “Tatrupapattijananato” means because it generates rebirth there;
the meaning is because it produces it. “Setodakā” is that which has white water. That by which [an object] is seen more clearly in a particular state is [the cause].
To show this, he said: "at the place where the waves have broken. Because it is a place easy to cross and free from defects such as mud, it is a beautiful landing-place (*tittha*).

"Not being drunk" means that water not being consumed by anyone. "One who performs the duty to be performed by oneself" means one who carries out the duties consisting of the tasks to be done by oneself, both by way of consumption and by way of gathering what is to be gathered.
And the meaning is "one who enjoins. "One who performs wholesome deeds" means one who performs the merit that ought to be performed by oneself.
The commentary on the first *Aputtaka-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the second *Aputtaka-sutta*.
131. Regarding the phrase "with alms-food" (*piṇḍapātena*), this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*).
It means "he joined it with that," or "he provided it along with it"; thus he said, "He joined [it] together with alms-food; the meaning is that he gave the alms-food.
It was stated, "having eaten choice food," but in the Pāḷi it says, "he eats broken rice with sour gruel as a side dish. This refers to what was generally practiced at that time.
It should be understood that this has been said. Now, the statement, "Give this to some ascetic or brahmin," had never been heard before;

however, because those known as paccekabuddhas have indeed become well-known in the world through the power of their own virtues, it was for this reason that the merchant’s wife thought, "Not to just anyone," and so forth.
For indeed, even when giving to them, people generally give with due respect and mostly only what is excellent.

He struck his own nostril by means of his supernatural power. Because of his greed, being unable to restrain or control his mind with the thought, "Oh, may I have much grain," he spoke the words beginning with "This is better" in order to show the manner in which remorse had arisen. [He said: "The alms-food of this ascetic..."
For one who says, "Give [me]," the accomplishment of the purpose does not occur by means of a single cognitive process (*javanavīthi*) alone.
Rather, there is both a cognitive process that occurs at the beginning and one that occurs in the middle; it is with reference to this that he said, "by way of the prior and subsequent volitions.
Regarding the statement, "A single volition does not give two rebirths," the definitive conclusion is to be understood by way of the Sāketa question.
It is "ancient" because it was performed earlier and prior to the fourteen types of volition.
It is called "appropriation" (*pariggaha*) because one grasps it; thus he says, "the appropriated object. They live by following and depending upon [it], thus they are "dependents.
"All this" refers to all this aforementioned object of appropriation, such as wealth, grain, and so forth. "Leading to being laid down" means...
"Of that which leads to being cast off. He said "of the nature of being cast off" because it possesses the essential quality of being cast off.
He said "of the very nature of being abandoned" because "that which must be left behind" is the meaning here.
The commentary on the second *Aputtaka-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. The Third Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Persons (*Puggala-sutta*).
132. “Born into a low family,” and so forth: it is called *tama* (darkness) because it passes beyond (*atīti*) manifestation due to its state of non-manifestation;

one who is possessed of that *tama* is called a person of darkness (*tamapuggala*). Due to that association, the designation for the person is applied to the quality itself, just as one is called "miserly" due to the association with miserliness (*macchara-yogato maccharo*).
Therefore, *tama* means one who has become dark through the state of non-manifestation, having become like darkness; this is the state of being darkness (*andhakārattaṃ*).

The meaning is "has reached. That which has darkness as its very characteristic, and whose course, destination, and conclusion proceed from that [darkness] in succession, is "one for whom darkness is the final resort" (*tamaparāyaṇo*);

or the meaning is "one who has reached the state of having darkness as the final resort. By the term "darkness" used here according to the method [of exposition], only the darkness of the aggregates (*khandhatama*) is spoken of, not the darkness of physical gloom.
And the "darkness of the aggregates" should be understood as the mere occurrence of the aggregates when they are devoid of attainment (*sampatti*).
“Born into a high family,” and so forth—it is called *joti* because it shines (*joteti*) by way of making things manifest. One who is endowed with that *joti* is thus [called] *jotimā*;
all such [terms] are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. The other two refers to the two types of persons:

*jotitama-parāyaṇo* (one whose ultimate destination is darkness) and *jotijoti-parāyaṇo* (one whose ultimate destination is light). Those who make baskets and the like from bamboo, rattan, and so forth, are *vilīvakārakā*. Those who kill deer, fish, and so on for the sake of hunting are *nesādā*, namely, hunters, fishermen, and the like.
Because they kill with leather on chariots, they are called *rathakārā* (chariot-makers) and *cammakārā* (leather-workers). "Pu" is a name for dung;
those who remove it—that is, take it away—are *pukkusā*, meaning flower-scavengers. "Dubbaṇṇo" means ugly or misshapen. "Okoṭimako" means one who is at the bottom end due to a lack of height;
the meaning is "short-bodied. Therefore he said, "a *lakuṇḍaka*. He moves (*ḍeti*) like a *laku*—that is, like a small jar.
He is called *lakuṇḍaka* because he is short. He is called *kāṇa* because his eye closes; as for that closing of his eye, it may be by one eye or by both, hence it is said:
"blind in one eye or blind in both eyes. *Kuṇa* means crookedness, namely a deficiency of the hand;
one who has this is *kuṇī*. One with a deficiency of the feet is called *khañja*. [The term refers to] the lower part of the body of the physical frame.

“One whose side or portion is struck” (*pakkhahata*) means one who has been struck in a part. Therefore, he said “a cripple. That which is to be brought or led to a lamp or a lighting is “lamp-fuel” (*padīpeyya*);
it refers to accessories such as oil-jars and so forth. “Stated” means stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

“Failure of arrival” (*āgamanavipatti*) refers to a failure by way of the place of arrival, based on the derivation that “arrival is here. “Failure of requisites already arisen” (*pubbuppannapaccayavipatti*)...

Failure by way of the conditions present at birth: for his parents, being outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) and so forth by nature, are the conditions present at his first arising, or the conditions for that first arising; these very factors constitute his failure, not his success.
"Failure of conditions during life" means failure of the conditions for happiness during one's lifetime. Even someone born into such a low family might be endowed with great wealth.
But this person is unfortunate and ill-favored. "Failure in the means of livelihood" refers to failure by way of the means of subsistence.

For he lacks the skills such as elephant-training that serve as the means for maintaining a livelihood with ease; instead, he maintains his life by performing work such as clearing away flowers or grinding stones.
Therefore, it is said: "in a life of hardship. "Failure of personal existence" refers to failure of the physical basis (upadhi).

The "conjunction of the causes of suffering" is the coming together of conditions for the arising of bodily and mental suffering. The "failure of the causes of happiness" is the loss of favorable conditions for happiness.
The "failure of enjoyment" is the destruction or non-attainment of the happiness derived from enjoyment.
Both light and the state of being destined for light constitute the bright side (the waxing phase).
“By means of the ten bases of abuse” is a defining statement, just as in the expression, “If they are ill, this medicine must be given.
Therefore, the meaning is: he reviles him by means of any one of those ten bases of abuse.
“With a one-pointed mind” means with a concentrated mind due to the desire to give the gift.
The commentary on the *Puggalasutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Ayyikāsutta* 133.
*Jarājiṇṇā* means decayed by old age. By this, he expresses that the peak of manifest old age has been reached. *Vayovuḍḍhā*...
“Advanced in age”: by this, he speaks of the onset and progression of the final stage of life. “Great in birth” means having attained greatness by birth.
“Having passed a long time” means having gone beyond two or three royal successions.

Although the word *vaya* (age) is a general term, because it occurs in proximity to the word *jiṇṇa* (old/decayed), it refers specifically to the final stage of life; thus he says, “having reached the final stage of life. “Aunt” (*ayyikā*).
He speaks with reference to the maternal grandmother. He says "the elephant-treasure" because the elephant itself is a treasure; he says "worth a hundred thousand," and so forth.

"All those" refers to the pottery vessels. Showing the measure of the continuum of the seven [beings] along with those [vessels], he says "among them," and so forth; that is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the *Ayyikāsutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Issattasutta*. 135.
Regarding the phrase "the origin of the matter": what is the origin of this matter here? It is [the occasion] when the sectarians [challenged] the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
And there was the striving for non-gain and ill-repute. To show this in detail, it is said: "It is said that of the Blessed One," and so forth.

Just as a great twin-cloud might arise in all directions and produce a great flood, so too did all the perfections (pāramīs), as if gathered together with the thought, "We shall give our fruition in this very existence," produce a great flood of gain and honor.

Then, from here and there, Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and others, with food, drink, vehicles, clothing, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and so forth in their hands, arrived and sought out the Blessed One, asking, "Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of Gods, the Bull among Men, the Lord of the World?
Even after bringing provisions by means of hundreds of carts, they were unable to find space, for the area extending for a league all around was filled with the ruts of the carts.
They stand pressing against the yoke of the cart and follow along, like the Brahmins of Andhakavinda and others.
All this should be understood according to the method set forth in various sections of the Khandhaka and the Suttas.
Just as it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus. As it is said: "At that time, the Blessed One was honored..."
“...honored, esteemed, revered, and venerated, receiving robes... [and so on] ...requisites;

and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as well,” and likewise: “Cunda, as far as any Saṅgha or group has arisen in the world today, Cunda, I do not see any other single Saṅgha or single group that has attained such a pinnacle of gain and a pinnacle of fame as this.”
"Cunda, [this is] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. "Thus" means in the manner now being described. "Conciliation" (*nijjhatti*) means persuasion (*saññatti*). "This" refers to the discourse.
It is improper to ask in this way because the talk of the non-Buddhist sectarians has been presented in the assembly of the great multitude.
That [gift] should be given; for even when giving with mere confidence of heart (*cittappasāda*), merit increases. The intention is that it was announced by himself.
"Bhagavāti" is the Teacher’s address. "Citta" means that which proceeds according to its conditions;
[the Nigaṇṭhas... [etc. "...is clear; the intention is 'of one who is clear'. Previously, the place where the gift should be given was asked about without distinction;
now, he speaks of the specific quality of the recipient (*dakṣiṇeyya*) that makes that gift bear great fruit: "Another thing was first asked by you..."
“...another later. Consider this: the intention is that you should bring the latter together with the former.
Indeed, it is my own burden to provide the explanation for the question asked. “Arrayed together” means gathered as a mass from one side by way of an army;
thus he said, “become a heap. “Untrained” refers to [one who has not practiced] the art of archery for seven or eight years.
"Trained": although someone may have trained in the art of archery, they might not yet be one who has mastered the hand;
however, this person is not untrained, nor is he one who has not mastered the hand—the state of shooting arrow after arrow [is such that] the fist remains bound within the fathom-length range.
"Upon heaps of grass, heaps of clay, etc.": by the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes heaps of sand, heaps of gravel, wooden planks, iron clubs, and so forth. "One who has not practiced" means:
He has not practiced in their presence in the sense of piercing [the truth]. Having approached kings, royal ministers, and so forth, he has not performed service (*upāsana*);
thus, he is one "who has not performed service" (*akatūpāsano*). Because of his lack of training and so on, or due to a state of timidity, his body trembles, shakes, and is seized with fear;
thus he is "trembling" (*chambhī*), which is why it is said: "with a quivering body" (*pavedhitakāyo*).
Because it is intended in the sense of being worthy of offerings, he said, "Sensual desire is abandoned by the path of arahantship.

Because absolute abandonment is intended, remorse (kukkucca) is abandoned by the third [path] along with its association with aversion (paṭigha). It belongs to one who is beyond training (asekkha), thus it is "of the beyond-training" (asekkha);
this refers to the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). This does not refer exclusively to the virtue of the highest fruit, but rather to whatever [virtue] there may be.
Virtue that occurs in the continuum of one beyond training (asekkha) is intended as supramundane alone, because it is born of the training;

the same applies to the aggregate of liberation. Alternatively, a "learner" (sekkha) is so called because this [virtue] belongs to him, or because he trains himself since his training is not yet completed.
The aggregate of virtue pertains to the four paths and the first three fruits. It is excluded from the higher [stages] because there is nothing further to be trained in.
One who is beyond training (*asekkha*). One who has reached growth while still in training (*sekkha*) is called "one beyond training.

While it might be said that the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) constitutes the highest fruit, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), the meaning is stated in that way because the virtue of one practicing insight (*vipassaka*) is intended. "In all instances" refers to the passages beginning with "by one beyond training," and so forth.
And here, just as the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom are intended as mixed together, so too are the aggregate of liberation (*vimuttikkhandha*).
Liberation through its factors (*tadaṅgavimutti*) and others should also be understood;
it is not only liberation through subsiding (*paṭippassaddhivimutti*). Regarding the statement "the craft of archery," he says this because that craft by which one becomes an archer is "archery.
Or, regarding the wind element by virtue of which the body gains strength, he says "strength is the wind element" with reference to that condition for power.
For the element that prevents uneven activity by means of even activity is called "strength" (*bala*); there is no other kind of strength apart from that.
Since only the Arahant is absolutely gentle (*sorata*), his state is "gentleness" (*soracca*);

thus it is said: "Gentleness is Arahantship. These two refers to these two qualities: patience (*khanti*) and gentleness (*soracca*). A *papā* is a place where people drink water; anyone [who goes there]...
He said, "whatever water reservoirs there are, such as square ponds and so forth," meaning any place where water is kept for drinking.
"Crossings" (*saṅkamanāni*) are those by which one moves across or traverses bodies of water, such as bridges and the like.

Herein, one should construct a bridge in a place suitable for building a bridge, a walkway (*caṅkama*) in a place suitable for constructing a walkway, and a path in a place suitable for making a path. This is the meaning here.
This is the intended meaning. Therefore, he said, "The fifties," and so forth.
"The conduct of the alms-round" refers to the practice of the observances that are beneficial to the Noble Ones (*ariya*).

By the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "giving even," he shows this meaning: that even when giving to anyone at all, including one whose taints (*āsava*) have not been exhausted, it must be done with a mind of serene confidence, having faith in the fruit of kamma.
Because it ought to be given. "They thunder"—this is a demonstration of its state as a great cloud;
for that which pours down a great rain does so while thundering and emitting garlands of lightning. "Having prepared and assembled"—that is, having gathered together various kinds of solid food.
Therefore he said, "having made a heap."
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, "scattering" (*pakiraṇa*) can also mean "dispersing" (*vikiraṇa*); thus he says, "he scatters" (*vikirati*).
Alternatively, by saying "he gives a gift as if scattering," he shows that one performs great giving not only after searching for a field of merit, but also within the field of compassion.
By this term "he scatters," the Blessed One refers to the doctrine of the non-Buddhist teachers mentioned in the introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
The state of being unopposed is also illuminated. "Streams of merit" means streams consisting of merit, floods of merit.
"Moistening" means making something smooth and supple even with a thick stream of moisture. "Wetting" means bringing it to a state of dampness.
Just as this stream of merit moistens, fills, and floods the interior of the giver, so too does it moisten the interior of the recipients.
It fulfills and satisfies. For this very reason it was said: “Giving, one becomes dear; many resort to one,” and so forth.
Even though this is so, because it was stated that “the rain falls upon the giver,” the Commentary says “he feels affection” specifically from the perspective of the donor.
Alternatively, since the arising of affection in the recipient is dependent upon material gifts, it is stated specifically from the perspective of the donor.
The commentary on the *Issattasutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Pabbatūpamasutta* (The Simile of the Mountain) 136.
“Khattiyas” refers to those who have received consecration (*abhiseka*). “Arrogance of power” is the lust for sensual pleasures. [This arises] from the vastness of the circle of the earth.
“Following those who dwell there”—this entire statement is a description of the causes for the easy accomplishment of whatever royal business is desired.
To show in detail the kind of royal business for which he had become diligent, it was said, “It is said that he...,” and so forth.
“Intervening journeys” means intervening journeys between three continuous journeys. “The thieves thought... [End of excerpt].
A certain internal official, having offended the king, was wandering about committing theft with a retinue of five hundred men; it was with reference to them that this was said. The construction is:
"If I were to say, 'What you have done is improper'... "In the head monastery" (*dhuravihāre*) means in the monastery that serves as the head of the city, just as the pole is the head of a chariot.
"To stand firm" (*santhambhitum*) means to present oneself through a state of confidence. "One who is trustworthy" (*saddhāyiko*).
It is to be believed by means of faith; the meaning is "one who is to be trusted. Therefore he said, "to be believed. "Trustworthy" means one who is to be relied upon.
"Like the sky" refers to its broadness. "Grinding down" means crushing. "Grinding what is to be made fine" means grinding it exceedingly finely, like a small millstone grinding [grain].

"Practicing the Dhamma" (*dhammacariyā*) means that even disregarding one's own burning head and clothing, one must practice correctly alone, because only through that does one find a firm footing in the next world. "I declare" (*ācikkhāmi*) means I speak;

and in speaking, I cause the King to understand that matter exactly as it is. "Success" (*nipphatti*) is the accomplishment of the purpose to be achieved through battle. "He binds" (*visinoti*) means he fetters.

"Object" (*visaya*) means that by which the intended thought is directed; it is the state of capability. "Endowed with spells" (*mantasampannā*) means those who possess the king’s secret incantations.
"Great ministers" (*mahāmaccā*) refers to ministerial officials who, like Mahosadha and others, are experts in the science of political ethics (*nīti*).
"To win over" (*upalāpetuṃ*) means to gather [them] among others for the purpose of creating dissension.
"Only two mountains" means that only those resembling mountains were taken. "In the *Rājovāda*" refers to the *Rājovāda Sutta*.

"Has indeed come to its true state" means it has attained its appropriate condition. "Plundering": here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning. "Calamity" (*vipatti*) means destruction, such as the loss of wealth and so forth.
It is not possible to conquer old age and death through elephant battles and the like, because they are outside the domain of a living being. But by which...
The Blessed One said, "One should establish [them] in the Buddha... and so forth, showing that it is possible to conquer [suffering].
For faith established in the Triple Gem—having taken root and become firmly grounded—is absolutely for the sake of victory over aging and death. Therefore he said, "Therefore, O faithful one.
The commentary on the Mountain Simile Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
The Elucidation of the Obscure Points in the Commentary on the Kosala Saṃyutta of the *Sāratthappakāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, is completed.
4. Connected Discourses on Māra 1.
First Chapter 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Ascetic Practices (Tapokamma-sutta)
137. Near Uruvelā is the village of Uruvelagāma. Because he perfectly awakens to all phenomena by facing toward that village of Uruvelā, it is called *abhisambodhi*;
this is omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). And because he is endowed with that, the Blessed One is called "the Fully Awakened One" (*abhisambuddha*).
Of his forty-five years, the first fifteen years were the period of the First Awakening.
However, since what is intended here is specifically the period within seven days, he said: "Having attained full enlightenment, [he thought] 'within these very seven days.
Because it is difficult for others to perform due to its lack of ease, one who performs such a thing is a "performer of difficult deeds" (*dukkarakāra*);
that same term, by way of the feminine gender, becomes "the performance of difficult deeds" (*dukkarakārikā*). He thought, "I am indeed liberated from that. If this is so, why [did he do it]?
Why did the Lord of the World apply himself to that for six years? It was on account of being oppressed by his past karma. For this is said in the Apadāna:
“I, Jotipāla, then spoke to the Sugata Kassapa:
‘Whence indeed can there be enlightenment for one who is shaven-headed? Enlightenment is exceedingly difficult to attain.’”
“By the ripening of that karma, I practiced many hardships for six years at Uruvelā;
thereafter, I attained enlightenment.
It was not by this path that I reached supreme enlightenment.”
“I sought [the path] by a wrong way, but was held back by my former karma.
“To kill” means to afflict. For the fetter of failure and so forth is, in the ultimate sense, the death of the virtuous, because it kills the penetration of truth;
and because it is most evil, it is called the “Evil One” (Pāpimā). And his state of being most evil is due to his evil conduct; thus he says, “he is intent upon evil.”
*Adhipati* means the lord of sensual desire (*kāmādhipati*). Because he brings those who have not abandoned sensual lust under his own control, he is *vasavattī*.

Because he brings an end to those very same wholesome kamma-acts, he is *antaka*. Because he is a condition from which one is not yet liberated from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*), he is *namuci*.
Because he is a kinsman to those who are intoxicated and negligent, he is *pamattabandhu*.
“Ascetic practice” means from the pursuit of self-mortification. “Has failed” means he has missed the mark.
There is also the reading “aparādho,” which has the same meaning. One who devotes himself to bodily mortification mostly devotes himself for the sake of immortality;

and since such a person, when questioned by those who profess the efficacy of karma, might be thought to do so for the sake of becoming a deity, he says, “for the sake of the state of immortality. “All asceticism”...
All self-mortification is not conducive to enlightenment because it lacks the proper means (*anupāya*). "Kiñcassa" means "might there be anything [of benefit] for him.
Regarding "phiyārittaṃva dhammanīti": *dhamma* here refers to a "grove" (*vaṇṇu*); that which is called "dhamma" is used in this context to mean a grove, specifically a location consisting of groves.
Therefore he said, "in the forest" (*araññe*). One would pull [the boat] with ropes from both sides.
And one should press down with hostile forces.

Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are included because the virtue of the path is intended here. By the inclusion of concentration, right effort, mindfulness, and concentration are also included, owing to their supportive nature.
The same principle applies here regarding "by wisdom" (*paññāya*). It is called "awakening" (*bodha*) because one awakens by means of it. The path...
He said: "For the sake of awakening means for the sake of the path. But how does one develop the path for the sake of the path? To this he said: "Just as," and so forth.

By this he shows that just as the undertaking of cooking rice-gruel is solely for the purpose of the gruel, so too the undertaking of the development of the path is for the purpose of attaining the path. And "undertaking" should be understood as the application to the development of the Noble Path.

Some, however, say: "‘The path’ means the noble path; ‘for awakening’ means for the full awakening of arahantship. And by taking it thus, this statement, ‘I have attained supreme purity,’ is also justified.
Others, however, say: "It is for the awakening of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), for that is superior to all other forms of awakening.
He has been struck down, brought to a state of being rendered powerless. Therefore he said, "He is defeated."
The commentary on the *Tapokamma-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Hatthirājavaṇṇa-sutta*.
138. "Causing blindness" means causing blindness by obstructing the arising of visual consciousness in ordinary people.
“Great darkness” means in great darkness. “Placing the great outer robe upon his head on the stone slab” shows that he was sitting leaning against that slab.
“Exertion” means meditative development (*bhāvanā*). “Grasping” means grasping it completely without letting go;
it refers to one who is devoted to meditative development, attending to the successive attainments and the attainment of fruition.
This is the meaning. Therefore he said, “Is it not so,” and so forth. “Ariṭṭhaka” means having the color of ariṭṭhaka; therefore he said, “black.

“For a long time” means for a very long duration. “They wander” means moving about with the intention of attacking; the intention is: “Enough of this for you, as it is useless. For by that, no purpose whatsoever was accomplished for Māra.
The commentary on the Sutta of the Elephant King’s Form is finished.
3. Commentary on the Subha Sutta 139.

"Well-restrained" means well-restrained by the restraint of the path. "Well-shielded" means well-shielded. "Under the sway of their own impulses" means they do not exercise mastery over the doors of the body and so forth. "Bound by conduct" means having a conduct that is fettered.
The commentary on the Subha Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the First Mārapāsa Sutta 140.

"By means of appropriate attention" (*upāyamanasikārena*) means by attending to impermanence and so forth as impermanent and so forth. "By means of skillful energy" (*upāyavīriyena*) means by energy that functions according to the method for the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states.
"By means of causal energy" (*kāraṇavīriyena*) [refers to energy] for the purpose of the non-arising of what has not yet arisen, and so forth.
By means of energy as a cause. For energy has the purpose of preventing unarisen evil from arising and so forth;
the word "right" (*sammā*) illuminates this meaning by showing that it accomplishes whatever purpose those energies serve.

Indeed, with the word "right" (*sammā*) used in the sense of "methodical," it is said "by methodical energy, by causal energy," referring to its function of indicating the means and the cause. [This refers to] liberation through the fruit of arahantship.
By way of an exalted description. Having heard the Blessed One’s words beginning with "Monks, it is by me," and so forth, Māra said:
"Even having attained arahantship, he is not satisfied," and so on.
"By the snare of defilements" means by that which serves as a device for the Māra of defilement. For the Māra of defilement binds sentient beings with the snares of the strands of sensual pleasure.
But he did not do so by himself. Therefore he said, "Those which are called the divine strands of sensual pleasure," and so forth.
"In the bonds of Māra" means in the place of bondage for the Māra of the defilements; the meaning is "in the prison of existence.
"O ascetic, you shall not escape from me"—this was said by Māra because he did not believe the Blessed One’s words: "Supreme liberation has been attained; I am released from all snares."
Or, even while having faith, one might say this out of one's own deceit, thinking, "In this way, he would not exert himself for the liberation of other beings.
The commentary on the First Mārapāsa Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Snare of Māra (Dutiyamārapāsasutta) 141.

"A wandering tour by gradual journeying" (*anupubbagamanacārikā*) means a wandering characterized by traveling in succession through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. "When you had thus gone" (*evaṃ gatesu*) means when many of you had gone together in this manner.

"Good in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇaṃ*) refers to that which is good at its start; the same applies to the subsequent terms. The beginning of the Teaching (*sāsana*) is ethical conduct (*sīla*), because it is the root.
For him, serenity and the rest constitute the middle, because they represent the intermediate stage of the attainment of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
The fruits and Nibbāna constitute the end, because once these are attained, there remains nothing further to be done. Right practice in the Dispensation occurs through wisdom;
since virtue and concentration are the roots of that wisdom, he said, "Virtue and concentration are the beginning. This is because wisdom functions by way of initial awakening and penetration.
Since there are two kinds [of paths], he said, "The insight and the path are the middle," thereby including both.
The fulfillment of wisdom is the function of the fruit, while the realization of Nibbāna is the conclusion of right practice, because there is nothing further to be done beyond that;
thus he said, "The fruit and Nibbāna are the conclusion. By the mention of the "fruit," Nibbāna with residue remaining (saupādisesa-nibbāna) is included.
By means of one [factor], there is another; by means of both of these, there is the culmination of practice. Thus he said: "The fruits and Nibbāna are the conclusion.
Because of the statement, "Therefore, bhikkhu, you should first purify yourself in regard to wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states?
It is virtue that is perfectly pure and view that is straight," [the practice] culminates in the perfection of virtue and straightness of view.
"Insight, and the virtue and concentration based upon it—these are the roots of that Dispensation," thus he said, "Virtue, concentration, and insight, or the beginning.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Although there is no whole (samudāya) separate from its parts (avayava), yet when those parts are considered in their collective form...
"Gāthā" is a conventional designation; showing that [the sutta] is as if distinct from that [designation], he says, "First, the first quarter-verse of a four-line gāthā," and so forth.

By mentioning the beginning and end of five-line and six-line gāthās, it is established without being explicitly stated that the others—the second, third, and fourth quarters—are the middle three or four lines respectively;
therefore, they are not mentioned. Regarding the phrase "of a sutta with a single connection," this [sutta] has many divisions.

This was said with reference to a sutta having a single sequence of exposition (*ekānusandhika*). However, for the other type [of sutta], those same beginning, middle, and concluding portions are found through the differentiation of the teachings to be taught.
"Nidāna" (the introduction) has the meaning of the characteristics of the indication of time, place, assembly, and so forth.

In the phrase "Idam avoca" (Thus he spoke), the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*); by that, it includes the remainder of the concluding passage (*nigamana-pāḷi*). [This applies] to that which has multiple sequences of exposition (*anekānusandhīka*).
The first [division], together with the introduction (nidāna), is the beginning; the last, together with the conclusion (nigamana), is the end;
and by the others, the middle is to be understood—thus the beginning, middle, and end are to be known.
"Meaningful" means made meaningful through the perfection of meaning; "well-phrased" means well-phrased through the perfection of phrasing.
"Perfection" (sampatti) means having complete phonetic components; thus he said, "by the phonetic components... [and so on]... the teacher.

"Entirely perfect" means completely perfect through the fulfillment of the five aggregates of dhamma, beginning with virtue (sīla). "Free from defilement" is due to the absence of defilements such as wrong view and conceit.
Without distinction, the three trainings exist throughout the entire Dispensation. However, the term "dhamma" here refers to the holy life (brahmacariya).
As it is said in such passages as: “Venerable sir, under which Blessed Buddhas was the holy life (brahmacariya) long-enduring?
It is like being covered by a fine cloth (*dukūla-sāṇi*), but not like being covered by a wall, rock, or the like.
By this, he speaks of the power of the Dharma’s terminology (*dhamma-nirutti*) to abandon all defilements (*kilesa*). [It is] through the loss of gain (*alābha-parihāni*).
There is no loss of what has been attained. "Three thousand four hundred and fifty" means three thousand five hundred miracles. "Sāta" means happiness.
The commentary on the second Mārapāsasutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Sappasutta.
142. “Of those who make liquor” means of those who mix flour-liquor (*piṭṭhasurā*). “Lord of the Kosalans” means he is a Kosala;
because he belongs to the King of Kosala, they are called “Kosalikas. “A bowl for use” means a bowl for the purpose of eating food; it is a bowl for use.

“At the mouth of the blacksmith’s bellows-pipe” means at the opening of the blacksmith’s bellows-pipe. “While blowing” means while being blown. And that [bellows] is [blown] by means of the wind from the bellows.

It is called "filled"; therefore, it is said, "being filled by the wind of the bellows. "On the ground of certainty" means having seen Māra moving about in the Blessed One’s place of seclusion even with the fleshly eye.
For this reason, he said, "by the light of a flash of lightning. "For the sake of a bed" means for the benefit of a bed.
For this reason, he said, "I shall stand," and so forth. "Self-restrained" means restrained in one's own person.

Therefore he said, "one whose self is restrained. Regarding the phrase "of one established therein": it means of one who is firmly settled in that Sage-Buddha who is free from the restless agitation of hands and feet.
By saying, "having relinquished [all else], he should move about therein," the Blessed One was answering him:
"What will the terrifying [forms] do to the Buddhas? There is no fear. He spoke thus as if merely pressing down upon what is utterly worthless.
"You alone shall undergo exhaustion"—thus he threatens Māra.

"Terrifying" means producing fear in those who have not yet transcended passion (*avītarāga*). "Therein" means for that purpose. "It might burst" means it might split. "A spear-point" refers to a broad arrow known as a *satti*.
"They would direct it at the chest" means they would place it there to pierce comfortably, or they would discharge it.
"In the acquisitions consisting of the aggregates" means in those acquisitions designated as the aggregates.
"They call themselves a refuge" means they call themselves a refuge from that cause of fear.
The commentary on the "Sleeping Snake" is finished.
7. Commentary on the Supatiṭṭhasutta 143.
[The feet] were washed for the purpose of removing the heat, not for the purpose of washing away dust and dirt. Therefore he said, "But for the Buddhas," and so forth.
"In a house where the feet have been washed" means in a place to be stepped upon by those whose feet have been washed. There is no breach of the rule because of their status as Masters of the Dhamma.
They wash while standing at the edge of the water so as not to fall into the imitation of others. Regarding the phrase "by one who encompasses sleep":

here, "sleep" (*soppa*) refers to the continuous flow of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), which is devoid of the mental activity consisting of intermittent functions during the intervals of drowsiness.
One should encompass this by way of its intrinsic nature, its purpose, and its temporal limits; that which encompasses it is the mindfulness and clear comprehension to be described below.
It was said with intentional meaning: "by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension that encompasses sleep. However, some say "sleeping while in a state of deep slumber";
this speaks in disparagement of the Blessed One’s sleep.

Regarding the phrase "kiṃ nu," he says, "Why indeed do you sleep?"—here *kiṃ* is used as a personal pronoun (*paccatta-vacana*) in the sense of an interrogative particle (*hetu-nissakke*). [The word] *dubbhago*...
He is called "devoid of splendor" and "with broken limbs"; moreover, he is like one who is dead and like one who is unconscious, which is why it says, "as if dead and as if unconscious.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the category of craving mentioned in such passages as "eighteen [factors] based on the external" is included.
"By way of being attached here and there" means by way of a state of specific clinging to this or that object.
It is "rooted in poison" (*visamūlā*) because it is the cause of "poison"—that is, of karma which produces suffering;

or, craving is "rooted in poison" because poison, in the form of feelings such as the suffering of pain (*dukkhadukkha*), is its root. It is the enjoyment of that suffering consisting of form and so forth, not of the Deathless.
"Consumption by poison. "To lead somewhere"—is it to lead [them] entirely to some state of existence? "By exhaustion"—because of being completely destroyed.
"What is this to you?"—what is your reproach regarding my practice, for me who am purified through the total exhaustion of all acquisitions (*upadhi*)?
He shows that it is merely a source of vexation for you alone.
The commentary on the Supatiṭṭhasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Nandatisutta: 144.
The eighth sutta has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the Nandatisutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the First Āyusutta 145.
One lives for fifty years, or even more than a hundred years, such as the Elder Anuruddha; [or] sixty...
Or for years, just like the elder Bākula. One who finds pleasure (*sāta*) and happiness (*sukha*) in being contrary is "one who delights in contrariness" (*paccanīkasāta*);
the state of being such is "delight in contrariness" (*paccanīkasātatā*), by means of which [he spoke]. Having overcome [the situation], he spoke the reply even while knowing [the truth].
He would neither despise nor loathe [him]. Thus, like that boy, a true person (*sappurisa*) should conduct himself without thinking about anything at all.
The intention is that in this way there is no mental suffering for him. "One should walk as if with a head on fire" means:

just as a man whose head is ablaze would make an effort solely to extinguish it without doing anything else, so too the true person (sappurisa), knowing that life is limited, should likewise practice insight (vipassanā) into how all conditioned things are impermanent, and because they are impermanent, they are suffering, and because they are suffering, they are non-self.
Having descended [into the world], even while striving for that [liberation], one should practice and proceed toward the disappearance of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).
The commentary on the First Discourse on Life is finished.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Life.
146. By "as if by the felly," he speaks of the wheel by means of its rim. "It revolves around the hub" means it turns around the hub.
Being thus situated, yet not abandoning it, he says, "it does not leave it. "The life-span revolves" means that the life-span of mortals, even as it passes away, returns again;
speaking thus as a foil for the Blessed One, the Blessed One, however, having overcome it—
With the words, “The days and nights pass away,” and so forth, he made known precisely the passing away of life and the state of death.
The commentary on the Second Discourse on Life is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. Second Chapter. 1. Commentary on the Rock Sutta (Pāsāṇasutta). 147. *Pavijjhi*:
he pierced [the mountain], causing it to fall from all sides, discharging it from here and there. *Sakalaṃ*: possessing all parts; the meaning is "without remainder."
The commentary on the Pāsāṇa Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Kiṃnu Sīha Sutta: 148.
“For the sake of making him blind” means out of a desire for his eyesight to be impaired. [She thought: “So that he, while the Dhamma is being taught by the Blessed One...”
He is unable to see [the truth] with his own eye of wisdom because of his desire to act in such a way. Therefore he said, "of the assembly," and so forth.
He is unable to destroy it because there is an absence of fear toward a terrifying object. "One who has attained the ten powers" means one endowed with the ten powers.
The commentary on the Kīṭāgiri Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Sakalikasutta* 149.
"By way of dullness" means by way of stupidity, by way of bewilderment—that is, through great delusion.

"Intoxicated by the composition of poetry" means having become intoxicated by the practice of composing poetry, such as being devoted to the act of writing verses. "What is this addiction to sleep?"—this refers to your sleeping.
"For what purpose, indeed, should a man who is called a 'man' act like a man? He must not simply sleep.

'Having approached the goal' means having approached and attained the ultimate goal, which is Nibbāna. 'Unattached'... [as above] ... because there is no state of being one whose aims have failed in any respect whatsoever.
'Watching' means like a man who is awake; I do not fear, because of the absence of any cause for fear. They do not regret anything anywhere."
"Always," because of its state of being released; "māmaṃ" means "to me. It is stated with a long vowel for the sake of metrical ease in the verse.
"Established" (*ṭhitatta*) means being delimited by summary and interrogation. "Loss" (*hāni*) refers to the ruin of someone.
The commentary on the *Sakalika-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Patirūpa-sutta* 150.
That by which one is drawn toward is "conformity" (*anurodha*), which is lust (*rāga*). That by which one is repelled is "opposition" (*virodha*), which is aversion (*paṭigha*).
Regarding those two—conformity and opposition—one "clings" (*sajjati*) to them, meaning one forms an attachment (*saṅga*) to them; that is, it is simply the arising of conformity and opposition.
And here, "the virtuous person" refers to one who instructs others. That instruction of others is a seeking of their welfare and a compassion for them;
therefore, you speak falsely with the intent to cause wavering by imputing partiality and hostility toward the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is compassionate and seeks the welfare of others.
The commentary on the *Patirūpa-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the Mānasa Sutta (151) "Moving through the air":

this is said with reference to those possessing the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhiññā*). Although they move in the sky (*antalikkha*), they are called "sky-goers" (*antalikkhacara*) because they accomplish their tasks [there].

"Born in the mind" (*mānasa*): it is so called because it is produced in the mind. Furthermore, since it is associated with the mental continuum (*manasantāna*), he says, "associated with the mind" (*manasampayutta*).
The commentary on the Mānasa Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Patta Sutta 152.
The characteristics and so forth of the five aggregates of clinging, as well as their origin, gratification, danger, and escape—
And because the correct grasping of their characteristics and so forth occurs by means of taking them up, he said, "having taken up the five aggregates of clinging.
Being affected, feeling, perceiving, forming, and cognizing are the individual-essence characteristics (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*) of the aggregates.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he includes their functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*), as well as their origination and other such factors. He "shows" [them] through direct perception.
He shows; having made it manifest and clear like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, he makes it known.
