"He causes to grasp" means that by causing those phenomena to be examined by the mind and thoroughly penetrated by view, he causes them to be acquired.
"In the undertaking" means in the correct taking up of the meaning therein, and in the undertaking [of practice] by way of the comprehension of the aggregates and by way of other phenomena.
"By the quality penetrated" means by the quality penetrated by them through that teaching, by means of it, and through their own individual personal effort.
"He causes to shine" means he makes their mental continuum radiant by dispelling the stains of defilements such as lack of faith.
"Making it a bone" means making firm the purpose and the goal to be attained through that teaching. Therefore he said: "This..."

“Not,” and so forth. The mind that performs the action is called the *otaraṇacitta* (the mind of entry). Some say it is the “mind of insight (*vipassanā*) preceded by wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
“With attentive ears” means having the ears applied to hearing the Dhamma because of being undistracted; for that very reason, having the ears fixed upon its meaning.
These aggregates, beginning with form, and whatever is conditioned (*saṅkhata*)—that which is produced by fully present conditions—that too, “this is not I... [and so on].
The construction is: "I am; this is not mine"—thus one sees. *Khemattā* means "the self that is secure" (*khema-attā*); it refers to that state of being secure.
Therefore he said: "the secure state of selfhood. "Māra’s army" is searching for [it].
The commentary on the *Pattasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Six Bases of Contact (Chaphassāyatana-sutta) 153.
It is called *sañjāti* because it is born (*sañjāyati*) from this; it is called *samosaraṇa* because associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) converge (*samosarati*) therein.
It has that same meaning; thus, it is by way of being a "birth-convergence" (*sañjātisamosaraṇa*). It is called "fear and terror" (*bhayabherava*) because one fears (*bhāyati*) from this.
Fear (*bhayaṃ*); that very thing is "terrifying" (*bheravaṃ*) because it brings terror to anyone; the meaning is the sound of gods and so forth.

The "divine drum" (*devadundubhi*) is the sound arising by way of a portent when the sky is free from clouds. The "sound of a thunderbolt strike" (*asanipātasaddo*) is the sound of a lightning bolt falling.
"It reels" (*undrīyati*) means it turns over. "The world is infatuated" (*adhimucchito*) means it has fallen into a swoon, like one whose body is completely rigid.
"Of Māra" means of the defilement-Māra (*kilesamāra*). "Become a place" means become a locus for the process [of existence].
The commentary on the *Chaphassāyatana-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Piṇḍa-sutta*.
154. “In this and that” means in various families of kinsmen and friends. “Gifts for guests” means articles to be sent as presents.
“Gifts for visitors” means articles to be given to those who have arrived.
“On the day of their own festival” means on the day of a festival to be celebrated by the boys and girls themselves. Now, to explain this matter in detail:
Showing this, he said: “Of equal age, birth, and clan,” and so forth. The word *sama* (equal) should be applied to each term:
equal age, equal birth, and equal clan. Furthermore, equality of clan should be understood in terms of being suitable for marriage alliances, not in terms of belonging to the same specific clan.
From various villages. When there was no one else to give [the gift]. A cake prepared to be sent on account of a festival.
*Chaṇapūvaṃ*: "Of their success" means of that twofold success, namely, their giving and their hearing of the Dhamma.

Knowledge is preceded by adverting; therefore, having stated "due to non-adverting" as the reason for one who does not know, he spoke the words beginning with "of the Buddhas" while stating the remaining reasons.
"Distinction in formal conduct" refers to the formal conduct to be performed by people upon seeing the Buddha.
"Bhindanaṃ" means "to shatter" (*bhindituṃ*), that is, to destroy.

The word "pana" (however) indicates a distinction. By it, this specific point is illuminated: it was not merely because the Blessed One wished to avoid being ridiculed that he did not re-enter that village; rather, it was out of compassion for Māra. "Janesi" means he generated demerit (*apuñña*);
and in generating it, he did so in such a way that in the future there would arise from it even firmer and greater suffering.
It will be accomplished; thus he accomplished it. Regarding the word *āsajjana*: here, *naṃ* is merely a particle.
As for *kiñcana*, since it means "it crushes," "it grinds," or "it overcomes," he said, "capable of crushing.
The commentary on the Piṇḍasutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the *Kassakasutta* 155.
“Referring to Nibbāna” means relying upon Nibbāna, having Nibbāna as one’s object; this is the meaning.
“With hair disheveled and scattered” means with hair that is disarrayed because it is strewn hither and thither. Regarding the phrase “the sphere of visual-contact-consciousness,” here, just as...

By the mention of "eye," contact is specified, and by that very term, the sphere of consciousness is also [specified]. If that were the case, it would follow that eye-consciousness itself is being mentioned.

[Objection: But surely, because it is specified here by the mention of "eye," there is the inclusion of all consciousnesses belonging to the eye-door? [Reply: That is true; however, that is by means of the first mention of "eye."

This is not a fault. To specify that what is intended by "life-continuum consciousness" (bhavaṅgacitta) is precisely that which serves as the immediate condition for the adverting consciousness (āvajjanā), it is stated as "accompanied by adverting.
Therefore, the phrase "together with its object-receiving [consciousness]" (tadārammaṇa) includes the object-receiving consciousness along with the impulsive consciousness (javanacitta).
Furthermore, when "the sphere of consciousness" (viññāṇāyatana) is mentioned, it refers exclusively to that which is stainless.
However, because it was stated without qualification as "the eye," it is shown that this meaning also applies to Māra by saying, "Whatever in the world...
and so forth. "Rotten and putrid" means completely cooked and seething with disease in the upper and lower parts of the eye-socket.
By the phrase "in the same manner," it refers to whatever in the world is afflicted by leprosy, white leprosy, boils, itch, and so on, by way of wounds, pustules, and the like.
He points out such things as: "Let all that impurity, even that which is dripping and most loathsome in appearance, belong to you alone.

Regarding what householders call "possessions"—gold, silver, fields, lands, and other requisites—and what those who have gone forth call "my bowl and robe," while they are indeed clinging to them with the thought "this is mine"—in these objects of attachment, for them...
And if your mind is directed toward those persons who possess property, or if your mind arises with reference to them, the meaning is that you are thus bound to them.
Therefore he said: "O ascetic, you shall not escape me. Regarding what they call "belongings":
the people of the world say of the aforementioned requisites, "This is mine."
"That is not mine" means that it does not belong to me; there is no "mine" there by way of craving.
"I am not those" refers to those persons bound here; I am not they either, and there is no bondage of views for me therein.
"You shall not see even my path"—thus, O Māra, you shall not see even the path gone by me who am liberated through the total absence of bondage.
"You shall not see, you will not behold, those states of existence and so forth which are your domain;
among those existences, wombs, and destinies, you will not see the path traveled by me, because I have emerged from existence.
The commentary on the Kassakasutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Rajjasutta* 156.
Regarding the phrase “ahanantena,” he explains that it is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental;

or rather, it is the nominative case used in the sense of the nominative itself, with the intended meaning being that there must be an ellipsis of the words “having not killed. This same principle applies to the remaining terms as well.
He says, "by one who does not cause another to suffer loss of wealth," because the word *ajinanti* expresses the sense of an included cause (*antogadhahetu*).

"By one who does not cause [another] to do" means by one who does not cause another to suffer loss of wealth. "By one who does not grieve" means by one who does not grieve for another on account of the loss of possessions and so forth.
He states the reason why the Blessed One thought thus with the words beginning "for this reason" (*iti*), etc.: "In a kingdom and a conquered territory oppressed by fines and taxes..."

When oppressed by the powerful through punishments such as fines and the like, the "sections for success" (*ijjhanaka-koṭṭhāsa*) are the sections that accomplish mastery over the mind and so forth. "Increased" (*vaḍḍhita*) means reinforced by way of the fulfillment of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
"Repeatedly performed" means set in motion again and again through the frequent practice of cultivation. "The yoked vehicle" (*yuttayāna*)...
Just as well-yoked noble chariots, when controlled by a charioteer, proceed according to his wish, so too it has been brought to proceed according to his wish.

"In the sense of a foundation" means in the sense of a basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*). "Made into a ground" means made like a thoroughly cleansed site for obstacles, because it has become a state of foundation through the complete purification of defilements and the attainment of the range of psychic power (*iddhi*). "Not abandoned" means...
Because they have been well-cultivated and have distanced themselves from their opposites, they have not been abandoned due to their fitness for their respective foundations.

"Constantly bound" means that for that very reason, they have been made as if constantly attached. "Well-mastered" means they have been brought to the accumulation of development through every aspect.
"Like one whose hand is unerring at hitting the mark" means like one whose hand is capable of hitting the mark because it does not miss. Well...

“Exerted” (*samāraddhā*) means properly accomplished for the arising of meditative development (*bhāvanā*). “One should reflect” (*cinteyya*) means one should reflect by way of extracting the meaning.

“Of a mountain” (*pabbatassa*) means it is a mountain (*pabbato assa*). Regarding the phrase “it would be a mountain” (*pabbato assa*), [the author] asks, “Of what kind? and says, “Of gold,” and so forth.
“Of gold” (*jātarūpassa*) means of that which is endowed with the nature of being born (*jāta-rūpa*). “Even twice as large” (*dvikkhattumpi tāva mahanto*) refers to the extent of that mountain.
"It is not enough for one person"—that is, it is not sufficient or adequate even for a single individual, because craving is so difficult to satisfy.
"Knowing thus" means knowing the danger of craving’s insatiability and so forth.
"One should live equanimously" means that, having abandoned the grasping at others' possessions and the like, one should act with complete impartiality through body, speech, and mind.

Suffering has craving as its source; craving has the strands of sensual pleasure as its source. Therefore, it is said that suffering has the strands of sensual pleasure as its source by way of the condition of craving.
"That" refers to suffering. "From whatever source it arises" means that from whatever source, whatever cause, it proceeds.
"Thus he who saw" means he who, having fully understood the basis [of suffering], saw suffering and the strands of sensual pleasure—which constitute its source—in their true nature.
He saw with the eye of wisdom. For what reason would he bow down? The meaning is that such a reason does not exist.
"The substrate consisting of the strands of sensual pleasure" means the substrate known as the strands of sensual pleasure.

Having understood that this is an attachment—that which one clings to—one should not indulge in that very thing, being overcome by sensual desires; one should train for the sake of discipline and pacification so as not to become attached.
The commentary on the Rajjasutta is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. The Third Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Sambahula-sutta 157.
"With a mass of matted hair bound upon the head" means with a bundle of matted locks fastened to the head.

For those brahmins who have gone forth without worldly possessions maintain their livelihood by gleaning while wearing matted hair. Indeed, the carrying of a staff of udumbara wood, taken up for the sake of self-protection, is a manifestation of their state of having few desires.

Therefore he said, "for the purpose of manifesting the state of having few desires. Regarding the phrase "shaking his head," it was stated "striking his chest with his chin and making it hang down" in order to show the extreme degree to which the head was shaken.
Regarding "having thrust out the tongue," this means having drawn it out from the mouth by means of its hanging and moving.
Therefore he said, "upwards," and so forth. "Tisākha" refers to [a frown] on the forehead like a three-fold bend.
Because it is born there, it is called the "forehead-mark. Therefore he said, "the three-fold wrinkle arisen on the forehead," meaning having formed three wrinkles upon the forehead.
"In his own oil" means in the oil produced by his own evil karma; the intention is that it should be cooked in the place where [the oil] is obtained.
The commentary on the *Sambahula-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta 158.
"My gain" means: the gain of such a Teacher, a Perfectly Enlightened One;
the gain of such a True Dhamma that leads to liberation; and [the gain] of such fellow-celibates who have practiced well.

This is my gain; these are gains well-obtained by me. "Well-obtained by me" means that this going forth and full ordination in my dispensation leading to liberation, and my delight therein—all of this has been well-obtained by me.
To show how such a reflection arose in his mind, it is said: "It is said that he... and so forth. [This was] according to the nature of his temperament.
The basic meditation subject (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*) was taken up. "Inspiring" (*pāsādika*) means bringing about confidence.
"Thus it occurred" means that such a reflection arose, beginning with "What a gain for me! and so forth. "Appearing as if seated" means as though he were actually sitting.
"In that very place" means in the very spot where Māra approached him while he was seated. "Of him" refers to the Elder Samiddhi. The meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
“Suitable” means that it will be beneficial and conducive to the practice of developing the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
“Mine” means by me. “Mindfulness and wisdom” (*satipaññā*): these are understood through their capacity for knowing by means of the Noble Path.
It is said that at that time the Elder intensified his insight (*vipassanā*). “As one wishes” (*kāmaṃ*) means according to one’s liking. Some [read] “*kāmaṃ*... [and explain it as follows:]...
"Karassu" means "Do [it]," while "Kāmā" is said to be the Venerable One’s address to Māra. "Vibhiṃsakarā hāni" means terrifying losses.
"Rūpāni" means distorted forms; for the word *rūpa* also carries the sense of a distorted state, as in such expressions as "He displays no small amount of *rūpa*.
"Na kampessasi" means you will not waver from the performance of the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
The commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Godhika Sutta: 159.
“On the side of a mountain” means near the foot of a mountain. It is called “occasional” (*sāmayika*) because it is obtained from time to time.

Therefore he said: "At each moment of absorption, one is liberated from opposing states. For mundane liberation (lokīyavimutti) is called "occasional liberation" (samaya-vimutti) because it is not an absolute abandonment;
supramundane liberation (lokuttara-vimutti), however, is "non-occasional liberation" (asamaya-vimutti) because it is an absolute abandonment.
Those endowed with these are called "occasionally liberated" and "non-occasionally liberated. [This continues] until the production of the first jhāna.
What is the meaning of "why does he fall away"? It means because of illness (*sābādhattā*), that is, because of being diseased.

"By way of wind, bile, and phlegm" means sometimes by way of wind and bile, sometimes by way of wind and phlegm, and sometimes by way of the combination of both. "Latent" (*anusāyiko*) means lying down following after the body;

the meaning is that it persists in the state of a chronic ailment. "Of concentration" (*samādhissa*) means of the cultivation of concentration. "Conducive factors" (*upakāraka-dhamme*) refers to such things as the climate and food.
"To fulfill" means to bring together. "He declined" because of the physical frailty of his body.

"Should be brought" means it should be brought for the purpose of taking away his life. His destiny is fixed solely in rebirth in the Brahma-world, not in the limited sense as is the case for stream-enterers and others. Therefore he said, "He is reborn in the Brahma-world.
"Blazing" refers to the splendor of a retinue that is unique and not shared by others, due to the supernormal power (*iddhi*) that has arisen and is fixed, within the world including the devas.

Shining in the world. He is "possessed of eyes" by means of the five eyes: the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*), the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), the Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*), the wisdom-eye (*paññācakkhu*), and the universal eye (*samantacakkhu*).
They are "endowed with majesty" (*ānubhāvadharā*), meaning they are possessed of the inconceivable and immeasurable majesty of a Buddha.

For the word "splendor" (*juti*) is also used as a synonym for "majesty," as in such expressions as "the splendor, power, energy, and attainment of psychic potency" (*iddhijutibalavīriyūpapatti*). [They] destroy pride without remainder.

"It completely cuts off" refers to the path of the summit cutting off conceit (*māna*). However, the state of being "mental" (*mānasatā*) regarding Arahantship should be understood as arising from that [path].
"Virtue and so forth" refers to the unsurpassed virtue and so forth. "One who is training" means one who is cultivating the trainings, causing them to arise within their own continuum.
This is not the cultivation of the mind (*cittabhāvanā*). Therefore he said, "one who still has work to do. "He generates it in the body of a being, in the world with its devas"—this is the meaning.
"Renowned" means she is renowned for her qualities such as virtue (sīla), which are not shared by others.
"Having suppressed the feeling" means having suppressed the arisen bodily pain—which had arisen in dependence upon the arisen painful feeling—by way of not producing self-exhaustion;
this is said because, having grasped that very feeling, she enters the path of insight (vipassanā) as it proceeds.

It is called the "fundamental meditation subject" (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*). Having stated, "He attained final Nibbāna as one whose head was level [with the rest of his body]," he spoke the passage beginning with "There are three kinds of those whose head is level" in order to analyze its divisions and show which one is intended here. One who is level-headed by way of posture is "one whose head is level in posture.
This same method applies to the other two as well.
"And the disturbance of the postures" means non-conformity with the postures. "All at once" means in a single moment.
"By way of final Nibbāna" means by way of Nibbāna without residue, not merely by the destruction of the defilements. "In this" refers to these two methods.
This being so, having established insight while in that very posture, in that very posture, in one...

Even while still afflicted by illness, if many who have established insight and attained Arahantship were to attain final Nibbāna through that very illness, they would all be "equal-headed" (samasīsino) as those whose taints are destroyed.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.
And herein, there are thirteen "heads": craving is the head of impediments; conceit is the head of bonds; and views are the head of misapprehensions.
Restlessness has agitation as its head; ignorance has the defilements as its head; faith has resolution as its head; energy has exertion as its head;
mindfulness has establishment as its head; concentration has non-distraction as its head; wisdom has seeing as its head; the life-faculty has occurrence as its head;
liberation has the range [of objects] as its head; and cessation has formations as its head. Among these thirteen heads:
The "heads" such as the obstacles (*palibodha-sīsa*) and so forth, as well as the head of occurrence (*pavatti-sīsa*), are what must be exhausted;
the heads such as resolution (*adhimokkha-sīsa*) and so forth are the exhausters; and the head of the range (*gocara-sīsa*) is the fruit of exhaustion.

For that fruit, which is liberation (*vimokkha*) consisting in the internalization of the object, has the head of formations (*saṅkhāra-sīsa*)—namely, cessation (*nirodha*) which is the seclusion from formations—as its object; this is for those things that must be exhausted.

In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, thirteen "heads" (*sīsāni*) are stated in order to show that the state of being "same-headed" (*samasīsibhāva*)— the simultaneous accomplishment through vision of the exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*), the fruit, and the object— is as if they were together. However, here, based on the statement,
"The exhaustion of the taints and the exhaustion of life occur neither before nor after," the application is made specifically by way of the heads concerning the occurrence of defilements (*kilesa*).
While doing so, he said: "And here, the head of occurrence," and so forth.

In that context, although the path—which emerges from occurrence—is exhausted by way of preventing further occurrence after death (*cuti*), it is nonetheless called the "head of occurrence" because occurrence exists as long as death has not yet taken place; thus, "the life-faculty is the head of occurrence."

"...exhausts the final consciousness," he said. However, the series of reviews—which must be accomplished by the path-consciousness immediately following itself through the exhaustion of the defilements—deserve to be called a "series of the exhaustion of defilements" as well.
This is because of the statement, "When liberated, the knowledge arises: 'It is liberated,'" which indicates that the series is completed by the reviewing.

The exhaustion of the defilements is said to be "completed"; however, if that completion occurs through the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), then by that very same [consciousness] there is also the completion of life.
Thus, showing that the exhaustion of the defilements and the exhaustion of life are neither prior nor subsequent due to this equality of the time of death, he said:
"There is no simultaneous arising of two consciousnesses," and so forth.
"Of two kinds of consciousness" refers to the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) and the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*).
"That" refers to the reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa*), which occurs seven times for those with a complete cognitive process (*javana*), or five times for those with an incomplete one.
Although it is said, "one or two," just as it is said, "one or two moments of resultant-representing consciousness (*tadārammaṇacitta*"), at the very least, two occur.
"Having uprooted" means having extracted. "Without residue" means by means of *nibbāna* without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*).
"The state of being smoky" refers to the mode of occurrence that is like the state of smoke. "Smoke-clouds" are clouds resembling smoke;
"darkness-clouds" are those where the mist is called "darkness" (*timira*). "Without a foundation" means not obtaining a footing.
This is an instrumental case used in the sense of a characteristic of a state (itthambhūtalakkhaṇe); the meaning is "by means of a phenomenon that does not arise.

For if there were arising, it would indeed be called "established"; however, in the Commentary, it is stated that "the very cause for that consciousness not being established is itself the cause for its final nibbāna," thus [it says] "because of the cause for non-establishment."

"Of one touched by grief" means: of one overcome by grief, thinking, "Alas, my effort has become fruitless. "It slipped away": for one pierced by intense grief, due to a lapse of mindfulness, the belt that had been held loosely fell off.
The commentary on the *Godhika-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Sattavassānubandha-sutta*.
160. Since Māra began following the Lord of the World from the moment he departed from Kapilavatthu, seeking an opportunity [to harm him], it is therefore said:
“six years before the Bodhi tree. “Having closely followed” means having pursued him and acting as if conforming to his practice according to his own desire.

“Meditating” (*avajjhāyanto*) means reflecting deeply (*pajjhāyanto*). “Are you conquered? means “Are you defeated, deprived of your wealth? “Exceeding measure” means “more weighty. “Having dug up” means “having uprooted.
“Free from taints” (*anāsavo*) refers to one who abandons the taints of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and so forth.

“Go away! (*pehī*) means “depart. “Those going to the further shore” (*pāragāmino*) means those whose nature is to go to the further shore. He says “those who too,” etc., because this word “going” (*gāmi*) applies to all three times.
“Māravisūkāni” means the thorns of Māra; they are like thorns, being the wicked deeds of Māra.
“Viruddhasevitāni” are synonyms for those very same things, in the sense of being opposed to them. To show their actual nature, the passage beginning with “Appamāyū” was stated.
“Nibbejanīyā” means providing penetration (into the truths). “Ukkaṇṭhanīyā” means bringing about weariness [with the round of existence].

It should be understood by way of a mental construct (*vikappa*), because that verb refers to the domain of a metaphorical supposition (*opammaparikappa*). Therefore he said, “one would go all around.
“In this” means in this matter of the appearance of fat. “Soft” means one would find or obtain a soft, sweet flavor.
“Taste” means that which is to be tasted.
The commentary on the *Sattavassānubandhasutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Māradhītusutta* 161.
"He thought" means he reflected while overcome by grief. "Prostitutes and female elephants" refers to female elephants from the island [of Ceylon]. "One hundred" [is the number].
“*Ekasatan*” means one hundred; that is, one hundred each, meaning a hundred for each. Therefore he said, “having made them into a hundred each.
“A hundred maidens’ forms” means a hundred individual bodies of young women. It is said they first showed themselves in the form of girls;
for the conventional designation “girl” (*kaññā*) applies to those who have not yet reached the age of menstruation. Then, [they appeared] again in the aforementioned form of maidens.
For the maiden had already borne flowers. Again, she appeared in the form of a bride; with reference to her, it was said, "one who has not yet given birth to a hundred forms.
In the third instance, she appeared in the form of a young woman (*yuvati*). For a woman who has given birth and has not yet passed the middle age is a young woman.

Up to this point, among the three types of women—the foolish, the youthful, and the mature—two of the former have been shown. In the final instances, [the characteristics] of those belonging to the human species are described.
Thinking, "Only human women are pleasing," they showed themselves in that human form.
"The attainment of the goal" means the absolute arising of welfare. "The peace of the heart" means the supreme tranquility of the mind.
"The first army of defilements" refers to the group of sense-pleasures; for that army of defilements, though its nature is as fleeting as a snap of the fingers, [is formidable].
Because it is to be cherished and desired due to its state of being dear and pleasant, it is called "dear-form" (*piyarūpa*) and "pleasant-form" (*sātarūpa*) by virtue of its own function.

"I am meditating alone" means that through the meditation on characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*), I am meditating alone, without a companion, due to the absence of both social company and the company of defilements.
"I have awakened" means that I have awakened gradually according to the sequence of the paths.
I awakened. Therefore: for the purpose of attaining the aforementioned bliss of seclusion.
By non-performance: by not performing intimacy with friends.
Witness: the state of being a witness. By which dwelling: by which dwelling among the meditative attainments (jhānasamāpatti). Herein, the meaning of the second word [is as follows].

This will be made clear in the commentary on the verses of response itself. By saying "that person" (*taṃ puggalaṃ*) without having addressed [the Buddha], he speaks as if the Blessed One were not present even though He is standing right before him; the meaning is "how could you?

Since it will be said later, "one who meditates without applied thought" (*avitakkajhāyī*), it should be understood that bodily tranquility (*kāyapassaddhi*) is precisely what is meant here; thus he says, "by the fourth jhāna."
“Because the body of inhalation and exhalation has become tranquil, he is one whose body is tranquil. Regarding the formative acts of merit and so forth, these are the formative acts of karma.

Because of the absence of attachment to sensual pleasures and the like, he is “without attachment” (*anālaya*). He does not flow out, thus he is “not flowing” (*na savati*); for it is through passion that beings flow along in *saṃsāra*.
He is not sluggish; he is not one whose mind is overcome by sloth and torpor. For it is through delusion that beings fall into sloth and torpor. “One thousand five hundred defilements” refers to...
Among the eight hundred defilements mentioned in the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, after removing the one hundred modes of craving (*taṇhāvicarita*), there remain one hundred and fifty defilements.
When these are combined with the sixty-two views mentioned in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, they total seven hundred and fifty-five.
These, when doubled by way of their being either arisen or unarisen, constitute one thousand five hundred defilements.
It is more than ten; however, that small amount—whether deficient or in excess—is not included in the calculation, which is why it is called "one thousand five hundred defilements.
The others are not mentioned because their past and other states are not intended here, as the abandonment [of the defilements] is what is meant.
This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Abhidhammaṭīkā*. By the first phrase...
By the phrase "does not waver" (*na kuppati*), [the first quality is shown]. By the second, the phrase "does not remember" (*na sarati*). By the third, the phrase "is not dull" (*na thino*).

By the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), he demonstrates the state of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*); what is intended is the absolute and complete abandonment of the hindrances without remainder.
"He has crossed the flood of defilements pertaining to the five doors" means that he has crossed over the flood of defilements that arise by way of the six doors.
He stands firm. Because they consist of the flood of sensual desire, the flood of views, the flood of existence, and the underlying tendencies, he says:

"Or, by the mention of the five floods, the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana) are to be understood. Since attachment to the form realm and so forth do not specifically pertain to the five sense doors, he says:
"By the mention of the sixth [door], the five higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) are to be understood."

By saying "from the hand of King Māra," [the commentator] shows that the genitive case is used here in the sense of a relationship. By stating "while they were being led away," he indicates that the genitive is used in the sense of disregard (anādara), as in "among those being led.
"Having uprooted" means having relied upon the Buddha. By the phrase "having concluded the teaching with 'This he said,'" he demonstrates that this is the concluding passage for the Saṃyutta Nikāya;
however, because it does not follow in the sequence below, it is not written in some manuscripts.
“Daddallamānā” is a designation formed by changing the sound *jajja* into *dadda*. Therefore, he said, “blazing exceedingly.
“He took them out” means that, without paying attention to their bodily or verbal movements and regarding them as no more than blades of grass, he took them out without any concern.
“Fallen from the fruit” means fallen from the fruit-basket. “Kuṇḍatṛṇādigacchatūlaṃ” refers to the cotton of wild grasses and so forth, or the cotton of the *poṭaki* plant.
The commentary on the Māradhītusutta is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
From the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the *Mārasaṃyutta* is completed.
5. *Bhikkhunīsaṃyutta* 1.
Commentary on the *Āḷavikāsutta*.
162. "Born in Āḷavī" means having been born in Āḷavī and having grown up there. Therefore he said:
"Having gone forth after departing from the city of Āḷavī itself. "Having incited [them] to give wealth" means:

the king gave one portion for the cetiya, the prince gave one, the commander-in-chief, being the chief among the ministers, gave one, and the merchant, being the chief among the people of the countryside, gave one.
While the construction work was thus being carried out on the four faces and the work on the face undertaken by the merchant was lagging behind,
a certain lay follower, a noble disciple, had five hundred carts yoked and traveled to the countryside, proclaiming: "Whoever is able to give—
be it bullion, gold, the seven kinds of gems, yellow orpiment, or realgar— let them bring their wealth."
Having exhorted him with the words, "Do this," and having sent him off with the first meditation subject he had received, [the teacher] heard that the new construction was finished.
As the man was traveling alone, robbers waylaid him on the road;
finding nothing at all there, they thought, "If we let him go, he will cause us harm," and so they took his life. Thus it was for a noble disciple who was innocent of wrongdoing.
It is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā: "Those thieves who committed offenses became blind; therefore, that place was known as 'Andhavana' (The Blind Forest).

Because those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) possess mental seclusion (cittaviveka) wherever they may be, due to the attainment of seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviveka), it is said [of the bhikkhunīs]:
"desiring bodily seclusion" (kāyavivekatthinī).
"Escape" (*nissaraṇa*) means *nibbāna*, because it has escaped from all that is conditioned (*saṅkhata*). "By reviewing knowledge" (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇena*);

the intention is that this is by means of reviewing knowledge, let alone by means of the knowledges of the path and fruit. "The state of *nibbāna*" (*nibbānapada*) refers to the category of phenomena known as *nibbāna*.
"In the sense of piercing through" (*vinivijjhanaṭṭhena*): by piercing the heart, having pierced the heart and produced suffering, [it pierces] the aggregates.
These five sensual pleasures are like spears and spikes. "Adhikuṭṭana-bhaṇḍika" refers to the executioner’s gong.
The commentary on the Āḷavikā Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Somā Sutta.
163. “A position” (*ṭhāna*) means a place of sovereignty, that is, a state within one’s own domain. It is “difficult to overcome” because of its immovability.
Regarding the phrase “by the wisdom of two finger-breadths”: here, from the time they are young girls, women attend to the process of cooking rice;
having heated water in a cauldron and added the rice, they use their own intelligence to determine the exact measure of time required for it to cook.
Even after removing those [fruits] with a pair of tongs, they are unable to know whether they are ripe or unripe by merely grasping their color and shape;

rather, they know them only when squeezed with two fingers. Therefore, because they are designated as having weak wisdom by means of two fingers, they are called "those of two-finger wisdom" (*dvaṅgulapaññā*).
By describing the occurrence of the knowledge of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), in the four...

It is said that "the dwelling in non-delusion regarding the truths is illustrated" by the words, "while knowledge is occurring," meaning while the knowledge of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is proceeding.
"Of one who is seeing clearly" means of one who sees with distinction through the penetration of non-delusion;

specifically, of one who is seeing clearly during the preliminary stage prior to the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the five aggregates as the truths. "Or something else" means something other than a woman or a man.

“Regarding the basis”: he says, “by way of craving, conceit, and views in the sense of ‘I am’,” referring specifically to the very basis grasped through the grasping of views and the grasping of craving based on the conceit “I am.
The commentary to the Soma Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Kisāgotamī Sutta 164.
Regarding the phrase "Kisāgotamī": who indeed was this Kisāgotamī? Why did this woman, having become a bhikkhunī, bring the practice of the ascetic life (samaṇadhamma) to its ultimate perfection?
To clarify this matter, the passage beginning with "It is said that formerly... is commenced. "Aṅgārāva" refers to coals having the color of burnt bricks.
Thus she was born. Thinking, "I will fetch wood and vegetables for half a māsaka," she went to the market into the middle of the street.
*Siddhatthaka* means mustard seed. *Sālāyaṃ* means in the hall for the destitute (*anāthasālā*). *Khuraggeyeva* means on the very tip of the razor; the meaning is "at the very moment of shaving.
In the word *ekamāsī*, the letter *m* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*), and by way of phonetic combination (*saṃhitā*), the short vowel occurs in the preceding word.
Or, in another sense, "long-lasting" means she said, "I was alone. This is a neuter gerundive (bhāvanapuṃsaka), as in such expressions as "sat down to one side.
She has transcended the end of her son’s death because, at present, there is no longer any death of a son for her. For this very reason, she said, "There is no such thing as the death of a son.
"Seeking a man" means that, just as for me there is absolutely no seeking for a man whatsoever—
In the same way, there is no longer any search for a son; therefore, my son’s death is now its end.

By declaring the absence of craving and delight regarding all aggregates, elements, and states of existence, craving has been completely dried up in respect of all beings, and the aggregate of ignorance that acts as its cause has been shattered.
Thus, proclaiming her own freedom from defilements, the Elder Nun uttered this lion’s roar.
The commentary on the Kisāgotamī Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Vijayā Sutta: 165.
That which has five factors is "fivefold" (pañcaṅga); that which is fivefold is itself "five-factored" (pañcaṅgika); by means of that five-factored [sacrifice].
Regarding the terms beginning with *ātata*: *ātata* refers to a single-surfaced musical instrument among those such as drums (*bheri*) that are covered with leather.

*Vitata* refers to one with two surfaces. *Ātatavitata* refers to instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*) which are strung with cords. *Susira* refers to flutes and the like. *Ghana* refers to solid objects such as gongs.

The qualification "among those covered with leather" is used because even though there are distinctions such as *tata*, they are all included within *ātata*. *Ekatala* refers to [instruments] such as the *kumbha-thūṇa* and the *daddara*.

The *ubhayatala* (double-sided) refers to the *bherī*, *mudiṅga*, and so forth. That which is covered with leather, while the rest is bound with strings, is all called *ātatavitata* (stretched and spread).
The inclusion of the *gomukhī* and others should be understood as falling within this very category. "Flutes and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), conchs and horns are also included.
*Sammatāḷa*, *kaṃsatāḷa*, *silātāḷa*, *salākatāḷa*, and so forth, are called *sammādi*. Among these, *sammatāḷa*...
“*Nāma-daṇḍa-maya-tāḷaṃ*”: a drum made of wood; *kaṃsa-maya-tāḷaṃ*: a gong made of bronze; *tāḷana-tāḷaṃ*: the striking of a stone with an iron plate.

All [these refer to] the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). “In the sense of trickling and streaming forth” means by way of dripping from above and flowing out. “Thus” means “with this putrid body.
“Abiding in the formless” refers to this teaching of the Dhamma being expressed by way of the person (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*); therefore he said, “in all cases.”
“In all form and formless existences. This is because both those form and formless existences have been included.

Since the sense-sphere existence has also been included by virtue of the commonality of being an “existence” (bhava) and by virtue of its being the basis for those [other two], ignorance’s darkness is destroyed, having been utterly eradicated by the highest path.
The commentary to the Vijayā Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Uppalavaṇṇā Sutta 166.
“Starting from the top” means beginning from the very summit down to the roots; it refers to the *sāla* tree that is properly in full bloom throughout its interior.
By way of the heading “color-element,” he speaks of the second bhikkhunī as being endowed with the color-element. Thus it was said.
“There is no other bhikkhunī like her. By “the eyelashes,” the eyeball is meant; thus he said, “between the eyelashes,” meaning in the middle of the two eyes.
“On the bridge of the nose” means at the base of the bridge of the nose. Having said, “Do you not see? he stated the reason for his not seeing: “I have become masterful [in concentration].”
The commentary on the Uppalavaṇṇā Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Cālā Sutta 167.

"This" refers to this view. "Caused to adopt" means he incited them, saying, "Do not find pleasure in birth. "Another" refers to acts such as cutting off [limbs] other than binding or killing. "Caused to enter" means he made them enter [into that state].
The commentary on the Cālāsutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Upacālāsutta 168. "Again and again...
they come" because the cause has not been eradicated. "Tormented" by the torments of the defilements. "An improper resort" means an unsuitable domain.
The commentary on the Upacālā-sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Sīsupacālā-sutta, 169.
“Like a female ascetic” means like a female ascetic by virtue of bearing the outward marks of an ascetic, because she does not find favor with any religious sect whatsoever.
The intention is: "Because you do not practice the path of solitude, I do not perceive in you the state of a female ascetic.
"Setting snares" means they prepare snares; the meaning is that they prepare them so that the minds of beings become entangled there in the snare of views (*diṭṭhipāsa*).
And being thus disposed, they are as if cast into the minds of beings; therefore he said: "In their minds, the snare of views..."
The meaning is "they cast off. "He releases from the snare" means that by means of the excellence of the Dhamma, he draws beings out from the mental continuum of the snare of views.
Therefore, because he releases them from the snare, he is not called a *pāsaṇḍa*. This is the conclusion of the meaning stated [in the verse]: "Only those outside of this [Dhamma] are *pāsaṇḍas*.
And having done so, with reference to all the non-Buddhist systems, in the *Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta*...
It is said, “ninety-eight sects. They “sink” means that they sink deeply and without support in the mire of wrong views and the mire of saṃsāra.
“Having overcome” means having surpassed by means of the abandonment of all defilements. “Ajitā” (Unconquered) means he has conquered because of his invincibility.
“The destruction of all kamma” (sabbakammakkhayo) refers to Arahantship, for it is there that all unwholesome and wholesome kamma-karmas are exhausted.
The destruction of acquisitions (*upadhisaṅkhaya*) is that wherein the acquisitions are completely exhausted; it is Nibbāna.
The commentary on the Sīsupacālā Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Selā Sutta.
170. "By whom was this image fashioned?"—this refers to the image designated as the "personal body" (*attabhāva*).

He asks this, wishing to create confusion regarding the agent, as to whether it was made, fashioned, or produced by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Puruṣa, Pajāpati, or others. "Evil" (*agha*) means the basis for evil.
Therefore he says, "because it is the foundation of suffering. "By the cessation of the cause" means by the non-arising and cessation of the cause conditioned by craving (*taṇhā*).

"By way of deficiency in conditions" means by way of the state of deficiency in conditions such as the remaining defilements and volitional formations; the meaning is "by way of their reaching the state of being non-conditions.
The commentary on the Sela Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Vajira Sutta.
171. "A mere heap of formations" (*saṅkhārapuñja*) refers to the collection of defiled formations within the classification of the material and immaterial.

"In the ultimate sense" (*paramatthato*) means by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Just as a so-called "heap of formations" designated as a "being" (*satta*) is not found in the ultimate sense, so too nothing whatsoever exists apart from those [formations], because such a thing does not exist.
"While they exist" (*vijjamānesu*) means while they are being obtained through the fulfillment of their respective conditions.
"By way of ten aspects" means by way of the aspects of woman, man, and so forth.

"In those that are determined" means in those occurring through attachment [to them] as "man," "elephant," "horse," and so on, based on the specific configurations produced by their respective particular conditions.

"Designation" (sammuti) means the conventional expression "a being. Therefore he said, "merely a common appellation. "The suffering of the five aggregates" refers to that which is designated as the five aggregates.
It is suffering. For this was said by the Blessed One: "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Nothing else arises, because there is no conditioned phenomenon other than the aforementioned suffering.
"It does not cease" means that nothing other than that ceases; thus, cessation occurs from arising.
The commentary on the Vajirā-sutta is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Bhikkhunī-saṃyutta within the Sāratthappakāsinī,
the commentary on the Saṃyutta-nikāya, is completed.
6. Connected Discourses on Brahmā 1.
First Chapter 1.
Commentary on the Sutta of Brahmā’s Entreaty
172. "The reflection arose" means that a state of indifference toward teaching the Dhamma arose, caused by his contemplation of the profundity of the Dhamma.
Why did this reflection arise, and where did it arise? To clarify all of this, the passage beginning with "Of all Buddhas" is commenced.
Therein, "habitual and customary" means both practiced and practiced by those who practice.
And the meaning is that he practiced exactly correctly. By this, he shows that this reflection arises indeed for all Buddhas at their first attainment of full enlightenment;

this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) in this regard. Therein, the phrase "on the eighth day" is stated because it arose within the seventh week, and not because there was an eighth week as in the case of others.

Because of the actual existence of what has been set in motion. *Sapaccaggha* means of great value. Alternatively, the reading is *paccagge*, meaning "new. *Selamaya* means made of stone, specifically of green-gram-colored stone (*muggavaṇṇasīla*).

*Paṭividdha* means reached by means of direct penetration through the knowledge of self-enlightenment (*sayambhuñāṇa*) in the manner of breaking through toward [the truths] such as "this is suffering," and so forth.
The meaning is: "understood according to reality. "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, because there is no other dhamma to be penetrated apart from those.

"Profound" means that, like the great ocean, it cannot find a footing for the knowledge of others—except by those who have accumulated and matured the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*)—just as a gnat’s proboscis or a needle [cannot reach its bottom]. Therefore he said: "This is a statement negating superficiality. That which finds no footing...
Because it cannot be fathomed, one is unable to see it either in its essential nature or in its specific details; thus he said, "Precisely because of its profundity, it is difficult to see.
It is to be seen with difficulty means it can be seen only with hardship, by someone, and only at some time.

As for that which cannot even be seen, there is never anyone who, having fathomed it, understands it step by step; thus he said, "Precisely because of its difficulty to see, it is difficult to penetrate."

It is to be understood through suffering because awakening is difficult to achieve. At this point, the Sutta passage should be cited: "What do you think, monks, which is more difficult or more hard to accomplish?

Or, it is "peaceful" (*santo*) because its object is peaceful; it is "extinguished" (*nibbuto*) because all feverish distress has been extinguished. It possesses a state of preeminence by means of its own conditions.
Or it is "excellent" (*paṇīta*) because it has been brought to excellence. It is "satisfying" (*atappaka*) in the sense of producing no further craving, like delicious food.
In this context, the truth of cessation is "peaceful" as its object, and the truth of the path is "peaceful" both in itself and as having a peaceful object; thus it is "having a peaceful object.
It is "peaceful" because of the absence of defilements and formations whose intrinsic nature is not peaceful, and because all feverish distress has been extinguished.
It is "extinguished" (*nibbuto*). By the very fact of its being peaceful and sublime, it should be understood as being non-satiating and insatiable for that purpose.
Therefore he said: "This dyad is spoken of with reference exclusively to the supramundane. Because it is the object of supreme knowledge, it cannot be fathomed by mere reasoning.
For that very reason, because it is the domain of subtle knowledge and because its intrinsic nature is delicate and refined, it is "subtle. To the foolish...
It is "to be experienced by the wise" because it is to be understood only by those who are wise as described above, owing to its being beyond the scope [of ordinary cognition].

They are called *ālayā* (attachments) in the sense that they are clung to and resorted to for the sake of delight; these are the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*). They are called *ālayā* in the sense that one clings to them, adheres to them, and resorts to them for the sake of enjoyment;
these are the modes of craving (*taṇhāvicaritāni*). "They delight" means they find pleasure, play, and sport. "Delighting in attachments" (*ālayaratā*) means being devoted to those attachments.
"Referring to the word *ṭhāna*" means referring to the term *ṭhāna*. However, what is intended by "condition" (*ṭhāna*) is precisely dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

It is called a "condition" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands (*tiṭṭhati*) depending upon it for its existence; thus, it refers to ignorance and the other factors that serve as conditions for volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth.
The conditions for these volitional formations and the rest are "this-condition" (*idappaccaya*), namely ignorance and the others. These very [factors] are "this-conditions."
"Conditionality by way of this" (*idappaccayatā*) is like saying "the god himself is the deity.

Alternatively, conditionality by way of this (*idappaccayatā*) is the state of being a condition, or the capacity to produce, of the conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*) with respect to their own fruit.

By this, dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is shown to have the characteristic of a condition in the ultimate sense. It is called dependent origination because the fruit arises dependently (*paṭicca*) from it.
By both these lines, the meaning of conditionality (*paccayaṭṭha*) alone is elucidated for phenomena. Therefore he said:

"This is a designation for the conditions such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*)," etc. "Conditions for volitional formations, etc. means the conditions for volitional formations and so forth; that is, ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The stilling of all formations" (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatha*): "all" refers to everything denoted by the phrase "the stilling of all formations" and so forth; in its actual meaning (*atthato*), it is exclusively Nibbāna.
Now, in order to demonstrate its nature as Nibbāna, the words beginning with "for because" (*yasmā hi*) were spoken. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to Nibbāna.
"Having come to" (*āgamma*) means depending upon it, by way of the noble path’s object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). "They are stilled" (*sammanti*) means by way of subsiding and pacification.
They subside. And being thus subsided, they are said to be "especially calmed"; therefore, it says "they are stilled" (*vūpasammanti*).
By this, it shows that Nibbāna is the "stilling of all formations" (*sabbasaṅkhārasamatha*), because all formations subside therein.

For it is precisely in the commentary that the expression "the stilling of all formations" is stated with respect to Nibbāna, which is dissociated from all formations. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
“Basis” (*upadhi*) refers to the aggregates and so forth, because suffering is built up (*upadhīyati*) therein.
“Relinquished” means they have been abandoned by way of complete eradication. “All craving” refers to all craving, including its eight hundred varieties.

“All defilement-passions” (*kilesa-rāga*) refers to all passions that are defilements, such as the divisions of sensual passion, form-passion, and so forth; or alternatively, all defilements here are termed “defilement-passions.”
[These] are intended [here], and not merely specific types of greed, because they bring about a state of feverish burning in the mind.
As it is said: "A lustful mind is transformed; a hateful mind is transformed; a deluded mind is transformed.
They "become detached" means they fall away, through suppression and by way of being entirely disconnected from it. "All suffering" refers to the various forms such as aging, death, and so forth.
All the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). By means of becoming, one is bound from one state of becoming to another state of becoming through the nature of craving for becoming.
Or, karma is [bound] together with its fruit because, for one who possesses craving, there is the occurrence of renewed becoming in the future.

It is "withdrawn" (*vāna*) from that [craving], because that [craving] is entirely absent therein. Due to sitting for a long time or speaking for a long time, [it arises] by way of backache, dryness of the palate and throat, and so forth.
Physical fatigue and physical affliction are indeed to be understood; however, these apply only to those who do not understand the meaning of the teaching and do not practice accordingly.
But for those who understand and do practice, even the bodily exhaustion resulting from the teaching is no exhaustion for the Teacher.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "And the matter of the Dhamma did not afflict me."
For this very reason he said: “That which is called teaching those who do not know would be weariness for me.

Both—namely, mental weariness and mental vexation—these two do not exist for Buddhas because they were utterly eradicated even at the foot of the Bodhi tree. *Anubrūhanaṃ* means gathering together or compounding.
*So* is a particle meaning “also indeed. Or, *anacchariyā* refers to wonders that have reached growth; it also has the sense of growth.

The particle *hi* is used here as in the expression “the qualities of one beyond training” (*asekkhā dhammā*). Having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons solely for the purpose of sharing the Dhamma with the world including its devas, he has now attained the sovereignty of the Dhamma;
this verse indicates his lack of concern regarding that sovereignty and demonstrates the marvelous nature of the meaning of the verse as well as its attainment of excellence.
This should be understood. For the lack of wonder regarding verses is due to their meaning (*atthadvāra*). "They became objects of the range" (*gocarā ahesuṃ*) means they appeared (*upaṭṭhahiṃsu*).
And appearance means being fit for reflection; thus he said, "they reached the state of being to be thoroughly reflected upon" (*parivitakkayitabbataṃ pāpuṇiṃsu*).
If it is indeed an easy practice (*sukhāpaṭipadā*), how can there be difficulty? To this he said, "But at the time of fulfilling the perfections," and so forth. Such passages as these...
"Of one who gives what is difficult to renounce. *Ha* or *byattaṃ* is a particle used in this sense. Some say it is used in the sense of "certainly" (*ekaṃsatthe*).

The construction is: "O wise one (*ha byattaṃ*), or certainly (*ekaṃsena vā*), it is sufficient (*alaṃ*)—that is, it is indeed useless—to proclaim or teach that which has been attained with such difficulty.
Or, *halantaṃ* is a word synonymous with *alantaṃ*, as seen in expressions such as "I say it is enough" (*halanti vadāmīti*).

"By those touched by lust and hatred" means by those overcome and afflicted by lust and hatred, as if by a snake touched by its venomous fangs. "Followed by lust and hatred" means pursued by lust and hatred. "Of the permanent, etc.
refers to the four perversions (vipallāsas) beginning with the perception of permanence. "Thus gone" means in such a manner, namely, by way of [the perception of] impermanence and so forth.

The process must be awakened to. Those who are stained by passion for sense-pleasures and passion for existence, whose minds are shrouded by the hindrances, and who are stained by passion for views through their adherence to distortions, will not see the Dhamma as it truly is; they will not penetrate it.
"By its own nature" means by its undistorted nature. "To cause them to grasp thus" means to grasp it according to its true nature as impermanent and so forth.
In order to make [them] understand the Dhamma. Since their state of being overcome by lust and hatred is due precisely to their state of delusion, he says, “shrouded by a mass of darkness.
To clarify the reason for his lack of concern regarding the teaching of the Dhamma, he raises the objection himself with the words, “But why,” and so forth.
“In the guise of one who has not yet known” means in the guise of one who has attained the status of a disciple of this Blessed One.
“By means of a certain ascetic’s guise,” some say; however, that guise would have vanished through his very attainment of *arahantship*.
Three reasons for his falling into a state of indifference were presented:

the strength of the opposing factor, the profundity of the Dhamma, and the Blessed One’s extraordinary reverence for it. To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “For him, indeed... was commenced. Therein, the opposing factors...
Indeed, the defilements such as lust and the rest are so called because they create obstacles to right practice.

Due to their powerful nature, having been cultivated for a long time, and being difficult to purify from the continuum of sentient beings, they—like intoxicated elephants—overpower and overwhelm weak men, leading them to ruin and calamity;
[they do this] toward a well-constructed, dense settlement measuring many hundreds of yojanas in length and breadth.

They even lie upon a thorny path. However, in order to demonstrate that it is difficult to purify due to its being far-reaching, diverse, and hard to sever, the passage beginning with “Then for him” was spoken.
In that context: a gourd filled with sour gruel because it is not polished on the inside;

a wooden tub filled with buttermilk because it has been stored for a long time; a rag soaked in fat because of its weakness from being saturated with oil; and a hand smeared with ointment because of its mixture with oil.
They are said to be difficult to cleanse. These [defilements] are compared to inferior things because they are a continuous succession of forms and because their impurity is of recent duration;

however, the corruption by the defilements (*kilesa-saṃkileso*) alone is even more difficult to cleanse, because it is beginningless and because it does not depend on the form-aggregate. Therefore he said, "extremely corrupted.
And just as there is this greater difficulty in cleansing, so too the similes already mentioned apply to its depth, its difficulty of seeing, and its difficulty of being understood.
[The simile] is inferior. Even though the Dhamma is profound, it may become well-manifested through knowledge that has attained clarity by means of the destruction of its opposites;
yet the destruction of those opposites is dependent upon right practice, which is dependent upon hearing the true Dhamma, which in turn depends upon confidence in the Teacher and the Dhamma.
That [confidence] is caused by an entreaty to those who occupy the position of venerables—thus [it is said] by way of a conduit.
Showing that this was prompted by Brahmā’s entreaty for the sake of beings’ correct practice of the Dhamma, he said, “Moreover,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase *apparajakkhajātiko*: that which has little dust (*raja*) consisting of defilements (*upakkilesa*), such as lust and so on, is *apparaja*;
those whose eyes of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*) are such, being of that nature, are *apparajakkhajātiko*. Demonstrating this meaning, he said, “Consisting of wisdom,” and so forth.
"Those whose nature is such that the dust of passion and so forth is slight are 'of a nature with little dust' (*apparajakkhajātiko*); this is how the meaning should be understood here.

Regarding "by way of non-hearing," he says "by way of non-hearing" (*assavanatāya*), because—as in the case of "having known for oneself by direct knowledge" (*sayam abhiññā*)—the word is in the instrumental case used as a nominative.

"By way of the ten bases of meritorious action" means by way of the ten types of bases for performing merit, such as giving and so forth. Therefore he said, "those who have performed their duties," and so on.

In the *Papañcasūdanī*, however, it is stated: “By way of the twelve types of meritorious action. This is said by including such acts as taking refuge and the dedication of merit for the benefit of others within [the category of] giving and so forth.

That which was “thought out” is that which was produced by one’s own ingenuity, accompanied by investigation, and struck by reasoning; this was done by the six teachers who claimed to be teachers—such as Pūraṇa and others—who were defiled by the stains of lust and so on, and who stood in the position of poets of thought and the like, composing their works through mere conjecture.

It is said that, deceiving the world which had become filled with curiosity by hearing the clamor regarding the Buddhas, they stood in hypocrisy, claimed omniscience, and proclaimed whatever was contrary to the Dhamma as "the Dhamma. Therefore he said: "For they, having arisen earlier," and so forth.
"Open this" refers to the great door of Nibbāna, which has been closed since the disappearance of the Blessed One Kassapa’s dispensation.
He opened and disclosed the Noble Path by means of the hand of teaching the True Dhamma.
He said, "as upon the summit of a rocky mountain," because a rocky mountain is high and firm, whereas a mountain of earth or a mixed mountain is not.
By "the palace made of Dhamma," he refers to the supramundane Dhamma; for that indeed brings about complete confidence.

And it is like a palace in the sense of having risen above all phenomena (*dhamma*). Alternatively, the word *dhamma* here is used in the sense of wisdom (*paññā*), as stated in the phrase "consisting of wisdom.
For that [wisdom] is described in the Abhidhamma as a "palace" in the sense of having risen above [all things]. And so it is said:
"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, Free from sorrow, amidst a grieving people..."
“As one standing on a mountain looks down upon those on the ground, so does the wise man look upon the foolish.

Regarding the phrase “Just as,” and so forth: just as when a man stands on a mountain and looks down into the darkness below, his fields, rice-paddies, boundary walls, and huts, as well as the people sleeping therein, are not perceived because they lack luminosity; yet, within those huts, the flames of a fire are indeed perceived.

Because they lack such radiant quality, beings who have not performed wholesome deeds do not come within the range of the Blessed One’s knowledge as he ascends the palace of the Dhamma and surveys the world of sentient beings;

due to their lack of radiance and their inferior state, they are like arrows shot into the night. However, those fortunate individuals who have performed wholesome deeds, even if they stand at a distance, [come within the range of the Blessed One].

The construction should be understood as follows: they come within range because of their state of being ablaze through the fire of fully matured knowledge, and because of the loftiness of their mental continuum, like the Himavanta mountain.
Having attended upon one who occupies the position of a teacher, the aspiration directed toward a more weighty purpose is the entreaty; that too—
In terms of its meaning, it is simply a request; thus he said, "‘Entreaty’ means ‘asking.
Because this pair of knowledges is not a knowledge and vision that has a limited scope, but is unique to the Buddhas alone, they are called the "Buddha-eye";
thus he said, "The name ‘Buddha-eye’ belongs to these two knowledges. [This refers to] the three knowledges of the paths, namely, the lower ones...
The name "Dhammacakkhu" (the Eye of Dhamma) belongs to the three knowledges of the path because they consist merely in the seeing of the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
Since those knowledges are described as being like lightning, the knowledge of the supreme path—because it has reached the culmination of the function of knowledge—is not merely a matter of seeing;
therefore, it is not called "Dhammacakkhu," since it is described as being like a thunderbolt.
"By the method stated" means by the method stated here [in the passage] beginning with "those of little dust in their eyes.
Since those with dull defilements are called "those of little dust," it should be understood that those with abundant defilements are "those of much dust.

Because they are capable of destroying opposing factors, they are sharp, keen, and clear; by way of the opposite of what was stated, they are blunt. The "modes" such as faith refer to the various aspects of believing and so forth.
It says: "Sundara" means beautiful. In the *Sammohavinodanī*, however, it is stated: "Those whose factors such as disposition (*āsaya*) and so forth are beautiful are 'of good character' (*svākāra*).
This should be understood as being entirely consistent with this commentary on the meaning.

"Cause" (*kāraṇa*) refers to the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) or the Truths (*sacca*). "The other world" (*paraloka*) refers to the future life (*samparāya*). That brings about suffering and is blameworthy (*vajja*).
“It should be viewed with fear as if it were [a danger]” means: “viewing both the next world and wrongdoing with fear.

Or, because the state of misfortune (vipattibhava) is other than the state of success (sampattibhava), the state of misfortune is called the “next world,” as stated: “viewing... [the next world]... with fear.
“But this is the canonical text here” means: regarding the elucidation of the meaning of the words “few with little dust in their eyes,” this is the canonical text that establishes that very state.
For the strength of the qualities that ripen liberation—such as faith and the rest—occurs when their opposites, the unwholesome states, are weak;
and the weakness of those [unwholesome states] occurs when faith and the rest are strong.

Thus, according to the specific presence or absence of these qualities that ripen liberation, the Pāḷi analyzes them into categories such as "those with little dust in their eyes" and "those with much dust in their eyes."

It is shown by such passages as, “A person endowed with faith has little dust in their eyes,” and so forth. The aggregates and so on are themselves the world (*loka*) in the sense of breaking apart and disintegrating.
The world consisting of the world of success (*sampattibhava-loka*) refers to the world of existence as success, which is the world of rebirth known as a happy destination (*sugati*).

That by which success comes to be is the world of the origin of success (*sampattisambhava-loka*), namely, the kamma-existence that leads to a happy destination. [The remaining two worlds are] the world of rebirth known as an unhappy destination (*duggati*) and the kamma-existence that leads to an unhappy destination.
The world of misfortune and the world of the origin of misfortune. Furthermore, having analyzed and shown the world by way of single and dual categories and so forth, it is said:

"One world," and so on. For just like the nutriments, all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) that subsist by means of nutriment are called "the world" (*loka*) in the sense of being subject to disintegration (*lujjana*).
In that context, "one world: all beings subsist by means of nutriment"—this is a discourse based upon the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).

It is stated that all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) exist in dependence upon conditions; by this, the entire world of formations is one and of a single kind, because there is no other mode of being.
The meaning in such passages as "two worlds" and so forth should also be understood according to this method.
Furthermore, in this context, Nibbāna is not included by the mention of "name" (nāma), because its intrinsic nature is not that of the world (aloka).

But would it not follow that even the Path and its Fruits possess the nature of the world (*lokatā*), since they exist in dependence upon conditions, as expressed in the phrase "subsisting by nutriment"? It does not follow;
for here, the term "world" is intended to refer to those phenomena belonging to the Truth of Suffering which are to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).

Alternatively, the "world" is defined as that which is not subject to breaking up or disintegration—that is, that which does not remain as it was grasped—and thus it excludes the supramundane (*lokuttara*) states, which are free from such grasping.
There is no worldliness (*lokatā*). The aggregates that serve as the objects of clinging are the "aggregates subject to clinging" (*upādānakkhandhā*).

The eight worldly conditions, such as gain and so forth, which serve as the basis for attachment and the like, are the "worldly phenomena" (*lokadhammā*). "The ten bases" refers to the ten sense-bases consisting of form. The remainder is easily understood.
Because one whose inclination is toward the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭajjhāsaya*) is intended here, all kamma pertaining to the three planes must be censured and abandoned by him.
It is said: "Having offered [the sacrifice], one stands near"; thus it is stated: "All volitional formations are to be avoided; all kamma leading to existence is to be avoided.
Regarding the five dyads beginning with "having little dust in one's eyes," having taken ten aspects for each of them, it is stated:
"One knows these five faculties through fifty modes. Alternatively, [it is known] through the positive and negative concomitance of the faculties such as faith and the rest.
It was stated thus because [the Buddha] knows the higher and lower degrees [of beings' faculties].
And here, as the Blessed One adverts to them by way of their having little dust in their eyes, their being capable, and so forth, those beings appear to him as masses of beings, not individually.
"There are blue lotuses here" is *uppalinī*; it refers both to a grove of blue lotuses and to a body of water. But here, it refers to a body of water.
“Intended” means he said, “in a grove of blue lotuses. For those that grow and flourish while remaining submerged within the water are called “those nourished while submerged.
“Illustrated” means they are explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, or shown right here by the phrase “others as well,” and so forth.

“One who gains knowledge by a condensed statement” (*ugghaṭitaññū*): “condensed statement” (*ugghaṭana*) refers to the condensing of knowledge; it is one for whom [the goal] is achieved by the mere condensing of knowledge.
The meaning is "he knows. One who knows the meaning that has been elaborated—that is, fully detailed—is a *vipañcitaññū*.

One who is to be led toward the realization of the Dhamma by means of the *Niddesa* and other such texts is a *neyya*. A *pada* is so called because the meaning is reached (*pajjati*) by it, or because the meaning is known (*pajjate ñāyate*); such is its sense.
One for whom the *pada* (the word) is supreme, but not the full awakening to the Truths, is a *padaparamo*.

"At the moment of being uttered" means at the time of the proclamation, the recitation, or the mere utterance of the Dhamma. "The breakthrough to the Dhamma" (dhammābhisamaya) is the realization (abhisamaya) together with knowledge of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

"This is called" refers to the attainment of Arahatship by directing one's knowledge according to the teaching, while the matrix (mātikā) is being established in brief by way of the method beginning with "the four foundations of mindfulness."
A person capable [of attaining realization] is called "one who understands through a condensed statement" (*ugghaṭitaññū*). This is what is meant by "is called":

when the matrix (*mātikā*) has been set forth in brief and the meaning is being analyzed in detail, a person capable of reaching *arahantship* is called "one who understands through elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*).

"From the point of recitation" (*uddesato*) means for the sake of recitation; the sense is: for one who is reciting or causing [another] to recite. "From the point of interrogation" (*paripucchato*)...
"For one who asks about the meaning": "The realization of the Dhamma occurs gradually" means that the attainment of Arahatship occurs by way of successive stages.

"The realization of the Dhamma does not occur in that very birth" means that by means of that particular individual existence (attabhāva), one is unable to produce either the Path or the Fruit, or even at least meditative absorption (jhāna) or insight (vipassanā). This is called "one for whom the words are the limit."

The meaning is this: because for this person the "sixfold phrasing" (*byañjanapada*) and the "sixfold meaning" (*atthapada*) constitute the ultimate word itself, he is called "one for whom the word is supreme" (*padaparama*). "There is a residual impression" (*vāsanā hoti*):
the teaching is spoken of as a "residual impression" by way of a metaphorical designation for its fruit; for there is no teaching whatsoever of the Buddhas [that does not bear fruit].
They are useless for two kinds of persons. In the *Vibhaṅga*, "by the obstruction of karma" refers to the fivefold karma of immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*).
"By the obstruction of ripening" refers to rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) without roots.

Since even those with two roots lack penetration of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), it should be understood that rebirth-linking with two roots is also indeed an obstruction of ripening. "By the obstruction of defilements" refers to...
It is certain due to wrong view such as desire. "Lacking faith" means being devoid of faith toward the Buddha and so forth. "Lacking desire" means being devoid of the desire for the wish to act.
The humans of Uttarakuru have entered the state of lacking desire. "Lacking wisdom" means being deficient in the wisdom of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
However, even for one whose wisdom of the life-continuum is complete, if the movement of the life-continuum does not become a condition for the supramundane, [it is still considered lacking].

He is indeed called one of little wisdom. "Incapable of entering into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states" means they are incapable of entering—that is, attaining—the path known as the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.

The phrases beginning with "not by obstruction of karma" and so forth are to be understood by way of the opposite of what was previously stated. Regarding those of a lustful temperament and so on, whatever is to be said—
This should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā* (The Elucidation of the Path of Purification) within the *Paramatthadīpanī*.

It is called "the door to Nibbāna" because it has been opened and established as the path of entry, having been attained by the self-enlightened wisdom (*sayambhuñāṇa*) through the proximate cause of great compassion (*mahākaruṇūpanissaya*).
"Let them release their faith" means: having made their own faith capable of receiving the Dhamma...
"Let them answer" means let them establish it by way of faith. "Well-functioning" means being able to proceed with ease and without difficulty.

"I thought: 'I shall not speak, nor shall I speak,'" [refers to the fact that] for the gods and Brahmas who have approached the presence of the Teacher, there is no such thing as "disappearance" before him; rather, it is their non-remaining [there].

He said, "He has gone back to his own place. The faculty of faith and so forth, as well as the factors beginning with right view, are called the *dhammacakka* (Wheel of Dhamma) in the sense that they proceed within the mental continuum of those to be trained.
Alternatively, *cakkam* means command; *dhammam* means teaching.
Or else, because it does not deviate from the meaning and the Dhamma, it is both *dhamma* and a wheel in the sense of proceeding—thus it is the *dhammacakka*.
