The "Wheel of Dhamma" (dhammacakka) refers to the wheel that is both by way of Dhamma and by way of method (*ñāya*). As it has been said: "It is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion the Dhamma and the wheel;
it is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion the wheel and the Dhamma; it is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets [it] in motion by means of the Dhamma;
it is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets [it] in motion through the practice of Dhamma," and so forth. "Set in motion" (*pavattesi*) means he established [it].
The commentary on the Brahmāyācana Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Gārava Sutta: 173.
“This thought” refers to the thought that has arisen thus: “How might I dwell? “In another” [refers to]...
Regarding the word *parasmiṃ*: "another" (*para*) means one who is not oneself (*attā*). However, in this context, it does not refer to just anyone;

rather, it refers to one who occupies the position of a teacher (*garuṭṭhānīyo*). Therefore, he said: "without placing anyone in the position of a teacher. One who responds to a teacher with "Yes" (*āmā*) is *patissa*;
one who is not *patissa* is *appatissa*. The meaning is: devoid of deference, lacking reliance upon a teacher.
In the compound *sadevaka*, the analysis (*viggaha*) is by way of its parts (*avayava*), while the collective whole (*samudāya*) is the meaning of the compound (*samāsa*).

By the inclusion of "with the devas" (*sadevaka*), the deities of the five sensual-sphere realms (*pañca-kāmāvacara*) are included through the principle of elimination (*pārisesa-naya*), since the others are already comprised by the other terms. By the inclusion of "with Māra" (*samāraka*), the deities of the sixth sensual-sphere realm are included through the principle of proximity (*paccāsatti-naya*), for Māra is both born there and resides there.
By the expression "with Brahmā" (*sabrahmaka*), the deities of the Brahma-world such as the *Brahmakāyika* and others are included.

It is by the principle of proximity alone. In the phrase “of the generation together with recluses and brahmins,” there is the inclusion of those recluses and brahmins who are adversaries of the Dispensation.
This is merely an illustration, because by that same expression, those recluses and brahmins who are not adversaries and have neither restrained their evil nor cast out their evil are also included.
Granted, the word *loka* (world) refers to the realm of sentient beings by virtue of the qualifiers such as “together with devas.”

It is understood [that this compound applies] because their grammatical construction (*yoga*) is identical. However, since this compound is found even in cases where the construction is not identical—as in the phrase "having hair and having wings" (*salomako sapakkhako*)—the word *pajā* (progeny) is included to demonstrate that there is such deviation. By the term *pajā*, the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is intended.

Although Māra and Brahmā are included by virtue of their commonality as divine beings (*devabhāva*), the mention of the others is for the purpose of showing the specific distinctions that apply to them.
Showing that the mention is separate, he said, “Māra by name,” and so forth. He said, “of all,” because Māra is capable of causing even the Brahmās to lose their vision.
“Above” means in the higher realm. He said, “Brahmā,” referring to the ten thousand Brahmās; thus he said, “with ten fingers,” and so forth.
Here, as in the Dīgha Nikāya and others, there are also collections of texts belonging to outsiders.
He says, "by way of the single *nikāya* and so forth," because [the term] is obtained [in that sense].

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the science of sites (*vatthuvijjā*) and so forth," the various branches of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*) are included. Because they are born and produced by their respective kamma and defilements, they are called "beings" (*pajā*), meaning the class of sentient beings (*sattanikāya*).
[The phrase] "of that being" refers to this. Alternatively, by the expression "together with gods and humans" (*sadevamanussāya*), conventional gods (*sammutideva*) are included.

And the inclusion of the human world (manussaloka) should be understood as remaining [from that]. Having thus taken the world by way of its parts and shown the *yojana*, now, in order to show the *yojana* by taking the world without regard for its parts, it is said: "Moreover, here...

These [terms] are stated by way of the world (*loka*), having been made in the sense of "wherein karma and the fruits of karma are manifested" (*lokīyanti*); and by way of beings (*pajā*), in the sense of "it is produced (*pajāyati*) by means of causes and conditions."

Having made [this point]. Regarding the phrase "more perfected in virtue" (*sīlasampannataran*), here it is the state of being complete and perfected that is intended, as in such expressions as "the rice field is well-perfected" (*sampannaṃ sālikedāraṃ*).

Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'more abundant'. Even that which is complete deserves to be called "more abundant. "In the remaining cases" refers to [the phrases] "more perfected in concentration" (*samādhisampannataran*) and so forth.

Regarding the terms "reason" (*kāraṇa*) and so forth: "reason" means logical justification; "meaning" (*attha*) means the non-perverted meaning; "growth" (*vuḍḍhi*) means the cause of further increase.
"By this statement" refers to the statement spoken immediately following in this sutta.
To show that he should be refuted not only by this [statement] but also by bringing forward another sutta, he said, "I have no teacher," and so forth. Regarding what should be said here:

This has already been stated in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*. He said "by those who remember" (*sarantena*), taking this as the nominative case in the sense of the instrument;
or rather, the meaning is "those who remember by means of the causes for remembering.
The commentary on the *Gāravasutta* is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Brahmadeva Sutta 174.
"Alone" (*ekako*) means being detached due to abiding in seclusion. By this, his freedom from the company of crowds is indicated;

however, his freedom from the company of defilements is revealed by the words "heedful" (*appamatto*) and so forth. "With mind directed toward" (*pesitatto*) means having one's consciousness directed toward Nibbāna. "Truly" (*sammadeva*)...
It is indeed according to the proper method. However, if it is obtained starting from the arrival [of the path], there is nothing further to be said;
yet, if it is obtained starting from the commencement of the practice, this too is certainly appropriate—to show this, the phrase "in whatever way or that way" and so forth was stated.

Because the penetration of non-delusion has reached its culmination through the attainment of the supreme path, the non-delusion regarding the qualities of the fruit is even more eminent than that regarding the qualities of the path.
Because it is said, "by his own direct knowledge" (*sayam abhiññā*), he says, "having known for himself.
Furthermore, because his knowing is a realization—a making manifest to oneself—he says, "having realized" (*sacchikatvā*), meaning "having made it manifest.
Likewise, because this realization for him is the attainment of insight (*vipassanā*), he says, "having entered upon" (*upasampajja*), meaning "having acquired it. By this...
By the statement beginning with “Birth is exhausted” (*khīṇā jāti*), etc.:

here, by the heading “birth,” the aggregates (*khandha*) that possess its characteristics are meant. “Exhausted even before” means because it was already exhausted in the past, prior to the attainment of the Path.
In that regard, [it is said] concerning the future; “due to the absence of effort” means because of its non-existence.
This was stated by way of a figurative expression, having taken the commonality of the state of being "future. The ellipsis to be supplied is:

"They are not present because they do not exist," and "the development of the path is defiled. Just as when the root of a young tree that has not yet borne fruit is cut, the fruits that were destined to arise in the future do not arise due to the condition of the cutting and are thus said to be "lost," so too [is it] in the absence of development.
By the passage beginning with "But as for the path," [the author] shows this meaning: that when the path is cultivated, those defilements liable to arise and the birth conditioned by them,
being not arising, are said to be "abandoned" because they have reached the state of non-arising through knowledge characterized by the destruction of lust.
*Soḷasakiccabhāvāyā* means for the state of having sixteen functions, or for the production of the state of sixteenfold function.
In the text, *sapadānaṃ* refers to walking in regular succession (*sapadānacāra*), expressed by means of a neuter abstract noun; thus he says, “walking in regular succession.
*Anukkammaṃ* means without overstepping. *Āhutipiṇḍaṃ* means a lump of offering, that is, a lump of porridge to be cast into the fire by way of sacrifice.
The intention (*adhippāya*). "Offering of food" (*bhūtabalikamma*) means performing the offering by having [the food] placed there in that manner.

"Smeared with green [cow dung]" (*haritupalitta*) means having the ground plastered with fresh cow dung. "Encircled by forest garlands" (*vanamālaparikkhitta*) means surrounded by beautiful garlands of wild flowers.
"Incense ladle" (*dhūmakaṭacchu*) means the inhalation of smoke. "Fragrance of virtue" (*sīlagandha*) means the fragrance of reputation arising dependent upon virtue (*sīla*).
"Of one who is being struck" means of one who seizes what has approached [him].
"From this place" means from this dwelling-place of humans; the intention is "from the surface of the great earth.

"The lowest of all" refers to the Brahma-world of Vāsava, the abode of the Brahmapārisajja devas. The "Brahma-path" refers to the four wholesome jhānas, because they constitute the path to the Brahma-world.
The "path of life" (*jīvitapatha*) is so called because it serves as the means for the continuation of life. He says, “Why do you mutter?

and so forth, with reference to the words, “May your lordship, Great Brahmā, eat. “Grains of grass” (*tiṇabījāni*) refers to rice grains and the like. He speaks of “cow’s milk” (*goyūsa*) while feeling disgust.
This meaning is also clarified by the statement, “The food of Brahmā is not of this kind.”

Even though he has attained the state of surpassing the gods (*atidevapatta*), because the five aggregates as a basis still exist, what is grasped is his being devoid specifically of the defilements as a basis (*kilesūpadhi*) and so forth.
For that meaning is understood through the abstract suffix (*bhāvapaccaya*) [in *atidevatā*]; thus it says, "he has attained the state of surpassing the gods" (*atidevabhāvaṃ patto*).
Since even the Brahmās, being included within the divine realm (*devagati*), are indeed gods, it is therefore said, "he has attained the state of surpassing the Brahmās" (*atibrahmabhāvaṃ patto*).
"Having developed himself" means having stood after increasing and nourishing himself with qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).

Ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) are "trembling" because of their trembling due to craving, conceit, views, and limited taints (*āsava*). Those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are called "steadfast" because of the total absence of wandering among the realms of existence (*gati*).
For it is thus: because they have completely seen the Four Truths, there is no longer any inheritance of becoming (*bhavadāyajja*).
Because they still possess the state of being slaves to craving and because their nature is to wander through certain realms of existence, those in training (sekha) are not stable.
"Bhajamānā" means being associated with; they associate specifically with the side of stability—the most excellent side—which is exclusively praised, by virtue of their state of associating with it.

One whose defilements have been abandoned, whose taints are destroyed, and who is free from the poison [of craving], is happy; he shines with happiness in the future. That which brings about his happiness is "happiness-making" (*sukhāyitika*).
The commentary on the *Brahmadeva Sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Baka Brahmā Sutta*.
175. The view that occurs as “the self and the world are eternal” is the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*).
“Together with the body” means together with that state of existence as a Brahmā. “The Brahmā-abode” refers to his own basis as a Brahmā.
He says what is impermanent is “permanent” because, due to its impermanence, he himself is not clearly perceived. “Firm” means strong; it is “substantial” because of the absence of destruction.

The meaning is as follows: It is "ever-present" because it exists at all times due to the absence of arising and transformation. It is "absolute" (*kevala*), which means complete; therefore he said, "unbroken.
Alternatively, "absolute" means unmixed with birth and so forth; the intention is that it is devoid [of them].

Precisely because of the absence of arising and so forth, it is "subject to no passing away. There is no one who is born... [or] who undergoes rebirth, because of its eternal nature, together with its station.
“Of those dwelling therein. For he (the Buddha) acknowledges their state as permanent. “The three planes of jhāna” refers to the planes of the second, third, and fourth jhānas.

For the non-percipient beings (*asañña*), the pure abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), and the formless realms (*arūpabhava*) are specific distinctions within the plane of the fourth jhāna. Alternatively, in the phrase “Nibbāna,” the word *iti* has the sense of “beginning” and not the sense of “conclusion”;
therefore, by the word “all,” that which was stated as “non-percipient beings... [and] the states of existence” is included.

He conceals it. "He denies" means that, while the state actually exists, he rejects it by saying "it does not exist," as if he were unaware of its presence. Some are residents of the Uttaravihāra monastery.
"One reborn in a lower plane" means one who has been reborn in the lower planes. Now, in order to explain this matter, the words "when it has not arisen," and so forth, are stated.
"Having made it a rebirth [jhāna] in a lower plane" means having produced the rebirth-jhāna in the third-jhāna plane, which is below the plane where one currently resides.
The intention is that this is not merely a matter of aspiration, as is the case with higher jhānas.

"At the first moment" means at the initial moment of that existence. He "knew" because of its proximity. "Both" refers to both the specific kamma performed by himself and the place where he was reborn.
Having forgotten [the cause], he did not reflect upon his rebirth.

“Gone with ignorance” means proceeding together with ignorance. For this is an instrumental expression used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). Therefore he said, “endowed with. “Ignorant” means one who does not know.
Because he is deprived of the eye of wisdom, he has become blind; the meaning is that he has fallen into a state of blindness.
Regarding the future tense, this word [“will speak”] occurs through the employment of the particle *yattha* (where), whereas the meaning refers to the present time. Therefore he said:
"He speaks" means: therefore he says "where," and so forth.
"A highway robber" means a thief who lies in wait on the road. "Being terrified" means being terrified by such [words] as, "Alas, sir, the Brahmā Baka has fallen into ignorance!
"Having regained mindfulness" means, through that very terror, having emerged with wise reflection regarding the object of his previous birth.
"Having obtained mindfulness. "Desiring to press" means desiring to rub, desiring to show up the fault [by saying], "Look at this!
To such an extent have you transgressed! "Performers of merit" means those who do meritorious deeds. "Because they have gone forth and proceeded by means of wisdoms" (*vedehi*).
"The final rebirth in the Brahma-world" means the attainment of the state of a Brahma for the very last time. "They long for us" means they long for us (*asmā*).
He is a *brahmā* because his qualities have been developed through [the perfection of] life-span, beauty, and so forth. He is a *mahābrahmā* because he is greater than others.
He is "overpowering" (*abhibhū*) because he stands having overcome that Brahma-world by way of being the eldest. He is "unoverpowered" (*anabhibhūta*) because he is not overcome by others.
"Exclusively" (*aññadatthu*) is a term used for emphasis. He is "all-seeing" (*dasa*) by way of vision; the intention is that he sees everything. He is "masterful" (*vasavattī*).
He brings all people under his control. He is the Lord in the world; he is the Lord. He is the Maker and Creator of the world; he is the maker and creator. He is the Best and the Distributor;
he is the supreme one and the apportioner of this world. He is the Ruler and the Father of beings past and future;
because he exercises habitual mastery, he is the Ruler. He is the father of beings who have been born and of those yet to be born—those who seek existence—who desire, boast of, envy, and honor him.
The Blessed One, having delimited that which was described as "this is permanent, this is stable, this is eternal" by way of perverted perception, shows it to be "little, trifling. For instance,
if one were to remove a single sesame seed every hundred years from a Kosalan cartload of sesame seeds, those seeds would reach exhaustion [only after a vast number of years].
"But not even for an Abbuda [hell] is there such a lifespan"—thus it is called Abbuda;
by that measure, Nirabbuda is twenty times greater, and by that measure of Nirabbudas, there are one hundred thousand Nirabbudas. This is the summary here;
however, the calculation of the years of the lifespan in Paduma will come later in this very Saṃyutta. "Anantadassī" means of infinite vision.

One who sees the knowable without remainder. "Vata-sīla-vatta" means that which has become a *vata* (vow) by way of undertaking, and because it is practiced through the conduct of virtue (*cāritta-sīla*), it is a *sīla-vatta*.
However, since that is one and the same, he said, "merely virtue" (*sīlam eva*).
Regarding the word "apāyesi" (he caused to drink): when he caused thirsty people to drink water, [the merit arose] starting from the very moment of that performance.
The passage beginning with “Therein” was commenced in order to demonstrate this. “In the past” means in a previous birth.
This Brahmā, having developed jhāna through the inclination, “I shall bring about an end to aging and death,” was reborn in the Brahma-world;
there, he perceived it as Nibbāna. “He passes his time delighting in jhāna” refers to the continuous occurrence of that activity at that time.

The application [of the verb] occurs based on [the action] currently taking place. Because the carts that were following behind a cart traveling ahead through the thick darkness of night turned back by virtue of [hearing] the sound [of it], it is said: "all the carts having likewise turned back.
"Ready for battle" means prepared for war. "Loot" means plundered goods. Regarding the phrase "at the bank of the Eṇī": here, [the word] "panihatāya" [is used].
Some say it is called "Niccagaṅgā" (Ever-flowing Ganges). Others say that because of the abundance of black antelopes (*eṇimiga*) there, that region on the bank of the Ganges is called "Eṇikūla.
A "Gaṅgeyyaka" is one who dwells near the Ganges. A "baddhacara" is one whose conduct is bound [to another];
thus he said, "a resident pupil (*antevāsika*). Because the Buddha is omniscient, therefore...
"He understood" means that he knew everything that had been forgotten by me here; this is the intended meaning.
Illuminating the entire Brahmā-world, the Blessed One stands illuminating his own light—which is not shared with others—having surpassed all other light in this Brahmā-world.
The commentary on the *Baka-Brahma Sutta* is concluded.
5. Commentary on the *Aññatarabrahmasutta* 176.

“Having performed the preliminary work for the fire-kasiṇa”: here, the preliminary work for the fire-kasiṇa is simply the arising of the thought, “I shall attain the jhāna that is the preliminary work for the fire-kasiṇa.
For it is not as with others that the Buddhas [attain it] by means of entering into jhāna therein.
There is an elaboration of preliminary work (*parikamma-papañca*) because [the Blessed One] has attained mastery in all respects and reached the state of supreme excellence.
It is said that this Brahmā held the view, "There is no other who possesses such great power as I," with reference to which it was stated:
"There is no ascetic or brahmin who could come here. The Blessed One [addressed] him...
In order to relinquish his resolve, he entered the fire-element and sat in the air above him. Therefore it was said: “Having seen the Tathāgata... having entered the fire-element.
It is “penetrating to the bone” (*aṭṭhivedhī*) because it can be pierced as far as the bone;
the meaning is that it should be pierced just as [an arrow] pierces a bone and remains striking against the marrow. But this—
"Like a bone-piercer" means "like a bone-piercer"; the meaning is that one should act in such a way that he relinquishes his adherence.
"Of the others" refers to the elders Mahākassapa, Mahākappina, and Anuruddha.

"The radiance of the bodies, celestial mansions, ornaments, and so forth of other Brahmās" refers to the radiance of the bodies of Brahmās, the radiance of their celestial mansions, and the radiance of their ornaments, garments, and so on.
It outshines all these splendors in this Brahma-world by means of its own radiant nature.
"There is no more for me" (*natthi me sā*) means: "Now I have no such view; I no longer hold the conviction that 'there is no ascetic or brahmin who could come here.
Therefore he said: "In that regard, for him... [etc. ...they are abandoned. "In this" (*ettha*) means in this [state].
In that assembly, he gave such a great teaching on the Dhamma that the Brahmā was completely liberated from his wrong views and the eye of Dhamma arose within him.
[The Buddha spoke] with just as much [as was necessary], as stated in the words beginning, "Even today, friend... and so forth. These were spoken in their specific form by means of the first line.

With four [powers] under the first [heading] and one under the second, thus five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) are stated according to their specific forms. Why is the divine ear (*dibbasota*) not included here?

He says: "It is indeed included by virtue of those [other powers]. For one who has attained these supramundane (*lokuttara*) direct knowledges, the accomplishment of the divine ear is not difficult, because it succeeds with ease through the removal of its opposites.
The commentary on the Aññatarabrahma Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Brahmaloka Sutta. 177.
*Paccekaṃ dvārabāhaṃ* means "each doorpost. Here, the word *pacceka* is used in the sense of repetition (*āvutti*).
It should be understood; [the commentator] said "each one, each one" to mean "individually, individually.
For among them, one solitary Brahmā stood leaning against one door-post of the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī), while the other leaned against the other.

And "solitary Brahmā" (paccekabrahmā) means a Brahmā who wanders alone, not a Brahmā who wanders with a retinue. [The name] Samiddhi refers to the celestial enjoyments in heaven and to the [qualities of] the Brahmās.
"Meditative absorption (jhāna) is an accessory to happiness" means it is enriched by the bliss of jhāna.

Because of the attainment of abundance in prosperity, and because of the Brahmās' attainment of abundance through the qualities of direct knowledge (abhiññā), he said: "It is 'thriving' (phīta) because it is well-flowered with the flowers of direct knowledge.
"Unable to endure" means not being able to endure, or not approving.
“Satapadaṃ” means the word *sata*. “By way of form” (*rūpavasena*) means by way of the word *rūpa*; the sense is: together with the word *rūpa*.
The same applies here to “by way of the remote” (*pantivasena*). “Ekacce” means some deer; the sense is: five hundred of those tigress-disguised ones.
“Whose attendant shall we go to?”—this was said out of pride (*ahaṅkāra*), looking on with wonder at the excellence of the celestial mansion (*vimānasampatti*).
He speaks thus: "They clash and cause reproach; therefore they are called *raṇā*, which means faults (*dosā*).

The arising of a transformation upon the convergence of opposing conditions is 'distortion' (*ruppana*); it is the shaking (*pavedhana*) of form (*rūpa*). Thus he said: "It is constantly shaken by cold and the like.

The Teacher Sumedha, possessing beautiful wisdom, does not delight in forms; what then of one of dull wisdom who delights in forms, failing to see both their vulnerability and their constant shaking? This is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the *Brahmaloka Sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Kokālika Sutta*: 178.
Because of the absence of lust and other defilements that cause measurement, one whose taints are destroyed cannot be measured by way of lust and so forth.

It is immeasurable; or, because it stands having pierced through the four noble truths which are immeasurable, there is no "measured" (*pamita*) object of measurement (*pameyya*) for it that could be measured (*parimeyya*).
Therefore he said: “The one whose taints are destroyed... illuminates. “That” refers to the one whose taints are destroyed.

“To measure” means, being a seeker of faults, to delimit [him] by way of defects. Regarding his measuring according to true nature, it is “downward-turned wisdom” due to the inferiority of his own wisdom.
The commentary on the Kokālikasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Katamodakatissasutta 179.
Why is wisdom called *kissa*? It is that by which one hears "What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? and so forth, in the search for what is wholesome (*kusalagavesitāya*). Thus it is called *kissa*.
The commentary on the Katamodakatissa Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Turū Brahmā Sutta. 180.
“Ābādhika” means one who has an affliction (ābādha). “In the immediately following sutta” refers to the sutta that follows next. “Wretched” (varāka) means...
This is merely a word of encouragement, not a statement made in its literal sense.
By the term "piyasīlā," he shows that the word "pesalā" is established in this sense according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*).
"Kabarakkhīnī" means eyes that have become clouded due to their color being impaired by the force of the disease. "Yattakaṃ" means as much of the Blessed One’s word as you are altering.

The meaning is that there is no measure for what has been transgressed by her. Since for one called a non-returner (anāgāmin), sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill will (byāpāda) have been abandoned, and yet you have come here having been seen through the influence of sensual desire and ill will, therefore the meaning to be understood here is simply this: "Insofar as this has been transgressed by you."
"One who has not attained vision" means one who has not reached the sign of vision; he stands like one who has swallowed poison, as if he were a "poison-swallower.
Shears are like an axe in the sense that they cut at the root. "In the supreme goal" means in Arahantship.

He says, "He is one whose taints are destroyed," just as Sunakkhatta spoke of the naked Korakkhattiya. One whose taints are destroyed is worthy of praise, like the Chief Disciple; yet he calls such a person "immoral."

Or, for one who says: "The praise of one worthy of praise and the blame of one worthy of blame are equal in their result"—this blame, which proceeds by way of destroying existing virtues, has a more bitter result due to its great culpability;

likewise, even the praise of one worthy of blame has a result equal [in culpability] due to its great culpability, because by superimposing non-existent virtues upon another, it becomes a cause for both oneself and others to engage in wrong practice toward the one worthy of praise.

And because it brings about equanimity for him. For even in the world, people regard one who was previously worthy of respect as a recluse with equanimity, let alone one who has now fallen into wrong practice; thus they treat them as equals. "By his own" means by his own property.

This offense is minor because it pertains to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and because it can be remedied. This [other] is a much greater *kali*, because it pertains to future lives (*samparāyika*), is accumulated through intentional action, and cannot be remedied.
"Nirabbuda" is a specific numerical designation meaning "one"; thus he says "by the calculation of nirabbudas," which refers to one hundred thousand nirabbudas.

This is the meaning. As for the calculation of the *nirabbuda* hell, it has already been explained above. Regarding the statement, "The reviler of noble ones goes to hell," it should be understood that the lifespan mentioned there refers to one who reviles ordinary noble ones (*ariya*).
However, they say that because of the greatness of the virtues of the Chief Disciples (*aggasāvaka*), the lifespan in their case is even much greater than that.
The commentary on the Turūbrahmasutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Kokālikasutta 181.
There were two monks named Kokālika; in order to distinguish and identify the one intended here, [the text says]: "Who..."
“Is this Kokālika?”—this is the question. To show the origin (*aṭṭhuppatti*) of the sutta, [the text asks]: “And why did he approach?”—this is the question.

“It is said that this one,” and so forth, is the answer to those questions in due order. Because they desired to dwell in seclusion and because of their fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), they dwelt [there] lest anyone... [should disturb them].

"They will depart" means he conceived resentment because his own desire was frustrated. The elders handed them over to the Saṅgha of monks because they had not performed the formal act (*payuttavācā*) and because it had not been announced by the elders. With the words "Even before...
and so forth, up to "I think," he suspects that the elders are standing in hypocrisy, like one who sees a wound in a healthy place, as if looking at the surface of a clean mirror.
And it was as if he were raising up a letter.

"Having offended" means having said in the presence of the Blessed One, "Evil bhikkhus have arisen. He said, "A mine of faith, bringing forth serenity"; the meaning is "one who possesses active faith," hence he said, "one whose words are to be trusted.
As for a boil, it breaks through the bone starting from the outside; but these [abscesses] break through the bone first of all.

*Uggatā* means risen up. *Taruṇabeluvamattiyo* means the size of young jackfruit fruits. *Visagilito* means one who has cast down a weapon; in common worldly parlance, that [weapon] is designated as "poison" (*visa*).
The phrase "having heard the guardian deities" (*ārakkhadevatānaṃ sutvā*) is to be connected by supplying the word [from the previous context].

A bowl from the Magadha kingdom is called a *māgadhaka* bowl because it was traded in the Magadha country; by that [measure], a cartload of sesame seeds is said to be a *tilavāha*. "Of the place to be boiled" refers to the location where one is to be boiled by the suffering of hell. This is the name "Abbudā."
Regarding the calculation of years: in the case of the lifespan in the Abbuda hell, it is tenfold starting from one;
beyond that, in the Nirabbuda and subsequent hells, the calculation of years should be understood as being twentyfold. "In all" refers to all the hells beginning with Abbuda and ending with Paduma.
"The same method applies" extends by analogy the state of being twentyfold for each successive higher hell above the preceding one.
The commentary on the Kokālikasutta is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Second Chapter.
1. Commentary on the Sanaṅkumāra Sutta 182.

"Of old" (*porāṇaka*) means because he has existed for a long time since his birth. He is a "person" (*jana*) because he is born; one who leads people from this [world] is a "leader of men" (*janetā*), and [the term refers to him] in that sense.
A "noble" (*khattiya*) is preeminent because, through the protection of worldly boundaries and by enjoining beings toward right practice, he leads them.
Because of its great helpfulness. For one who thus establishes others therein becomes established therein oneself; therefore, it is called "supreme.

In the sense of piercing through opposing factors and in the sense of making known past lives and so forth, it is called "clear vision" (*vijjā*). These seven true qualities (*saddhamma*) are faith, moral shame, moral dread, erudition, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom.
They are called "bases of conduct" (*caraṇa*) because by means of them one travels toward a direction not previously gone; they are fifteen factors beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
The commentary on the Sanaṅkumāra-sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Devadatta-sutta: 183.
Since the act of causing schism had already been committed even before the training rule was laid down, and because he remained [in that state] with his very own characteristic marks...

“It should not be said that ‘Devadatta has departed from the teaching’; rather, regarding the phrase ‘not long after he had departed,’ it is stated that he went ‘from Veḷuvana to Gayāsīsa,’ instead of saying ‘having departed from the teaching.
For one who is a regular member (*pakatatta*) may cause a schism in the Saṅgha of monks, but not one who is not a regular member (*apakatatta*).
*Vaḷavāya* means born from the womb of a mare.”
The commentary on the Devadatta Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Andhakavinda Sutta: 184.
"Janata" means a multitude of people; the meaning is a place where people congregate. "In a place not frequented by men..."
To whatever extent there is movement for those performing duties such as plowing, beyond that distance is the non-proximate area (*anupacāra*).
"For the sake of release from the fetters" means for the purpose of liberation from the fetters. "Not obtaining the delight in seclusion, the bliss of seclusion, and the jhāna":
previously, people thought of me as one who was secluded by living in the forest, unassociated with others, and energetic; now—
Seeing him living in a village, people might lose confidence in him, thinking, "He has become settled in the company and socializing of crowds.
Even if one has no personal delight here, one should not live with a distracted mind, thinking, "Even though this is so, I shall live right here.

The intended meaning is: "What is the point of falling under the sway of the mind? One who is devoted to the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) is one who delights in the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness.
For in this way, even living in a community is praiseworthy for him, since the duties of a recluse cannot be accomplished without dwelling in seclusion.
The intention is that he is liberated from the fear of the round of existence by virtue of his underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*).

By the words "he sat there with the monks," he shows their sitting according to their preference because he is not dependent on the perception of a self (*sattūpaladdhi*). Therefore he said, "by this," and so forth.
The phrase "born in this and that manner" is neither a vision based on hearsay nor the grasping of hearsay.

The construction is: "I do not speak because of mere reasoning (takkahetu) or because of a methodological principle (nayahetu). That from which the basket (piṭaka) or the text (gantha) is acquired is "the acquisition of the basket" (piṭakasampadāna);
by means of the grasping of the text—that is, by way of being the one who grasps the basket through the mastery of that text—according to some following of the text, thus...
The meaning is: "I do not speak. It is called *brahmacariya* because the conduct (*cariya*) of the supreme Dhamma, which is the Brahmā, proceeds verbally;
that is, the teaching of the Dhamma. By means of the cultivation [of the path], there is the complete relinquishing through the total abandoning of death for those who have renounced death.
And as for them, he said "those whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsavānaṃ*) because they have exhausted birth.
"Ten times ten" means ten times ten, that is, one hundred. "Another" means other than the one thousand five hundred. "Partakers of merit":
he shows that he is unable to count how many beings were born as a result of that teaching who partake of the merit associated with the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭanissita-puñña*).
He says it was "the teaching on the qualities of a Brahmā" because it was spoken by Brahmā.
The commentary on the *Andhakavinda Sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Aruṇavatī Sutta*: 185.
"Abhibhū" and "Sambhava" are the names of those two great elders (*mahāthera*). To show their distinction:
The words beginning with “tesu” have been stated. This shows that these two were the foremost disciples (aggasāvaka) of that Blessed One.
“They disparage” (avajjhāyanti) means they think of [him] by placing him below. “They revile” (khiyyanti) means they cause him to be regarded as inferior; they treat him as something base.
“They expand upon it” (vitthārayantā) means they cause that very inferiority to be thought of to reach a state of abundance. All the various sectarians (pāsaṇḍa)... their own...

The construction is as follows: at their own time and according to their own tenets, all gods and humans praise human effort (*purisakāra*) upon obtaining their respective systems and having attained their respective goals.

"Exertion-energeticness" (*ārambhavīriya*) refers to the energetic exertion in shaking off the defilements comprised within the army of Māra; that which is called the "element of exertion" (*ārambhadhātu*).
It is called "exertion-virya" (nikkamavīriya), which is the virya that is the opposite of indolence; it is what is referred to as the "element of exertion" (nikkamadhātu).
"Exert yourselves" means: by stepping from one stage to the next, proceed with an even more powerful application of cultivation;
thus he said, "Strive. The so-called "army of defilements" (kilesasenā) is the collection of defilements such as lust and the rest.
Because it is the condition for death, it is called "the army of Death. It is with reference to this that it was said: "by Death with its great army.
With the intention that the first manifestation of the aggregates is "birth," while their subsequent successive occurrence is "saṃsāra," he said:
"both birth and saṃsāra. This is because, in such passages as "even one birth, or two births," and so forth...
The occurrence of the aggregates (khandhas), delimited by the taking up and laying down [of the body] in each respective existence, is called "birth" (jāti).
That very same process, proceeding from one state to another until final Nibbāna, is "saṃsāra," because it involves wandering here and there;
therefore, he said, "or saṃsāra, which is synonymous with birth. "Limit" (pariccheda) means the end. "He pervaded with radiance" (obhāsaṃ phari): [this refers to the light].
The connection [is as follows]: "In a place where there is light" means in a place where light has been produced by oneself.
"There is no need for light" means that just as there is no need to see light in a place of darkness, there is no need to see light in a place where light already exists.
Therefore, as those beings investigate and reflect, "What is this light? Whose light is this?"—the word "all" refers to [those within] the thousandfold world-system.
"All gods and humans. "To the assembled multitude" means to the entire gathered and well-defined assembly that had come together for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
"They heard the sound" means they did not merely hear the sound, but also the meaning;
thus, it became as manifest to them as if within the range of their ordinary hearing, making itself known throughout the three-thousandfold world system.
The commentary on the Aruṇavatīsutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Parinibbānasutta 186.
"Thus it was at Kusinārā" means that just as the Thūpārāma of Anurādhapura is situated in the south-western direction, [so was this place].

Thus, that park was situated to the south-west of Kusinārā. Therefore—because those desiring to enter the city approach it from the park, proceed toward it, and move along it, it is called "Upavattana" (the Approach)—for that reason.

"That" refers to the Sāla grove standing in the form of a row of Sāla trees. "Between" means in the middle. "Appamajjana" is diligence (*appamāda*); as for its meaning, however, it is associated with knowledge.
Because mindfulness has a preeminent function therein, it is said: "by non-separation from mindfulness.
He spoke this by including it within the very term *appamāda* (heedfulness), since it encompasses the entire word of the Buddha in its meaning.
And because of his supreme mastery over the mind in regard to the jhānas and so forth, [he could enter] "in such a time, such attainments..."
"Having attained [this attainment], I shall attain final Nibbāna"—having thus set a time limit, the entering into that attainment is what is intended by "preparation for final Nibbāna.
"The Elder" refers to the Elder Anuruddha.
And this too—the discourse on the entry into the fifty-six aforementioned jhānas—is merely a summary exposition.
Why? Because the Blessed One, at that time, entered all the daily functional attainments (*vaḷañjana-samāpatti*) without exception;
thus, showing this, he said, "Entering the city of Nibbāna," and so forth. Regarding the passage "Having entered twenty-four...
and so on, some first say: "The Blessed One, daily, twelve hundred thousand times ten million [times] entered the attainment of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*)."

He enters [the attainment]; he enters the attainment of fruition exactly one hundred and twenty million times; therefore, even then, he enters attainments numbering two hundred and forty million. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, two types of thoughts frequently occur to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One...”

“the thought of security and the thought of seclusion. For the thought of security stands having fulfilled the Blessed One’s attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*), while the thought of seclusion stands having fulfilled the attainment of the fruit of arahantship.
Indeed, for Buddhas, the latent tendency of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is light, and their mastery over attainments has reached its peak;
therefore, their entry into and emergence from attainments occurs in only a few moments of consciousness (*cittakkhaṇa*).
They succeed. The Blessed One enters these twelve attainments— the five fine-material-sphere attainments, the four immaterial-sphere attainments,
together with the attainment of the measureless states and the attainment of cessation, as well as the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship—
each one a hundred thousand times ten million times every day before his meal, and likewise after his meal.
“Thus, there are twenty-four hundred thousand kasiṇa attainments that are practiced daily.

Others, however, say: “On the day of his full enlightenment, during the last watch of the night, the Blessed One—having applied his knowledge by way of the factors of dependent origination in reverse order starting from aging-and-death, and having begun the insight into phenomena as they arise one after another—”
Just as a man cutting through a vast, dense, and very difficult forest might from time to time whet his axe on a sharpening stone,
even so, by entering the attainments— which are like sharpening stones— from time to time, one should,
in both forward and reverse order, individually [contemplate] the factors of dependent origination in order to bring about the sharpness and clarity of knowledge.
He exercises the knowledge of comprehension by means of entering into millions of attainments;

following that, even though he has become a Buddha, the Blessed One enters into millions of attainments of fruit every day by way of insight through the factors of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order—it is with reference to this that it was said: "numbering twenty-four hundred thousand crores..."
"Having entered the attainments.

These two [attainments] also, for the most part, do not possess the quality of immediate succession (ānantariyakatā) even with respect to their reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), because they belong to the side of jhāna.
Since the very last life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta) is called "death" (cuti) because of its falling away from this or that state, therefore [the attainment of cessation] is not...
It was stated, beginning with "whosoever," in order to show that it is not only this Blessed One, but rather all sentient beings pass away by means of the *bhavaṅga*-consciousness alone.
"By the truth of suffering" (*dukkhasaccena*) means they pass away—that is, they reach the end of their time—by means of the death-consciousness included within the truth of suffering;
or, they pass away (*pecca*) because of the act of dying.

"Devoid of a counterpart" means being without a person who is his equal due to the incomparability of his virtues such as morality (*sīla*). "Cessation" (*vūpasama*) is so called because here all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) are stilled;
thus, Nibbāna—so designated, known, and described—is itself bliss.

"Causing the hair to stand on end" means bringing about a state where the hairs of the body bristle with joy. "Terrifying" means it was something that produced fear in those who have not yet abandoned lust. "Endowed with the qualities of excellence in every aspect."
He was endowed with all excellent modes and supreme causes, namely the virtues of morality and so forth. "Uncontracted" means not bent, due to the absence of contraction.
"As if fully blossomed" means well-expanded through the association with rapture and joy.
He endured the feeling because he had thoroughly understood it by way of its intrinsic nature, origin, and so forth. "Unobstructed liberation" is the state of complete dispassion.

Therefore he said: "The arrival at the state of non-designation. "Like the extinguishing of a light" means like the extinguishing of a lamp, because after it has dissolved there, there is no remaining.
The commentary on the *Parinibbāna Sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Brahma-saṃyutta* within the *Sāratthappakāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, is completed.
7. Saṃyutta Nikāya: Brāhmaṇa Saṃyutta 1.
Arahanta Vagga 1. Dhanañjānī Sutta Commentary The commentary on the Dhanañjānī Sutta, the first in the Chapter on Arahants within the Saṃyutta on Brahmins.

187. Regarding the term *Dhanañjānigotta*: here, *gotta* refers to that which protects (*gāyatīti*) the lineage (*gaṃ*)—that is, the designation by name of the family line descended from one's ancestors.

(What, then, is this? It should be understood as a common form shared by all members included in that family, originating from the first ancestor of that family and not shared with other family successions. This [lady] has the *Dhanañjāni* lineage.
[They were] of the Dhanañjāni clan. Having asked the reason for that *udāna*, the passage beginning with “So kira” was spoken in order to explain it from the very beginning.

The construction is: “He gives food of various flavors. The meal of the brahmins consists of rice prepared with the five products of the cow (*pañcagorasa*), accompanied by soups, vegetables, and condiments, and possessing various flavors.
“A sword with a circular tip” means a sword known as a *maṇḍalagga*. It is of two kinds...
For there are three kinds of swords: the circular-edged, the broad-edged, and the long-edged. In this context, that whose edge is positioned in a circular shape is the circular-edged;
whereas that which is as long as a sword-blade is the long-edged.
"Instruction" (*sāsana*) means teaching. It refers to the five-line stanza beginning with "Homage... to the Fully Enlightened One. In the Teacher’s instruction...
Indeed, this should be understood as a five-line verse (*pañcapadikagāthā*) that disregards worldly desire.
"Okkāvaradharā" means those who maintain the noble lineage of Okkāka, which is reckoned as their ancestral line. "Sakka" means that which is possible.
"Evaṃ" refers to this manner, beginning with the words "If my limbs... [and so forth]. Furthermore, the five hundred verses [of the *Saccasaṃyutta*] are the commentary...
They say, "Though [many] have ascended, only two have been extracted here.
"Unable even to strike" means being unable to strike or touch it even once with the hand or the foot.
For he, though having threatened her in order to bring her under his control by means of his own power through the majesty of that noble female disciple, followed after her and became fruitless.
It was so. Therefore he said, “Lady,” and so forth.
“Of that brahmin” means of her own husband, the brahmin. “Offering” means presenting. “At that time” means at the moment of the arising of suffering;
having recollected the Blessed One’s words, “All conditioned phenomena are suffering,” [she thought], “Of the One Possessing the Ten Powers...”
In such passages as "of the Blessed One," he recalled the epithets of his qualities as they were familiar to him; hence he said, "the possessor of the ten powers.
"Having become angry" means due to a lack of patience and gentleness. "Having been broken" means that, because of the absence of self-restraint, the friendship within that brahmin was broken.
"Just so" means just as it is now without cause, so too at another time it was without cause.
This is the meaning. The word *evaṃ* (thus) serves to illuminate the state of being groundless; however, the word *eva* (indeed) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
Furthermore, "groundlessness" means pointlessness; one should seek the application of the word *evaṃ* here in its sense of being idle chatter that is devoid of purpose.

Alternatively, this word *evaṃ* has the sense of censure (*garaha*), because indeclinables possess multiple meanings. And its status as having the sense of censure is evident from its proximity to the word *vasali*.

By the phrase "honored by villages, towns, and kingdoms," the state of being honored by the owners of villages, towns, and kingdoms is indicated, because one must conduct oneself according to their will.
"Of such-and-such a person" refers to the remainder— namely, the words beginning with "excellent" (*abhikkanta*),
as well as whatever else has come down here and was described below.
The commentary on the Dhanañjānī Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Akkosaka Sutta: 188.
"He was indeed a Bhāradvāja" means that this brahmin was named Bhāradvāja; for this name is derived from his clan (gotra).
Furthermore, in order to show that this [conflict] has specifically arisen, it is said, "by about five," and so forth.
"Causing the destruction of kinsmen" means causing the destruction of the circle of relatives. "The faction was split" means that for that very reason, the faction of kinsmen was lost.
Just as one who is dejected may be called "displeased," so too he says "and by dejection" regarding one who is angry. "By ten" is used in the sense of an exhaustive enumeration.

It was stated [in the commentary] with five hundred verses, considering that one who reviles should likewise be reviled. In this context, however, even if one reviles by any means whatsoever, it is indeed called "reviling.
"You are performing the renunciation of my brother" [is said]. "He associates" (*sambhuñjati*) means he engages in social enjoyment (*sambhoga*).
He eats together with [others] through insults and so forth. "He exchanges" (*vītiharati*) means he performs an exchange (*byatihāra*).
"Karoti" means he makes an exchange by reviling in return for one who reviles him; thus it is said, "he makes a recompense for what has been done. The construction is:
fear arose in him (assa), who—having heard [the words] through hearsay—perceived, "He curses me.
"His" (assa) refers to the brahmin. The word "sutvā" (having heard) should be connected with both instances: "Having heard, 'This is yours alone, O brahmin...'"
And [the phrase] “having heard by way of oral tradition. Granted that Kisavaccha and the others did not utter a cry of lamentation, for that was intended only for the deities;
nevertheless, such a perception arose in beings, and he too perceived it as such. Therefore he said, “by way of oral tradition.
Because he had completely attained the state of being tamed, he is “tamed. “Free from agitation” means devoid of the mental vibration caused by greed, hatred, and the like.
“Of that very person” means that for the person who is reacting with resentment, evil arises through that anger, because there is no transmigration from one continuum of existence to another.
Some, however, explain the meaning here as follows: “Of that very person” refers to that very man who is reacting with resentment;
“more evil” means more base than the person who is reacting with resentment. One who is endowed with mindfulness...
Having offered [the sacrifice], he endures while established in reflective discernment; the intention is that he does not endure having become deluded.
"Healing both" means healing—that is, pacifying—the disease of the defilements known as anger that has arisen in both. By the words "That person who...
and so forth, he shows how the phrases occurring in the preceding verses are connected. In the five...

"Those who have been trained according to reality regarding the aggregates are called 'skilled in the noble Dhamma,'" he said; thus, "of the Dhamma" means "of the Dhamma consisting of the five aggregates.
Now, demonstrating that same meaning in its fullness, he said, "or of the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
The commentary on the Akkosasutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Asurindakasutta* 189.

“By that very same [person]” means by the brother who has gone forth. “Of him alone” refers to the one who practices forbearance (*titikkhassa*). Regarding the phrase “that victory is his,” he says “that victory belongs to him” because it is stated with a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*);
the intended meaning is: for one who conquers anger—which is difficult to conquer—by means of forbearance.
Because patience and the like are not the burden of one who is a slave to anger, but rather are merely a conceit of fools, this point is clarified here by the passage beginning with “Of what?
Victory belongs only to the one who understands, not to the one who does not understand, because there is no patience for the latter.
Indeed, an ignorant fool who lacks understanding is unable to conquer anger; he merely conceives of victory.
The intended meaning is: "even though he has been defeated by the defilements.
The commentary on the *Asurindakasutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Bilaṅgikasutta*.
190. *Suddhaṃ* means pure, devoid of any ingredients. *Sambhārayuttaṃ* means mixed with ingredients such as pungent spices and so forth.
It is called *kañjikaṃ*, *āranālaṃ*, or *bilaṅgaṃ* because it is produced from sour gruel; this is the meaning. The name was recorded at the time of the Council by way of a qualification:
"Bilaṅgikabhāradvāja. There are three [Bhāradvājas]: Bhāradvāja, the husband of Dhanañjānī; Akkosakabhāradvāja; and...
The three [discourses] beginning with the *Asundarikabhāradvāja* appear at the outset of the first three suttas. "Me" means "mine.
The commentary on the *Bilaṅgika-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Ahiṃsaka-sutta*.
191. It is said that the brahmin spoke thus because he wished to establish that meaning for himself, thinking, "I am a non-harmer";

therefore it is said, "he asked the question regarding non-harming. "If it were so" means: if this were the case according to the meaning of your name—that is, if you were one whose name corresponds to its meaning—you would be a non-harmer indeed. "He does not cause suffering" means he does not produce even the slightest bit of pain.
The meaning is that it removes [one] from suffering.
The commentary on the Ahiṃsaka Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Jaṭā Sutta.
192. Regarding "of the question on tangles" (*jaṭāpañha*): this refers to the question concerning the synonyms for "tangle," namely, "internal tangle, external tangle.
The commentary on the *Jaṭāsutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Suddhikasutta*.
193. Regarding "the question concerning purity": this refers to a question based on purity, namely, "A non-Brahmin is not purified.

"Endowed with virtue" means possessed of virtue characterized by the fivefold restraint. "Ascetic practice" (*tapokamma*) refers to performing ascetic practices such as fasting and the five-fold heat-exposure (*pañcātapa*).
"Knowledge" (*vijjā*): they say it is the three Vedas, for "by means of them, one knows what is beneficial in this world and the next world."
"Having made [it so]. *Gottacaraṇaṃ* means conduct characterized by lineage (*gotta*). "A brahmin is purified because of his superior birth.
For he alone is permitted to practice asceticism (*tapa*), not another.
"Other base births" refers to the other castes. "Even a thousand words" refers to even many thousands of verses. "Rotten within by defilements" means rotten by nature.
By means of defiled bodily actions and so forth, that is, by bodily misconduct and so forth.
The commentary on the *Suddhika-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Aggika-sutta*.
194. "By way of attending the fire" means by way of offering the *aggihutta* sacrifice. "Mixed" (*sannihita*) means brought into a state of combination.
And being thus, it is said to be "joined" (*saṃyojita*) because it has been mixed with ghee.
It "enters the path to the states of loss" because wrong view, wrong intention, and so forth arise within one's own continuum. Therefore he said, "This tenet," and so on.

"By birth" means by a birth that is pure due to the absence of any fault arising from defiled actions. "In various kinds of texts" refers to the eighteen branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*). "Learned" means having heard them and reached a definitive conclusion; the intention is that he is the most worthy of offerings (*aggadakkhiṇeyya*).
"By the knowledge of past lives" is stated here because this term is conventionally established both in the world and in the Dispensation (*sāsana*).

For others who know their past lives do so specifically by the knowledge of past lives, but the Blessed One knows them also by his omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). "By the divine... [The text continues:]...by the divine [eye].
"By the eye": here too, the method is the same. "The destruction of birth" (*jātikkhaya*) means that by this [path] birth is entirely exhausted;

it is the supreme path (*aggamagga*). Because it is to be attained and reached by that [path], "the destruction of birth" refers to *arahantship*. "Having known, one has completed the completion" means:
having known with the knowledge of the path the Dhamma of the Four Truths which is to be fully understood, one has completed the completion of all sixteen tasks.
“Having explained its origin” means having made known the provenance of the gift of milk-rice. “Chanted with verses” means it was chanted by me with two verses.
“It should not be eaten” means it is not fit to be consumed. Why was it called “unfit for food”?
Is it not true that the Blessed One’s intention is absolutely pure? This is true; however, the brahmin previously did not wish to give.
Having heard the verses later on, his heart became softened by the teaching of the Dhamma and he desired to give;

therefore, he rejected that [gift] so that the monks would not fall into following his example in the future. For he acted in exactly this same way in the immediately preceding sutta and in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.
Thus he said, "You, O Brahmin," and so forth. By the words "on the palm-leaf mat... were made manifest," [he indicates...]
This shows that the Blessed One, having set aside the verse for the purpose of recitation, taught the Dhamma to the brahmin in detail.
"By singing" means by one who sings, or by song. "Both the meaning and the Dhamma" refers both to the welfare of the world including its devas and to the cause thereof.
"Of those who see correctly" means of those who perceive rightly. "Dhamma" refers to the conduct-dhamma handed down through tradition.
It does not exist. To show the excellence among foods, he said, "a meal of fine rice-porridge" (*sudhābhojana*). Regarding the phrase "when the Dhamma exists":

since this discourse arose concerning the statement, "One should eat the Soma-rice-porridge," it refers to those living by taking as their support the noble ones' conduct and Dhamma, for whom this very [conduct] is supreme when that Dhamma exists.
"This brahmin reflects" (sallakkheti). The remaining conditions are faultless because no discussion arises concerning them.
The grammatical derivation (*saddasiddhi*) of the term *kukkuccavūpasanta* should be understood as being like that of the word *aggiāhitapada*.

"With food and drink" is a characteristic statement (*lakkhaṇavacana*), just as one says, "The ghee must be guarded from crows. Therefore he said, "This is merely for the sake of the teaching" (*desanāmattam*).

It is prepared like a fertile field that yields abundant grain and fruit; that is to say, this field of merit is prepared through the accomplishment of specific qualities such as virtue (sīla), just as a field is well-prepared by means of proper plowing, sowing, and the bringing and removing of water.
The commentary on the Aggika Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Sundarikasutta 195.
It is called *āhuti* because it is to be brought and offered. It is *aggihutta* because one offers into the fire (*aggi*) with ghee, honey, milk-rice, and so forth;
this should be understood as including the location [of the sacrifice]. Therefore he said, "the abode of fire," and so forth. And "well-cleansed" refers to those of low birth.
And by this, it would be thoroughly purified. The word “me” is brought forward and connected [to the following].

“He makes fruitless” refers from here until the word “I give. This section is established by way of abbreviation (peyyāla) because it is exactly the same as what has been explained in the commentary on the immediately preceding sutta;
it is not an establishment for the purpose of preparing ghee. And it is for the purpose of warding off the falling snow and the cold wind.
Thinking, "This is not the reason," and not accepting that, he said "capable" (*paṭibalo*) and so forth in order to show another, indeed, a good reason.
"Having recognized" means having recognized, "This is not a brahmin.

"With short hair-tuft" means with a short tuft of hair at the crown. He said, "without seeing even a mere tuft of hair," because for brahmins a tuft of hair is for the sake of purification; some say it refers to "the requisites of a paramahaṃsa."
Birth is not the cause of being worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*), because it does not exclude those evil qualities which are the causes of unworthiness.

"This" refers to conduct consisting of virtue and so forth. It is the cause of being worthy of offerings, because one abandons the evil qualities that produce unworthiness by means of the abandonment of specific factors (*tadaṅga*) and other methods.
"His" refers to the brahmin. "That meaning" refers to that state of being worthy of offerings.
He clarifies the meaning expressed as "causality" by means of a simile: "Born from pure wood such as sal-tree timber" means born from pure wood like that of the sal tree.

Wood that is not pure, such as from a dog's trough or a donkey's trough, does not fail to perform the function of fire. "In this way" means just as fire performs its function of fire regardless of where it is born, so too one who is worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya), even if born among outcaste families and the like, [performs his function].

He is not so called merely because he was born into the lineage of the Noble Ones by virtue of his perfection of qualities; rather, it is said, "born of noble birth through the perfection of qualities.

To show the preeminent status of that perfection of qualities through steadfastness (*dhiti*), the passage beginning with "For he" (*so hi*) was spoken. In this context, "through steadfastness" means through energy (*vīriya*);
for it is by that energy that one sustains those wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) by producing them when unarisen and by further developing them once arisen. Through moral shame (*hiri*)...
He restrains the defilements; for when there is a genuine loathing of evil, there is no opportunity at all for them to arise.
By means of the "duty to oneself," which is the quality of moral dread (*ottappa*) characterized as knowledge.
"One who knows what is cause and what is not cause" means one who knows, as they truly are, the proper place for various states (*dhammas*), or the state of the adverse nature of evil qualities.
He is "tamed" by the Noble Path, which serves as the object-condition for Nibbāna, the ultimate truth.
By the "taming of the faculties," he has likewise attained the Noble restraint of the faculties. They are called "Vedas" because they know the Truths;
the "end of the Vedas" is the Noble Fruit. The "end of the defilements" is the state of their non-arising and cessation. The "Sacrifice" is the supreme fruit.

"Useless" means fruitless because they do not come, and even for those who have come, it is because there is no one among them worthy of the highest offerings (*aggadakkhiṇeyya*). "He sacrifices" and "he gives.
"Well-offered" (*suyiṭṭha*) refers to a good gift by virtue of obtaining the recipient who is worthy of the highest offerings. "Well-sacrificed" (*suhuta*) is a synonym for that same thing.

Alternatively, "well-offered" means it has been properly and correctly offered, brought to its essence, thinking, "This object of mine to be given [is now well-bestowed]. The same method applies here for "well-sacrificed" as well.
"Upahaṭamattā" means as soon as it has been brought forward by the brahmin with the words, "May your honor eat.

"Only the nutritive essence produced" means that the nutritive essence has been separated from its physical basis (*vatthu*) without taking the basis itself. By this, it is said that "it has reached a state of subtlety," meaning that the remainder of the food has entirely attained a subtle condition;
this refers to its no longer being manifest in its previous form due to the non-coarseness of the nutritive essence.
This was stated, but it does not refer to the grasping of nutriment (*ojā*) alone. For that [nutriment], because it exists in inseparable association, cannot be grasped separately;
therefore, even by deities, it is grasped together with its physical basis (*savatthuka*). By "the bases of humans," he refers to the body composed of the four great elements.
Because the physical basis is coarse, the digestive faculty is not as sharp as that of deities; thus, due to the admixture of divine nutriment, there is a proper digestion.

It does not go [to them]. This shows the meaning that even though the divine food is subtle, when mixed with that milk-rice, because of being mixed with something gross, it does not provide pleasure to the gods whose physical bases are subtle—this is shown by the passage beginning with "But in the case of cow's milk.
Alternatively, due to the grossness of the object of enjoyment, it is difficult for the gods to digest it properly; and due to the greater weight of the divine food, it is difficult for humans.

Therefore the Blessed One said, “Indeed, I do not...,” and so forth. It is stated that “the fire element produced by the mind of attainment (samāpatti-citta), intensified by the power of jhāna, becomes more acute,” which is why it says, “he should transform... [eightfold]... into fire. However, in the case of the Blessed One, it transforms by its own nature alone;
thus it says, “by the ordinary [nature],” meaning by that which is established through its own intrinsic nature, without the jhāna having reached the power of jhāna.
Regarding the phrase “in a place not overgrown with grass” (*appaharite*), the word *appa-* here has the sense of non-existence, as in such terms as *appiccha* (“having few desires”).

Thus he says: “‘In a place not overgrown with grass’ means in a place overgrown with grass. “Even in a hundred pots of milk-rice”: it does not become turbid; that is, it does not become muddy. He would go away without returning, overcome by dejection, thinking:
“He neither consumed it himself nor gave it to others; he simply wasted the milk-rice.”

"He completely burns the wood" means that he, being one who burns it, consumes the wood by means of the yellow wood-fire (*dāruhariddi*). "If," and so forth, is the proof for the external nature of the burning of the wood;
this is because there is no counter-agent to the impure causes of that [burning].

"Skilled in the aggregates and so forth" means those who are clever and wise through knowing them by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), their arising, their passing away, their gratification (*assāda*), their danger (*ādīnava*), and the escape from them (*nissaraṇa*). "The light of knowledge" means consisting of knowledge.
"Light": "I kindle it" means I cause it to blaze up. Because it is a state of singular radiance due to the removal of the darkness of delusion, it is a fire that blazes perpetually everywhere.
Because there is no distraction whatsoever, its nature is eternally concentrated.
"He speaks thus" means he speaks as if saying, "Having undertaken the holy life (*brahmacariya*), I live it," placing this very proximity within his heart.
“Like a load of a khāri” means similar to a load of a khāri. Therefore he said, “Just as,” and so forth.
“Carried on the shoulder” means having been placed upon a carrying-pole (kāja) and carried on the shoulder. “It touches the ground” is due to the weight of the load causing the carrying-pole to tilt.
Regarding one who exalts his own birth and so forth through conceit (māna), another cannot endure those [qualities]; thus he said: “In this and that situation...”
"Generating envy"—the intention here is that one would sink by grasping excessively at various grounds for pride, such as birth and so forth.
"Anger is the smoke": just as a brilliant fire is defiled by smoke, so too is [the mind] defiled by anger.
"The fire of knowledge"—of that [fire], anger is the smoke. False speech itself is the stain of lying (*mosavajja*). Just as when there is knowledge...
"There is no lying. Thus, when there is lying, even knowledge [is obscured]; it is as if that [knowledge] has been suppressed by it. Therefore he said: "Knowledge concealed by lying.

Just as the sacrifice of the brahmins does not succeed without a sacrificial ladle (*sujā*), so too the Teacher’s sacrifice of Dhamma does not succeed without an abundant tongue; thus the tongue is spoken of by way of a synonym for the sacrificial ladle.

The "place of light" (*jotiṭṭhāna*) is the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), which is the fire-pit, because light is established there. The heart of sentient beings is the place of light, because the fire of wisdom blazes forth therein.
"Self" (*atta*) refers to the mind (*citta*), by way of the conceit "I am established here.

"Dhamma is a lake" because it is free from the sloth of faithlessness and so forth, because it washes away the stains of the defilements, and because it brings about the supreme extinction of the fires [of passion].
The noble path-dharma is an untroubled lake. "Sand from bottom to top" means that the sand has been turned over.
"Agitated" means it has become disordered. "Praised by the wise" means it is the best in the presence of the wise.
Because it is excellent and praiseworthy, and because it breaks and utterly cuts off the defilements, it is called "sabhī. Therefore he said, "in the sense of being supreme."
And thus the Blessed One said: “Of paths, the eightfold is best.
By the phrase “truth of speech,” he shows right speech as that which is “utterly pure speech endowed with four factors.
He says “Dhamma” because the path-factors shown by the words “truth” and “restraint” are what is intended here by the term “Dhamma.”
“By this... [etc. ...he shows,” he says. The Truth of the Path (maggasacca) is included because it was spoken with many qualifications in the immediately preceding verse.
“In meaning” means in the sense of being the forerunner, and so forth; for while she performs her own function, all the others become her followers.
“Because they share the same destiny” means that by virtue of their state of being supportive to right view, they have the same destination as it does. For the object—
Wisdom is able to investigate what has been brought forward by applied thought (*vitakka*); for that reason, it is included within the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*).
By the term "Dhamma," concentration (*samādhi*) is understood in its essential nature, while the other two [factors] are included because they are conducive to it.

For instance, in such passages as "Those Blessed Ones were of such a nature" (*evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto*), concentration is referred to as "Dhamma. Ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) is understood to be included in all [three].

Because it is the most excellent state. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is declared to be the foremost among them.
Because of its ultimate meaning—that is, because it is the ultimate reality—or because it serves as the object-condition for the path-phenomena that will be discussed immediately hereafter.
Five factors are included because they constitute the nature of those paths; [the remaining] three factors are [included].
"Called the holy life (brahmacariya)" means that this is called the "holy life of the path" in the sense of being supreme as it leads to Nibbāna.
"Situated in the middle" means it is based on the cultivation of the Middle Way by avoiding the two extremes, such as dullness and agitation.

Here, the mention of the grasping at eternalism and annihilationism is merely an illustration, as these are the primary [extremes]. "Attainment of the best" means the attainment of the state of excellence.
The letter *ta* functions as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*). Where it should have been said "sa ujubhūtesu," the letter *ta* is inserted in the middle to effect the euphonic junction.
Some read "sa dujjubhūtesu"; for them, the letter *da* functions as the euphonic conjunction.
Having considered that the Brahmin Sundarika was addressed with the word "sa" (he), he says "sa tvaṃ" (you, he); the meaning is "so tvaṃ" (thus you). Dhamma is the noble garment.
“Dhammasārī” means one whose ornaments are the Dhamma. Alternatively, “dhammasārī” means one who is strung together by the Dhammas;
the sense is that he stands having been strung together by them. Therefore he said, “by wholesome states,” and so forth.
The commentary on the Sundarikasutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Bahudhītarasutta 196.
"On all sides" means on every side by way of both the right and the left. "The cross-legged posture" (ūrubbaddhāsana) refers to sitting by way of binding the thighs.
He says, "having folded [the legs]" (ābhujitvā), with reference to the manner of sitting with the two thighs mutually bound together.
Regarding the phrase "having bound," the straightening of the lower body is already indicated by the mention of "sitting";
therefore, he says, "having placed the upper part of the body straight," explaining that in the expression "the body straight" (*ujuṃ kāyaṃ*), the word *kāya* refers specifically to the upper body.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "eighteen" is stated to demonstrate both the actual form and the purpose of that straightening.
Regarding the term *parimukhaṃ*, the prefix *pari-* has the same meaning as *abhi-*. Thus it is said: “facing toward the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānābhimukhan*”).

The meaning is that, having turned away from external, manifold objects, one holds the meditation subject alone in front of oneself. The sense of “encompassing” (*pariggaha*) is as in such terms as “a guide” (*pariṇāyikā*).
The sense of “door” (*mukha*) is the sense of “exit” (*niyyāna*), as in such terms as “the door of liberation that is emptiness” (*suññatavimokkhamukha*).
For the meaning of "going forth" (*niyyāna*) is the sense of emerging from its opposite;

therefore, "having discerned the way out" means having established mindfulness that is entirely free from confusion and has abandoned all confusion, having set up supreme mindfulness and circumspection. The six-colored [rays]...
[he] sat down for the purpose of inspiring confidence in the brahmin. "Wandering toward the forest entrance" means taking their range of movement.
*Ajjasattiṃ*: this means that six full days have passed since today; the sense is "six days beginning from today.
This is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). *Ajja chadivasamattakā*: meaning "lasting only until the sixth day from today.
*Lāmakā*: inferior and fruitless. Therefore he said, "sesame stalks," and so forth.
“With exertion” means by stretching upwards and upwards, that is, by overcoming. To demonstrate that overcoming of theirs, he said, “the ears, the toes, and so forth.
“Skin-tearing insects” refers to insects such as ticks and *maṅgula* worms that eat as if they were tearing away the skin.

“Black-and-tawny” (*kaḷārapiṅgalā*) means those with tawny eyes protruding; or alternatively, those whose limbs are reddish-black and whose eyes are tawny. “Struck by spots” (*tilakāhatā*) means struck by spots; their bodies are covered all over with spots the size of sesame seeds.

"He increased the Brahmin's teaching of the Dhamma with responsive verses" means that he naturally expanded the Dhamma teaching which the Brahmin was to deliver himself by way of praising the virtues of the renunciant life through seven [verses].
"Having gone forth" means having gone forth after making his creditors understand his situation as an obstacle in various ways.
To show how the Blessed One acted in that matter, the passage beginning with “On the following day” was spoken.

“Having sent her to this or that family home” means that while giving his daughter to various brahmins suitable for her, he sent her to this or that family home because of his lack of respect for the duties of a brahmin. [As it is said:
“When she is lost, dead, gone forth, a eunuch, or when the husband has died...”
“For a woman who has the most excellent husband, no other husband is desired.”—This, indeed, is the duty of a brahmin.
“In the position of a grandmother” means he placed her in the position of a maternal great-grandmother by way of pleasing the Teacher’s heart.
