The commentary on the Bahudhītarasutta is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Chapter on Lay Followers (Upāsaka-vagga). 1. Commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.

197. "In Dakkhiṇāgiri" means in the district of Dakkhiṇāgiri; in that district of Dakkhiṇāgiri, in the Dakkhiṇāgiri Monastery. "Having placed them on the poles and yoked with thongs" means they were joined and set in motion by means of thong-ropes—this is the meaning.
"On the first day" refers to the first day among the days of sowing, the day the work was commenced.
It is stated as "with the five factors complete" in order to show that even the other factors were complete, let alone the rest. [They were adorned] with yellow orpiment, realgar, and collyrium.
Because they were placed upon the chest and other parts [of the body], their limbs were radiant with light. The rest were oxen.
"Releasing the exhausted bull" means unyoking the one who was tired and yoking one who was not tired;

this is the "exchange for the exhausted. "Lion-earrings" means earrings with lion faces. "Brahmā’s turban" means resembling the turban of Brahmā; the meaning is that it resembles the turban of Assanaka.
The duties of the Buddhas are divided according to time into five types of duties.

"The duty before the meal" (*purebhattakicca*) refers to the duty that must be performed by the Buddha prior to the meal. "Having passed the time" means having passed the time in the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"Sometimes alone," and so forth, demonstrates the practice appropriate for training various disciples. "By nature" (*pakatiyā*)...

By way of the natural appearance of a Buddha. For the "appearance of a Buddha" consists in the physical body of the Buddhas being adorned with the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the bodily radiance, the fathom-wide aura (*vyāma-prabha*), and the variegated array of the *ketumālā* (halo).
Sometimes, while many miracles (*pāṭihāriya*) are taking place, these miracles—which are the outflow (*nissanda*) of the perfections (*pāramī*)—manifest themselves according to his own inclination.
This shows that they do not exist at all times. And by taking it thus, the statement beginning with "as soon as his right foot was placed within the threshold" is justified.

Having stated that because of the predominance of yellow rays in the Blessed One’s body, it is "as if sprinkled with liquid gold," he refers to the fact that here and there on the body, the yellow is intermingled with blue and other rays, saying: "as if draped with variegated cloths."
And it is said, "as if. They make a sound in a sweet manner because of their joyful and excellent voices.

"Therein" means in the monastery (*vihāra*). "In the perfumed pavilion" (*gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe*) means in the circular hall that has been plastered by hand and where garlands of fragrant flowers have been gathered together.
"In the attendance area" (*upaṭṭhāne*) means in front. Having said, "He exhorts," in order to show the nature of that exhortation in general, [the text says] "Bhikkhus," and so forth.
It has been said. "Attainment" (*sampatti*) refers both to the perfection of the faculties such as the eye and so forth, and to the possession of hands and other limbs.
"The body is comforted" by the removal of fatigue; they say this occurs "by means of entering meditative attainments" (*samāpajjana*).
By the phrase "in the second part," having divided the latter portion into three parts, he spends the first part in sleep and sitting, and the [remaining] parts in meditative attainments.
He shows this. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the world of beings to be trained—those who awaken either in Rājagaha and other such places where he dwells at that time, or elsewhere.
He surveys it with his Buddha-eye. "Appropriate to the time" (*kālayutta*) means according to the period suitable for the ripening of their faculties.
"Appropriate to the occasion" (*samayayutta*) is a synonym for that same term; or alternatively, it means according to the attainment of the specific distinctions they are to understand.
"Secluded" means having entered into meditative attainment after fixing a time limit. "Fulfilling his purpose" means not failing in that [purpose]; the sense is: "in accordance with his inclination.
Regarding the phrase "the entire... of the deities," the totality here should be understood as referring to the world-system (*lokadhātu*), not the totality of the deities themselves.

For it is not the case that, as during the Great Occasion (*mahāsamaya*), all deities everywhere in the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassacakkavāḷa*) are present at all times during the middle watch of the night.
They approach the presence of the Teacher. *Kilāsubhāva* means weariness.

"By way of exchanging the robes of the monastery" means by way of exchanging the inner and outer robes worn in the monastery. "Having taken up" means having taken [the robes] for the purpose of wearing them; thus he said, "having put them on. *Bhikkhācāraṃ* means the place where one must go for the sake of alms.
*Atirocamānaṃ* means shining forth in all directions, surpassing this or that [object]. *Sarīrappabhaṃ* means the radiance of the body.
His own bodily radiance was like a moving lotus pond, with jeweled filaments and silver pericarp, filled on all sides with blossoming golden lotuses, resembling a lake in motion.
The vault of the sky was like the surface of the atmosphere perfectly purified by the removal of defilements such as clouds and mist;
for that too shines forth on all sides due to the brilliance of the web of rays from the clusters of stars.

"Kanakasikhara" means the peak of the Golden Mountain. "Shining with glory" means blazing with the splendor of the form-body (rūpakāya)—a glory that is entirely blameless, perfect in every respect, and unique, not shared by any other;
the radiant nature of which surpasses even the full moon's orb on a clear, cloudless night, when its perfectly round and beautiful disk is fully manifest.
Its radiant nature surpasses the solar disc, which is brilliantly illuminated by a network of rays from a thousand-spoked sun;

and its gold-like brilliance, having surpassed both of those, shines, blazes, and glows, overwhelming the mass of light of a Great Brahmā who is capable of illuminating ten thousand world-systems in a single moment.
*Samantapāsādikā* means "bringing about confidence on all sides. And because it must be remembered in its entirety, he says, "inspiring confidence.
*Uttamadamathasamatham anuppattā* means having attained the supreme state of being tamed through body and speech, as well as the supreme tranquility of the mind.
*Appasādena* means by the absence of confidence, or by the opposite of confidence—that is, by lack of faith (*assaddhiya*). In both cases, [the meaning remains the same].
“Neither lack of confidence nor stinginess”—it is not so in either case;

rather, he spoke thus because, being displeased and with the intention of finding fault, he wished to point out something from the Blessed One’s own mouth. Showing the reason for this, he said, “But of the Blessed One,” and so forth.
“Unsatisfied” means not reaching satiety. “Destruction of karma” means the loss of merit.
This brahmin possesses sharp wisdom; for he will realize arhatship before long. He spoke thus even for the sake of initiating conversation, thinking:

"In this way, I shall obtain the opportunity to hear some Dhamma from him. "By way of the person to be trained" means by way of the individual who is to be guided, through the manner of proclaiming his own role as a tiller of the soil.
“Coarse” means ordinary. “He is the most worthy of offerings”—thus he conceives great respect.
In the text, the word “or” (*vā*) in the phrase “a yoke or a plough” has the sense of an unstated alternative. By this, it includes seeds and so forth; therefore, the meaning shown is:
“seeds, or a ploughshare, or the ropes for binding,” and so on. For thus did the Blessed One [speak] to the brahmin.
Giving his reply, he said, "Faith is the seed," and so forth. "By way of similarity to the preceding dhamma" means by way of similarity to the dhamma previously grasped.
Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood as it is recorded in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, whether from the literal word or through the implication of the meaning.
This is the power of the Buddhas: that they teach by way of dhammas introduced in the course of a relevant discussion.
Having begun with the taming of those to be tamed (*vineyya-vinayana*).
"Without connection" (*ananusandhika*) means without a sequence of questions. "In this way" (*evaṃ*) means in the manner now being stated.

"Therein" (*ettha*) means in this teaching. "He" (*so*) refers to the Blessed One. "Of him" (*tassa*) refers to the brahmin. "Out of compassion" (*anukampāya*) [means out of compassion for one who is] not omniscient.
For even if one were to remain after merely asking out of compassion, such a person would be compassionate without truly knowing;
however, the Blessed One, for the sake of fulfilling both qualities, speaks without omitting anything, thinking, "This was not asked.
Expanding upon the meaning stated briefly in the passage beginning with "With its root," he says "Therein," and so forth. In that context, the state of being the root of the seed through cultivation—
He says, "Because of that... because it must be performed," referring to both the immediate succession and the manner of its application.
By this, he clarifies, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that plowing is the primary cause for the seed.
By the word "wholesome" (*kusala*), he shows that unwholesome actions perform the task differently, and furthermore, that [the wholesome] is immeasurable.
“Of that” means because of the state of being a benefactor to the brahmin’s dhamma, which stands in the place of seed.
“Because of the capacity to connect with the dhamma” means because of the capacity to join and connect the dhamma spoken in that manner with its fruit.
This was said with reference to the statement, “Austerity is rain. To make the meaning briefly stated clear, [the text says] “For this,” and so forth.
It has been stated. When rain is mentioned immediately after the seed of a farmer’s assistance, it is not said to be "out of place.
Why? Because at the time of sowing the seed, rain appropriate to that occasion is expected;

therefore, if it were mentioned at the very end or in the middle [of the sequence], its capacity to connect with the preceding phenomena would not be manifested. [This applies] when it is outside of its own proper scope.
Regarding "superhuman states such as jhāna and so forth": "even afterwards" means even after the subsequent explanation of the requisites for cultivation (*kasi-sambhāra*).

"Must be stated" means it must be stated categorically. "Immediately thereafter" means immediately after the seed. By the very word "immediately," it is demonstrated that the rain being spoken of is capable—namely, capable of connecting with the fruit of the seed.
Because it illuminates that which is proximate in its assistance.
"Characterized by serene confidence" means having the characteristic of being properly confident toward an object worthy of confidence.

"Characterized by conviction" means having the characteristic of leaping forward toward an object worthy of faith with the thought, "It is exactly so. In the phrase "root-seed" and so forth, the root itself is the seed.
"Root-seed" (*mūlabīja*). This same method applies to the remaining [categories] as well, because it is the "group of seeds" (*bījagāma*) that is intended here.
However, "element-group" (*bhūtagāma*) should be understood as "that which has roots and seeds" (*mūlaṃ bījaṃ etassa*), thus "root-seed," and so forth.

As for the fifth, "seed-seed" (*bījabīja*), the word "seed" (*bīja*) is conventionally used for a hard fruit capable of sprouting, because it serves as the specific cause for the production of a similar fruit when combined with other conditions.

Since it occurs in some cases, such as the root [of a plant], for the sake of establishing that meaning, it is stated as "seed-seed" (bījabīja) by qualifying it with the word *bīja* alone, in order to exclude those other instances—just as one says "suffering-suffering" (dukkhadukkha) or "form-form" (rūparūpa).
Thus, showing that even in this sense this [kamma] possesses the status of being a seed in the primary (non-figurative) sense, he said: "All that... goes."
Now, in order to clarify the nature of faith as a seed within the simile of faith—which must somehow be explained—the passage beginning with “In this regard, just as...

is commenced. Granted that virtue has faith as its proximate cause, nevertheless, because it is the primary root for all blameless states just as concentration is, faith also serves as its foundation; thus he says: “Below, by means of the root of virtue...”

"It is established. Since the undertaking of serenity and insight occurs for every person by means of faith, it is therefore said that "it causes the sprout of serenity and insight to emerge above. "That" refers to the seed of grain.
"The essence of earth and the essence of water" refers to the essence found in the earth and water together with their constituent parts. "Having taken" means by way of a succession of conditions.
"Having taken. "For the purpose of grasping the ripening of grain" means for the purpose of producing the ripening of grain.

"Taking the essence" means having taken the essence of the cultivation of faith, virtue, the roots of causes, serenity, and insight. "By means of the noble path-stalk" means by means of the stream of the noble path;

"for the purpose of grasping the ripening of the grain of the noble fruit"—since the noble fruit itself is to be treated as wealth, it is called "grain," and this is for the purpose of its production. A "grain-stalk" refers to the stalk of the stem.
The western region is the support; the stalk is within it, and the stem is its very support. "Cattle" refers to the flower.
"Growth" means growth by way of the completion of its parts. "Increase" means the state of having grown through the strengthening of the root-continuum.
"Expansion" means the state of abundance by way of leaves, stalks, and so forth. "Having produced milk" means [the attainment of] the state of being a young sprout.

Having produced milk that serves as the seed for the seed of rice. "This" refers to faith (*saddhā*). "Having become established" means having become established initially through mere virtue (*sīla*) that has arisen, accompanied by right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*)—both that which constitutes a path of action and that which does not.
Regarding "growth" and so forth: growth occurs through the complete purification of virtue and mind; increase occurs through the purifications of overcoming doubt and the views;
and [maturity] occurs through the purification of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path and the way.
"Having reached abundance": having produced the "milk" known as purification of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*), because it possesses a state of exquisite purity and delicious flavor.

"It bears fruit manifold... etc.: it brings to fruition the summit of the fruit of Arahatship, which is perfected by manifold analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and manifold direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
"By performing the function of a seed": by performing the function of a seed; for that [seed] which is similar to itself and dissimilar to others...
The function of the seed consists in establishing, connecting with, and bringing forth the fruit;

because it performs this—because it produces it—it is said, "Thus, faith is the function of the seed. By this, he shows that faith possesses the state of being the seed for wholesome states, a quality not shared by anything else.
He supports this very point with the words beginning "And that... Now, showing the scriptural authority (āgama) on this matter:
He said, “born of faith,” and so forth. By this he shows that just as there is reliance on true persons and hearing the true Dhamma, so too faith is the root cause for complete right practice.
Sense-faculty restraint and energy [counteract] unwholesome states, and the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*)—which involve performing difficult deeds—[counteract] both unwholesome states and...

It is called *tapa* (heat) because it heats and afflicts the body. What is intended here is restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*), since it is grasped as the "burden-bearing" quality of energy (*vīriya*), while the others are occupied with the state of being its outflow.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of the *kalala*, the *iṅgāla-vuṭṭhi* (firebrand-rain), and so forth is intended.
"Well-supported" (*samanuggahita*) means approached. By the terms "germinating," "withering," and "accomplishment," [the stages] of the continuity of the grain-seed are described.
This shows how, for their growth, the continuity of the seed of faith receives assistance through the rain of asceticism (tapas) at the beginning, middle, and end.

Regarding the phrase "in the preceding words as well," by means of the word *api*, the meaning should be understood as "also in the subsequent words. This is because [the text] intends to say, "Shame is my plowshare, the mind is my yoke";
thus, in the expression "mindfulness is mine" (*sati me*), the word *me* must be brought over and connected. Even water, for its part...
It must be brought from rivers, tanks, and so forth. Having yoked the fourfold oxen of energy (*vīriya-balībadda*). "At all times" is the remainder of the statement.
By "together with insight," path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) is intended, because it is intended for the cultivation of the fruit of the Deathless.
Both types of wisdom—insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) and [path-wisdom]—are the decisive support (*upanissaya*), because of their distinguished nature. Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth.
"Paññā": it is wisdom because it knows by way of various modes (*pakāra*).

Wisdom stands foremost for those possessed of wisdom, because it serves as a specific condition for appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and because it is the most preeminent among the co-nascent dominant factors (*sahajātādhipati*). "Sirī" means beauty or fortune.
"The qualities of the good" refers to faith and the rest; "anvāyikā" means accompanying or following along. "Bound to the pole" means bound to the pole known as moral shame (*hiri*).
Because concentration sometimes arises through the application of wisdom, it is said here that "concentration is called the 'mind-thread'" (*manosīsena*).
It is called the "concentration-thread" because it binds by leading evenly, acting as a binding rope.
"Going in one direction" prevents wandering toward either laxity or over-exertion; rather, it proceeds along the middle path of insight (*vipassanā-vīthi*).

Because it provides the specific condition for wisdom (paññā) regarding the removal of the notions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and selfhood from the body and so forth, it is said that "wisdom is conjoined with mindfulness" (satiyuttā paññā), since there is no dissociation from that mindfulness.

This is the distinction between continuity (santati) and compactness (ghana): the occurrence of preceding and succeeding phenomena as if they were unified due to their uninterrupted succession is "compactness of continuity."
The density of the collection (*samūhaghanatā*) is the occurrence of those [mental factors] as if they were unified by way of being contained within a single group.

The density of function (*kiccaghanatā*) is the occurrence of those [factors] as if they were unified by way of the differentiation of their functions, which are difficult to discern. The density of the object (*ārammaṇaghanatā*) is the occurrence of those [factors] as if they were unified by way of a single object.
"All" refers to all the root-continuities (*mūla-santānaka*) of the defilements; or "all" refers to all the continuities (*santānaka*). Non-application (*anuppayoga*).

This is the meaning. "It splits" means it breaks and utterly cuts off. And that which is called "it splits" is specifically supramundane wisdom (*lokuttara-paññā*), because the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) is intended here.

However, mundane wisdom (*lokiya*) also effects the breaking of the compactness of continuity and so forth, because it accomplishes the resolution of the compact through insight (*vipassanā*). Therefore, he said: "But the other may also be mundane."

"Hiriyatī" means he feels shame; the meaning is that he feels loathing. Therefore, "from evil states" (pāpakehi dhammehi) should be understood as an ablative expression, or alternatively, as an instrumental expression used in the sense of a cause.
"Ottappa" (fear of wrongdoing) is also implicitly included, for there is no such thing as shame that is devoid of fear, nor is there a lack of shame that does not involve fear of evil.
"Rukkhalaṭṭhī" means a tree-staff; it is so called because one plows by means of that part.
Specifically, because it is called "the plough," he said: "The pole bears the yoke and the plough.
Granted that there may be moral shame (*hirī*) devoid of wisdom (*paññā*), but there is no wisdom devoid of moral shame; thus he said: "Because of the absence of... [moral shame]...
It is "immovable" because there is no shaking at the point of connection. It is "not loose" because of its firmness. Wisdom bound to moral shame, by way of its opposites...
And because it is unshakable and not lax, it is said to be "unshakable and not lax" by the phrase, "uninterrupted by moral shamelessness.
It is called *mano* (mind) because, like a person measuring with a tube, it measures the object and knows it by way of delimitation.

By the expression "by means of the mind as its vanguard," it refers to the mind itself. By the phrase "associated with that," concentration—which accompanies the mind just as a spear accompanies a man who carries it—is designated as "mind."
He shows that it is "said. By "the driver" (*sārathi*) is meant the plowman; for here, he is intended as the "driver" because he drives and matures the oxen.
"Single-fastening" (*ekābandhana*) means making them bound together as one. "In its own task" (*sakakicce*) means when they are yoked to their own task.
For when they have been tied appropriately to the pole and so forth and made into a single unit, the work on the plow succeeds.
"Not otherwise" means that it "establishes its own function. "By way of its own non-distraction-nature" means by way of its own nature of non-distraction (*avikkhepa*).

"Having bound" means having connected itself through the state of being a co-nascent and other conditions. "Its own function" refers to the respective functions to be performed by shame (*hirī*) and the others.
"The meaning of what was long ago spoken, etc. refers even to a meaning that was spoken long ago. "Recalls" means remembers; it contemplates the body and so forth as foul (*asubha*), and so on.
It is called *padāleti* because it cleaves (*phāleti*). They drive it, they go with it; thus it is a *pājana*.
Here, in this sutta, it is stated as "pācana," having changed the letter *ja* to *ca*. To show this meaning—namely, "the plough and the goad"—it was said:
"Just as, O Brahmin... [pe] ...being mindful. Now, showing that meaning in detail, he said: "In that regard, just as... and so forth. [The word] *naṅgalaṃ*.
It guards [the plough] from breaking or splitting. "And it goes before it" means that when this plough is tilling the earth—that is, scratching the ground—it goes ahead, acting as its precursor.
"Courses" (gatiyo) refers to the modes of proceeding. "Seeking" (samanvesamānā) means searching by way of recollection;
or, while establishing the body and so forth as objects, it guards the plough of wisdom by way of the meditation on foulness (asubha) and the like.

In the sense that it guards against all that is harmful, mindfulness is called "protection" (*ārakkhā*), just as the ploughshare is called the "protector" (*ārakkha*) of the plough when it encounters both its proper and improper objects. For it is thus manifested as protection.

Having stated that mindfulness stands before the plough of wisdom by way of not forgetting what was done long ago or spoken long ago, [the text] says "mindfulness... in order to demonstrate its position in front.

He said, "It is forgotten. "Cultivated by mindfulness" (*satiparicita*) means established by mindfulness. There is also a reading, "established" (*upaṭṭhāpita*), which has the same meaning. "Does not allow it to sink" means it does not allow it to become despondent through its failure to perform its own function. "Sinking characterized by indolence" (*kosajjasaṃsīdana*) refers to sinking in the form of indolence. The virtue of restraint according to the *Pātimokkha* is mentioned because bodily and verbal self-restraint have been discussed. By demonstrating the state of restraint regarding food that is to be consumed, the state of restraint regarding all four requisites is illustrated;
thus he said, "by way of food," and so forth. And here, the state of restraint is the absence of improper search (nesanā) caused by the requisites;
hence it is stated, "the meaning is 'free from defilement' (nirupakkilesa). This is said because the word *bhojana* is conventionally established in the sense of the consumption of food.
“By way of moderation in eating”: however, when it is said “by way of the word *bhojana* (food) in the sense of consuming,” the intended meaning is indeed obtained.
“By that” refers to the statement beginning with “guardians of the body. “They do not plunder” is to be connected by bringing forward the word “illuminates” (*dīpeti*).
"In two ways" means: by way of the unseen and so forth for those things that are unseen, and by way of the seen and so forth for those things that are seen;
thus, in these two modes. Non-deception is speaking truthfully. Cutting (*chedana*) is severing at the base. Mowing (*lunana*) is cutting anywhere.
Uprooting (*uppāṭana*) is pulling out by the roots. "By what is eaten" (*asitena*) means by what is given; the sense is "by what is consumed. Of those things termed deception...

The meaning is: of the three [types of] grass and the eight ignoble modes of speech (*anariya-vohāra*). "Knowledge according to reality" (*yathābhūta-ñāṇa*) is the knowledge that discerns name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

It is to be understood as "truth" (*sacca*) because its mode of existence is non-perverted; it is "cutting" (*chedaka*) in the sense of cutting through. It is "removing" (*niddāna*) in the sense of removing.

The view that "only this is truth, all else is vain" is called "truth of views" (*diṭṭhi-sacca*). "In two ways of conceptualizing" (*dvīsu vikappesu*) is by way of the grammatical derivation from the abstract noun (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kattu*).
In two alternative interpretations, the meaning of “niddāna” is understood solely in the sense of the accusative case (the object).
Virtue itself is called “soracca,” considering it to be the action of one who has thoroughly refrained (*orata*) from killing living beings and so forth.

Because of the absence of the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*) and because of its excellence, he is “surato”—one who delights (*rata*) in the beautiful Nibbāna by taking it as his object; thus, he is an Arahant.
Its state is gentleness (*soracca*), which is *arahatta*. Non-release itself is not ultimate release.

To the extent that wisdom through insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) and the energy associated with it possess the nature of a plough and yoke, and likewise the cultivation of wholesome states proceeding in that manner possesses the nature of ploughing, to that same extent do the perfections of wisdom and energy that previously occurred possess the nature of the plough and yoke.
Showing that the state of being a "draught-animal" (kasibhāva) should likewise be understood regarding the cultivation of wholesome states that have already set in, he said, "Just as," and so forth.

*Dhorayha* means that which carries a burden (*dhuraṃ vahati*). The "dense mass" mentioned above refers to the dense mass consisting of the various types of conceit, such as the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), and so on.

Those who possess a burden (*dhura*)—that is, a primary burden to be carried—are called *dhurā*; they are those who carry the initial burden. Carrying another burden based upon that [initial one], they...
*Dhorayha*: *Dhurā* (the yoke) and *dhorayha* (the draught-ox) together form *dhuradhorayha* by way of their unity. "Carrying" (*vahan*) means proceeding by means of plowing.

Because it is secure and free from calamity due to the bonds of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) and so forth, [it is called] *khema*. Having that Nibbāna as its object—that is, aiming toward it—it is "carried" (*vāhīyati*) accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*).
That which is included within the Path (*magga*) is "carried forward" (*abhimukhaṃ vāhīyati*). "The furrow-limit" (*khettakoṭi*) means the boundary of the field.
"In the seen, etc. (*diṭṭhekaṭṭha*) means: co-existent with views (*sahajāta-ekaṭṭha*) and to be abandoned by the same [path] as the views (*pahāna-ekaṭṭha*).

"Gross" (*oḷārika*) is said in relation to those things to be abandoned by the higher paths; otherwise, even those to be abandoned by seeing would be grosser than those to be abandoned by the second path.
"Subtle" (*aṇusahagata*) means minute. This is said in relation to those things to be abandoned by the lower paths. "All defilements" (*sabba-kilesa*) refers to all remaining defilements.
It goes along with one who abandons [defilements] without turning back, because there is no further need for what is to be abandoned.
"Without turning back" means not returning; the sense is that it proceeds in such a way that there is no turning back. Therefore he said, "devoid of turning back," and so forth.
And this is your foremost draft-ox.
"Thus is this plowing" is a restatement of what was previously said. Therefore he says, "making a conclusion.

For it is a repetition of the very meaning already stated. "Having struck with the plowshare of mindfulness using the plow of wisdom" means having struck by making the plowshare of mindfulness and that which is reckoned as wisdom into a single, unified whole.
Regarding the word "plowing" (*kaṭṭhā*), here the term "plowing" (*kasī*) [is used].
Having brought [the terms] together, they should be connected as "wood is the plough. "The conclusion of the work" means that which constitutes the conclusion of the aforementioned work of ploughing.

Although this ploughing with the fruit of the Deathless was previously shown from a personal perspective in such passages as "Wisdom is my yoke and plough," nevertheless, the teaching of the Blessed One, who possesses great compassion, is for the sake of the entire assembly of beings.
Showing that this [passage] is indeed common [to both versions], he said, “But as for this...,” and so forth. “On that very day” means on that same day.

Regarding the phrase “he said at the beginning,” the word “beginning” (ādi) here includes the textual portion at the conclusion of the discourse; thus, referring to other textual passages such as “When this was said,” etc., he said, “and after that.
The commentary on the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Udaya Sutta 198.
"This was said" refers to the statement, "He filled [the bowl] with rice.
They say, "He was not able to take it because of the power of the Blessed One’s resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-bala). It is said that this was [said] out of a desire to discipline that brahmin.
The Blessed One did so.

"Out of fear of reproach" means out of fear of being censured by others. He turned back without speaking because it is stated in the *Brāhmaṇadhamma* that "even when a heretic has approached, he should not be honored even with mere words.
"He departed" means he departed without having spoken the Dhamma to the brahmin.

The brahmin’s knowledge had not yet reached maturity. This statement... [etc.]... was spoken because he necessarily desired to preach the Dhamma beginning with the words, "Again and again they sow the seed," and so forth.
One who plows thoroughly (*pakaṭṭhako*) is so called from the perspective of the mode of action;
the meaning is that he is preeminent in craving for flavors (*rasataṇhā*). Therefore, he said, "one who is greedy for flavors."
The connection is that he began this teaching with the words, “Again and again they sow the seed. The word *bījaṃ* (seed) and the particle *iti* have the sense of illustration;
by means of that part, he illustrates the whole. *Osakkasi* means you shrink back. *Vuttaṃ* means sowing has been performed.
Therefore it was said, “Enough with that much. *Vassitvā* means having caused rain to fall.
The teaching... [etc. ...shows that even when turning back the improper words spoken by the brahmin, "going for alms day after day" is indeed the bodily practice of the monks.
"Leading milk with the hand" means *khīranikā*. "Is wearying" (*kilamati*) means one becomes exhausted through the performance of various duties.
"Quivering" (*phandati*) means one struggles due to being joined with what is unwholesome. "For the sake of non-becoming" (*apunarbhavāya*).
"For non-arising in the future. "The path" means the means; it is Nibbāna, because when that is attained, there is no further becoming (*punabbhava*).
Taking the word "again and again" (*punappuna*) as a basis, since activities such as sowing seeds are called "repeated phenomena," he said:
"by one teaching the sixteen repeated phenomena."
The commentary on the Udayasutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Devahitasutta 199.
"By abdominal winds" means by the abdominal winds that circulate repeatedly through the piercing, thrusting, and so forth, produced by the wind-element.
Or [he lives] by means of its transformations. However, during the time when he has fixed attendants, he is merely the treasurer of the Dhamma.

"In the forest" refers to a penance grove (*tapovana*) that serves as a dwelling place for the Blessed One and his monks. That [grove] is smokeless because even the heating of water is not performed there.
"Therefore" means: because his livelihood is maintained through the practice of selling hot water, therefore [he does so].
This is appropriate because it is permissible to perform such things as praising [the physician] for the sake of repaying his kindness.
Now, in order to show the reason for this within its own context, the passage beginning with “vaṇṇaṃ hi” was stated. For the Blessed One [thought]:
“This highly esteemed preparation for medical treatment will belong to the venerable Upavāṇa, the Brahmin Devahita, and by means of it, there will be the alleviation of my own illness.”

Furthermore, knowing all this— that in connection with that very matter, the brahmin Devahita would come into my presence and, by hearing the Dhamma, become established in the refuges and the precepts—
I said, "Come now, Upavaṇa, find some hot water for me.
It was appropriate to speak thus in order to explain the path leading to arrival, the preliminary practice, and the preliminary performance.
Because they possess the unsurpassed human qualities (*anuttara-manussa-dhamma*). By the phrase "by the world with its devas," there is a complete inclusion of the entire world.

They are "worthy of worship" (*pūjanīya*) because they should be honored out of a desire for distinguished fruits; it is these very ones who are referred to here as "those worthy of worship" (*pūjaneyyā*).

Likewise, because they should be honored with reverence, they are "to be respected" (*sakkāriya*); by shortening the vowel *ā* and substituting *re* for the sound *ri*, it is stated as "they should be respected" (*sakkareyyā*).
“Apacayeyya” should have been said; however, by eliding the letter *ya*, it is stated as “apaceyya. “Of them” refers to those who are worthy of worship by the world including the devas.
“To bring” means to lead. “Even by this much”:
by performing even such a slight duty as approaching [the teacher] and so forth, he becomes one who possesses fame... and gives rise to joy.

"Of the sacrificer" (*yajamānassa*) means of one who is giving the object of offering (*deyyadhamma*). "The success of the sacrificial gift" (*dakkhiṇāya ijjhanaṃ*) means its state of having abundant fruit;
thus he said, "it becomes of great fruit" (*mahapphalo hoti*). "Known" (*viditaṃ*) means realized and made directly manifest.

"He understands" (*ājānāti*) means he knows and penetrates, having brought to an end the cycle of existence and so forth. "Having known" (*jānitvā*) means having penetrated the Four Truths in the sequence of the paths.

He has reached the state of having accomplished his task through the attainment of the highest state. Since the service performed by the brahmin is actually presented as being performed for the Blessed One himself, it is said:
"for one who sacrifices in this manner, characterized by the sacrifice of those whose taints are exhausted.
The commentary on the *Devahita Sutta* is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Mahāsāla Sutta 200.

Because that brahmin, being without support, had become especially coarse in body due to his old age, and because his cloak was pieced together from fragments of worn-out rags, the meaning of the term "wearing a coarse cloak" (*lūkhapāvuraṇo*) is stated as "wearing a worn-out cloak" (*jiṇṇapāvuraṇo*).
“Pāṭiyekkaṃ” means one by one among the sons, separately with each individual word.
“Sampucchanā” here means consultation; thus he said, “having consulted together. “Nandissaṃ” means he rejoiced.
This is a future tense used in the sense of the past; therefore he said, “he was filled with joy... [etc. ...he became. “Bhussantā” means crying out with a loud, resonant sound.
"Vayogataṃ" means one who has reached the final stage of life. Since he has passed beyond the first two stages of life, and has partially passed beyond the final stage as well, it is therefore said:
"One who has gone through the three stages of life, having transcended them, and is established in the final stage."

"Unusable" (*nipparibhoga*) means that because of its worn-out state, it has lost its vigor and excellence; it is unusable and should not be consumed. "The fodder is removed" means that those who do not give the fodder take it away from there. "Elder" (*thera*) means one who is aged. "Disobedient" (*anassava*) means they do not carry out one's instructions.

"Lacking respect" (*appatissa*) means devoid of deference. "Not acting under one's control" (*avasavattino*) means they do not conduct themselves according to one's will. "More excellent" (*sundaratara*) means more excellent by virtue of providing support.

"Having placed in front" means having made it a support by placing it before one. "He finds a footing in the water": because he stands there, he gains a firm footing; for a staff that is half-submerged provides a footing for the man holding the staff.
"Brahmin women" refers to his own Brahmin wives. "Individually" means separately, specifying them by saying, "in such-and-such a house, in such-and-such a house.
"Do not give them away," meaning, "they are precisely what we desire for our sons."
"Whatever place among our homes pleases us, there we shall go"—the Blessed One spoke thus, desiring to show favor to all of them.
"From that time forth" means from the moment of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). "For the purpose for which we [came] to this brahmin..."
The Teacher had rendered assistance through gifts of great prosperity and other means, and since that benefit had also been accomplished for his sons and attendants,
the Teacher did not go to the house of that brahmin’s sons at all times; rather,
the intention is that they themselves would go to the presence of the Teacher from time to time and perform honors and hospitality according to their means.
The commentary on the Mahāsāla Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Mānatthaddha Sutta 201.

"Stiff with conceit" means: stiff and bound by a conceit that has been aroused [by thinking] "This one indeed... and so forth; like a stiff iron rod, he does not bow down to anyone. He knows nothing at all in the world, because he does not even know the mere basics of social courtesy (*paṭisanthāra*).
*Abbhutavittajātā* means those in whom wonder has arisen. *Vitta* and *vitti* are synonyms for satisfaction (*tuṭṭhi*).
*Abhūtapubbāya* means that the satisfaction which arose in that assembly at that time had not occurred before. Therefore he said: "Endowed with wonder... [as above]...
*Assa puggalassa* means by this person. *Apacitā* refers to the general sense of being worthy of worship through supreme reverence.
In this context, skill in teaching consists in adapting the instruction to one's own disposition.
The commentary on the *Mānatthaddha-sutta* is concluded.
6. Commentary on the *Paccanīka-sutta*.
202. When someone says, “All is white,” it is for this very brahmin who is making a rebuttal to that statement.

“Having disciplined” means having destroyed. “One hears”—this is the meaning; by bringing forward the verb “one hears,” the meaning of the verse should be understood, because it is said, “one should know what is well-spoken. For indeed, it is not possible to know what has been taught without hearing it.
The commentary on the *Paccanīkasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Vanakammikasutta* 203.
One who is engaged in forest-work; because he has forest-work (*vanakamma*) being performed by him, he is called a "forest-worker" (*vanakammika*). In this [context]...
"In this forest grove" means in this very vast forest grove. "I have no business in the forest as you do, O Brahmin"—this is the intended meaning.
However, as for that great forest of defilements (*kilesa*), its roots have been completely severed by the axe of path-knowledge upon the whetstone of concentration;
therefore, it is "without forest" (*nibbana*), being devoid of the thicket of defilements. [This is] due to delighting in seclusion (*viveka*).
He delights in being alone because of the departure of opposing factors. Therefore, he said: “Having abandoned discontent... [and so on]... having abandoned.
The commentary on the *Vanakammika-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Kaṭṭhahāra-sutta*.
204. "Dhammantevāsikā" means those who are pupils solely by virtue of being students, without having given any wealth at all. Therefore he said:

"those who acquire a craft by performing services. "Of profound nature" refers to its depth due to being surrounded on all sides by dense, thick, and vast trees, shrubs, and creepers, and because, at that time, it was like a mass of snow and slush, making it impossible even for peacock-vehicles to stand upon it.
"Bahubherave" means full of many terrors. "Aniñjamānena" is an instrumental expression used in the sense of a state of being (itthambhūtatthe).
"Atisundaraṃ vata" means: "In such a place as this forest, while sitting with your body thus motionless and meditating, you are indeed meditating upon an exceedingly beautiful jhāna," he says.

“Of a wonderful nature” (*accherarūpaṃ*) means the state of being marvelous (*acchariyabhāvaṃ*). “Through the attainment of excellence” (*seṭṭhappattiyā*) means through the attainment of the state of being supreme (*seṭṭhabhāvappattiyā*).

By the phrase “desiring companionship with the Lord of the World,” the brahmin asks about association with the Lord of the World; however, by the words “Why, sir? and so forth, he asks about a desire for other specific qualities.

Thus it is said: “He asks in another way. “Doubt” (*kaṅkhā*) is craving (*taṇhā*) as it occurs in a continuous manner. “In things of manifold natures” (*anekasabhāvesu*) refers to [things] by way of form (*rūpa*), etc., and by way of the internal, etc.
Thus, with respect to various objective conditions (*ārammaṇa*): greed for gratification (*assāda-rāga*), covetousness (*lobha*), and longing (*abhijjhā*) are of many kinds;

or alternatively, the remaining defilements (*kilesa*) such as views (*diṭṭhi*), conceit (*māna*), and hatred (*dosa*). They are "constant" (*nicca-kāla*) because they are the necessary support for sentient beings.
"By way of yearning" (*pajappāpanavasena*) means by way of various modes of craving (*taṇhāyana*). "Without interval" (*nirantara*) means vanished and without remainder.
"Anupagamanoti" means "without clinging. This illuminates the knowledge of omniscience;
for it is by virtue of that very knowledge that the Blessed One perceives all diverse natures with his universal eye, and thus he is called "the one who sees all... [as they really are].
This is said with reference to Arahantship, for that is called "unsurpassed" in the primary sense.
The commentary on the Kaṭṭhahāra Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Mātuposaka Sutta 205.

"Iti" means from the human state of existence. "Paṭigantvā" means having gone toward. For one being reborn in heaven, by the power of the fruit of their karma and according to the natural law (dhammatā), from the moment of conception onwards, they truly do delight with a sense of rapture.
The commentary on the *Mātuposaka-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Bhikkhaka-sutta*: 206.
"It emits a foul odor" means it is *visso*, that is, ill-smelling. "Having cast out" means having expelled from one's own mental continuum (*santāna*).
"Having removed" means having abandoned that without remainder; thus he said, "having abandoned by means of the supreme path.
It is called *saṅkhā* because by it one correctly calculates (*saṅkhāyati*) and delimits; thus he said, "by calculation (*saṅkhāya*), that is, by knowledge (*ñāṇena*).
He explains the derivation of the word *bhikkhu* according to the method of etymology as "one whose defilements have been shattered" (*bhinna-kilesatta*).
The commentary on the Bhikkhaka Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta:
207. "Pacceti" means he trusts; he has faith. And being thus, one who desires that goal is said to be "seeking after it."
It is said: "He desires, he yearns. Regarding the phrase "Very well, venerable sir," the word *sādhu* here has the sense of a request (*āyācana*), not the sense of approval (*abhinandana*).

Having stated "he spoke while making a request," the author says "it is said that for the Elder... and so forth, showing the reason for the request. One who purifies by water is not necessarily bound for a state of misery (*apāya*);
however, because [the practice] is, according to his own tenet (*laddhi*), a blameworthy defilement (*sāvajja-kilesa-bhūta*), he makes the request. There is another reason.
Referring to this, he said, "And furthermore," and so forth. He stated that it is the "basis of meaning" (*atthavasa*) because its purpose (*attha*) consists in the fruit;

thus he said, "the basis of meaning, the cause of meaning" (*atthānisaṃsaṃ atthakāraṇaṃ*). However, in the *Papañcasūdani*, it is stated: "It is 'meaning' (*attha*) because it is to be sought (*araṇīya*) by means of the fruit;
taking it as the cause, 'the basis of meaning' is simply the meaning itself. Therefore, 'two bases of meaning' means two meanings, two causes."
The commentary on the Saṅgāravasutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the Khomadussa Sutta:
208. The construction is: “He who had thus acquired that name entered for alms. “In this very way” means by himself, without being invited by anyone.
As they were approaching, [the Buddha thought: "An unpleasant physical condition" refers to an unsuitable form.
"The duty of the assembly" (sabhādhamma) refers to the conduct that ought to be practiced within the assembly. "Without causing him to move" means without making him rise from his seat.

The Blessed One, the Leader of the World, the supreme among all beings, comes directly forward; because there is no one in the world superior to himself, he does not display the formal courtesy expected of the world.
By the words beginning with "these," he shows that those who abandon all defilements entirely are indeed the wise ones called "the peaceful.
The commentary on the *Khomadussa Sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the *Brāhmaṇa-saṃyutta* of the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the Commentary on the *Saṃyutta-nikāya*, is completed. 8.
The *Vaṅgīsa-saṃyutta*.
1. Commentary on the Nikkhanta Sutta 209.
"At Āḷavī" means in the vicinity of the city of Āḷavī. "At the Supreme Shrine" (aggacetiye) refers to the supreme shrine among those such as the Gotamaka Cetiya.
It is said that because of its delightful natural beauty, its charm, and its excellence in being conducive to striving (*padhāna*), it surpasses other shrines.
"Esteemed as the best. By the Elder Kappa: "Kappa" is the name he received from his clan; this great elder was among the thousand jaṭila ascetics. "Ohīnaka":
when the elders had entered the village for alms, he remained behind in the monastery itself.
He states the reason for this with the words "monastery guardian," and so forth. "Having adorned evenly": by means of equal adornment.
"Having adorned": by way of not allowing a wholesome state of mind (*kusalacitta*) to arise, he destroys it.
"When this" means when this lust has arisen. Alternatively, there is the reading "in one" (*ekasmiṃ*); that is, when lust has arisen toward a single object of a different class (*visabhāgavatthu*).
"Or another phenomenon" (*dhammo vā*) means a phenomenon other than that which arises in my own mind. By which reason another, having dispelled his lack of delight...
The construction is: "How could that cause be obtained so as to produce delight right now? The meaning is: "That cause does not exist. This is the statement of the reason for its absence.

Regarding "the homeless life" (*anagāriya*): it is the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), which is "homeless" (*anagāra*) because of being devoid of a home (*agāra*). Because one is devoted to that, it is called "the homeless life"; [this is the derivation] of the letter *ka*.
Having used the letter *ya*, the meaning is "one who has gone forth" (*pabbajita*). "They run toward" means they run, having overwhelmed the heart. "Of those who have risen up" means of noble sons.
Therefore he said, "of great influence, being of royal lineage. "The supreme measure" means a thousand *palas* all around;
that is, on every side. "They would surround" means they would pierce. "From this thousand" means from the aforementioned thousand archers.
"Many thousands more women, casting glances, smiles, frowns, weeping, and cries, will neither bewitch me nor captivate me.
Regarding the reading "byādhayissati," it is stated that the meaning is "they will not be able to shake me.
"In the Dhamma" means in one's own presence, in the Sāsana-Dhamma firmly established. Therefore he said:
“Having dispelled discontent,” and so forth.
The word *magga* is stated here with a change of gender where it should have been called *maggo*. Therefore he said: “For that is the preliminary path to Nibbāna.
The commentary on the Nikkhanta Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Arati Sutta 210.
"This elder, it is said, was fond of his dwelling" means that this elder had no opportunity to exhort his own pupil Vaṅgīsa.
By this, he shows that from time to time lust would agitate the latter's mind. "Discontent with the Teaching" (sāsane aratiṃ).
Discontent with the fulfillment of virtue and the cultivation of serenity and insight; delight in the strands of sensual pleasure—that is, gratification in the five categories of sensual objects;
and evil thoughts—that is, sensual intention. "In every way" means by all modes: the mode of partial suppression, the mode of suppression, and the mode of eradication.
Just as a great wilderness is called a "thicket," so too the great forest of defilements is called a "thicket."
*Pathaviñca vehāsan* is the nominative singular used in the sense of the locative; therefore, the meaning is "on the earth and in the sky.
Hence he said, "established on the earth," and so forth. *Jagatī* is a synonym for the earth. Hence he said, "within the earth.
*Parijīrati* means it reaches complete decay. *Samāgantvā* means having come together with knowledge. Hence he said:
“*Mutattā* means having known the state of being.

By the term *paṭigha*, odors and tastes are included because they function by striking against the nose and tongue. By the term *muta*, the object of touch (*phoṭṭhabba*) is included because it is to be grasped after being touched. “*Na lippati*” means he is not smeared.
The word *saṭṭhi* has the same meaning as the word *cha*; thus, the phrase “*saṭṭhinissitā*” means “dependent on the six objects.”

The meaning has been stated. "Diverse unrighteous thoughts" (*puthū adhammavitakkā*) refers to many various types of thoughts—such as thoughts of form (*rūpavitakka*), and so forth—which are wrong intentions (*micchāsaṅkappa*).
"Established among the people" (*janatāya niviṭṭhā*) means firmly rooted in the great multitude. "By way of those" (*tesaṃ vasenā*) means by way of those very wrong thoughts.

"In no object whatsoever" (*na katthaci ārammaṇe*). "One would not have entered into a mass of defilements" (*kilesavaggagato*) means one would not have fallen into a collection of defilements (*kilesasaṅgaṇikaṃ*).

The meaning is that defiled thoughts should not be generated. "Vulgar speech" refers to talk connected with sensual desire. "Of a fickle nature" means of a frivolous character. "By means of circumspection" means by means of skillfulness.
"Depending on Nibbāna" means depending on the unconditioned element as an object. "At the time of final Nibbāna" means at the time of Nibbāna without residue.
The commentary to the *Arati Sutta* is concluded.
3. Pesalasuttavaṇṇanā 211.
"Of these" means of these elders. "The text does not come [to them]" because they are not well-versed in it.
"And the text does not appear" means that even when one portion of the text is present, they lack the ability for the text to appear to them in its various aspects; thus he says.
The same method applies here as well regarding the phrase "not in the commentary" (*na aṭṭhakathā*).

Sweetness of words and syllables (*padabyañjanamadhuratā*) consists in pronouncing them without losing the perception of the specific phonemes, such as those that are lax or hard (*sithila-dhanitādi-tantaṃ*). He thinks of other bhikkhus as being surpassed;

having overcome them by means of his inspired eloquence (*paṭibhāna-suta*), he praises and esteems himself out of a sense of contempt. Because of the occurrence of pride (*māna*), there arise states that serve as its co-nascent, support, and other types of conditions.
Those phenomena co-arising with it. "May you not be remorseful on account of pride"—this is the construction.
"Praising" means the extolling of virtues being performed by others. "Without barrenness" means free from the five mental barrennesses (*cetokhila*).

"Entirely the ninefold" means that all nine types of pride, without exception, [are abandoned] even in their slightest part. "By clear knowledge" means by the clear knowledge of the supreme path. "Absolutely" (*accantameva*).
One who has become tranquil through tranquility is a "tranquilized one" (*samitāvī*).
The commentary on the *Pesala-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Ānanda-sutta*.
212. Here, in order to clarify the cause for the arising of Venerable Vaṅgīsa’s lust (*rāga*), it is said, beginning with “Venerable Ānanda.
“Him” refers to the Elder Ānanda. “To comprehend the object” means to take as the range of mindfulness the objects classified as body, feeling, and so forth;
or rather, each single object among the six—such as the foul, the painful, or the form and so on—from the perspective of impermanence, suffering, and so forth.
To grasp means to discern and know. "With the female form as its object" means with the object that is the nature of form within the continuum of a woman.

"Extinguishing" (*nibbāpana*) means that by which one extinguishes; thus it is "extinguishing. "By way of perversion" means by reason of the state of perversion, such as [perceiving] the "beautiful" in what is unattractive.
"A basis for lust" means a cause for the arising of lust. "A desirable object" means an object of beauty. And here, under the heading of the "desirable object,"...

In this context, he speaks of grasping at the desirable aspect; for that is indeed what is to be avoided. "From another" means from something else, in the sense of not being subject to one's own control.
For even when formations are desired with the wish, "May they not break up," they nevertheless break up; therefore, because they are not subject to one's control, they are called "other.
And since that otherness of theirs becomes evident through the vision of impermanence, it is said: "See them as 'from another,' that is, as impermanent."

"See! Although insight (vipassanā) does not abandon the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta), because it proceeds by taking formations as its object, it is nevertheless worthy of being grasped as "signless" (animittā) through the non-grasping of certain signs. To show this, it was said: "of the signs of permanence, etc.
The convergence of vision (dassanābhisamaya) regarding conceit occurs by way of seeing both specific characteristics (salakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa).

The realization of abandonment through insight (*vipassanā*) is what they call "by means of the path. However, it is the realization of seeing by way of penetration through full understanding (*pariññā*), due to non-delusion by the path itself;

and it is the realization of abandonment by way of penetration through abandonment. "By way of the subsiding of lust and so forth" means by way of the state of peace (*santa*), because lust and the rest are to be pacified through their eradication and their subsiding.
The commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Subhāsita Sutta: 213.
They are called *aṅga* because they are known as causes, as traditional authorities, or as constituent parts; that is, reasons.
He says, “By means of parts,” meaning “by means of causes (kāraṇehi) or by means of constituent members (avayavehi).
Since the abstentions are established prior to well-spoken speech, he says, “False speech... [etc. ...are the causes,” meaning they are the specific causes for that [speech].
Because noble modes of expression are specifically of the nature of volition (cetanā), truthfulness in speech and so forth are the constituents of the collection of verbal good conduct.
“Being constituent parts,” he says, “the four factors beginning with truthful speech. “The ablative case” refers to the ablative used in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
Therefore he says, “attained and occurring. For speech is said to be “endowed” (*samannāgatā*) because it has come forth and proceeds in accordance with—that is, in conformity with—that abstinence.
“The instrumental case” refers to the instrumental used in connection with association (*sahayoga*). Therefore he says, “joined.”
For even a co-nascent volition (cetanā) deserves to be called "properly conjoined" with the abstinence (virati) as it has been undertaken, in accordance with its nature.

"Speech of utterance" (samullapanavācā) refers to vocal sound; because it is spoken, it is called "speech" (vācā). But it is called "speech" (vācā) because communication (viññatti) is effected by means of it;
likewise, abstinence and volition are "speech. However, that [kind of] speech of volition is not intended here; rather, it is the speech of communication (viññattivācā) that is meant.
In this sutta, they are not intended [in that sense], because of the statement, "it is well-spoken. Therefore he said, "because it should not be spoken [otherwise].
"Well-spoken" means spoken correctly according to the proper method, because it constitutes verbal good conduct (*vācīsucarita*). "Bringing benefit" refers to the time when it brings welfare.
"Purity of cause" refers to the purification of the cause through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*). "Absence of fault" refers to the absence of faults such as following wrong courses of action.
For when one speaks that which is free from lust, hatred, and so forth, because of the avoidance of partiality and hostility, the treading of wrong paths is indeed utterly eradicated.
"Free from reproach" means devoid of censure. It illuminates perfection in every aspect; for if there were no perfection in every aspect, there would also be grounds for reproach.
Although the teaching was previously commenced with a reference to the Dhamma, it is now [presented] with a reference to the person, owing to the inclination of the individual...pe...

This is the statement. Although here it is stated without qualification as "the word of a certain faultless person," because [the Buddha] speaks with speech that is free from the faults of non-Dhamma and so forth—as expressed in the passage beginning "he speaks only the Dhamma"—here too, well-spoken speech is intended.
By the restrictive term "only well-spoken," he shows by way of its specific form what is excluded: "not ill-spoken."
By this [phrase]. Therefore he said: “The prevention of speech that is the opposite of that very vocal factor.
For the word *eva* has the sense of excluding its contrary; by it, the rejection of malicious speech (*pisuṇavācā*) is shown.
Or, since the fourfold good verbal conduct is included by the term “well-spoken,” it is said: “By the phrase ‘not ill-spoken,’ the abandoning of wrong speech (*micchāvācā*) is illustrated.”

For "well-spoken" (*subhāsita*) is a term common to all well-performed verbal actions. Therefore, it should be understood that even the speech of Bodhisattvas that involves causing division in others and so forth, as well as that which is unwholesome (*asabbha*) and so on, falls within the scope of non-slanderous speech and the rest.
The phrase "the characteristic of speech that ought to be spoken" is connected by supplying the words:
"it elucidates the essential characteristic (*sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*) of speech that ought to be spoken. If this is so, is it not [the case that...]?
Having stated first that which should not be said, one should state afterwards that which should be said, as in: "Release the left, take the right.
[The phrase] "But for the purpose of indicating the parts," and so forth, refers to this.
"By the first" means by the word "well-spoken" (*subhāsita*). "Not departing from the Dhamma" means not departing from the Dhamma that brings about welfare and happiness for oneself and others.
“Not departed from. *Mantāvacanaṃ* means speech that should be set forth through wisdom (*mantā*).
For one who possesses wisdom and whose speech is not scattered does not utter speech that brings no benefit. “By the other two,” refers to the third and fourth phrases. Some say:
“In ‘by these,’ etc., this is the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental. That speech is the fourfold speech as previously described. And whatever speech—

The connection is with the word "they imagine. "Others" refers to those outside of this [teaching], namely the proponents of logic (*ñāyavādino*) and the grammarians (*akkharacintakā*). They say: "The thesis (*paṭiññā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*) are the members (*avayavā*) of a statement.

"By means of nouns and so forth" means by means of the words for nouns (*nāma*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*). "Gender" (*liṅga*) refers to feminine gender and so forth; "number" (*vacana*) refers to the singular and so forth.

"Case endings" (*vibhatti*) such as the nominative and so forth [indicate] time (*kāla*) such as the past and so forth. [The case endings indicate] the agent (*kattā*), the recipient (*sampadāna*), the point of departure (*apādāna*), and the instrument (*karaṇa*).
“Basis, action, and agent”—the phrase “endowed with attainments” is stated having fulfilled these [three] factors and so forth.
“He negates that” means that the Blessed One, by saying “Indeed, by these,” negates even that aforementioned qualification of speech.
Here, the word *kho* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). Therefore he said, “factors and so forth. Whatever possesses the characteristic of being an improper linguistic expression.
That was the language of the Mlecchas. "By means of the Sinhalese alone" means by means of speech included within the Sinhalese language.

"They attained arahantship" means that, having become intensely stirred by the terrors of saṃsāra and having directed their minds toward its escape, they exerted themselves in insight (vipassanā) and attained arahantship through the successive stages of the path.

"Early in the morning, like a full-blown *kokanada* lotus" means a lotus that has fully blossomed at dawn. "It is broken open" means it is split apart; a bursting forth occurs. "Having gone to the human state" means having attained the condition of a human being.
"In the interval between Buddhas" means during the period between the appearance of two Buddhas, while the teaching of the *paccekabuddhas*—and not the teaching of a Buddha—is shining.
"Worn down by old age" means just as the limbs such as the hands and feet become flaccid, so too do the faculties such as the eyes [deteriorate].
They become incapable of grasping their respective objects; youth has completely vanished; physical strength has departed;
mindfulness, intelligence, fortitude, and so forth, have been dissociated; even one's own children, wife, and others, who formerly followed one's advice, now show no regard;
there is the state of needing to be helped up by others and being led to bed by them, and once again the attainment of the condition of a fool—thus, through old age, [one is] entirely...

"Crushed. "This" refers to the body. "Dependent on withered skin and hide" means it is supported by elements whose youth has passed away and which are withered due to being devoid of flesh and blood through the process of aging.
"Food and meat" refers to the bait that is like food, because it must be established [as sustenance] after being swallowed, as it were, by death.
It is filled with various kinds of filth such as hair, body hair, and so forth; for that very reason, it is a vessel of impurity.
This [is so] because it is entirely devoid of essence, like the trunk of a plantain tree.
"Suitable" means appropriate for the Perfectly Enlightened One. "One should not scorch" means one should not scorch either the mind or the body;
and here, "scorching" refers to despondency both in the present and in the future. "One should not oppress" is a synonym for the phrase "one should not overcome."
The vision of the goal. "By way of non-slanderous speech" means by way of having entirely abandoned slanderous speech. "Evil things" means base and inferior things;
therefore he said, "unpleasant," and so forth. "Without taking up" means without grasping.
"By way of being wholesome" means by way of being faultless and sweet. "Like the Deathless": this is a designation for what is similar [to it], or else it is used here in the sense of the cause.

It is called "conventional usage" (kāriyavohāra) because it says, "or because of its being a condition for the name 'Nibbāna'. For at that time, its manifestation as seeing occurs by way of a condition.
"Conduct" (cariyā) means behavior (cāritta). The "ancients" (porāṇa) are those of the first eon, or the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas.
"Established" (patiṭṭhitā) means having made a firm resolve through immovability; because its state is dependent upon conditions, it is non-deceptive. In both ways...
He spoke of practice [when he said]: "Established in the welfare of oneself and others.

Because they are established in welfare—namely, in benefit pertaining to the present life, the future life, and so forth—they are likewise established in the Dhamma, that is, in qualities such as non-violence.

By the term "non-obstructive," he shows that the word *attha* (welfare) is a synonym for *hita* (benefit). "Dhammic" means not departing from the Dhamma, or else, it means endowed with both welfare and the Dhamma.
"For the attainment of Nibbāna" means for the purpose of attaining Nibbāna. "For the making of an end to suffering" means for the purpose of bringing about its cessation.
Since the Buddha speaks for the sake of security (*khemā*), it is therefore secure (*khemā*) because it is the cause for the arising of security;
thus, it should be understood here that it is the supreme among all words. "By way of being a mantra-word" means by way of being free from all defects.
The commentary on the Subhāsita-sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Sāriputta-sutta: 214.
That which becomes full by filling the causes of the qualities of speech through skill in verbal expression is "polished" (*porī*); [it is] by means of that polished [speech].
Therefore he said, “complete in its syllables and so forth. “Unbound” means not bound by bile and the other humors, that is, unafflicted.

Therefore he said, “unobstructed,” and so on. “Faultless” means free from defects in both meaning and phrasing. “With words and phrases that do not falter” means with words and phrases that do not slip;
“sufficient for making the meaning known” means adequate for awakening one to the meaning, such as matters pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) and so forth.
"Bhikkhunī" is stated with a short vowel for the sake of metrical convenience.

The phrase "he teaches in brief and speaks in detail" does not refer to a statement made after first reciting [the text] and then praising its meaning; for that [latter case] would indeed be an exposition in detail.

However, this was said with reference to both types of teaching: that which is sometimes set forth in brief according to the disposition of those receiving the Dhamma, and that which is sometimes given in detail. Therefore he said, "These four," and so forth.
To show that what is sweet by its very nature becomes even sweeter through the influence of conditions, he said, "Just as," and so forth. In various ways...
“Patibhāna” (inspiration) means that which manifests as the ability to speak on the Dhamma; it is the knowledge of the manner of teaching. Therefore, he said, “From the ocean,” and so forth.
“Odahanti” means they immerse themselves by way of understanding.
The commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Pavāraṇā Sutta 215.
Regarding the phrase *tasmiṃ ahu*: it means "on that day," as he says, "on that day. *Anasanena* means by the total abstention from food. The construction is:

"having been endowed with either the ascetic virtue (*sāsana-kīla*) of the Buddhist dispensation or the external (*bāhiraka*) practice of fasting. By the word "or" (*vā*), [the two alternatives are indicated].

It also includes the drinking of milk, honey, sugar-cane juice, and so forth. It is called *pavāraṇā* because by means of it one restrains [faults] through various modes such as what has been seen, causes [others] to remember their bodily actions and so on, and makes them objects of censure;
it is the granting of an opportunity for the purification of practice—that is, for the purification of one’s own faults.
Since this teaching of purification is generally to be performed by those who have completed the rains-residence (*vassa*), it is therefore said:

“[It is] the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) for those who have completed the rains-residence (*vassa*). It is also called ‘the invitation of purity’ (*visuddhi-pavāraṇā*). At that time, in order to show the praise for the complete silence of that community of monks (*bhikkhu-saṅgha*), it was stated in the Canon as “having become silent”; thus he said, “From whatever [point]...
there is none. Hand-fidgeting (*hattha-kukkucca*) is lack of restraint and unwise action of the hand.

In the same way, "foot-worry" (pādakukkucca) is to be understood; the word *vā* has the sense of an unstated alternative (*avuttavikappa*), by which it should be seen that the absence of anything other than those [two] is indicated.
"With five sensitive parts" means with the five types of sensitive matter (*pasāda*). "The sense of relinquishment" (*vossagga*) is the letting go (*vossajjana*) of action according to one's desire.
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of questioning" (*pucchanatthe*): the negative particle *na* is used here in the sense of questioning by way of negation.
The meaning is: "Do not reproach me for any action, whether physical or verbal; why indeed would you reproach me with body or speech?

Some say that by the term "gates" (*dvārāni*), they refer to the conduct proceeding through those gates. Because the invitation to purity (*visuddhipavāraṇā*) is intended here, it is by the very person who has invited [to confess] that [the confession is made].
It is known as "purity" because it has not been abandoned. Might some worldling (puthujjana) have the suspicion that it is "impure"?
To prevent that, he said: "Not because of impurity. The mind-door is pure because the defilements that produce impurity have been removed.
"Now" means at this present time, during the era of a Buddha. "In this" refers to the purity of the mind-door.
Since the purification of mental conduct is already implied by the teaching on the purification of bodily and verbal conduct, he said, "whether bodily or verbal. For it has been stated:
"The Elder spoke 'whether bodily or verbal' with reference to the four things that are not to be guarded. [He said] "I invite you, monks," because this refers to the community of monks.
On that occasion of the *pavāraṇā*, the Dhammasenāpati, while giving his reply to be spoken by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, was addressed as "one who bears the burden of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Therefore he said, "Indeed, venerable sir," and so forth. They are "not to be guarded against" because they need not be feared in the face of reproach from others, owing to their state of complete purity.
“*Anuppannassā*” (of that which has not arisen) is a statement with a specific underlying intention (*adhippāyika-vacana*).

Expounding upon that intention, he said: “From the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa,” and so forth. In the analysis “from the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa,” the ablative case is used;

therefore, the meaning is “descending from the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa. “By another” means by someone other than this Blessed One. “Never previously produced” means [never produced] in the mental continuum of another.
"Previously arisen": it cannot be said that [these qualities] have not arisen in the personal continuum of the Paccekabuddhas.

"Endowed with" (samanuāgatā) means having properly approached (sammā anu upagatā). Regarding "the Blessed One’s qualities such as virtue," he says, "they have come about by depending on the path of arahantship itself," because the qualities of one who has become a Buddha are intended here.
"All qualities" refers to all the Buddha-qualities, such as the knowledge of the ten powers (dasabalañāṇa), and so forth.
In the word *bhanteti*, the particle *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*). By this, everything up to the passage in the text beginning with "But for these...
or verbal [invitation]" is included. Therefore he said: "The Elder, while performing the invitation ceremony, spoke thus...
That which is established by the power of his own merit—the Wheel-Treasure—is, in the primary sense, what is called "set in motion by him. It is not...

"Otherwise" refers to the first method mentioned. Since this is a continuation of what has already been set forth, and because the first method was stated by applying that designation to things similar to it, the second method is stated without taking that into account. "Tenfold" refers to:
the provision of protection, defense, and security for the inner circle of family, the army, and the guards; and [provision] among the devoted kṣatriyas, brahmins, and householders.
The tenfold [duty] consists of: the prohibition of unrighteous conduct among merchants and countryfolk, ascetics and brahmins, and beasts and birds;
the bestowing of wealth upon the poor; and approaching ascetics and brahmins to ask questions.
Therein, by including householders and birds as separate categories, it is twelvefold. This is the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-vatta*).

The conduct that brings about the state of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). Because it is practiced according to reality, it is said to be "practiced in accordance with the proper method" (*ñāya-yutta*);
thus he says, "by the right method, by way of cause and reason.
He shows that the meaning here is "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), which means liberated from both parts, or liberated from both sides, by saying, "liberated by two parts."

By this [phrase], "formless... [and so on]... from the mental body. "The state of possessing the three knowledges, etc. means the state of being one who possesses the three knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the four analytical insights.
For those liberated by wisdom alone have not attained that threefold [state], but are liberated by wisdom alone.
"For the sake of purification" means for the sake of the invitation to purity. In the sense of fettering, they are designated as "fetters," and in the sense of binding...

And regarding what is designated as "bondage": "one who has conquered the battle" means that the Noble Path-army has won the battle in such a way that lust and the other defilements will never again raise their heads; thus he said, "one who has conquered the battle of lust, hatred, and delusion.

"Of the power of Māra" refers either to the army of Māra or to the capacity of Māra. "The multitude of those to be guided" refers to the assembly of people who are to be led [to liberation]. This is because it shares the common characteristics of a caravan, such as a wagon-train and so forth.
"Having trained those who are to be trained" refers to that army of those to be trained (*vineyya-sattha*). It is "hollow within" due to the absence of the core of virtue (*sīla-sāra*) and so forth.
The commentary on the *Pavāraṇā-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Parosahassa-sutta*.
216. Regarding the statement that at that time two hundred and fifty monks, more than a thousand, were attending upon the Blessed One, he said: “More than a thousand” means exceeding one thousand.
There is no fear in Nibbāna from anything whatsoever; for no reason at all is there fear in Nibbāna, because it is entirely secure due to its unconditioned nature.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: “And, bhikkhus, what is secure for you...”
“I shall teach the Dhamma and the practice leading to security,” and so forth. Because there is no fear from any quarter once this has been attained, it is called *akutobhaya* (fearless);
[this refers to] Nibbāna. Therefore he said, “of one who has reached Nibbāna,” and so on.

The phrase “starting from the time of Vipassi” is stated for the purpose of showing that our Blessed One was the seventh among the seers (*isī*) by way of name; for they [the previous Buddhas] were in various places...
