"Extolled many times in the Suttas. Regarding "of the seers" (*isīnaṃ*): the meaning is that he is the seventh, the highest and most excellent among the seers—the Paccekabuddhas, the disciples, and the external ascetics.
"By way of the origin of the matter" (*aṭṭhuppattivasena*) means by way of the arising of the cause. To clarify that origin of the matter, it was said: "In the midst of the Saṅgha," and so forth.
He is called Vaṅgīsa because with his speech endowed with inspired eloquence (*paṭibhāna*), he "sees" or overcomes others. Therefore, he said: "The perfection of inspired eloquence," and so forth.
“Hundreds of immersions of the defilements” refers to the improper arisings of the defilements—such as lust and so forth—within their respective objects by way of being excited, corrupted, and so on.
If there are many hundreds, why then is it called a “path of wrong ways”? To this he says:

“But it is called a ‘path’ because it is the path of the round (saṃsāra). By way of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views, there are the five barren soils, beginning with the barren soil of lust. “They divide” means...
"Speaking by way of analysis": having analyzed, that is, having distinguished by means of knowledge.

"Proclaimed the Deathless": the teachings that bring about the Deathless have been taught. "Seers of the Dhamma": through the penetration of the Truths. "Unshakable by the winds of views. "Having pierced through":

having penetrated. "Become transcendent": become transcendent in the sense of having gone beyond. "Of ten halves": of ten [units], each being a half. Therefore he said, "of five. "By one who knows": by one who knows the extreme rarity of the Dhamma.
The commentary on the Parosahassasutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Koṇḍaññasutta: 217.
"One who has thus received a name" refers to [the Buddha] being addressed by the monks, based on the Teacher’s words: "Koṇḍañña indeed has understood! (Aññāsi vata, bho, Koṇḍañño).
He was given this name for the purpose of distinguishing him from others who also bore the name Koṇḍañña. "After a long time" refers to the period of twelve years.
"In the abode of Chaddanta" means in the dwelling place of the Naga king Chaddanta. "The wise great disciple" [is so called] because of his long-standing seniority.
"Of the gods and humans in ten thousand world-systems" means of the gods in ten thousand world-systems.
"In this world-system (cakkavāḷa) of gods and humans"—thus they say [it applies] "to the gods and humans in the ten thousand world-systems.
*Agga* means from the beginning. *Tattha* means on the bank of the Mandākinī.
*Vassaggena* means by the sequence of years. *Taṃ* refers to the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña. Like the Great Brahmās, worldly humans...

They were filled with longing. The Venerable Elder, being the leader, stayed here and there in various regions along the way, and in due course arrived at the banks of the Mandākinī; therefore it is said: "Venerable sir, I wish to dwell in the countryside.
Those elephant-lords were endowed with majesty and possessed divine lifespans; thus it is said: "Because of their former service to the Paccekabuddhas..."
"Having completed his practice. Having cleared away the obstructing branches from the Elder’s walking path and removed them, he provided water for rinsing the mouth and tooth-sticks;

that is, having produced fire by rubbing together pieces of *saḷala* wood, *devadāru* wood, and so forth, and having kindled it, he heated stone fragments therein, rolled them on sticks, and [placed them] at the water-holes in the ponds.
Having thrown it away and ascertained that the water has become hot, he brings a *nāgalatā* tooth-stick and sets out water for rinsing the mouth.
He performs his duties (*vatta*) by sweeping with broken twigs both inside the hut and outside at the entrance and in the courtyard,
and by bringing food in the manner to be described.
"At the measure of its base" means at the measure of the waist; or this reading itself means "of such great extent," that is, as great as the white lotus grove is.
This same method applies to the red water-lily groves and so forth. "Men eating" [them].
"Like well-cooked thickened milk" means like well-cooked *payoghana* (thickened milk). Because of its density, however, it contains small amounts of honey.
It is as if it were so; therefore he said, “This is called ‘lotus-honey. *Muḷāla* is the root of white lotuses. *Bhisa* is their very bulb (*kanda*).
“In one joint” means in each individual internode. “A foot-measure jar” (*pādaghaṭaka*) refers to a small vessel, being a quarter of a *doṇa* in size due to its shape;
therefore, it is the measure of a jar, about the capacity of a *tumba*. “In a small pit” (*soṇḍiāvāṭe*) refers to small pits.

And also in small enclosures. "This food" refers to the aforementioned meal of milk-rice without water. Some recognize [this]—those elders who are more senior; some do not recognize it—those who are new, having recently gone forth.
"Enlightened after the Buddha" means enlightened following the Buddha. "Possessing strong energy" is by way of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
“Of long-accumulated vigor”: the construction is that he is one who has obtained the three kinds of seclusion—namely, seclusion of body, mind, and requisites.
The Elder Vaṅgīsa speaks of four [knowledges] out of his own inspired eloquence, not because the other higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are absent; thus he says, “the others,” and so forth.
“The assembly sat down” means they became silent by way of being noiseless. “He caused permission to be given” means that first, by himself...
The meaning here should be understood as follows: having known and established for himself the time of his own final nibbāna, he subsequently made it known to the Teacher.
"That" refers to that first sight at Isipatana on the full moon of Āsāḷha, or rather, that initial sight of you during the period of difficult ascetic practices;
"that, Bhante, was the first sight. "Onata-vinata" means inclined both downward and upward.
Vinatā. "Having shaken" means having moved slightly for the sake of showing [them].

"With a single roar" refers to the sound of those elephant-lords (*hatthināga*), as well as the *nāgas*, *yakkhas*, *kumbhaṇḍas*, and deities. "The Brahmās showed the gods" is the grammatical connection.
They performed recitation (*sajjhāya*) for the purpose of generating faith in the Blessed One within the assembly that had gathered out of faith toward those things that inspire faith.

"Having gone out" means having gone out from the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi) when the Blessed One had emerged. "It remains indeed" means that, having reached a state of non-corruption, it simply persists.
The commentary on the Koṇḍañña Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta.
218. *Paccavekkhatīti*: He reviews, that is, he looks back upon and examines the minds of those noble ones with his own eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*).
*Pabbatassā ti*: Of the Isigili mountain. *Dukkhapāraṃ gatan ti*: Gone to the further shore, the limit, of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
*Sabbaguṇasampannan ti*: Endowed with all qualities, both the qualities of a Buddha and the qualities of a disciple. *Anekākārasampannan ti*: Endowed with manifold aspects.

It is endowed with those various modes by which beings—whether they be limited to form, sound, smell, taste, or touch—can place their confidence, and with all the many infinite and immeasurable modes of inspiring faith.
Since those modes are indeed the unique qualities of a Buddha (buddhaguṇā) not shared by others, he said: "endowed with manifold qualities."
The commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Gaggarā Sutta, §219:
"Those" refers to those gods and humans. Regarding the phrase "by the color of the body," they say it means "by the color of the skin on the body. By the color of the body...
Or [it is] by virtue of his body of Dhamma. There is also the reading “yasasā,” which has the same meaning. “Vigatamalo” means one who is free from defilements such as clouds, mist, and the like.
“Bhāṇu” refers to radiance; because he possesses an exceeding radiance, he is “bhāṇumā. He is called “sūriyo” (the sun), as expressed by the words “like the Ādicca.”
The commentary on the Gaggarā Sutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta. 220.
"He, it is said, wanders about"—this is the connection. "Just as this island, Jambudīpa, is known by the name 'Jambu,' so am I..."
Thinking, "By means of that rose-apple tree he will be known," she carried away a branch of the *jambu* tree. "Having made a wager" means:
having made an agreement such as, "In this debate, if you are defeated, you shall become my slave; if I am defeated, I shall become your wife.
"By the power of victory or defeat in the debate" means: by the power of the wanderer's victory in the debate thus conducted.
"And by one's own defeat. "By resorting to a craft" means by resorting to the practice of learning a craft. "Vijja" means a spell (*manta*).
It is called a "corpse-defiling craft" (*chavadūsaka-sippa*) because it defiles—that is, destroys—the state of a corpse-head by way of manifesting the destiny of rebirth;
such is the phrase of the spell as it functions. "By its own power" refers to where the head of a being reborn in hell [is located].
Having brought and shown [the skull] which was located somewhere by means of the Buddha’s supernormal power:

"The head of one whose taints are destroyed" refers to the discarded skull of a *khīṇāsava* who, out of supreme fewness-of-wishes, had entered the forest without letting anyone know and attained final nibbāna.
"He showed it" means he brought it by his own supernormal power and displayed it.
“Do you know, Master Gotama? Vaṅgīsa asked this with reference to the place where he himself had been reborn;
however, the Blessed One, referring to *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*), replied, “Yes, Vaṅgīsa... I know the destination. For it has been said:
“Nirvāṇa is the destination of the Arahant. Vaṅgīsa, through the power of his own mantras, knew the destination of one who was included within the cycle of rebirths (*gati-pariyāpanna*).
Thinking of the Blessed One as well, "He too is such a one," he said, "Do you know by means of a charm, Master Gotama?
The Blessed One, taking his own Buddha-knowledge itself as the charm and demonstrating it, said, "Yes, Vaṅgīsa, I know by means of that very same charm.
"Groundless" (amūlika) means that which should be given for nothing. "Sleeping on the bare ground" (thaṇḍilaseyyā) is lying down on ground that has not been cleared away.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes such acts as descending into water for a third time and carrying earth. With the phrase "he...
attained Arahantship," it appears as though the Elder Vaṅgīsa, having gone forth, attained Arahantship by means of the pleasant way of practice before long;
however, this should not be viewed in that way. For in the future, after the Elder had gone forth, [he applied himself] to serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
Even after undertaking the task and spending such a long time on a difficult path of practice, he attained Arahantship. Therefore he said:
“While I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness, these impudent thoughts of the Dark One pursue me.”
Discontent arose in the Venerable Vaṅgīsa; lust agitated his mind, [and he thought], "I am burning with sensual lust; my mind is consumed by fire," and so forth.

"The bliss of liberation" means that he was experiencing—the very one who was experiencing—the bliss of the fruit of Arahantship that had arisen at that moment within the total liberation from defilements and in Nibbāna, feeling it correctly for the duration of time as determined. By the poet.
*Kāveyya* means that which was spoken by poets (*kavi*), or that which has come from them, or that which belongs to them; it is this very thing that is called *kāveyya* here.

"Those who have reached the fixed course and see the fixed course" refers to those bhikkhus who are noble disciples of the Buddhas, having reached the fixed course (*niyāma*) by virtue of being established in the fruit (*phalaṭṭha-bhāva*) and seeing the fixed course by virtue of being established on the path (*maggaṭṭha-bhāva*).
For "the fixed course" (*niyāma*) is intended here as the fixed course of rightness (*sammatta-niyāma*). "A welcome arrival."
My coming into the presence of this Teacher, my approaching him, and my coming into this Dhamma and Vinaya—my going forth and my full ordination—is a beautiful coming.
Regarding that, he states the reason with the words, "The three knowledges," and so forth.
Although not explicitly stated in the verse, it is indeed understood from its meaning, because the Elder possessed the six supernormal powers (*chaḷabhiññā*).
The commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta,
within the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, is completed.
9. Vanasaṃyutta 1.
Vivekasuttavaṇṇanā 221.

“Desirous of causing spiritual urgency” means, in terms of meaning, desirous of producing a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Being thus disposed, [they should avoid] him from the company of defilements and so forth.
"Desirous of discerning" means it is said, "desirous of causing [the mind] to enter into seclusion. "In external objects" means in those things that lie outside the range of one's own domain.
"On various objects" means on diverse objects such as visible forms and so forth. "Wanders" means it proceeds.
"You, O person" means you are born separately from your own defilements; thus, toward another person of that same kind, by way of this improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra)...

"Subdue and dispel the desire and lust that arise. "We shall remind the mindful one"—meaning that having gone forth in the liberating dispensation and received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the Teacher, we too shall remind that mindful and wise person dwelling in the forest to dispel whatever thoughts have arisen;
or else, [we shall remind him] of the state of the removal of defilements belonging to the mindful and virtuous ones.
We remind him—who dwells having practiced [the path]—of the suffering of saṃsāra. "Pātāla" refers to the pit of delusion (mohapātāla), the dust of the defilements;
it is that very thing which is called "pātāla. "Do not carry away" means: do not lead downward into the stream of the miserable states (duggati).

This connects with "sitam" (cold). Therefore, he said: "clinging to the body. "One who has attained seclusion" means one who has attained the seclusion from defilements through the cultivation of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).
"Supreme energy" (*uttamavīriya*) refers to energy that has attained the characteristic of exaltation, or the fourfold energy of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*) that has been reached.
"Exerting" (*paggayha*) means having applied [the mind]. "Supreme seclusion" (*paramaviveka*) refers to supreme seclusion by eradication (*samuccheda*).
The commentary on the *Viveka-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Upaṭṭhāna Sutta 222.
There is indeed bodily distress as a rule, but not mental distress, because that has already been eradicated by the path itself.
"Afflicted by old age" means afflicted precisely by being overcome by old age. This same principle applies to both phrases. Because it stands above, it is "surrounding" (parito).
"Because it pierces exceedingly due to its length and breadth, it is called 'the taking up of the spear and arrow' (*sattisallagga*).

For in this way, there is a similarity between [the body] and the arrow of craving (*taṇhāsalla*). However, there is a dissimilarity with ignorance (*avijjā*) because of its production of delusion and its production of suffering.
Regarding "it is afflicted" (*ruppati*), the meaning is "undergoing change" or "being oppressed"; thus he said, "of that which is being struck."
“Pabbajitaṃ” means either one who has gone forth from the continuity of the [defilements] or one who has gone forth from the stains such as passion (rāga).
“Tasmā” means because this is the word of the Elder himself; therefore, this meaning of the verse now being stated is as follows.

“Devatāya hi,” etc., is for the purpose of making clear the very meaning already stated. “Ettha” refers to the remaining verses. Since the meaning follows the method already explained, it is called “anuttānapadavaṇṇanā” (a commentary on the non-obscure words).

He said: In the phrase "from discipline" (*vinayā*), there is an ablative case expressing cause; its meaning is stated by means of an instrumental expression of cause as "by means of discipline" (*vinayena*).
The same applies to the word "through surmounting" (*samatikkamā*). It is supremely pure because it cuts off defilement. "One who has aroused energy" means one whose energy is cultivated.
And this cultivation consists of both exertion and fulfillment; thus he said, "one whose energy is exerted" (*paggahitavīriyaṃ*).
“Perfected in energy.
The commentary on the *Upaṭṭhāna Sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Kassapagotta Sutta*.
223. It cuts off the life of deer; therefore it is called a "deer-hunter. "A red deer" refers to a small deer of a reddish color; some say it means a "large red deer.
Having received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from the Teacher, he went to that region and lived there because alms-food was easily obtained;
it is with reference to this matter that [it is said] in the first sutta...
It is said, “in the manner already described. Now, this elder was one who possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and was a practitioner of insight (*vipassanā-kammika*).
“Having stood” means having halted his walking by following the sequence of steps and standing in a place near the elder; he began to listen to his words.
“He caused his thumb to blaze” means that by the power of his resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-bala*), he caused his own thumb to blaze like a staff-lamp.
He sees even with his eyes a thumb [of a deer] as it leaps; he also hears with his ears the Dhamma being taught by that [hunter] in part.
"But his mind runs away" is the connection. "Of this one too" means "of the hunter too.
Regarding the term *appa-pañña*, the word *appa* here has the sense of non-existence—as in such expressions as *appaharita* (scarcely any greenery)—therefore he says "without wisdom" (*nippañña*).
"By one capable of knowing the cause" means by one capable of knowing the cause through such conduct as "by this cause there is happiness for beings, by that [cause] there is suffering";

the meaning is: by a mind associated with the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakata-ñāṇa*). "He hears" means he hears merely by way of the act of hearing, not by way of its meaning. Therefore it was said: "he does not know its meaning. "The forms of the causes" means...

The causes of worldly involvement. Having abandoned [the thought], "What is the use of this to me?", thinking, "This is proliferation (papañca)," he exerted energy—that is, having applied the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna).
The commentary on the Kassapagotta Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Sambahula Sutta 224.
"A number" (*sambahulā*) means a number according to the method of the Suttas. "Those who have rehearsed the Suttas" (*suttantika*) are those who have recited the Suttas.

"Those who uphold the Vinaya" (*vinayadhara*) are those who maintain the Vinaya. "They apply themselves" (*yuñjanti*) means they exert effort in their respective duties. "They strive" (*ghaṭenti*) means they apply energy therein.
“They are doing it. The connection is: “While they were still doing it, the dawn broke.
“Who are these? means “What are these? Therefore he said, “Where are these? “They have gone to the Vajji country, the kingdom of the Vajjis,” thus [it is] “to the Vajji country.
Therefore he said, “They have gone facing toward the kingdom of the Vajjis. “There is no fixed dwelling place for them” means there is no permanent residence for them.

Because he is homeless, he is called "homeless" (*ageha*). It is suitable by way of the climate, or it is suitable because of the well-being of body and mind due to the climate. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
The commentary on the *Sambahula-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Ānanda-sutta*.

225. *Ativelam* means for too long a time. A bhikkhu, having spoken merely the words of a conversation with those who have approached and sat down, should keep his mind engaged in the task of study or the task of meditation; he should not spend excessive time in frequent attempts to win them over.
However, on that occasion, the Elder, for some reason, spent much time frequently attempting to win over householders; it was with reference to this that [the Buddha said].
It was stated: “excessively,” and so forth. Now, in order to clarify that meaning, it was stated: “the Blessed One,” and so forth.
“That” refers to such a form of persuasion; with reference to this, the statement “excessively full of entreaties from householders” was spoken.
“Having heard the speech of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus” is said because [the Buddha] spoke while seated in the midst of the Saṅgha by means of the Elder.
"The Teacher’s instruction" refers to the Three Pitakas.
"Having approached" means having gone near; he says "having entered" because that involves plunging into it.

For one whose heart is weary of the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*), and who contemplates, as they truly are, Nibbāna which is completely detached from all conditioned things—

He said, "Nibbāna... indeed makes one enter," meaning that while standing by him as one who properly provides consolation, he exerts himself for further attainment and thus places Nibbāna within his heart.
The connection is to be understood by bringing in the phrase, "Nibbāna... indeed makes one enter from the perspective of its object. The activity occurring as "biḷibiḷī" is devoid of actual meaning.
“Biḷikā”: this discourse on the householder’s entreaty is called “biḷibiḷikā” because, since it did not achieve the Elder’s own goal of the ascetic life, it was like a deity’s whimpering.
The commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta 226.
"In the immediately preceding existence" means in the divine existence immediately preceding the past one. For the Elder had passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and was reborn here.
"The chief queen" refers to a certain attendant goddess who, by the mere power of her mental aspiration, [was reborn] even now.
Thinking, "She will be reborn in the realm of the gods because she has accumulated wholesome qualities," he spoke as if it were happening right now, saying, "You shine.
Thus, showing that his divine ear regarding her past was as if it were present—because not much time had passed—he said, "You shone even before.
He further remarked, "You are ill-fated now on account of your miserable state in sugati (happy realms) or niraya (hell), etc."
The intention [is as follows]: because of being mired in sensual pleasures due to a miserable state of practice.

"Taking a stand" means settling down. "By eight causes" refers to the eight causes being mentioned, which have roots grown firm through long-term cultivation and which are rooted in conditions such as improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
"Passionate by way of lust" means through the influence of lust.
"Attached" means being stained, greedy, and obsessed by the power of lust arisen toward the personality (sakkāya) in its desired aspect, according to its intrinsic nature and one's intention.

"He stands" means he stands having descended [into it]. "Hated" means being corrupted and with a corrupted mind by the power of hatred arisen toward the personality in its undesired aspect, according to its intrinsic nature and one's intention. "Deluded" means by the power of delusion...

"Deluded by way of non-regard" means through the process of being deluded. "Bound" (*vinibaddho*) means bound specifically to the ground of conceit (*mānavatthu*) because of being fastened by the sense of "I-making" (*ahaṃkāra*).

"By way of conceit" (*mānavasena*) means by various modes of conceiving (*maññanākāra*). "Misapprehended" (*parāmaṭṭho*) means grasped erroneously from the outside as being permanent and so forth, contrary to the true nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.
"By way of views" (*diṭṭhivasena*) means by way of wrong vision. "Firmly established" (*thāmagato*) means by way of the defilements such as lust (*rāga*) and the rest.
He has attained strength and stability. "By way of latent tendency" means by way of lying down repeatedly in the continuum because they have not been abandoned by the Path;

for their meaning of being unabandoned is the meaning of latent tendency (*anusaya*). "Fallen into uncertainty" means fallen into doubt. "Fallen into distraction" means having reached a state of being distracted.
"By way of restlessness" means by way of the mind's state of agitation. "One who torments" (*tāpī*) means one who causes torment.
"Devakaññāyo. Thus "established" means they are indeed established in *sakkāya* (the existing body) by way of the aforementioned method, such as through their state of passion (*ratta-bhāva*).
"Of the god-men" (*naradevānaṃ*) means of those gods who have become men.
"To go back" (*paṭigantuṃ*) means, by way of expectation, to depart from that [state] and to relinquish that expectation. "Dussantaṃ" means biting.
“Clothing,” some say. “Having joined the needle” means having joined the needle with the sewing thread and having inserted it into the loop.
“Those of lovely body” (manāpakāyikā) refers to those born in the class of gods of lovely body. To demonstrate their power, the words beginning with “with the mind” (manasā) were spoken.
“They gather together” (samajjanti) means they come together. “The state of going” (gamanabhāvaṃ) means the intention to go. “Exhausted” (vikkhīṇo) is by way of cutting off.
"He has reached destruction. There is no fault in deities announcing superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma); therefore, he declared his attainment of Arahatship so that they would not return again.
The commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Nāgadatta Sutta.
227. *Atikālena*: at an excessively early time, meaning at the very morning; *kālasseva* is the sense. *Koṭisammuñjaniyā*: by the tip of the broom;
by only a portion of the broom is the sense. By this, he shows that the sweeping was performed in an unpleasant manner.
*Majjhanhike vītivatte*: when midday has passed; while spending time through association with householders, it is when much of midday has elapsed. By others...
"By the monks" means by those who have entered [the village] not too late; this is an ablative expression (*nissakkavacana*).
"I fear Nāgadatta"—saying this, the deity, having made his conduct something to be feared, speaks thus to urge him toward right conduct.
"Suppagabbha" means one who is exceedingly possessed of bodily immodesty (*kāyapāgabbiya*) and so forth.
The commentary on the Nāgadattasutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Kulagharaṇīsutta 228.
“Having gained entry” means having obtained access by way of trust. “A certain family” refers to that family.
He speaks with reference to his wife and husband. He thought: "This family has been very helpful to me for a long time by providing suitable food and other necessities;
therefore, I have become the foremost recipient of offerings here. By accepting gifts from them alone, I shall increase my merit.
That is why he said, "What would I do by going elsewhere? and so forth. "Sā" refers to the deity. "Ubhopeta" refers to both of them.
He speaks with reference to both the monk and the housewife. "Having reached a firm footing" means having attained a firm footing through mutual trust and confidence.
It is called a "meeting place" (*saṇṭhāna*) because they meet and settle there; it is a place of rest. "Having come together" means...
Having assembled. It is called *mantana* because one deliberates by means of admissions and examples; it is an indicative reason (*ñāpaka-kāraṇa*).

"Words that are contrary" (*paṭiloma-saddā*) refers to words that reveal what is untrue because they have fallen into a state of contrariety. "By that reason" means by that false speech which is a counterfeit of a reason.
One should not be dejected because of the state of being a non-doer. "One is agitated by the word" means [agitated] by others regarding oneself.

One who is habitually agitated by the mere sound of a word that is intended [to provoke him]. "The vow does not succeed" means that due to a light-mindedness, the vow as it was undertaken does not reach completion.
"One whose vow is fulfilled" refers to one whose qualities of virtue (sīla) and other vows are complete.
The commentary on the *Kulagharaṇīsutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the Vajjiputtasutta 229.
A prince of the Vajjis means one born and raised in the kingdom of the Vajjis, a son of the Vajji king.

A "night-long festival" (*sabbaratticāra*) refers to a festival of constellations (*nakkhattamaho*) to be enjoyed by people wandering here and there during the attainment of a festive occasion. Therefore he said: "The Kattika constellation..."

"Having proclaimed," and so forth. "It becomes a single connected whole" means that because on that day the Cātumahārājika devas, having proclaimed the festival, experience the great pleasure of festival games through their divine prosperity accomplished by the power of their own merit, it therefore appears as if it were a single connected whole with them.
"Of the musical instruments such as drums" refers to drums (*bherī*), kettledrums (*mudiṅga*), conchs (*saṅkha*), small drums (*paṇava*), lutes (*vīṇā*), and other such instruments.
“Struck” (*tāḷitānaṃ*) means beaten in accordance with the rhythm that has been commenced. “Lutes and so forth” (*vīṇādīnaṃ*) refers to lutes, flutes, *gomukhī* drums, and the like.
“Played” (*vāditānaṃ*) means struck together in accordance with the tuning that has been commenced.

“He spoke” (*abhāsī*) means that, his heart being drawn by that sound, he emerged from his state of improper reflection and spoke while lamenting, “Oh, what a great loss for me! It was like a piece of wood that had been cast away.
Like a useless piece of wood cast away in the forest. "Lāmakatara" means inferior.
Just as a deity might pull out a wedge previously driven in, the deity spoke the words, "Many will envy you," showing that she was removing the meaning stated by that bhikkhu;
thus he said, "The Elder," and so forth. As for those going to heaven...
The denizens of hell long for this; likewise, many long for you who have practiced rightly.
Therefore, the intention is that you should not think of yourself as "worse.
The commentary on the Vajjiputta Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Sajjhāya Sutta (230).

"By way of the study that leads to escape" means: "Surely, by relying on this study, it is possible to escape from the suffering of the round of existence"—thus it is "by way of the study that leads to escape.
"From recitation" means: from reciting while standing at the head of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*).

Now, in order to show his recitation by way of mastery over the means of escape (*nissaraṇapariyatti*), his performance of duties and counter-duties by way of practice (*paṭipatti*), and his development of insight (*vipassanābhāvanā*), the passage beginning with "It is said that he...
was spoken. By praising his practice on the day he attained Arahantship, it is shown that he practiced in the same manner even on the preceding days;
however, it shows that he was unable to bring his insight to its highest excellence.
“Kālam ativatteti” (he lets time pass) is an explanatory gloss for the word “saṅkasāyati. “Therassa” refers to the elder who was engaged in recitation.
“Dhammapadāni” are words that illuminate the aggregates of Dhamma, such as virtue and so forth. Therefore he said, “The entire word of the Buddha is intended.
The intention is that he did not grasp the oral instruction. By the phrase in the text, “living together with the bhikkhus,”...
This shows that the Dhamma must be mastered even for the purpose of hearing it. It is called "dispassion" (*virāga*) because one becomes dispassionate by means of it;

it refers to the Noble Path. "Having known" means having understood and penetrated what is seen, heard, and so forth, according to its true nature, by way of the clear realization of full comprehension (*pariññābhisamaya*).
"Relinquishing" (*vissajjana*) means abandoning; it does not mean the relinquishing of the Buddha’s word, nor even of the learning (*pariyatti*) of the storehouse-keeper (the Tipiṭaka).
Since [the practice] was permitted even for the sake of escape, he said "to this extent," etc., showing that the proper measure must nevertheless be known therein.
The commentary on the *Sajjhāyasutta* is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Akusalavitakkasutta*.

231. He thinks unwholesome thoughts: that is, wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) which are unwholesome in the sense of being produced by lack of skill (akosalla-sambhūta). "Yoni" is said to mean a means;

therefore, attention directed toward things such as the foul (asubha) by way of the beautiful (subha), etc., is "attention that is not based on the proper ground" (ayoniso-manasikāra); thus he says, "by means of attention that is not a proper means.

A "serene meditation subject" (pāsādika-kammaṭṭhāna) is a meditation subject such as the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), which brings about confidence. "Strong rapture and pleasure" (balava-pītiñca sukhañca)...
The joy and happiness accompanied by access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) are powerful because they suppress the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
The commentary on the *Akusalavitakka-sutta* is finished.
12. Commentary on the *Majjhanhika-sutta*.
232. Regarding the "Nandana Chapter": in the commentary on the Nandana Chapter, this [chapter] is included here as well because there is no distinction in the verses.

If that is so, why was it recited there yet taken up here? Although it was included in the *Devatā-saṃyutta* by virtue of its connection with deities, it is taken up here because it is connected with an "occasion for discourse" (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
The commentary on the *Majjhanhika-sutta* is finished.
13. Commentary on the *Pākatindriya-sutta*: 233.

The construction is that whatever needs to be said regarding the thirteenth [sutta] has already been explained in detail. Regarding the *Jantudevaputta-sutta*, it refers to the commentary on the *Jantudevaputta-sutta*.
“*Tattha saṅgītaṃ idhāpi*,” etc., follows the same method as explained in the commentary on the immediately preceding sutta.
The commentary on the *Pākatindriya-sutta* is concluded.
14. Commentary on the *Gandhatthena-sutta*.

234. "It contemplates the odor-object" (*gandhārammaṇaṃ upanijjhāyati*) means that it approaches and contemplates the object designated as "odor," just as consciousness contemplates a visible form through the medium of a visible-form object. It approaches and contemplates that [odor] by means of the odor-object directly, face-to-face;
the meaning is that it penetrates it according to its true nature and its actual essence. "It will smell" (*upasiṅghissati*) means that it will smell after having approached by way of craving.

"One part of this theft": when the bases of theft are being analyzed by way of their objects, he says "of those things to be stolen," etc., meaning that among them, this [scent] is one part, namely the object of scent.

Although there might be the state of having mental phenomena as its object when theft proceeds with a view toward nutritive essence (*ojā*), that is not a sweet form of theft; therefore, it is said, "of the five portions. And although—
That scent-object is not possessed by anyone else, so it is permissible to take it; however, because it has not been authorized by the Teacher, its consumption is not appropriate.
As for what that bhikkhu said—“I do not carry it away, nor do I break it”—this same justification applies there as well.
It is called *vaṇṇa* because fruit is produced by means of it; thus it is said, “by way of *vaṇṇa* means by way of cause.”
"In each such monk": "One whose actions are crowded" means one whose unwholesome actions consist of craving, views, and so forth;
for from the very beginning, through views, delusion, and craving, they obstruct wholesome actions.
And because of being rigid, harsh, and rough due to views, it is said: "one whose actions are not exhausted, one whose actions are harsh."

*Ākiṇṇaluddo*: being crowded with cruelty, he is harsh. Therefore he said, “one who is full of evil,” and so forth. *Makkhito*: smeared. *Taṃ*: that exhortation to the deity. *Tasmā*: because he stood having transgressed [the bounds], he spoke thus: “And you are worthy to be spoken to. *Gavesantassa*:
of one seeking, by way of producing [the result] within his own continuum.
[It was as large] as a mass of clouds arisen, spreading across the vault of the sky for many yojanas in length and breadth. *Suddho*: pure through virtue.
"You know" means you understand. "Sugati" means a beautiful rebirth; by this, the inclusion of Nibbāna is also established.
The commentary on the Gandhatthena Sutta is finished.
[From] the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Vanasaṃyutta* is completed.
10. *Yakkhasaṃyutta*. 1.
Commentary on the *Indakasutta*.
235. Because he is a leader (*pariṇāyaka*) of himself, he is of great power and named *Inda*; because he possesses the designation (*samaññā*) "Inda," he is also called "Indaka.
[The phrase] "of that Indaka" refers to him. "Dwelling on Mount Indakūṭa" means one who resides on Mount Indakūṭa; [the phrase] "of that dweller on Indakūṭa" refers to him.
A *yakkha* is so called because he is to be sacrificed to and worshipped with offerings (*balikamma*). [The phrase] "which has become the dwelling place of Indra" refers to that location.

*Kūṭa* means *Indakūṭa*; it received its name from the *yakkha* Kūṭa. *Indakūṭa*—where *inda* is the first member and *kūṭa* the latter—is like "Kelāsakūṭa" [meaning] "Kelāsa," where the latter member (*kūṭa*) has been elided.
*Indo yakkho* means it received its name from the *yakkha* Kūṭa.

Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence here, because they serve as mutual characteristics, just as in the case of "the meditation subject of the body. By *rūpa*, he refers to the entire aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).
"Not the sphere of visible form" means: one challenges [this] by asking, "Having passed away from this body, what does this [being] obtain?

By asking "From where does it come?", [it is shown that] since the soul (*jīva*)—which is a dependent form (*parādhāra-rūpa*) and the self (*attā*)—is not present when the physical form arises in the mother's womb, from what place indeed could it come?
Therefore he said: "And these bones, and these pieces of flesh," and so forth. How?
He asks how [the embryo] remains attached within the womb, which is designated as the "belly" (*kucchi*).

By the passage beginning, "Like roaring lions with tusks in a mountain cave," it is shown that "cave" (*gabbhara*) is a synonym for the belly. Therefore he says: "In the cave means in the mother’s belly.
The "proponent of the person" (*puggalavādī*) is one who clings to the doctrine of a self (*attavāda*). For just as fish-flesh, when eaten, becomes froth...

Just as [milk] becomes something else and dissolves, and is no longer perceived because it no longer exists as a being, even so, if the material form (rūpa) arisen in the mother’s womb in the state of an embryo were not a being, it would not grow; rather, having dissolved, it would pass away.
Yet that material form is indeed perceived. Therefore, by this conviction, they say: "The material form... [is] in the womb. Thus he spoke.
Thus it was said. "First" means the first among these five. Therefore he said: "together with the first rebirth-linking consciousness.
Regarding "with the woolen threads of birth," they say it means "with the woolen threads of a birth-goat.
The intention of the reciters of the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* is: "Birth-wool is the wool taken after splitting open the womb; with three threads made from that, [the cord] was fashioned at its tip."
"Unclouded" (*anāvila*) means clear; the meaning is "well-purified. "Possessing such a color and appearance" refers to that which is delimited by the aforementioned dimensions and shapes.

"It is called *kalala*" means that the personal existence (*attabhāva*), consisting of the primary elements and derived matter, as it proceeds by way of a continuum, is designated by the name *kalala*.

"Kalala" means by way of the cause of the material form of the kalala as previously described, depending upon it and making it a condition. "The color of meat-washing water" means that in terms of color it has the appearance of meat-washing water; in terms of shape, however, it is like melted wax.
"Fully matured" means having reached full maturity, having reached a state of complete ripeness beyond the stage of the kalala.
"Massed together" means become a mass, gathered together. "Rotating" means changing or transforming. "That state" is used here in the instrumental sense as an accusative case.
The meaning is that they transform into that state. Alternatively, the accusative case is used in the sense of the ablative:
transforming from that state—that is, from the state of the *kalala*—it transforms into the *kalala*. "An *abbuda* is born" means that what is called an *abbuda* comes into being.
Regarding its shape, it is said to resemble a withered lotus bud; as for its color, however, they say it is neither white nor red. It is called *maṇḍa*.
Just as from the pressing of young mangoes there arises the essence of the flavor of the ripe pepper, [so it is here].
"It is released on all sides" means that this *maṇḍa* (scum), without adhering to the bowl, having been released from all parts, remains as a mass.
"Such is the *pesi*" means that this *pesi* does not adhere anywhere within the womb, but remains as a mass just like the aforementioned *maṇḍa*.
“Having been offered, it remains. Therefore he said, “resembling a melted drop of ghee.
Regarding the phrase “the *pesī* is produced,” here the word *pesī* is used in the nominative case with an ablative sense; thus he said, “from that, the *pesī* is sent forth.

It is the shape of the *ghana*. “Produced by kamma-conditionality”: that shape arises from the production of material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*). For it has been said: “Old age and death are impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.”
"Pustules" means that masses of flesh resembling pustules arise.
"The seventh and so forth": by the word "and so forth," it includes the thirty-four seven-day periods starting from the eighth week up to the forty-first week.
"The time of maturity" refers to the time when the embryo has matured; it is fully ripened after nine months.
It is so called because it is produced from the hair of the head, body hair, and so forth. Therefore he said: "These are born during forty-two days.
"Of him" refers to the being dwelling in the womb. It is connected as one with the membrane of the mother's belly;
for when the food consumed by the mother has settled in the stomach, it reaches the body of the being in the womb via the umbilical cord and performs the function of nutriment.

It produces [matter]. It means that it acts as a condition for the nutritive essence (*ojā*) within the body of the one in the womb, thereby producing matter consisting of the "nutritive octad" (*ojaṭṭhamaka-rūpa*).
Having obtained that condition, it produces the materiality of the nutritive octad. Thus, by means of the condition of the food consumed by the mother, the one in the womb subsists for ten months;
indeed, he subsists solely through that which has entered via his own umbilical cord, lasting for as long as the seven-day period of nutriment-produced matter.

From that point on, it is so called because of its being brought [into the womb]. Some, however, say: "The food consumed by the mother permeates and saturates his body like an external application; by means of that, he is sustained.
Because what has entered the womb is hidden by the membrane of the belly and thus does not deserve to be called "standing outside," he said, "having gone inside the belly."
"A man gone into the mother's womb" means one who has entered across the mother's womb. "In this way" means that by the manner just described, this being...

[as before] ...is produced; therefore, matter is not the life-principle (*jīva*). For it is not accepted by the holder of the view that the being, having reached growth through the sequence of seven days, attains impermanence.
The commentary on the Indaka Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sakka-nāma Sutta. 236. “Named Sakka”:
like the son of Bali, he received his name by virtue of being Sakka’s [son]. The reading is: “It is said that this one...”
Some also write “eko kira. One who has gone over to the side of Māra is a “mārapakkhika.
In the phrase “what belongs to another,” the word *yaṃ* is a reference to the action; therefore, the construction is: “Whatever instruction belongs to another, that is not good for a recluse.
By reason—that is, by mere reason—companionship arises with anyone at all, whether a householder or one who has gone forth.
The Wise One, the Fully Enlightened One, does not need to feel compassion for that person who has arrived due to some other cause, because there is no attainment of distinction [in him].
However, when such a person is present, faith becomes especially intensified. "If by mind... and so forth... he is not bound by that [mind] through the influence of affection;
for compassion (*anukampā*) and pity (*anuddayā*) have an undefiled nature.
The commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta: 237.
A village situated not far from Gayā is called “Gayā”; thus he said, “at Gayā,” meaning “not far from Gayā.”
The meaning is "in dependence upon the village where one has settled. This is an indication of the village used as a resort for alms.
There is no irregularity in the sequence [of the bed's parts], because the two sides of the bed-legs are long.
They place it in the place of the deities with the intention that it is a consecration for the deities performed for the sake of an offering. It is said to be like a bed with eight legs.
Because it must be turned over from bottom to top. "Kathina-needle" (*kathinasibbanasūci*) means a needle for sewing the *kathina*.
"Without having spread out" (*apaccattharitvā*) means without having spread any covering over a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha.
"Like pierced by a lattice-work" (*gavacchivijjhitam viya*) means that, as if by those needle-hairs, it has become completely covered over, like a lattice-work of cow-hair.
Here too, having stated "he has a rough body," he says "it is said that he...
and so forth, showing the cause for his being such by explaining that the roughness of the body is due to the hair being like stiff needles.
"With his own hands" means he smeared his own body with oil belonging to the Saṅgha. "In this way" means in the manner described.
“Place of assembly” means a place where *yakkhas* gather. “He” refers to the *yakkha* Sūciloma. “And me” he says, referring to himself.
“Having raised up” means having made it point upwards. “He pushed away” means he pushed it back slightly, acting in such a way that the *yakkha* was unable to bring his body near.
“Unpleasant” means not pleasing due to its roughness and sharpness; or [it refers to] the mind...
“I will hurl them” means that by my power I shall cause a distraction of your mind.
To show how he might cause such a distraction, the passage beginning with “For those who... was spoken.
Or, “terrifying” means frightening—whether in the manner already described or otherwise—in such a way that the mere sight of it produces fear, trepidation, and horripilation in beings.
“Capable. Alternatively, the reading is “while they were speaking. The construction is: “We shall seize them by both feet and hurl them to the other side of the Ganges.
“From what source? means for what reason? In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is shown that this is a compound word explained through the elision of a case ending;
thus the meaning is stated as “from what source, from what condition? “They let go of their minds” means [they let go] so that a wholesome mind might arise.
They cast them forward by way of non-giving. "From what source do they arise?"—this asks for the origin of wrong thoughts (*micchāvitakka*).

Sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and the rest have as their cause improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) toward signs of beauty and so forth. However, since both sensual desire and improper attention are included within one's own internal self (*niyakajjhatta*), he says:
"This personal existence (*attabhāva*) is the source of these; thus they are 'from this source' (*itonidāna*)," and so on.
"Even so": in the commentary, wrong thoughts are to be seen as like boys absorbed in play;
this world of the personal existence (attabhāva-loka) is like the world that serves as their place of origin; the mind is like the vulture being released by them;
and the fetter that follows it from afar is like the long cord tied to its feet—thus should the correlation with the simile be understood.
Craving is the specific condition for evil thoughts and the defilements associated with them, because in its absence they do not exist;
thus he says, "born from the moisture of craving. Because they are included within the personal existence (*attabhāva*), it is said, "arisen within oneself.
By this, he shows that they have no other cause, and by the phrase "like the sprouts on a banyan tree," he shows their abundance.

By the words "clinging" (*visatta*) and so forth, it refers to that which is difficult to relinquish. "In various objects of sensual pleasure" (*vatthukāmesu*) means in the various objective bases such as visible forms.

"Various sensual defilements" (*puthū kilesakāmā*) refers to craving for sense-pleasures, craving for form, and so on. "By those sensual defilements acting as instruments" (*tehi kilesakāmehi karaṇabhūtehi*). "The personal existence" (*attabhāvaṃ*) refers to the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*).
Those who are engaged and devoted to insight meditation know [this] according to reality.
Since the word *yato* is used here in the sense of an ablative of cause (*nissakkavacana*), he said, "that which is its source.

Regarding the term "dispelling" (*vinodentī*), since it is expressed as an agentive noun, the means by which they dispel it must necessarily be the instrumental cause; thus he said, "dispelling by means of the Truth of the Path.
Furthermore, "dispelling" here means drawing out from the continuum, casting outside, and total abandonment; and when those defilements have been abandoned, they "cross the flood" (*oghaṃ taranti*).

Demonstrating this, he spoke the verse beginning with “difficult to cross. Since there is no further becoming once this has been attained, it is called “non-renewal of existence” (apunarbhava), which is Nibbāna;
thus he said, “of that which is termed non-renewal of existence,” and so forth.

Because here, by the two phrases “those who understand it” and “from what source,” the truths of suffering and its origin are indicated, by the mention of “dispelling” the truth of the path is indicated, and by the mention of “non-renewal of existence” [the truth of cessation is indicated].
The truth of cessation has been elucidated; therefore it was said, "while elucidating the four truths.
"In that very place" means standing in the same spot where he had stood when he asked the question beginning with, "Lust and hatred...
"By following the teaching" means by recollecting the Teacher’s proclamation of the Dhamma. "Having directed his knowledge" means...

Having directed and set in motion the knowledge of realization toward Nibbāna by means of the sequence of insight (vipassanā), [the text says] "he is established in the fruit of stream-entry" (sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito).
The construction is: through the attainment of the first path, which is adorned with a thousand methods, he is established in the first fruit and thereby obtains it.
They do not remain in a defiled state of existence because of the great power of the Noble Dhamma.
"Setakaṇḍupīḷakasūciyo": the white scabs and the hair-needles, having reached a state of whiteness, have all fallen away, been cast off, and disappeared without remainder.
"Bhummadevatāparihāraṃ": [referring to] the state of existence as a terrestrial deity.
The commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Maṇibhadda Sutta 238.
"He obtains happiness" means he attains happiness distinguished as pertaining to the present life and so forth.

"It is always better for one who possesses mindfulness" is because of his practice of what is beneficial for the future. Maṇibhadda [said]: "A person possessing mindfulness, acting with mindfulness, does not presently produce enmity."
With this underlying intention, he said, "one is released from enmity.

However, the Blessed One stated, "one is not released from enmity," in order to negate that [former claim], because the release from enmity achieved through mere mindfulness is neither absolute nor final, since its opposite has not been abandoned by oneself or by others.
He then spoke of that release from enmity which is both absolute and final, being independent of another.
Showing this, he spoke the verse beginning with "yassā" (of whom). "Karuṇāya" means by means of compassion that has reached absorption (*appanā*).
"Karuṇāpubbabhāge" means in the access (*upacāra*) of the first jhāna produced through the cultivation of compassion. "So" refers to the person who is cultivating the meditation on compassion.
"Mettaṃso" means one whose "aṃsa"—that is, a portion or a single wholesome factor—is loving-kindness; thus, he is "mettaṃso. Of him...

Regarding the phrase "by anyone": because that Arahant possesses an extraordinary degree of compassion (*karuṇā*) and the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*), there is no possibility of enmity with any person whatsoever due to the absence of those qualities.

By this it is meant that even one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) might harbor enmity toward someone else who lacks the cultivation of loving-kindness and compassion, owing to a defect in his own mind;
however, this does not apply to one who is endowed with the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness and compassion.
No one would harbor enmity. This shows that the development of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) possesses such great power.
The commentary on the Maṇibhadda Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Sānu Sutta.
239. "He was seized by a *yakkha*" means he was possessed by a *yakkha*.
To show the cause of that seizure in detail from its very root, he says "he," and so forth.

Because he was in his final existence (*antimabhavika*), [the Buddha] shows that he fulfilled the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) with diligence from the very beginning, by saying "from the time of his going forth," and so forth. "Paccāhāraṃ" [means...]
A rejection. "In this recitation" means in this my preaching of the Dhamma. "Merit" means the giving of merit.
They become dear; therefore the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu should desire:
'May I be dear, pleasing, respected, and esteemed by my fellow celibates,' he should be one who fulfills his virtue. And so it was said:
“Regarding that novice,” and so forth.
*Vuḍḍhimanvāyā* means by way of the growth of the limbs and members due to the attainment of youth. By virtue of being capable of enjoying sensual pleasures, his faculties have reached maturity.
*Anuyojetvāva* means having dismissed him, or having directed him toward the state of a householder. “Previously... [text continues]
"Your son was esteemed as virtuous, of noble character, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training;
now he has become otherwise than that"—lest such a proclamation among the deities cause me shame.
And "on the occasion of the miracles" refers to the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, respectively, from the beginning, the end, and both the beginning and the end.
And the side that must be brought back again and again toward the Uposatha precept by way of entering and exiting.
"Also on the thirteenth" means even on the seventh and ninth days.

For the teachers maintain that the virtue undertaken on the seventh days is the "entry" (paṭipadā) for the Uposatha virtue, while on the ninth days it is the "exit" (nikkhamana). In the Porāṇa-ṭīkā...
However, because it was stated by way of both approaching and following after, he said "people," and so forth. "Half a month" means the entire fortnight of time;
for in this way, the following of the rains-residence (vassāvāsa) is accomplished. "Well-arrived" means having come into one's own continuum after making it thoroughly purified and perfected.
Furthermore, that [continuum] is endowed with modes that are equal to one's own mind.
He said, “Associated. This refers to the conduct of the noble ones by emulating the Arahants.
He spoke thus because he considered his own son’s attachment to his body to be like his own play, saying, “Those spirits do not play [with him].

The female lay follower was virtuous through the aforementioned Uposatha precepts, while the novice was virtuous through his own novice precepts. “Leaping up” means leaping up into the air. There is no liberation because of the accumulation of karma that brings about suffering.

"Both kinds of sensual pleasure" refers to sensual pleasure as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasure as defilements (*kilesakāma*). For it is only by relinquishing sensual pleasure as defilement that one is said to relinquish sensual pleasure as objects.
He "comes back by way of disrobing," meaning he returns from the duties of one who has gone forth, such as wandering for alms.
Even if he lives merely by means of inhalation and exhalation, one who has disrobed and lives without virtue is as good as dead. For this has been said:
“Sunakkhatta, in the discipline of the Noble One, he who renounces the training and returns to the low life has indeed died.
“In the sense of heat” means in the sense of burning fever. “Run forth!”—having said, “May it be well with you in this task of running forth,” [he says] “run forth toward the state of a householder.
“Having led out” means having caused to go out. By eleven...
Because it was ablaze with fires, it was like a great conflagration. "Having observed" means having observed the danger in the state of a householder and the benefit in going forth.
"Having acquired a sense of shame and dread of blame" [he thought]: "My fellow-celibates will know my desire to disrobe.
"Having shaken all of Jambudīpa" by way of agitating the minds of the four assemblies.
The commentary on the Sānu Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Piyaṅkara Sutta:
240. *Paccante* means at the border. *Pāṭiyekkaṃ* means separately at the time of the recitation. [This refers to] the section beginning with the Yamaka Vagga and ending with the Brāhmaṇa Vagga.
“Chabbīsativaggā” means that which has twenty-six sections; “tantī” means the Pāḷi (the textual tradition).

Such bad food as excrement, urine, and so forth—considering it “bad food” because of its impure and loathsome nature—or by the inclusion of the term “bad food,” one extends the reference to vomit, womb-impurity, and so on.
“Chetvā chaviādīni” means having pierced through the skin and the other [layers] excessively.
Having entered, it remained touching the marrow due to the arising of gross material form produced by rapture (*pīti*). Therefore he said, "having become heart-gladdening.
"By nature undertaken" means that without having received [the precepts] from anyone else, at that very moment they themselves became self-restrained.
"According to their restraint. By the third phrase means by the phrase "let us train in virtuous conduct. "The rest" refers to what remains after what has been stated.

The three [abstinences]—from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, and from the drinking of intoxicants—are included according to the principle of "the cow and the ox" (where the whole includes the parts).
"Chātakadubbhikkhā" means that which contains famine and scarcity; the meaning is "abounding in hunger and scarcity. "From the wombs of *pisācas* and *yakkhas*..."
The construction is: "May we indeed be released from this womb of ghosts, which resembles the realm of the *petas*.
The commentary on the Piyaṅkara Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Punabbasu Sutta.
241. By the inclusion of the "place where it dwells," it encompasses the night-quarters, day-quarters, and so forth.
It extends only to the measure of twelve cubits, because that is the extent of the ordinary range for movement.

It follows the assembly according to its size; wherever the assembly stands, it goes to that place, because it is coextensive with the limits of the assembly. This is because there is no distortion of the Teacher’s facial expression.

Observing the permission for entry, she saw that the supporting condition (*upanissaya*) was established through inference, thinking, "Surely this person must have performed meritorious deeds in the past.
"By going into a state of unity" means by coming within arm's reach, thereby attaining a state of mingling with the assembly. "Little sons" refers to sons and grandsons;
for the syllable *ka* is used here in the sense of endearment (*anukampā*).
The fetters that are being released by the Noble Path having Nibbāna as its object are said to be "released by coming to Nibbāna.
Regarding "exceeding the limit," it is said to be "exceeding measure" because it cannot be delimited by any measure. "Piyāyanā" means longing.
Since longing is the seeking and yearning for the object of love through the power of affection, it is said to be "seeking" and "yearning."
“Than that”—meaning than a beloved son and so forth. “Of beings” (*pāṇīnaṃ*) is a plural form used in the sense of the genitive, referring to the word “suffering.
When one asks “Who liberates? (*ke moceti*), one is asking about the object of the action of liberating. However, since the case ending can be shifted according to the sense of the meaning, he said:
“It should be stated by bringing it as ‘of beings’ (*pāṇinaṃ*). “Abhisambudhaṃ” means “while fully awakening. Therefore, he said: “Fully awakened” (*abhisambuddho*).
Regarding "of the true Dhamma" (*saddhammassa*), it is the genitive case used in the sense of the accusative; thus he said, "without even knowing the true Dhamma.
"Offering a blessing of thanksgiving for her son" means offering a blessing of thanksgiving for her son’s practice.
Regarding "exalted": here, those who were submerged in the mire of the suffering of saṃsāra and were unable to lift their heads from it, today, by the power of the Buddha—
They rose up fifty finger-breadths high. Because they rose up perfectly, without falling back again, they were "well-risen" (*samuggatā*).
Being thus, they became well-risen even within the Dispensation (*sāsana*). "The state of penetration of the Four Truths" means the existence of the penetration of the Four Truths.
By the word "etc. in "itch, scabies, etc.," one includes things such as loathsomeness and unpleasantness. [He attained] divine success (*dibbasampatti*).
She obtained it because, during her lifetime, she had created the opportunity for karma that bestows prosperity.

Having accepted her mother’s words, “Be silent and superior,” through the correct application that removes obstacles to that specific attainment, the daughter—by virtue of her mother who had thus attained excellence as desired—became a recipient of prosperity in the present life;
therefore, it is said, “solely by the power of her mother.”
The commentary on the Punabbasu Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Sudatta Sutta: 242.
Regarding the phrase "on account of business" (*karaṇīyena*), "business" (*karaṇīya*) here is intended to mean the work of trade; explaining that, [the text says] "Anāthapiṇḍika..."
He spoke these words beginning with “and so forth. “Is being sold” means it goes to sale.
“Acts in exactly that same way” means he acts in the very same manner as the merchant of Rājagaha did when he went to Sāvatthī; that is, having gone to Rājagaha, he acts in that same way.
“Svāyaṃ” refers to Anāthapiṇḍika. “On that day” means on the day that the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the vicinity of Rājagaha.
*Paṇṇaṃ* means the teaching (*sāsana*). *Na suṇī* means not hearing; he was called "one who does not hear the *paṇṇa*" because he did not hear it.

Indeed, out of reverence for the Dhamma, that merchant did not consider any other duty even as worth a blade of grass. Therefore, he said, "For the sake of hearing the Dhamma," and so forth. *Dārakarūpānaṃ* means of the children.

The word *rūpa* here has no other meaning, just as in the expression "of the cattle" (*gorūpānaṃ*). *Pañcavaṇṇaṃ* means [the offering] consisting of the five colors, such as the small ones and so forth.
He obtained fivefold rapture (*pīti*). Indeed, these arise in him in gradual succession. The phrase “rising up with his head...
he goes” is stated by way of characterizing the material form (*rūpa*) originated by rapture.
“He dwells in a charnel ground” means he dwells near a charnel ground; for that monastery was situated in a place close to a cemetery.
"Athassa" means that this thought occurred to Anāthapiṇḍika: "It is not the right time... [etc. ...I shall go to visit him.
With mindfulness directed toward the Buddha—without thinking of anything else—he lay down upon his excellent bed with mindfulness fixed solely on the Buddha.
Therefore it is said: "On that day," and so forth.
"Strong confidence" (*balavappasāda*) is powerful faith directed toward the Buddha. "Joy and light" (*pīti-āloka*) refers to an exceptional radiance,
similar to the illumination of insight (*vipassanobhāsa*), which arises from the condition of the mind and the temperature-born (*utu-samutthāna*),
produced by the sublime joy that occurs at the mere hearing of the name "Buddha" due to the power of strong confidence developed through long-term familiarity with previous Buddhas.
Therefore he said, “All darkness has vanished,” and so forth. Some say, “It was indeed done by deities (devatā),” but the former [explanation] alone is appropriate here.
“Non-humans” (amanussa) refers to deities who have attained distinguished qualities; for they had witnessed the merchant’s prosperity with their own eyes.
Therefore he said, “This great merchant,” and so forth. “A moist body” (allasarīra) means a corpse that has been discarded or left unburied at that very moment.
"Another [kind of] corpse" refers to a putrid corpse. "They surrounded it" means they flowed around it on all sides. "The light disappeared" because of the dullness of the force of the joy;
due to that dullness, the material phenomena (*rūpa*) arising from it became weak.
These [verses] should be connected with the thousand-footed verse by way of this context. "A *pada*" is so called because one steps upon it there.
"Step-taker" (*padavītihāro*) means the place where one takes a step. "In equal pacing" (*samagamane*) means without making the pace either too fast or too slow.
"From there" (*tato*) means from among those sixteen parts. "One portion" (*eko koṭṭhāso*) means one part of the aforementioned place for taking a step when it has been divided sixteenfold.
"Active volition" (*pavattacetanā*) refers to the volition engaged in leaping or running over the aforementioned place designated as a "fraction" (*kalā*).
"Padavītihāra" means that by which one steps forward; it is wholesome volition occurring in such a manner.
They say, "Having divided its fruit into sixteen ways. The construction is: "It is taken by way of one who is establishing himself.

This is for the purpose of the worship of the Triple Gem, the hearing of the Dhamma, the undertaking of the training rules, and the going for refuge—[all] based precisely on that which is dependent upon turning away from saṃsāra (vivaṭṭanissita).
It is permissible even for one who is traveling. The first mode of travel mentioned is certain for the attainment of the distinction of the supramundane;
the second is not certain. Thus, the phrase "it is indeed permissible" is spoken with reservation.
"He" refers to the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. "Followers" means those who go along as companions; he speaks with reference to them. "Sivaka..."
"Others say, 'It is a non-human being. Why was he so brave as to think, 'I have those who are devoted to me;

why should I fear? Rather, it was said beginning with 'Moreover' (*apicā*) to show that he went forth even after trampling down all dangers by means of the sharp and clear nature directed toward the Buddha.
For faith has the characteristic of leaping forward, and one who is endowed with it is a true person (*sappurisa*)."
It should be understood that by means of the qualities of the true Dhamma, one overcomes all perils and leaps forward.
By virtue of such great qualities as the fulfillment of all desires, the habit of renunciation, noble aspiration, the desire to remove the suffering of others,
the wish for the welfare of others, and rejoicing in the success of others— one constantly [protects] those who are without a protector.
Because he was a giver of alms-food (*piṇḍadāyaka*), the name "Anāthapiṇḍika" arose for him in this way. "He spoke thus" means he said, "Come, Sudattā.
"By the complete extinguishing of the defilements" (*kilesaparinibbānena*) means by the total subsiding of the defilements such as lust and so forth.

"Having attained the complete subsiding of all defilements" means having reached the total pacification of all defilements by means of the supreme path (*aggamagga*). "The gradual discourse" (*anupubbikathā*) refers to the discourse on giving and so forth; for that indeed proceeds by way of sequence.
Because it is to be told in successive order, it is called "the gradual discourse" (*anupubbikathā*). With reference to this, it was said:
"Then the Blessed One gave a gradual discourse. That is to say: he expounded a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, a talk on heaven;
he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the blessing of renunciation. "At the summit" refers to the gradual discourse.
"Further on" means above. "He proclaimed the Four Truths":

just as the Great Merchant was established in the fruit of stream-entry adorned with the thousand-fold method, so too, by analyzing both progression and cessation together with their causes, he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths.
The commentary on the *Sudatta Sutta* is concluded.
9. Commentary on the First Sukkā Sutta 243.
*Rathikaṃ* means a carriage road (*raccha*). *Gahetvā* means having gone along it. *Siṅghāṭakaṃ*: elsewhere a triangular road is so called;
here, however, it is stated as "a crossroads" (*catukkaṃ*). Regarding the term *madhupīkā*, here the word *madhu* refers to a specific kind of honey.
He said, "They have drunk the drinking of fragrant honey. For a general designation stands for a particular;
thus, "fragrant honey" refers to a certain specific kind of honey that is exceedingly sweet and intoxicating. Therefore he said, "Having become unconscious, one simply lies there.
"Irresistible" means not to be countered or removed; therefore he said, "External," and so forth. Whatever...
It is called *asecanaka* because it brings about a state of being cooled and does not require sprinkling (*na secanam*); for that very reason, it is *anāsittaka*.
It is *ojavanta* because it resembles that which is highly esteemed as being full of vitality (*ojas*). Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth.

By its own nature (*dhammatāya*) means by its very intrinsic character. "Sweet" means desirable. "As if drinking" refers to the taste of the nectar of the True Dhamma being offered to the bhikkhunī Sukkā.
As if filling their own cupped hands with ears and listening intently. From the cloud, [he heard] the one who had come from the cloud.
The commentary on the First Sukkā Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Second Sukkā Sutta.
244. Indeed, one generates much merit by giving food to the Elder Nun Sukkā, who is endowed with virtue and is the foremost among those worthy of offerings, due to her liberation from all fetters.
The commentary on the Second Sukkā Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Cīrā Sutta.

245. The eleventh [sutta] is self-evident, as it is similar to the tenth. For in that case, food was brought for the lay follower (*upāsaka*), whereas here it is the gift of a robe; this alone is the distinction.
The commentary on the *Cīra-sutta* is concluded.
12. Commentary on the *Āḷavaka-sutta*.
246. *Āḷaviyaṃ* refers to both that kingdom and that city by way of the feminine gender.

Even when the kingdom is intended, the plural number is not used here because such a conventional usage does not exist. *Tañca bhavanaṃ* means "and that abode," namely, the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka.
*Tattha* means "in the abode of Āḷavaka. [The text continues: "Then the yakkha Āḷavaka approached the Blessed One."
"Herein" means in that textual passage. "This gradual discourse" means this discourse now being spoken, which has come down in successive order.

"The lord of Āḷavī" refers to the king called Āḷava or Āḷavaka. Sometimes for the purpose of warding off thieves, sometimes for the purpose of suppressing rival kings by demonstrating his energy and power, and sometimes for the purpose of employing those fit for training—[he was so called].
And for the purpose of exercising. "Migava" (deer-hunt) is a conventional designation given because deer "wander" (*vana*), "dwell" (*vasa*), or "move about" (*vāna*) in the forest.
"Tasseva" means of the king alone. "Migo" refers to a single eni-deer. "Tiyojanaṃ" is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection.
"Standing as if having entered the water" means that, like one who has reached exhaustion and stands having entered the water, he is breathless.
It was thus situated. "Root" means nearby. Upon seeing the yakkha, the king was seized by fear, trepidation, and paralysis of the thighs;
therefore, the king was unable to flee. Hence it is said: "He approached to devour [him].
Then the king, having offered the deer cut in two, desired to save himself. The yakkha [thought], "Is it not mine..."
"From the moment it came into my hands, even the deer was mine; why then do you show such stinginess in giving it back to free yourself?
Thus he did not release the king. Then the king made a similar promise to him.
Therefore it is said: "The king with him," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "not having come to my abode": this means "not having come to my residence."

"Unpermitted" means not permitted by the owner who has approached [the food] as his own. By this, he shows that one may eat what was previously unpermitted by such a person once they have now given permission.
"In the path of death" means within the domain of death; they spoke thus because of their proximity to death.

The construction of the sentence is: "They departed, taking that prince Āḷavaka with them. The chief queen of that king is referred to as the mother of the prince Āḷavaka. The phrase "of the thousands of queens wailing" should be applied [to the mother].

"At the conclusion of the teaching" means at the end of the discourse taught by the Blessed One to the great assembly including the king, after he had returned from taming the yakkha and was sitting at the foot of a tree near the city gate. "He" refers to the Blessed One. In his abode...
"Even there" means even in that very celestial mansion (*vimāna*). The Blessed One also sees [them] with his natural eye (*pakaticakkhu*) because they have been reborn above Nigrodha.

"Therein" refers to that statement, "with the desire to cause annoyance. "Of them" refers to Sātāgiri and Hemavata. The "five great observations" (*pañcamahāvilokita*) have as their objects time, continent, country, lineage, progenitor, and the measure of lifespan.
The thirty-two [marks] are those that come down in such passages as, "The cold has departed, and the heat is stilled," and so forth.
The preceding signs. From the waist, the lower body, the garment, and the ear—thus in three ways. "Sound" refers to the sound of Āḷavaka’s shouting.

By way of this context, in order to show that just as these [other] three sounds occurred, spreading throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, so too did the sound of Āḷavaka’s shouting, it is said: “Four,” and so forth. “While declining” means while waning.
"Crushing" is said with reference to the capacity to crush, but not in the sense of actually crushing. Therefore he said, "May it not [harm] anyone," and so forth.

"Even a mere drop of dew" means even a quantity as small as a falling drop of dew. "Khurappa" is an arrow. "Supreme" means excellent by virtue of being invincible and unopposed. "Cloth-weapon" refers to a garment that performs the function of a weapon.
It is said that these were produced through the power of the merit of Sakka and others, possessing unimpeded efficacy and fit for destroying adversaries.
Weapons are not to be killed [with]. Therefore he said, “If indeed,” and so forth.
“Like a thunderbolt-wheel” means like a circle of lightning.

“Bile” means the bile of a venomous snake (*alagadda*). “Should pierce” means should pour out. “Easy” means easy to do. “For the purpose of establishing the mind that has become pliant” means for the purpose of effecting the establishment of one’s own mind once it has become pliant.

“When it was said thus”: when it was said, “Indeed, I do not [say so]. Because he had learned [the teachings] while attending upon the Blessed One who was established in the Dispensation of the Blessed One, he said, “He learned from Kassapa...,” meaning that he indeed learned them by attending upon the Blessed One. “Questions asked”:
questions asked by the Perfectly Enlightened One. Since they were questions asked within the domain of a Buddha, they therefore pertain exclusively to the domain of a Buddha.

"Having rejected" means having rejected by way of the fact that it cannot be accomplished through speech alone. Regarding the phrase "when you desire," he says "if you desire" because it is an exposition based on the euphonic combination (*padasandhi*) of words.
By this, he shows that they will first listen to your question and then provide an answer. Therefore, he says "not for me," and so forth.
In the second alternative, the letter *da* functions as a euphonic conjunction; thus he says "that which you desire."

Without saying, "Ask, friend; having heard, I shall know," [the Blessed One] said, "All of this to you," and so forth, because the word of an omniscient Buddha, when not restricted, has universal scope.
