Here, *kiṃ* is used in the sense of an inquiry (*kinti*), while *su* is used in the sense of doubt (*saṃsaye*); thus the meaning is "what indeed? (*kiṃ nu*). *Idha* means in this world.
Therefore, "wealth" (*vitta*) is so called because it makes one wealthy. "Well-done" (*sukata*) means done thoroughly and with care.

"Happiness" (*sukha*) is a desirable fruit. To show what is primary therein, it is said: "bodily and mental pleasure," and so forth; for by that mention, the outflow-fruit (*nissandaphala*) is already included.
"Brings about" (*appeti*) means it causes one to attain. It is a term that illuminates the sense of excellence.
Regarding the word *tara*, he says, "exceedingly sweet" (*atisayena sādū*). This refers to those things designated as "flavors" (*rasa*) which are desirable objects for phenomena such as lust.

As for the phrase "in what manner," he states the meaning of the word *kathaṃ*. If this is a compound word, namely *kathaṃ-jīviṃ*, he explains that the nasalized vowel was added for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition, and so forth.
“Faith is wealth here” is a way of referring to the whole by means of a part, like pointing to the ocean or a mountain.
The word *iti* should be understood as having the sense of “beginning with. The phrase beginning with “For just as...

was spoken in order to demonstrate, by means of reasons and similes, the meaning already stated—that it is “wealth because it produces wealth”—by way of bringing happiness, warding off suffering, and pacifying poverty.
Because it is the cause for obtaining the jewels and because it brings about the continuity of the world, faith is like wealth—just as gold, silver, and so forth.
Therefore he said, “Thus,” and so on. [An objection: But surely volition, right view, and the rest bring about an especially superior happiness of result;

how then does faith bring that about? [The answer: Because its intrinsic nature consists in having faith as its primary burden. Therefore he said, “for those who have practiced with faith as their primary burden.”
And this should be applied to the remaining phrases as well.

Now, in order to show that the wealth of gold, silver, and so forth—which serves as a simile for the wealth of faith—is inferior, whereas the wealth of faith alone is supreme, the word "best" (*seṭṭha*) is employed in the text;
thus, the passage beginning with "But because... was stated. [It refers to one] who has gone to the next world.
It is "conducive" (*anugāmika*) because it follows after. It is "not shared by others" (*anaññasādhāraṇa*) because it is not common to others.

It is "the cause of all success" (*sabbasampattihetu*) because it is the cause for all successes, both mundane and supramundane, such as the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*). It leads to misfortune through practice that lacks the proper means (*anupāyapaṭipatti*).

Therefore, because it is conducive, because it is not shared by others, because it is the cause of all success, and because it is the source of wealth such as gold and so forth— [it is thus described].
And faith alone is the best wealth. The teaching regarding the highest limit is as in the passage, "The Teacher of gods and humans.
By the phrase "the ten wholesome states," there is an inclusion of only certain qualities such as giving and so forth, but not all;

therefore, in order to include those not included [by that], it is said, "or the quality of giving, virtue, and meditation. The term "happiness" is a common designation for all three kinds of happiness.
Showing that same [attainment] as it was specifically acquired by a particular person, he said: "The merchant Soṇa...

brings about... Taking as an illustration King Mahāpaduma—the son of Queen Padumavatī—who, after experiencing the bliss of sovereignty comparable to divine bliss, subsequently became a paccekabuddha and experienced the bliss of Nibbāna, he spoke thus.
“It brings about the bliss of Nibbāna, like the Great Lotus and others.
Thus, explaining the word *sacca* by way of extracting its meanings, he said: “It is seen in many senses.

The intention is that the word *sacca* is seen in the sense of verbal truth (*vācāsacca*), because it was stated [in the Sutta]: “Speak the truth. It is seen in the sense of abstinence-truth (*viratisacca*) among the [three] abstentions (*veramaṇī*).
For it is because they are established in this that recluses and brahmins are called "established in truth.
Based on the mode of occurrence—namely, taking one's own position as the basis and asserting "this alone is truth, all else is vain"—it is precisely view that is called "truth";

thus, the construction is: "that which is seen in that truth of view" (diṭṭhisacce). "Truths of the brahmins" (brāhmaṇasaccāni) refers to the truths of those who are supreme brahmins in the ultimate sense (paramattha). Those [truths]...
“‘All living beings are not to be slain; all sensual pleasures are impermanent; all states of existence are impermanent;
I am nothing belonging to anyone, anywhere’”—these and other such [passages] appear in the Catukkanipāta. Ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) is Nibbāna.
“Having made it internal” means having included it within oneself; the meaning is “together with those [other truths],” because even among the ultimate truths, this one is the most excellent.
"By whose power" means by the power of whose word-truth (*vācasacca*).
"He runs upon the water" means he runs and goes upon the surface of the water as if on solid ground that cannot be broken through, like King Mahākappina.
"The wise destroy even poison with truth" refers to those such as Kaṇhadīpāyana and others. "With truth" [means...]
Just as in the Maccha Jātaka, by the truth of the Bodhisattva, the deity caused rain to fall from the sky.

"Established in truth" means established in both the truth of abstinence (*virati-sacca*) and the truth of speech (*vācā-sacca*); these are the three types of Bodhisattvas. "Seeking Nibbāna" means they aspire to Nibbāna.
"More excellent" means more constant, because it yields a more desirable result.

The genitive case (*sāmivacana*) in *rasānam* is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Showing that this selection—whether by someone, from something, or for the sake of someone—does not establish the statement of "anyone," he says "these which...
and so forth. For by that, Nibbāna is selected from the collection of flavors (*rasa*) on account of its specific excellence as the most superior.
Therein, the construction is: "those which are called these. [The term] *sāyanīyadhammā* means...
Dhammas to be tasted by the tongue. He says that the taste-base (*rasāyatana*) is "taste," such as "the taste of roots, the taste of trunks," and so forth.

"Fruit-taste" (*phalarasa*) means the taste of a fruit; the meaning is the taste to be obtained after squeezing and heating the fruit. "Lacking the nature of taste" (*arasarūpo*) means having a nature devoid of proper conduct.

"Tastes of form" (*rūparasā*) are those wholesome states of happiness arising by way of the relishing of form. This same method applies to the "tastes of sound" (*saddarasa*) and so on. "Taste of sound" (*saddarasa*)...

"Flavor produced from the letter" means the flavor consisting in the attainment of liberation (*vimuttirasa*). "Flavor of the meaning" (*attharasa*) refers to the happiness that arises through the penetration of the meaning;
likewise, the flavor of the Dhamma (*dhammarasa*) should be understood in the same way.

In the passage beginning with "modes of beauty," the term "flavor" (*rasa*) refers to the flavor of the fruit. For that [fruit] is both the beauty of the fruit and, because it is to be savored and experienced, it is its flavor.
And "taste" (*rasa*) is called "the taste of form" (*rūparasa*). However, conduct (*ācāra*) is called "taste" because it is the cause for the "taste" of harmony (*sāmaggīrasa*).
Regarding the phrase "it brings truth" (*saccaṃ haveti*): here, *haveti* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (*ekaṃsattha*), and the sense of emphasis is indeed restriction;
thus he says, "truth alone is more sweet," and so forth. It nourishes the body, not the mind. But surely, since its purpose is the arising of happiness, it [nourishes] the mind as well?
"Do they nourish? No; because it arises dependent upon the physical nourishment of happiness.

"Truthful speech of abstinence" refers to the attainment [of the path] through a specific kind of truth. One nourishes the mind by means of truthful speech characterized by abstinence, because when the essence of truth exists, the full nourishment of the mind through serenity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and so forth becomes possible, whereby one attains the benefits of the paths and fruits.
It brings about undefiled happiness because it is based on the turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭa*).
"The flavor of liberation" refers either to the happiness of the fruit or to the happiness of Nibbāna. The "flavor of ultimate truth" is the flavor of Nibbāna;

for it is described as "the flavor of immortality" and "the flavor that provides consolation. "Pervaded by that" is stated for the purpose of showing the superior excellence of the flavor of liberation.

Even so, by the phrase "because it is permeated with the flavor of liberation" (*vimuttirasa-paribhāvitattā*), he shows that either the flavor of liberation or the flavor of ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) is the most excellent flavor.
"Serving as the means for its attainment" (*tadadhigamūpāyabhūtaṃ*) means serving as the means for attaining that ultimate truth.

"Based on the meaning and the Dhamma" (*atthañca dhammañca*) means that because it proceeds by depending upon both the fruit and the cause, it possesses the flavor of meaning (*attharasa*) and the flavor of the Dhamma (*dhammarasa*).
"Excellent! Even better than that, the intended meaning is that the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) alone is the most excellent flavor.
One who does not know both the supramundane (lokuttara) and mundane (lokiya) welfare is blind; one who knows only mundane welfare is one-eyed; one who knows both is two-eyed.
One who does not know both the welfare of others and one's own welfare is blind; one who knows only one's own welfare is one-eyed."
One who knows the meaning of both is "two-eyed. That person with two eyes lives by wisdom (*paññājīvī*).

To show this by dividing it according to householders and those gone forth, the words "or a householder" and so forth were spoken. The construction is: "and having accomplished the path of the householder.
And "having accomplished" (*ārādhetvā*) means "having achieved" (*sādhetvā*).

“By the same method as before” means by the very method set forth by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa. “Kiñcāpi” (even though) is a particle used in the sense of indicating permission (*anujānana*).
What does it permit? It permits that when one of the meanings expressed by the four lines of the verse is established, the others are also established.
Therefore he said: “He who [avoids] the fourfold fruitlessness... pe ...is purified. What?
"Shows clearly" means: it is the showing, by way of removing doubt, of those counter-agents through whose strength of evil qualities the crossing of the flood and so forth are not accomplished.
Therefore he said, "Even though this is so," and so on. "Crossing the flood" refers to the practice for crossing the flood.
"Not believing" means not believing that one who practices in this way crosses the flood by means of this practice. Not...
"He leaps forward" means that he does not enter [the teaching] because he is not opened up by faith, which has the characteristic of leaping forward.
"By the relinquishing of the mind" means by the surrendering of the mind through acting according to its own whims. "He is negligent" means he has fallen into negligence.

"Right there" means precisely in sensual pleasures. "Because of being attached" means because of being stuck. "Interspersed" means intermingled. "Therefore" refers to the fourfold meaning already stated.

It is the grasping [of the object] by way of its being a cause. "Its opposite" means the opposite of lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) and so forth, because it provides the occasion for faith (*saddhā*) and the rest.

"By this" refers to this word in the verse; such is the connection. Among these factors for the attainment of the stream-entry path—namely, association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma—the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is the proximate cause.
He said: "The faculty of faith is the proximate cause for the factors of stream-entry. For this has been stated: "One who has conceived faith approaches;
approaching, he pays homage; paying homage, he lends an ear; lending an ear, he hears the Dhamma," and so forth.
It is called "crossing the flood of views" because by means of it one crosses the flood of views; that is, the crossing of the flood of views. And here, although "crosses" [is used]—

It is said, "the flood"; however, it is appropriate to speak of something as if it were currently occurring even when it is in close proximity to what is currently occurring, because the state of having crossed the flood seen [by one] is absolute.
Therefore, it is said, "it proclaims the stream-enterer. This same method applies to the others as well.
Because evil states that act as obstacles to the practice regarding views, doubt, and so forth, have been utterly eradicated, he is a stream-enterer... [and so on].
"Endowed with diligence. When it was said, "The stream-enterer... crosses over," the possibility of returning to this world even once might have been implied;
therefore, to exclude that, it was said: "Having reached... the remainder. [Objection:
But surely, because of the word "the remainder," only that portion of the basis for the flood of existence which has not been crossed by the path of stream-entry is included, and thus not everything?
"Could it be so? No; because those [fetters] which are to be crossed by the two higher paths are spoken of subsequently as being abandoned.
He also avoids the scope of the exception [by stating]: "Thus this objection does not find a footing within its own domain.

Because the perception of sensual desire has existed since beginningless time, the crossing of the flood of sensual desire must be accomplished with great effort; therefore he says, "by energy. This is the third [section].

Having attained the path. The basis for the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*) is the "basis of the flood of sensual desire" (*kāmogha-vatthu*), which is the entire existence of sensual desire (*kāmabhava*) together with the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).

"Designated as the flood of sensual desire" means reckoned as the flood of sensual desire. It is "sensual-desire-suffering" (*kāmadukkha*) because it is both sensual desire in the sense of being desirable and suffering.

"Perception of sensual desire" (*kāmasaññā*) is the perception that is itself sensual desire in the sense of relishing; [here] the perception of sensual desire has vanished because it has been completely cut off.
"Of these" refers to those whose perceptions of sensual desire have departed.

Because it is the root of all stains such as lust and because it specifically brings about a state of defilement within the continuum of sentient beings, it is the "supreme stain," that is, ignorance (*avijjā*). Therefore the Blessed One said: "Ignorance is the supreme stain."
"Having grasped the footing of wisdom" means having placed the aforementioned footing of wisdom in one's heart.
"In connection with that," by means of one's own ingenuity, according to the method learned by all alike. "In all respects" means in all five places.

"Inquiries into the meaning and the method" refers to inquiries into the cause—the method—by which the attainment of the meaning of wisdom and so forth occurs. Therefore he said, "For this... and so on. [The purpose is] the meaning of wisdom and so forth.

"Having known" (*ñatvā*) means having understood through knowledge that brings about the penetration of truth, in its true nature, the welfare (*attha*) consisting of the wealth of wisdom, fame, friends, and the future life.
One might ask: "Is it not the case that this [wisdom] stands surpassing both the supramundane wisdom of the path and fruit of stream-entry and the mundane wisdom that is the means for attaining it?
Why, then, does he inquire regarding the application of welfare therein? This is true; however, further on...

Desiring to ask about the application (*yutti*) of concentration because of the preeminence of wisdom (*paññā*), and because that [preeminence] has been attained only in part, he asks beginning with that very [wisdom].

The commentary on the meaning of the passage beginning with “By what application? is seen to extend to wealth and so forth as well, according to the principle: “This method applies to wealth and the rest.
Furthermore, the fact that this is a question regarding the application of meaning is clarified by the phrase “in all cases indeed.”

By means of the four causes known as faith (*saddhā*), eagerness to hear (*sussūsā*), heedfulness (*appamāda*), and exertion (*uṭṭhāna*). By means of that which constitutes the eightfold virtue of livelihood (*ājīva-aṭṭhamaka-sīla*), distinguished by bodily good conduct and so forth. By means of that which consists of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
When taking only the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*) in their primary sense (*nippariyāya*), he said, "at a later stage" (*aparabhāge*).

However, the factors conducive to enlightenment in a secondary sense (*pariyāya-bodhipakkhiya*) are obtained specifically even at the time of insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāmini-vipassanā*). [The term] "in the prior stage" (*pubbabhāge*)...
Or it refers to the time of nascent insight (*vipassanā*). He says "at a later stage" again with reference to the preliminary practice prior to that;
the meaning is "subsequent to that. "Dhamma" means the Dhamma of practice. The construction is: "One does not obtain wisdom by mere faith alone.
If this is so, why was it said "one who has faith"? To this he says: "But because... and so forth. What is meant?
He explains the very meaning already stated by the words "it occurs" and so forth.
To show that the acquisition of wisdom does not come through mere desire to hear, but rather that one acquires wisdom through heedfulness (*appamāda*), the text says "heedful and discerning.
Demonstrating this point, he says "thus," and so forth.
Now, having extracted and demonstrated the specific conditions for the acquisition of wisdom (paññā) by means of faith (saddhā) and the other faculties, he says "Thus.

"Through desire to hear" (sussūsāya) means through the wish to listen; in its actual sense, this consists of approaching [the teacher] and so forth. "The means for attaining wisdom" refers to the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma).
Therefore, he says, "he hears it. [Wisdom] does not forget what has been grasped; its characteristic is the non-departure of mindfulness (sati).
"Indeed, it is heedfulness. Not only is discernment the skill in grasping things as they truly are, but it is also the thorough expansion of wisdom according to reality;

thus he says, "he makes it extensive. Now, having brought the cause for the acquisition of wisdom to its ultimate conclusion, he says, "or through a desire to hear," and so forth. "He examines the meaning" refers to the teachings already heard.
Preceded by an investigation into the meaning of the scriptures, he investigates and examines the distinction between the material and the immaterial, and the ultimate reality (paramattha),
both by way of specific characteristics (salakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa). "Gradually" means that having thus attained full understanding through knowledge (ñātapariññā),

he proceeds step-by-step from there toward the culmination of full understanding through examination (tīraṇapariññā) and full understanding through abandonment (pahānapariññā) according to the sequence of the Path.
One realizes Nibbāna, which is the ultimate truth.
Showing that these four factors, beginning with faith, must be brought to their highest perfection, he said:
"without neglecting the place, time, and so forth. This refers to the place, the time, and the companions by relying upon whom a particular task is to be accomplished.
One who desires their own advancement without overstepping [the bounds] should practice after examining everything as follows:
"This is the place where I currently dwell; this is the time; these are my friends; these are my enemies; these are my gains and losses;
and such am I in terms of birth, clan, locality, strength, wealth, retinue, and so forth. This task should now be undertaken; this task should not yet be undertaken. Thus one should proceed.
One who practices in this way indeed employs a fitting means for the acquisition of worldly wealth;

however, in the case of the supramundane, it should be understood by way of the purification of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. It is called *dhura* because it is like a yoke (*dhura*) in its quality of being borne; thus, it is a burden.

Here, however, "the exertion of the yoke" (*dhurasampaggaha*) is termed *dhura* through the elision of the final member of the compound; it is energy (*vīriya*). One who possesses this [energy] in an eminent degree is [described as such].

“Dhuravā. Since the term “one who exerts himself” (*uṭṭhātā*) will be explained as referring to physical energy (*kāyika-vīriya*), it is specified here as being “by way of mental energy” (*cetasika-vīriya*).

“One who does not cast off the yoke” (*anikkhittadhura*) because of his state of being a bearer of the burden (*dhorayha-bhāva*). “He does not think more highly than a blade of grass” means that he conducts himself with excessive humility, treating [himself] like a blade of grass.
Regarding the phrase “in this manner and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) includes—
“He who performs his human duties does not depart from happiness.
It is not possible for one who habitually sleeps by day, who shows no regard for rising at night,
and who is constantly intoxicated and addicted to drink, to dwell in the household.”
This is the summary of such [cases]. "Exerting unwavering effort" means because of his tireless nature. "By means of a single mouse" means by means of one dead mouse.

"Before long" means within four months itself. "Numbering four hundred thousand, like the junior pupil" refers to two hundred thousand [kahāpaṇas] obtained through the sequence of taking one kahāpaṇa, two kahāpaṇas, sixteen kahāpaṇas, and twenty-four kahāpaṇas;
and another two hundred thousand [kahāpaṇas] obtained through the acquisition of the daughter of the junior chief merchant (cūḷaka-mahāseṭṭhi). Thus, it numbers four hundred thousand.
Just as Cūḷantevāsī obtained wealth by means of a single root, so too does another who is worthy, diligent, and industrious obtain wealth.
And this matter is to be illustrated by the Cūḷakaseṭṭhi Jātaka. For it is said there:
“Even with a small load, the wise man, being discerning, ... [obtains great profit].”
"He raises himself up, like a tiny fire burning. Regarding "having performed the duty":
having performed the duty of resolve (*adhiṭṭhānavatta*). The construction is: "He attains fame as one who speaks truth, one who speaks reality.
"What is desired and prayed for" means: by those with whom he desires friendship, that which is other [than mere friendship] is prayed for. "He binds friends together."
One cultivates friendship. Because giving creates endearment, it is said: "By giving, one becomes beloved.
Showing that which is a gift that brings about friendship in an absolute sense, he says: "Or by giving what is difficult to give, one binds [friends].
And since "giving" is a term used as a characteristic (lakkhaṇa), he says: "Or by way of giving," and so forth.
He answers according to the inclination of Āḷavaka, by way of a householder. "Saddho" means one who has faith; thus, it refers to that faithful person.
"Gharamesino" means one who seeks a home, which here signifies the household life.

Because they depend upon the household life, the "home" is said to be the five strands of sensual pleasure; therefore, he says, "the five strands of sensual pleasure. By the words "These four qualities," and so forth...
Showing that the phenomena mentioned in the immediately preceding verse are indeed these very ones, he says, “The truth of the aforementioned kind,” and so forth.

Therein, it is called *dhamma* because of its holding (*dhāraṇa*), maintaining (*upadhāraṇa*), and supporting (*atthassa yāthāvato*) those meanings through such expressions as “these are wholesome, these are unwholesome.
Perception (*saññā*) is the holding of mind and mental factors; it is the continuous sustaining of the wholesome continuum by way of non-interruption.
*Dhiti* means that by which one holds firm; it is energy (*vīriya*). *Cāga* means that by which one relinquishes; it is generosity (*dāna*).

It exists by way of being capable of producing a fruit despite the deficiency of conditions. "Others too" means: if there are other qualities besides this collection of qualities already mentioned, ask about those qualities as well.
*Dama* means that by which one tames the defilements or the body, speech, and so forth; it is wisdom (*paññā*). *Uṭṭhāna* means that by which one rises up or exerts oneself.
*Vīriyaṃ*. “In this” (*ettha*) means in this question. “Together with” (*saddhiṃ*) means together with the concise connection of the words expressing the essential meaning.
“Each single word” (*ekamekaṃ padaṃ*) refers to each individual word beginning with “wisdom” (*paññā*).

“Extraction of the meaning” (*atthuddhāro*) is the drawing out of the meaning of wisdom and so forth by means of such statements as: “In this place, ‘wisdom’ is mentioned as a phenomenon (*dhamma*),” and so on. Of that respective meaning, “wisdom... [and so forth].
The extraction of synonymous terms, such as "understanding" (*pajānanā*) and so forth, is the "extraction of words" (*paduddhāra*). To explain the word: "it understands, thus it is wisdom (*paññā*);
it bears [the truth], thus it is the Dhamma (*dhammo*); it tames, thus it is self-control (*damo*)"—this is the "word-commentary" (*padavaṇṇanā*).
"Today" (*ajja*) means "now" (*etarahi*). "In the manner already stated" refers to the manner described in the passage beginning with "having faith in the Arahants."

Alternatively, by means of the penetration and comprehension of the Truths, through having seen the Truths in the manner described, he knows the welfare of this world and the world beyond as they truly are.

And thus, the Teacher explains that the Yakkha, by asking a question established through the power of the Master’s teaching, demonstrates his own success in acquisition, saying, "How does one obtain wisdom? and so forth. "Of the future life" (samparāyiko) means...
And here, the word *ca* (and) is indicated as being elided; thus, showing that the meaning “both pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammiko*)” has indeed been stated, he says:
“The meaning which... shows. It is called *attha* because the fruit (*phala*) is attained (*arīyati*) from it;

it is the cause. Because of its purposefulness for those with discerning eyes (*vicakkhaṇe*). “Of that knowledge” means of the knowledge that makes that meaning manifest. And because there is no other equal to him in his special qualities, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is the foremost among those worthy of offerings (*aggadakkhiṇeyyo*). Therefore he said:
“In this world or in the next,
there is no one equal to the Buddha, for he alone is supreme.
He has reached the highest state of those worthy of offerings.”
"For those seeking merit who desire abundant fruit.
"Accompanied practice" (*sahitapaṭipatti*) refers to one's own practice accompanied by wisdom (*paññā*). "Beautiful awakening" (*sundarā bodhi*), "good awakening" (*subodhi*);

the awakening of the Buddha is "Buddha-awakening" (*buddhasubodhi*), and that itself is "the state of Buddha-awakening" (*buddhasubodhitā*). [This was said] by the deities who had assembled for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
And there arose the sound of a universal shout of "Well done! (sādhukāra).

Regarding the "marks of a hundred merits" (*satapuññalakkhaṇa*): because the equipment of merit was performed over a hundred thousand eons, by virtue of those merits, they are called the "marks of a hundred merits," which are marks produced by manifold merits.
They are endowed with all their limbs in a manner that is to be greatly rejoiced in by everyone.
“Endowed with” means possessing. They are called *byañjanāni* (limbs) because they manifest the state of having performed merit;

that is, the major and minor limbs. Because these are complete, it is “complete in its limbs. The Yakkha... [as stated] ...filled them; for the Blessed One indeed made them such as those solely for the purpose of completing the verse.
“Free from disease” (*abyādhita*) means healthy. Some read “*abyathitā*,” which means free from self-terror.
Where "Hatthayo" should have been said, "Hatthako" was stated. "Āḷavinagara" refers to the inhabitants of the city of Āḷavi;
for when one is situated in a place, the word for that place is used [to denote its inhabitants], as in "the village has arrived" or "the beds are making a clamor.
This was while a great tumult was occurring.

"Sampiṇḍitvā" means having assembled. Although it is not the case that the preparation was made by him, because he had repeatedly exerted himself for the sake of battle, it is said, "having begun with the battle.
He preached that very Āḷavaka Sutta because it was suitable for the assembly gathered for that very teaching. Therefore he said: "The discourse... [was] thus... By four.
"By means of the bases" means by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*). "His own assembly" refers to his own retinue; some also say it means "the other [assembly].
The commentary on the *Āḷavaka-sutta* is finished.
From the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta-nikāya*.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the *Yakkhasaṃyutta* is completed.
11. *Sakkasaṃyutta*, Chapter 1. First Section.
1. Commentary on the Suvīra-sutta 247. *Abhiyaṃsu*:
They went forth having become ready for battle and facing [the enemy]. *Tatra*: In that context, regarding the advance of the asuras, this is now the discourse being told in successive order.
*Tettiṃsa purise gahetvā*: Having taken thirty-three men for the performance of meritorious deeds...

Having taken [them] as companions; having fulfilled the seven rules of conduct (*vatapada*) undertaken with the thought, “May I be a supporter of my mother and father for as long as life lasts,” and so forth.
*Adhigaṇhantaṃ* means overcoming or surpassing. *Puttahatāya* means one whose son has been killed.
That was not *surā* (liquor); the intention was, “We did not drink *sura*. *Tato paṭṭhāya* means from the time it was said, “It is not *surā*. “Na...”
Some say they are called *asura* because "they do not shine" (*suranti na*). On the lower surface, within the earth, it extends for ten thousand *yojanas* in length.
He says "in the five places beginning with the uraga" to refer to the locations frequented by uragas and others.
"In the first *ālinda*" means in the first veranda. On all four sides of Sineru, there are [terraces] five thousand *yojanas* wide, broad, and thick.

There are four sub-ranges (paribhaṇḍa). For on each side of Sineru, in relation to the great purpose to be obtained from the great islands surrounded by five hundred minor islands such as Yugandhara and the rest, they are "of great significance" (mahattha). "With minds agitated by anger" means with minds disturbed by anger.
"Seeking battle" means desiring battle. "In the others" means in the remaining sub-ranges. "The others" refers to the Supaṇṇas and so forth.
“Ant-ants” refers to ants together with their wings. “Having retreated” means having turned back by way of the rear.
“He fell into negligence” means he became negligent at the command of Sakka. “Sixty yojanas in width. “The great golden street” refers to a street consisting of a ground-level pavement made of gold.
“Not exerting” means not performing exertion, which is physical energy (*kāyika-vīriya*). “Not striving” means not applying effort, which is mental energy (*cetasika-vīriya*).
"Not doing" means not performing any task whatsoever—any duty such as farming, trading, or other similar activities that ought to be done.
"Excellent" (*vara*) means preeminent; thus he said "supreme. Furthermore, since it is specifically the place for cultivation that is intended, he said "space.
"Without having performed work" means without having performed even any work that serves as a means of livelihood. "A place of livelihood" refers to that [place].
"For the sake of life" means for the purpose of living. "The path to Nibbāna" means the path that serves as the means for the attainment of Nibbāna.
The commentary on the Suvīra Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Susīma Sutta.
248. *Antareti* means "within. *Evaṃnāmakan ti* means "one who has such a name," namely, one named Susīma. *Ekaṃ puttaṃ eva* means "only one son," that is, one of his own sons.
The commentary on the Susīma Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Dhajagga Sutta.
249. *Samupabyūḷho*: the meeting of both [armies] together; or the meaning is that it was "intensely arrayed" (*bhusaṃ byūḷho*).
Its intense arraying was due to the two armies having come together and become massed; thus he said, "massed, formed into a heap.
*Pacchimanto*: the end of the chariot-fender; the rear limit, the rear section. *Rathasandhito*: from the chariot-junction.
From the point where it is connected with the crossbar of the chariot-fortress. "That very same measurement" means that very measurement already stated as "one hundred and fifty yojanas in length.
"Having doubled it" means having doubled it according to the description beginning with "the western end is one hundred yojanas," and so forth.
[This refers to] the remaining ornaments, such as the various moon-discs, sun-discs, networks of tinkling bells, and so on. [This is for] the gods who are looking [at them].
“Rājā no” means “our king, the best of gods. “He receives the second seat” means that when Sakka is seated, he receives the second seat immediately following him.
Therefore, because of his status as the best of gods, he is worthy of honor just like Sakka;
which is why Sakka said, “You should look toward the top of his banner. This same principle applies to the others as well. “Defeated by the asuras” means by the asuras.

He was brought to defeat. "Upon seeing the dust-banner" means that even when standing still, upon seeing even a mere cloud of dust raised by an approaching enemy army, one who possesses the nature of flight does so out of fear;
this refers to the power of the *Dhajaggapārisuddha-paritta*, because it must be received with the head bowed even by deities who are not present in person.

Regarding the phrase "from fear of thieves, etc.," by the word "etc. (ādi), one should understand the inclusion of the fear of disease and so forth, as well as the suffering of the round of existence (saṃsāra).
This is because when a protective chant (paritta) is cultivated according to the proper method, even access-concentration (upacāra-jhāna) and the like are achieved for its purpose.
The shrine named after the village of Dīghavāpi is called the Dīghavāpi Cetiya. A "head-railing" (muddhavedikā) refers to a pavilion (hammiya) that has been enclosed [with a railing].
Having constructed the railing, he established mindfulness directed toward the Buddha and recited the protective paritta.
By the power of that paritta, two bricks... [and so on] ...stood firm. For it was thus that while standing upon that ladder... [and so on] ...they stood firm.
The commentary on the Dhajagga Sutta is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Vepacitti Sutta (250).
They say that he is called "Vepacitti" because his mind trembles due to the great power of the asuras.
However, when the seers requested freedom from fear, he replied, "I give you fear itself! and by way of cursing them, [said], "May your fear be inexhaustible."
From the time it was uttered, because of its trembling nature, it is called "vepacitti," which worldly people call "puloma.
He says "merely a particle" because no causal meaning or the like is possible here; for even certain particles serve to indicate specific meanings.
"Tam" refers to Sakka, the lord of the gods. "With the five [strings] on the neck" means with the five strings bound around the neck.
The description is by means of the elision of a case ending (*vibhattialopa*). "By the mind alone" means by the very mind that has arisen [thinking], "I shall bind this;
let this be bound. It is bound, it becomes bound; this is the power of the gods (*devānubhāva*). "Is released"—here too the same method applies.

"By ten" means by the ten stated here, beginning with "You are a thief. Therefore he said, "by these. By way of censuring (*khuṃsana*) based on the fact that [the being] has been produced for a long time.
He says, “I am old. He does not take that abuse to heart because his disposition has long been established in patience and gentleness.
“A great receptacle” means a great sign of tranquility (*upasama*). “Of him” refers to Vepacitti.
“Would counter-attack” means that, having become an adversary, he would engage in conflict. Therefore it is said, “he would oppose. [Tranquility...]
I think [this is so] because of the suppression of anger—which has become the leader of its adversary—by means of tranquility alone.
For when anger finds no counter-action from such a person, it subsides like a fire that lacks fuel. The word *yadā* (when) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*), not the sense of time;
thus he said, "because he perceives that. "At that very moment, two oxen fight" means at that very same [moment].

At the moment when two bulls are fighting, there is no purpose found superior to forbearance (*khanti*), because it immediately wards off hostility and harm, providing for both the present life and the life to come. They call that forbearance supreme; it is the best power.
Because it proceeds by overcoming the condition of opposition. It is "foolish" (bāla) because of association with folly;
its "strength" is "the strength of folly" (bālabala). Thus he said: "The so-called 'strength of folly' is the strength of ignorance.

That which is the strength of such a person—that strength of ignorance—is indeed powerless, because it must be shattered by the power of wisdom. "There is no opponent" refers to the established nature of phenomena (dhammaṭṭha).
There is nothing that proceeds by way of opposing or overcoming. However, someone might even offer a mere rebuttal;
showing that such a thing is no reason [for the Buddha’s silence], he said, “or by opposing,” and so forth. “By the power of a fool” is the statement of the reason for the expression “by opposing.
It refers to that very person who is retaliating. Because of the occurrence of discursive thought regarding diversity (*nānattavitakka*).
"For the benefit of both. "Desiring to treat" means warding off [harm] by way of preventing what is unbeneficial, through performing the duties of a wise person.
They are called "fools" because they do not understand cause and effect, and thus are unskilled in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.
The commentary on the Vepacitti Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Subhāsitajaya-sutta* 251.
Having stated "by way of skill," he said "it is said that... and so forth, in order to demonstrate his state of being skilled in speaking that matter.

They "grasp" means they adopt a conviction (*laddhi*). "Having released" means having liberated him in such a way that one is no longer able to further say of him, "He is a thief. Thus, having released him.
It is not possible to speak first. "Heavy" (*garu*) means burdensome; the sense is that it is difficult.
As for "afterwards," when one has spoken of "another's" [view], if one speaks something first, one reveals one's own intention;
then, having understood his mind according to one's ability, one is able to speak further. Therefore he said: "But after following another's speech, afterwards it is easy."
"...let it be said. Furthermore, the Lord of Asuras first spoke, saying, "Let there be victory for you, O Lord of Devas, through well-spoken words";

and a distinction follows that which is introduced first. Sakka, the King of Devas, being skilled in speech, introducing that very distinction first by way of persuasion, said, "It is you indeed here," and so forth. "Former gods" refers to those headed by Sakka.
Because they appeared in the world even before the assembly of gods, the term "pubbadevā" (former gods) is a word of praise.
Since it was said "you" and "former gods" with reference to Vepacitti, it is stated: "First, tell [us] that which has come down through your own lineage.
The plural form is used for Vepacitti because he is worthy of respect. "Daṇḍāvacaro" means the range of punishment; that is, the sphere of punishment (*daṇḍa-avacara*).
"Adaṇḍāvacarā" means those that do not fall within the scope of punishment; these are the verses spoken by Sakka.
The commentary on the *Subhāsita-jaya-sutta* is concluded.
6. Commentary on the *Kulāvaka-sutta*.

252. "The sound of chariots" (*rathasadda*) refers to the sound of the networks of small bells (*kiṅkiṇika*) and other ornaments that adorn the chariots. Likewise, there is the sound of banners (*dhajasadda*). "The sound of noble steeds" (*ājānīyasadda*) refers to the neighing of well-bred horses.
"With a heart imbued with compassion" (*karuṇāsamāvajjitahadaya*) means having a mind directed toward non-harming of living beings.

"By means of the pole-head" (*īsāmukhena*) means by means of the front of the chariot-pole. "Produced as a condition for merit" (*puññapaccayanibbatta*) means produced from a sublime and vast [cause].
He was reborn by making merit the condition. He does not cling anywhere, moving without encountering resistance.
"Through the *simbali* grove" means through the midst of the *simbali* grove. "Shattered and crushed" means shattered here and there and completely crushed without remainder.
The commentary on the *Kulāvaka-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Nadubbhiya Sutta* 253.

"A true adversary" (*supaccatthiko*) means one who is thoroughly, exceedingly hostile, an enemy. "You are captured" (*gahitosi*) means you have been seized after being bound by the divine noose (*devapāsa*).
He was indeed bound by the power of Sakka’s merit. It is said that the King of the Cetiya [Mountains] in this [place]...
Prior to that [eonic] period, he uttered a harsh lie never before spoken by anyone;
at that very moment, having fallen away, he plunged into a fissure opened in the great earth and was crushed by the flames of the Avīci hell. It is with reference to this that it is said:
"with reference to the evil of Cetiyarāja. "Great evils" means great, more grievous evils. For thus:
These [examples] have been included in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) as illustrations for Vepacitti’s making of an oath.
The commentary on the *Nadubbhiyasutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Verocanāsuriṃdasutta*.
254. “Like figures of doorkeepers” means like images fashioned in the form of doorkeepers. “One should indeed strive” means one should not fall into despondency midway;
this is the intended meaning. “In those beautiful when completed” means in those that are lovely by virtue of being finished.
For all things that are incomplete do not shine. “A multitude of tasks” means tasks that have arisen because they have been left unfinished.

"Akiccajāto" means one for whom no duty has arisen; there is indeed nothing devoid of duty, because [the body] exists for the purpose of dispelling the suffering that arises through such acts as going, standing, lying down, and sitting. "Sambhogā saṃyogaparamā eva":

for these beings, the objects of enjoyment are by nature contrary to one another, yet they are not unattractive when not conjoined; rather, those things reach their perfection through preparation, cooking, and conjunction.
They are to be understood as such because they have attained the state of being fit for communal consumption. Therefore he said, "rice-gruel and so forth for those on probation," and so on.
The intention is that they should be shared out after having been heated, provided they are suitable for consumption.
The commentary on the *Verocana-asurinda-sutta* is concluded.
9. Commentary on the *Araññāyatanaisisutta* 255.
A *jāmātuka* is called the husband of one’s daughter; a *sasura* is the father of one’s wife.

Therefore, these two people who live within the household—the son-in-law and the father-in-law—are so called by way of their relationship to the daughter (*sujā*). Regarding the phrase “for those long-initiated,” having been initiated...

Having gone forth long ago, by virtue of their undertaking of vows, they are those who have gone forth outside of this [Buddhist fold]; thus he said, "those who have long undertaken the vows. "Withdraw from here" means:
depart, move away from this place where you currently stand. It is not because they perceive repulsiveness that they do so, but because of their application of reverence toward virtues.
For the devas, for the most part, think: "In the past, we attended upon those possessed of virtue, and by abiding by their instruction, we performed meritorious deeds..."
"Having accumulated [merit], they have been reborn here"—thus do they establish a sense of reverence toward those possessed of virtues.
The commentary on the Araññāyatana-isī-sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Samuddaka-sutta.
256. "On the surface of the great ocean surrounding the world-sphere" means on the surface of the shore of the great ocean all around the base of the world-sphere mountains.
Just as the great ocean near Sineru slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and slants gradually, so too it is for the most part near the base of the world-sphere.
Therefore he said: "on the sandy beach with the color of a silver plate. "In those of the aforementioned kind" means...
In the modes described in the immediately preceding sutta. "By way of the hermitage path" means by way of the middle of the hermitage path.
"They thought thus" means they deliberated in the manner that has come down in the Pāli, beginning with "What if we...

"One who does what is desired" means one who performs whatever is wished for. "Of the wicked" means of those who are difficult to satisfy; moreover, they are those whose underlying intentions are corrupt.
"They are opposed" means "of those that are corrupted and opposed. "Sown" refers to the seed;
thus he said, "planted in the field.
"Evening meal" means food to be eaten in the evening. This is consumed according to its turn, like that of the gods.
Because there was neither anything subtle nor any heavy food, it is called "alms-food" (*bhatta*). "Born of illness" means that illness has arisen.
"Trembles" means it shakes and quivers.
The commentary on the Samuddaka Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Second Chapter: 1.
Commentary on the Vatapada Sutta.

257. They are called "sections of vows" (*vatakoṭṭhāsāni*) because they are to be undertaken as vows; because one must go forth [into homelessness] by means of their mutual non-confusion of nature, they are called "steps" (*padāni*); and for that very reason, because they are unmixed portions, they are so designated.

They are "fully accomplished" (*samattāni*) because, by way of being a distinction of merit, they produce the fruit of a praiseworthy existence and through the recognition of fame, they are equally attained (*samattāni*). They are "complete" (*paripuṇṇāni*).
"Entirely full" means full in every respect by way of being unbroken and so forth. "Well undertaken" means properly undertaken therein through careful performance.
"Matula" means the father's sister; it does not refer to any wife of a maternal uncle, because the elders of the family are intended here.
Alternatively, even a wife may be included by virtue of her connection to a maternal uncle; if that were the case, the inclusion of the wives of paternal uncles and others should also be understood.
By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the elder sisters is intended. "One who performs acts of reverence" means one who rises up to greet them.

Anyone who gives while still being full of longing does not possess "freely bestowed generosity" (muttacāga); however, since this person is not like that, it is said, "he is one of freely bestowed generosity.
"Freely bestowed generosity" (vissaṭṭhacāga) means giving without expectation. Just as one who is abundant in the taking of life is called "red-handed" (lohitapāṇī).
He is called "one with hands cleansed" because he is one who is abundant in giving; thus it was said:
"Always having washed his hands for the purpose of giving gifts. "Delighting in relinquishment" means being delighted in the renunciation of things to be given.
"Worthy of being entreated by others" means being fit to be asked by others, because he immediately bestows whatever desired object is requested. "Devoted solely to giving" means...
He was constantly devoted to giving because he frequently engaged in great acts of almsgiving.

Furthermore, he delighted in— and took great pleasure in— both "giving" (*dāna*), which consists of relinquishing after having fulfilled the needs of others, and "sharing" (*saṃvibhāga*), which consists of distributing among those who are to enjoy it himself.
The commentary on the Vatapadasutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sakkanāmasutta 258.
“Manussabhūto” means born among humans, or having attained the human state. “Āvasathaṃ” means a dwelling place.
Because he gave [the name] after having caused [it] to be made, he is called Vāsava, meaning "he who gave a dwelling.
The word *attha* here is used in the sense of "cause"; thus it is said, "even for a thousand causes. This matter has already been explained above. He judges;
therefore, because he has a thousand eyes of wisdom (*paññā*), he is "Sahassakkha" (Thousand-eyed). *Magha* is said to mean wealth; that, moreover, is defined as faith (*saddhā*).
He possesses *magha* (wealth/gift), thus he is *Maghavā*. Because he gave gifts in former times, he is *Purindada*, [the term being formed] without eliding the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*).
He is able to perform meritorious deeds, thus he is *Sakka*.
The commentary on the Sutta on the Name of Sakka is finished.
3. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta 259. "He" refers to Sakka, the king of the devas. Although the plural number should have been used, the singular has been employed.

"Vacana" (speech) means that which is spoken; thus, it means "meaning. Therefore, "in the plural" means "in many meanings. Just as one who practices [the path] proceeds by way of successive stages... [te]... them.
Having undertaken the Dhamma, Sakka attained the state of Sakka; in order to show that practice, the passage beginning with “Sakka, it is said,” was spoken.
In the immediately preceding [existence] means in the personal existence (attabhāva) immediately prior to his becoming Sakka. “All of that” refers to all of it:
both the right practice during the time he was the youth Magha and the attainment of the state of Sakka through that practice. It was spoken; therefore, according to the method explained therein—
"It should be understood"—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the Mahāli Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Dalidda Sutta.
260. "Poor among humans" means one who is miserable among humans. "Pitiable among humans" means being extremely lowly among humans.
"Miserable among humans" means being extremely base among humans. "In that place" means in the place of birth of that son of the gods.
"They think of him as inferior" means they consider him to be lowly based on his former state.
"They speak" means they speak that very thing to others. "They elaborate" means they expand upon the meaning already stated.

At all times, having been distinguished and endowed with a retinue, he sat upon the back of an elephant worth seven and a half *ratanas* with the great majesty of royalty, being gazed upon by the multitude of people.
"They hang down" means they dangle. Or [it refers to] a mere salutation.
He did not [expect anything else], but rather he expected from the Paccekabuddha the same treatment as that accorded to his own peers. Therefore it was said:
“So,” and so forth. “Kvāyaṃ” means “Where is this man?”—he speaks thus because of his being afflicted.
Having observed a change in color due to being sewn with black and red threads, he said, “He is wearing the robes of a leper. Having been reborn in the Great Hell, he experienced great suffering.
He experienced [the results]. By means of the remaining ripening (vipāka) of a corresponding evil deed, having found an opportunity, he took rebirth in Rājagaha...

[etc. ... He took rebirth there. And although the taking of rebirth here occurs through wholesome karma alone, it is nevertheless stated as "by the remainder of the ripening" because of the powerful nature of that unwholesome karma’s ripening.
Therefore he said: "From the time of his being taken [in the womb]... [etc. ... he emerged."
From the time he was capable of going for alms, due to the severity of his illness, his flesh... [and so on] ...fell away.
"Having directed his knowledge" means having directed and applied the knowledge of cultivation through the sequence of insight (vipassanā) toward Nibbāna.
Because his faculties were fully matured, by means of the Teacher’s skillful teaching, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). "A cushion" (cumbaṭaṃ).
A foot-cushion. For those with leprosy, thinking "May my entire sole of the foot not be painful," they make a cushion and go about binding it to the sole of the foot;

just as one who, having fallen from a base human existence like a broken clay bowl, takes up a divine state as if recovering a golden bowl, he was reborn in the world of the gods at the moment of the second consciousness following the death-consciousness, at the instant of the consciousness of grasping.

“Attained by means of the path” means arrived at or arisen through the realization of the path. “Virtue dear to the Noble Ones” refers to the dhamma of virtue that is beloved, pleasing, and delightful to the Noble Ones.
He said “even though” and so forth because the training in higher virtue is, like the trainings in higher mind and higher wisdom, exceedingly dear to the Noble Ones in every respect.
But in this context—namely, in this context of the stream-enterer’s existence—
When the meaning is being stated after having been extracted: even the five precepts, like [wrong] view, are not abandoned even in another existence.
The commentary on the *Dalidda-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Rāmaṇeyyaka-sutta*.
261. Beings delight (*āramanti*) here, thus they are called *ārāmas*, such as delightful groves and the like.

These very things are also called *cetiyas* because they cause one to accumulate (*cetenti*) within oneself joy and gladness through faith. "Of the state of being delightful to humans" means of the state that is pleasing to human beings.
Furthermore, by way of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), it possesses an inconceivable and immeasurable majesty.

"It is so," said the Blessed One; "it is not worth a sixteenth part. The beauty of an insentient piece of ground is to be understood as resulting from its association with noble ones who are distinguished by their virtues;
thus it was said: "Now... [he spoke] beginning with 'in a village' and so forth.
The commentary on the *Rāmaṇeyyaka-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Yajamānasutta* 262.

Regarding the phrase "to those sacrificing" (*yajantānaṃ*), it means those giving with reference to one worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). Having shown that this is a discourse established on the basis of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppattika*), the commentary was composed beginning with the words "At that time, indeed...
in order to explain the meaning. "Supreme" (*aggam*) means the best. Or rather, [it refers to] the ghee and other substances obtained by each of them according to their means.
"Let not the ghee and other substances, which were taken as the foremost, perish merely by being burned in the fire;
let not gods and humans perish through wrong grasp. "By mere reasoning" means by mere logic.
The construction is: "How do you think of us? Now see! This [truth] comes to you from direct perception... they said.
"Resulting from the substrata" (*upadhivipāka*) means either that it ripens within the substrata, or that its results are the substrata themselves;

thus it is "resulting from the substrata. It is expansive because of its vastness. They gave it to the community of monks, saying: "The Fully Enlightened One and Great Brahmā have given this exhortation."
The commentary on the *Yajamānasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Buddhavandanāsutta* 263. "Arise" means exert yourself;
perform physical energy (*kāyikavīriya*). Therefore he said, "wander in the world. [This refers to] mental energy (*cetasikavīriya*).
But this has indeed been brought to its ultimate conclusion by the Blessed One. Therefore he said, "Victorious in battle. Because of its height of twelve yojanas;
and because it stands pervading the Cakkavāḷa, which measures many hundreds of thousands of yojanas in width and length.
"Pannabhārā" means those who have laid down their burden. Since it is that which must be set aside, he said, "Those who have lowered the load from their shoulders," and so forth.
For these are called "burdens" in the sense of bringing down upon the person who possesses them; thus it is said: "The five aggregates are indeed burdens.
And their specific components are the defilements and volitional formations.
Just as on the night of the fifteenth of the waxing moon—the full-moon night—the moon shines forth, liberated from all impurities at the time of its fullness, so too...
The intention is that your mind shines thus, being entirely liberated from all defilements.
The commentary on the *Buddhavandanā-sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Gahaṭṭhavandanā-sutta*.
264. "In many directions" means in numerous directions. If one asks which those are, he says: "the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions.
By including the intermediate directions here, he shows that the zenith and nadir are also included. "Dwellers on earth" refers to those whose livelihood is dependent upon the earth;
by this, those dwelling in trees and mountains are also included. "With a mind long concentrated" refers to access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-jhāna*).
Having generated [these states], with a mind long concentrated through the non-decline of jhāna.

"Until the end of life" (*āpāṇakoṭika*) means for the duration of one's lifespan, as long as life lasts. By the word "and so forth" (*evamādi*), the remaining bases of meritorious action are included.

According to the morality of constant observance there are five; according to the morality of restricted observance there are ten. By the word "also" (*pi*), there are also eight according to the morality of the Uposatha on certain days.
...he shows. "By those who are righteous" means by those who have not departed from the Dhamma. "Pamukha" means release.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Homage of Householders is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Homage to the Teacher.
265. Having placed his right knee-circle upon the earth and bowing down, he was one who touched the ground with his knee;
thus, being such, he is called *brahmajāṇuka*. Because he is to be sacrificed to, he is a *yakkha*; he is worthy of worship.

Thus, because of his connection with this particular kind of veneration, [the Buddha] said, "He is a *yakkha*, that is, Sakka. For Mātali, inquiring about him who was the vessel for the homage of Sakka, [said]:

“Who indeed is that *yakkha*? he asked. [The answer was: “By means of his qualities (*guṇa-nemittakehi*). For the names of the Buddhas are infinite, and all of them are indeed based on their qualities, because of their infinite virtues. For this has been said:
“Incalculable are the names of the Great Seer according to his qualities.”
“By virtue of his qualities, his name should be proclaimed even beyond a thousand names.
Therefore, “of wondrous name” means one whose name is endowed with perfect qualities. “By transcending” means by means of transcending through the process of complete eradication.

“Apacaya” means the removal of the accumulation of the enemies that are the defilements; those for whom this is a pleasure (*ārāma*) in the sense of being worthy of frequenting are [the *apacayārāmā*].
They delight in diminution. Therefore it is said: "Delighting in the destruction of the round.
The commentary on the *Satthāravandanā-sutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Saṅghavandanā-sutta*.

266. “From lying upon a putrid body, the mother’s corpse, or else upon one’s own own putrid body, having spread oneself out by remaining within it—this is the construction for ‘lying on a putrid body.

‘In a mass of carrion’: these people have been submerged for ten months in this carrion known as the mother’s womb, which is impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive. What is it that you desire in them? This is the construction.
“I shall fly through this space of theirs”: I shall fly through this right practice of these seers (isī).
Now, in order to show that practice, it is said: “They do not open their granary. They do not put grain into the granary because there is no more to be put there.
Therefore he said: “For they have no grain. “Finished for others” means taken by others.
It was finished for their cooking. "By the practice of wandering for alms" means by the act of seeking food. "Seeking" means searching. "In this manner" refers to the way they have sought it.

"They maintain themselves" means they do not seek through improper search (*anesana*). "Possessing a beautiful character well-undertaken" means possessing a lovely character that has been properly undertaken.

"Thus speaking what is well-spoken" refers specifically to the well-spoken words measured by virtue, by way of the burden of the scriptures (*ganthadhura*) and the burden of insight (*vipassanādhura*).
They are of a nature to shine. They are silent through noble silence. For that very reason, they move with the mind in an especially harmonious way.

They are extinguished because, among those who have taken up the staff—that is, those engaged in grasping and so forth—they lack the fever of the defilements arising from the cause of taking up the staff and so on.
Therefore he said, "those who have laid aside the staff. Regarding "among those who take up": this refers to those who take up existence. "Without taking up" means being devoid of that.
Therefore he said, "Existence as a womb," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Saṅghavandanā-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3. Third Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Chetvā Sutta. 267.
The meaning has already been stated below in the commentary on the Devaputta Saṃyutta.
The commentary on the Chetvā Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Dubbaṇṇiya Sutta: 268.
“Ugly, unsightly, and misshapen” means having a short stature, he was at the very lowest limit. By Sakka...
This is merely a name taken [for him], but there was no such yakkha at all. Therefore he said, "A certain brahmā of the fine-material sphere.
If this is so, why did he come having assumed such a form? To answer this, he said, "It is said that Sakka [did so].

But how is it known here that "he was a certain brahmā of the fine-material sphere and not that obstructive yakkha"? Demonstrating the reasoning for this, [the text says]: "The obstructive yakkhas..."

He spoke these words beginning with “pana. Having heard the speech of the devas, he—without giving rise to impatience by thinking, “Who indeed is sitting upon my seat?”—remained established in patience through his harsh conduct (*pharusasamācāra*).

He [offered] great mental attention (*balavacittīkāra*), that is, profound honor and respect. This was shown through his humble behavior (*nīcavutti*) and his most excellent self-surrender (*paramanipaccakāra*) and perfect tranquility. Of Sakka...
Being unable to stand upon Sakka’s throne or reveal himself by virtue of that very perfection of conduct, he vanished.
“I am one whose heart is wounded”—Sakka speaks thus of his own nature, meaning that because of the absence of patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, his heart is wounded toward others.
“To bring [them] under my control through the power of anger”—it is not easy for me to produce [this state] within myself through anger.
The intention is: "Now, anger does not remain under my control.
"I do not remain angry for long" means that even if anger should ever arise in me, by following after that anger, I do not remain angry for a long time.
"I do not harbor resentment" means that if anger should arise within me, I quickly subdue it; thus, this vow of mine has been fulfilled beforehand.
The commentary on the Dubbaṇṇiya Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Saṃvarimāyā Sutta 269.

“Afflicted” (*ābādhika*) means one who has an affliction (*ābādha*); thus, he is called afflicted. “He taught” (*vācesi*) means he trained him. *Saṃvara* is the name of a certain asura’s magical art (*māyā*).
The primordial being, the ancient lord of the asuras—referring to him, he said, “Just as Sāmbara,” and so forth. In this way, another magician also suffers when he employs his magic.
The obstacle known as “insult” (upavāda-antarāya) disappears when there is an act of forgiveness; it returns to its normal state.
Therefore, he said, “In this way, he would find comfort. “By him” means by Vepacitti, because of his failure to grant the Sāmbara spell.

Because of being deceived. "Without having done so" means without having done what ought to be done—namely, leading [the person] into the presence of the seers (isī) and making them confess their transgression.
The commentary on the Saṃvarimāyā Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Accaya Sutta.
270. *Sampayojesun* means they engaged in harsh verbal speech toward one another.
Therefore he said, “They made a quarrel,” which means they engaged in dispute. *Atikkamma-vacanam* means speech that transgresses the restraint of speech (*vacī-saṃvara*).
Because when an offense is confessed, it is exhausted for the one who forgives while the other accepts the forgiveness.
Therefore it was said: “‘Does not accept’ means ‘does not tolerate. Let him be under your control; let him be one who may be dealt with as you wish, without being treated with special favor.
Regarding the phrase “in the duty of a friend,” he says this because the word “friend” is used here by eliding the latter member of the compound (*mittadhamma*).
It is an instrumental expression—“by friends”—used in the sense of a locative; hence he says “among friends. Just as [it is said] of a nature that has arisen...
Aging is the alteration of state; thus, by way of the opposite of friendship, the quality of enmity is spoken of as a synonym for aging.
That which is unassailable, blameless, and has entirely abandoned the defilements—therefore he said, "the person whose taints are exhausted.
The commentary on the Accaya Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Akkodhasutta* 271.

Regarding the phrase "Do not let anger overcome you": here, the state of being unconquerable by anger is achieved through the cultivation of its opposites—patience, loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth.
For it is said that the anger of one who possesses these qualities is thus overcome: "You yourselves must overcome anger; for those who are angry..."

"Do not retaliate. "The practice" refers to this very conduct. "Loving-kindness" (mettā) is loving-kindness that has reached absorption; its "access" (upacāra) is the preliminary stage of loving-kindness.
"Non-cruelty" (avihiṃsā) means that by means of it, one does not cause harm to anything. "Compassion" (karuṇā) should be understood as compassion that has reached absorption;
its "access" is the preliminary stage of compassion. "Base people" refers to those who, due to the absence of wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) regarding patience and other virtues...
And by association with reprehensible conduct, one becomes an inferior person. Through the purity of requisites, anger crushes the individual;
therefore, it must be properly abandoned by means of the power of reflection and meditative development.
The commentary on the *Akkodha Sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the *Sakkasaṃyutta* within the *Sāratthappakāsinī*,
the commentary on the *Saṃyuttanikāya*, is completed.
The commentary on the Sagāthāvagga of the Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathā, titled the Sāratthappakāsinī, is completed.
The first part is finished.
